en: The Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll One.
Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Paramiti of the Tang Dynasty.
The Commentary on the Text by the Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera Guwu Zhixu;
Revised and Compiled by the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Wenling Daofang.

The title of the sutra is as explained in detail in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning); here, I shall further briefly outline its essential framework. This sutra is [titled] according to both person and dharma.
Regarding its name: this Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dharma is neither cause nor fruit; there is no cause or fruit whatsoever that does not rely upon it.

Because those who have attained the fruit of the Tathāgata take this as their secret cause, whether they practice or realize it, there is nothing that is not of definitive meaning, and the fruit penetrates to the source of the cause.
Furthermore, because Bodhisattvas on the causal stages also rely upon this to fulfill the ten thousand practices, it is called the "Root."
The dust-sensory consciousnesses and the great elements all attain ultimate solidity, such that the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition.
Taking the wondrous true *tathatā* (suchness) of the *tathāgatagarbha* as its essence—since every phenomenon is the *tathāgatagarbha*—it is called the "Great Buddha-Ushṇīṣa.
Taking non-arising and non-ceasing as the cause and effect of its thesis—since both cause and effect are neither born nor extinguished—it is called "Esoteric" (*mi*).

The cause is that by departing from craving one attains liberation; its function is to bring about eternal separation from all cravings and ultimate emancipation, and for this reason it is titled *Śūraṅgama*.
The "curd-butter" (mṛdvīkṣīra) that gives rise to poison represents the characteristics of the teaching; this is the flavor of the Perfect and Sudden within the Vaipulya section.
In explaining the scriptural text, it is divided into three major sections: first, from "Thus have I heard" up to "returned to the Buddha."

That which constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*) extends from "Then Ānanda saw the Buddha" up to the tenth fascicle, where it is known that there is *nirvāṇa* and one does not cling to the three realms;

this is the main body of the teaching (*saddharma*). That which follows, from "Ānanda, if there should be another person" until the end, is the section on the dissemination of the teaching (*parīndanā*).

The initial preface is divided into two parts: first, the general preface; second, the specific preface. Regarding the general preface, it is the "Preface of Certification and Faith" (*saddharmapratyayana-nidāna*), as it is common to all sūtras and is therefore termed "general.
Because these six meanings certify and establish that [the teaching] is trustworthy, it is called the "Preface of Certification and Faith. As for the six meanings:
the two characters *evam* (thus) manifest the accomplishment of the essence of the dharma to be believed; the two characters *ahaṃ śrutam* (I have heard) [manifest the person who heard].
The term "able to hear" (*śrotṛ*) manifests the accomplishment of the audience; the two characters "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) manifest the accomplishment of the responsive inspiration;

the character "Buddha" (*buddha*) manifests the accomplishment of the Dharma-preacher; the phrase "in the city of Śrāvastī," etc., manifests the accomplishment of the location where the Dharma was preached;

and the section beginning with "with a great assembly of bhikṣus," which fully enumerates both the constant followers and those gathered from afar, manifests the accomplishment of the assembly of listeners. Now...
Fearing that splitting the text would make it inconvenient for reading and punctuation, the entire section is divided into two parts: first, the designation of the time and place of the teaching;
second, the citation of the great assembly who heard it together. Regarding the first part, the designation of the time and place of the teaching:

that which is heard is the Dharma-body (the essence of the teaching), and that which hears is "I" (the speaker), who is likewise the Dharma-body. That which speaks is the Buddha. The time and place may be understood [from the text].
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove monastery.
The phrase "thus" (*evam*) is a term used to indicate the Dharma; it refers generally to the textual meaning of the ten fascicles that follow.
Furthermore, it carries the sense of faith and compliance. Generally speaking, those who believe say, "This matter is thus," whereas those who do not believe say...
This matter is not as [previously] stated; what is now called "thus" (evam) clearly indicates faith and compliance. As for "I" (ātman), Ānanda refers to himself;
this is neither the "self" falsely imagined by non-Buddhists nor the "self" falsely grasped by ordinary worldlings.
Rather, it is one who has profoundly realized the eight kinds of mastery over the self—a state that is neither self nor non-self—yet follows worldly convention by provisionally designating it as "I."

The "hearer" refers to the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) giving rise to auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), which is capable of penetrating the nature of sound as it is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).

"At one time" means that the capacity of the audience and the response of the teacher were in perfect accord, such that the preaching and listening reached their conclusion; this is collectively termed "at one time. "Buddha" means self-awakened and awakening others, with the perfection of awakening and practice;
this refers to Śākyamuni, the Teacher of the Sahā world. "Is present" indicates his manifestation of traces here in this realm.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, [the Buddha] was always said to be "in the city of Śrāvastī.
Some say "Śrāvastī" is a distinction between the "Chū" and "Xià" dialects of the Sanskrit original; it is translated as "Abundant Virtue," also as "Object of Hearing," and also as "Delightful Path.
This is the name of a city in the kingdom of Kośala. As for Jetavana, it was originally the garden of Prince Jeta; in Sanskrit, "Jeta" is...
Regarding this so-called "Vijayārāma" (Victory Monastery), it was a place where the householder Anāthapiṇḍada constructed for the Buddha and the Saṅgha to cultivate pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Now, although these five elements of authentication generally apply universally, the specific details recorded in each instance differ:
namely, "Thus" (*evam*) differs from "I have heard" (*śrutam*); "I have heard" differs from "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*); and "at one time" differs from [the location].
If the "attainment" and the "abiding" were entirely distinct, how could one know this to be the general preface of this sutra unless it were briefly elucidated?

Furthermore, since the phrasing and intent are so broad, what could serve as a ladder for entering contemplation according to the text? Therefore, I dare not avoid prolixity and shall provide two types of exegesis for each point:
an interpretation according to the teachings (*jiao*) and an interpretation of the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*). First, the interpretation according to the teachings is as follows:
This means that while conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) contains words and letters, ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is devoid of words and letters.
Ānanda transmitted the conventional words of the Buddha, which are no different from what the Buddha himself spoke; therefore, they are called "thus" (*tathā*).

Because these conventional words and letters accord with the principle of ultimate truth, they are called "this" (*iti*). Thus, at the beginning of the Tripiṭaka sūtras, it is clarified as "Thus" (*evam*). If...
The Buddha’s teaching states that form is emptiness and emptiness is form; form and emptiness are non-dual and without distinction, and emptiness and form are not different.
This is what it means for the suchness to be identical to phenomena, and for it to be thus. Ānanda transmits the Buddha’s words as being no different from suchness;
the signifier is identical to the signified. This is how the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching) sutras clarify "thus" at their outset. If...
The Buddha taught that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) has a limit while nirvāṇa is limitless; that one emerges from the limit of birth-and-death and enters the limitlessness of nirvāṇa;
and that emerging from the limitlessness of nirvāṇa, one enters the Middle Way.

Ānanda transmitted this teaching on "emerging from existence and entering non-existence" and "emerging from non-existence and entering the middle," which is no different from what the Buddha taught, and is called the progression from the shallow to the deep.
There is nothing that is not this; thus it is clarified at the beginning of this Separate Teaching (biejiao) scripture.
If one says that the Buddha clarifies that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa* and is also the Middle Way, how much more so must *nirvāṇa* itself be the Middle Way?

True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) pervade all places; there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma. Ānanda transmitted this, which is identical to what the Buddha taught.

Because there is no difference, it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*); because Suchness is immovable, it is called "This. This *Yuanjiao jing* (Perfect Teaching Sutra) first clarifies "Thusness" (*evam*) in this manner.

In the present sutra, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are all the Tathāgata-garbha; their nature is truly perfect and harmonious, fundamentally without arising or ceasing.
This is the "Thusness" of the Perfect Teaching. Furthermore, in the third fascicle, it says: "This dharma is also a condition, yet not [a conditioned thing]."
Those who have attained the Dharma-nature do not go beyond the causes [of their practice];

because the delusions of those suited to the teachings are heavy, they temporarily borrow the meanings within the Tripiṭaka to further break through the habitual tendencies within the Tripiṭaka—this is precisely what is meant by "rebuking the partial and disparaging the small. Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*):

such contemplation of the mind is exclusively that which examines birth-and-death (*saṃskāra*) with thorough scrutiny so as not to err; this is "thusness" (*tathatā*). By breaking through birth-and-death, one realizes the Truth.
The term "truth" (*satya*) signifies the intention of "breaking through emptiness": observing that the arising and ceasing of the mind lacks inherent nature is "as-it-is" (*tathatā*);

realizing that its very substance is unborn is the intention of "substantial emptiness. Observing the Middle Way within the mind as unchanging is named "as-it-is," while forever relinquishing the two extremes is named the "sequential intention.
Observing the mind as the entirety of the *dharmadhātu* is named "as-it-is," wherein the extremes are identical to the Middle.

The name is one mind and consciousness. Next, explaining "self" according to the teachings: if one speaks of ordinary persons, they possess three kinds of self—namely, the self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the conceit of self (*asmimāna*), and the nominal self.
Those in training (*śaikṣa*) lack the self-view and thus have only two kinds of self.
Those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) lack both the self-view and the conceit of self, possessing only the nominal self. Now, Ānanda, being one who is still in training, is free from the false self.
The intention of the Tripiṭaka is that one who can subdue pride may refer to themselves as "I" by following worldly conventions without fault.

If it were said that using the four phrases to refer to oneself all follows from false views, then since there is no self within the Buddha’s True Dharma, who would hear this? This is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna).
If it is said that Ānanda, the man of great learning, knows both self and non-self yet does not bifurcate them into two, this is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna).
The distinction between self and non-self is the intent of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*).

If it is said that Ānanda knows that self and non-self are non-dual, acting as an attendant to transmit and uphold the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom, using his sovereign voice to transmit both the provisional and the real—there being nothing that cannot be so transmitted—this is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*). In this present sutra, [it concerns] the *tathāgatagarbha* nature.
The perfect fusion of these three meanings—wherein "non-self" is "self," "leaving self" is "leaving non-self," and "is" is "is not"—is precisely the meaning of the True Self of the Perfect Teaching.

Regarding the interpretation of "Self" through the contemplation of the mind: to contemplate that a single thought-moment belongs to what is produced by causes and conditions is to see it as a provisional name, the "Self.
To contemplate that this mind is empty is the "Self that is no-Self. To contemplate that this mind is provisional is "discrimination."
The contemplation of self and non-self, wherein the mind itself is the Middle Way, is the truly wondrous self. Next, the explanation according to the teachings:
regarding "hearing," there is hearing-hearing, hearing-not-hearing, not-hearing-hearing, and not-hearing-not-hearing. As for "hearing-hearing":

when the faculty of the ear is unimpaired and sound is within the range of audibility, one directs the mind with the desire to hear; through the convergence of these various conditions, hearing occurs.
The meaning of the *Zang* (Āgama) teachings is that "hearing" or "not hearing" is spoken of according to worldly convention as a provisional name;
yet in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is neither sound nor letter—how could there be a hearer or anything heard? This is the meaning of the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching).

"Not hearing yet hearing" means that the wondrous nature is fundamentally free from names and transcends all dependence; it is only through provisional conceptualization that there is hearing and non-hearing.

The meaning of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) is that "not hearing" means not hearing; since the nature is already free from names and transcends forms, all sense organs and objects do not fail to accord with this principle of being free from names and transcending forms.

This is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), as clarified in this sutra through the seven elements (*qida*), each of which is pure, inherently so, and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
Regarding the "interpretation of hearing by contemplating the mind," it means contemplating that which is produced through causes and conditions.
The Dharma is the contemplation that the conditions for hearing what is heard are empty; this is the contemplation that the conditions for not hearing what is heard are empty, which is provisional;
this is the contemplation that the conditions for hearing what is not heard are empty, provisional, and middle. This is the contemplation of not hearing what is not heard.
Next, explaining according to the teachings: "at one time" means that time has no substantial dharma; it is based upon the characteristics of form and mind.
The meaning of the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao) is that there are differences in the number of kalpas across the various stages (*avasthā*).

The meaning of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) is that when not a single thought arises, the three periods of time (*tryadhvan*) cannot be apprehended. The meaning of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) is that within the non-abiding *dharmatā*, one discriminates the infinite distinctions of worlds and kalpas.
[In the Perfect Teaching,] the ten periods of past and present, beginning and end, do not depart from the present moment of thought.
To universally contemplate immeasurable eons in a single thought—neither coming nor going, nor abiding—is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Furthermore, from those who have realized the Truth (Jian-di) above down to those who are not yet beyond training (Wuxue) below, this is called the "Single Moment" of the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao). That the three vehicles enter the primary truth together is called the "Single Moment" of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
From the stages of the Grounds (Deng-di) upward is called the "Single Moment" of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao). First...

To attain perfect enlightenment at the very moment of generating the bodhicitta is called the "Sudden Perfect Teaching" (*yīshí yuánjiào*). In this present sutra, one attains the Dharma-body without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
the deluded mind suddenly ceases, and this cessation is itself Bodhi—this is the Perfect Teaching. Regarding the "sudden" (*yīshí*) observation of the mind:
when observing that dharmas produced by causes and conditions are merely provisional names, this is the "sudden" observation of the mind as empty. This is not...

When one contemplates the mind at the stage of "attainability," it is provisional; when one contemplates the mind at the stage of "discriminating various phenomena," it is the Middle Way; and when one contemplates the mind at the stage of "inconceivability," it is suchness.
Next, the explanation according to the teachings regarding the Buddha: *Buddha* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "the Awakened One" or "the Knower.
If one says that beneath the Bodhi tree, through thirty-four moments of mind, the fetters and both the active and residual habits were severed and exhausted, this constitutes self-awakening.

To awaken to the four truths of arising and ceasing and likewise to cause others to awaken through the four truths of arising and ceasing is the characteristic of a Buddha according to the Tripitaka Teaching (*zàngjiào*).

If it is said that one who has previously severed [afflictions] now, when the conditions are ripe, attains the wisdom of a single thought-moment of correspondence beneath the Bodhi tree to sever the remaining residual habits,

and manifests an inferior *saṃbhogakāya* (lesser *saṃbuddha-kāya*) while turning the wheel of the Dharma of the four truths of non-arising— this is the characteristic of a Buddha according to the Shared Teaching (*xiōngtóngjiào*).
That which refers to the simultaneous realization of both self-awakening and awakening others by a Buddha is the characteristic of the Universal Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others.

If one speaks of sequentially severing the three delusions and sitting upon the Lotus Treasury World to turn the wheel of the immeasurable Four Noble Truths, this is the characteristic of the Particular Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others.
If one speaks of the single mind completely severing the three delusions to reach the ultimate and realize the inconceivable Dharma, [this is the characteristic of the Universal Buddha].

To possess a body that can manifest all Buddha-bodies, with each individual body identical to space and inconceivable, and to be able to turn the wheel of the unconditioned Four Noble Truths, as well as to skillfully turn the wheels of the three previous teachings—this is the characteristic of the Perfect Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others.
As this sutra says: "I, by means of wondrous clarity and non-extinction..."
It does not arise in conjunction with the *tathāgatagarbha*; rather, the *tathāgatagarbha* alone is wondrously enlightened and luminous, perfectly illuminating the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, within it, the one becomes the infinite and the infinite becomes the one; the small appears within the large and the large appears within the small.

One should know that these are the characteristics of a Buddha according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). As for the "contemplation of the mind" (*guanxin*) interpretation of the Buddha, the Buddha arises from the causes and conditions of contemplating the mind.
The Dharma is the Treasury Buddha; contemplating the causes and conditions of the mind as being immediately empty is the Penetrating Buddha;

contemplating the causes and conditions of the mind as first empty, then provisional, and finally the Middle is the Distinct Buddha; contemplating the causes and conditions of the mind as immediately empty, provisional, and middle is the Perfect Buddha.
Next, the explanation according to the teachings: "Abiding" (zai) refers generally to walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; "abiding" is precisely "dwelling" (zhu). "Dwelling" is...

This now includes the remaining three modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*). We shall now explain "abiding" (*sthiti*) by means of "dwelling" (*vihāra*). Furthermore, there are two aspects: the Buddha as the "one who abides" (*sthātṛ*) and the dwellings as the "place where one abides" (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
The dwellings consist of such dharmas as the celestial dwelling (*devavihāra*), the Brahma-dwelling (*brahmavihāra*), the noble dwelling (*āryavihāra*), and the Buddha-dwelling (*buddhavihāra*).

Alternatively, the dharma is the "one who abides" and the monastery (*vihāra*) is the "place where one abides. The ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) are called the "celestial dwelling" because they are the causes for the celestial realm.
Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are called the Brahma-abodes because they are the causes for becoming a Brahma-deva.
The three samādhis are called the Noble Abodes because they are supramundane dharmas. The Śūraṅgama Samādhi is called the Buddha-abode because it is the unsurpassed dharma.

If one says that [the Buddha] emerged from the contemplation of the emptiness of reduction to give rise to true outflow-free wisdom, dwelling in *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* while manifesting his traces in the human world by means of the ten...
The four wholesome *brahmavihāras* correspond to the capacities of worldly beings, while the three *samādhis* correspond to the capacities of those seeking transcendence;

this refers to the Buddha’s dwelling according to the *Tripiṭaka* teaching. If one says that he dwells in *nirvāṇa with remainder* by developing true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) from the contemplation of essence-emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and manifests his traces in the human world—therein employing both the celestial and Brahma-dwellings to respond to worldly capacities, and the noble dwelling (*āryavihāra*) to respond to transcendental capacities.

This refers to the Universal Buddha-abiding (*sāmānya-buddha-vihāra*). If one says that [the Buddha] abides in the secret treasury of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa-guhya-kośa*) by proceeding through the sequential three contemplations (*krama-tri-vipaśyanā*), manifesting traces in the human world and universally employing the four modes of abiding (*catvāro vihārāḥ*) to respond to both mundane and supramundane capacities, this refers to the Particular Buddha-abiding (*viśeṣa-buddha-vihāra*).

If one says that [the Buddha] abides in the secret treasury of the three virtues by means of the three contemplations within the single mind (*ekacitta-tri-vipaśyanā*), manifesting traces in the human world and likewise universally employing the four modes of abiding...

To be able to abide in the four modes of dwelling according to the capacities of both mundane and supramundane beings—such that every single place where one dwells is none other than the secret treasury of the three virtues—is precisely the dwelling of a Perfect Buddha.

As this sutra says, "Manifesting jeweled king lands upon the tip of a single hair, and turning the Great Dharma Wheel within a minute speck of dust," this is the dwelling of a Perfect Teaching Buddha. This is the explanation of "dwelling" through the contemplation of the mind.
This refers to observing that one dwells within an object— whether it be the object of impermanence, the conventional, the Middle Way, or emptiness—
because by dwelling in an object through the dharma of non-dwelling, one is said to "be present. Next, regarding the explanation according to the teachings (*yāna*),
the phrase "the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī" means that if one perceives the earth, sand, grass, wood, stones, and walls of this place as they are, this is the Treasury Teaching (*pitaka-yāna*).
If one sees this place as pure and adorned with the seven treasures, it is the realm of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
If one sees this place as the Flower Treasury World (Huazang Shijie), it is the realm of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).
If one sees this place as the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas, it is the realm of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). As the present sutra says: "All sentient beings are turned by external objects."
Within this, one who observes the great through the small and can thus transform objects becomes identical to the Tathāgata;

their body and mind are perfectly luminous and unmoving within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and they are able to universally contain the lands of the ten directions within a single hair-tip.

One should know that this place is precisely the Constant, Quiescent Light (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa*), yet it manifests as various distinctions according to the perceptions of sentient beings. This concludes the "Explanation of the City by Contemplating the Mind."
The "House" (śaraṇa) refers to the City of Nirvāṇa; "Compassion" (maitrī-karuṇā) refers to the House of Contemplation on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda).

To dwell in the City of True Reality (satya-nagara) and enter the House of Compassion based on the arising of conditions while contemplating the cessation of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination is the Treasury of the Teaching of the Tripitaka (Tripiṭaka-śāsana).

To dwell in the City of True Reality and enter the House of Compassion based on both the arising and the dharmic nature of conditions while contemplating that the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are neither produced nor extinguished is the Teaching of the Shared Vehicle (Sādhāraṇa-śāsana).

Contemplating the inconceivable twelvefold dependent origination as ceasing within the abiding Middle Way, one enters the city of Nirvana through the sequential stages of the conditions of birth, the conditions of phenomena, and the unconditioned;
this is the distinct teaching of the three types of compassion residing in the house of mercy.

Contemplating the inconceivable twelvefold dependent origination as neither arising nor ceasing, one abides in the city of Nirvana within the Middle Way and enters the Great Compassion of the single mind and its three conditions.
If one abandons the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), how can one know that all phenomena are identical to principle if one does not rely on the teaching?

How can one know that the entire nature constitutes practice if one does not contemplate the mind? May readers reflect deeply upon this. Second, citing the great assembly as witnesses, which is further divided into three parts:
first, the assembly of Śrāvakas; second, the assembly of Pratyekabuddhas; third, the assembly of Bodhisattvas. The Śrāvakas are those who constantly follow [the Buddha].
The two remaining groups [of the assembly] are both "assembled clouds. Regarding the first, the assembly of śrāvakas, it is further divided into three parts:

first, indicating the category and stating the number; second, revealing their status and praising their virtues; third, listing the names of the leaders. First, regarding the indication of the category and the statement of the number:
"great bhikṣus" indicates the category, and "one thousand two hundred and fifty people" states the number.
He was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
"Together with" (yǔ) carries the meaning of "in company. According to the *Śāstra*, it is explained through seven points:

"together" means being at the same time, in the same place, observing the same precepts, having the same mind, holding the same views, following the same path, and attaining the same liberation. "Great" (dà) is the Sanskrit term *mahat*, which signifies "much," "many," and "superior."

Regarding the three meanings [of "Bhikṣu"]: first, because he is respected by great beings such as kings and celestial lords due to his dignified capacity and measure, he is called "Great" (*mahā-*) [i.e., *Mahā-bhikṣu*].

Second, because he has extensively mastered both internal and external scriptures, he is called "Much" (*bahu-*) [i.e., *Bahu-bhikṣu*]. Third, because he has transcended the ninety-five types of non-Buddhist paths, he is called "Victorious" (*jina-*) [i.e., *Jina-bhikṣu*].

The term "Bhikṣu" now encompasses these two meanings of "much" and "victorious. Furthermore, it contains three meanings: first, terrifying Māra; second, destroying... [the afflictions]; third, begging for alms.
The "evil *tri-bhikṣu*" (three types of mendicants) may also be translated as "remover of hunger" (*atibhikṣu*) or "frightener of Māra.
As for the "Frightener of Māra," the King Māra dwells in the sixth heaven and governs the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*); he is terrified that people will cultivate the Way and thus escape his domain.

When the True Dharma remains in the world, there is a man of faith who possesses the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), has reached the age of twenty, and is free from the thirteen grave obstacles (*trayodaśa-antarāyika-dharma*).

Furthermore, there are no sixteen minor impediments that prevent one from receiving the *bhikṣu* precepts through the ritual of formal ordination (*jñapticaturtha-karman*) upon ascending the platform, performed by three masters and seven witnesses—or, in a border region, by three masters and two witnesses—in accordance with the Dharma.

Once this is completed, it is called "attaining the nature of a fully ordained monk" (*śikṣā-sampanna-bhikṣutva*), and one enters the ranks of the Sangha Jewel. At that time, the earth-walking rākṣasa...
He raised his voice and proclaimed, "Excellent! Here there is a son of good family who has gone forth from home in accordance with the Dharma;
he shall cause the gods to flourish and the asuras to diminish. Upon hearing this, the yakṣas who roam the air also raised their voices and proclaimed, "Excellent!

This sound reached the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, where the devas there again raised their voices and proclaimed, "Excellent! The sound was transmitted thus through the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven up to the Yāma Heaven.
The sound was transmitted successively from Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin up to the Brahma Heaven;
when the Māra King heard this proclamation within his palace, he gave rise to great sorrow and fear, and thus it is called "Frightening the Māras.

To destroy evil means that by leaving the household life and upholding the precepts, one gives rise to concentration through the precepts, and wisdom is developed through concentration; thereby one destroys the seven branches of body and speech and eradicates the views and afflictions of the three realms.

Regarding "all evils": once a *bhikṣu* (alms-seeker) has left the household life, he is forever free from the four kinds of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*) and begs for food to sustain his physical life;
he forever abandons all false dharmas and begs for the Dharma to sustain his life of wisdom. The four kinds of wrong livelihood are:
first, "looking upward" (*ūrdhvamukha*), which means observing the stars and calculating the waxing and waning of the heavens to seek food thereby.
The second, "downward-facing mouth" (adhomukha-bhakṣa), refers to planting fields and orchards. The third, "three directions-mouth" (trimukha-bhakṣa), refers to subsisting on favors from patrons.

The fourth, "four directions-mouth" (caturmukha-bhakṣa), refers to forming alliances with the wealthy and noble. The fifth, "four intermediate directions-mouth" (vidigmukha-bhakṣa), refers to commerce and the accumulation of wealth.

These four matters may be practiced by householders, but they are not to be practiced by those who have left the home life; therefore, he has forever abandoned them. "False dharma" refers to false precepts.

Wrong concentration, wrong wisdom, and wrong precepts—namely, the precepts of cattle and dogs, as well as all the prohibitions and observances of the devas and rishis—cannot produce one who transcends birth and death.
Wrong concentration refers to the twelve gates of dhyāna practiced by ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists based on a mind of longing for the pleasant and aversion to the unpleasant.
Wrong wisdom refers to the two views of existence and non-existence, the sixteen types of knowledge, and the sixty-two views.

Having now forever abandoned the two views, the one hundred and eight views, and so forth, they seek only the training in higher ethics, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom;
therefore, they are called "Bhikṣus" (mendicants). As for those who "eliminate hunger," they maintain pure precepts and can serve as a field of merit for the world of humans;
they are able to perform the pure gift of Dharma, removing all sentient beings' lack of merit and wisdom.
Regarding the "two kinds of assemblies": *saṃgha* in Sanskrit is translated here as "harmonious assembly. There are two meanings of harmony:
first, harmony in principle (*li-he*), which refers to collectively realizing the unconditioned state of cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);

second, harmony in practice (*shi-he*), which consists of harmony in precepts (*śīla-sāmagrī*), harmony in views (*dṛṣṭi-sāmagrī*), harmony in benefit (*lābha-sāmagrī*), harmony in conduct (*vṛtti-sāmagrī*), harmony in speech (*vāc-sāmagrī*)—meaning freedom from contention—and harmony in intention (*manas-sāmagrī*)—meaning sameness of mind.
The term "one who pleases the assembly" (*saṃgha-rājin*) refers to four or more [monks]; a single bhikṣu is not called a *saṃgha*, nor are two or three bhikṣus.
When four bhikṣus dwell together, they are able to perform all legal acts of the *saṃgha* (*dharmika-saṃghakarma*), with the sole exception of the three types of formal procedures (*karmavācanā*):

the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), the conferring of full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the removal of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*). If five bhikṣus dwell together, they may perform these themselves.
It may also be permitted to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) in frontier regions;

if ten bhikṣus reside together, then full ordination may be conferred throughout the five regions of India, and when twenty bhikṣus reside together, all formal acts (*karmavācanā*) may be performed—therefore, this is called the "harmonious assembly.
As for the number one thousand two hundred and fifty, these were those whom the Buddha first delivered after his initial attainment of enlightenment.
In the Deer Park, five people were first ordained; next, Yaśas and others, fifty people; next, the three Kāśyapas, one thousand people;
and next, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, two hundred people. These one thousand two hundred and fifty-five individuals, moved by the Buddha’s profound kindness, became his constant retinue;
here, however, only the general number is cited. "Together" (saha) refers to the teacher and disciples.

"Constantly following one another" means that the phenomena of the Dharma are harmonious and not distinct; the principles of the Dharma are harmonious and not distinct. There are two further explanations:

first, the explanation according to the teachings (*yàojiào*), and second, the explanation of contemplating the mind (*guānxīn*). First, regarding the explanation according to the teachings: "One hundred and seven" refers to the *Zàngjiào* (Tripitaka Teaching);

"one hundred and seven" refers to the *Tōngjiào* (Shared Teaching); "immeasurable one hundred and seven" refers to the *Biéjiào* (Distinct Teaching); and "one hundred and seven" refers to the *Yuánjiào* (Perfect Teaching). "Great, many, and superior" refers to the *Zàngjiào*.

As previously stated, it is called "Great" (Mahā) because it is revered by Arhats of great power; it is called "Universal Knowledge" (Sarvajña) because arising and ceasing are themselves non-arising and non-ceasing;

it is called "Many Victorious" (Bahu-jina) because it encompasses the four gates of the Tripiṭaka; it is called "Victorious" (Jina) because it refers to the meaning of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna);

furthermore, it is called "Great" because it is revered by Arhats who have realized the reality of dharmas (dharmatā), and it is called "All-Knowing" because it fully understands the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Because he surpasses those of the Two Vehicles, he is called "Victorious" (jaya); this is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (bye-kyo).
Furthermore, because he is revered by all great Bodhisattvas, he is called the "Great Dharma Realm"; because he fully knows immeasurable dharmas, he is called "Many-Victorious";

and because he surpasses all Bodhisattvas, he is called "Victorious"—this is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (won-gyo) in the present sutra. Regarding the bhikṣu of the Treasury Teaching (zang-kyo), it is as previously explained; furthermore, he begs for alms.
The term *śramaṇa* (士) means one who traverses the conditions to seek the Truth and breaks through evil; "breaking through obstacles" refers to destroying delusions regarding principles;

"fearing Māra" refers to using the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to destroy the four kinds of Māras; and "removing hunger" refers to eliminating the hunger for analytical dharmas—this is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānya-śāsana*).

Furthermore, the term *bhikṣu* (乞士) means one who traverses the Three Truths to seek the Principle; "breaking through evil" refers to removing both the delusions common to and specific to the Shared and Distinct Teachings; and "fearing Māra" refers to destroying [them].
Within and outside the realms, the eight māras are eliminated; the term "removing the famine" (除饉) removes the famine of partial emptiness, which is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
Furthermore, the "mendicant" (*qishi*) seeks the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha within the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and the seven great elements;

the "eliminator of evil" (*poezhe*) realizes that madness has ceased, which is Bodhi; the "terrorizer of Māra" (*bumo*) awakens to non-delusion within the very state of *dhyāna*, knowing the realm of Māra.

The *tathatā* (suchness) of the Buddha-realm is the same as that of the *kṣatriya* (those who remove hunger). To "remove hunger" means to eliminate the deficiency of not possessing all dharmas; this is precisely the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) in the present sutra.

There are four kinds of *saṃgha*: first, the non-gradual *saṃgha*, referring to those who have broken the precepts; second, the "dumb sheep" *saṃgha*, referring to those who are ignorant and do not understand the laws and regulations;
third, the pure *saṃgha*, referring to those at the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*); fourth, the true [saṃgha].
The "true Sangha" refers to the four stages of approach and the four fruits; according to the meaning of the Tripitaka (Agama) teachings, it refers only to these, excluding the previous three types.

Furthermore, according to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), those from the stage of seeing (darśana-bhūmi) upward are called the true Sangha. According to the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), those from the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) upward are called the true Sangha.
Furthermore, according to the [Perfect Teaching], those from the Abiding in the Initial Resolve (prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra) upward are called the true Sangha.
This is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya) regarding the Sangha. As for the interpretation through the contemplation of mind (*cittāvalokana*):

the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is the teacher, and the various mental states and functions (*caitta-caitasika*) are the assembly of disciples. This single moment of wondrous contemplation is called the Buddha;

the harmonious union of these various mental states and functions that follows and constitutes wondrous contemplation is called being "together with a great assembly of bhikṣus numbering several myriads. This can be understood by clarifying the contemplation according to the four teachings (*catvāra upadeśāḥ*).
The second part, "the phrases praising the virtues of the Great Arhats who manifest their stations," consists of twelve phrases beginning with "sons of the Buddha who manifest their stations";
these constitute the praise of their virtues.
They are all untainted Great Arhats, sons of the Buddha, who maintain and uphold the Dharma, skillfully transcend all realms of existence, and are able [to purify] lands.

He has perfected his dignified deportment; he follows the wheel of the Buddha and is worthy of being entrusted with the sublime teachings. He strictly purifies the Vinaya and establishes a grand model for the three realms.
His response-bodies are infinite as he delivers sentient beings, rescuing those of the future and transcending all worldly entanglements.
The "outflow-free" (anāsrava) refers to the exhaustion of all afflictions—the absence of the outflows of desire, existence, and ignorance.

"Great" (mahat) possesses the three meanings of being vast, abundant, and supreme, as previously explained. The Arhat contains three meanings: first, the meaning of "one worthy of offerings" (dakṣiṇīya), which is the fruit of the mendicant;
second, the meaning of "slayer of thieves" (vadhaka), which is the fruit of destroying evil; and third, the meaning of "non-arising" (anutpāda), which is [the fruit of] fearlessness.

Regarding the fruits of Māra, one should know that for a bhikṣu, three meanings apply to both cause and fruit; these three, however, pertain only to the fruit. Furthermore, there are three types of Arhats:

those who cultivate the *smṛtyupasthānas* by nature and sever the delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), yet attain only the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) without possessing the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and are thus called persons liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*).
Those who cultivate the shared *smṛtyupasthānas*, sever delusions, realize the Truth, and are fully endowed with the three insights (*vidyā*) [are another type].
Those who possess the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) are called "persons liberated both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).

By cultivating the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), severing delusions, realizing the truth, and fully perfecting the supernormal powers, clarities, and liberations—while simultaneously manifesting the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—they are called "persons of unimpeded liberation.

Because the present subject is one of unimpeded liberation, they are designated as "Great. Regarding the classification by teaching (*yāna*): the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) and *Śrāvaka* (Shared) teachings are as explained above; furthermore, there is no... [text continues].

The outflows of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the outflows of the sands of phenomena (*dharmas*), and the outflows of the non-abiding ground of ignorance (*apratiṣṭhita-avidyā*) should receive the offerings of humans, devas, and the two vehicles;

having slain the thieves of view, thought, the sands of phenomena, and ignorance, one is free from the two kinds of birth and death—segmented and transformational—this is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*).
Furthermore, within a single mind, when all outflows are perfectly exhausted, one should receive the offerings of the nine realms.
That afflictions are themselves bodhi is called "slaying the thief"; that birth-and-death is itself nirvana is called "the non-arising.

This is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching. As for the contemplation of the mind: contemplating the mind as empty means there are no outflows of view or thought; contemplating the mind as provisional means there are no outflows of the sands of phenomena;
contemplating the mind as the Middle means there are no outflows of ignorance. That one mind possesses the ten dharma-realms is the principle of correspondence.
Regarding the contemplation of the mind: that afflictions are themselves bodhi is the contemplation of "slaying the thief"; that birth-and-death is itself nirvana is "non-arising.
From the words "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) onwards, there are twelve phrases consisting of general and specific praises of his virtues.

"The Son of the Buddha abides and sustains, skillfully transcending all realms of existence" is the general praise of his two virtues of precept and wisdom. The ten phrases beginning with "He is able [to purify] lands" are the specific praises.

This is a separate praise of precepts and wisdom. Regarding the term "Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*): because they are born from the mouth of the Buddha and transformed by birth from the Dharma, they are called Sons of the Buddha.

If one says that those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) sever delusions and realize the truth and are thus true sons of the Buddha, while Bodhisattvas merely suppress delusions without severing them and thus their status as "sons" is remote—this is the meaning of the Tripiṭaka Teaching (*pitakavāda*). If, however, one says that all three vehicles sever delusions, yet the Two Vehicles [do not realize the ultimate truth]...

The meaning of "sons of the Great Compassionate One" being weak refers to Bodhisattvas whose great compassion is predominant; their ability to succeed the Buddha-seed is strong, which is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*).

If it is said that Bodhisattvas who universally practice all the path-dharmas of the Buddhas are called "Sons of the Buddha," while the Two Vehicles, who seek only their own liberation, are like hired laborers or lowly servants, this is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*pieh-chiao*). If one says [this applies to] the beginning...

To give rise to the bodhicitta is itself the seed of the Buddha; it is like when the crown prince of a Wheel-Turning King first enters the womb, he is immediately of the lineage of the Holy King—this is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
"Abiding" means dwelling securely without movement; "maintaining" means upholding without loss.
If one says that abiding in the *mokṣa* precepts maintains the wheel of the Dharma of the four noble truths of arising and ceasing, this is the meaning of the Tripitaka Teaching (*zangjiao*). If...
To say that one abides in the precepts of ultimate truth and maintains the Dharma-wheel of the four truths of non-arising refers to the meaning of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
To say that one abides in the threefold pure precepts and maintains the Dharma-wheel of immeasurable four truths refers to the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).

To say that one abides in the unsurpassed, wondrous precepts of the single mind and maintains the Dharma-wheel of the four truths of non-action refers to the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). To say "neither is nor is not" refers to the meaning of the Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao).

If one thinks that when the retribution of the realm of perception is exhausted, one returns to fall [again], this is not called "skillfully transcending"; only when one does not fall back is it called "skillfully transcending"—this is the meaning of the Tripitaka Teaching (*zangjiao*).

If one says that fearing the three realms as being substantially real, one transcends them yet does not skillfully know that the three realms are empty, this is not called "skillfully transcending"—this is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).
If one says that one not only transcends the three realms of cohabitation (*tongju*), but also...

Because it transcends the three realms of existence through skillful means and also transcends the three realms of existence as actual retribution, it is called "good"; this is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).

If one says that all three lands are identical to the Constant, Quiescent Light (*changjiguang*), and thus there is neither transcending nor not-transcending, yet one speaks of transcending, it is called "good";
this is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). As for the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*): if one contemplates that the mind is produced through causes and conditions...

These are the sons of the Buddha of the Tripitaka Teaching who abide in the *vinaya* precepts and maintain the Dharma-wheel of the Four Truths of Arising and Ceasing; they transcend the prison of the triple world.

If they contemplate that the causes and conditions of the mind are empty, these are the sons of the Buddha of the Shared Teaching who abide in the precepts of the Truth of Reality and maintain the Dharma-wheel of Non-arising;
they transcend the triple world while remaining within it. If they contemplate that the causes and conditions of the mind are first empty and then provisional...

The latter middle [stage] refers to the sons of the Buddha of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), who dwell in the three clusters of precepts (*tri-śīla-skandha*) and maintain the wheel of immeasurable Dharma, successively transcending the three lands.

If they contemplate that the causes and conditions of the mind are empty, provisional, and middle, they are sons of the Buddha of the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*), who dwell in the unsurpassed precepts and maintain the wheel of unconditioned Dharma, perfectly transcending all realms of existence. Next, they are able to achieve perfection within the lands.

"His majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*)" is a specific praise of his virtue of ethical discipline (*śīla*). "From the Buddha, he turned the wheel [of Dharma] and was worthy of being entrusted with the sublime legacy" is a specific praise of his virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*).
"He strictly purified the *vinaya* and established a grand model for the three realms" is a comprehensive praise of his accomplishment in the virtue of majestic deportment;

that is to say, it does not merely refer to the establishment of decorum within a single nation, but rather that he served as a teacher and model throughout the three realms. His manifested bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are immeasurable.
"Delivering sentient beings" is a broad praise of the merit of turning the wheel of Dharma following the Buddha;

it means that one does not merely turn the wheel after a single transformation-buddha, but rather shares in the immeasurable response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of all Buddhas. "Rescuing and liberating those of the future, transcending all worldly dust and burdens" is a broad praise of the merit of being wonderfully worthy of the final entrustment;
it means that one does not merely protect and uphold the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*), but rather embodies compassionate vows.

Regarding the teaching that extends to the end of the future: if one refers only to the five regions of India as the "land," the *prātimokṣa* precepts as "dignified conduct" (*vīrya*), the four truths of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising as the "wheel," the realm of shared residence as the "three realms," and the hundred billion worlds as "immeasurable," this corresponds to the meaning of the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* [teachings].
If, however, one refers universally to the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*), [this corresponds to the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* and *Dharmatā* teachings].

Regarding the "land," it refers to the three clusters (*triskandha*); regarding "dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*), it refers to the immeasurable and unconditioned Four Truths; regarding the "wheel," it refers to the four lands;

regarding the "three realms," it refers to horizontal pervasiveness as the immeasurable and so forth—these are the meanings of the Separate and Perfect [vehicles]. As for the contemplation of the mind:

if one contemplates that the mind arises through causes and conditions, this accomplishes the land of the Shared Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), and its dignified deportment proceeds from the Buddha of Inferior Response.

Turning the wheel of birth and death, they establish a broad model for co-residence within the three realms, even extending to the rescue of future beings so that they may transcend the defilements of this shared world.
If one contemplates the causes and conditions of the mind as being empty, one accomplishes the two kinds of lands—the land of common residence and the land of skillful means.

Their majestic deportment proceeds from the superior or inferior response-bodies of the Buddha, turning the wheel of non-arising to establish a broad model for both the land of common residence and the land of skillful means.
From the three realms up to the deliverance of future beings, transcending the dust-like burdens of the two lands;

if one contemplates that the causes and conditions of the mind are simultaneously empty and provisional, one accomplishes the three kinds of lands—concordant, expedient, and of true reward—and their majestic deportment.

From the Victorious Response Buddha, he turns the immeasurable wheel of Dharma, establishing a grand model for the three kinds of realms within the three worlds, up to the deliverance of future beings and their transcendence [of suffering].
If one contemplates that the dust and burdens of the three lands arise from causes and conditions, they are immediately empty, provisional, and middle;

thus the four kinds of lands—*sahā-loka*, *upāya*, *saṃbhoga*, and *dharmakāya* (the land of tranquil light)—are accomplished. The majestic deportment proceeds from the Dharma-body and Reward-body Buddhas as they turn the wheel of unconditioned action, establishing a grand model for the four types of triple-world realms, even extending to the salvation of future beings who transcend the dust and burdens of these four lands. Question: Regarding "tranquility" (*śānti*)...
[The questioner] asked: "How could there still be dust-like defilements in the Light? [The Master] replied: "This refers to the 'Quiescent Light' (Jiguang) realized through partial enlightenment.
[The questioner] asked: "The Son of the Buddha possesses immeasurable virtues; for what reason do you specifically praise only the two types, Precept and Wisdom? [The Master] replied:
"Though virtues are immeasurable, none are not fully subsumed within the three—Precept, Concentration, and Wisdom. This sutra first establishes the name of the Great Samādhi, calling it 'Great'..."
The Śūraṅgama-samādhi, the King of Samādhis at the Buddha’s Crown, takes the rational nature of the true cause as its essential substance;

yet although this essential substance is inherently possessed by all sentient beings, it relies entirely upon the efficacy of the conditional and developmental causes for the true cause to become manifest.
Therefore, the fourth fascicle states: "If you merely do not follow after the three types of continuous succession—worldly karma, its fruits, and sentient beings—"
Because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise; thus, the madness of the *Yajñadatta* within your mind naturally subsides.
This subsiding is itself Bodhi—the supreme, pure, and luminous mind that is fundamentally coextensive with the Dharma-realm and is not obtained from others.
Indeed, this supreme, pure, and luminous mind of Bodhi is what is called the "True Cause" (*dharmatā-hetu*) of the Great Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King.
Because it is the essence of nature, it is said that it fundamentally pervades the dharma-realm and is not obtained from others;
yet, because it does not follow after discrimination, it is entirely the wisdom-mind of the "enabling cause" (*paripūri-hetu*), which is the very "virtue of wisdom" praised here now.

Furthermore, because the three conditions are severed, it is entirely the wholesome mind of the "contributory cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*), which is the very "virtue of precepts" praised here now. Moreover, this sutra begins by investigating the mind and discerning the vision.
Following the exposition of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements, the text subsequently reveals the great sevenfold perfect interfusion;

this is nothing other than opening up this perfect understanding to serve as the primary stage for entering the stream. Next, it elaborates upon this by means of the four kinds of pure precepts and demonstrates the ritual procedures for reciting mantras and establishing the altar;
this is nothing other than supporting these rules of discipline to serve as an aid for correct cultivation.
Only when aided by the practice of integration do the three gradual stages become complete;
only then can one traverse the fifty-five positions of the true path to Bodhi and ascend to Wondrous Enlightenment.

One should know that every position traversed from beginning to end is none other than the fundamental substance of the Principle-nature (li-xing), and every practice traversed from shallow to deep is none other than the conditions and the consummation (yuan-liao).
Second, there is still the fear that those whose practice remains lax regarding the precepts will inevitably sink into ruin despite possessing empty intellectual understanding;

therefore, using Sunakṣatra and the jewel-lotus as a point of inquiry, one must once again investigate the seven destinies in detail. Only then does one realize that without true precepts, there can be no true wisdom.
For without the *vimukti* (liberation) precepts, one cannot avoid the three evil realms; and without the *dhyāna* precepts, one cannot avoid the realm of desire.
If one possesses untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) yet lacks them, one cannot escape existence in the realms of form and formlessness; how then could one attain supramundane wisdom?

Furthermore, fearing that those who are negligent regarding wisdom might possess preceptual goodness yet remain subject to delusion, I have borrowed the example of the "unlearned bhikṣu" as a point of discourse.
Thus, I shall again provide a detailed analysis of the five aspects of the Dharma, so that it may be known that without true wisdom, there is likewise no true [preceptual purity].
Because the precept-canopy lacks the wisdom of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the *prātimokṣa* precepts may be broken, leading one to become a companion of Māra.

Because it lacks the wisdom of the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*), the bodhicitta-precepts may be broken, leading one to become a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha; how, then, could one obtain the threefold pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*)?
Thus, the Āgamas state: "By the purity of the precepts, wisdom is purified; by the purity of wisdom, the precepts are purified. As it is said:
Washing both hands alternately without allowing one to precede the other is not only the case in the Tripitaka teachings;

one should know that among all the essential methods of practice in the Shared, Distinct, and Complete Teachings, none surpass this. Furthermore, these precepts and wisdom correspond to what the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* calls the "vehicle" (*yāna*) and the "precepts" (*śīla*).

If both the vehicle and the precepts are lax, one will remain forever in the three miserable realms; if the precepts are strict while the vehicle is lax, [one may attain a higher rebirth but not liberation].

Although one may dwell among humans or devas, there is no way to transcend the world; even if one’s aspiration for the vehicle is urgent while their observance of the precepts is lax, they will only attain transcendence after passing through the three evil realms.
Only when both the vehicle and the precepts are urgent can one advance steadily upon this Path.
This is the profound reason why the present sutra first extols the two virtues of precept and wisdom. Third, the names of the principal leaders are listed.
Their names were Śāriputra of Great Wisdom, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila,
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Upāliśata, and others who served as the leaders.
The Great Wise One was foremost in wisdom among the assembly of Śrāvakas. "Śāri" means *śārikā* (a kind of bird);
because the Venerable One’s mother had eyes like those of this bird, he was named after her. "Putra" means son;
thus, he was designated by his maternal lineage. His formal name was Upatiṣya Mahāmaudgalyāyana, which translates as "Great Mung Bean Clan."
The Venerable One’s clan name was Kauṇḍinya; he was so named because he was born from the deity of the *kūṭadanta* tree, a species of tree found in the Western Regions.
Mahākauṣṭhila—translated as "Great Thigh"—was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra and was also known as the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha, foremost in debate. Pūrṇa is translated as...

Pūrṇa was his father’s name; Maitrāyaṇī—translated here as "Compassion"—was his mother’s name. Because he was named after both his parents, he is called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. He is foremost in preaching the Dharma. Subhūti is translated as "Born of Emptiness," also as "Well-Appeared," and also as "Good Fortune"; he is foremost in understanding emptiness. Upāli... The instruments for killing are also called the smith’s tools—the various furnaces, bellows, hammers, and vessels.

As the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "If bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, they employ the mind of pure awakening to grasp stillness."
As one practices by clarifying all thoughts, the agitation of consciousness and the adventitious defilements of body and mind are forever extinguished, and tranquil serenity arises within.
Because of this tranquility, the minds of all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions appear therein like reflections in a mirror; this skillful means is called *śamatha*.

If those bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, they realize through their pure enlightened mind that both the nature of the mind and the sense organs and objects are all produced by illusion.

With a mind of pure awakening, one does not grasp at illusory transformations or various states of stillness; one clearly understands that both body and mind are but obstructions.

The three Tathāgatas’ responses and instructions consist of two parts: first, from the current text until the conclusion of the "Eighteen Dhātus," which reveals principle through phenomena;

second, the section on the "Seven Substances," which clarifies that characteristics are inherently possessed by nature. Within the first of these two, there are again two sub-sections: first, following [the text]...

This section consists of two parts: "Shattering Delusive Attachments" and "Secretly Revealing the True Mind. The second part, "Displaying the Sublime Principle," simultaneously shatters other delusions.

Within the first part, there are three sections: first, questioning the original cause for generating the resolve; second, demonstrating the direct path of the eternal mind; and third, extensively refuting seven rounds of deluded calculations.
The first of these [three] has two sub-sections: first, the Tathāgata’s question; second, Ānanda’s answer. This is the first [of the two].
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "We are of one breath; our feelings are as equal as those of brothers.
When you first resolved your mind, what superior signs did you perceive within my Dharma that caused you to suddenly renounce the profound and heavy bonds of worldly affection?"
Ānanda was the Buddha’s younger cousin and a blood relative of this world; therefore, they were called "of the same breath" (*tongqi*), their feelings equaling those of the natural order (*tianlun*).

While father and son and brothers are termed the "natural order" because they are joined by Heaven, here it is clarified that his affection was no different from that toward his own siblings, which is why it is said they were "equal.
There is no profound kindness greater than that of one's parents, and no profound love greater [than theirs].
If one does not perceive the excellence of the Buddha-dharma, how could one suddenly renounce wife and children?
However, although the Buddha-dharma perceived here lacks the three [ordinary] objects, the mind that perceives it must distinguish between the true and the false;
therefore, wishing now to demonstrate the essence of the fruit of Bodhi, he first asks about the initial cause for generating the aspiration. Second, Ānanda answers.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "I see that the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks are supremely wonderful and peerless;
his physical form is translucent, like lapis lazuli. I constantly reflect that these marks are not produced by desire and attachment. Why?

Because the breath of desire is coarse and turbid, characterized by the mingling of stench and the chaotic mixture of pus and blood; it cannot give rise to such supreme, pure, wondrous, and luminous purple [radiance]."
The Golden Light Assembly [states that] because of his yearning and longing, he followed the Buddha to shave his head.
The conditions for the arousal of the mind were fundamentally free from any crookedness; it was only to be regretted that he had not yet recognized his own mind.
Therefore, the text below interrogates him, saying: "Who is it that loves and delights? ... down to ... what do you take to be the mind? When my fist shone forth, [he failed to see].
This refutes the mind that clings to [erroneous] attachments; it does not mean that the arising of the resolve for awakening (*bodhicitta*) based on perceived characteristics is itself a fault.
Second, demonstrating the direct path of the eternal mind, which has two parts: first, pointing out and demonstrating the eternal mind; second, exhorting the cultivation of the direct path.
Now, the first part.

The Buddha said, "Excellent, Ānanda! You and all others should know that all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, undergone the continuous succession of birth and death because they do not understand the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of pure nature and luminosity—and instead employ various deluded thoughts.
Because these thoughts are not true, there is cyclic wandering."
Because one wishes to shatter delusion and reveal the truth, I shall first provide a direct, thorough explanation. There are two kinds of birth and death:

first, *paricchinna-utpāda-vyaya* (segmented birth and death), which is restricted solely to the co-resident realm (*sahabhū-bhūmi*) within the triple world; second, *pariṇāma-utpāda-vyaya* (transformative birth and death), which extends throughout both the stage of expedient means (*upāya-bhūmi*) and the land of true retribution (*bhūtāvasthāna-bhūmi*).

As for the essence of the eternally abiding true mind—the luminous substance of intrinsic purity—it is the principle of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). It is not... [the object of] birth and death.
The "Knower" refers to the wisdom of primordial enlightenment (*abhisambodhi-jñāna*). "All deluded thoughts" refers to the afflictions of ignorance, the sands of views, and the fetters of thought.

That these thoughts are not real means they are formed based upon the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure nature and luminosity, and possess no separate self-nature of their own—just as there is no nature of a snake apart from the rope, no nature of a ghost apart from the stump, and no nature of waves apart from the water. It is the same with respect to space.

It is because there is no nature of flowers. Generally speaking, since beginningless time, sentient beings have possessed only original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) but not initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*).
Therefore, True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not maintain its own nature; it manifests its entire substance as delusive thought (*vikalpa*).
This is what is meant by "the unchanging following conditions. Yet, this very delusive thought has no separate self-substance; it takes True Suchness itself as its substance. As it is said:

While following conditions without changing, one now seeks to strip away false conceptualization; thus it is said, "this perception is not real," which is merely saying "this snake is not real," and so on up to "these flowers are not real.

Since the appearance of the snake has arisen, the appearance of the hemp must necessarily be hidden, and since the appearance of the flowers has arisen, the appearance of emptiness must necessarily be hidden;
therefore, they are called "not real. In truth, this does not mean they are separate from reality.
If there were a separate deluded thought, and if that separate delusion existed, then deluded thought would conversely possess its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and could not be dismantled.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states, "Deluded thought has no intrinsic nature," and the Second Patriarch said, "Seeking the mind, it is utterly unattainable.
These are the great outlines of this school's teaching and the true lifeblood of this scripture; now, I shall briefly elaborate upon them.
This scripture clarifies that the principle of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) cannot be increased or diminished by delusion or awakening;
rather, its diligent emphasis lies solely in reminding the person of the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*).

If one possesses this wisdom of initial awakening, the principle of original enlightenment is inherently and spontaneously realized, so there is no need to worry about lacking great utility. Therefore:
The beginning of the sutra states that the Tathāgata knows the application of those sexual arts;
later passages state that he even knows the number of drops of rain outside worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

and it further states that his "awakened clarity" analyzes subtle demonic affairs—all of these clarify that the Tathāgata’s wisdom of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is perfected. The subsequent text says: "These soldiers must be known."
The "thief" being located here refers to the wisdom of the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi-citta*) that encourages the beginner;

the current text states, "All this is due to not knowing the eternally abiding true mind. Later, Ānanda reproaches himself, saying, "It must be because I do not know the destination of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*)," and throughout the section on the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), he repeatedly reproaches himself, saying, "You originally did not know," and "You plainly did not know," and so forth.
All of these lament that there is no initial awakening. That which is the eternally abiding true mind is fundamentally real;

its substance is beyond all dependence, vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive. Its nature is pure, being primordially free from faults and devoid of non-virtue, thus untainted by defilement.
Its nature is luminous, being primordially void and spiritual, penetratingly clear and without obscuration. It perfectly possesses these three wondrous qualities.
Because its essence is defined by its meaning, it is called the "eternally abiding true mind" (*nitya-sthita-bhūta-citta*) and the "essence of pure and luminous nature.

This is precisely the meaning of the title *Mahā-buddha-uṣṇīṣa*. It is called "Great" (*mahā*) because it is eternally abiding; it is called "Crown" (*uṣṇīṣa*) because its nature is pure; and it is called "Buddha" because its nature is luminous.

Furthermore, as the essence of the three Tathāgatas, because it is eternally abiding, it constitutes the Dharma-body Tathāgata; because its nature is pure, it constitutes... [the Sambhoga-body Tathāgata]; and because its nature is luminous, it constitutes... [the Nirmāṇa-body Tathāgata].
Because the nature of the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata is luminous, it constitutes the Saṃbhogakāya Tathāgata. Furthermore, these three causes of Buddha-nature are eternally abiding:

the eternally abiding nature is the *dharmatā-hetu* (causal nature); the purity of nature is the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditional nature); and the luminosity of nature is the *pariniṣpatti-hetu* (fulfilling nature).

Moreover, because the essence of the myriad practices is eternally abiding, there is the *deva-caryā* (divine conduct); because its nature is pure, there is the *brahma-caryā* (holy conduct); and because of its infant-like and sickly [adaptability], there is the *bāla-caryā* (childlike conduct) and *glāna-caryā* (sickly conduct).

Because its nature is luminous, there is noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*). Furthermore, it is the essence of the Śūraṅgama-samādhi: by virtue of the meaning of permanence, it is established as the samādhi of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

by virtue of the meaning of intrinsic purity, it is established as the samādhi of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); and by virtue of the meaning of luminosity, it is established as the samādhi of the absolute truth (*tattva-satya*).
Moreover, it is the essence of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*); permanence is the true nature of enlightenment.
The purity of the nature is the expedient means (upāya) of bodhi; the luminosity of the nature is the ultimate wisdom (prajñā) of bodhi.
Furthermore, it is the essential substance upon which wondrous śamatha and so forth depend. Based on the meaning of permanence, there is wondrous dhyāna;
based on the meaning of the purity of nature, there is samāpatti; and based on the meaning of the luminosity of nature, there is śamatha. Moreover, it is the Tathāgatagarbha.

The three meanings of *xing* (nature) are eternally abiding: "immediate" (*ji*) refers to the meaning of being both separate and not separate; "separate" (*li*) refers to the meaning of being neither immediate nor non-immediate; "purity" (*jing*) refers to the meaning of being immediately all-inclusive;
and "clarity" (*ming*) refers to the meaning of being simultaneously all-exclusive. Furthermore, "immediate" corresponds to the true nature of permanence;

"purity" corresponds to the true nature of pervasiveness; and "clarity" corresponds to the true nature of perfection. Moreover, "immediate" refers to the true nature of permanence; "purity" refers to the true nature of pervasiveness; and "clarity" refers to the true nature of perfection. Furthermore—

That is to say, because the essence of the seven destinies—afflictions, karma, and suffering—is based on the principle of permanence, there is delusory suffering, just as flowers appear based on space;
because it is based on the principle of pure nature, there is delusory karma, just as knots appear based on a cloth;

and because it is based on the principle of luminous nature, there is delusory affliction, just as cataracts appear based on the eyes. Furthermore, the essence of the three nirvāṇas likewise arises from the principle of permanence.

Therefore, there is *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of intrinsic purity) by virtue of the meaning of intrinsic purity; there is *upāya-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of purity through skillful means) by virtue of the meaning of the luminosity of nature;

and there is *pariniṣpanna-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of perfected purity). The employment of various deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) arises from not knowing that the essence of the mind is eternally abiding;

the employment of ignorance-delusion (*avidyā-vikalpa*) arises from not knowing that the essence of the mind is intrinsically pure; and the employment of [delusions as numerous as] the sands of the Ganges arises from [not knowing this].
Delusive thoughts arise because one does not know that the essence of the mind is luminous; thus, one employs views and thoughts as delusions.
These thoughts are not true because one mistakes the eternally abiding for ignorance (*avidyā*). Ignorance is not true because one mistakes the purity of nature for the "dust-and-sand" afflictions.

The dust-and-sand afflictions are not true because one mistakes the luminosity of nature for views and thoughts. Furthermore, these three—[ignorance, dust-and-sand, and views-and-thoughts]—are likewise [not true].

Delusions are all false perceptions within that which is eternally abiding; they are false perceptions of defilement within the intrinsically pure nature, and false perceptions of obscurity within the intrinsically luminous nature.
Therefore, they are not real. Thus, there is the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*): because ignorance and the sands of afflictions are unreal, there is the cycle of transformation;
because views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are unreal, there is the cycle of segmentation (*bhavāgra*).
This has already implicitly indicated the two kinds of fundamental [delusions]; what follows below specifically clarifies and explains them.
Second, the exhortation to practice the direct path:
"If you now wish to investigate the true nature of the luminous clarity of unsurpassed bodhi, you should respond to my questions with a straightforward mind."
Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share the same path, they all transcend birth and death by means of a direct mind;
since both mind and speech are direct, from beginning to end throughout the stages of realization, there is never any trace of crookedness.
"Research" (*yan*) carries the meaning of exhausting the source and investigating the root. Truly illuminating the nature (*xing*) is unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Although this is what all Buddhas have realized, it is in fact the innate nature possessed by all sentient beings. While enmeshed in delusion, it is called "concealed";
when freed from entanglement, it is called "illuminated. Now, if one wishes for this nature to accord with reality and become illuminated, one must research and exhaustively investigate it.
One must investigate thoroughly and seek to exhaustively penetrate this nature. Such thorough investigation requires a direct mind;
a "direct mind" is what the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* calls right mindfulness of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding the stages from beginning to end:

starting from the stage of "names" (*nāmamātra*) and ending with the ultimate stage, the intermediate levels constitute the fifty-five stations of the true path to Bodhi. Although these various stations exist, [they are all subsumed within this direct mind].
Although the levels of depth differ, cause and effect are none other than the true mark (dharmatā), unlike the circuitousness of the first three teachings;

therefore, it is said that there are "forever no signs of detours. These two characters, "direct mind" (*ṛju-citta*), already lay out the essential tenet of the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in its entirety.
Because Ānanda appeared to be as yet unenlightened and unable to grasp it, [the Buddha] spoke thus.

The arising of false conceptualizations regarding these seven locations—each and every one of them—is nothing other than inverted, frivolous proliferation; the mind and speech are in every case not upright.
