Third, the extensive refutation of the seven rounds of false conceptualization consists of seven parts: (1) the primary refutation of the conceptualization that [the self] is within; (2) the refutation of the counter-conceptualization that it is outside;

(3) the refutation of the counter-conceptualization that it is hidden in the roots; (4) the refutation of the counter-conceptualization that it is seen within; (5) the refutation of the counter-conceptualization... [and so forth].
Following the arising of the six refutations, there is a shift to the intermediate seven refutations, which then lead to the refutation of non-attachment.

Regarding the first five [of these], the first raises the inquiry concerning the mind that takes conditions as its object; the second clarifies subduing through analogies; the third restates their internal attachments; the fourth prefigures the definitive name;
and the fifth correctly refutes that [the mind] is not internal. Now, the first [section].
"Ānanda, I now ask you: when you first resolved to attain enlightenment, taking the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks as your object, what did you see that caused you to feel such love and delight?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, it was by means of my eyes and mind that I felt such love and delight.
With my eyes I beheld the Tathāgata’s sublime appearance, and from this arose a heart of love and delight; therefore, I resolved to cast off birth.'"
Death.
Among the most weighty inquiries of the Tathāgata, what is seen and who is cherished—these two phrases—are followed by the later School of the Gate (Zongmen) question:
"Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? This is precisely the attainment of this function, as the saying goes: "To catch a thief, one must [seize him at the moment of the crime]."
The mention of "seeing" and "defilement" (zāng) in the response serves as the foundation for the subsequent investigation of the mind and the discernment of seeing.

Because the deluded mind is difficult to eliminate, it must be extensively refuted through seven rounds of inquiry; however, regarding the locus of the deluded eye, it suffices to refute it by means of the two phrases:
"the faculty of seeing does not die" and "it sees all objects. This is sufficient because the true seeing is difficult to manifest.
Therefore, although ten points must be carefully distinguished, for the place where the mind is true, it is sufficient to clarify it with the single phrase:
"To see this nature is the mind, not the eye. Second, two analogies clarify subduing.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you have said is true; that which you truly love and delight in arises from the mind and the eyes.

If you do not know where the mind and the eyes are located, you will be unable to subdue the dust and toil of worldly afflictions. It is like a king who, having been invaded by bandits, dispatches troops to eliminate them;
those troops must first know the location of the bandits. It is the fault of your mind and eyes that causes you to wander through the cycle of rebirth."
Ānanda’s falsely conceptualizing eye can by no means see anything, and his falsely conceptualizing mind can by no means give rise to attachment or delight;
this is because the eye is but a fleeting sensory dust and the mind is but a conditioned reflection.
Yet Ānanda mistakenly believes that he can certainly see and certainly feel attachment and delight—this is what is called "mistaking an object for oneself," a most profound inversion.
The king represents fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*); the thieves represent that which is falsely conceptualized—the mind and its objects;
and the soldiers represent initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*) and the wondrously discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*).

Although fundamental enlightenment is invaded by thieves, the power of the *tathatā*-nature naturally gives rise to the wisdom of initial enlightenment, which is like mobilizing an army. One who knows the location of the thieves has no [fear of] the thieves.
One’s own cave-dwelling is nothing other than the king’s land and the king’s subjects; it is only because of a failure in governance that they have become great rebels.
If one can pacify them according to the Dharma, they will once again be the king’s land and the king’s subjects, and truly no more "bandits" can be found.
This applies equally to the mind and the eyes: if one knows that the floating roots and their conditioned shadows all belong solely to [the nature of mind], [then delusion ceases].
What manifests as the mind is merely the floating sense-organ; the original source is not the eye. The shadow is originally not the object; the original source is not the mind.
Vastly returning to the sovereign transformation, where else could there be any defilement to be found?
That which causes you to transmigrate now is simply because you falsely reckon what is not the mind to be the mind, and falsely reckon what is not the eye to be the eye; thus, guilt is incurred. (3)
The second part [of the refutation] further addresses their internal assertions, which is divided into two sections: first, the formal citation of their position;
second, the establishment of a counter-example. Herein is the first section. "I now ask you: where do this 'mind-only' and the eyes currently reside?

Ānanda replied to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, all ten types of ordinary beings in the world alike maintain that the consciousness-mind resides within the body. Even when looking at the Tathāgata’s blue..."
The lotus-eye is also upon the Buddha’s face; yet as I now observe these four sensory objects of the floating roots, they reside only on my own face.
Thus, this conscious mind truly dwells within the body.
As for the ten kinds of ordinary beings, among the twelve classes of living beings, they merely exclude those whose spirits have been transformed into earth or wood.
The two types—the mineral-metal and the empty-dispersed-dissolving-sinking—are for a time identical to mindless objects;
the remaining ten types all manifest with conscious awareness. To calculate that the mind resides within, one extensively cites the ten modes of birth as evidence;
to calculate that the eyes reside on the face, one loftily cites the Tathāgata as evidence. How certain this is! Thus, Ānanda demonstrated the false attachments of all heterodox outsiders.
To be identical and to emulate it accordingly. Second, establishing the precedent:
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "As you are now sitting in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall, look at the Jeta Grove; where is it now?
[Ānanda replied,] "World-Honored One, this great multi-storied pavilion and pure lecture hall are in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden; the Jeta Grove is actually right here."
“Ānanda, what did you first see within this hall? ‘World-Honored One, within this hall I first saw the Tathāgata, and next I observed the great assembly;
it was only when looking outward that I beheld the groves and gardens. Ānanda, by what cause do you behold the groves and gardens?
‘World-Honored One, because the doors and windows of this great lecture hall are wide open, I am able to see afar from within the hall.’”
"Beholding.
This uses Ānanda’s own body as an analogy for the mind; the Tathāgata and the great assembly as an analogy for the liver, intestines, stomach, and spleen;
the doors and windows as an analogy for the eyes; and the gardens and groves as an analogy for all external objects. This is easy to understand from the text.
Fourth, the provisional designation of the samādhi is announced:
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden-hued arm from amidst the great assembly and stroked Ānanda’s crown,
informing Ānanda and the entire multitude that there is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the ten thousand practices.
"The path of wondrous adornment through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend all at once—listen attentively now, Ānanda!
Prostrating yourself, receive my compassionate instruction.
To shatter deluded attachments, I first proclaim the name of the Great Samādhi; for where deluded sentiments are shattered, true nature is fully revealed."
If one possesses sharp faculties, it is sufficient to internally examine and shatter [the notion of] the mind;
when the mind is sought and cannot be found, the mind becomes settled and at peace, which is precisely the Śūraṅgama King Samādhi.

Because those of dull faculties have heavy attachments, once they have shattered the internal, they inevitably shift their calculations to the external, proceeding through successive stages until they give rise to infinite conceptualizations. Ānanda demonstrated this by appearing as if he had not yet [realized it].
This passage clarifies the deluded state through the melody of awakening, so that the Tathāgata’s skillful means may break it open and reveal it, thoroughly elucidating the ultimate principle.

One should know that from this point in the text until the end of the third fascicle and the beginning of the fourth, every section perfectly manifests the fundamental substance of the principle upon which Great Samādhi relies;
it must by no means be fragmented or distributed according to three names. This applies to *samādhi* as well.

*Samādhi* is also called *samāpatti*; this is translated as "right concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*). There is the *samādhi* of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the *samādhi* of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and the *samādhi* of middle truth (*madhyama-satya*).
Furthermore, there is the *samādhi* of the three truths taken separately and the *samādhi* of the three truths in their perfect fusion.
This present [state] is the *samādhi* of the three truths in perfect fusion; it encompasses all phenomena, and all *samādhis* are entirely contained within it.
For this reason, it is called "the King. Regarding the old interpretation:

seeing that the characters for *samādhi* here are identical to the characters for *samā* asked about by Ānanda, [the commentators] proceeded to force a connection between them through various adjustments until they were utterly bewildered;

they did not realize that what Ānanda asked about was precisely what is called *samāpatti* within the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, which is simply an abbreviation formed by omitting the two characters *patti*. Now...
What is stated in the text refers to the three samādhis; the differences in their terminology are merely variations in the local dialects of the Sanskrit *brahman* sound.
One must know that the samādhi of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is accomplished through *śamatha*; the samādhi of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is accomplished through *samāpatti*;

and the samādhi of the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*) is accomplished through *dhyāna*. Furthermore, the samādhi of ultimate truth ceases the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), while the samādhi of conventional truth...
The Samādhi of the Middle Truth that halts the delusions of *rajas* (dust-like afflictions) is the *śamatha* Samādhi of the Ultimate Truth;
the Samādhi of the Conventional Truth clarifies the contemplation of emptiness; the Samādhi of the Middle Truth clarifies the contemplation of the provisional;
and the Samādhi of the Middle Truth clarifies the contemplation of the Middle. This is the essence of *samāpatti*: there are no delusions to be destroyed and no contemplations to be established.
To shatter [delusion] and immediately realize *dhyāna* is the Great Buddha-Crown;
as explained in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), this is the true nature (*tathatā*) upon which this samādhi relies.

Furthermore, *Śūraṅgama* is also explained in the *Xuanyi* as the true cultivation arising from that nature, fully endowed with the ten thousand practices. First, it is "endowed" because it is inherently possessed. This means:
First, it is called "complete" because its principle encompasses and includes everything without exception. Second, it is called "complete" because it is all-inclusive;

that is, practicing this samādhi is itself the practice of all samādhis, as well as the six perfections, the five practices, and so forth, such that nothing is not perfectly subsumed—therefore, it is called complete. Third, it is called "complete" because it is an accumulation; that is to say:

Since beginningless time, all sentient beings possess various seeds of causal conditions—such as snapping the fingers, gathering sand, raising the hands, or bowing the head—which constitute all manner of wholesome roots.
When they attain this samādhi, these seeds are simultaneously awakened and manifested; therefore, it is called "endowment.

This is termed "endowment" with respect to the direct cause (*nidāna-hetu*), "endowment" with respect to the inclusive aspect, and "endowment" with respect to the accumulated aspect of the understanding cause (*vidyā-hetu*).

Furthermore, the three causes of conditions are all inherently present, and are thus called "inherently complete" (*benju*); the three causes all encompass and include [all phenomena], and are thus called "comprehensively complete" (*gaiju*);
the three causes all unfold and manifest, and are thus called "cumulatively complete" (*jiju*). Here again appears the meaning of being neither vertical nor horizontal.
Practice is the gateway for entering principle: one practice is all practices, and all practices are one practice.
Therefore, it is called the person of the single gate who is perfectly enlightened and perfectly cultivated, forever free from all traces of circuitousness; thus it is named "Transcendence.

The two kinds of adornment—merit and wisdom—arising from that which accords with the nature are themselves used to adorn the single nature. Cultivating non-duality within this nature is called "Sublime Adornment.
Beginning from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-jñāna*) and culminating in Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), it is therefore called the "Path."
The fifth [section] correctly refutes [the objection] that [the eye] is not internal; it has two parts: first, citing an example, and second, the actual refutation. Now, for the first:

The Buddha told Ānanda, "Is it as you say—that while the body is in the lecture hall and the doors and windows are wide open so that one can gaze far out at the groves and gardens, there might be sentient beings within this hall who do not see the Tathāgata, yet see what is outside the hall? Ānanda, [replied].
He replied, "World-Honored One, it is impossible that one who does not see the Tathāgata within the hall could see the groves and springs outside.
Second, the direct refutation:
"Ānanda, you are also like this. Your mental faculty is all-encompassing and clearly aware; if what you currently perceive is clear..."

If you truly believe that the mind exists within the body, then you should first understand whether there is any sentient being who first perceives what is inside the body and only afterwards observes external objects.
Even if one cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach, one certainly ought to clearly perceive the growth of nails and hair, the movement of tendons, and the throbbing of veins;
how could it be that one does not know these things? It must be that one does not know them from within.
How do we know this is external? Therefore, you should understand that your claim—that the mind capable of cognition and awareness dwells within the body—is impossible.

The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "One falsely identifies the reflected images conditioned by the six sense-objects as the characteristics of one's own mind. This sūtra says: "A single delusion..."
"To hold that the mind is fixed as a delusion within the physical body is the common calculation of all sentient beings;
the six subsequent sections below are merely further refinements of this calculation. Although this passage refutes that deluded mind, it does not establish anything real;
rather, it reveals that the deluded mind has no substance. Because it has no substance, it has no location. Furthermore, because it has no substance, it has no location.

Yet all things are clearly manifest; this is precisely what is meant by "the nature is identical to empty space. Furthermore, no characteristics of empty space can be apprehended—how could this be anything other than the entire body of the true mind?
For this reason, it is said that the true mind is secretly revealed. If one cannot realize this, one utterly辜负 (gains nothing from) the perfect sound [of the Buddha's teaching].
Second, refuting the further calculation that [the mind] exists externally. Part one: the initial shift.
This consists of two refutations; now, for the first:
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying, "I have heard the Tathāgata’s such sounds of Dharma, and I have realized that my mind truly resides outside the body.
Why is this? For example, if a lamp is lit within a room, that lamp must necessarily—"

If one can first illuminate the interior of a room and then [illuminate] from its doorway through to the courtyard, yet all sentient beings today cannot see within their own bodies but only see outside their bodies—this is like a lamp placed outside a room being unable to illuminate the interior.
This principle must be clear and free from confusion; it accords with the Buddha’s definitive meaning (nītārtha). Is there no error here?
The second part, the refutation, is also twofold: first, establishing an analogy; second, the actual refutation. Regarding the first:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "These bhikṣus have just now returned from Śrāvastī city, where they went on alms-round for solid food and returned to the Jeta Grove.
I have already finished my meal. Observe, Ānanda: when one bhikṣu eats, are all the others satiated?"
Ānanda replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Although these bhikṣus are all arhats, their physical bodies and life spans differ;
how could one person alone cause the multitude to be satiated?"
"Kabalīṅkāra-āhāra" (solid food) refers to substantial food that can be grasped in physical portions;
"sūpaviṣṭa" (having sat down for the meal) means having finished eating, which carries the sense of concluding the fast. Second, the actual refutation.

The Buddha said to Ānanda, "If the mind that perceives, knows, sees, and cognizes truly exists outside the body, such that the body and mind exist as separate entities and do not interact with one another, then what the mind knows, the body could not feel; and what is felt at the boundaries of the body, the mind could not know.
I shall now show you my hand, which is as soft as tūla-cotton. When your eyes see it, does your mind discern it? Ānanda replied:
Thus the World-Honored One told Ānanda: "If they were mutually cognizant, how could it be that [the mind] is outside?
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of cognition and awareness dwells outside the body—is impossible."
The Buddha’s hands are like *tūla* cotton—white, pure, soft, and supple—and for this reason they are called "tūla-cotton hands.
Third, the refutation of his shifting arguments, which consists of two parts: first, the shifting of the argument; second, the refutation and rejection. Now, the first part.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has stated: because one does not see the interior, it does not reside within the body;
because the body and mind know each other and are not separate, it does not exist outside the body. As I now reflect, I know it must reside in a single location.
The Buddha asked, “Where, then, is that location? Ānanda replied, “This cognizing mind neither knows the interior yet is able to see the exterior.”
As I reflect upon it, the faculty of perception lies latent within, just as if someone were to take a crystal bowl and cover both eyes with it;
although there is something covering them, it does not obstruct the vision. That faculty perceives objects and immediately discriminates them accordingly.
Yet, this conscious mind of mine that is capable of knowing cannot see inwardly because it resides within the faculties; it clearly gazes outward without obstruction.
Because its roots are latent within, the lapis lazuli gem is named for its transparency both inside and out; it is similar to modern spectacles.

Here, the eye is used as a metaphor for the mind, and the lapis lazuli bowl is used as a metaphor for the pure matter (*rūpa*) of the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). Therefore, it is said that "the eye follows what is seen, and the mind follows in discrimination."
The second section, the refutation, is further divided into two parts: first, establishing the analogy; second, the actual refutation. Now, for the first part:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "As you have said, if this mind were hidden within the roots [of the sense organs], it would be like [the eye being inside] lapis lazuli.
When that person covers their eyes with a lapis lazuli lens, they should see the mountains and rivers outside, yet they should also see the lapis lazuli itself. This is not the case."
“World-Honored One, this person should see the lapis lazuli clearly with eyes made of lapis lazuli.
[The Buddha] broke it into two pieces.
The Buddha told Ānanda, “If your mind were united with the lapis lazuli, you should see the mountains and rivers; why do you not see your own eyes?”
If the eye were a seer, it would be identical to its object and thus could not function as a perceiver;
if it cannot see, how can you say that this cognizing mind is latent within the sense organ like a crystal?
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of conscious cognition dwells hidden within the organ like a crystal—is untenable.
If it is granted that the eye is seen, then the eye would be identical to external objects in its lack of the capacity for seeing;
thus, the principle that "as one sees, so one discriminates" would not be established. Since the eye is not seen, it is clear that the mind does not reside potentially within the sense organ.
Fourth, the refutation of the alternative position regarding the seeing of the internal, which has two parts: first, the presentation of the alternative position; second, the refutation.

First: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I have now further reflected thus: within the bodies of these sentient beings, the viscera and organs reside inside while the apertures are situated on the outside;
where there are viscera, it is dark, and where there are apertures, it is bright. Now, as I stand before the Buddha, [my eyes] are open."
To see light with the eyes is called seeing the external; to see darkness with the eyes closed is called seeing the internal.

What is the meaning of this? This is further a calculation that the mind resides within. When he first calculated it to be within, the Buddha refuted him by questioning how one could see the internal.
Now, by saying that seeing darkness is seeing the internal, [the opponent] is precisely turning back to rescue his initial position. Second, the refutation: Furthermore—
Third, there are three parts: first, the direct refutation; second, the refutation by way of shifting the argument;

and third, the refutation by way of tying up the conclusion. Now, for the first: The Buddha told Ānanda, "When you close your eyes and see darkness, does this objective realm of darkness face the eye or not?
If it faces the eye, the darkness is in front of the eyes; how then could it be 'internal'? If it were internal,"
If one dwells within a dark room where there is no sun, moon, or lamp, this darkness within the room is entirely your own scorched entrails.
If it does not face [the eyes], how can it constitute seeing?
Herein, first both "facing" and "not facing" are stated together, and then both are refuted. Regarding the phrase "if it faces the eyes," [the following applies] first:
The refutation of "confrontation" (pratimukha) also has two points: first, that once there is confrontation, it is not internal; second, that if one grants it is internal, there is a logical fallacy.
If it is not confronted, the following refutes non-confrontation; it simply requires the single phrase: "How can it constitute seeing? Second, the sequential refutation also has three parts:
first, refuting the counter-argument that it is internal and confronted; second, refuting the counter-argument that it exists in space; third...
To refute their shifting arguments, there are two points of realization. First:

If you claim that when the eyes are closed, one sees darkness because of an internal object formed by separation from external objects, then why does one not see one's own face when opening the eyes to see light?
If one does not see one's own face, then an internal object is not established. If it were established, this would be a cognition that clearly perceives [the face].
Furthermore, since the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) resides in empty space, how could it be said to be "inside"?

Fearing that the opponent might further attempt to defend this by saying: "When one opens the eyes and sees the external, it is called the 'external correspondence'; when one closes the eyes and sees darkness, it is called the 'internal correspondence,'" [the author replies:
even then, darkness would still be in correspondence with the eye, yet one does not take the darkness of the room as being within the internal organs.

Now, I shall cite these points and refute them: since you allow for internal confrontation, then at the time of opening one's eyes, one should likewise be able to internally confront and see that face.
If, when the eyes are open, one cannot internally confront and see that face, then how could one possibly achieve internal confrontation when the eyes are closed?
Furthermore, if you were to concede that one sees the face through internal confrontation, then both the eye and the mind would have to reside within empty space.
This still contradicts your plan that the mind resides within the body. Second, it refutes your alternative concession that it resides in space.
If [the mind] were in empty space, it would not be your own substance; thus, when the Tathāgata now looks at your face, it would also have to be your body.
Furthermore, since your eyes already perceive this, your body would lack sensation.
Fearing that he might offer this defense: "Even if it were granted that both the mind and the eyes are situated in empty space, what fault would there be?
We shall now restate and refute this point. If [the eyes] were in empty space, they would not be your own body;

consequently, when the Tathāgata now sees your face, the Tathāgata would likewise possess the eyes of your body. If your eyes have already perceived [the face], your body ought still to be unaware of it.
Third, he refutes their shifting defense regarding the two cognitions.
If you maintain that the two cognitions of the body and the eye must each possess its own distinct knowledge, then your single body would necessarily become two Buddhas.
Fearing this, they might further shift their defense, saying: "Even though the eye is in space, what prevents the eye from knowing [the body]? The body is likewise perceived accordingly. Now...

Furthermore, he refutes this by saying: "If you grant that the eye exists in empty space and yet both locations—the eye and the body—are perceived, then the two present cognitions would constitute two Buddhas.
Now, although at the time of attaining Buddhahood there may be countless transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), they are merely like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers;
how could one say that the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) possesses two distinct entities? This concludes the third refutation.
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that seeing darkness is called "seeing the internal"—is untenable.
This consists of two parts: first, the presentation of the revised position, and second, its refutation. Now, the first part.
Ānanda said, "I have often heard the Buddha reveal to the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
and because phenomena arise, all manner of minds arise. Now, as I contemplate this very essence of contemplation, it is truly my own mind-nature.
Wherever it joins with something, the mind exists accordingly; yet it is not located within, without, or in between these three places."
The preceding four chapters all involve conceptual constructions of one's own mind; the following three chapters all rely on the sacred teachings for erroneous inference.

Although they rely on the sacred teachings, they fail to understand their true purport because they mistakenly identify the reflected image of conditions (*ālambana-pratibimba*) and do not know the actual meaning of the mind.
For instance, the four propositions regarding "the arising of the mind" and "the arising of phenomena" reveal that causes and conditions are themselves emptiness and the provisional.
Although the terminology of the Middle Way is the same, its meaning pertains to the four teachings. If one were to say that "with the arising of the mind, dharmas arise;

with the cessation of the mind, dharmas cease," such that the arising of dharmas is the mind arising and the cessation of dharmas is the mind ceasing—wherein mind and dharmas mutually serve as causes and conditions—then although arising and ceasing appear vividly, they are merely a provisional conjunction of causes and conditions, devoid of any separate time, space, atoms, or a Great Self (Maheśvara).
To hold that [phenomena] can arise, yet do not arise spontaneously because they lack causes and conditions—this is the meaning of the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao).
If one says that with the arising of the mind, phenomena arise, such that there are no phenomena outside the mind and phenomena are fundamentally unarisen;

or that with the arising of phenomena, the mind arises, such that there is no mind outside of phenomena and the mind is also unarisen; and that both mind and phenomena are, in their very essence, unarisen—this is called the "cause" (hetu).

That conditions are themselves empty is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). If one says that the non-awakening of ignorance gives rise to the three subtle states, this is called "the arising of mind";
that the wind of objective realms moves to produce the waves of the evolving consciousnesses, this is called "the arising of dharmas.

Because mind and dharmas mutually serve as causes and conditions, there are the distinctions of the ten realms and the provisional names of immeasurable varieties; this is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).
If one says that when the mind arises, dharmas arise, then everything is merely the arising of mind-dharmas; if the mind arises, then everything is merely dharmas.

If these two mutually negate each other, then both mind and dharmas vanish; if they are both illuminated simultaneously, then mind and dharmas remain distinct, yet their essence is the inconceivable Dharma-realm.
This is what is called the Middle Way within causes and conditions, the meaning of the Perfect Teaching. Now, Ānanda—

Although they recite the texts, they do not comprehend their meaning; they stubbornly cling to the "reflected image of conditions" (*pratibimba*) as the nature of their own mind, claiming that it arises in accordance with conjunctions and lacks a fixed location—whether internal, external, or intermediate.

This does not even accord with the sense of the arising of the mind taught in the *Āgama* teachings, let alone its full meaning. Second, the refutation has three parts: first, restating their position; second, the actual refutation; third, the conclusion.
Refutation. First:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "As for what you have just said—that because dharmas arise, various kinds of mind arise, and wherever they encounter conditions, the mind follows and exists there—"
Although Ānanda cited both the passages concerning the arising of the mind and the arising of dharmas, his intention lay solely in the arising of dharmas; thus, he neglected the arising of the mind.
Furthermore, not realizing that the deluded mind has no substantial essence, he reckoned this conditioned reflection to be the "agent" that conjoins with various dharmas as the "objects" conjoined.
Therefore, the Buddha addressed his misconception and did not need to further produce the two preceding [passages].
The first two lines of the verse do not serve as the basis for their false conceptualization; therefore, they are excluded. Second, the actual refutation, which has two parts:
first, the refutation of non-existence; second, the refutation of existence. This is the first part.
If this mind has no substance, then there is nothing with which it can conjoin. If that which lacks substance were able to conjoin, then the nineteen elements would conjoin with the seven objects;
such a principle is not tenable.
Indeed, the deluded mind has no substance, yet Ānanda has long clung to the notion that it does, failing to realize its fundamental non-existence.
Now, one may challenge this by means of its lack of substantiality: this "mind" refers to that grasped "reflected image" (*pratibimba*).
Since you do not know that the reflected image is not the mind, you must falsely claim it has substantiality; you simply dare not accept the principle that it lacks substantiality.
While the six sense objects and eighteen realms are in their entirety identical to one's own mind, you now single out only this reflected image and calculate it [as real].
If one considers the shadow to be one's own mind, then the sensory objects and the realms would both be external dharmas apart from the mind.

To then wish to take this essence-less causal mind and attempt to unify it with all dharmas—how is this any different from wishing to synthesize the essence-less seventh object with the essence-less nineteenth realm?
This principle is necessarily untenable. Second, the refutation of existence.

The nature [of the mind] is further analyzed in two parts: first, refuting it by means of its internal and external movement; second, refuting it by means of its unity, multiplicity, pervasiveness, and non-pervasiveness.
This is the first part.
If there were such a substance, then as you yourself touch your own body with your hand, does the consciousness that perceives this emerge from within?
"If [the seeing] enters from outside or emerges from within and returns to see within the body, or if it comes from outside, one should first see the face.
Ānanda said, 'Seeing is the function of the eye; the mind knows, but the eye does not. Therefore, for the eye to be the act of seeing is illogical.

The Buddha said, 'If the eye were able to see, when you are inside a room, would the door be able to see? Furthermore, those who are already dead still have their eyes remaining; should they all be able to see?'"
If an object were to see another object, how could it be called "death"?
This primarily refutes the deluded mind, while taking the opportunity to incidentally refute the deluded eye. The ephemeral physical eye cannot perceive;
how then could the mind that clings to reflected images possess cognition? Alas, this is something one must contemplate! (2. Discussing the One in Terms of the Two)
The refutation through [the categories of] pervasive and non-pervasive:
Ānanda, furthermore, as for this mind of yours that perceives and knows, if it must have a substance, does it have a single substance or multiple substances?
Is it currently located within your body as a pervasive substance or a non-pervasive substance? If it were a single substance, then your—
When you prick one limb with your hand, the other four limbs should feel it; yet if all were to feel it, there would be no specific location for the prick.
If the prick occurs at a specific location, then your "single entity" cannot be established. If there were multiple entities, you would become many people—of which entity would you be?
If your body were pervasive, it would be the same as the case of the prick previously mentioned; if it were not pervasive, then when you touch your head, you would also be touching [your feet].
If the head of the foot were that which perceives, the foot itself should be devoid of cognition;

yet this is not the case for you. First, I shall establish four propositions and then refute them one by one. The first is the proposition of identity, asserting that the four limbs share a single mental essence;

therefore, I challenge this by asking how they could all perceive simultaneously. If they were all to perceive at once, then when one part is pricked, the sensation would not be localized. Now, when it is pricked...
If it were to exist pervasively in all locations, then the principle of universal awareness would collapse, and the four limbs could not share a single mental substance.

Next, the phrase "multiple substances" refers to multiple minds; therefore, this is equivalent to multiple persons. Third, the phrase "pervasive substance" means that a single mind fills the four limbs;
since this is identical to the previous case where the four limbs share a single mental substance, it is likewise the same as before.
The four "non-pervasive" propositions raised as objections mean that because a single mind cannot respond universally, it should possess cognition in one place while lacking cognition in another;
however, your position is not so, as these four propositions are all refuted by the summary statement. This concludes the third section on refutation.
Therefore, one should know that wherever there is a conjunction, the mind follows accordingly; it is impossible for it not to exist.

This section on the refutation of the six [positions] regarding the transition [of consciousness] has two parts: first, the refutation of general speculations, and second, the refutation of the specific position. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, the general speculation, and second, the general refutation. Now, the first [section].

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have also heard the Buddha, when conversing with Mañjuśrī and other Dharma-princes regarding the true nature (dharmatā), say that the mind is neither within nor without. As I reflect upon this:
if one says it is within, then nothing is seen; if one says it is without, then there should be no mutual cognition, for since there is no cognition within, it cannot be within."
If the mind and body have become mutually aware while being outside, this is not logical; yet since they are now mutually aware, and there is no seeing within, it must be in between.
Now, when the Buddha says that the mind is neither within nor without, he is precisely demonstrating that the mind has no essential substance or characteristics.
Furthermore, because it has no directions or corners, and neither form nor non-form, it is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Yet Ānanda currently identifies with the shadow of conditions, whereby there is clearly a form that can be apprehended; how utterly illusory and false this is!
However, since he has not yet precisely pointed out what constitutes the "middle," his view is termed a "vague calculation. Second, the general refutation.
The Buddha said: "What you call 'the middle' must necessarily not be confused, for it cannot be without a location.

Now, when you investigate this 'middle,' where does it reside? Does it reside in a place, or does it reside in the body? If it resides in the body, then what is at the periphery is not the middle; if it were in the middle, it would be the same as the interior.
If it resides in a place, is that place something indicated, or is it something unindicated? If it is unindicated, it is the same as non-existence. If it is unindicated, then—"

Why is there no fixed [direction]? For example, when a person uses a marker to designate the center, if they look toward the east, it becomes the south; if they look toward the west, it becomes the north.
Since the substance of the marker is inherently indeterminate, the mind should likewise be disordered.
Because Ānanda had only explained the meaning of the term "middle" without clarity, it must be determined by means of the two meanings of "abiding in a place" and "abiding in the body";
therefore, it is said that the middle must not be confused with being without a location. Second, the refutation of the false calculation, which has two parts:
first, the false calculation; second, the formal refutation. Now, the first part.
Ānanda said, "Among what I have spoken, it is not these two kinds [of mind]. As the World-Honored One has said, 'With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
Since the eye possesses discrimination and the object of form lacks consciousness, when consciousness arises therein, that is where the mind resides."

Ānanda’s original intention was precisely focused on this; however, these two phrases—"the eye and form serve as conditions to produce eye-consciousness"—relate their meaning to the four teachings (*catur-yāna*).

If one understands that consciousness is produced by these correct causes and conditions, and does not belong to false causes or causelessness, then the consciousness produced by such causes and conditions lacks substantial reality and is devoid of self or what belongs to a self (*anātman-anātmiya*); this is the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) teaching.
If one understands that the producer and the produced are both devoid of self-nature and that their essence is entirely empty, this is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).

If one discriminates the infinite provisional names of dependent origination— namely, that visual consciousness arises from nine conditions while auditory consciousness arises from only eight, and so on,
up to a full clarification of the differences between the causes and results of the transformation of the eight consciousnesses— this is the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).

The meaning is this: if one knows that the nature of consciousness has no source and arises falsely from the six kinds of faculties and objects, then the nature of consciousness is clear and knowing, and the true consciousness is wondrously enlightened, profound and still, pervading the entire dharma-realm. It contains and exhales the ten voids, having no fixed location;
it merely manifests according to karma and is called "conditioned arising. The nature of this conditioned arising is itself the true nature.
What is called "the unchanging following conditions" and "following conditions while remaining unchanging" is precisely the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Some claim this is a provisional teaching of the Dharma-character school (Xiangzong), but this is because they have not deeply sought its underlying intent.

Now, what Ānanda calculates is to falsely point to the shadow of conditions as the mind, claiming it is produced by the co-arising of the faculties and objects, and that it possesses a substantial essence that can be apprehended. This is still [a misconception].

How much less could the teachings of the Non-Store (Tripitaka) convey the meaning of the absence of substantial reality, let alone the meanings of the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect [Teachings]? Second, the formal refutation:
The Buddha said, "If your mind were located between the sense organs and their objects, would this essence of the mind encompass both, or not?

If it encompasses both, then the substance of the object and the essence of the mind would be intermingled; since the object is not the essence of cognition, they would stand as two opposing entities. How could this be?"

If one were to claim that the middle simultaneously possesses both [aspects], this would be untenable; for if it is neither cognition nor non-cognition, it lacks intrinsic nature, and thus what could serve as its characteristic?
Therefore, one should know that there is no such possibility for it to exist in the middle.

This refers to your reckoning of the intermediate mind: does it take both the sense organ and the object as its common substance, or does it possess a distinct substance of its own that does not include the sense organ and the object? This is the double citation [of the opponent's position].
In refuting this, we first refute the inclusion of both; if it includes both, then the material object of form and the eye-organ—
If their natures were mutually intermingled and confused, then objects would ultimately not be as they are;

if the nature of the body possesses cognition, then cognition and non-cognition would remain as two opposing forces standing in opposition to the end—how could this be called the "Middle"? Next, to refute the position that it does not include both:
if neither of the two [possibilities] is established when including them, then your mental substance is neither the cognition of the sense organs nor the non-cognition of the sense objects.
If one asks what its essential nature (*svabhāva*) might be, since even an essential nature does not exist, how could there be any characteristics?
[This consists of] seven refutations of shifting positions regarding non-attachment. Part One: The Initial Shifting Position; Part Two: The Refutation. Now, the first.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in the past I saw the Buddha together with his four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—turning the wheel of Dharma.

He constantly spoke of awakening to and discerning the nature of the mind, saying that it is neither within, nor without, nor in between; it has no location at all and is entirely free from attachment."
If one names it "mind," does that mean there is attachment to a self? No, there is no such attachment.

The meaning of being "without location" and "without attachment" also pertains to the four teachings (*catur-yāna*). If one says that "mind" is merely a provisional name (*prajñapti*) and lacks any substantial reality, such that it is without location and without attachment, this is the meaning of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching.
If one says that since the provisional name is empty, the provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) are likewise [empty]...
If one says that the dharma of the empty mind is itself empty—where could it be, and where could it be attached? This is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

If one says that the mind has no location, yet is not not-located, and because it is not not-located, it has nothing to which it is attached, this is the meaning of the Distinct and Complete Teachings (*bhedavibhāga-pūrṇa-yāna*).
Now, Ānanda stubbornly clings to the reflected image as being the mind, yet claims it does not reside in the three locations; this is much like a monkey leaping about restlessly.

If even the teachings of the Tripitaka (Zangjiao), which lack fixed abodes and are merely provisional names without ultimate reality, cannot be established, how much less so the Distinct and Complete Teachings?

Only by examining these three chapters can one know that although the words are the same, their underlying meanings are vastly different. When heterodox people preach the True Dharma, the True Dharma itself becomes heterodox;
in the final age, those who borrow the ultimate discourse of the definitive meaning to form their own biased interpretations are as numerous as [the stars].
This is the second refutation.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Regarding your statement that the mind-nature of awareness and discernment has no location whatsoever—consider all things in the world, such as empty space, water, land, and flying creatures, which are called 'all things. If you do not cling to them, do they exist or do they not exist?"
If it were non-existent, it would be the same as a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns; how then could one not be attached? To say there is no attachment is to name it "non-existence.
If there is no characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), then there is nothing that is not non-existence; if there is a characteristic, then it exists. How can there be non-attachment?
Therefore, one should know that to say all non-attachment is called the awakening mind—that is impossible.
Since Ānanda has identified the shadow of conditions as the mind, there must be another entity that simply does not abide in any single location;

therefore, the Buddha refutes this by saying: "The empty space of the world, water, land, flying creatures, and all such material phenomena are called 'all things,' for there is nothing that is not included therein.
Since you say that [the mind] does not abide in any of these 'all things,' then as for this non-abiding..."
Does the mind exist apart from all things, or does it have no separate location at all?
This is the double proposition. First, the refutation of non-existence: If it has no separate location, then this mind would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit;
how then could it still be called "unattached"? Next, the refutation of existence: If there were one [separate location]...
That which is non-attached cannot be termed "non-existence" without first being "free from characteristics.

Since that which is free from characteristics can be termed "non-existence," if it were not non-existent, it would possess characteristics. Once characteristics have become existent, there must necessarily be a location for them;

how then could it be termed "non-attachment"? The refutation of these attachments is thus evident. Up to this point, the preceding section has been a sequential refutation of false attachments, implicitly revealing [the truth].
The true mind is precisely the refutation of the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which means that there is truly no snake upon the rope.

Second, it reveals the sublime principle while simultaneously refuting other delusions; this reveals that the essence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is itself the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), while simultaneously refuting the view that the dependent nature is not real—just as revealing the essence of the rope to be hemp refutes the view that the hemp definitely possesses a rope.
This is divided into three parts: first, a general demonstration that all phenomena are mind-only; second, a specific elucidation of the nature through the seeing-essence;

and third, a comprehensive traversal of the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements to realize the principle. Regarding the first part, the general demonstration that all phenomena are mind-only, previous commentaries have all classified this as "refuting the deluded.
They maintain that while the preceding section refuted the non-existence of the deluded mind, this section now proceeds to refute the deluded mind itself.
Because it has no substance, the deluded mind is not perceived; precisely because it lacks substance, there is nothing that is deluded.

In the voidness of the deluded mind, the entire body is the True Reality (*tathatā*). Therefore, although the preceding section provisionally refuted the deluded, it already implicitly revealed the True;

how much more so now, when auspicious signs manifest the permanence of the True, clearly indicating the two fundamental sources and pointing to the fact that all phenomena are Mind-only, proclaiming the existence of the wondrous mind.

As for the substance [of this teaching], it does not merely directly manifest the true nature; rather, the act of "shouting" to shatter old delusions is simply a supplementary maneuver following the destruction of the false.
Therefore, one should regard the manifestation of the truth as primary and the destruction of the false as secondary. This is further divided into two parts:
first, the direct demonstration that the two are not separate from the one mind; second, the detailed demonstration that the substance of the mind differs from false attachments. First:
In the first of the two middle sections, there is the request made by the appropriate recipient and the revelation given by the Tathāgata. Now, for the first part:
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am the youngest brother of the Tathāgata, having been favored by the Buddha’s compassionate love."

Although I have now left the household life, I still rely on my former charm and affection; thus, despite my extensive learning, I have not attained the outflows-free state and am unable to subdue the *sāpīya* spell.
Consequently, I was turned by it and fell into a house of debauchery. This must be because I did not know the destination of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will reveal to us the path of *śamatha*, so that those of the icchantika class may [attain liberation].

After Huimili Che had spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; the great assembly likewise waited expectantly with thirsty longing, desiring to hear his instructions.

Those who had not yet attained the outflow-free state (anāsrava) had not only failed to reach the exhaustion of outflows, but had not even attained the outflow-free truth of the first fruit (srotāpanna).

It is clear that because Ānanda had partially realized the untainted (anāsrava) attainment of the path-concomitant precepts through the first fruit (srotāpanna), even though he had not yet severed desire-attachment, he could not have been turned by the power of the licentious incantation;
how much less so since the seven points of false attachment mentioned in the preceding text are all subsumed under the delusions of views (dṛṣṭi-kleśa).
The old commentary’s claim that Ānanda had previously realized the first fruit is likely not necessarily the case; one should instead rely on the third fascicle [of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*].
It is only when one realizes the *tathāgatagarbha* that one’s traces become identical to those of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*);

thus, it is only in the fourth fascicle that it says, "You have now attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. The "True Limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*) refers to the ultimate principle of the secret treasury of the three virtues, which is called the "abode of the True Limit.
The "one mind and three types of cessation" (*ekacitta-triśamatha*) are, for example, like the path by which one arrives there.
When people see the name "śamatha" mentioned, they immediately seek to dissect and categorize it, failing to realize that in the Perfect Teaching, raising one [name] implies all three.
*Icchantika* means "one who has severed the roots of goodness"; *mleccha* means "evil views.

Not knowing that the nature is inherently endowed with the Perfect School, they cling to fixed notions of Buddha-nature—asserting that the three [natures] are non-dual or that two exist while one does not—and this is precisely to sever the Buddha-realm.
The roots of goodness of these [beings] are collectively termed "evil knowledge and views. Second, the Tathāgata reveals two parts: first, the auspicious omen indicating the true and eternal;
second, the formal demonstration of the two fundamental natures. Now, for the first part.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face; the radiance was as brilliant as hundreds of thousands of suns, and the entire Buddha-world shook in six ways.
Thus, lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions were simultaneously revealed.
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, all these worlds were merged into a single realm, and within that world, everything that existed—
All the great Bodhisattvas, each residing in their own land, joined their palms and listened attentively.
Because he was about to correctly reveal the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of pure and luminous nature—he first emitted light and manifested auspicious omens to indicate this.
As for the "face-gate" (*mukha-dvāra*), it is the place where the six sense-faculties converge, and it is also the point from which the front and back emerge.
The reason for emitting light from these [six] parts is to cause sentient beings to turn their backs on the dust of sensory objects and unite with awakening.

For sentient beings turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust, giving rise to various false conceptualizations; thus, the seven locations are all "not" (non-existent). Because the Tathāgata turns his back on the dust and unites with awakening, wondrously accords with the true and eternal;
thus, the six sense organs are all "are" (existent). As for the phrase "like hundreds of thousands of suns," it means illuminating the myriad dharmas.
There is nothing left out. As for the sixfold earthquake, it is to shatter ignorance and bring about awakening. Regarding the manifestation of the ten directions as merging into a single realm:
when one is deluded by the false, there is neither sameness nor difference; yet within this, one fiercely perceives difference.
When one awakens to the Real, all distinct natures are non-distinct. That the Bodhisattvas all abide in their own lands means that they do not...
The movement of the Dharma-realm is such that those who join their palms in reverent listening all accord with the true source. What the auspicious signs manifest fully reveals the wondrous Dharma;

for those of sharp faculties, it is a matter of meeting the truth upon seeing it and realizing it within the mind, while for those who do not yet understand, these words are spoken again to provide further clarification.
The six kinds of trembling—namely, moving, surging upward, rising, shaking, roaring, and striking—the first three pertain to form, while the latter...
The third point concerning sound indicates that the Buddhas provide both physical and vocal benefits. Second, it correctly demonstrates the two fundamental natures.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed various inverted karmic seeds that naturally cluster like *akṣa* fruits;
thus, practitioners are unable to achieve unexcelled Bodhi, or even [attain] anything else."

Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, as well as those who have become non-Buddhist practitioners, devas, māras, and their retinues—all fail to realize the two kinds of fundamental roots and thus practice erroneously, like boiling sand in hopes of producing fine food; even if they pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, they will never achieve it.
What are these two kinds, Ānanda? The first is the root of beginningless birth and death, which is your...
Now, as for you and all sentient beings who take the攀緣心 (攀緣心, *pān-yuán-xīn*—the攀緣心, or "clinging-and-conditioning mind") as your own nature:

the beginningless essence of Bodhi and Nirvana is fundamentally pure. Yet, it is your present *vijñāna*-essence (*shì-jīng*), which is fundamentally luminous and capable of giving rise to all conditions, that is what remains after those conditions have passed.
Because sentient beings have abandoned this original luminosity, although they act all day long, they do not realize it themselves; thus they enter [into suffering] in vain.
Regarding the various realms of existence:

previously, it was explained in general that the continuous succession of birth and death for all sentient beings arises entirely from their failure to know the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of pure luminosity—and instead employing various false thoughts; because these thoughts are not real, there is cyclic wandering. However, it remains...
It has never been clearly stated that this true mind and delusive thoughts possess no two distinct essences, being like hemp and a snake that do not exist apart from a single rope.

Now I shall further clarify that these two natures are inseparable from the one mind, so that people may not neglect the true while pursuing the delusive, but must understand the delusive in order to return to the true.
"All sentient beings" is a general term for those who are deluded regarding the truth and pursue the delusive.

The proliferation of delusion is as extensive as that listed in the following section on the seven destinies; it specifically refers to those practitioners who loathe delusion and seek the Truth, as detailed extensively in the following section on the *skandha-māras*.
"Akṣa" is the name for a fruit from the Western Regions (India) that does not exist in this land;

"cluster" (*pu*) refers to three things that necessarily arise together and form a single cluster, used as a metaphor for the triad of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*).
If they were never to separate from the beginning until the end, one could not achieve unexcelled bodhi;

this refers to the provisional teaching’s bodhisattvas who separately become śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, referring to the two vehicles of the *Zang* (Treasury) and *Tong* (Penetration) teachings; the rest may be understood accordingly.

Although these two streams are one in essence—one following delusion and the other tending toward enlightenment—the gap between the wise and the ignorant is vast and distinct, yet they have not yet reached the truth regarding reality and falsehood.
Since the source has no beginning and true wisdom (*tathatājñāna*) is but one, it is summarized as a reprimand:

"All [suffering] arises from not knowing the two kinds of fundamental natures. The sand is a metaphor for the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arising upon the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*);

the food is a metaphor for the nature of perfect reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) inherent within the nature of dependence on others. If one does not abandon pervasive conceptualization, how can one attain perfect reality?

Toiling through kalpas of dust-like eons for nothing but empty loss—how can one not be cautious? That which "climbs" (the subject) is the mind capable of cognition, namely the eight consciousnesses, each possessing its own *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving portion).
That which is "climbed upon" (the object) is the realm perceived, namely the eight consciousnesses, each possessing its own *nimitta-bhāga* (image portion).
These two portions—the perceiving and the image—arise based on the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying portion) of the eight consciousnesses; this is called "dependence."

The "arising from conditions" refers to this mind that fails to realize that its own objects are merely manifestations of the self-attestation of the eight consciousnesses, and which horizontally gives rise to the dual grasping at self and phenomena.
This is what is meant by taking the攀緣心 (pān-yuán-xīn, the攀緣心 or object-grasping mind) as one's own nature;

it is precisely what is called "falsely identifying the four great elements as the form of one's own body" and "falsely identifying the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects as the nature of one's own mind."
This is taken as the root of beginningless birth and death because one fails to realize that the mind and its objects are entirely devoid of self-nature;
this very essence is the eternally abiding true mind, a body of pure and luminous nature.

Therefore, when ordinary beings give rise to craving and attachment, grasping at the conditions of the six sense-objects within the triple world, it becomes the root of birth and death through segmentation. When those of the Two Vehicles give rise to revulsion...

If a Bodhisattva abandons both extremes and separately clings to the object of the Middle Way—the rational nature (*dharmatā*)—this becomes the root of *parinirmita-vaśavarti* (transformative) birth-and-death. Enlightenment (*bodhi*) is the fruit of the four kinds of wisdom-virtue;
Nirvana is the fruit of the three kinds of cessation-virtue; and the primordially pure essence is the fundamental nature itself.

Purity does not depend upon cultivation or realization to become pure. "The consciousnesses are each precisely aware" refers to the eight consciousnesses being individually and precisely cognizant, which is the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-verifying portion).

"Original luminosity" generally refers to the one mind that serves as the basis for the eight consciousnesses, which is the *svasaṃvitti-svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-verifying portion of the self-verifying portion).
However, this does not mean that the one mind is divided and partitioned into eight separate *svasaṃvitti-svasaṃvittibhāgas*.

Nor is it the case that the eight consciousnesses share only a single *svasaṃvittivijñāna* (self-witnessing division). This is because the essence of the mind is free from faults, transcends all distinctions, and is inconceivable;
this very body of primordial luminosity pervades the eight consciousnesses, and each consciousness possesses it in its entirety as its own self-witnessing division.
It is like eight people together gazing at a single full moon as they travel along.
In each of the eight directions, there is a complete moon; as it follows the eight people, it is neither divided into eight parts nor is it a single moon seen by all together.

Reflect on this, reflect on this: it can give rise to various conditions, namely, based upon this self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) and the realization of self-realization (*svasaṃvitsaṃvedana*), the two divisions of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the appearance-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) are established.
The seeing-part possesses four conditions, namely, the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and so forth.

The immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) possess two aspects, namely the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition.
That which is omitted by these conditions refers to this self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) and the cognition of self-cognition (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti*).

Since the entire substance manifests as the illusory duality of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), its own essence becomes concealed, just as when the entire substance of sesame seeds is extracted [the husk remains].
Once it has become a rope, people see it only as a rope and no longer regard it as hemp;
yet, since you have cited self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) as the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), there is nothing that is not self-realization within that seeing-aspect.
Just as when hemp is taken to be a rope, the rope is itself the hemp, so now we point directly to this very self-realization of the seeing-aspect as the original state of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
Because its essence is pure, it is said to be "that which is left behind by conditions.

The subsequent passage states, "This seeing and these conditions are fundamentally the wondrously pure and luminous essence of Bodhi," which is identical to this point. Referring to the eighth consciousness, it is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom;
Bodhi is the fundamentally pure essence. Referring to the seventh consciousness, it is the Wisdom of Equality.
The primordial pure essence of the sixth consciousness refers to the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wonderful observation wisdom);
the primordial pure essence of the first five consciousnesses refers to the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (performance-of-duty wisdom).

These four wisdoms of *bodhi* are likewise inherently possessed; they differ from the provisional teachings of the *lakṣaṇa-vāda* school, which claim they are produced by causes that give rise to them.

The "pervasively imagined" (parikalpita) refers to the fact that the self-nature of the self and phenomena is fundamentally empty and utterly unobtainable, like the absence of the nature of a snake upon a rope;

this is the inherently pure Nirvana, the primordially pure essence. The "dependent" (paratantra) refers to the illusory ten realms of existence, which are mere provisional names with immeasurable distinctions, like hemp that can be made into a rope; this is the Nirvana of skillful means, the primordially pure essence.
The finger is the perfected manifestation, while the inherent dharmas are entirely True Suchness; the rope is the hemp, which is the inherently pure Nirvana and the primordially pure essence.

Thus, these two kinds of roots are not separate from the One Mind. To awaken to and see that the perceived characteristics are merely self-realization is like realizing that the rope is hemp—this is Bodhi and Nirvana.
To be deluded regarding the perceived characteristics and take them to be self and dharmas is [the state of ignorance].
For example, seeing a snake in a rope constitutes the very root of birth and death;

therefore it is said that although one abandons this fundamental luminosity, though one acts all day long, one remains unaware and enters the various realms of existence by way of error. This is the most essential point of this sutra and the secret instruction for the transmission of the mind from the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The old commentaries mistakenly identify the "clinging mind" (*pān-yuan xin*) solely with the six consciousnesses, and thus insist on its destruction.

If one eliminates the six consciousnesses until they are exhausted, then within the fruit [of enlightenment], what could possibly serve as the substance of the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (the wisdom of wondrous observation) and the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (the wisdom of accomplishing tasks)?

This is truly lamentable. To single out the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-ghana*) specifically as the eighth consciousness and insist on using it exclusively as the substance [of these two wisdoms] is for a person of delusion—whose root of birth and death has lasted for immeasurable kalpas—to mistake that very thing for their original self.

Second, it is deplorable; how much more so now that the text and its meaning are inherently clear and manifest, yet people offer a flurry of false interpretations that misrepresent and deceive the core of the Sūtra—what is the purpose of such actions?
Second, a detailed demonstration that the essence of the mind differs from false attachments, in four parts:

first, a repeated censure of false conceptualizations as not being the true mind; second, a direct demonstration that the true mind possesses an essence; third, a detailed clarification that discrimination has no inherent nature.
Fourth, a general refutation of long-standing misconceptions. First:
"Ānanda, if you now wish to know the path of *śamatha* and desire to transcend birth and death, I shall now question you further.
At that moment, the Tathāgata raised his golden arm, bent his five fingers into a fist, and said to Ānanda: "Do you see this? "I do, World-Honored One," Ānanda replied.
The Buddha asked, "What do you see? Ānanda replied, "I see the Tathāgata raising his arm and bending his fingers into a radiant fist that illuminates my mind and eyes.
The Buddha asked, "By means of what do you see this? Ānanda replied, "Together with the great assembly, I see it with my eyes.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Now answer me: when the Tathāgata bends his fingers into a radiant fist..."

"I shall illuminate your mind and eyes for you. Your eyes can see; what do you take to be the mind? When the Buddha pointed his fist at Ānanda, Ānanda said, "The Tathāgata is now inquiring about the location of the mind.
As I use my mind to investigate and pursue it, that which is capable of this investigation—I take that to be the mind.
The Buddha said, "Stop, Ānanda! This is not your mind. Ānanda was startled; he left his seat and joined his palms in reverence.
Rising, he addressed the Buddha: "This is not my mind; what should it be called? The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This is a false appearance and perception of external objects that deludes your true nature. From your beginningless past until this present life, you have mistaken a thief for your own son, thereby losing your original constancy and undergoing the cycle of rebirth."

The false appearances and conceptualizations regarding the preceding sense-objects (*viṣaya*) are precisely what is meant by "the reflections conditioned by the six objects" within Perfect Enlightenment.
The six objects are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of consciousness; these [reflections] are merely the shadows of the six objects appearing within the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect).

Since they are not even the *darśana-bhāga* of consciousness itself, how much less could they be the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) or the cognition of that self-cognition? Yet, one mistakenly identifies them as such.
The mind is not only not the true mind, but it is also not the deluded mind; therefore, it is directly rebuked by saying, "This is not your mind.
As for the seeing-part of consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is luminously penetrating, without substance or form;
although it is entirely within the realm of delusion, there is no such reflection to be found therein. Thus, the subsequent text says: "It contains and exhales..."
How could the ten directions have a fixed location? Thus we know that what Ānanda reckons as "the capacity to infer" is in reality merely the shadow of that which is inferred;
it is certainly not the true inferrer, for the true inferrer has no substantial essence or characteristics that can be apprehended.
Later generations, failing to understand this, point to this conditioned shadow as being the six consciousnesses.
Furthermore, they do not know that the six consciousnesses are profound. Second, this correctly demonstrates that the True Mind has a substantial body.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I am the beloved younger brother of the Buddha; because my heart loves the Buddha, he caused me to leave the household life.
Why would my mind seek only to make offerings to the Tathāgata, even if it were to travel through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to serve all Buddhas?"
"Virtuous friends, it is by means of this mind that one gives rise to great courage and performs all those difficult dharmic practices;
even if one were to slander the Dharma and forever lose their roots of goodness, it would still be because of this mind.
If what I have thus revealed were not the mind, then I would be without a mind, identical to earth or wood. Apart from this awareness, there is nothing else. How could the Tathāgata say..."

"This is not the mind; I am truly terrified, and there is not one among this great assembly who does not harbor doubt. I pray that you will deign to show great compassion and reveal what we have not yet understood.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause the minds of Ānanda and the great assembly to enter the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena), stroked the crown of Ānanda’s head while seated upon the lion throne and addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata has constantly taught all..."
All that arises from the Dharma is but a manifestation of the mind; all causes and effects, worlds, and even the finest motes of dust, derive their substance from the mind.

Ānanda, if one were to investigate the fundamental source of every single thing within all these worlds—even down to blades of grass, leaves, threads, and knots—they would all possess an inherent nature.
Even empty space has its name and appearance, let alone this pure, wondrously pure, and luminous clarity.
Since the mind-nature is itself all minds, how could it lack a substance?
Ānanda doubted that the mind was non-existent, yet the Tathāgata answered that the mind possesses substance.

Because he had long clung to the notion of "conditioned shadows," the Buddha suddenly stripped away his head [of this delusion], abruptly severing his doubt; how could he have imagined that this very [mind] would be subject to annihilation?

Furthermore, can one attain the cessation [of afflictions]? Entering the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)—the character "entering" refers to cultivation and realization;
"non-arising dharmas" refers to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); and "patience" refers to the stages and positions. The nature of non-arising is without distinction from beginning to end;
yet, in terms of entering and in terms of patience, it begins with the stage of names and culminates in the ultimate. This is the first.
The passage that thoroughly reveals the nature is subtle as the Middle Way Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), pure as liberation (*vimukti*), and luminous as prajñā;
thus, the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*) may be said to be presented in its entirety.
"Nature is the nature of all minds" means that it is the fundamental nature pervading all minds. This is explained in detail in the third section.
It is without intrinsic nature.
If you maintain that the nature apprehended by the conceptualization of vitarka and vicāra must necessarily be the mind, then this mind should exist as a distinct,
complete entity apart from all objects of the senses— form, odor, taste, and touch— and apart from all activities, just like your own self at present.
To listen to my Dharma is to have discrimination arising from sound;

even if you were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, cognition, and awareness, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness, it would still be a mere shadow of discrimination regarding the dharma-dusts. I am not commanding you to hold this as being non-mind;
rather, you must subtly examine the mind itself: if there is a nature of discrimination that exists apart from the external objects, then that is your true mind.
"If the nature of discrimination is devoid of objects and lacks substance, then these objects before one are merely shadows of discrimination;
if those objects are not permanent and perish when they change, then this mind would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.

In that case, your Dharma-body would be subject to annihilation—who then could cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas? At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly fell silent, overcome with self-reproach.

These two sections, through the method of concession and refutation, clarify that discrimination lacks intrinsic nature. The first sixteen characters constitute a general restatement of the attachment;
"those who are stubbornly attached and do not relinquish" refers to those who cling tenaciously.

The phrase "that which is known" (the object of cognition) is intended to reveal that although what they grasp as the objective reflection (ālambana-pratibimba) considers itself to be the subject capable of knowing, in reality it is merely that which is known.
This is not truly able to fully comprehend; this mind should then proceed to that which has a distinct nature of its own. This is the first point of concession.
Even as you are now, up to the point of discerning reflected images—this is the first point of refutation.

Not only is the discernment at the time of listening to the Dharma entirely dependent upon sound, but even if the six sense organs do not engage with external objects and one internally maintains a state of profound stillness...
