This state of pure leisure and vastness is still merely an internal object (dharmaviṣaya) perceived by the solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Thus, from the *anāgamya* concentration up to the *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*, all are subsumed under the category of "reflected images of conceptualization regarding dharmas" (*dharmavikalpa-pratibimba*).

At present, those who attain realization through darkness mistakenly claim this to be their "original face" or an event prior to the void kalpa (*śūnyakalpa*), even reaching back to the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvara Buddha.
"Pointing upward toward the nostrils is also utterly foolish. Next, "I do not command you; it is that which reaches the 'True'—that is your mind.

This is the second instance of speaking with indulgence. Since I have already refused to allow you to mistakenly take this [discrimination] for the mind, yet I also do not command you to grasp it as being non-mind—because there are no phenomena apart from the mind, even these discriminations of dust-like reflections are themselves merely mind.
Because things that appear are established as entities by the causal mind, to grasp them as being the mind itself is like mistaking a thief for one's own son;

to grasp them as not being the mind is like abandoning the waves while seeking the water—both are impossible. If, below, one discriminates according to the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), this constitutes the second refutation:
if one resolutely grasps these as being the mind, then the mind would conversely become annihilated, and the cultivation of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) would be undermined.
Since both [the subject and object] are proven to be unobtainable, this is why the great assembly does not know their whereabouts and remains silent, overcome with self-discomfiture.
Fourth, a general refutation of long-standing erroneous attachments.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "All those practitioners in the world who have currently attained the nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) yet fail to achieve the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) or the state of an Arhat, do so because they cling to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistaking them for reality.
Therefore, although you now possess great learning (*bahuśruta*), you have not attained the fruit of sainthood."

The nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*) consist of the four dhyānas, the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya*), and the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) as the ninth.

Of these, the first eight attainments are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*). By means of the pure contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*) from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one is able to cause the sensation and perception associated with the defiled *manas* to be suppressed and cease functioning;
therefore, it is called the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception. This is the third fruit for the noble ones (*ārya*).

To introduce the subject: Kātyāyana and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa are the names of two non-Buddhist teachers. In Sanskrit, *nirvāṇa* is translated here as "extinction" (*mie-du*).

The nature of our present single thought of seeing and hearing is detached from names and transcends forms; therefore, it is called "wondrous" (*miao*). It is profoundly penetrating and vacuous yet spiritual;

therefore, it is called "luminous" (*ming*). Its substance is free from falsehood and delusion; therefore, it is called "true" (*zhen*). Its nature is free from admixture and defilement; therefore, it is called "refined" (*jing*).
Because these four meanings are united in an inconceivable manner, it is called the "wondrous mind" (*miaoxin*). As for "form," this refers to the eleven categories of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*).

Right now, it is manifest and fully accomplished, without remainder and without deficiency. Why do you all refuse to recognize it, even though it is directly before your faces?
Having lost it, one instead takes from within this fundamental awakened essence merely a single point of deluded emotion;
thus, this ocean of original enlightened nature becomes obscured and turns into a stubborn void. Within that empty obscurity, darkness coagulates into illusory form.
This illusory form mingles with deluded emotion and discursive thought, and according to whatever forms are conceived, [one clings to them].
This body is a collection of delusive thoughts; it gathers the vital energy within, causing it to sway and fluctuate as it pursues external objects, racing and surging forth.
One calls this state of confused agitation the "nature of the mind," not realizing that it is in fact not the nature of the mind.
Once one is deluded by this and takes it to be the mind, one will certainly become confused, thinking it resides within the physical body.

One does not know that this physical body, extending outward to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, are all objects within the wondrously luminous true mind of my present single thought.
"In a state of confused turmoil" means that because one is deluded regarding the wondrously luminous mind, the entire substance becomes a state of stupor;
because one is deluded regarding the wondrous nature of luminosity, the entire substance is in turmoil; and because one is deluded regarding the fundamental wondrous nature of the mind.
You take the delusions pervading your entire being as the interior of your physical body;
you do not know that you are mistakenly identifying your own state of confusion as the mind, yet the perfectly wondrous, luminous mind manifest before you has never been confused.

You mistakenly identify your own state of agitation as the mind, yet the precious, luminous, wondrous nature manifest before you has never been agitated. You mistakenly identify what is within your body as the mind...
The fundamental nature of the mind, which is originally wondrous and sublime, has never been within;

examine the meaning of the preceding passage, "The blind man sees darkness," and even the subsequent passage, "Awakening is not among the eye-diseases," and you shall understand this for yourself. It is like the great ocean:
although its entire body forms bubbles, how could the substance of the ocean ever diminish? This refers to what the Tathāgata pointed out above as being present before us.
The "seeing of the nature" mentioned previously refers directly to the entire body of the great ocean;
yet what Ānanda currently conceives as seeing and hearing must be neither produced nor extinguished, and it remains confined within the body, just like the substance of a single bubble.
To recognize a single bubble as such is already a state of delusion; to point to this one bubble and call it the entirety of the vast ocean—how could this not be delusion within delusion?
To be deluded regarding this is to have one's head and tail inverted to such an extreme that it is like my hanging my hand downward;
though there is nothing diminished thereby, the whole world considers it to be upside down—how pitiable this is!

However, the meaning of being deluded within enlightenment is somewhat difficult to understand, so I shall now further explain it through two points: first, in relation to beginningless ignorance; second, in relation to...
Observing and illuminating what is present, first regarding that which is beginningless: the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) is termed "awakening to True Suchness" (*tathatā*).
Yet, because it does not maintain its own nature, unenlightened thought arises and ignorance (*avidyā*) comes into being; this is termed "delusion within awakening.

Based on the clarity of consciousness, an objective realm is established, whereby the self-substance transforms into the characteristic of stubborn emptiness (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*); thus it is said that "obscuration becomes emptiness," for the clarity of awareness becomes the dullness of emptiness.

When mutual dependence gives rise to movement, the wind-element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*) comes into being; this extends to the full manifestation of the four great elements as explained in the fourth fascicle.

Therefore, it is said that by binding darkness one forms the delusive conception of form (*rūpa-vikalpa*), and by grasping a portion of the four great elements, one takes them as one's own body, thereby giving rise to the distinctions among the twelve classes of beings.
Thus, it is said that the characteristics of thought constitute the body; all else may be understood accordingly.

Second, regarding those present before us: if, for even a single moment, the wisdom of contemplation is clear and distinct, then the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and sublime luminous mind—the wondrous nature of the jewel-like clarity—will manifest in its entirety as it truly is;
this is called "awakening. At this time, no characteristics of space, the four great elements, body, or mind can be apprehended.
If, for even a single moment, one loses the illumination of contemplation, then immediately the entire substance reverts to becoming [the world of delusion].
Through delusion, emptiness and form, body and mind suddenly manifest as an illusion—this is what is meant by "the obscuration of darkness becomes emptiness," and so forth.
Furthermore, one should know that if there were no beginningless ignorance (*anādikāla-avidyā*), there would be no present single thought-moment;

and if one were separated from the present single thought-moment, there would likewise be no separate beginningless ignorance. Thus, these two meanings constitute but a single meaning; it simply requires...
Ānanda and the great assembly should recognize the nature of seeing and hearing present before them, merely ensuring they do not fall into deluded sentiments;
thus, the wild mind will suddenly cease, and this cessation is itself Bodhi.

When one thought-moment accords with this, one is a Buddha—how could there be any further accumulation of beginningless ignorance from which to seek out and sever its locus? This is something students must know.
V. Clarifying that the nature of seeing has nothing to return to by means of pointing and indicating. Part one: The request; part two: The instruction. Now, the first:
Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction, wept and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying: "Although I have received the Buddha’s..."
Thus, through this wondrous sound, I have awakened to the wondrously luminous mind—the fundamental ground of the heart that is originally perfect and eternally abiding.

Yet, as I contemplate the Buddha’s present preaching of the Dharma, I perceive it with my conditioned mind; I merely obtain this mind and do not yet dare to recognize it as my own fundamental ground of the heart.
I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim his perfect voice to uproot the source of my doubts and lead me back to the Unsurpassed Way.
Generally speaking, if one has long clung to the shadows of conditions and cannot let them go entirely, one will certainly be unable to directly realize the wondrous, luminous nature of seeing.
This is the common ailment of those who merely listen to the Dharma without reflecting back upon the nature of the mind;
because they refuse to reflect upon the nature of the mind, they continue to reckon that the conditioned mind is truly capable of hearing.
If one does not know that the dharmas are but shadows of conditions and lack intrinsic nature, one will certainly lack the functional capacity to hear the Dharma;

that which is able to hear the Dharma is precisely the power and function of the fundamental mind-ground. Second, the detailed exposition has two parts: first, a general clarification by means of analogy;
second, a specific differentiation according to its essence. Now, the first part.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you and the others still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind, this Dharma is itself a condition and not the realization of the Dharma-nature.
It is like a person pointing at the moon with their finger to show it to another; that person should look at the moon because of the finger.
If, however, they gaze at the finger and take it to be the substance of the moon, would such a person not only lose sight of the lunar disk, but also lose the finger? Why is this?"
Since that which is pointed to is intended to be the bright moon, you have not only lost the finger, but furthermore do not recognize brightness or darkness. Why is this?
Because you take the substance of the finger itself to be the nature of the moon’s brightness; thus, you fail to discern the two natures of brightness and darkness.
You are just like this.
The meaning is this: the mind that takes the reflected image as its object is clearly incapable of hearing the Dharma, yet you still falsely imagine that it can hear.

Since you falsely reckon that the mind taking the reflection as its object can hear, then even the Dharma I have preached becomes a mere sensory object (*viṣaya*) rather than the attainment of the *dharmatā*.
It is like a person looking at a finger who ultimately fails to see the moon. [End of section on] the "knot."
If you say that you are also like this, it should be reconciled with the Dharma as follows: Now the Buddha has pointed out your nature of seeing to you by means of sound;
because of my preaching the Dharma, you ought to turn back and contemplate your own nature of seeing.
If you instead discriminate the sounds of the Dharma and take them to be the nature of seeing, you will not only lose your nature of seeing, but you will also lose—
Why is this? Because one takes the sound of the Dharma as the nature of seeing.
Not only does one lose sight of this Dharma-sound, but one also fails to recognize who possesses cognition and who lacks it. Why is this?

It is because one takes the reflected image conditioned by the Dharma-sound to be that which possesses cognition and is able to hear the Dharma—just as if one were to take a finger to be light while the true [hearing] is actually listening.
As for the wondrous clarity of the Dharma, the mind conversely does not yet dare to recognize it as its own fundamental ground, like taking the moon to be darkness;

would this not be an error? Herein, the moon is used generally as a metaphor for the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*), the pointing finger as a metaphor for the sound of the Dharma, and the reflection pointed at as a metaphor for the conditioned mind (*pratyaya-citta*).
Second, distinguishing the two based on their essential natures: first, distinguishing that the conditioned mind can be returned.

As in the observation of the finger and its reflection, these two demonstrations show that the nature of seeing has no place of return, like the moon in the sky. Regarding the first of these two [sections], there are two parts:
first, a proximate analysis based on sound to clarify the absence of intrinsic nature; second, an extensive examination through various phenomena to demonstrate what may have a place of return.
This is the first part.

If you consider this discriminating mind that perceives the sounds of my teaching as being your own mind, then this mind should inherently possess the nature of discrimination even apart from those discriminating sounds (only then could it be called your mind).
It is like a traveler staying overnight at an inn who departs after a brief halt and never remains permanently;
yet the innkeeper, who stays on without ever leaving, is called the master of the inn. This [discriminating sound] is likewise.
Furthermore, if this were truly your mind, it would have no place to go;
why is it that now, upon leaving the sound, it lacks the nature of discernment (and thus does not resemble the person at the marketplace)?
Of these, the first two phrases are concessive statements; the following passage beginning with "Just as below" provides an analogy;

and the passage beginning with "This is also like this below" applies the principle to the case at hand to refute it. Second, [the text] extensively examines various phenomena through analysis to demonstrate that they are subject to return.
This is not merely a matter of the discrimination of sound or the discrimination of mind; my appearance is detached from all forms and characteristics, possessing a nature free from discrimination.

Thus, even down to the point where all discrimination is entirely absent—neither form nor emptiness, like Kauśika and others who mistake it for the obscure Primal Truth (Tattva)—if one is detached from the conditions of all dharmas and possesses a nature free from discrimination, then your own mental nature will each have its respective place of return. How can it be the master?
This is an ultimate statement that all conceptual discriminations lack intrinsic nature and are all subject to reversion;
they must never be mistakenly taken as a self. Continuing from the preceding words:

this is not only the case for the mind that discriminates based on sound—it has no intrinsic nature at all—but it is also true for your mind that discriminates my thirty-two marks and wondrous countenance.
Apart from all forms and appearances, there is likewise no further nature of discrimination;

and so it continues even unto the mind that discriminates odors, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas—apart from those odors, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas, there is likewise no further nature of discrimination.

Even if one were to discriminate them, none of these constitute a realm that is neither form nor emptiness. That which the Kauśīnāgaras and others are deluded about, taking to be the "Dark Principle" (Tattva), is entirely non-existent.
Furthermore, it is precisely by means of this *pradhāna* (the principle of primordial matter) that one takes phenomena as objects;
apart from this *pradhāna* as an objective condition, there is no further nature of discrimination. From this it follows that when one discriminates sound, one returns it to sound;
when one discriminates form, one returns it to form; and even when one discriminates *pradhāna*, one returns it to *pradhāna*. You—
If you wish to take this discrimination to be the nature of the mind, then each aspect of your mind-nature has its own place of return;
how, then, can it be the master? This passage must be interpreted in this way for it to have a valid foundation;

the old interpretation erroneously takes the four characters "du wu fen bie" (all discrimination is non-existent) to mean "all discrimination is non-existent," and mistakenly claims that since discrimination is refuted, [the nature of the mind] is simultaneously established.

To refute non-discrimination while failing to understand what fault lies in not knowing non-discrimination, and then abruptly refuting it—furthermore, how could the *tattva* (ultimate principle) ever belong to that which is non-discriminative, since it is actually subsumed under the delusions of discriminative views?

Such a failure in logic and textual coherence is lamentable and regrettable. Now, you claim that the two characters "entirely" (*dou wu*) refer to the object of discrimination, rather than being form (*rūpa*).
The four characters "not empty" (fei kong) are themselves entirely without commentary; this "neither form nor emptiness" is truly the realm of the self-mind’s direct perception (*svasaṃvedana*).
Because those heterodox outsiders, through their false views and discrimination, do not realize that all is but mind, they obscure it and call it the "Dark Principle" (*tattva*).
Second, showing that the nature of seeing has no place of return, like the moon in the sky; this has two parts, the first of which is as follows:
The second part, the formal instruction on the absence of anything to which [the mind] returns, consists of two sections: the request for instruction and the actual teaching.

Herein is the first. Ānanda said: "If my mind-nature has various things to which it returns, then why does the Tathāgata say that the wondrous, luminous, original mind has nothing to which it returns?
I pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me."

Second, the correct demonstration that there is no returning, which has three parts: first, using the analogy of the moon to reveal the essence of the Dharma; second, using that which can return to demonstrate that which does not return;
third, concluding that this non-returning is the original mind. Now, the first part.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "Furthermore, you see me; this essence of seeing is the fundamental source of clarity. Although this seeing is not the wondrous, pure, and luminous mind, it is like a second moon—it is not a reflection of the moon.
This directly points to the present essence of seeing as being like the moon in the sky, unlike the discrimination that takes sensory objects as its conditions."
The moon is but a reflection; one merely takes the act of seeing as the "seer" and the Buddha as the "seen.

Within this single entity, one falsely creates the two aspects of the seeing-subject and the seen-object, just as one who presses upon the eyes falsely sees two moons. One cannot immediately call this the wondrously pure and brilliant mind.
If one realizes that the subject and object are non-dual and there is only the single true mind, then the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is directly perceived.
The substance [of the nature] is left without remainder. Second, by means of that which can be returned, one reveals that which cannot be returned.

You should listen attentively; I shall now show you the ground of non-returning. Ānanda, when this great lecture hall is opened wide toward the east and the sun rises in the sky, there is bright radiance;
yet at midnight during a dark month, when clouds and mist shroud it in gloom, it returns once more.
When darkness fills the gaps between doors and windows, one again perceives the openings; when looking through the spaces between walls, one again observes the obstructions;

in places of distinct differentiation (i.e., distinctions), one again perceives the conditions; within the stubborn void, there is everywhere the nature of emptiness; when the earth and dust are thick and turbid, the appearance is obscured and dark;
when the sky clears and the mists subside, one again observes the purity. Ānanda, you have all witnessed these various transformations.

"Regarding these manifested forms, I shall now each return them to their original causes. What are these original causes? Ānanda, these various transformations: clarity returns to the sun; why is this?
Without the sun there would be no clarity, for clarity fundamentally depends on the sun as its cause; therefore, it returns to the sun. Darkness returns to the black moon;
penetration returns to doors and windows; obstruction returns to walls and eaves; and conditions return to discrimination (which also carries the sense of differentiation)."

When the turbid void returns to emptiness, the swirling dust returns to the earth, and the clear brightness returns to a cloudless sky, then all that exists within the world does not, in total, transcend these categories.
You now perceive these eight kinds of objects; as for the clarity of your faculty of seeing, toward which of these would you wish it to return? Why is this?
If it were to return to brightness, then when it is not bright, there would be no further perception of darkness. Yet, even now, though there is both brightness and darkness...
Although various distinctions are perceived, [in reality] no distinction is seen; how could there be a return [to the original state]?
Seeing no distinction precisely reveals that it differs from the conditions of the eight kinds of objects; therefore, it can never return.
The three fetters do not revert to this original mind.

All things that can be returned are naturally not you; as for that which cannot be returned by you, if it is not you, then who is it? Thus you should know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure.
You have merely become deluded and confused, losing your fundamental nature and undergoing the cycle of birth and death, where you are constantly adrift and submerged.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called "One Who Is Compassionate.
As for what is said regarding the eight kinds of objective conditions that can be returned:
since they are naturally not you, this luminous nature of seeing cannot be something returned by you. It is neither your own fundamental original mind-ground; then whose is it?
Ah! Because this mind is inconceivable, it is fundamentally wondrous; because this mind can perceive the eight kinds [of consciousness], it is fundamentally luminous;

because this mind is not the eight kinds themselves, it is fundamentally pure. Yet now you are deluded and distressed by yourself, and instead of daring to recognize it as your original, fundamental ground of the mind, you have lost that foundation and undergone cyclic existence, wandering pointlessly and drowning in the sea of birth and death.
This is very much like the case of the deluded Śāṇakavapā who mistook his own head for its reflection;

is this not deeply pitiable? Sixth, by means of pervasiveness, it is shown that the nature of seeing is not a material object. Part One: Showing the meaning of non-differentiation. Part Two: Showing the meaning of having neither small nor large dimensions.
Master Jiaoguang divides this into two sections, or alternatively, into three sections; all of these are due to a failure to understand.
Because Ānanda’s question was based on a specific point, the answers themselves were largely superficial; moreover, dividing them into three sections is particularly far-fetched and laughable.
Of the first two parts—consisting of the initial question and the subsequent answer—the first is as follows.
Ānanda said, "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has no place to return, how can I know it to be my true nature?
You should know that at this time Ānanda had still not entirely abandoned the mind that pursues external conditions;

therefore, while listening to the sound of the Buddha’s Dharma, he was unable to directly turn back and contemplate his own nature, instead allowing the sound of the Dharma to transform into a distinct, luminous object before him.
This state of luminous clarity manifest before one’s eyes is called "seeing one's nature. Therefore, I dare not claim it to be my true nature;
I do not know if this segment of brilliant, luminous clarity might be a material object rather than the seeing-nature itself.
Thus, the Buddha refuted it by stating it is "not a thing. In the second answer, there are three parts: first, regarding... [text truncated]
1. Delusion and enlightenment are shown to be non-differentiated yet differentiated; 2. Differentiation and non-differentiation are shown in terms of self and other;
3. The true nature of the seeing-nature is shown to be not a material object.
Now, for the first [point]: The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "I now ask you: at present, you have not yet attained the untainted purity, though you rely upon the Buddha's spiritual power."
While Aniruddha attained unimpeded vision within the first dhyāna and could see Jambudvīpa as clearly as observing an *āmala* fruit in the palm of his hand,
the various bodhisattvas could behold hundreds of thousands of worlds and the pure lands as numerous as atoms throughout the ten directions of the Tathāgatas,
seeing everything without exception; yet the clear-sighted vision of ordinary sentient beings does not extend beyond a mere inch.

Aniruddha—here translated as "Without Poverty"—was foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), for he could see through the great trichiliocosm as clearly as one views the fruit of a *jambu* tree in the palm of one's hand.
The *āmra* (mango) does not exist in this region; it is sometimes translated as "difficult to distinguish," because it is hard to differentiate between its ripeness and unripeness.

The meaning of this passage is to reveal that the nature of seeing is fundamentally one, yet the distinction between delusion and awakening is as vast as heaven and earth. Nevertheless, regarding delusion...
Although awakenings differ, the seeing-nature is non-dual. To see clearly within a mere inch is itself the seeing-nature that exhausts the entirety of the lands.
It is like a single spark of fire that can set an entire field ablaze; yet, alas, sentient beings confine themselves through their own deluded emotions.
This seeing-nature is precisely the true nature inherently possessed by each and every one. (2)
In terms of the distinctions between self and others, they are both distinct and non-distinct.

Ānanda, consider this: when you and I observe the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings dwell, surveying everything across the waters, the land, and the air, although there are various forms—some obscured and some bright—they are all nothing other than the obstructions left behind by the discrimination of external objects. You should...
Regarding this discrimination between self and other, I shall now lead you to discern within these perceptions: who is your true self-substance, and what are the external objects?

Ānanda, exhaustively trace the source of your vision from the palaces of the sun and moon; these are material objects and not you. Proceeding as far as the Seven Golden Mountains, observe them thoroughly and completely;
though they possess various kinds of light, they too are material objects and not you. Gradually continue your observation to the rising clouds and the flying birds.
Flying winds stir up dust; trees, mountains, rivers, grasses, weeds, humans, and livestock—all these things are not you, Ānanda.
Although the natures of all these things, whether near or far, differ from one another, they are equally illuminated by your own pure essence of vision.
Thus, while the various categories of objects possess their own distinctions, the nature of seeing has no difference. This subtle, wondrous, and luminous clarity is truly your own nature of seeing.
Those who differentiate between self and other regard objects as "other" and not "self," while they view their own vision as "self" and not an "object.
When it says "exhausting the source of your vision," this refers, for the time being, to the extent and boundaries of that visual essence (*darśana-vijñāna*).
The meaning of this passage precisely reveals that those various things which possess distinctions are "objects" and "others," whereas the pure visual essence is neither.
That which is without differentiation is neither a thing nor something else; it is your own true nature.
This answers his question, "How can one know that this is my true nature? Third, it correctly demonstrates that the seeing-nature is not a thing.
If you see this object, then you should also be able to see my seeing. If we see the same thing, that is called "seeing me.
When I am not seeing, why do you not see the place where I do not see? If you see my non-seeing, then it is naturally not the characteristic of that non-seeing.
If you do not see the ground of my non-seeing, then it is naturally not a material object; how then could it not be yours?
Furthermore, at this moment when you see an object, since you have seen the object, the object must also see you.

If the essential natures of subject and object were thus intermingled, then you, I, and all the world would fail to be established as distinct entities. Ānanda, if it is you who see, then you are not me;
since the nature of seeing is all-pervasive, if it is not you, then who is it? Why do you doubt your own true nature? This nature is yours.
"Not grasping at the unreal self while seeking the real":
this is a direct anticipation of Ānanda’s internal error—mistaking that which is "bright and numinous" for the nature of seeing—and thus it is stepped upon and refuted.
The text has three sections; first, from "If seeing were an object" downward, [it uses] seeing...
Since each and every object should be capable of being refuted, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, you now" uses the faculty of seeing— which, like objects,
is also capable of being refuted— to refute it. The section beginning with "Ānanda, when you see" combines both meanings and concludes by attributing them to the person concerned.
The meaning of the initial passage is as follows:

if this seeing were not your own nature but were instead a distinct entity, then since your seeing would be one entity and the Buddha’s seeing would likewise be another entity, you should also be able to see the Buddha’s seeing.
Furthermore, if you were merely seeing the same object before you as the Buddha does, that alone could be called "seeing."
Regarding the Buddha’s vision: when one sees the Buddha’s vision, one has already seen the locus of that vision;
why then would one not also see the locus where the Buddha does not see? This is because he erroneously claims that "seeing" is a discrete entity;
thus, when the Buddha emits this entity, he perceives it placed before his eyes, and when the Buddha withdraws this entity...
Furthermore, you should see that they are all gathered together in one place.
Moreover, if you falsely claim that there is a Buddha whom you do not see in certain places, this is merely a state of non-seeing within your own field of vision;
it is naturally not a state of non-seeing within the sphere of that Tathāgata. How could you possibly take the state of non-seeing conceived by your deluded mind and call it such?
Is this not the mark of the Tathāgata’s non-seeing? Having thus proceeded through successive stages of refutation, the conclusion is shown:
"If you truly do not see the Buddha and the ground of seeing, then this nature of seeing is naturally not some distinct entity characterized by brilliance and clarity;
how could it not be your own nature? The meaning of the subsequent passage is further that, if it were delusory...

If you reckon that the seer and the object are one thing, then the object should likewise be able to see; thus, at the present moment when you see an object, since you see the object, the object would also see you.

The substance of the object and the nature of seeing would then be in a state of chaotic confusion—unknowing who is the agent and who is the object, who is self and who is other, and what constitutes the primary retribution and what the secondary environment—and this would destroy conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If this were the case regarding the characteristics of dharmas, then you, I, and all the world would fail to be established; how could such a principle even exist?
This is because Ānanda is entirely deluded regarding the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) and mistakes it for a single entity; therefore, it can be refuted by this [analysis].
If one realizes that everything is but mind, then object and wisdom illuminate each other, thereby establishing the profound manifestation of the fourfold logical gate (*catuṣkoṭi-dvāra*).
In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the characteristics of conventional phenomena (*saṃvṛti-dharma*) remain unimpaired.

Regarding the third passage, following the conclusion of the preceding refutation, it formally concludes by saying: "Ānanda, if when you see, it is merely your seeing and not the Buddha's seeing, then this nature of seeing is pervasive;
it is not your true nature—then to whom else does it belong? How can you say [it belongs to you]?"
I suspect that while your true nature is inherently present within you, you do not regard it as real, but instead seek the truth through my words—why is this so?
Second, demonstrating the meaning of there being no distinction between large and small: first, the inquiry; second, the explanatory response.

First: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing is necessarily mine and not that of others, then when I and the Tathāgata were observing the Palace of the Supreme Treasury of the Four Heavenly Kings and dwelling in the palaces of the sun and moon, this seeing was all-encompassing and pervasive throughout the Sahā world; yet now it has receded."
Returning to the vihāra, I saw only the monastery; my pure mind beheld only the halls and the corridors.
World-Honored One, this vision of mine is such that its substance is originally all-pervasive throughout the entire realm, yet now within this room it fills only this single room.
Is it that this vision has contracted from large to small? Or is it that the walls and buildings have constricted it, causing it to be severed? I do not know the meaning of this.
I pray that you will bestow your vast compassion and expound this for me.
This is because Ānanda, in his mind, still takes that which is "brightly manifest and spiritually luminous" to be the nature of seeing;
therefore, although the Tathāgata has repeatedly defined and attributed its true nature, he remains in constant doubt and does not dare to recognize it. It must be so.
I am not anyone other than you—this statement follows from the preceding remark, "If it is not you, then who is it?
Even at this point, [Ananda] still refuses to recognize it as himself; therefore, the Buddha rebukes him for mistaking his own self for an external object.
Thus, we know that the preceding section and this one together reveal the principle that the nature of seeing is not an object, though they are divided into three and two parts respectively.
All of these [views] are erroneous. Part Two: The Response and Explanation has two sections: first, the refutation of attachments; second, the reconciliation [of contradictions]. Now, for the first:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "All worldly activities, whether large or small, internal or external, each belong to their respective objective fields (*viṣaya*).
One should not say that the faculty of seeing expands or contracts. For example, when one looks into a square vessel, the space within appears square. I shall ask you again."
Regarding this square vessel, the space seen within it—is it definitively square or indefinite as to its shape?
If it were definitively square, then when a round vessel is placed there instead, the space should not be round. If it were indefinite, then within the square vessel, there should be no square space.
You say you do not know where this principle resides; yet the nature of principles is such—how could it have a location? Ānanda, if furthermore...

If you wish to have the [visual] field enter a space that is neither square nor round, you must merely remove the squareness of the vessel; the essence of space itself has no directionality, so one should not say that there is a further location where the directional characteristics of space are removed.
If, as you ask, when entering a room your vision contracts and becomes small, then when looking up at the sun, would you pull your vision back to make it equal to the surface of the sun?
Furthermore, if building walls and houses can obstruct and sever your vision, then by piercing them...
If you say that small apertures must necessarily have a continuous trace [of light], this reasoning is not correct.

"that which is seen" refers to the image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses which serves as the object.

These two are precisely the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), just as a rope is formed from hemp, or as two moons are perceived due to pressing upon one's eyes while looking at a single true moon. Regarding "the images that are conceptualized," it is with respect to these [two divisions] that they arise.
The inability to discern the nature of the two divisions of appearance is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);

the false arising of the two attachments to self and phenomena is called the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). This is like mistaking a rope for a snake, or like being deluded regarding the moon in the sky and grasping at its reflection in water.
Just as a flower in the sky fundamentally does not exist, not only is the imagined nature empty by nature, but furthermore—
The dependent nature is like an illusion, like a rope on a heap of hemp that lacks not only the appearance of a real snake but also the appearance of a real rope;
the true moon lacks not only the appearance of a reflection but also the appearance of duality.

This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi, for True Suchness does not abide in its own nature and thus manifests as an illusion upon its own realization.

The perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*)—these two parts, together with the self-verifying essence (*svasaṃvitti*), constitute these three divisions, all of which are entirely the substance of self-verification.
This means that while it constantly accords with conditions, it remains eternally unchanging.

Just as the entirety of the two strands of a rope is nothing but hemp, or as the entirety of the two moons in the sky is nothing but the true moon, how could one distinguish between what is "this" and what is "not this"? Once one knows the rope...
This refers to the hemp, the second month, and the single [digit];

thus, although pointing to the snake as the hemp and pointing to the shadow as the moon would also be permissible, they are not mentioned because they lack substantiality through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

This *bodhi* likewise points to the four wisdoms of *bodhi*, wherein the seeing and image aspects (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness are fundamentally the *ādarśa-jñāna* (Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom) *bodhi*.
The essence of wondrous purity and luminosity—the seeing and perceived portions of the seventh consciousness—is fundamentally the Bodhi of the Wisdom of Equality;
the essence of wondrous purity and luminosity—the seeing and perceived portions of the sixth consciousness—is fundamentally the Bodhi of the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation;
the essence of wondrous purity and luminosity—the seeing and perceived portions of the first five consciousnesses—is fundamentally the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done.

Because the essence of the wondrously pure and luminous wisdom of Bodhi is the non-duality of stillness and illumination—being wondrously illuminating while eternally still, and being pure in its stillness while eternally illuminating—it is "luminous" (ming).
Furthermore, since it is the wondrously pure and luminous essence of Bodhi, it is also the primordially pure essence of Nirvana.
Because it is wondrous, it is the Nirvana of inherent purity; because it is pure, it is the Nirvana of expedient purity.
Because Nirvāṇa is luminous, it is precisely the Perfectly Pure Nirvāṇa. Second, citing an example to explain and establish this point:
"Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: as for you, Mañjuśrī, is there yet another Mañjuśrī who is Mañjuśrī, or is there ultimately no Mañjuśrī at all?
[Mañjuśrī replied: "World-Honored One, I am the true Mañjuśrī; there is no such thing as 'Mañjuśrī. Why is this so?"
"If there were such a thing, then there would be two Mañjuśrīs; yet today, it is not that I lack a true Mañjuśrī—it is simply that within this reality there is truly no duality of 'is' and 'is not.
The Buddha said: "This vision of wondrous clarity and these various empty objects are likewise so.

Originally, they are the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi, the pure, perfect, and true Mind. It is through delusion that they are falsely perceived as form and emptiness, as well as hearing and seeing."
"Just as in the case of a second moon, who is the real moon and who is not? Mañjuśrī, there is only one true moon;
in the interim, there is naturally neither 'this is the moon' nor 'this is not the moon.
In this passage, there are also three sections: first, taking Mañjuśrī as an example; second, from "This seeing is wondrously luminous" onwards... [the rest of the text follows].
The dharma corresponds to this explanation of the three [aspects] as in the second month; below, it further cites a metaphor to explain and establish [the point]. The first passage is clear.
Regarding the second passage—"this wondrous clarity and these various empty objects are likewise so"—it is also like Mañjuśrī’s [realization that] there are truly no two aspects of "is" and "is not.
This is because it is fundamentally the wondrously clear, unsurpassed Bodhi, the pure, perfect, and true [nature].
The mind’s perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is falsely manifested as the object-aspect of form and emptiness, and the subject-aspect of hearing and seeing.
Third, he provides an analogy to explain this: "It is like pressing the eye and falsely seeing two moons; how can one say that one is real and the other is false?
Once one realizes that the essence of the moon is fundamentally true, the conceptual proliferation of 'is' and 'is not' will forever cease. (2)
This demonstrates delusion and enlightenment, gain and loss.
Therefore, what you now perceive and observe, along with the various manifestations of sensory objects, is called "delusive thought" (*vikalpa*). You cannot escape from within this;

that you are unable to do so is because this is the true, essential, wondrously enlightened, and luminous nature. It is precisely because of this that it can cause you to transcend both the "pointing" and the "not-pointing."

This means that if one does not realize the absence of intrinsic nature in the dependent nature, yet perceives this perception as perception and views objects as objects, then all such various elaborations for the sake of others are collectively termed "delusive thought" (*vikalpa*).
Such a person is definitively unable to transcend the two gates of "is" and "is-not";

these words describe the loss incurred through delusion. Because this seeing and its objects of seeing are themselves the essence of true, wondrous, and luminous awakening-nature, [they are not separate].
One who attains this can cause you to transcend the two doubts regarding that which is indicated and that which is not indicated;
this statement refers to the attainment through awakening. Thus, we know that the wondrous principle is non-dual, and the point of contention lies solely between delusion and awakening.
How could one not regard the opening of the perfect understanding as an urgent task? (8) This concludes the section contrasting with the conventional truth of external paths.
Briefly clarifying that the nature of seeing is neither a causal condition nor spontaneous. This section has three parts: first, distinguishing it from spontaneity in contrast to non-Buddhists;

second, distinguishing it from causal conditions in contrast to worldly truth; third, concluding by clarifying its own nature. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the inquiry and request;
second, the revelation. Now, the first [of these].
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, it is truly as the Dharma King has taught:
that the nature of enlightenment, which pervades the ten directions, is profoundly still and eternally abiding, its essence being neither arising nor ceasing.

How does this differ from the ‘Dark Principle’ (Tattva) spoken of by the former Brahmin Śāṃkara, and from the ‘True Self’ (Ātman) that various non-Buddhist sects, such as those who smear themselves with ashes, claim exists and pervades the ten directions?”

The World-Honored One has also previously expounded this meaning on Mount Laṅkā for Mahāmati and others. Those non-Buddhists always speak of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), whereas I speak of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*);
it is not within their realm of experience. Now I observe that this nature of awakening is spontaneous, neither arising nor ceasing, far removed from all false and inverted views;
it appears as if it were not a matter of causes and conditions, yet it is [merely] the same as their [non-Buddhist] notion of spontaneity.

However, there must necessarily be a distinction [between them]. How then can it be revealed that one does not enter among the various heterodoxies but attains the wondrously enlightened and luminous nature of the true mind?
Within this passage, there are also three sections: the first section concerns the doubt that [the Buddha's teaching] is confused with the externalist calculations;
"The World-Honored One has also once... serves as the second section, concerning the doubt that it contradicts past sūtras; and "With that spontaneity... serves as the third section.

Jie Zheng requests an exposition of the true meaning. One must know that the profound doctrine taught by the Buddha—revealing the wondrous principle of "the unchanging following conditions" and "conditions following the unchanging"—is as vastly different from that of the non-Buddhists as heaven is from an abyss.

Since the non-Buddhist theories of *tattva* (ultimate reality) and the *ātman* (self) have already been refuted without exception by the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings, how could they possibly be conflated with the Perfect Teaching? However...
In this degenerate age, those who speak of the Perfect [Teaching] often have words but lack its true intent; they are not far removed from the heterodox calculations of external paths.

Therefore, it is necessary to briefly demonstrate the source and flow of their differences. When the Buddha says that the pure, perfect, true mind is delusively manifested as form, emptiness, hearing, and seeing, he is referring to the unchanging nature of True Suchness (tathatā).
This is like taking up the entire substance and following along with conditions—just as one might take up the "True."
The entire moon is falsely perceived as two moons, yet beyond these two moons, no true moon can be found.

When non-Buddhists postulate that the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) or the *ātman* (self) can produce all phenomena, they hold that this *pradhāna* or *ātman* is the producer of all things and is itself produced.
This is inconsistent, for the producer would be eternal while the produced would be impermanent; thus, the two cannot be one.
Furthermore, the Buddha said that these views and their conditions are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi;
this is the aspect of True Suchness (tathatā) conforming to conditions, yet it remains its entire substance without changing. It is like two moons:
the entirety of both is simply the true moon, and outside of the true moon, there is no separate substance for the two moons. This is what the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) falsely calculate.
All things each have their own essential nature and characteristics, yet you collectively infer the *tattva* (ultimate reality) and the divine self (*ātman*) as their abiding cause;
thus, the child does not resemble the father, and both cause and effect are untenable, for they are not two and are not identical.

Furthermore, since the Buddha taught that all phenomena arise solely as manifestations of the mind, those realms which are neither form nor emptiness, and those realms of "luminous clarity" and "spiritual alertness," do not exist at all.

The realms (*dhātu*) are likewise a single type of objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of one's own mind; yet, they obscure this and take it to be the "Dark Principle" (*tamas-tattva*) or the "Self" (*ātman*).
Failing to realize that all is but mind, they differ greatly from us.

Because there are these three kinds of differences, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras alike expound the profound meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in order to shatter [these misconceptions]. Now, Ānanda persistently...
Is this intended to lead those who deeply understand the corruptions of the末法 (mofa) era to agree with him? Second, the Instruction:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I have now thus revealed to you the provisional and the ultimate truths. Yet you still do not realize them and are deluded into thinking they are 'spontaneous' (*svabhāva*).
Ānanda, if they were truly spontaneous, you would have to clearly discern the essential substance of that spontaneity; for now, you..."
Contemplate this wondrous clarity within the faculty of vision: what constitutes its self-nature?
Does this seeing take light as its self, or darkness as its self, or space as its self, or obstruction as its self? Ānanda, if light were its self, it should not perceive darkness;
if emptiness were its essential body, it should not perceive obstruction, and so on for all such characteristics as darkness.
If [the seeing-nature] were self-originated, then when light is present, one would see the nature as being annihilated;

how then could one see the light? This precisely reiterates that the unchanging seeing-nature manifests its entire substance while following conditions, such that no separate self-substance can be found.
Even if one seeks the self-substance of the seeing-nature within light, darkness, obstruction, or emptiness, it is utterly unobtainable, for it is detached from them.

If one seeks a separate self-substance for the nature of seeing apart from light and darkness filling space, how could such a thing ever be found? If one were to take the "Primal Darkness" (Āṇḍa) postulated by the non-Buddhists as its self-substance, or the "Spirit-Self" (Puruṣa) they postulate as its self-substance, these would take emptiness and darkness or emptiness and light respectively as their essence; how utterly incongruous this would be! The first section consists of two parts: the initial formulation of the argument and its subsequent refutation. Now, for the first part:
Ānanda said, "If this wondrous nature of seeing is not self-arisen, and I now discern it to be produced through causes and conditions, my mind is still not clear regarding this meaning;
I ask the Tathāgata: how does this accord with the nature of causes and conditions?"
Since it is neither spontaneous, it must belong to causes and conditions; this is an unavoidable conclusion according to common worldly reasoning.

Therefore, I shall now propose that it belongs to the teaching of causes and conditions. However, since it is said that "this seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi," how can this be made to accord with the meaning of causes and conditions? Second, the refutation.

The Buddha said: "Regarding what you say about causes and conditions, I shall question you further. Now, as you perceive the nature of seeing manifest before you, does this seeing arise because of light? Does it arise because of darkness? Does it arise because of space?

Or does it arise because of obstruction? Ānanda, if it arose because of light, you should not see darkness; if it arose because of darkness, you should not see light. This applies likewise to all others."
The causes of emptiness and obstruction are identical to light and darkness. Furthermore, Ānanda, this seeing also arises in dependence on light;

there is seeing in dependence on darkness, seeing in dependence on emptiness, and seeing in dependence on obstruction. Ānanda, if it were to exist in dependence on emptiness, one should not see obstruction;
if it were to exist in dependence on obstruction, one should not see emptiness. This applies even further to its dependence on light and dependence on darkness, which are likewise identical.
"Empty and obstructed.
This precisely re-emphasizes that the nature of seeing, which follows conditions in its entirety, remains itself entirely unchanging;

it does not rely upon light, darkness, obstruction, or emptiness as causes and conditions. "Cause" refers to the direct cause, while "condition" refers to the auxiliary condition; these are merely the direct [causes].

This is merely a distinction within the category of "remoteness. Regarding the three fetters that clarify the self-nature, there are two parts: first, the direct demonstration of the true essence free from faults;
second, the concluding rebuke for those who remain attached to names and marks. Now, for the first part:
one should know that such a subtle, awakened, wondrous clarity is neither caused by conditions nor by causes, nor is it spontaneous, yet it is not non-spontaneous.
"Neither non-being nor not non-being; neither being nor not being"—this is the departure from all marks and the identity with all dharmas.
Within this, the two phrases "neither cause nor condition" and "nor spontaneous" constitute a double negation and a double refutation.
The phrase "nor not-spontaneous" should, by analogy, be preceded by "nor not-cause-and-condition," which constitutes a double illumination and a double establishment.
The two phrases "neither non-being nor being" and "neither being nor non-being" are simultaneous negation and illumination, refutation and establishment;
they are not separate from the phrase that transcends all marks. The phrase "all dharmas" takes up the aforementioned various phrases to collectively negate and refute emotional attachments;
once such attachments are refuted, it immediately illuminates and establishes the substance of the Dharma. This is to be free from all [marks].
The phrase "the characteristics are themselves all dharmas" (xiāng jí yīqiè fǎ) is a statement that penetrates all principles of perfect interfusion without exception;
please further elaborate upon it. When the head and hands move, shake, open, and close, one sees that there is no movement; in their extension and contraction, they are free from all characteristics.
It is not the wind or the banner that moves—it is the mind of the worthy one that moves. This is precisely what is meant by "all dharmas": that which is unchanging.
Fundamentally without arising or ceasing, it is free from all marks. After death, casting off this life to proceed toward the next birth, it is precisely all dharmas.
The essence of emptiness has no fixed location; being free from all marks, even when within a spatial vessel, it is not that the space itself lacks a location—it is precisely all dharmas.
Pointing with the finger, everything is an object; there is no such thing as "seeing"—it is free from all marks. Subtle.
That which is revealed as nothing other than seeing is precisely all dharmas.

Seeing, the objects of seeing, and the characteristics of what is conceptualized are like flowers in the sky—they fundamentally do not exist; they are free from all marks. This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi;
this is precisely all dharmas. Furthermore, as stated in the subsequent text, they are not produced through combination.
To be free from all marks is not non-harmony; it is precisely all dharmas.
Within the true and eternal nature, seeking coming and going, delusion and awakening, or birth and death, nothing at all can be found—this is being free from all marks.
Birth, cessation, coming, and going are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha—this is precisely all dharmas. Being pure and fundamental by nature is to be free from all marks.
"Manifesting according to karma" refers to all phenomena; the Tathāgata-garbha, as the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind, is neither any of the ten realms and is free from all marks.
"The Tathāgata-garbha, originally luminous and the mind’s wondrousness," is identical to all ten realms and is thus all phenomena.
"The Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrously luminous mind's origin," is free from both identity and difference, and is free from all marks.
"This is precisely non-identity, which is identical to all dharmas. To state the essential point:
being free from all marks is what is called "following conditions all day long while remaining unchanging all day long," which is identical to all dharmas;
this is what is called "remaining unchanging all day long while following conditions all day long. This is the fifth passage that thoroughly reveals the nature. Second, the conclusion.
"You are attached to and detained by names and characteristics.
Why do you now apply your mind to them, attempting to differentiate them through the various worldly, frivolous names and characteristics?
It is like trying to grasp empty space with the palm of one's hand; it only increases your own exhaustion. How can empty space ever be caught according to your grasping?"
The wondrous nature is inconceivable, transcending the paths of words and thought; only by directly observing the mind below may one perhaps attain a point of resonance.
Should one wish to apply the mind to it through thought or discuss it in words, it would be no different from grasping at empty space.
Nine: Examining the two delusions together to clarify that the nature of seeing is not "seeing. Part one: citing past instances to raise doubts;
part two: refuting through logical inquiry; part three: correctly demonstrating the nature of seeing. Now, the first [part].

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if the nature of wondrous enlightenment is neither caused by conditions nor produced by causes, why did the World-Honored One formerly declare to the bhikṣus that the nature of seeing possesses four kinds of conditions—namely, depending on space, depending on light, depending on the mind, and depending on the eyes?
What is the meaning of this?"
To say that the nature of seeing possesses four kinds of conditions means that the manifestation of visual consciousness requires ten conditions to arise;
here, only four are mentioned for brevity. This refers to the nature of false seeing and not to the true nature elucidated here.

Because false seeing relies upon conditions, it has no inherent reality of its own; thus, it lacks a self or what belongs to a self, which distinguishes it from the erroneous causes of externalist paths.
If one understands the meaning of dependent origination as being devoid of intrinsic nature, then one knows that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and manifest according to karma;

if one understands that they manifest according to karma, then one knows them to be fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. This profound meaning of causes and conditions is why it serves as the foundation for the Shared, Distinct, and Complete Teachings alike;
yet Ānanda clung to the literal text and was obscured by its intent, failing to reach this realization.
If causes and conditions are themselves empty, how could one know them to be also provisional and the Middle? The four conditions encompass the ten conditions:

the empty condition and the manifesting condition encompass the objective-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). The single character "mind" (*citta*) fully encompasses six conditions: namely, the attention-condition (*manasikāra-pratyaya*), the discernment-condition (*viniścaya-pratyaya*), the defilement-purity-condition (*saṃkleśavyavadāna-pratyaya*), the fundamental-condition (*mūla-pratyaya*), the seed-condition (*bīja-pratyaya*), and the opening-and-guiding-condition (*āvāhaka-pratyaya*). The eye is the faculty (*indriya*).
Regarding the classification of these ten conditions according to the standard four conditions: the seed serves as the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*);

the objective aspect of one's own representation (*sva-bhāga*) serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); the opening and guiding support serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);

and the remaining seven, along with the external objective reality (*bimba*), all serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Second, the refutation through reasoning and inquiry has two parts; first, the direct explanation of the past.
The first part explains that the two [types of causes] spoken of according to worldly sentiment clearly demonstrate that the nature of seeing is not a causal condition.
First, the Buddha said: "Ānanda, I say that the various characteristics of causes and conditions in the world are not the ultimate truth."
The Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma always relies upon the two truths: that which relies on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is called "teaching according to [sentient beings'] dispositions";

that which relies on ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called "teaching according to wisdom"; and that which reveals both truths simultaneously is called "teaching according to both dispositions and wisdom.

What has been explained here is directed toward the conventional truth; it serves only to refute false conceptualizations and does not mean that causes and conditions truly exist within the ultimate realm.
Furthermore, [this section] secondly directly reveals that the nature of seeing is not dependent on conditions.
Ānanda, I ask you again: when people in the world say, "I am able to see," what do they call seeing, and what do they call not seeing?
Ānanda replied: "People in the world rely upon the light of the sun, the moon, or lamps to see various forms; this they call seeing."
If there were no three kinds of light, one would be unable to see Ānanda. If "not seeing" were defined simply by the absence of light, then one should not see darkness;
yet since one certainly does see darkness, this is merely the absence of light—how can it be called "not seeing"?
Ānanda, if one is in the dark and does not see light, it is called "not seeing"; now that you are in the light, you do not see darkness.
If the mutual concealment of these two characteristics were called "not seeing," then both characteristics would equally be called "not seeing.

Furthermore, if these two characteristics were to mutually suppress one another such that your nature of vision were temporarily absent therein, then you would know that both are actually instances of seeing; how then could they be called "not seeing"?
The statement "because of the existence of seeing" refers to the deluded conceptual grasping of the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

The statement "seeing both light and darkness" refers to the essence of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*) and its aspect of seeing (*darśanabhāga*), which is the nature of dependent origination (*paratantrasvabhāva*). This aspect of seeing is like a second moon; it is distinct from the moon's own reflection. III.
The Correct Demonstration of the Nature of Seeing has three parts: first, the direct demonstration of the true nature; second, the raising of doubts and detailed explanation.
Now, first:
Therefore, Ānanda, you should know now that when seeing light, the seeing is not the light; when seeing darkness, the seeing is not the darkness;
when seeing emptiness, the seeing is not the emptiness; and when seeing obstruction, the seeing is not the obstruction.
You should further understand that the four meanings are thus accomplished. When you perceive seeing, that seeing is not [itself] seeing;
even seeing is detached from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it. Why, then, do you speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, and the characteristics of combination?
You śrāvakas are narrow-minded, inferior, and ignorant, unable to penetrate the pure true reality (*dharmatā*). I now instruct you: you should contemplate this well.
Do not become weary on the sublime path to Bodhi.

Having already established that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) is not the cause of the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect), this further clarifies that the *darśana-bhāga* is not the *svasaṃvedana* (self-cognizing aspect).
Phenomena such as light and darkness, or obstruction and space, are all the *nimitta-bhāga*; perceptions such as seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all the *darśana-bhāga*.
Within the single essence of self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*), one falsely gives rise to the duality of the perceived (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiver (*darśana-bhāga*).
Apart from the fundamental essence of self-realization, where else could these two parts exist? These two parts ultimately are not the fundamental essence of self-realization;
it is like falsely seeing two moons when there is but one moon—apart from the substance of the moon, where else could two moons exist? And yet, these two moons...

Since the true substance is ultimately not identical to the single month, it is said: "You should further know that when the nature of seeing arises from the portion of seeing, the nature of seeing is not that portion of seeing.
You should know that the nature of seeing is already detached from the delusion of the portion of seeing; it is beyond the reach of the portion of seeing.
How, then, can you speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, or the characteristics of their combination? It is like the True [Nature]."

When the moon arises during the second month, the true moon is not the second month; one should know that the true moon is already free from the delusion of the second month and cannot be reached by it.
How, then, can one further speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, or the characteristics of their conjunction?
Furthermore, taking the meaning of the metaphor from the subsequent passage: at the time of an eye disease, the eye itself is not the disease.
The eye is already free from cataracts; how could cataracts reach it? How much less can one speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, or the characteristics of combination?
For the essence of vision, already tainted by delusion, is no longer a characteristic of causes and conditions, spontaneity, or combination—how much more so this true nature of vision?
This true nature of vision is called the pure *dharmatā* (real mark), because it is detached from all things.

This is because appearances are identical with all phenomena. That which is free from all appearances is likened to the true moon, while the absence of the appearance of a second moon is likened to the essence of the true moon alone.
This nature of "seeing" as non-seeing is likewise so: only when one negates both its nature and its aspect of seeing can one negate its aspect of appearance.
Therefore, you should contemplate this with skillful thought and deeply take it as your own;
for this is the true essence of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King Samādhi, and it is the single gate that transcends to the wondrous path of Bodhi.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has for our sakes proclaimed the characteristics of both causal conditions and spontaneity—both those that are in combination and those that are not—my mind was still not yet enlightened. Now, having further heard and seen...”
"Seeing what is not seen only increases our confusion and distress; we pray that Your Great Compassion will bestow the eye of great wisdom upon us, revealing the luminous purity of the awakened mind.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated with tears of sorrow and received the Sage’s decree.
This question specifically seeks to clarify the meaning of "seeing seeing" as being "not seeing"; therefore, the answer below states: "This is truly seeing seeing.
How can it again be called perceiving, hearing, knowing, or seeing? This is indeed "seeing seeing, not seeing.

Regarding the commentary, some judge this section as a response to the request for *samādhi*, claiming it is entirely unrelated to the preceding chapter; this may be described as a failure to grasp the text.

To lose the essential intent and fall into error is indeed grave. When one asks whether "harmony" (*samavāya*) and "non-harmony" are identical to "causality" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*), at first glance they appear the same, but upon further investigation, they differ.
The reason they seem the same at first glance is that "causality" carries the meaning of harmony, while "spontaneity" carries the meaning of non-harmony.
The reason they differ upon further investigation is that causality refers solely to the function of responding to conditions (*anupratyaya-vṛtti*), which is the primary [meaning].
The natural, singularly reckoned, and unchanging essence proclaimed in the Teachings is something that non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) fail to understand.
If one were to claim that a portion of the unchanging essence and a portion of the随缘 (following conditions) function interactively and restrict each other, this is called "harmony" (*saṃyoga*).

Alternatively, if one were to claim that the unchanging remains unchanging by itself and the following-conditions aspect follows conditions by itself, such that they are strictly separate and distinct, this is called... [the name of the error].

The non-concordance of these two [views] applies to both the internal and external, as well as the Great and Small Vehicles; one must distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, the partial and the perfect, by means of the Three Seals or the Single Seal.
I shall not elaborate further here, for this can be understood through reflection. Having heard the Buddha’s reprimand, Ānanda asked:

Because the refutation of the meanings of conjunction and non-conjunction has not yet been elucidated, it is said that "the mind is as yet unopened.

Furthermore, since one has not yet attained mastery over the subtle principle that the essence of nature remains unchanging while following conditions, and that while following conditions it remains unchanging, even upon hearing it is said to be neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous, one still does not fully comprehend it; thus it is said that "the mind is as yet unopened. Moreover—
Those who, upon hearing and seeing that "seeing is not seeing," find their confusion and distress redoubled, have not yet fully mastered even the meaning of the "essence of seeing" (*jien-jing*);
how much less could they grasp this further layer of profound depth?

Yet, when the Tathāgata first directly pointed out that the nature of seeing is the mind and not the eye, he had already precisely indicated this very substratum (*tixing*) upon which the two aspects—seeing and its object—rely; it is precisely this [first point].
Because they have seen this single word, their lamp-eye is lost yet not extinguished; their lamp-eye is attained yet does not arise;
their hands open and close yet do not open or close; their head moves and shakes yet does not move or shake; their years pass and change yet do not pass or change;
they follow after inversion without diminution or loss, even to the point of being without contraction or expansion, without interruption or continuity, and without "is-ness."
It is not that there is nothing which is neither spontaneous nor caused by conditions;

rather, they are bound together such that by departing from all marks, one realizes that all dharmas are the constant and unchanging nature pointed out within the midst of following conditions. Alas, Ānanda, you have missed it face-to-face;

you merely grasp it as the "seeing-essence," yet even with this grasping, your realization remains un-intimate. However, this— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. This translation reflects the full meaning of the preceding segment.)
