Upon realizing the substance of this nature, then [harmony and disharmony]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Both union and non-union are entirely transcended. Second, the Tathāgata’s detailed explanation has three parts:
first, the censure and permission to teach; second, the combined clarification of the two delusions; third, the manifestation of the return to truth. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, the narrative by the scribe describing the intent; second, the Tathāgata’s censure and permission. This is the first.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and the great assembly, was about to expound the Great Dhāraṇī and the sublime path of practice for the various samādhis.
*Dhāraṇī* is here translated as "total retention" (*zongchi*), meaning to retain all phenomena and uphold all meanings. This is the Great [Dhāraṇī].
"Dhāraṇī" refers to the essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristic of the Dharma-realm;
that is to say, as will be explained below, the aggregates, bases, elements, and the seven great elements are all the wondrous True Suchness of the Tathāgata-garbha.

Therefore, whichever of these dharmas—aggregates, bases, elements, or the seven great elements—one may take up, each is the entire body of the Tathāgata-garbha nature, and each is capable of encompassing all as one.
Because it upholds all dharmas and maintains all meanings, it is called the Great Dhāraṇī. By practicing in accordance with this, one attains various samādhis, namely:
the samādhi of the eye faculty up to the samādhi of the mind faculty; the samādhi of the object of form up to the samādhi of the object of phenomena;
the samādhi of eye-consciousness up to the samādhi of mind-consciousness; and the Samādhi of Holding the Earth.
Because it encompasses everything from the state of obscurity up to the samādhi of consciousness-only, it is called "all samādhis.

There is not a single one of these samādhis that does not arise entirely from the nature, nor is there any cultivation that does not reside entirely within the nature; all are the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King Samādhi.
Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend [samsara] through this single gate, it is called the "wondrous path of practice. Now, I am about to expound upon it.

The preceding passage has already revealed the great aggregate of the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*); now, with few remaining doubts, we shall take this opportunity to further reveal the nature of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-svabhāva*).
For within the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), that which sees by means of the eye stands at the beginning.
Since the nature of seeing is thus established, the natures of the others may be known; therefore, one should proceed through all phenomena in their entirety.

This reveals the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* and opens up the understanding of the Perfect and Sudden [teachings] as the foundation for true cultivation. Second, the Tathāgata’s admonition and permission:
He addressed Ānanda, saying, "Although you possess a powerful memory, it only increases your erudition; it does not pertain to the subtle and secret contemplative illumination of *śamatha*."

Your mind has not yet attained full understanding; listen now attentively as I shall analyze and reveal it for you, so that all future beings subject to outflows may likewise attain the fruit of Bodhi.
This passage rebukes those who hear the Dharma but do not contemplate the mind, failing to penetrate the practice of the complete nature. It is exhaustive.
"Meditative absorption (samatha) and subtle, secret contemplation-illumination" refers precisely to the Perfect and Sudden Calm Abiding and Contemplation;

from the initial stage of names and words up to the ultimate realization, there is nothing that does not proceed by way of this. Yet, if one now merely relies on rote memorization of phenomena, one will have hearing but lack wisdom.
Consequently, one fails to understand the calm abiding and contemplation that arise from the entirety of the nature, and fails to penetrate the essence of "seeing seeing" as non-seeing.

Second, the combined elucidation of the two delusions. This section has two parts: first, the direct demonstration of the two delusions; second, the combined elucidation through progressive and regressive analysis.
Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the general heading; second, the detailed explanation. This is the first [of those two].
Ānanda, all sentient beings revolve in the world due to two kinds of inverted, discriminative, and deluded views;
these arise in their respective places and cause them to revolve according to their karma. What are these two views? First, the deluded view of individual karma;
second, the deluded view of commonality.
"All sentient beings" refers to the sentient beings of the nine dharma-realms.

"Transmigrating through the world" refers to the segmented transmigration within the Shared World (tongju shijian) and the transformational transmigration within the Worlds of Expediency, True Reward, and Realization (fangbian, shibao, and shibao shijian).

"The two inverted, discriminative views of delusion" specifically point to the two types of false vision: those of individual karma (bieye) and collective karma (tongfen). Both of these are afflictions (huo).

These refer to the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the sands of dust (*rajas*), and ignorance (*avidyā*). "Arising in their respective places" means that wherever there is delusion, there must necessarily be karma:

the views and afflictions give rise to outflowing (*sāsrava*) wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable (*āniñjya*) karmas; the sands of dust give rise to non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) karma of partial truth;
and ignorance gives rise to both outflowing and non-outflowing karma of the two extremes. This constitutes the wheel of karma.

As for "transformation," whenever there is karma, there is necessarily suffering—namely, the transformation of the realm of cohabitation through the karma of views and afflictions (*kleśa*), the transformation of the realm of skillful means through the karma of *rajas* (dust-like delusions), and the transformation of the realm of true retribution through the karma of ignorance (*avidyā*).

These three—delusion, karma, and suffering—are like a mass of filth that does not separate for even a moment; furthermore, they are manifestations of the mind alone, entirely illusory, and have no place from which they originate.
Because there is nowhere to which one goes, it is said that [the mind] arises in its own place and revolves through its own karma.

Regarding "delusive vision of individual karma," this refers to what one sees alone; regarding "delusive vision of shared karma," this refers to what is seen by a multitude together. Although the individual and the shared differ, their delusiveness is one and the same.
All sentient beings, in every moment of thought, fully possess these two kinds of vision: the shared and the individual.
It is because of deluded views that one deludedly undergoes saṃsāra; yet, though one spends all day within these two delusions, the nature of seeing remains as it was.
This so-called "seeing of seeing" is not [ordinary] seeing; if one awakens to this, saṃsāra ceases. Part Two: A Separate Explanation, in two sections.
First, an explanation of individual karmic deluded seeing; second, an explanation of collective karmic deluded seeing. Now, the first section.
"What is meant by 'delusive vision caused by individual karma'? Ānanda, it is like a person in the world who has a red film over the eye;

at night, they see a lamp-light and perceive a separate circular shadow with five overlapping colors. What do you think? Is this circular light manifested by the lamp-light at night the color of the lamp, or is it the color of the seeing?
Ānanda, if this were the color of the lamp, then it would not be seen by one with the film."
Why is it that while their views differ, this circular shadow is seen only by the one with the visual impairment?
If seeing color were itself the formation of color, then what would you call the person with the impairment who sees the circular shadow?

Furthermore, Ānanda, if this circular shadow existed separately from the lamp, then when looking at the side walls, curtains, tables, or mats, a circular shadow should likewise appear; yet it does not exist apart from the sight [of the lamp].
There may be things that should not be within the range of the eye; how then could a person with cataracts see a circular shadow?

Therefore, one should know that while the color-form actually resides in the lamp, it is the visual ailment that constitutes the shadow. Both the shadow and the seeing are equally the result of the cataract. Yet, the one who perceives this cataract is fundamentally free from disease.
Ultimately, one should not say that this is the lamp or the seeing; even less should one say that there exists within this something that is neither lamp nor seeing, as in the previous case.
The second month is neither substance nor reflection. Why? Because the second observation is produced by pressing.
No wise person should say that this pressed root-cause is either form or non-form, or seeing or non-seeing; this [second moon] is likewise produced by a cataract in the eye.
Now, whom would you name as being the lamp and the seeing? How much more so regarding the distinction between what is not the lamp and what is not the seeing?

[The Master] says: "I see it. Within this passage there are four sections: first, from the beginning up to "the five colors layered," which establishes an analogy to demonstrate that the vision is distinct;
second, from "What do you mean? up to "the eyes see a circular shadow," which uses interrogation and refutation to demonstrate its falsity; third...
Therefore, one should know that reaching the state where there is neither lamp nor seeing is the manifestation of the delusion that fundamentally relies upon the True.

This fourth section, from "like the second moon" up to "neither lamp nor seeing," serves as an extended analogy to further harmonize with the preceding examples. The meaning of the initial passage is as follows:
first, one must take the pure eye as a metaphor for correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), and take the light of the pure lamp as a metaphor for Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus it is covered.
The perfection of seeing the nature and the perfection of the light-nature are boundless and shoreless, without "is" or "is not.
This so-called suchness beyond ignorance is that which is realized by wisdom; there is no wisdom outside of suchness that can realize suchness.

Furthermore, the eye has three meanings, namely: the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), and the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*). The lamp has three meanings... [text continues]
This refers to the lamp of the ultimate truth, the lamp of the conventional truth, and the lamp of the middle truth. The afflictions of views and thoughts are like a cataract on the eye of wisdom;

The afflictions as numerous as motes of dust in a sunbeam are like a cataract on the eye of the Dharma; one falsely perceives the five aggregates of the expedient means and the five colors upon the lamp of the conventional truth.
The overlapping delusions of ignorance are like the red cataracts of a Buddha’s eye; within them, one falsely perceives the five colors of retribution layered upon the lamp of ultimate truth.
This analogy illustrates the vertical discourse on the three delusions. Furthermore, these three delusions are entirely empty in their own nature;
all three delusions are established as mere provisional names, and all three delusions are themselves inconceivable.
Failing to realize that the three delusions are fundamentally empty is collectively termed "view-delusion and thought-delusion" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);

failing to realize that the three delusions are provisionally established as various medicines and ailments through immeasurable causes and conditions is collectively termed "delusion like fine dust" (*rajas-sama-kleśa*);

and failing to realize that the essence of the three delusions is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*). This explains the three delusions horizontally within the context of the three vertical delusions. The second passage clarifies...
This circular reflection is neither the lamp nor the seeing, yet it is not separate from the lamp or the seeing; its entire substance is illusory and devoid of any real dharma.
This intends to reveal that while the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the three lands are neither true wisdom nor suchness (*tathatā*), they likewise do not depart from true wisdom and suchness.
In the third passage, the phrase "form actually resides in the lamp" intends to reveal suchness.

The "five aggregates of the fundamental nature inherent in truth" indicates that seeing illness as a shadow means the five aggregates of the nine realms are all established through delusive confusion.

"Shadow and vision are both cataracts" indicates that for sentient beings, the perception of an internal body and external objects—the seer and the seen—is nothing other than delusion. "Seeing the cataract is not the illness" indicates...
When one observes that which sees, the seeing is not [itself] seeing. This is because the two aspects—the perceived and the perceiver—entirely depend upon self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*).

Although the clear eye manifests its entire substance as these two illusions, the eye itself still remains present.
It says: "To see the cataract is not the disease" refers precisely to what is called being in delusion all day long while remaining eternally true all day long.
It should never be said that "this is the lamp" or "this is the seeing," for within this there is neither non-lamp nor non-seeing.

This concludes and clarifies the meaning of the absence of "is" and "is-not," summarizing the previous second section’s refutation through inquiry. As for the fourth section, it further raises [the point].
The analogy of the second moon corresponds to the preceding examples: the true moon is like the lamp, while the second moon is like the five colors superimposed;
it is not the moon itself, yet it is not separate from the moon.
It is like a shadow—just as mentioned above, it is neither the color of the lamp nor something existing apart from the lamp. One should not say that this distorted sense-faculty is a shape.

It is not that form is separate from seeing; it is not that the seer lacks eyes. The eyes are still used as a metaphor for the eyes, just as pressing on the eyes is a metaphor for the red cataract (timira).

Since the eyes are fundamentally not being pressed, one should not say that form is separate from the eyes. Since there is no pressing upon the eyes, one should not say that form is not separate [from them].
Because two moons are seen when the eyes are pressed, one should not say that seeing is separate [from form]; since the essence of seeing has no pressing, one should not say [that it is separate].
"Free from non-seeing"—or perhaps the character "free" (*li*) should be read as "this" (*shi*); the text is even more direct here. "Form and non-form" refers to the physical body (*phu-ch'en*);
"seeing and non-seeing" refers to the essence of seeing (*chien-ching*). This is generally as stated above:
it is neither the seeing of form, nor is there something else apart from seeing that exists. "This is also like this" below provides an example once again.

The analogy of the moon combined with the explanation of the "knot" reveals that this view is merely illusory; the text is easy to understand. Second, the explanation of the deluded vision of those of a similar class (*sabhāgatā*).
What is meant by the "deluded vision of those of a similar class"? Ānanda, in this Jambudvīpa, excluding the great oceans, in the space between them...
The plains consist of three thousand islands; the central island among them, encompassing its east and west, contains two thousand three hundred large nations.
As for the remaining small islands scattered throughout the various seas, some contain two or three hundred nations, while others have only one or two, up to thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty.
Ānanda, if there were even a single small island within this [central region], [it would likewise be filled with nations].

If there are two countries where the people of only one share the same karmic affinity for misfortune, then the sentient beings within that small continent will perceive all manner of inauspicious phenomena;

they may see two suns or two moons, or even such various evil omens as halos, solar spots, rings, crescents, comets, meteors, falling stars, "burdened ears," and rainbows. These are seen only by the people of this particular country.
The sentient beings of that country have never before seen or heard of this.
Although this is a correct explanation of how the divisions of countries arise from deluded vision, if we consider it in relation to this country, they may be called "the same";

yet if we consider it in relation to that country, they remain "distinct" as before. Whether they appear the same or distinct, they are all nothing but a single delusion. The term "halo" (yùnhuì) here refers to an optical aberration.

When the qi encircles the sun and moon, those who are attuned perceive it as an eclipse of the sun or moon; those wearing jade rings and pendants perceive it as the arrival of baleful vapors near the sun and moon, appearing like rings and pendants.
A *sui* (comet) is when the radiance of a star points in a single direction; a *bei* (meteor shower) is when the radiance of a star radiates in all directions;

a *fei* (flying star) is when a star suddenly shifts away; a *liu* (flowing star) is when its luminous traces are connected; and a *fu-er* (star with a "back-ear") is when the qi of yin and yang turns its back upon the sun.
"Like a sun on the side of a shoulder" and "like a rainbow on the ear" refer respectively to what appears in the early morning and what appears in the evening.
[This section] consists of two parts: first, a general indication of their progression and retreat; second, a detailed explanation. Now, the first part.
Ānanda, I shall now clarify these two matters for you by advancing one and retreating the other.

Although there are two types of seeing, their falsity is no different; I use that which is easy to understand as an analogy for that which is difficult to understand, so that what is difficult to understand may likewise become easy to understand.
Thus, by advancing one point and retreating another, we can clearly demonstrate that both are false. This is because the lamp...
The illusory unreality of the upper circular shadow is most easily understood, for it is because many do not suffer from cataracts that this inauspicious object is known to be false.
However, the illusory unreality of the [other] objective realms is already difficult to understand, as they are perceived by many who share the same vision.
Nevertheless, one still relies on the fact that the sentient beings of those other lands neither see nor hear them, which serves to manifest their falsity; this applies even to the two lands.

If one contemplates the nine realms of the primary and secondary worlds as being identical, how could one know that all are equally like circular reflections were it not for the Tathāgata’s own abiding samādhi?
Now, by clarifying this through two matters, one comes to know that all that is able to see and all that is seen are nothing but illusory;
yet the nature of seeing—that which sees—is non-seeing, and thus within delusion, it is eternally true. Second, the specific clarification.
Second, first, the specific analogy for advancement is the same as the second [section], while the analogy for regression is distinct. Now, for the first:
Ānanda, it is like the deluded vision of individual karma among those sentient beings, whereby they perceive a circular shadow appearing within a lamp’s light;

although it seems to be an external object, it is ultimately produced by the cataract of the seer’s own eyes. This cataract is the affliction of the seeing itself, not something created by external form.
However, one who perceives this visual defect ultimately incurs no fault from that perception. Take yourself today as an example:
when you observe with your eyes the mountains, rivers, lands, and all sentient beings, these are all produced by the visual disease of beginningless time.

Although the seeing and its objects appear to be present before you, they are fundamentally not external objects; rather, they are the visual defects perceived by the essence of my enlightened awareness. Therefore, they arise from the body of that awareness.

Seeing (and hearing, sensing, and knowing) is what is called a cataract; however, the originally enlightened, luminous mind that is able to perceive this seeing and its objects is ultimately not a cataract.

Therefore, when this awareness perceives the cataract that is being perceived, this awareness is certainly not itself fallen within the cataract. This is truly what is meant by "the nature of seeing-seeing.
How, then, could it again be termed seeing, hearing, knowing, or perceiving? For this reason, you now see me, yourself, and all the world.
The ten classes of sentient beings all perceive this as a cataract (of the visual faculty), yet it is not the true vision of the one who perceives this cataract.
Because that true essence of vision is by nature fundamentally not a cataract, it cannot be called "vision."

This passage uses the individual karmic obstacle of the false vision experienced by the person Angulimālya as an analogy for the collective deluded vision shared by Ānanda, thereby clarifying in depth that the "seeing of seeing" is not true seeing. The text is also divided into three sections:

first, from the beginning up to "there is no fault of not seeing," which reiterates the analogy previously established; second, from "I shall now give you an analogy" up to "feeling, hearing, knowing, and seeing."

This is the correct analogy for Ānanda’s vision; therefore, what you now perceive cannot be called "seeing. This passage clarifies that while the knots are manifest in delusion, they are eternally true.
The initial section concludes with the phrase "there is no fault in not seeing"; here, "fault" also refers to a disease.
If seeing were indeed a disease, how could one see the optical aberration (*mièng*)? It is as stated in the preceding text: "then that person with the aberration sees the wholeness."
"What is meant by 'shadow'? This refers directly to the "eye-disease" (the *śuṅga*), while the seeing-nature—which is eternally true and not subject to delusion—is not the disease.

In the subsequent passage, the four characters "with the eyes one observes and sees" correspond to the "delusory seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) and serve as an analogy for the aforementioned "eye-disease.
The mountains, rivers, lands, and all sentient beings correspond to the "delusory object-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) and serve as an analogy for the aforementioned "circular shadow."

"All these are produced by the disease of vision since beginningless time" means that both this perceiving subject (the *darśana-bhāga*) and the perceived object (the *nimitta-bhāga*) are equally the disease of the seer;
this exceeds the previous example, as it concludes that the seer is produced by a cataract (*timira*).
"The vision and its conditions appear like a present object" follows back to the previous example, wherein although they appear before one...

The objective realm is originally my own luminous awareness; that which perceives the object is a cataract. Since the perceiving awareness is itself the cataract, following the previous analogy, the cataract is simply the fatigue of seeing, not something created by form.
When the fundamentally enlightened, luminous mind perceives objects, it is not a cataract.
Furthermore, as for why it is called "awareness, hearing, knowing, and seeing," this follows the previous analogy; yet, one who perceives the cataract ultimately incurs no fault of seeing. However—

Regarding the three characters: "You now see" refers to the character for "seeing" (*jian*)—that is, the seeing of light, the seeing of darkness, the seeing of emptiness, and the seeing of obstruction—which points to the "seeing-part" (*jian-fen*), the faculty of seeing, like the visual aberration of a cataract.

"I and you, as well as all ten classes of sentient beings in the world" refers to the "characterized-part" (*xiang-fen*), the objects of what is seen, like the circular shadow [of a cataract]. These two—the seeing and the characterized—are...
All these divisions are merely the optical aberrations (*taimira*) of the essence of vision itself; they are not the self-essence of the one who perceives these aberrations.

Just as the aberration and its shadow are both not the eye, so too the true essence of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*), though it remains amidst delusion throughout the day, is by nature fundamentally free from aberration.
The aberration cannot reach it, for although the eye may possess an aberration, the nature of seeing is not lost. Therefore, this nature of seeing cannot be [obstructed].
It is designated as "seeing"; yet if it were not designated as seeing, it could likewise not be designated as hearing, smelling, tasting, sensing, or cognizing.
Since it is the nature of seeing, it is also the nature of hearing, the nature of smelling, the nature of tasting, the nature of sensing, and the nature of cognizing.
This is why it is called the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature; one should rely upon this for cultivation.
The practitioner practices for the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King Samādhi. Second, the cases of regression are analogous, though their particulars differ.
Ānanda is like those sentient beings with common deluded vision; his particular deluded vision is like that of a single person with a diseased eye.
The circular shadow seen by all in that country corresponds to the visual aberration produced by the cataract; what is manifested here by this community of shared destiny is likewise so produced.
Inauspiciousness appears together within the karma of the afflictions, all arising from the delusive perceptions of beginningless time;
this is analogous to the three thousand continents of Jambudvīpa, including the four great oceans, the Sahā world, and extending to all impure lands and sentient beings throughout the ten directions—
all are equally the pure, untainted, wondrous mind of enlightenment (arising from) the voidness of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Regarding the conditions for delusory illness: because of the conjunction [of causes], there is delusory birth; because of the conjunction, there is delusory death.
This first withdraws the commonality of a single nation’s delusory vision as an illustration, which is then applied to the individual karma of a single person’s delusory vision;

subsequently, it generally withdraws the commonality of the ten directions’ environment and its inhabitants as delusory visions, all of which are likewise illustrated by the example of a single person.

These are delusive visions resulting from individual karma. Although the people of a single country may be numerous, if one views them from the perspective of another country, they can be compared to a single person;

the karmic miasma produced by a country can be compared to the cataract-like film on a single person's eye, and the inauspicious sights seen by a country can be compared to the circular shadows seen by a single person. Thus, these layered and manifold delusions are all of the same nature.

That which arises from beginningless false views has no other cause; this is analogous to tracing back from Jambudvīpa downward through successive stages to the ten directions, each step being reduced to an individual case of deluded perception.

That they share the same enlightened, luminous, and untainted wondrous mind is analogous to the single person’s eye mentioned above—specifically, the first "seeing" in the phrase "the seeing of seeing is not seeing" from the preceding text.
Regarding "the illusory conditions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as a disease," this corresponds to the "red cataract" in the eyes mentioned above;
"illusory birth through combination and illusory death through combination" corresponds to the "perfect shadow of the lamp-light" mentioned above;
and "the various realms of outflows" refers to the shared residence (sahā-loka). These correspond respectively to the phenomena of light, darkness, space, and obstruction cited in the preceding text.

The realm of the outflows of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-āsrava*) refers to the *tongju* (co-resident) *fenduan* (segmented) birth-and-death; the realm of the outflows of dust-like sands (*rajas-āsrava*) refers to the *fangbian* (provisional) and *guobao* (retributive) [birth-and-death];

and the realm of the outflows of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) refers to the *zhongsheng* (sentient beings) of the nine dharma-realms who undergo false birth and false death—the *fangbian* (provisional), *guobao* (retributive), and *bianyi* (transformative) birth-and-death.
By traversing these two categories of the "same" and the "different," one attains insight.
The nature of non-seeing is as luminous as the sun and moon. Third, this reveals the return to truth:

if one can remain far removed from all conditions of conjunction and disjunction, then one further eliminates the causes of birth and death, perfecting the nature of bodhi which is neither arising nor ceasing—the pure original mind, the eternally abiding fundamental awakening.
This follows from the preceding text which clarifies that although the two types of delusion arise from the entirety of Reality (*bhūtatathatā*), within delusion Reality remains eternally present.

Thus, one should know that if one now wishes to turn back from delusion and return to Reality, there is no other method than simply to distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction as well as non-conjunction;
thereby, the causes of the two forms of birth and death—segmented and transformational—will be extinguished, and Bodhi will be attained.

Only when one realizes that the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing is perfect within its own essence does one know that the pure original mind and original enlightenment are eternally present, and are not something obtained through cultivation or realization.

However, if one wishes to distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction and disjunction, one must penetrate this seeing-nature—the nature of seeing that is not seeing. For this seeing-nature is not merely clarity; it is...
The objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*), such as darkness, space, and so forth, are likewise not the subjective seeing part (*darśana-bhāga*), such as seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
Just as a true moon is never two moons, these two divisions—the seeing and the perceived—are distinct from the true moon and lack any inherent self-nature (*svabhāva*) apart from it;
they are like two moons, whereas in reality there is only one moon. When one knows that at the very moment of seeing the two moons, the true moon has never [actually] been divided.
Once one has broken [the illusion] and knows that these two moons are in reality but a single true moon, one will certainly not twist these two moons with the hand to force them together,
nor will one certainly pull these two moons apart with the hand to cause them to separate.

Just as ordinary beings greedily pursue forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles— like twisting the moon to make it appear as two— the followers of the Two Vehicles revile and abandon the three realms.
The five sensory desires within the realms are like pulling at the moon to make it appear; they cause all conditions to harmonize, which is the cause of *pariccheda-śīti* (segmented birth and death).
Conditions that do not harmonize are the cause of *pariṇāma-śīti* (transformative birth and death).

The tenth section refutes both harmony and disharmony to eliminate remaining doubts and reveal the nature of seeing as being free from faults and transcending non-dharmas, thereby manifesting realization through the principle of *dharmatā*. This has two parts: first, rebuking delusion; second, interrogating and refuting.
Now, first: Ānanda,
although you have previously realized that the wondrously luminous nature of original enlightenment is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it a spontaneous nature,
you have not yet clarified how this source of awakening is neither born from combination nor from non-combination.
Those who calculate based on "nature" (svabhāva) claim that apart from the aspect of characteristics (nimitta-bhāga), there exists a separately obtainable aspect of seeing (darśana-bhāga);

this constitutes the calculation of the non-Buddhist heretics regarding the self (ātman). Those who calculate based on "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) claim that apart from the aspect of characteristics, no separately obtainable aspect of seeing exists;

this constitutes the minor tenets of those who calculate based on non-self (anātman). Those who calculate based on "conjunction" (saṃghāta) claim that the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing intermingles with the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
The calculation of disharmony refers to the notion that the characteristics of arising and ceasing are entirely unrelated to the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing;

this belongs altogether to frivolous conceptualization. It arises because one fails to realize that the entirety of the real gives rise to delusion, and the entirety of delusion is itself the real—therein, in truth, there is no such thing as right or wrong.
Knowing that Ānanda must harbor this calculation, the Buddha therefore rebuked his confusion.
He then investigates and refutes it. This investigation and refutation consists of two parts: first, the refutation of conjunction; second, the refutation of non-conjunction.
Regarding the first [of these], there are two sections: first, restating the doubt; second, the actual refutation. Now, the first [section].
Ānanda, I now ask you again regarding the external objects previously mentioned;

you still harbor doubts based on the nature of all worldly delusions and the combination of various causes and conditions, wondering whether the mind that realizes Bodhi arises from a combination of factors.
What was stated above—that through false conjunction one is born and through false conjunction one dies—refers only to the nature of worldly delusive thoughts and causal conditions;
it concerns merely the affairs of the periphery of the eye's cataract. It does not mean that the wondrous mind of Bodhi which is realized also arises by depending on conjunction.
Since you have not yet awakened to the essence of the Bodhi-mind inherently realized by all sentient beings, you will surely harbor doubts.
Since it arises through conjunction, one must instead borrow the objects of the external world (*viṣaya*) in order to refute that [conjunction] as being non-existent.
This second section, "The Actual Refutation," is divided into two parts: first, the refutation of conjunction; second, the refutation of synthesis. Herein is the first.
Then, as for this wondrous, pure essence of seeing within you now: does it blend with light, or does it blend with darkness, or does it blend with openness, or does it blend with obstruction?
If it blends with light, then when you observe light and that light appears before you, where is the seeing mixed in?

Can the characteristics of the seeing be distinguished from the light, and what would the form of that mixture be? If it were not the seeing itself, how could it see the light? And if it were identical to the seeing...
What is meant by "seeing seeing"? It must be that seeing is complete and perfect. Where does clarity and seeing harmonize? If clarity were complete and perfect, it would not harmonize with seeing;
seeing would necessarily differ from clarity. If they were mixed, the nature of that clarity would be lost; if their names were mixed, the harmony between clarity and seeing would be lost.
This is not the true meaning. The same applies to darkness, openness, and all various obstructions.
"Harmony" is like water and earth mixing together. First, the four lines are listed in general; next, harmony is specifically examined and extensively refuted;
finally, the remaining three lines are concluded by analogy. The first section is understandable. Regarding the second section, the text says:
"If your visual essence were in harmony with light, then at the very moment you perceive light, when the manifestation of light is directly before you, where would there be any admixture?"
Is it the essence of seeing? If the essence of seeing were a distinct substance, then since these two things would each have their own separate parts, how could they be mixed?
Furthermore, what form would they take? If the light were not the essence of seeing, how could one see that light?
If the light were indeed the essence of seeing, how could that seeing itself be seen? Since the nature of seeing must be perfect and pervasive, where [could it be located]?
Furthermore, it would be even more evident that if the characteristic of light were already fully integrated, there would be no further room for the essence of seeing to harmonize with it;

how much less so when the essence of seeing must necessarily differ from the characteristic of light? Now, if you cause these two to intermingle, you lose both the nature of seeing and the characteristic of light.
Since their names are lost through this confusion—namely, the names "seeing" and "light"—you should know that they are not truly harmonized with the light.

To claim they are severed is contrary to reason; the conclusion can be inferred from this analogy. For if the faculty of vision and its clear manifestation were two distinct entities, one could speak of their "conjunction" or "union.
Since they are in fact nothing other than the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi, how can one speak of their conjunction or union?
Second, the refutation of union.
Furthermore, Ānanda, as for this wondrous, pure essence of seeing that you now possess: does it unite with light, or does it unite with darkness?

Does it unite with openness, or does it unite with obstruction? If it united with light, then when darkness arrives and the appearance of light has already ceased, this seeing would no longer unite with the various forms of darkness;
how then could it see the dark? If, when seeing the dark, it does not unite with the dark...
If it were conjoined with light, it should not see light; since it does not see light, how could it perceive light through conjunction?
To perceive light as distinct from darkness, that darkness, space, and all various obstructions would likewise be the same.

Regarding "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), it is like the joining of a box and its lid. First, the four propositions are listed in general; next, the conjunction is specifically examined and extensively refuted;
finally, the remaining three propositions are concluded by analogy. The first section is self-evident. As for the subsequent text:
"If the essence of seeing conjoins with light, then when darkness occurs and light ceases, this seeing should not further conjoin with darkness, for light and darkness are mutually exclusive."
Conversely, if a circle were different from a square, it could not become circular by being placed inside a square box. Since it does not conjoin with darkness, it should not perceive darkness;
yet if you grant that it perceives darkness, then it need not conjoin with darkness. By the same logic, one must grant that it need not perceive light even when conjoining with light.
Now, since you grant that it need not perceive light when conjoining with light, how is it that it currently encounters and conjoins with light?
At that time, would it still be the case that one perceives light but does not perceive darkness? The conclusion may be inferred by analogy. Second, refuting that [perception] is not a composite.
Part one: the opponent’s preliminary argument; part two: the refutation. This is the first.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as I reflect upon this wondrous source of awakening, it does not seem to be in union with the various sense-objects and the mental deliberations of the mind.
Previously, [the Buddha] rebuked the delusion regarding karma and simultaneously swept away the notion of non-union; now, although Ānanda accepts the preceding refutation of union...

Combining these texts, one further reflects that the nature of seeing—which is neither seeing nor non-seeing—is utterly transcendent beyond the two divisions of the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).
Therefore, it is said: "Is it not a case of non-conjunction with the various objective conditions, sensory objects, and mental deliberations?
Here, "objective conditions" refers to the object-aspect, and "mental deliberations" refers to the seeing-aspect. This is like hearing it said that the true moon is not the double moon.
Consequently, it is claimed that there is a distinct "true moon" apart from the two [reflected moons]. This refutation has two parts:
first, the refutation of non-duality; second, the refutation of non-union. Now, the first part.

The Buddha said: "You have now further stated that awakening is not a composite. I ask you again: this wondrous essence of seeing, if it is not a composite, is it because it does not combine with light?
Or does it not combine with darkness? Does it not combine with openness? Or does it not combine with obstruction?
If it did not combine with light, then there would necessarily be a boundary between seeing and light. You should observe closely: where is the light, and where is [the seeing]?"

This seeing exists within seeing; from what does its boundary arise? Ānanda, if within the limit of light there were no seer, then they would not reach one another, and one would not know where the characteristics of that light reside. How, then, could its boundaries be established?
It is the same for darkness, openness, and all various obstructions.
Two distinct objects must be in separate locations to be called "disharmonious. Since this is originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi, it is not two things at all;
thus, even to speak of harmony or union is already impossible, let alone to speak of disharmony. The meaning of the text is easy to understand.
Second, the refutation of non-conjunction:

Furthermore, this wondrous seeing-essence is not a product of conjunction; it does not conjoin with light, nor does it conjoin with darkness, nor does it conjoin with openness, nor does it conjoin with obstruction.
If it did not conjoin with light, then the nature of seeing and the nature of light would be mutually opposed, just as the ear is to light.

Since they do not touch or see one another, and one does not even know where the characteristic of light resides, how can one distinguish between what is reasonable for them to combine and what is unreasonable?
It is the same with darkness, openness, and all various obstructions.

Only when two things do not interfere with one another can they be said to be "not conjoined"; the textual meaning is thus clear. This concludes the section specifically addressing the essence of seeing (*darśana-viśuddhi*) to reveal the true nature.

Third, the universal traversal through the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) to realize the principle is divided into two parts: first, a general demonstration; second, a detailed explanation.
Now, first:
Ānanda, you have not yet clearly understood that all these floating dust-like, illusory, and transformative appearances arise from their very place and perish in that same place;
they are called "appearances" because they are illusory and false, yet their nature is truly the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity. This is true even for the five aggregates (*skandhas*).

The six sense bases, from the twelve *āyatanas* to the eighteen *dhātus*, arise falsely through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and are falsely said to cease when causes and conditions separate.
Yet they are utterly incapable of knowing that arising and ceasing, coming and going, are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha—eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading;
that this wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the true permanence, wherein one seeks coming and going, delusion and awakening.
Birth and death are ultimately unattainable.

This vehicle distinguishes the views through ten stages; by thoroughly understanding that the nature of seeing is itself the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity, one realizes that this essence universally extends to the nature of all phenomena, such that not a single thing is anything other than the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity. This constitutes the sixth stage, which reaches the very bottom.
The passages clarifying the nature extensively explain that all phenomena produced by causes and conditions are none other than emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Regarding "all floating dust-like illusory and transformative appearances," this refers universally to the faculties, bodies, and the physical world formed through the interaction of subject and object;
it means that the four sensory objects—form, odor, taste, and touch—are illusorily constituted as earth, water, fire, and wind.
The four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—illusorily constitute all sense organs, bodies, and the vessel-world;
these are precisely the dharmas produced by causes and conditions. "Arising in their own place" means they arise like flowers in the sky, having no place from which they come;
"extinguishing everywhere" means they perish in each moment, and in their extinction, there is no place to which they go. This is what I call emptiness.

Furthermore, regarding what is called "illusory appearances," this refers to the various distinctions between the ten realms of beings and their environments as spoken of according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

these are also termed "provisional names. As for the statement that "their nature is truly the essence of wondrous enlightened clarity," this means that every phenomenon is entirely the essence of the nature itself;
it is like the nature of flowers being identical to emptiness, or the nature of the second moon being identical to the true moon.
This is also called the meaning of the Middle Way. The phrase "likewise up to the five aggregates" reiterates the intent of the preceding text and provides a detailed explanation.
What are referred to as "various illusory appearances" are nothing other than the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.
What is called "illusory falsehood designated as appearance" is merely the conjunction of causes and conditions.
Falsehood has arising because of causes and conditions, and falsehood is called cessation when they separate;

that which is said to be its true nature—the wondrously enlightened and luminous essence—is simply because this arising and ceasing, coming and going, is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading nature of wondrous True Suchness.
That is to say, it arises where it is and ceases wherever it goes.
"Exhaustion" means that within the true and eternal nature, one seeks in vain for coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death, and finds nothing at all.
This concludes the brief explanation of the text. Now, this serves as the general outline for the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
It is precisely what is called the Great Dharani of Perfect Contact; by means of this, one opens up the perfect practice, and by relying upon this...
From this point forward, a more detailed explanation must be provided so that the essential purport of this sutra may be made fully manifest. This shall be presented in four points:
first, to clarify why the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are used to encompass all phenomena;

second, to clarify why the five aggregates are listed first rather than being established as a comprehensive system, while the seven elements are instead established separately as a comprehensive system.

The three knowledges (vidyā) discuss the aggregates, bases, elements, and realms of all ten dharma-realms; the four knowledges [discuss] that each and every aggregate, base, element, and realm is a great dhāraṇī.
Regarding the first meaning: the single true dharma-nature consists solely of suchness-reason and suchness-wisdom, which fundamentally lack any distinction between subject and object.
Because true suchness does not maintain its own nature, it gives rise to non-awakened thought.
Arising with ignorance, it subsequently forms the duality of subject and object;
all aspects of seeing are merely nominal and are called "mind," while all aspects of perceived phenomena possess substance that can be taken as objects and are all called "form.
One should know that these two dharmas, form and mind, do not transcend the one true suchness-mind; it is only because sentient beings dwell within deluded habituation that they [perceive] this form.

Regarding the two dharmas of mind, the delusions of sentient beings vary in their degree of gravity. If both delusions are equally light, the Buddha then teaches the dharma-gate of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);
this is because form and mind are conjoined, and by knowing that all things are merely name-and-form, one finds that "self" and "what belongs to self" are utterly unobtainable.
If the delusion regarding the mind is heavy while the delusion regarding form is light, the Buddha then teaches [the following].

The Dharma-gate of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) combines form (*rūpa*) and opens up the mind, causing one to seek "self" and "what belongs to self" within the deluded mind and find them utterly unobtainable.

If one is deeply deluded regarding form and lightly deluded regarding the mind, the Buddha then teaches the Dharma-gates of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) and the twelve sense fields (*dvādaśāyatana*),
which combine the mind and open up form, causing one to seek "self" and "what belongs to self" within deluded form and find them utterly unobtainable.
If both delusions regarding form and mind are equally heavy, the Buddha then teaches the Dharma-gate of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*).
This opens up both form and mind together, so that when one seeks the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) within these illusory forms and illusory minds, neither can be found.

Previously, this was used to reveal that the illusory has no intrinsic nature; now, returning to this very point, it reveals the nature of that which lacks intrinsic nature—which is precisely the true nature.
Furthermore, the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) do not exceed the two dharmas of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), differing only in their expansion and contraction.
The two terms "name-and-form" encompass all phenomena without exception;
likewise, the teaching of the five aggregates also encompasses all phenomena exhaustively, as do the twelve bases and the eighteen elements. All of them encompass every phenomenon.

How much more so when explained in full? Now that it has been fully explained that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are all the Tathāgata-garbha, what further dharma could there be that is not of the nature of the Garbha?
For this reason, these four categories are fully elucidated.
The second intention is that since the five aggregates and the eighteen elements have no distinct substance, the perfect penetration of the eighteen elements is itself the five [aggregates].

Regarding the *āyatana* (entrance) of the *skandha* (aggregate) of form: although it is said that the two dharmas of form and mind mutually open and close, this is merely a skillful means to explain away the deluded mind;
in reality, their nature has no opening or closing. Therefore, one dharma is all dharmas, and all dharmas are one dharma.
To speak of the *skandha* of form, for instance, the eighteen *dhātus* (realms) are all form. To speak of the *skandha* of sensation, the eighteen... [are all sensation].

If one speaks of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), then all eighteen realms (*dhātu*) are perception; if one speaks of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), then all eighteen realms are formations;

if one speaks of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), then all eighteen realms are consciousness. Furthermore, although the six sense objects (*viṣaya*) appear as external, they refer only to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*);
that is to say, they are the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of consciousness, which constitutes the activity of conditioning and flux.

That which is manifested by false conceptualization is precisely what is experienced by the six sense organs; therefore, each and every object (*viṣaya*) is fully endowed with the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Since the objects already fully possess the five aggregates, it is even more evident that each of the six sense organs and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) is likewise fully endowed with the five aggregates.

Consequently, in the first section on "Definitive Meaning" (*ekāntārtha*), the following text provides a general demonstration of the delusive characteristics of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) that must be destroyed.
Within the twenty-five methods of perfect penetration (*āveṇika-samyak-prativedha*), the true nature of the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) is specifically elucidated;

one should know that this must be clearly revealed because destroying the delusive appearances of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) is precisely destroying the delusive appearances of the eighteen realms, and revealing the true nature of the eighteen realms is precisely revealing the true nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Therefore, within the perfect penetration of the ear faculty, the clarification of turbidity and the destruction of the aggregates are fully explained.
After practicing with effort, one breaks through the five aggregates (*skandha*) and transcends the five turbidities;
since these remain the common application of the twenty-five kinds of perfect penetration (*pariṣuddhi*), it is unnecessary to establish a separate "perfect penetration of the five aggregates.

Furthermore, although the seven elements (*mahābhūta*) are listed separately, they do not constitute distinct dharmas outside of the aggregates, sense bases, fields, and elements; earth, water, fire, wind, and space [are all subsumed therein].
The five gross elements and the six sense organs of the superficial level—all of which, in their ultimate sense, are the five sense organs—are all the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing are the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Consciousness (*vijñāna*) constitutes the three aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Furthermore, among the six sense organs and six sense objects, all characteristics of solidity are collectively termed the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*); all characteristics of moisture are collectively termed the water element (*ap-dhātu*); and all characteristics of warmth... [are collectively termed the fire element].
The collective characteristic of movement belonging to the fire element is termed the wind element; the collective characteristic of emptiness is termed the space element;
the seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing of the six sense organs are collectively termed the organ element; and the six consciousnesses are collectively termed the consciousness element.
Since these eighteen realms and five aggregates are fundamentally not two distinct dharmas, they may nevertheless be distinguished as general and specific according to deluded perception.

Establishing these as the objects of contemplation within these seven great realms, one also universally shatters the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and universally transcends the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*);
for this reason, they must be established. Third, regarding why the ten dharma-realms all discuss the aggregates, bases, elements, and realms, there are three intentions:
first, to present their names collectively; second, to clarify that their characteristics are all empty and false; third, [to clarify]...

The nature of all things is truly real. First, to present their names collectively: the Buddha-dharmadhātu and the dharma-nature are neither with-outflows (*sāsrava*) nor without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
These are the so-called true, wholesome, and wondrous form; the foremost meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); supreme wondrous wisdom; true liberation; and the vision of omniscience.
They are the eighteen realms of the Buddha, namely the Buddha-eye, the Buddha-ear, and so forth, up to the Buddha-...

The Buddha’s mental faculty (*manas*) is the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done; the Buddha’s consciousnesses of form, sound, and so forth, up to the consciousness of the Buddha’s body, are the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation;
the Buddha’s mental organ (*manas-indriya*) is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the Wisdom of Equality.
The Bodhisattva’s dharma-realm consists of both the contaminated and the uncontaminated five aggregates, which are called "pure."
Impure forms, pleasure and non-pleasure, sensation, the self and the notion of no-self, formations, permanence and impermanence, consciousness—the Bodhisattva’s eighteen elements, namely:
the dharma-eye, the dharma-ear, and so on up to the dharma-mind; outflowing and non-outflowing forms, and so on up to outflowing and non-outflowing dharmas;
and outflowing and non-outflowing eye-consciousness, and so on up to outflowing and non-outflowing mind-consciousness—[these are the realms of] the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

The dharma-realm of the untainted five aggregates—namely, morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—up to the untainted eighteen elements such as the eye of wisdom and the ear of wisdom;
the dharma-realm of humans and devas consisting of the tainted good five aggregates up to the eighteen elements;
and the dharma-realm of the four evil destinies consisting of the tainted evil five aggregates up to the ten [elements].
Regarding the statement that the characteristics of the eight elements (*dhātu*) and so forth, as well as the two [aspects of] clarity and darkness, are all false and illusory:

each of the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) arises falsely through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and ceases falsely when causes and conditions disperse; these are merely illusory appearances designated by name.
Why is this said? Because the single mind is fully endowed with the seeds of both defilement and purity as its cause, and thus it manifests as defilement and purity.

All phenomena serve as conditions for the mind; apart from the mind, there are no other phenomena of defilement or purity, and apart from the phenomena of defilement and purity, there is likewise no other mind.
Not understanding this is called delusion. In relation to delusion, one speaks of awakening. Because of delusion, that which is not defiled becomes defiled;

because of awakening, that which is not pure becomes pure. If one is deluded regarding the causes and conditions of defilement, through their harmonious conjunction, the false appearances of the nine dharma-realms arise.
Then, as the characteristics of the Buddha-dharmadhātu cease in accordance with the cessation [of delusion], if one is deluded and separated from the causes and conditions of defilement,
the false characteristics of the nine dharma-realms (navadharma-dhātu) are said to cease; conversely, as the characteristics of the Buddha-dharmadhātu arise in accordance with their arising,

if one cultivates the awakening of virtue (*ādi-bodhi*) and achieves merit such that the pure causes and conditions harmonize and unite, the false characteristics of the Buddha-dharmadhātu arise, and thus the nine dharma-realms [cease].

When the characteristics [of the deluded states] are extinguished together with their nature, if the True Suchness of inherent virtue does not maintain its own nature, and one awakens to the causes and conditions of purity, becoming separated from the false, this is called the characteristic of the extinction of the Buddha-dharma-realm.
When these characteristics are extinguished, the characteristics of the nine dharma-realms arise accordingly;

thus, the three miserable realms are defiled while the human and celestial realms are pure, the out-flowing (sāsrava) is defiled while the non-out-flowing (anāsrava) is pure, and the partial truth is defiled while the... [is pure].
Provisionally, the two extremes are defiled while the Middle Way is pure; the partial Middle (but-madhya) is defiled while the perfect Middle (pariniṣpanna-madhya) is pure.

Furthermore, delusion regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is ignorance while wisdom regarding emptiness is awakening; attachment to emptiness is delusion while wisdom regarding the Path (*mārga-jñatā*) is awakening;

ignorance (*avidyā*) is delusion while the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is awakening. Such successive explanations concerning defilement and purity, as well as delusion and awakening, are transmitted in this manner.

The *Biographies* each contain accounts of union and separation; because these biographies speak of the delusory arising and delusory ceasing of phenomena, it is said that the characteristics of the ten dharma-realms, the aggregates (*skandhas*), bases (*āyatanas*), and elements (*dhātus*) are all empty and delusory. Question:

The characteristics of the nine realms may be called delusory, but the wondrous characteristics of the Buddha-realm are entirely in accord with the true nature. Why, then, are they also called delusory? Answer: This is said in contrast to delusion.
To speak of awakening in contrast to defilement and to speak of purity—though their essence is real, their names are illusory.

It is like the case of Yan-rda-da-da (Śaṇḍha), who suddenly realized that his own head was not obtained from the outside; though the head itself is real, the two words "realized" and "obtained" possess no reality whatsoever.
They are merely spoken of because of the loss and confusion [of the original state]. This is what is meant by saying that through the false, the real is revealed.
This refers to the statement that "the true and the false are identical, while both are false. Third, regarding the fact that their nature is entirely real:

the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) of each of the ten dharma realms are, in their very essence, the Tathāgata-garbha—eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading;
this is the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This nature is truly the essence of wondrous enlightened clarity. Take, for example, the form and mind of those in the hells.

In the six realms of mutual retribution, objects appear from nowhere and depart to nowhere; the various manifestations of suffering are distinct and vivid, yet they are all entirely what is manifested by the mind.
Since their substance is formed by the mind, are they not indeed the very identity of emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle?
If even the hells are the entire substance of the secret treasury of the three virtues, how much more so for the other destinies? A question is asked: Regarding the Buddha-realm...
Question: The nature may be called "true," yet the natures of the nine realms are entirely characterized by delusion and defilement;

how can they also be called "true"? Answer: When one’s vision is impaired by intoxication, the house appears to spin, yet the house itself does not actually spin. One who is deluded takes south for north, yet the north has not actually shifted.

A madman runs in terror, fearing he has lost his head, yet his head is not actually lost. One suspects a rope is a snake, yet the rope is originally hemp. Water completely turns into ice. (In these cases, the underlying reality remains unchanged despite the illusory appearances.)

Ice arises from original moisture; clear water becomes turbid. Since there is no water outside of the turbidity, it is said that "observing characteristics is originally false, while observing nature is originally true.
This means that if one observes the characteristics within nature, those characteristics are non-existent and thus not false;

therefore, all ten realms may be termed "false. Conversely, if one observes the nature within characteristics, that nature is non-existent and thus not true; therefore, all ten realms may be [realized as] suchness.
This is truly the essential core of the perfect cultivation and perfect realization. The two fundamental roots explained in the preceding text are not separate from the one mind;
the birth-and-death and nirvana explained in the subsequent text are nothing other than your own six sense faculties.
By extension, it may also be said that they are "only your six sense objects" and "only your six consciousnesses"—all of which refer to this very point. The connection is non-dual.
I do not decline this prolixity out of mere lightness; may the discerning reader grant me their trust.
As for the statement that each of the aggregates, bases, sense-fields, and elements of the Four Ming Mountains is itself a great *dhāraṇī*: take, for instance, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Since it is said to be fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), this *garbha*-nature has from the beginning possessed no divisions or portions, no spatial directions or boundaries, and cannot be dissected or torn apart.

Because it cannot be divided, any single atom of form that is cited is entirely constituted by the whole body of the *tathāgatagarbha* (storehouse nature), and is entirely endowed with its full function. As it is with one atom, so it is with all atoms;
as it is with one aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), so it is with all aggregates, sense-bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). It is, for example, like this:
The solar disc illuminates the four continents; each individual perceives the entire body of the sun.
That entire body of the sun perceived by each individual possesses the function of universally illuminating the four continents.
Furthermore, the full substance and great function of the sun perceived in even a single *kṣaṇa* extend through all time—past, present, and future.

This is the essence and function of the ultimate limit. Because raising any single form (*rūpa*) reveals the entire body and great function of the *tathāgatagarbha*, one attains the realization that form is the *dharmadhātu*.
All phenomena (*dharma*) converge in form; there is no convergence beyond this.

That sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) constitute the *dharmadhātu*, and likewise that the sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses (*indriya-viṣaya-vijñāna*) constitute the *dharmadhātu*—it is also thus. Furthermore, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)...

Regarding the "Great Dhāraṇī," although this sutra does not establish the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), the four teachings and the contemplations of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) all rely upon the five aggregates and are subsumed within the four foundations of mindfulness. Thus, the twenty-five kinds of perfect penetration are exhaustively and completely contained therein;
furthermore, the four kinds of foundations of mindfulness in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-jiao*) are all inconceivable, with each foundation of mindfulness being a single thought-moment.

Regarding all *smṛtyupasthānas*: even a single *smṛtyupasthāna* universally encompasses all Buddha-dharmas of the ten directions and three periods of time, and sustains all provisional and real meanings of the ten realms.
What dharma or meaning, then, would not be sustained by this as its *dhāraṇī*?
That the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) constitute the Great *Dhāraṇī* means that, for example, the eye base is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Because it is empty, it is called the Eye of Wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*); because it is provisional, it is called the Dharma-Eye (*dharma-cakṣus*); because it is the Middle Way, it is called the Buddha-Eye (*buddha-cakṣus*).
Therefore, it is said: "The entire earth is this mountain monk’s single eye. Aniruddha’s delight in seeing and illuminating is precisely the Vajra-samādhi;
it is by relying on this eye that one enters the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha and practices. It may also be said that this is...
The path to Nirvana through a single door has been traversed by countless Buddhas;

all Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this door, all Bodhisattvas of the present now each enter its perfect clarity, and those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this very dharma.
I too have realized it from within this; it is not only Naluduo—how could it be said that this principle resides solely in the faculty of hearing?

Specifically, because Ānanda has always been preoccupied with extensive learning, I now demonstrate to him the supreme and wondrous expedient of hearing, contemplating, and cultivating—namely, that one need only return home by way of the very path one is on, without changing the strings or altering the tracks.

If, however, the dualistic views of superiority and inferiority are not yet forgotten, one will fall entirely into the pervasive conceptualizations and delusions of ordinary beings; for the subtle essence of the meaning of "perfect penetration" lies precisely here.
One is all, and all is one. Thus, although the objects of contemplation differ, what distinguishes the truths revealed by them?
When deluded, one falsely speaks of six; yet upon awakening, they are not even called "one. The true nature of a single sense organ is the true nature of the other five organs;
it is also the true nature of the six sense objects, and it is also the true nature of the six consciousnesses.
Thus, regarding the true nature of the five aggregates and the seven elements, if one encounters a suitable recipient,
one may also utilize the case of Aniruddha to fully manifest the initial entry into the stream within the faculty of sight and the subsequent transcendence of the five turbidities;
one may likewise utilize the perfect penetration of the eye-faculty to fully manifest the thirty-two manifestations, the fourteen fearlessnesses, and the four inconceivable, effortless powers.
Wondrous Virtue, you should know that this is precisely the Great Dharani, the Vajra King, the Illusory and Inconceivable Mother of Buddhas, and the True Samadhi.
That the ear enters [this state] constitutes the Great Dharani, as detailed in the passage on the Perfect Penetration of the Great Being (Mahasattva);
one will know this for oneself upon reaching that text, so there is no need for further explanation. The same may be inferred for the nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as the six sense objects.
Regarding that which constitutes a great *dhāraṇī*: form-dust is itself emptiness; because it is empty within the provisional and the middle, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) form.
Because it is provisional, it is called "outflowing" (*sāsrava*) form. Because outflow-free form is itself the middle, it is called "truly good and wondrous form.
To take up the entire earth is to bring forth a single minute atom (*paramāṇu*); this single minute atom is the entirety of the Dharma-realm, the wondrous color of the Secret [Store].

The complete fulfillment of the thirty-two manifestations and so forth is as explained above; the remaining five sense objects may also be understood by analogy. That the six consciousnesses constitute the Great Dharani is as follows:
the eye-consciousness is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Because it is emptiness, it is called the "eye of all-knowledge" (*sarvajñājñāna*);

because it is the provisional, it is called the "eye of the knowledge of the paths" (*mārgajñatājñāna*); and because it is the middle, it is called the "eye of the knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*).
The visual faculty’s enlightened clarity is fully endowed with the thirty-two transformations, as described above; the remaining five consciousnesses may be understood by analogy.
Regarding the seven elements as the Great Dharani: the earth element is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Because it is emptiness, all things on the stage of cohabitation (*sahā-loka*) are level. Because it is the provisional, all things on the stage of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*) are... [all are level].
Because the level is itself the middle, the ground of retribution is entirely level.

The ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision of the wondrous lotus is fully endowed with the thirty-two manifestations and so forth, as explained above; the remaining six great elements may all be understood by analogy.
Therefore, the preceding text says: "Now, wishing to expound the Great Dharani, the various Samadhis, and the path of wondrous cultivation... This...

This is what is meant by that. If one attains realization through this assembly, more than half of the profound meaning of the cultivation of nature will have been understood. Second, the detailed explanation of the four [categories]:

first, explaining the nature of the five aggregates; second, explaining the nature of the six sense bases; third, explaining the nature of the twelve sense fields; and fourth, explaining the nature of the eighteen elements.
Regarding the first [of these], there are two parts: first, a general inquiry; second, a detailed explanation. Now, the first [part].
Ānanda, why are the five aggregates (skandhas) fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
In Sanskrit, *skandha* is translated as "aggregate" (*yùn*); in ancient translations, it was rendered as "covering" (*yīn*). "Aggregate" refers to accumulation; "covering" refers to concealment.

For ordinary beings, the five dharmas are accumulated, and their views and afflictions cover the Absolute Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). For the Two Vehicles, the five dharmas likewise [serve this function].
The five dharmas of the Bodhisattva of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are covered by an accumulation of dust as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

the five dharmas of the Buddha-realm of the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*) are covered by an accumulation of ignorance; and the five dharmas of the Dharma-realm of all sentient beings are covered by an accumulation of merit and wisdom in accordance with their nature (*dharmatā*).

All of these are termed "aggregates" (*skandha*) and are also termed "coverings" (*āyatana*). Second, the detailed explanation of the five [aggregates], beginning with the explanation of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

[The nature of the storehouse-consciousness] up to [the five consciousnesses]: the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) is precisely the nature of the storehouse-consciousness. Now, for the first [section]:
Ānanda, it is like a person with clear eyes who gazes at a bright, cloudless sky; there is only a vast, clear void, utterly devoid of anything.
For no reason, that person does not move their eyes, but stares fixedly until they become fatigued, whereupon they perceive something distinct within the empty space.
Furthermore, Ānanda, you should know that all these delusory flowers and the non-characteristic form-aggregate (rūpa-skandha) of total derangement are likewise so.
These delusory flowers, Ānanda, do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the eyes. If, Ānanda, they came from space, then having come from space, they would return to space.
If there were such coming and going, it would not be empty space; if it were not empty space, it would not be space.
One cannot admit that these floral forms arise and perish within [the body], just as Ānanda’s own body does not admit another Ānanda to arise and perish therein.
If the eyes were to produce them, then since they emerge from the eyes and return to the eyes, the nature of these flowers must likewise have emerged from the eyes;
therefore, there should be the faculty of vision [within them]. If there were such vision, then upon their departure, when they swirl in the void, they should naturally see their own eyes.
If there were no seer, then once [the flowers] had already vanished into space, the obstruction would immediately obscure one's own eyes;

furthermore, when seeing the flowers, the eyes should have been free of obstruction (and should rightly be called clear and bright). Why, then, is it that seeing the empty sky is instead called having "clear and bright" eyes?
Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
In each of these five sections on the aggregates (*skandha*), there are four parts.

From the beginning up to the phrase "it is likewise so," this raises the concept of phenomena produced by causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*), which generally indicates all the aforementioned superficial, delusory, and illusory appearances.
Next, from "these various wild flowers" up to "is called the eye of pure clarity," this clarifies that causes and conditions are themselves emptiness, which also serves as a general indication.

What is meant by "arising in its own place and perishing in that very place" is that within the true permanence of nature, one seeks in vain for coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death;

thus, nothing at all can be found. Thirdly, therefore, one should know that the single phrase "the aggregate of form is empty and false" clarifies that it is a provisional name based on causes and conditions;
this is a general indication of what is meant by "the false arising from the combination of causes and conditions."
