To define names by their meanings, there is not one instance where this fails; to define meanings by their names, there is not one instance where this errs. The textual meanings of today must be explained in this manner;

one must not be mired in the literal characters while remaining ignorant of the underlying principles. Furthermore, regarding the names of the eight consciousnesses, there are both general and specific applications.
Specifically, the first six are called *vijñānas* (consciousnesses) because they are capable of cognizing objects; the seventh is called *manas* (mind) because it is constantly deliberative.

Because it involves deliberation (*manana*), the eighth is called "mind" (*citta*); because all phenomena arise and gather therein, all eight are generally termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and designated as the "eight consciousnesses";
because they all possess the nature of deliberation, all eight are called "mind.

Since these are the sovereign minds (*cittarāja*), and because in the present context the two characters "consciousness" (*shí*) and "mind" (*xīn*) emphasize the character "consciousness," this refers specifically to the sixth consciousness, which has the nature of discernment (*prativijñapti*).
In these three characters, emphasis is placed on the character "nature" (xing);

thus, this eighth [consciousness] is precisely the faculty of thought (*manas*), which can be known through the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses], as they have been constantly dependent upon one another since beginningless time. This is indicated by the inclusion of the character "also" (jian).
This is the formal inquiry into whether the produced consciousness-mind and the producing faculty of thought are identical or different; thus, both the words and the logic are consistent.
This is consistent. Regarding the second [point], "the destruction of dharmas," this section directly clarifies that dharmas have no self-nature; how then could they produce consciousness?

For while the characteristics of the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) can all be pointed out and described, the dharma-object (*dharma-viṣaya*) is nothing other than the shadows of the arising and ceasing of those five sense-objects;
it has no separate self-nature. Therefore, the text now inquires: "You should first observe closely the nature of the dharma-object."

What shape could it have? If one is apart from the arising and ceasing of dharmas such as form and emptiness, movement and stillness, openness and obstruction, union and separation, then the dharma-object (dharmāyatana) can ultimately never be apprehended.
Its arising does not exceed the arising of these dharmas such as form and emptiness; its ceasing does not exceed the ceasing of these dharmas such as form and emptiness.
Where, then, could there be a self-nature or characteristic of a dharma-object? This is because of [the lack of such a basis].
Since the dharma-object (dharmāyatana) does not exist, what form would the consciousness that arises dependent upon that dharma-object take?
For this reason, Mahāmaudgalyāyana realized that the light of his mind was radiant, pervasive, pure, clear, sovereign, and fearless.
From the first fascicle, where the Buddha tells Ānanda, "We are of the same breath," up to this point, is the Tathāgata’s response and instruction.
The section on using phenomena to manifest principle is concluded. Second, the explanation that the nature is inherently endowed with characteristics is divided into three parts:
first, the question posed by the audience; second, the reprimand, admonition, and promise to teach; third, the formal exposition of the text. Now, the first part.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has always taught that all the various transformations in the world arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, specifically through the manifestation of the four great elements in combination. Why is it that the Tathāgata now rejects both 'causes and conditions' and 'spontaneity'?
I do not yet understand to which category this meaning belongs; I only pray that out of compassion you will grant us an exposition for the sake of all sentient beings."
The Middle Way of definitive meaning is the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

What has been explained above—revealing the principle through phenomena and correctly elucidating that the *tathāgatagarbha* remains unchanging while following conditions—is entirely the Middle Way of definitive meaning free from conceptual proliferation;
yet Ānanda has long been bound by the habitual tendencies of coarse and shallow causal terminology.
Falling back into the net of doubt, one might claim that this negates conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and thus inevitably falls into the emptiness of annihilationism (*uccheda-śūnyatā*);
therefore, one further seeks the revelation of the Middle Way and the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Tracing the origin of this state of doubt, there are three sources:

first, doubt arises proximately from the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), thinking: "If these are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor by spontaneous nature, then what of the sense faculties?"

First, although all things such as sensory dust and consciousness are entirely empty, they do not realize that what the Tathāgata reveals is the principle inherent within phenomena themselves, rather than a negation of phenomena in order to speak of principle.
Second, tracing back from the tenfold analysis of the seeing-nature, they give rise to doubt;
they claim that since this seeing-nature is neither sensation, hearing, cognition, nor vision, then both the seer and the seen are equally but illusory shadows, yet they fail to realize this.
What the Tathāgata has shown is precisely the eye that suffers from the cataract, not an eye sought outside of the cataract.
Next, [the interlocutor] raises doubts by refuting the three positions from seven perspectives, claiming:

"If the perceived object is neither the mind nor its cause, and both are rejected as being spontaneous, then the delusion would have no basis and the truth would have nothing to rely upon. Yet they do not realize that what the Tathāgata has shown is merely...

The reason why being free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is itself all phenomena (*dharma*) is as follows: secondly, [the Buddha] rebuked and cautioned [Ānanda], then granted permission for the proclamation.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Because you previously felt weary of and detached from the various Hinayana teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and resolved to diligently seek unexcelled Bodhi, I shall now reveal the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) for you."
How is it that you further entangle yourselves with the causes and conditions of worldly frivolous discourse and delusive thoughts?
Though you are learned, you are like a man who knows how to describe medicine but cannot distinguish it when the actual medicine appears before him. The Tathāgata says that you are truly pitiable.
Listen attentively now; I shall analyze and reveal this for you, so as to also benefit those who will practice the Mahāyāna in the future.
Having attained penetration into the true nature of reality, Ānanda silently accepted the Buddha’s holy command.
In this passage, from the beginning up to "truly worthy of compassion" is the word of reproach; "you should now listen attentively" is the word of admonition;
and "I shall, for your sake, [expound] up to the penetration of the true nature of reality" is the promise to proclaim. Ānanda silently accepted.
The Buddha’s holy intent is to lead [beings] by following the Buddha’s admonitions, listening with single-minded attention, and bringing the three karmas to stillness. The initial text states:

"You who previously felt weary of and sought to leave the various Hinayana teachings"—since Ānanda returned and saw the Buddha, he immediately and earnestly requested the expedient means for attaining Bodhi;
is this not because he grew weary of the Small Vehicle and sought the Great? Therefore, at this time, I act for his sake.

When you claim that the "Exposition of the Ultimate Truth" (paramārtha-satya) refers exclusively to each and every point previously explained—implying there is nothing other than the ultimate truth and no such thing as a gradual threefold truth (*krama-trisatya*)—your literal interpretation is as clear as the Buddha’s own words.
To attempt to allocate *śamatha* and so forth to the preceding text is, one might say, to openly cast a pitfall for the Buddha. Now...

One must further point this out individually so that the purport of the sutra becomes clear: at the very beginning of the sutra, the "ever-abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature" is proclaimed;

this is precisely the admonition to maintain a direct mind and right mindfulness toward *tathatā* (Suchness), which constitutes the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the true lifeblood of the teaching.
Next, wishing to successively shatter deluded attachments, the name of the "Great Samādhi" is first proclaimed to enable those of sharp faculties.
When the false attachments are shattered, the essential substance is definitively and perfectly revealed; when the mind is sought, it is utterly unfindable.

Since this mind is vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, how could it not be the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)? Next, it is clarified that the two kinds of fundamental [ignorance] are not separate from the one mind;
how could this not be the ultimate truth? Next, it is clarified that all phenomena that arise are manifested solely by the mind; how could this not be the ultimate truth?

In the second section on the Meaning of Truth, it is clarified that the nature of seeing is the mind and not the eye; yet this nature of seeing is fundamentally without movement, nor does it expand or contract.
It is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, nor does it increase or decrease. It is fundamentally not something to be returned to, nor is it definitively a material object.
It is fundamentally without expansion or contraction, nor is it discontinuous. It is fundamentally neither "seeing" nor "non-seeing," and it is fundamentally not self-originated.
Yet, causes and conditions are fundamentally neither light nor darkness, nor form nor emptiness; perception, hearing, cognition, and seeing are fundamentally neither conjoined nor unconjoined.
To state it in brief: to be free from all marks is itself all dharmas—how could this not be the ultimate truth?
Next, to clarify that the aggregates, bases, entrances, and realms are themselves empty, themselves provisional, and themselves the Middle—how could this not be so?
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is precisely the Middle Way, the definitive meaning, and the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
To abandon this and seek the definitive meaning of the Middle Way elsewhere is much like describing medicine while remaining ignorant of the true remedy;
this is because one possesses hearing but lacks wisdom (*śruta-viprayukta-prajñā*). Therefore, he again exhorts them to listen attentively, so that their efforts may not be in vain.
The true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of hearing is also the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and also the definitive meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

Because it is without marks and yet not without marks, it is called the "true mark. Having already deeply clarified the principle that marks are non-marks, [the text] now further clarifies the principle that non-marks are marks, so that one may attain thorough penetration. Third, the actual exposition for the sake of revealing [this truth].

Second, first, restating the doubt to provide a general indication; second, proceeding through the Great [Elements] to specifically reveal [the truth]. Regarding the first of these two, there are two parts:
first, refuting delusion by means of the dharmas; second, revealing the principle by means of a metaphor. Now, for the first:
"Ānanda, as you have said, the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world, Ānanda."
If the nature of those great elements were not a composite, they could not intermingle with one another,
just as empty space does not mix with forms. If they were indeed composites, they would be like transformations that arise and cease in continuous succession—
birth and death following birth and death, life and death following life and death— like a whirling firebrand that never rests.

This passage cites their false conceptualization in order to refute it. The causes and conditions of conjunction taught by the Tathāgata are intended solely to demonstrate that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

If one falsely conceptualizes the four great elements as having substantial reality and claims that all phenomena are produced through their conjunction, how would this differ from the heterodox views of the non-Buddhists? Therefore, he now cites and refutes this [position] first.
Having refuted the notion that [the elements] are not a composite, one next refutes the notion that they are a composite.

Failing to realize the nature of the unchanging following conditions, one must inevitably reckon that the substance is not a composite; failing to realize the nature of the unchanging while following conditions, one will inevitably shift to reckon that it is a composite.
Now, by refuting both, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is secretly revealed as being precisely the true nature of the four great elements.
That the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) lack intrinsic nature is precisely the true nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. First, to refute the notion that they are not a composite:
if one were to maintain that the essential substance of those great elements is necessarily non-composite, then each individual element would be unable to intermingle with the others;
just as space does not intermingle with material forms, there would then be no great elements at all.
If the nature of earth is always solid and does not become moist when meeting water, and the nature of water is always cold and does not become hot when meeting fire,
and so forth, how could these produce and sustain the myriad things? If one calculates that the natures of those great elements must necessarily be in a state of combination,

then they would be identical to various transformations where beginning and end mutually constitute one another, and birth and cessation continue in succession, such that having arisen, they arise again.
Dying and being born again, from birth to birth and from death to death, it is like a whirling firebrand that never ceases;
thus, there would be no substance to the great elements. If earth encounters water, it loses its solidity; if water encounters fire, it loses its moisture.
Once their own natures are lost, by what means could they give rise to and produce all things? Such [would be the consequence].
Is this not indeed frivolous conceptualization and deluded thought? Second, the principle is revealed through analogy:
Ānanda, it is like water forming ice, and ice returning to water.

This follows the preceding text’s refutation of his false calculations, demonstrating generally that while there is no change as conditions follow, there is also no change that does not follow conditions.
The principle of conditions is the "seven great elements" (mahābhūta); this must be noted as the general analogy for the totality.

The analogy of ice and water illustrates the aspect of following conditions (*anuparivartin*), while the fact that ice and water share the same nature of moisture illustrates the unchanging nature (*avikāra*).

Thus, when the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) follows defiled conditions to form the nine realms within the Buddha-dharma realm, the seven great elements serve as an analogy, just like water.
When ice is formed, if the nature of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) follows pure conditions, it manifests as the Buddha-realm within the nine dharma-realms.

The seven elements (dhātus) are illustrated by the analogy of ice returning to water; there is only the single nature of moisture. That the characteristics of ice and water differ while the nature remains one is called "the unchanging following conditions.
That although ice and water differ, the nature of moisture is non-dual is called "the following of conditions without changing. Because it follows conditions, it is...
Because they do not change, the seven great elements are none other than the true nature, perfectly interfused and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm;
because they do not change while simultaneously following conditions, the seven great elements all manifest according to the mind, in accordance with measure, and in conformity with karma.
Second, the detailed exposition of each element specifically reveals this: it demonstrates that following conditions does not change the unchanging, and the unchanging follows conditions.

The hidden nature (*tathatā-garbha*) of these conditions is precisely the true nature of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), which is the Dharma-gate of inherent presence (*xingju*) and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

One must understand that the seven elements are nothing other than the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and realms (*dhātu*); they differ only in their classification, combination, expansion, and abbreviation.

Specifically, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is expanded into the first five elements, while the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is designated as the element of the sense organs (*indriya-mahābhūta*), and the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are combined [into the element of objects].

Consciousness constitutes the element of consciousness; furthermore, the six sense objects are arranged horizontally as the five preceding elements, the six sense organs are subsumed into the element of the organs, and the six consciousnesses are subsumed into the element of consciousness.
Once one knows that these seven elements are nothing other than the Dharma, one must allow these two texts to mutually integrate through their sequence and position;
only then will the gate of perfect enlightenment open. The previous section clarified that the aggregates, bases, fields, and elements are all the Tathāgata.
One must know that the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; thus, the seven elements (mahābhūta) are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

Later, it is clarified that within the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, the seven elements are inherently endowed, pure, perfectly interfused, and pervading the entire Dharma-realm, manifesting according to karma.
One should know that this is precisely the inherent endowment of the aggregates, sense bases, and realms within the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is pure.
The perfect interfusion and universal pervasiveness throughout the Dharma-realm manifest according to karma;

that is to say, the principle within phenomena does not lack even the slightest aspect that is not subsumed within phenomena, and the phenomena within principle do not lack even the slightest aspect of phenomenal form that is not subsumed within principle.
Thus, a single hair can swallow the vast ocean, a mustard seed can contain Mount Sumeru, and in every infinitesimal moment of existence...
The subtle principle of the mind-nature throughout a thousand *kṣaṇas* and ten ages reaches its ultimate here;
as the three truths and the single truth leave no further residue, Ānanda attains great enlightenment and suddenly realizes the Dharma-body.

The subsequent questions posed by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra do nothing more than resolve the doubts and obstructions of those with heavy attachment to dharmas. Failing to understand this, some scholars have [misinterpreted it as]...

Next, regarding the third truth, some take this to refer to both the empty and non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, while others point to this alone as the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, reserving the non-empty *garbha* and so forth for what appears later in the text.
This is a misrepresentation of the Perfect Teaching and a slander of the Buddha’s words—how tragic, how tragic!
The text is divided into seven parts; the first clarifies that the nature of the *garbha* is identical to the nature of the earth element (up to section seven).

The clarification of the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is the very nature of the great element of consciousness (*vijñānamahābhūta*). This section consists of three parts: first, the refutation of false attachments; second, the revelation of the true nature (*dharmatā*);
and third, the censure of delusion. Now, for the first part: "Observe the nature of earth:
when coarse, it is the great earth; when subtle, it is minute dust, down to the *paramāṇu* (the smallest particle). Analyze that ultimate atom..."
The characteristic of the limit of form is composed of seven parts; if one further analyzes it down to the *paramāṇu* (the subtle atom), it is in essence emptiness.
Ānanda, if this *paramāṇu* were analyzed until it became empty space, you should know that empty space gives rise to the characteristics of form.
You have now asked how the various transformed phenomena of the world arise through combination; consider for a moment: how many [parts] does this single *paramāṇu* of dust employ?

If empty space exists through combination, it should not be formed by the aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Furthermore, if an atom were analyzed and dissolved into space, by how many material characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) would space itself be composed?
If it were combined with matter, then that which is combined would be matter, not space;
if it were combined with space, then that which is combined would be space, not matter. Matter may still be analyzed, but how can space be combined?
Within the ten dharma realms, all internal and external forms are collectively termed the earth element; for now, we shall distinguish them based on external forms as they appear before us.
The analysis of form into seven parts is merely a false calculation of non-Buddhist outsiders.

Because they do not realize that the nature of form is itself the *tathāgatagarbha* (store-nature), which is fundamentally non-dual and indistinguishable from emptiness, they falsely claim that one must first analyze form before it can return to emptiness. Now...
Therefore, I shall set forth [your position] and refute it: You claim that you agree with the calculations of common outsiders regarding the causes and conditions of combination;

you observe this earth as having a false nature, asserting that by analyzing matter down to its coarsest state, it becomes the great earth, and by analyzing matter down to its subtlest state, it becomes minute dust, until reaching the *paramāṇu* (ultimate atom), where one analyzes the boundary-mark of that extreme subtle matter into seven parts.
If that which is composed of parts were further analyzed down to the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal atom), would it then truly become emptiness?
If these *paramāṇu* particles could indeed be analyzed into empty space, one should know that within this empty space, material forms (*rūpa*) should likewise arise.
The following text will correctly refute this; the passage can be understood as a whole. The phrase "matter can still be analyzed" is also [to be understood in this context].
This is to comply with their mental calculations and temporarily let them be;

yet in reality, the coarse is the Dharma-realm and the subtle is also the Dharma-realm—all are manifestations that accord with the mind, respond to conditions, and follow karma. The coarse does not depend on combination, and the subtle does not depend on analysis.
Second, to reveal the nature of reality:
You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, essential form is true emptiness and essential emptiness is true form;

it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they can know, and manifesting in accordance with their karma.
This correctly demonstrates that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is precisely the true nature of form and also the true nature of emptiness;
therefore, form and emptiness are none other than this nature and none other than this reality.
Form does not exist only through conjunction, nor does emptiness arise only through analysis; it is simply because, while conforming to conditions, it is eternally unchanging. Thus...
Because it does not change while constantly following conditions, and because it follows conditions while remaining unchanged, it is called "Thus" (*tathā*).

Because it does not change while following conditions, it is called "Coming" (*āgata*). Because its nature inherently possesses the functional capacities for the ten realms—both defiled and pure—it is called the "Treasury" (*garbha*).
Because there is no phenomenon that is not contained within it, it is named the "Middle" (*madhya*). Because it has no fixed nature...
The nature of these is precisely the true nature of form and emptiness within the ten dharma realms; this nature cannot be altered, and its essence is devoid of falsehood.

Therefore, each and every one is the nature and is truly real. Because the forms of the ten dharma realms are all entirely free from faults and transcendent of non-existence, their essence is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*), and thus they are called "pure and fundamentally so. Because the forms of the ten dharma realms are each established vertically...

Because it exhausts the horizontal and pervades the vertical, it is called "pervading the dharma-realm. Now, the true nature of form and emptiness is precisely the intrinsically endowed, pure, and original nature;
this is the substance of nature. Its pervasion of the dharma-realm is the capacity of nature. This demonstrates that the essence remains unchanging while following conditions.
It responds to the deluded or awakened minds of sentient beings across the ten dharma-realms, manifesting according to what they perceive, whether defiled or pure.
The measure of purity follows the various karmas of good and evil within the ten realms, manifesting as the various forms of suffering and pleasure across those ten realms;

this demonstrates the function of the unchanging following conditions. That which follows conditions is precisely the unchanging, just as the moist nature of ice and water remains forever unchanged from beginning to end.
That which is unchanging is precisely that which follows conditions, just as the ice and water are always nothing other than the moist nature.
Just as ice forms from water due to conditions such as cold, yet its moist nature does not diminish,

so too the illusory forms of birth and death within the nine realms arise through conditions of delusion and defilement, while the nature of the treasury remains undiminished. Just as ice turns back into water due to conditions such as warmth, yet its moist nature does not increase,
so too one attains the true goodness of the Buddha-realm through conditions of awakening and purity, while the nature of the treasury remains unchanged.

Because the nature of the marvelous form does not increase as it is concealed within, we know that this serves as both a general and a pervasive metaphor for the essence and function, as well as the nature and characteristics, of the seven great elements.
Now, each passage must be interpreted by returning to the meaning of these metaphors; thus, the underlying intent will become clear.
Third, the refutation of delusion:
The ignorance of the world that takes delusion as its causal condition, as well as the notion of inherent nature, are all merely conceptual constructions and calculations of the conscious mind;
they exist only as verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
The "world" refers universally to the sentient beings of the nine dharma-realms.

Because they have not collectively realized this wondrous nature—which remains unchanging while following conditions, and which follows conditions while remaining unchanging—each harbors two kinds of deluded calculations: those based on causes and conditions, and those based on spontaneity.
Yet these deluded calculations are merely frivolous discourse; ultimately, they possess no real meaning that can be pointed out or articulated.
Generally, those in the mundane world outside the Buddhist teachings may reckon various false causes and conditions, such as time, direction, atoms, or Maheśvara;

or they may reckon the principle of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the divine self (puruṣa) as being spontaneous. These have already been refuted by the teaching of the arising of phenomena through causes and conditions as elucidated in the Tripitaka (the *Āgama* teachings).
Furthermore, there are those of dull faculties—Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—who receive the Buddha’s verbal instructions on causes and conditions.
Failing to comprehend the intent of the Tathāgata’s teaching— that the distinctions between the causes and effects of the mundane and supramundane,
as well as suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path, all belong to dependent origination— and that the Nirvāṇa of partial truth revealed by the Truth of Cessation is,

by its very nature, without arising or ceasing and is thus termed "spontaneous" (svayambhū)— this is the explanation of dependent origination as emptiness according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), which has already been refuted. Furthermore...

There are those of dull faculties among the three vehicles who, having received the Buddha’s teaching on "immediate emptiness," fail to comprehend the underlying intent of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.
Taking the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—to be entirely illusory, they designate them as "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya).

Yet, because the ultimate truth is unborn, suffering cannot oppress them and the origin cannot defile them; thus, they further designate this as "spontaneity" (svabhāva). This is what is elucidated by the Distinct Teaching (bhedavyavasthāna) regarding causes and conditions.

The provisional designation has already been refuted; furthermore, there are bodhisattvas of dull faculties who, having received the Buddha’s teaching through provisional words, do not comprehend the intent of the Tathāgata’s preaching.
They hold that the nine realms of birth and death are summoned by ignorance and thus name this "causal condition" (*nidāna*);
yet they maintain that the Buddha-nature of the "but-midway" (*zhong*) is immovable and unchanging, like the moon outside the clouds, and thus still name it "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*). This...

Only when the conditions and causes elucidated in our teaching are fully understood and exhausted without remainder can one realize that, prior to this, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision had not been opened;

thus, the nine realms are all designated as the "conscious mind," which is like water turning into ice. If the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*) is first opened, then the conscious mind immediately becomes the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (the wisdom of wondrous observation), just as ice turns back into water.
All subsequent cases should be understood accordingly. Only... (Note: The final character "惟" (*wéi*) appears to be a concluding particle or a marker for the following section.)

Because the nature of that storehouse is the nature of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder awakened to it; as defilements dissolved and wisdom became perfect, he attained the Unsurpassed Way.
Second, clarifying that the nature of the storehouse is the nature of the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*): First, the refutation of false attachments;
second, the manifestation of the rational nature; third, the censure of delusion. Now, the first [section].
Ānanda, the nature of fire has no self; it depends upon various conditions. Observe those households within the city who have not yet eaten:
when they wish to cook their food, they hold a magnifying lens (*ādityakānta*) in their hands and seek fire from the sun.

Ānanda, if you would call this "harmony" (*saṃghāta*), then consider me and you, along with these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus—now forming a single community. Although the community is one, if one were to interrogate it...
Each of its roots has its own body and possesses its own lineage and name of origin, such as Śāriputra’s Brahmin lineage, Uruvilvākāśyapa’s lineage, and so on, up to Ānanda’s Gautama clan.
(Only in this way can it be called "conjoined. Ānanda, if this nature of fire exists because of conjoining, then when that hand holds a mirror toward the sun, [the fire would arise].
As for this fire: does it emerge from the mirror, or does it emerge from the tinder, or does it come from the sun?
Ānanda, if it comes from the sun, it should be able to burn the tinder in your hand by itself; furthermore, all the forests where the sun passes should be consumed by fire.
If it emerges from the mirror, it should be able to ignite the tinder upon emerging from the mirror itself; why then does the mirror not melt? (Yet now) it merely follows your hand as you grasp it.

Since there is as yet no sign of heat, how could there be melting? If fire were produced from the tinder, why would it require the meeting of the sun’s light and the brilliance of the mirror before the fire arises?
You should observe closely: the mirror depends on the hand, the sun comes from the sky, and the tinder grows from the earth;
from where does the fire travel here? The sun and the mirror are far apart; they are neither blended nor joined, so the fire-light should not [arise from them].
There is no arising from self-existence.
Within the ten dharma realms, both internal fire and external fire are collectively termed the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*). For now, let us examine this based on the external fire manifest before us.

Regarding the selflessness of the nature of fire: this refers to the fact that the nature of delusion fundamentally lacks its own intrinsic substance, intended to refute the views of ordinary beings and non-Buddhists regarding the nature of things.

Regarding the phrase "reckoned as such and dependent upon various conditions," this first cites the objective realm of the primary causes and conditions, and subsequently clarifies their lack of intrinsic nature.
The passage beginning with "Ānanda, that which is called 'conjunction'" cites the characteristics of conjunction to, by way of contrast, reveal the nature of non-conjunction.
This analogy not only serves to contrast and reveal the fire element (*tejas*), but also universally illustrates the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) discussed below.
This is because the meaning is truly interconnected, even though the phrasing is not repeated. *Ādityakānta* (yang sui) refers to a fire-gathering mirror. *Uruvilvā* means "Pumpkin Grove";
it is the name of the Venerable One. *Kāśyapa* means "Tortoise Clan"; it is the surname of the Venerable One.
*Gautama* means "Supreme on Earth" or "Solar Lineage"; it is the secular surname of the Tathāgata.
The mirror is the *ātapamanthāna* (sun-stirring lens); "curved" (*yū*) refers to the appearance of being bent or winding. It is illogical that fire-light could arise spontaneously from nothing;
this single phrase simultaneously refutes the doctrine of non-conjunction. Second, it reveals the principle of nature (*dharmatā*).
You still do not understand that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true fire;

it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It responds according to the minds of sentient beings and manifests in accordance with the capacity of what they know. Ānanda, you should know that when a person holds a mirror in one place, fire appears in that one place;

if one were to hold mirrors throughout the entire Dharma-realm, fire would arise filling the whole world. When such manifestations arise everywhere throughout the world, how could there be [any lack of them]?
"Directions and locations manifest according to karma.
This reveals that the ten dharma realms are inherent within the nature; both fire and space are the nature itself and are all true.

Because they follow conditions while remaining eternally unchanging in their own essence, they can manifest according to the mind and respond to measures, appearing in accordance with karma. This is precisely the aspect of unchanging permanence.
According to conditions, there arise the various distinctions of the ten dharma-realms; the rest is as explained above.
Third, the refutation of delusion:
that the world takes ignorance and delusion as causes and conditions, or [asserts] a nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), is entirely the conceptualization and calculation of the conscious mind.
All verbal explanations are devoid of ultimate meaning.

The principle has been explained above: because the nature of the *garbha* (storehouse) is itself the nature of the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*), Ucchuṣma realized this and gave rise to great jewel-flames, attaining unsurpassed enlightenment.
Third, the nature of the *garbha* is itself the nature of the water element (*ap-dhātu*). First.
This section consists of three parts: first, the refutation of false attachments; second, the manifestation of the rational nature; and third, the censure of delusions. Now, for the first part:
Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing are without constancy.
For instance, in the city of Śrāvastī, there were the mahāsiddhas Kapila, Kāpya, and Padma-Hrasvaja, among other great illusionists, who sought the essence of the moon to use in their concoctions.
Regarding the magical elixir, masters such as these take a *fangzhu* (a concave mirror) in their hands during the daytime of the bright fortnight to catch the water from the moon.
Does this water emerge from within the pearl, does it exist spontaneously in the air, or does it come from the moon?

Ānanda, if it comes from the moon, then since it can cause the pearl to emit water even from a great distance, all the trees and forests through which it passes should likewise discharge streams; if they were to flow, why wait for anything else?
The clear water produced by the *fangzhu* (concave mirror) does not flow from the moon;

yet if it emerges from the pearl, then this pearl should constantly produce water—why wait for the midnight hour to receive the white moon? If it were born from space, then since the nature of space is boundless, water would likewise be limitless;
from humans to devas, all would be submerged in a vast deluge. How, then, could there still be those who travel by water, land, or air?
Examine this further with careful attention: the moon ascends from the sky; the pearl is held in the hand; the water-dish was originally set out by a person;

and as for the water, from what direction does it flow here? The moon and the pearl are far apart; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the crystal-like water arose of its own accord without a source.

Within the ten dharma realms, both internal water and external water are collectively termed the water-element (*āpas-mahābhūta*). For now, let us examine it in terms of the external water present before us.

The nature of water is not fixed; at times it flows, and at times it ceases. This also points to the lack of intrinsic substance in the nature of delusion (*mṛṣā-svabhāva*) in order to refute externalist calculations.
As in the passage from "In the city of Śrāvastī" onwards, which cites causes and conditions as the objective sphere, the phrase "Is this water... and so forth clarifies [the point].

The absence of intrinsic nature has already been extensively refuted regarding the combination [of elements]. Subsequently, the phrase "it is not possible for water-crystal to exist independently" further refutes the non-combination [of elements].
That which is called "water in the moon" is the lunar essence (*soma-rasa*); it occurs precisely on the night of the full moon when the moon's orb is in the sky.
It is called the "white moon. During the day, one takes water from the *fangzhu* (the "dew-dropping pearl"), the meaning of which can be understood from the context.
Second, it reveals the nature of reality:
You still do not know that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of water is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true water;

it is pure and fundamental, pervading the Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they can know—when one place grasps a pearl, water flows forth from that place.
Pervading the entire dharma-realm and filling it, the ten realms of existence arise throughout all worlds according to the karma of beings; how could they have a fixed location?
This clarifies that the ten realms are inherently complete within the nature. Water and space are both the nature and both are true;
though they follow conditions, they are eternally self-unchanging. Thus, because they are unchanging yet ever-folllowing conditions, there arises the differentiation of the ten realms of water.
Third, the refutation of delusion:
Ignorance in the world takes delusion as its cause and condition, or is considered to be of a spontaneous nature;
these are all merely conceptual constructions and calculations of the conscious mind, existing only as verbal expressions and devoid of any real meaning.

Because the nature of the treasury (garbha-dhātu) is precisely the nature of the water element, the youth Candraprabha realized it as a single flavor, attained the endurance of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and caused it to circulate. Regarding the four clarifications, the nature of the treasury is here the nature of the wind element. This means that the Tathāgata-garbha is the source from which all phenomena arise. Furthermore, the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata-garbha is the support for the arising of all dharmas. This indicates that the Tathāgata-garbha is the fundamental basis upon which all things depend. Moreover, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata-garbha is the storehouse of all seeds. Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance, for its movement and stillness are not constant.

When you regularly adjust your robes upon entering the great assembly, the corner of your *saṃghāṭī* moves and brushes against those beside you, creating a slight breeze that sweeps over their faces. From where does this wind arise?

Does it emerge from the corner of the *kaṣāya*, or does it originate from empty space, or is it produced on the faces of those people? Ānanda, if this wind were to emerge from the corner of the *kaṣāya*...

When you are wearing this robe, its fabric flutters and should therefore be separated from your body. Now, as I preach the Dharma within this assembly, my robe hangs down; look at my robe—where is the wind?
It cannot be that the robe contains a place where the wind is hidden. If it were produced from empty space, why would there be no breeze when your robe is motionless?
Since the nature of space is eternally abiding, the wind should be constantly arising; yet when there is no wind, [why does it not blow]?

If empty space were to be extinguished, one could see the extinction of the wind; what would be the appearance of the extinction of space? If there were arising and ceasing, it would not be called "empty space.
Being called "empty space," how could the wind emerge from it? If the wind arose of itself, then when you are brushed by it, the wind would have to arise from that very face being brushed.
It should then brush you yourself; why do you instead brush your own clothes? Examine this closely: it is you who are adjusting your clothes.
The face belongs to that person, while empty space is quiescent and does not participate in movement; from which direction, then, does the wind come to stir here?
Since the nature of wind and the nature of space are distinct, they are neither blended nor joined; yet it cannot be that the nature of wind exists spontaneously without a source.

The internal and external movements within the ten dharma realms are collectively termed the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*). Now, for the time being, we shall examine this based on the external movement manifest before us.
That the nature of wind has no substance and that its movement and stillness are not constant precisely reveals that delusion lacks self-nature; this refutes externalist calculations.

Ānanda, emptiness has no form; it is manifested through matter. For example, in the city of Śrāvastī, at a place far from the river, there were Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, as well as Pahlavas and Caṇḍālas, who had recently established a new residence and dug a well in search of water.
When they had excavated one foot of earth, there was one foot of empty space within it; it was thus.
Even when one excavates the earth to a depth of one zhang, one regains one zhang of empty space within; the shallowness or depth of this space corresponds exactly to how much has been excavated.
Does this emptiness arise because of the earth being removed, or does it exist because of the act of digging? Or does it arise spontaneously without a cause?
Ānanda, if this emptiness arose spontaneously without a cause, why was there no obstruction before the earth was dug? Why did one see only the great earth?
It is utterly devoid of penetration. If it emerged because of the earth, then at the time the earth emerges, one should see the empty space enter.

If the earth emerged first and there was no entry of empty space, how could empty space emerge because of the earth? If there is neither entering nor exiting, then empty space and the earth must fundamentally have no different cause.
If they are not different, they are the same; thus, when the earth emerges, why does the empty space not emerge as well? If it were to emerge because of the digging, [the same logic would apply].
If the empty space emerges from the excavation, it would not have emerged from the earth; yet the earth does not emerge without the excavation, for the excavation itself emerges from the earth.

How, then, can you see the empty space? Examine this again with utmost precision, observing with the most careful scrutiny: the excavation follows the movement of the hand in various directions, while the earth shifts according to the ground.
Thus, from what source does this empty space emerge? The excavation and the empty space—whether void or solid—are not mutually functional; they neither blend nor combine.
Space should not be thought to emerge from nowhere on its own.

Within the ten dharma realms, both internal and external space are collectively termed the "great element of space" (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*). For now, we shall examine this specifically with respect to external space as it appears before us.
That the nature of space is formless and is manifested through matter precisely clarifies that space lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), thereby refuting external [realist] views.

This is a summary; as in the case of Śrāvastī, we shall now again cite the causes and conditions for the arising of phenomena to extensively clarify that these empty things are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). The *kṣatriya* caste refers to the royal lineage;

the *brāhmaṇa*—translated here as "Pure Descendants" or "Brahmacārins"—refers to those like the families devoted to Confucian studies in this land; the *vaiśya* refers to merchants; and the *śūdra* refers to farmers.
Now, *pola-due* (Pulinda) here means "sharp faculties," referring to those such as the nine schools of artisans;

*caṇḍāla* here means "executioners," referring to those of the lowest castes such as butchers, tavern-keepers, and prostitutes. The shallowness or depth of space corresponds to the amount of soil from which it emerges;
this is what is called "dharmas produced by causes and conditions. Next, we clarify that within these causes and conditions there is no inherent nature.
The three propositions are collectively challenged; first, the absence of a cause is refuted.

Since "absence of cause" is equivalent to spontaneity (*svabhāva*), and because sentient beings mostly impute causal conditions to the four great elements while mostly impute spontaneity to the element of space, this [absence of cause] is refuted first.

Next, within the section on the emergence from the causal realm, the primary thesis is refuted first; then, in the passage beginning with "If there is no entering or exiting," its transformation is refuted.
The objection is as follows: if one calculates that emptiness has no coming or going, then prior to the emergence of the earth, emptiness must already exist;
since emptiness and the earth coexist in the same place and are of the same substance and interconnected, when the earth emerges, emptiness should likewise emerge.

This objection arises because [the objector] has not yet realized that both emptiness and earth are the Tathāgatagarbha and possess no separate intrinsic nature of their own. Therefore, this difficulty can be raised.

Next, regarding the refutation of [the claim that] it emerges because of boring: first, the primary refutation is established; next, the refutation of the view that it does not emerge because of boring follows.
In the passage beginning "You must examine this more carefully," because this principle is profound and subtle, he further exhorts them, saying, "Examine it with care!

Observe it with care! This is intended so that they may awaken to and enter into the wondrous nature. As for the phrase "boring through emptiness and reality": "boring" is a real thing, while "emptiness" is...
The substance is empty and pervasive; yet, if one has not yet realized the nature of the treasury, then emptiness and reality are diametrically opposed and cannot function for one another.

Therefore, it is said that they are neither blended nor joined. Nor should it be thought that empty space could emerge from nowhere on its own—this further refutes the notion that they are neither blended nor joined.
Second, this clarifies the great uniformity.

If this nature of empty space is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally immovable, you should know that the earth, water, fire, and wind manifest before you are likewise called the five great elements.
Their nature is truly and perfectly interfused; they are all the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction.

Ānanda, your mind is deluded and confused, failing to realize that the four elements are originally the Tathāgata-garbha. You should contemplate whether empty space goes out or comes in, or whether it is neither.
"Entering and exiting.

This means that by equalizing the four great elements through emptiness, one names them the five great elements to manifest that they are all of the same nature, all of the same reality, non-dual and without distinction.
Indeed, sentient beings of the nine realms have, for the most part, been unable to harmonize these two dharmas of form and emptiness.
First, ordinary beings reckon that the substantial matter of the four great elements stands in direct opposition to inert, empty space.
Second, those of the Two Vehicles reckon that the delusive matter of birth and death stands in direct opposition to the true emptiness of *nirvāṇa*.

Those who receive the teachings of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) reckon that entering emptiness from the provisional and emerging from emptiness into the provisional likewise stand in direct opposition. Those who receive the teachings of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) reckon... [text continues]
The two truths of emptiness and existence stand in direct opposition to the ultimate emptiness of the "Middle Only" (but-madhyama).

Who would know that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are themselves emptiness, and emptiness is itself the four great elements? Emptiness is the *tathāgatagarbha* (store-nature), and the four great elements are also the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The *tathāgatagarbha* is emptiness, and the *tathāgatagarbha* is also the four great elements. Therefore, the earth, water, fire, and wind of the ten dharma-realms are themselves the ten [realms].
The Dharma-realm is empty; the emptiness of the ten Dharma-realms is precisely the earth, water, fire, and wind of the ten Dharma-realms.

Now, following the preceding text, we extract from within this single well that which is neither caused nor conditioned, neither spontaneous nor a combination, and neither a non-combination—departing from all four propositions and transcending the hundred negations. Only then can one truly believe that the ten realms are void.
Emptiness is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unmoving;

its nature is truly interfused with each of the present elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and it is clearly evident that this is the Tathāgatagarbha, which is inherently without arising or ceasing.

Because you do not realize that the four great elements are originally the Tathāgatagarbha, you instead employ worldly frivolous discourse and deluded conceptualization to explain them as a combination of causes and conditions.
Yet you entangle yourself; now you should contemplate this empty space: does it emerge, does it enter, or is it neither emerging nor entering?
If you claim that empty space has emergence and entry, such conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) based on causes and conditions has already been refuted as above.

If you claim that empty space has no emergence or entry, such conceptual proliferation regarding spontaneity (*svabhāva*) has also been refuted as above. If one knows that the nature of the storehouse (*ālaya*) accords with empty space...
If conditions do not change, then entering and exiting are themselves non-entering and non-exiting.
If one knows that the hidden nature (garbhadhātu) is like empty space—unchanging yet following conditions—then there is no entering or exiting, yet this does not preclude entering and exiting.

If one knows that the hidden nature, like empty space, is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), then one knows that the four great elements of the hidden nature are likewise all free from conceptual proliferation. This third section clarifies the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
"You know nothing at all of the Tathāgata-garbha: its nature is awakening that is true emptiness, and its nature is emptiness that is true awakening;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of what they know.

Ānanda, it is like a single well: when a well is dug, emptiness arises within that well; the empty space of the ten directions is likewise so. Filling the ten directions, how could it have a fixed location? It follows the karma [of those who perceive it]."
[This] is discovered.
This clarifies that the ten dharma-realms inherent in nature—both emptiness and awakening—are both nature and both true.

Since the preceding text has already equated emptiness with the four great elements, the present mention of the single character "emptiness" (kōng) is equivalent to mentioning all five great elements.
That is to say, the five great elements are insentient phenomena and are termed "non-awakening," while the sense-faculties and consciousnesses are sentient phenomena and are termed "awakening.
Yet they do not realize that both the sentient and the insentient are, in their essence, the true nature.

Therefore, throughout the ten dharma realms—whether the primary or the derivative—there is not a single thing that is not pure and fundamental, pervading the entire dharma-realm; this is the principle of following conditions.

The essence of transformation follows the minds of sentient beings across the ten realms, responding to the capacity of their respective knowledge—whether great or small—and manifesting according to the various karmas of good and evil as the ten dharma-realms within emptiness;
this is the function of the unchanging following conditions. Fourth, the refutation of delusion.
In the world, ignorance and delusion serve as causes and conditions, and the nature of spontaneity—all these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind;
they are nothing but verbal expressions and possess no real meaning.

Worldly outsiders take the analysis of form until it returns to emptiness as their cause and condition, and take the immovability of inert emptiness as spontaneity; thus they receive [their teachings].

Those who do not grasp the intent of the *Zangjiao* (Tripitaka Teaching) take the extinction of form to realize emptiness as their causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), and take the immovability of true emptiness as their spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

Those who do not grasp the intent of the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching) take the realization that form is identical to emptiness as their causal condition, and take the non-arising of the principle of emptiness as their spontaneity.
Those who do not grasp the intent of the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching) take the two cultivations of conditions and understanding (*pratyaya-bhāvanā* and *pariniṣpanna-bhāvanā*)...

Revealing that suchness serves as the causal condition, and that the Buddha-nature of suchness transcends the two extremes by its very nature, [one sees that] all things ultimately yield no real meaning because of a failure to understand the nature of the *ālaya*.
Precisely because the nature of the *ālaya* is the great nature of emptiness, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha realized it, whereby his wondrous power became perfectly luminous. 6. Clarifying the *ālaya*.
The nature [of the sense organs] is precisely the nature of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

However, all Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras clarify only the six great elements—namely, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—and do not separately establish this category of "great sense organs.

This is because all phenomena are fully subsumed within matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*); the five great elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and space are collectively matter, while the great element of consciousness is precisely the mind.

Prior to this [classification], the five *bhūta* (elements), the two superior faculties (*indriya*), and the physical flesh-mass of the sensory bases were subsumed under the previous five great elements;
the ultimate sense-faculty of mind (*manas*) was subsumed under the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*). Therefore, they did not need to be established separately.

One must understand that in this present sutra, when establishing the faculties and the great elements separately, regarding the first five faculties, one does not take the two types of form—the superficial and the superior—but rather takes their functional capacity (*yogyatā*).
One function of the illuminating movement that perceives the objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not grasp the physical, fleshy form of the sixth sense organ,

but rather grasps the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) that silently accommodates all phenomena; one should know that this very function is the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*),
which, manifesting at the gateway of the six sense organs, takes as its object those six dust-like sensory realms of direct perception.
There are generally three purposes for establishing these faculties: first, to encompass the preceding teachings; second, to accord with the subsequent text;
and third, to establish the sphere of perfect penetration. Regarding the first purpose—to encompass the preceding teachings—there are again three points:
first, the ten previous investigations of seeing all relied upon the essence of seeing (*jianjing*) to manifest the wondrous nature; now, furthermore...
To clarify: the essence of seeing, hearing, and so forth is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha* (the nature of the treasury).

This *tathāgatagarbha* is like the true moon, while the essences of seeing, hearing, etc., and the objects such as form and emptiness, are like two moons. Because the two moons exist in dependence upon the true moon, pointing to the two moons is itself the true moon;
thus, the principle that "seeing is not seeing" becomes even clearer here. Second, previously, these were subsumed within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

All dharmas are exhausted without exception; now, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is opened up as the five great elements, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) as the great element of the sense-faculties, and the three aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the great element of consciousness.

Within each of these great elements, the ten realms and the five aggregates are still fully present, because the two dharmas of matter and mind are never separated from one another. Thirdly, previously...
The eighteen realms encompass all phenomena without exception;

now, by horizontally opening the six sense objects (*viṣaya*) to form the five great elements and combining the six faculties (*indriya*) into the faculty-element, and combining the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) into the consciousness-element—whether combined or separated—they all constitute the wondrous objects of contemplation.
This concludes the first intention. Second, to accord with the subsequent text: the text states, "the cycle of birth and death."
Peace, bliss, wondrous permanence, and the six sense faculties are one and the same; they are not other things.
Because he intends to expound this Dharma-door, he first establishes this "Greatness" [of the faculties]. Third, regarding the establishment of the realm of perfect penetration:

the six objects, the six faculties, and the six consciousnesses all serve as the foundational basis for the perfect penetration of the various sages discussed below. If these faculties were not established as "Great," then...

Since the claim that the "Perfect Expedient Means" (yuan-tong-bian) of Śrī-Ābhāsvara’s Buddha-remembrance lacks scriptural authority, it is necessary to establish this faculty (*indriya*) as being "Great.

The text is divided into four sections: first, refuting false attachments; second, clarifying the equality of the Great; third, revealing the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); and fourth, censuring delusions.

First: Ānanda, you perceive that awareness is devoid of cognition; yet it exists because of form and space, just as there is someone like you now in the Jeta Grove who experiences morning brightness and evening darkness.
Even if one stands in the middle of the night, under a full moon it is bright and under a dark moon it is dim; thus, brightness and darkness depend upon seeing.
Analyze this vision: is it of one essence with light, darkness, and the great void of space, or is it not of one essence?
Is it both the same and different, or neither the same nor different?

Ānanda, if this vision were fundamentally of one essence with light, darkness, and space, then when light and darkness—these two essences—are mutually extinguished, there would be no light at the time of darkness.

When there is light, there is no darkness; if light were identical to darkness, then when light is present, vision would cease to exist. If it were necessarily one with light, then at the time of darkness, [vision] should perish.
If it perishes, how can you see light or see darkness? If light and darkness are distinct, yet vision neither arises nor perishes, how can they be said to be one?
If this essence of vision is not of one substance with darkness and light, then, apart from light, darkness, and empty space, where would it abide?

Analyze this fundamental seeing: what form does it take when separated from light and dark, as well as from empty space? This fundamental seeing is identical to the fur of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit;
since light, darkness, and empty space—these three things—are all distinct, from what could seeing be established? Light and darkness are mutually opposed; how could they ever be the same?
Separated from these three, seeing fundamentally does not exist; how then could it be different? When dividing empty space and dividing seeing, there is originally no boundary between them.
How is it that this nature which sees light in the presence of light and sees darkness in the presence of darkness is not subject to change? How is it that it is not something separate from you?

Examine this more minutely—examine it with extreme care, with precision, and with deep observation. Light follows the sun; darkness follows the dark moon. Both belong to empty space when unobstructed, and return to the great earth when obstructed.
From what source, then, does this essence of seeing arise? The faculty of seeing is aware, while emptiness is inert; they are neither a mixture nor a union.
One should not view the essence [of vision] as emerging from nowhere on its own.

Within the ten dharma realms, seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition are all, for the time being, provisionally situated within the six sense organs; collectively they are called the "great element of the faculties" (indriya-mahābhūta), formerly referred to as the "great element of seeing.
This latter term retains the specific while omitting the general, and is thus not employed here. Now, we shall discuss this solely in terms of the single phenomenon of the faculty of seeing.
To analyze this by analogy with the other five faculties: the seeing of the ear, nose, and tongue lacks intrinsic nature because it depends on form and space;
this clarifies that seeing which arises through conditions has no self-nature, and by analogy, the opening, smelling, and perceiving are all likewise so.
Thus, the statement that brightness and darkness are analyzed by means of seeing intends to reveal that brightness and darkness also lack self-nature, returning [to the same principle].

Using the fact that seeing and cognition act as mutual causes and conditions as an analogy, one sees that all phenomena—such as motion and stillness, union and separation, and arising and ceasing—are likewise without exception.

This is the formal presentation of the principle of dependent origination; what follows is a detailed elucidation of their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), first by raising objections and then by refuting them.
Within the section on raising objections, six propositions are established: first, identity; second, non-identity; third... [and so forth].
"Either identical with the four [elements], it is not identical with the five; or different from the six, it is not different.

If one has not yet realized that the wondrous nature remains unchanging while following conditions, and follows conditions while remaining unchanging, then even with the sharpest wit and most lucid discernment, one cannot escape the conceptual trap of these six propositions.
Therefore, [the text] raises each point in turn to refute them, beginning first with Ānanda.
Regarding this "seeing-attainment" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), how can it be established? First, the refutation of its being a single entity is easy to understand from the textual phrasing.

Second, from the passage beginning with "if this essence of seeing" down to "from what could seeing be established," the refutation of its not being a single entity is shown. As for the statement that the three things—light, darkness, and empty space—are all distinct:

the character *yì* (distinct) is glossed as the character *lí* (separated). If these three things were one, they would collectively be separated from everything; thus, there would be nothing from which seeing could be established.
It is observed that light and darkness are mutually exclusive; therefore, to claim they are "either identical or not" is a statement of uncertainty.
Now, since light and darkness are definitively opposed, it cannot be said that they are identical. Fourth, apart from these three—light, darkness, and space—there is nothing that transcends them;
even if one were to separate from these three, there could be no self-nature of seeing whatsoever.

If one were to point out that the "perhaps different" (or-anya) could be distinct from the present, then since there is nothing else to be pointed out as distinct, it cannot be said that it is "perhaps different.
The division into emptiness and seeing originally has no boundaries; to subsequently deconstruct their non-identity is itself their identity-as-difference.

This is merely a shift in phrasing to prevent those who harbor shifting conceptualizations. Since the nature of seeing darkness and seeing light does not undergo change, this serves to refute [the notion of] non-identity.
"Neither different nor non-different" is simply a variation in phrasing intended to prevent those who hold shifting views from persisting in their calculations. You should examine this more closely;
my subsequent instructions urge you to investigate it with even greater precision, for I desire that you realize the nature of the storehouse (ālaya).

This is because, if one does not comprehend the nature of the storehouse, then the faculties such as seeing and hearing are merely the nature of conscious awareness, and the four great elements are merely the nature of insentient obstruction; thus, they do not constitute a true harmony.
This refutes the false conceptualization that they are combined;

the phrase "the essence of seeing should not be seen as emerging from nowhere on its own" further refutes the subsequent conceptualization that they are not combined. Second, it clarifies the great equilibrium.

If you see, hear, know, or perceive that the nature is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unmoving, you should understand that the boundless, unmoving void, together with the moving earth, water, fire, and wind, are all equally called the six great elements. Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious;

they are all the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction. Ānanda, your nature has sunk into delusion because you do not realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally such as this.
Ālaya, you should contemplate this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: is it born or does it perish? Is it identical or different?
Is it neither born nor perishing, or neither identical nor different?

This treats seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as equal to the previous five great elements, naming them the six great elements to reveal that they are all of the same nature and all of the same substance.

In truth, there is neither duality nor distinction. It is simply that the sentient beings of the nine realms have, regarding these two factors—the seeing and the conditions for seeing—failed altogether to integrate them into one.
Ordinary people reckon the five external elements to be real dharmas and reckon the six internal sense organs to be a real self; thus, they stand in diametrical opposition to one another.
The followers of the Two Vehicles cling to the five elements as external dharmas subject to arising and ceasing, while clinging to [the organs] as... [the internal self].

For those who receive the Shared Teaching (Paryāya-yāna), the six sense organs are considered internal dharmas subject to arising and ceasing, while the five great elements are considered external dharmas;
these two stand in direct opposition as being like illusions.

For those who receive the Distinct Teaching (Vaibhāṣika-yāna), although they know that the aforementioned five great elements constitute the "objective part" (nimitta-bhāga) and that seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing constitute the "subjective part" (darśana-bhāga), they must nevertheless...

Only by distancing oneself from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature) can one realize the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature). Now, while within the realm of delusion, the two parts—the seeing and the seen—are likewise set in direct opposition to one another.

Who knows that the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) are identical to seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and cognizing; that seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and cognizing are identical to the five great elements;

and that both the five great elements and seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and cognizing are identical to the *tathatā-garbha* (the storehouse of suchness)? The *tathatā-garbha* is [identical to them].
The nature is precisely seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; the *tathāgatagarbha* nature is likewise the five great elements.
Therefore, the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing of the ten dharma realms are themselves the earth, water, fire, wind, and space of the ten dharma realms;

and the earth, water, fire, wind, and space of the ten dharma realms are themselves the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing of the ten dharma realms. Now, following the preceding text, I shall single out the faculty of sight.
The seeds are neither one nor different, neither identical nor distinct; they are entirely free from the four propositions and transcend all hundred negations.
Only then does one truly believe that the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing within the ten realms is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving.
It is clear that this nature is truly interfused with space and each of the four great elements, all being the Tathāgatagarbha, originally devoid of arising or ceasing.
To speak of "boundless immovability" while referring to the movement of space and the shifting of earth, water, fire, and wind is merely speech conforming to the intentions of others.
Once the nature of the treasury (the *tathāgatagarbha*) is known, one realizes that space is neither moving nor non-moving, illuminating both movement and non-movement simultaneously;
likewise, earth, water, fire, and wind are neither moving nor non-moving, illuminating both movement and non-movement simultaneously, remaining ever-constant as they accord with conditions.

Because they do not change, the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) of all [realms] are moving yet not moving; because they do not change while constantly following conditions, the five great elements of all [realms] are not moving yet moving.
Furthermore, because they follow conditions while remaining constantly unchanging, the five great elements of the ten realms are neither moving nor non-moving;
because they do not change while constantly following conditions, the five great elements of the nine realms are not moving yet moving, whereas those of the Buddha-realm are not moving.
The five elements are all in motion, yet they are not moving; if you do not penetrate this principle, then both "motion" and "non-motion" are merely conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).

When it says, "You should observe whether this seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition arise or cease," the intent is to reveal that your present seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition are neither arising nor ceasing, neither identical nor different, and yet not non-arising.
If cessation were neither identical nor different, what else could it be than the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha? For the nature of the Garbha is constant and unchanging as it follows conditions;
therefore, it is not birth-and-cessation or identity-and-difference. Because it is unchanging yet constantly follows conditions, it is not "neither birth-and-cessation nor identity-and-difference.
If one is deluded regarding this wondrous nature, then one speaks of birth and speaks of cessation.
To speak of identity, difference, arising, ceasing, non-arising, non-ceasing, identity-and-difference, or neither—these are all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
If one realizes this wondrous nature, then all conceptual proliferations are extinguished.
Nevertheless, one may also skillfully employ various teachings of arising, ceasing, identity, and difference according to the four *siddhāntas*. Third, revealing the rational nature (*dharmatā*).

You have never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of seeing and the clarity of awareness, the essence of awareness and the purity of seeing, are fundamentally pure and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
According to the minds of sentient beings and the capacity of what is known, as with the single faculty of sight, seeing pervades the Dharma-realm;

so too, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the cognitive awareness of touch—all these wondrous virtues are brilliantly clear and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, filling the ten voids in their entirety.
"How could there be a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.

This clarifies that the ten dharma realms are inherently complete; that which sees, hears, perceives, and cognizes—both the seeing and the consciousness—is entirely of the nature [of the mind] and entirely luminous.

"Awakened luminosity" (*jue-ming*) and "awakened essence" (*jue-jing*) refer to what was called in the first fascicle "the fundamental luminosity of the consciousness-essence" (*shi-jing-yuan-ming*), speaking from the perspective of the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

Since the preceding passage has already shown that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all comprised within the five great elements, the present mention of the single character "seeing" (jiàn) effectively encompasses all six consciousnesses.

People say that among the six elements, five are the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the sense organ is the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), and thus the two divisions of subject and object are not self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*).
Little do they realize that the very subject and object are themselves self-realization.
Realization is itself the seeing and the seen; this self-realization of the seeing and the seen is nothing other than the wondrous nature and nothing other than true illumination.
Therefore, throughout the ten dharma realms, whether in terms of seeing or the seen, each and every thing is none other than the pure and original state, pervading the entire dharma realm.
This is called the essence that remains unchanging while following conditions; it responds to the minds of sentient beings across the ten realms, according to what they know.
The capacity of these [senses] is such that, for example, when a sentient being with a single visual faculty gazes through it, it does not exceed a mere inch, yet this is no diminution;

when a Tathāgata exhaustively perceives even the subtlest atoms of pure lands, there is nothing he does not behold, yet this is no increase. The same applies to hearing, smelling, tasting, and so forth;
each is inherently endowed with one thousand two hundred merits, pervading horizontally and penetrating vertically. Therefore...
