It is said: "The wondrous virtue is luminously pure; it is solely because the karma of the ten realms differs that [consciousness] manifests in accordance with that karma as the ten realms and the six sense organs.
Within the nature of non-differentiation, one falsely perceives various forms of differentiation—this is the function of 'the unchanging following conditions. (4) Refuting Delusion.
In the world, ignorance and delusion serve as causes and conditions, and [the notion of] inherent nature—all these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind;
they are nothing but verbal expressions and possess no real meaning.
Worldly outsiders calculate that the six sense organs are the self, arising from time, space, atoms, or Maheśvara.
Those who follow the *Pratītyasamutpāda* (Dependent Origination) teaching but fail to grasp its true meaning conceive of a self (*ātman*) that pervades the ten directions as being spontaneous;

they cling to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as the condition for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and when these six bases are extinguished, they take the realization of partial truth (*pratyekabuddha*) as spontaneity.

Those who follow the *Sāmānya* (Common) teaching but fail to grasp its true meaning regard the six sense bases as being like an illusion, taking the very substance of the six sense bases as the condition.

Emptiness is the spontaneous nature; those who receive the distinct teachings but do not grasp their meaning take the dependent-arising nature (paratantra-svabhāva) that constitutes the six sense organs as causes and conditions, and take the extinction of these six organs as the realization of the perfected-real nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) as the spontaneous nature.

This is entirely because they do not understand the nature of the storehouse consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna), and thus there is no true meaning [in their view]. It is simply because the nature of the storehouse is itself the nature of the great elements of the sense organs.

The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta realized this and attained the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection. Seventh, the nature of the treasury is precisely the nature of the great element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*).
While the Hīnayāna speaks only of the six consciousnesses, the Mahāyāna speaks of eight or nine consciousnesses.
One must understand that the name of the ninth consciousness is established based on the stage of fruition; in reality, it has no separate essence, being merely a designation based upon...

Because the nature of the eight consciousnesses emerges from obstructions and becomes perfectly luminous, it is further designated by the name "pure white" (*vimala*) and called the *āmalaka-vijñāna*.

In this present scripture, the eighth and seventh consciousnesses are collectively subsumed within the sense-faculty of mind (*manas*), which corresponds to what was previously described as having the nature of both deliberation (*manana*) and discernment (*vijñapti*). This, therefore, is already included within the category of the sense-faculties (*indriya*).
Therefore, I shall now specifically discuss the preceding six consciousnesses alone to clarify that they are all inherently complete (*xingju*). This section is divided into four parts:
first, refuting false attachments; second, clarifying the great equality; third, revealing the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); and fourth, censuring delusion. This is the first part.
Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely from the six kinds of sense organs and their objects.
As you now survey the assembly of holy ones in this gathering, your eyes move across them one by one; yet as they look around, it is merely like reflections in a mirror, without any further analysis.
Within that state, your consciousness sequentially identifies and points out: "This is Mañjuśrī," "This is Pūrṇa," "This is Maudgalyāyana," "This is Śāriputra."
"Bodhi! Śāriputra, does this consciousness that cognizes arise from seeing, or from forms, or from empty space, or does it emerge suddenly without any cause?
Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness arose within seeing, then in the absence of darkness, light, form, and emptiness—these four conditions—it would necessarily not exist;
yet since there is no such thing, even the nature of your seeing would not exist."
From what does consciousness arise? If the nature of your consciousness arises within the objective forms and not from the faculty of vision, then you neither perceive light nor perceive darkness.
When light and darkness are not perceived, there is neither form nor emptiness; since even those forms do not exist, from what could consciousness arise?

If it arises from emptiness—being neither form nor vision—then, lacking the faculty of vision, there would be no discernment, and you yourself would be unable to know light, darkness, form, or emptiness.
It is not that the conditions for the cessation of marks have been extinguished; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have no place where they can be established.
Since these two—place and non-place—are neither empty nor identical, they are not distinct entities. Even if you were to suddenly arouse your consciousness, what would there be to differentiate?
If it emerged abruptly without any cause, why do you not perceive a bright moon while differentiating it during the day? Examine this further in minute detail: seeing relies upon your pupils.

If they push one another toward the external objects so that those objects can be manifested as existent, yet cannot be established as nonexistent, then from what source does this consciousness arise?
When the consciousness moves, the seeing remains clear; they are neither blended nor joined. Hearing, listening, sensing, and knowing are likewise thus.
It should not be that consciousness arises from nowhere on its own.
The ten dharma realms and the six types of consciousness-mind are collectively termed the "great element of consciousness.
For now, we shall examine this by way of Ānanda’s visual consciousness, using it as an illustration for the other five consciousnesses.

That the nature of consciousness has no source and arises falsely from the six types of faculties and objects precisely clarifies that consciousness is dependently originated, thereby refuting the calculation of its having an inherent nature. "You now observe everywhere" below is a reiteration of the cause.

This consciousness cognizes dependently arisen phenomena; it subsequently investigates that these dependently arisen things lack intrinsic nature. Within the exposition of causes and conditions, it distinguishes the differing characteristics of the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Surveying them thoroughly and sequentially, it first discerns the characteristics of the faculties—namely, what was referred to in the previous section on the "greatness of the faculties" as the "greatness of seeing.
This is the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, which is provisionally manifested within the two [faculties of] the ear and the eye.
The various eye-faculties spontaneously cognize objects without distinct analysis; therefore, they are likened to what occurs within a mirror, yet they are not like a mirror’s lack of cognition.
Your consciousness sequentially points out and discerns the characteristics therein;
herein, there is also a distinction between the visual consciousness and the simultaneous mental consciousness, even though the Buddha did not explicitly state this principle.

One should understand this as follows: if one merely perceives the marks of Mañjuśrī, the śarīra, and so forth, without associating them with names and phrases (*nāma-pada*), this is the function of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
If, however, the names and phrases "Mañjuśrī" or "śarīra" arise, this is the function of the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Furthermore, the marks of Mañjuśrī, the śarīra, and so forth, which are the objects of visual consciousness, merely rely upon those [external] forms.

The objective realm that is the transformation of Mañjuśrī’s essential substance arises as the self-characterized portion (svabhāga-bhāga) of the visual consciousness, which serves as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
it does not directly take Mañjuśrī’s actual substance as its object.

This is because Mañjuśrī’s actual substance is the self-characterized portion of Ānanda’s eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), and thus serves as the object-condition for the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of that [eighth consciousness]. This is inferred.
Within the state of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*), one first establishes four propositions and then refutes each one individually. First, the refutation of arising within views;
second, the refutation of arising within characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). The texts for these are clear. Third, the refutation of arising within emptiness (*śūnyatā*):
Now, as for emptiness, it is neither a characteristic nor a view. Since it is not a view, there is nothing to be discerned, and it cannot itself know or manifest clarity.
If the dark color and emptiness are not characteristics, then where could the preceding conditions be applied?

Since they are perceived through seeing, hearing, knowing, and cognizing, are these two—place and [the object]—identical, such that both are entirely empty? Or is there a separate dharma apart from the characteristic of seeing?
If they are identical and both are entirely empty, then it is the same as non-existence; if there is a separate dharma, that too is not the same.
Regarding objects characterized by visible forms, even if you were to give rise to consciousness, what could you possibly differentiate? Fourth, the refutation of causeless arising:
both visual consciousness and the simultaneous mental consciousness take only present direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as their object;
there is absolutely no principle for a separate consciousness to perceive the moon at midday. Since one only cognizes the sun because one sees the sun, it is clear that this is not causeless.

This [analysis] takes the cause, the causal characteristic, and the emptiness of the cause as being equally subsumed under "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*); by means of the absence of a cause, it simultaneously refutes both the "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*) and the "causal.

You should examine this further in detail; below, I shall urge you to investigate it even more thoroughly, and I shall also refute the notions of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and "non-conjunction" (*asaṃyoga*).
The essence of seeing rests upon your pupils, while its form and characteristics are projected toward external objects; it merely possesses that which can be described.
If it were currently forming existence, it would not be the characteristic; if it were not the characteristic, it would then become non-existence.
Since such consciousness as a condition is neither the seer nor the characteristic, neither empty nor non-existent, from what ultimate cause could it arise?

Moreover, for one who has not yet realized the nature of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), consciousness belongs to movement while the seer belongs to stillness; in principle, they cannot be a union or a combination through hearing, listening, sensing, or knowing.
All [of these] belong to the state of clarity and stillness; the other five consciousnesses are likewise all fluctuating and unstable. Furthermore, it must not be their union or combination.

This refutes their calculation regarding the nature of union. The phrase "it should not be that consciousness arises from nowhere on its own" refutes their counter-argument regarding the nature of non-union.
Second, this clarifies the Great Equilibrium.
If this consciousness-mind is fundamentally without origin, you should know that its capacity for discerning, seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing is perfect and profoundly still;

its nature does not arise from external conditions. Furthermore, space, earth, water, fire, and wind are all equally termed the "Seven Great Elements. Their natures are truly interfused and perfectly harmonious, all being the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally free from birth and extinction.
Ānanda, your mind is coarse and restless; you have not yet awakened to the fact that seeing, hearing, and awareness are themselves the manifestation of enlightenment.
Having realized the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, you should contemplate these six bases of consciousness: are they identical or different? Are they empty or existent?
Are they neither identical nor different, and neither empty nor existent?

This takes the six types of consciousness and mind and combines them with the preceding six great elements to name them the "seven great elements," manifesting that they are all of the same nature, all true, non-dual, and without distinction.
Indeed, sentient beings of the nine realms have not yet been able to integrate these consciousnesses, along with the faculties and objects, into a single unity;
rather, those of the mundane and heterodox paths mistakenly take the reflected images of conditions appearing within consciousness to be the mind, and take the faculties to be [the self].

The body and its objects are in a state of mutual opposition like enemies; likewise, the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) hold that the sense organs and their objects are the producers while the consciousnesses are the produced, which is also a state of mutual opposition.

Those who receive the Common Teaching (p’unggyo), though they know that the producing organs and objects are like illusions and the produced consciousness is likewise illusory, ultimately do not regard them as one entity. This is the case for those who receive the Distinct Teaching (byeolgyo).

Although one knows that all things are but consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), the two divisions of the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*) and the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*) are not declared to be either eternally false or eternally true;

nor is self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) and the cognition of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti-saṃvitti*) established separately outside of these two divisions, for they would still stand in mutual opposition.

Who then knows that the perceiving subject and the perceived object are identical to self-cognition, that self-cognition is identical to the perceiving subject and the perceived object, and that self-cognition is identical to the *tathatā* (the nature of the treasury), while the perceiving subject and the perceived object are likewise so?
The nature of the treasury is itself the nature of the self-realized treasury, and this nature is also the perceived object and the perceiving faculty.

Therefore, the consciousnesses of the ten dharma realms are themselves the earth, water, fire, wind, space, and sense organs of the ten dharma realms; conversely, the earth, water, fire, wind, space, and sense organs of the ten dharma realms are themselves the consciousnesses of the ten dharma realms.
Now, following the preceding text, I shall single out the visual consciousness as an example.

This state of being free from faults and transcending all extremes does not begin with faith; rather, it recognizes that the ten dharma realms, the six consciousnesses, and the six sense organs are all entirely complete and profoundly still.

Their nature is not something derived from external conditions, but is identical to the true, perfect fusion of each of the elements—space, earth, water, fire, and wind—all of which are the Tathāgatagarbha, devoid of arising or ceasing.
Within this context, the two characters "discerning" (*liǎobié*) specifically refer to the seeing of the six consciousnesses.
The four characters "hearing, perceiving, cognizing, and knowing" still refer to the six sense faculties. Your mind is coarse and floating;

below this, he rebukes him for failing to realize that the consciousness-mind is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, and commands him to further investigate it. Regarding whether the consciousness-minds of the six locations are the same or different:
if one says they are the same, why does the eye-consciousness not distinguish sound, and why does the ear-consciousness not [distinguish form]?
If you say that its color is distinct, then since the ears themselves hear the Dharma, why does the body arise to show reverence and the mouth come to inquire about its meaning?
If you say it is empty, why is it so clear and bright, incapable of being severed or extinguished?
If you say it exists, why is it that internally, externally, and in between, it has no location? If you say it is not identical [to anything], why is it within its own nature...
If you say they are not different, why do they oppose one another within the middle way? If you say they are not empty, why are they sought and yet unobtainable?
If you say they are not existent, why should their application be inexhaustible?

Since these six bases and the conscious mind are neither identical nor different, neither empty nor existent, and are also neither non-identical nor non-different, neither non-empty nor non-existent—this is called "non-being."

The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is concealed by what? Because this nature follows conditions while remaining eternally unchanging, it is not identical to or different from [phenomena], nor is it empty or existent.
Because this nature is unchanging yet constantly follows conditions, it is neither non-identical nor non-different, neither non-empty nor non-existent.
If one is deluded regarding this wondrous nature, then one speaks of identity and difference, or speaks of emptiness and existence.
Some say that asserting identity or difference, or asserting neither emptiness nor existence, are all forms of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

If one realizes this wondrous nature, such proliferation will extinguish of itself; yet, one may also employ various explanations of identity, difference, and so forth, in accordance with the four *siddhāntas*.
Third, it reveals the nature of reality:

"From the beginning, you have not known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature-consciousness is luminously aware; this true consciousness of awakened clarity is wondrously enlightened, profound and still, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
It contains and exhales the ten voids—how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma."

This clarifies that the ten dharma realms and the six consciousnesses are both nature and are true, and that cognitive awareness (*vijñapti*) and fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) are both nature and are true.

"Cognitive awareness-enlightenment" (*ming-jue-ming*) refers to what is stated in the following passage: "the wondrous brightness of nature-enlightenment" (*xing-jue-miao-ming*) and "the brightness-wonder of fundamental enlightenment" (*ben-jue-ming-miao*);
these refer to the principle of *tathatā*. Since the preceding text has already equated the conscious mind with the six elements, it now cites one consciousness as a representative.

The "words" (characters) here refer to the totality of the seven great elements; these seven are nothing other than the entirety of the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses, which are fundamentally illusory.
They are not the wondrously luminous, true essence. One fails to realize that the nature-consciousness is itself clear knowing, and that clear knowing is itself the true consciousness.
Therefore, the consciousness-mind of each and every one of the ten dharma realms is none other than wondrous enlightened awareness.
That which is profoundly still and pervades the entire Dharma-realm is called the essence that remains unchanging while following conditions;
because of this, there exists the function of remaining unchanging while following conditions. This essence encompasses and emits the ten voids;

in whatever direction or location, all are manifestations arising from the karma of the ten Dharma-realms, appearing as the consciousnesses of the ten Dharma-realms. The two characters "encompassing" (han) and "emitting" (tu) apply universally to both delusion and enlightenment.
Furthermore, speaking in terms of the Buddha-realm: the ten periods of time across antiquity and the present, from beginning to end, do not depart from a single thought-moment;

the lands of even a speck of dust, whether self or other, are not separated by the tip of a hair. This meaning is like "containing": it is as when a single thought universally contemplates immeasurable eons. It is also like "emitting":
it is as when a single ray of light universally illumines the worlds of the ten directions. Yet, this containing is not truly containing, and this emitting is not truly emitting.
Therefore it is said: "How could there be a fixed location? This is stated next in terms of deluded perception.
One takes a *piṅgala* bottle, fills it with empty space, and names this "containing"; then one opens a hole and pours out the bottle, naming this "emitting.

Yet, in truth, there is nothing contained within what is contained, and nothing emitted from what is emitted. Thus it is said: "How could there be a fixed location? For when explained in its essential nature, it is non-existent.

Because it does not return from this dharma-realm, it contains [all things] throughout the ten voids; because there is nothing that does not flow from this dharma-realm, it emits [all things] throughout the ten voids.

In the Aspect School (Lakṣaṇavāda), what is called "the mind" (citta) is defined as "that which collects and gives rise to. "Collecting" is precisely containing, and "giving rise to" is precisely emitting.
It is not said that [the mind] "responds to the capacities of sentient beings' minds," for this consciousness is itself the sentient being.

The mind-element (*manas*) is precisely the cognitive faculty (*pramāṇa*); as for the preceding six elements, there is a fear that deluded sentiments might regard them as real dharmas external to the mind.
Therefore, it is necessary to state for each one that they "accord with the mind" and "correspond to the measure.

Since the present consciousness-element (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*) is a direct pointing to the mind currently manifest before sentient beings, yet they do not know that its entire substance is the *tathāgatagarbha*, [it is so designated].
Encompassing and exhaling the ten voids, how could there be any spatial location by which to name or describe it?
Only now do you realize that what you previously identified as the "conditioned shadow" is not only not the true mind; it is certainly and definitively not the six consciousnesses either.
(4) Refutation of Delusion.
In the world, ignorance and delusion serve as causes and conditions, and the nature of spontaneity—all these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind;
they exist only as verbal expressions and possess no real meaning.

When ordinary people and non-Buddhists reckon the discerning mind to be the self or what belongs to the self, or reckon it to be subject to annihilation, they fall under the influence of false causes and conditions.

Those who calculate that there is a permanent abiding [self] belong to the naturalistic view of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). They hold that these six consciousnesses are phenomena produced by causes and conditions, devoid of self or what belongs to a self (*anātman-anātmīya*).
If delusions and karma are both exhausted, the consciousnesses will no longer arise; it is like a fire being extinguished when the fuel is spent—the fire has no place to go.
The extinction of craving (*tṛṣṇākṣaya*) and *nirvāṇa* are likewise thus. In the realm of *nirvāṇa*, there is neither arising nor...

"Cessation" is termed "spontaneous" (natural). For those who follow the Shared Teaching (Prajñāpāramitā), taking the emptiness of the conscious mind as the condition for the principle of the emptiness of non-arising is termed "spontaneous.

For those who follow the Distinct Teaching (Tathāgatagarbha), the fact that the marks of consciousness—its four divisions—all belong to the nature of dependence on others is termed "conditioned" (causal);
the nature of consciousness itself, which is True Suchness and unconditioned, is termed [the spontaneous].
Naturally, all these [views] fail to reach the nature of the *ālayavijñāna* (store-consciousness) and ultimately possess no real meaning.

Because the nature of the *ālayavijñāna* is precisely the nature of the six consciousnesses, Maitreya Bodhisattva realized this and attained the Unsurpassed, Wondrously Perfect Samādhi of Consciousness-Mind.
The above clarifies that the characteristics are fundamentally inherent in the nature. From the beginning of the first fascicle, the Buddha told Ānanda: "You and I share the same vital breath..."
This concludes the third section within the correct elucidation of the principle of nature (*dharmatā*), wherein the Tathāgata’s response and instruction have been completed.

This consists of two parts: first, the narrative by the sūtra compiler regarding the benefits realized by the fourfold assembly; second, the verses of praise by those present who have attained realization. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the description of the benefits;
second, the description of the formal conduct. Within the first of these, there are again two sections: first, a brief description; second, an extensive description. Now begins the first.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, found their minds and bodies completely cleared away,
attaining freedom from all obstructions.

Regarding this "subtle and wondrous instruction," it is by means of this very passage on the inherent presence of both nature and form (*xingju-xiang*) that one now understands that what preceded was based solely on phenomena.
Every word of this text that reveals the principle is a definitive discourse of ultimate meaning.
Because one no longer falsely identifies the four elements as the characteristics of one's own body, one suddenly awakens to the pure Dharma-body, and thus the body becomes utterly vast and empty.

Because one no longer falsely identifies the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of one's own mind, one suddenly awakens to the eternally abiding true mind, and thus the mind becomes utterly vast and empty. Know this.
The delusory body and delusory mind do not depart from the Dharma-body or the wondrous mind; they are like bubbles that do not depart from the ocean, or dust that does not depart from space.
How could bubbles and dust obstruct space or the ocean? Therefore, one attains non-obstruction.
This is a brief account of the gate of awakening, which also serves as a general summary of what follows—the extensive account—which is to say, the specific exposition. Second, the extensive account.

Furthermore, regarding the two [sections], the first concerns the perfect realization of the three greatnesses (*trimahātmya*), and the second concludes by attributing them to the true cause (*bhūtahetu*). The first [section] also has three parts:

first, realizing the magnitude of nature (*dharmatā*) as the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇamahātmya*); second, realizing the essence of nature as the greatness of substance (*svabhāvamahātmya*); and third, realizing the endowment of nature as the greatness of function (*kriyāmahātmya*).
Now, for the first [part]:

This great assembly each and every one personally realized that their own minds pervaded the ten directions, seeing the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as observing a leaf held in the palm of one's hand.
This overturns the previous delusion of taking the mind to be within the physical body— a state of confusion regarding the determination of the self as being inside the material form.
One has already grasped the meaning of the seven great texts being all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm;

one has also grasped the meaning within the sections on the aggregates, bases, and elements that within the true, constant nature, seeking for coming and going, delusion and awakening, or birth and death, nothing at all can be found;

one has also grasped the meaning within the section analyzing "seeing" regarding the departure from all marks; and one has also grasped the sevenfold analysis within the section investigating the mind.
This fully accords with the meaning of "all locations being non-existent. Second, awakening to the nature-body as the "greatness of essence":

all things existing within the world are none other than the wondrously luminous, primordial mind of Bodhi; this essential mind is pervasive and perfect, encompassing and enveloping the ten directions.
This reverses the previous delusion of taking oneself to be an object; it addresses the deluded state of mind that views the great as small within this context.

As explained in detail, for example, when one raises a single hair-tip, it is immediately the wondrously luminous, primordial Mind of Bodhi, which is therefore able to universally contain the lands of the ten directions.
This is because one has already grasped the meaning of "pure and fundamentally so" from the passage on the seven elements.

In the passage concerning the aggregates, sense bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*), the meaning that their nature is truly the essence of wondrous awakening and clarity is also encompassed;
in the passage analyzing the seeing [faculty], the meaning that this seeing and its objects are originally the essence of bodhi’s wondrous, pure, and luminous substance is also encompassed;
and in the passage interrogating the mind, the meaning of the Great Buddha-Crown is secretly revealed. Third, the realization that nature is inherently endowed is...

Use this great method to turn the gaze inward and observe the body born of one's parents: it is like a single mote of dust blown into the empty space of the ten directions, appearing and disappearing as if existing or not;
it is like a single bubble floating upon a vast, still ocean, arising and ceasing without any trace of origin.
This reverses the previous [view] which took movement as the body and movement as the object;

it is like abandoning a clear, vast ocean of hundreds of thousands of miles and instead clinging to the substance of a single floating bubble—this is the deluded sentiment of the body. Because it is manifested solely by the mind, it is said that "if it exists, there is nothing outside the mind";
because it is produced through the false conjunction of causes and conditions, it is said that "if it perishes, there is no substance. Therefore, its...
Arising comes from nowhere because it is a false name for the separation of causes and conditions; ceasing goes nowhere because it is merely a covering.

Thus, one has already grasped the meaning of the "Great Elements" section—namely, that the nature of form is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true form, all appearing according to karma—and one has also grasped the meaning of the sections on the "Aggregates, Bases, and Elements"—namely, that they are called "marks" based on illusory falsehood.
One has likewise grasped [the meaning of the "False Consciousness" section].

In the "Discerning Views" section, the meaning of "your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the wondrously luminous, true essence of the wondrous mind," and so forth, also encompasses the point from the "Investigating the Mind" section that the eye cannot see itself.

Taking this as the nature-inherent and the simultaneous application of the Great [Vehicle], empty space is fully endowed with all phenomena; the nature of every phenomenon is fundamentally identical to the nature of emptiness.
The great ocean is fully endowed with all its bubbles, for the nature of the bubbles is none other than the nature of the ocean.
Second, the conclusion pertains to the true cause:
one clearly knows for oneself that the fundamental, wondrous mind has been attained, abiding eternally and never ceasing.

This points to the fact that the ten realms—the phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants, matter and mind—are all inseparable from the "present" single thought-moment of my own immediate mind.
The essence of this mind is fundamentally free from transgression and transcends all marks; it is vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive.
Its function is inherently complete, encompassing the sands of the Ganges. These three meanings are unified within this single mind; yet, while being one mind, they are perfectly distinct as three.
The meaning is that this is the wondrous mind inherently possessed by all people, which has been eternally abiding and indestructible from the beginningless past;
it is what is called the primordially pure essence of bodhi and nirvana. By practicing in reliance upon this, one is able to attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Thus, at the very outset, the Tathāgata spoke to Ānanda regarding the characteristics of birth and death for all sentient beings.
Continuing, [the text states]: "All this was due to not knowing the eternally abiding true mind, the nature of pure clarity;
now one knows it clearly and thoroughly, so that although it is an old possession, its significance is as if newly acquired. Second, the description of the ritual protocol.
Prostrating to the Buddha with palms joined, he attained what he had never before experienced; thus, in the presence of the Tathāgata, he spoke verses in praise of the Buddha.
Because he had not realized this until today, it is said that he "attained what he had never before experienced. Since his benefit was so profound, his gratitude became naturally keen;
therefore, by praising the Buddha and making vows, he seeks to repay the Buddha's kindness. Second, the Verses of the Appropriate Audience.

The first part, the praise, has two sections: first, praising the Perfectly Enlightened One’s person and Dharma; second, describing the depth and shallowness of what was realized. Regarding the first of these: The first part, the praise, has two sections:

first, praising the Perfectly Enlightened One’s person and Dharma; second, describing the depth and shallowness of what was realized. Now, the first [of these]: [The text continues with the specific verses of praise.]
"The Wondrous, Profound, Total-Mastery, Immovable Honored One, the Śūraṅgama King, rare in the world.
Here, the first phrase points to the speaker; the next four characters describe the Dharma taught;

and the final three characters offer a general praise for both the person and the Dharma, noting that both are rare. It is only through Ānanda’s thorough awakening to his own mind-nature that he comes to know this.
Because that which the Buddha realized is utterly no different from what is inherently possessed by me, I praise it spontaneously with these words:
"Wondrously profound, total retention, immovable. These six characters alone encompass the subtle purport of the three-fascicle sutra;
they encompass the subtle purport of its title; they also absorb the subtle purport of the subsequent text; and they are able to include the entire dispensation of a single lifetime.
Now, the subtle purport of all Buddha-dharmas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, as taught in this scripture, shall be pointed out one by one;
it is not the same as previous interpretations. "Subtle and profound" (*miaozhan*) refers to the meaning of being constant and unchanging while conforming to conditions.
"Total retention" (*zongchi*) refers to the meaning of being unchanging while constantly conforming to conditions. "Immovable" (*budong*) refers to... [conforming to conditions].
In the "Preface to the Realization of the Meaning of the Non-duality of the Unchanging Conditions and the Conditions Following the Unchanging," it says:
"The mind pervading the ten directions of space is like the leaves and objects; this is the wondrous clarity (*miāo zhàn*). The physical body born of parents is like dust and bubbles;

this is the universal retention (*zǒng chí*). Objects are the wondrous mind, and the essence of the mind contains and envelops them; this is immovability (*bù dòng*). Furthermore, these three meanings are in fact one."
Because it is the mind, it is called "wondrously profound" (*miaozhan*); because this one mind fully possesses three meanings, it is called "total retention" (*zongchi*).
Because it is neither one nor three, yet three and one, it is called "immovable. For all sentient beings, this principle is the wondrously profound, total retention, and immovability;
to produce understanding upon hearing its name is the stage of "name-and-word" (*mingzi*). To give rise to perfect cessation (*yuanzhi*) is the stage of "practice" (*xing*).
This contemplation is the "wondrously profound, total-holding, and immovable" state of the purification of the six sense organs, which is the stage of semblance-attainment (*sādharmya-niṣṭhā*).
This wondrously profound, total-holding, and immovable state where ignorance is first shattered is the stage of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha-niṣṭhā*).
This wondrously profound, total-holding, and immovable state that is fully and thoroughly realized is the stage of ultimate attainment (*niṣṭhā-niṣṭhā*). Now, it is called ultimate attainment.

Because he is one who has realized [the truth], he is called "Venerable," meaning that he is fully endowed with the Ten Epithets: the God among gods, the Sage among sages, and the one universally honored by the nine realms of the mundane world.
To summarize the seven great sublime principles mentioned previously: because it pervades the entire Dharma-realm, it is called "wondrously profound" (*miaozhan*).
Its nature is such that form is true emptiness and its nature is such that emptiness is true form; they manifest according to karma, and so forth.
Therefore it is called the Total-Holding (Dhāraṇī) that is Pure and Innate; therefore it is called Immovable. Furthermore, because the three are identical with the one, it is wondrously profound;
because the one is identical with the three, it is the Total-Holding. It is neither one nor three, yet it is both three and one; thus it is immovable.

It is designated as "Honored" because it refers to the ultimate state. To summarize the sublime meaning of the preceding aggregates, sense-bases, elements, and realms: seek within the true, eternal nature.

Because in the past and future, in delusion and enlightenment, and in birth and death, there is absolutely nothing to be attained; because the wondrous and profound is called "phenomena" due to its illusory nature;

and because the total retention of that nature is the true essence of wondrous enlightened clarity—remaining unmoved through the stages of one, three, one, and three, up to the ultimate state—it is called "Honored One," as explained above.
This concludes the preceding analysis of the wondrous principle of seeing, wherein both the faculty of seeing and its objects...

The characteristics of what is conceived are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent; therefore, the wondrously profound is originally the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed *bodhi*, the pure, perfect, true mind.
It is through delusion that it manifests as form and emptiness, as well as hearing and seeing.
Thus, this seeing and its objects are, in their essence, the wondrous, pure, and luminous substance of *bodhi*. Therefore, it is immovable and free from all marks.
Therefore, wondrous stillness (*miāozhàn*) is precisely all phenomena; because it maintains them as a whole without "is" or "is not," it is immovable.

Furthermore, seeing wrinkles on the face change while perceiving that which is not wrinkled or changing constitutes wondrous stillness; abandoning birth for the sake of proceeding toward birth amidst the absence of arising and ceasing constitutes maintaining [all phenomena].
That arising and ceasing and non-arising, non-ceasing are but this one mind constitutes immovability. Furthermore, taking emptiness as the master is...

The wondrously profound subject must have an object, and emptiness must possess objects; for the subject and object of the "total-holding" (dhāraṇī) and emptiness and its objects are in reality of no dual nature—this is immovability.

To summarize the subtle purport of the preceding inquiry into the mind, it is precisely to reveal that all seven locations are not [the mind], while subtly revealing that all seven locations are [the mind] as the principle of total-holding; in truth, there is no duality.
That which is not non-existent and that which is not identical to existence is called immovability (*aniñjya*).
Because one awakens to wondrous clarity, it is the initial expedient means of *śamatha*; because one awakens to total retention (*dhāraṇī*), it is the initial expedient means of *samāpatti*;
because one awakens to immovability, it is the initial expedient means of *dhyāna*. Furthermore, awakening to wondrous clarity, total retention, and immovability is called the three.
To realize that "one" is the initial expedient of *śamatha* for awakening to the wondrous, profound, and all-encompassing retention of immovability;
to realize that "three" is the initial expedient of *samāpatti* for awakening to the wondrous, profound, and all-encompassing retention of immovability;
and to realize that which is neither one nor three, yet is both three and one, is the initial expedient of *dhyāna*. Furthermore, it is the awakening to the wondrous *śamatha*.
He speaks of samādhi, dhyāna, and samāpatti; mentioning one, all three are established—this is the realization of the wondrous, profound stillness (*śamatha*), samādhi, and dhyāna.
Mentioning one, all three are established—this is the realization of the wondrous total retention (*dhāraṇī*).
This wondrous *śamatha*, samādhi, and dhyāna are neither one nor three, yet they are three and one—this is the realization of immovability. Thus, the essential meaning of the title is subsumed.

The "Secret Cause of the Tathāgata" refers to the ultimate meaning of cultivation and realization; it is named "Wondrously Profound. The "Ten Thousand Practices of the Bodhisattvas" refer to the *Śūraṅgama*;

it is named "Total Retention. The "Great Buddha-Crown" refers to the Immovable; furthermore, the two types of cultivation are entirely contained within the single nature, which is named "Wondrously Profound.
That the single nature is fully endowed with these two cultivations is named "Total Retention. That nature and cultivation are non-dual is named "Immovable. Furthermore, "Head" (śiras)...

"Lengyan" (Śūraṅgama) means that all phenomena are ultimately firm and solid; because the aggregates, bases, elements, and the seven great elements are ultimately empty, it is called "wondrously profound" (*miao-zhan*);
because they are ultimately provisional, it is called "total retention" (*zongchi*); because they are ultimately the Middle Way, it is called "immovable.
Even up to the ultimate state of "three-in-one" and "one-in-three," it is named "Venerable Endowment," as described above. Furthermore, it is fully endowed with the ten thousand [virtues].

The practitioner’s inherent possession [of these qualities] is called "Wondrously Profound" (Miaozhan); their accumulated possession is called "Total Retention" (Zongchi); and their intrinsic possession is called "Immovable" (Budong).

Furthermore, the three aspects—singularity, unity, and equality—are as explained above. Moreover, regarding the "secret cause": the *nirvedhabhāga* (penetrating) Buddha-nature is called "Wondrously Profound";
the *pratyaya* (conditional) Buddha-nature is called "Total Retention"; and the *mūla* (fundamental) Buddha-nature is called "Immovable. These three causes are intrinsically possessed.

Among the three causes within the cultivation of immovability (*acala*), they are named "wondrously profound" (*miaozhan*); among the three causes of realization and arousal, they are named "total retention" (*dhāraṇī*).

This continues up to the "three-in-one" and "one-in-three," as explained above. Furthermore, because it is immovable, it is called "Great"; because it is wondrously profound, it is called "Buddha"; and because it is total retention, it is called "Crown.

Moreover, because it is wondrously profound, its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is great; because it is total retention, its function (*vṛtti*) is great; and because it is immovable, its essence (*svabhāva*) is great.
Furthermore, because it is great and wondrously profound, it is self-awakened; because it is a dhāraṇī, it awakens others; because it is immovable, its awakening is full.
Moreover, because it is wondrously profound, its crown is invisible; because it is a dhāraṇī, radiance issues from the crown; because it is immovable, the mark of the crown is most honored.
Thus, each and every one of these three—each and every one as described above—is ultimately termed the World-Honored One (Bhagavān).

As stated above, those who extract the sublime purport from the subsequent text [should understand]: because the Tathāgata-garbha is fundamentally the wondrous, perfect, and round mind, it is "neither ten realms" (daśadhātu-aviviktatva), and thus the wondrous, profound Tathāgata-garbha is the original luminosity of the mind;
because it is wondrous, the ten realms are "all identical" (sarva-samāpatti) to it, and thus the Tathāgata-garbha is the wondrous luminosity of the mind's source;
because it is wondrously luminous, the mind's source is "separate from identity and separate from non-identity," being neither identical nor non-identical, and thus it is immovable.

Regarding "three, one, one, three," it is as explained above. Furthermore, because the Perfect is the true reality, the Wondrously Profound Penetration is the true reality, and the Total Retention is the eternal true reality;
"immovable three, one, one, three" and so forth are also as explained above.

This encompasses the teachings of all periods throughout the entire dispensation, even unto the sublime purport of all Buddha-dharma of the ten directions and the three periods of time—namely, the Buddha-dharma.
Though many [teachings] exist, they do not transcend the provisional and the real: establishing the provisional for the sake of the real, and opening the provisional to reveal the real.
The ritual protocols for the Dharma-preaching of all Tathāgatas do not, in total, go beyond this.

Now, because one knows that the nature of the nine realms is itself the nature of the Buddha-realm, and because the wondrously profound nature of the Buddha-realm is itself the nature of the nine realms, one upholds the single nature as all natures, and all natures as the single nature.
Because it is the nature [of reality], it is immovable. Because it reveals the provisional to manifest the real, it is called "wondrously profound" (miao-zhan);

because it establishes the provisional for the sake of the real, it is named "total retention" (zongchi); and because the provisional and the real are non-dual, it is called "immovable. To state the essentials: the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* is called "wondrously profound";
the merit of the *nirmāṇakāya* is called "total retention"; and the principle-body of the *dharmakāya* is called "immovable. Furthermore, all...
The wisdom of the path is called "wondrously profound" (*miaozhan*); the knowledge of the modes of phenomena (*sarvākārajñatā*) is called "total retention" (*zongchi*);

the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is called "immovable. The merit accumulated through practice is called "wondrously profound"; the merit inherent by nature is called "total retention"; the merit inherent by nature is called "immovable.

The principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called "wondrously profound"; the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is called "total retention"; the principle of the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*) is called "immovable."
Because they are immovable, the three bodies are all wondrously profound; because the three are one, the three bodies are all total retention (*dhāraṇī*);
because the one is the three, the three bodies are all immovable. Because they are neither one nor three, yet are three and one, Ānanda has now, with a single phrase, praised them exhaustively.
Were it not for perfect awakening, how could this be possible? The ancients called this "wondrous profundity."

The *Śūraṅgama-mantra* (Dhāraṇī) that governs the meaning of manifesting vision; the *Acalā-dhāraṇī* that governs the meaning of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); and the *Mahābhūta-dhāraṇī* that governs the meaning of the seven great elements—how far removed these are from the sublime intent!
This is indeed lamentable. The *Śūraṅgama-rāja-samādhi* is the name for the practice perfected through the entirety of the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*);

this is as fully explained in the *Xuan-yi* (Profound Meaning) and in the commentary on the first fascicle. Now, one understands the passages concerning the investigation of the mind, the discernment of vision, the four categories, and the seven great elements.
This is not to say that it does not manifest the essential nature of this samādhi;

rather, it is "rare" because the sentient beings of the nine realms have not yet awakened to the hidden nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), have not yet possessed the virtues of a Buddha, and were thus unable to expound this samādhi nor had they ever heard of it before—hence its rarity—and only now have they begun to hear it. Second, the description of the depth of what has been realized.
"May it eliminate my deluded thoughts of billions of kalpas, so that without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, I may attain the Dharma-body.
These "deluded thoughts of billions of kalpas" refer to the false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of recognizing delusion within enlightenment since beginningless time.
Based on this false conceptualization, there arise the causes and conditions, as well as the natural harmony and disharmony, within the nine realms of existence.

Now, because one understands that this various proliferation of conceptual play (*prapañca*) is the wondrous nature in which "the unchanging follows conditions" and "following conditions is unchanging," delusive thoughts of proliferation are suddenly extinguished, and the originally existing *dharmakāya* is attained.

Since it is called the *dharmakāya*, it must necessarily possess *prajñā* and *vimukti*; thus, it differs from the "original *dharmakāya*" explained in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). To point this out:
The locus where inverted perceptions are eliminated is liberation; the wisdom capable of eliminating them is *prajñā*.
Yet, these three virtues of the Dharma-body have never been diminished from the beginning; they merely exist as a principle and meaning that is not realized due to delusion, as if one has lost them.
Now, by attaining awakening from delusion, the "initial awakening" (*shiqiao*) becomes efficacious, which is termed "attainment. This [process] consists of five stages of varying depth.

The depths of these attainments are not the same; they are what are called attainment through names, attainment through contemplative practice, attainment through resemblance, attainment through partial realization, and attainment through ultimate perfection.
Ānanda, as for his inner secrets and outward manifestations, his original ground was secretly attained and cannot be recklessly measured;

however, based on his manifest attainments within his traces, he corresponds to the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) in the Hīnayāna teachings, while in the Perfect Teaching (*Vajrayāna*), he stands at the level of the first faith.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "You have now attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. This clear text is found here;

since you are only now realizing the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*), you must once again cultivate contemplation based on a settled meditative object (*samādhi-viṣaya*) as the means of entry into the gate of the "Flower Mansion" of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).
One should know that while still falling into the chamber of lust, one remains a worldling (*pṛthagjana*); thus, there is no untainted precept (*anāsrava-śīla*) at that time. However—

There is a discipline (*vinaya*) that requires the Buddha’s ultimate salvation; yet the passage concerning "reckoning the mind in seven places" is entirely subsumed under the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

The various old commentaries are in confusion, for they not only fail to recognize the characteristics of the medicine taught by the Tathāgata, but also remain ignorant of the characteristics of the illness pointed out by Ānanda.
Second, the request for empowerment through two vows; third, the initial formulation of the great vow.
Second, the request for the Buddha’s empowerment and three similes regarding non-retrogression. First:
"May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, returning to deliver as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges; with this profound resolve, I shall serve every dust-mote world-system.
This is called repaying the Buddha's kindness. I humbly entreat the World-Honored One to bear witness: in this evil age of the five turbidities, I vow—"
First entering [the path], one vows that as long as even a single sentient being has not yet attained Buddhahood, one will never enter *nirvāṇa* here.
The first verse constitutes the Four Great Vows; the subsequent verse constitutes the Superior Vow.

This vow to now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King represents the aspiration for the wondrous enlightenment of the ultimate fruit, which is the desire to realize the Path and Cessation within the ten realms.
This means that the vow to accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way encompasses the Dharma-gate of the immeasurable vow to know all phenomena;

likewise, the vow to deliver sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges encompasses the vow to sever the inexhaustible afflictions. These four great vows are based upon [the Four Noble Truths]:

the first two correspond to the truth of the cessation of suffering, while the latter two correspond to the truth of the origin of suffering within the ten realms—that is, the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings and the vow to sever inexhaustible afflictions.
Because one generates the aspiration by means of the Four Noble Truths, it is called the "profound mind. Next, regarding the increase of the superior vow:
within the evil world of the five turbidities, one vows to enter first; this is the superior covering of courageous vigor.

Furthermore, since the sentient beings of the five turbidities are stubborn and difficult to transform, one now realizes that the *tathāgatagarbha* is equal and non-dual, and thus becomes free from fear. Moreover, there is the great compassion of identical essence, like that of parents toward their children.

It is because of the added compassion for those who are sick. The two lines beginning with "As long as even one sentient being has not attained Buddhahood" refer to the superior power of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Because one realizes the *tathāgatagarbha*, which vertically exhausts the past and horizontally pervades all, one does not abandon a single sentient being nor does one weary of extending through the limits of the future.

Furthermore, this is because of the great compassion of identical essence (*samāna-sarīra-mahākaruṇā*), which gives rise to a love and mindfulness toward all beings equally, just as parents do toward their children.
*Nirvāṇa* is also called *nibbāna*; this is translated as "extinction" (*mie-du*). Second, he requests the Buddha’s empowerment:

"O Great Hero, of great power and great compassion, I pray that you will further examine and eliminate my subtle delusions, so that I may quickly ascend to supreme enlightenment and sit at the site of awakening throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
Because he has realized the essence of the Dharma, he is called the Great Hero (Mahāvīra); because he possesses both wisdom and the severance [of afflictions], he is called the One of Great Power;

and because he is able to rescue and deliver others, he is named the One of Great Compassion. "Great Power" is the virtue of wondrous stillness; "Great Compassion" is the virtue of universal retention (dhāraṇī); and "Great Hero" is the virtue of immovability.
Furthermore, because these three are one, there is wondrous stillness; because this one is the three, there is universal retention; and these three are [thus] one.

Because it is neither one nor three, yet is three and one, it is immovable; furthermore, because it realizes the essence of the wondrously profound, all-holding, and immovable principle, it is named the Great Hero (Mahāvīra).
Because it possesses the wondrously profound, all-holding, and immovable wisdom that illuminates, it is named Great Power.
Because it gives rise to the wondrously profound, all-holding, and immovable sublime function, it is named Great Compassion. Regarding "subtle afflictions" (*anuśaya*), based on...

In the following passage, the Buddha tells Ānanda: "You have now attained the fruit of Srotāpanna; you have already extinguished the afflictions of the world of sentient beings within the three realms that are abandoned through insight.
This refers to what was stated above: "I have eliminated my inverted perceptions accumulated over billions of kalpas. He further says:
"Yet you still do not know the beginningless, empty habitual tendencies accumulated within the faculties; those tendencies must rely upon causes [to be eradicated]."

"Attainment through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya-prāpti*) refers here to the afflictions of thought within the three realms. Furthermore, it says, "How much more so the divisions and counts of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing within these";
this refers to the distinct afflictions outside the [three] realms, namely what are now called the subtle afflictions.

"Unsurpassed enlightenment" (*anuttara-bodhi*) is ultimate enlightenment; by eliminating the subtle afflictions, one immediately ascends to Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is what is meant by "the culmination of clarity."
This refers to the Tathāgata; the worlds of the ten directions are the lands of serene light, true recompense, provisional means, and shared residence.
That is to say, when a single person attains Buddhahood, the entire dharma-realm becomes the environment and the body of that one Buddha.
The second metaphor illustrates non-retrogression:
"The nature of *śūnyatā* (empty space) may perish, but the *akṣara* (indestructible) mind does not waver or shift.
*Śūnyatā* here is translated as "empty emptiness," which cannot perish; however, it can still be said that while the bubble may vanish, the empty space itself is fundamentally non-existent.

"Melting away the kāra"—which here is translated as "vajra"—is used as a metaphor because the mind of firm resolve generated in accordance with the nature is identical to the storehouse-nature (ālaya-gotra);
therefore, it never wavers or shifts. The primary section on the correct elucidation of the rational nature is hereby concluded.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Fascicle Three:
Explanatory Text of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
Fascicle Four: Words and Phrases.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra during the Tang Dynasty;
the words and phrases compiled by the Dharma Master, Bodhisattva-Śrāmaṇera Gushu Zhixu.
Compiled by the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Wēnlíng Dàofǎng. Part Two:
Dispelling Remaining Doubts. The preceding section revealed the principle through phenomena, thereby fully manifesting the wondrous principle of the perfect and sudden nature-inclusion;
thus, those present attained perfect awakening and permanently severed their doubts. Now, this section is separately divided into two parts.

For those who ride upon the vehicle [of the Mahāyāna] but whose attachment to persons and phenomena is heavy, both doubts are simultaneously raised to seek an answer, demonstrating that the origin of delusion is thoroughly investigated so that they may know that both delusion and awakening are devoid of intrinsic nature;
from this point, one may speak of "arising cultivation according to nature," for cultivation is not external to nature.

The text is divided into two parts: first, clarifying that the phenomena and principle, as well as their characteristics, are fundamentally fused; second, clarifying the causes of delusion and awakening.

The conditions are without intrinsic nature. This consists of three parts: first, the initial inquiry and request; second, the granting of permission to proclaim; and third, the actual exposition. The first part [the inquiry and request] further has two sections:
first, the expression of reverence; second, the praise and narration. Now, for the first [expression of reverence]:
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat amidst the great assembly;
he bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Regarding "exposing the right shoulder": when sitting upright to listen to the Dharma, one’s robe is normally draped over both shoulders;

however, because one now rises from one's seat to inquire about the Dharma, one exposes the shoulder to manifest respect and compliance. Placing the right knee on the ground is called *hukuei* (half-kneeling), which likewise expresses an attitude of respect and compliance.
Joining the palms (*añjali*) signifies single-mindedness. Altogether, these constitute the formalities of reverent conduct.
The second part consists of two sections: first, praising the teaching; second, recounting the request. Now, for the first:
"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, you have skillfully expounded for the sake of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)."
Because wisdom can sever delusions, it is called "Great Majesty" (*mahātejas*); because compassion can benefit sentient beings, it is called "Great Virtue" (*mahāguṇa*).

Furthermore, because it subdues sentient beings, it is called "Majesty," and because it embraces sentient beings, it is called "Virtue. Since these two—subduing and embracing—are employed together, like a father and a mother, he is called the World-Honored One of Great Majesty and Virtue (*Mahātejogunabhagavān*).
As for the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), this praises what was previously mentioned.
Explaining how phenomena manifest principle, both the nature and its manifestations are the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
because only a Tathāgata can thoroughly realize this, it is called the "Tathāgata’s Primary Truth. Second, the description of the request, which has three parts: first, a general statement of doubt;
second, a specific statement of two difficulties; third, the request for the Buddha’s instruction. Now, the first part.
The World-Honored One has always declared me to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma;

yet now that I hear the Tathāgata’s subtle and wondrous sound of the Dharma, I am like a deaf person standing more than a hundred paces away listening for the buzz of a mosquito—what was originally invisible to me, how could it be heard?
Although the Buddha has proclaimed this clearly to remove my delusions, I still do not fully understand the ultimate meaning of these principles, nor have I reached the ground of freedom from doubt.
World-Honored One, although those like Ānanda have attained awakening, their habitual outflows have not yet been eliminated;

and although those among our assembly who have ascended to the state of being without outflows have exhausted all taints, even now, upon hearing the Dharma-sound preached by the Tathāgata, we still harbor lingering doubts and regrets.
This first describes the symptoms of his doubt and sets forth the reasons for his uncertainty. The deaf man is a metaphor for the śrāvakas who lack the wisdom of the Middle Way;
the hundred paces away is a metaphor for the Buddha’s realm being extremely distant from them;

and the mosquito is a metaphor for the subtle and wondrous Dharma-sound of the Middle Way, which they have never before perceived—this signifies that the śrāvakas’ eye of wisdom does not see the Buddha within.
How much more so regarding the realm of the Path! To even hear [of it] is like being deaf from ignorance, obstructed from hearing the true meaning that is expressed;
this describes the state of their doubt. Those such as Ānanda have light cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and thus were first awakened;

yet because their afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are heavy, their habitual outflows (*āsrava*) have not been eliminated. As for us Arhats, our afflictive obstructions are light, and thus we have exhausted all outflows.

"Knowing that the hindrances are heavy, one is still entangled in doubt and regret"—this explains the reason for giving rise to doubt, which stems from the heaviness of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Second, the specific exposition of the two difficulties is further divided into two parts: first, the difficulty of the contradiction between principle and phenomena arising from the sections on the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*);
second, the difficulty of the contradiction regarding nature arising from the section on the seven great elements (*mahābhūta*). Now...
First: World-Honored One, if all things in the world— the sense organs, objects, aggregates, bases, and elements— are all the Tathāgatagarbha, pure and fundamental from the beginning,
how is it that suddenly the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena arise, undergoing successive transformations and flowing on until their end?
It begins again.

[The Master] thought to himself: "Since the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are all the true nature of reality (*tathatā*), and this ultimate truth cannot admit of falsehood, why do we perceive these various false appearances?
From where does this falsity arise? It is surely because one has not realized that what the Tathāgata points to as false is...

This is because the principle is that the true is non-existent and the false is not to be negated. Second, from within the text on the seven elements, he raises the objection regarding their contradictory natures:
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata has said that the fundamental nature of earth, water, fire, and wind is perfectly interfused, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, serene and eternally abiding."
World-Honored One, if the nature of earth is all-pervasive, how can it accommodate water? If the nature of water is all-pervasive, why does fire not arise?

Furthermore, how can you explain that the natures of both water and fire are simultaneously pervasive throughout space without one subduing or extinguishing the other? World-Honored One, the nature of earth is obstructive while the nature of space is vacuous;
how can both be simultaneously pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm?
The meaning is this: [the interlocutor] considers earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth to be singular and all-pervasive, leaving no room for anything else.

This is because they fail to comprehend the Tathāgata’s principle that "nature is entirely identical with form, and form is entirely identical with nature," and instead falsely take solidity and obstruction to be the nature of earth, and moisture to be the nature of water, and so on.
Third, he requests the Buddha to provide further instruction.
Yet I do not know where this meaning leads; I only pray that the Tathāgata will flow forth with great compassion, dispel the clouds of delusion for me and the great assembly.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, thirsting for the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Tathāgata.

"Wherever one goes" (*yǒuwǎng*) means "where one returns"; "open my clouds of delusion and those of the great assembly" (*kāi wǒ míyún jí zhū dàzhòng*) means "open the clouds of delusion for me and the great assembly. Second, the permission to preach:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa and all the Arhats in the assembly who were free from outflows and had attained the stage of no-more-learning.
Today, the Tathāgata has universally proclaimed for this assembly the true nature of the ultimate meaning within the ultimate meaning,
so that those śrāvakas of fixed nature within your assembly, as well as all arhats who have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness and have turned toward the Mahāyāna,
may all obtain the ground of the quiescent extinction of the One Vehicle— the true site of *araṇya* practice for correct cultivation. Listen attentively now!
"I shall now speak for you; Pūrṇa and the others, who revere the Buddha’s Dharma-voice, listen silently.

Because those still in training (*śaikṣa*) have already attained realization, he addresses only those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). The preceding passage revealed the principle through phenomena, showing that the nature-inherent characteristics are none other than the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);
now, by further exhausting all doubts regarding phenomena, nature, principle, and characteristics, it is called the ultimate truth.
The nature of the true ultimate reality is not something added externally beyond the prior ultimate; it merely causes the true nature to become doubly manifest.

Those of fixed destiny as *śrāvakas* specifically refer to those who do not turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], meaning they have not attained the two kinds of emptiness—namely, that they have only realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) but have not realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). However, those who are willing to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle are not of fixed destiny. (1)

Those who mount the ground of the field of quiescent extinction—that is, the wondrous true *tathatā* nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, the single Buddha-vehicle which is primordially quiescent—take this as the basis for cultivating the cause.

This is the truly unadulterated place where one practices the correct conduct of arising from the entirety of *dharmatā*. Now, in expounding this Dharma, whether one has turned the mind [toward enlightenment] or not...

Turning their minds [toward the Way] so that all may attain enlightenment can be considered the preliminary stage (*pūrvāṅga*) to the *Lotus Sūtra*. Once they reach the *Lotus Sūtra*, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) have already been opened;
there would be no one left whose mind has not turned, nor would it be necessary to provide further instruction. Third, the Main Exposition, which has two parts:

first, answering the objection regarding the contradiction between principle and phenomena by explaining how delusion arises from the truth; second, answering the objection regarding the mutual accompaniment of characteristics.

The nature is all-pervasive; this explains the difficulty regarding the contradiction of its nature. In the first of the two initial sections, there is first a general exposition of true awakening, and second, a specific clarification of delusion and enlightenment.
The first section further has two parts: first, directly pointing to the fact that the nature of awakening is originally quiescent yet illuminating;
second, simultaneously refuting the views that awakening is either luminous or non-luminous. This is the first [part].
The Buddha said, “Pūrṇa, as you have said, it is pure and fundamental by nature; how then could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Have you not always heard the Tathāgata proclaim that the nature of awakening is wondrously luminous, and that fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous?
Pūrṇa replied, “Indeed, World-Honored One, I have always heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning.”
This first points out that the primordial awakened nature (bodhicitta) belongs neither to delusion nor enlightenment, yet serves as the basis for both delusion and enlightenment.

"Nature-awareness" (*xingjue*) and "original awareness" (*benjue*) have only two names; ultimately they possess no dual substance. Not changing is called "nature," while being inherently present is called "original.

"Wondrous clarity" and "clarity-wondrousness" are merely different ways of expressing the same reality, manifesting its state of being eternally luminous within stillness and its state of being eternally still within illumination.
Yet this constant quiescence cannot be diminished by delusion nor increased by awakening.
Although Pūrṇa claimed to have heard it constantly, he had not in fact grasped its essential meaning; therefore, the Buddha was able to test him with two critical questions.
These two pairs refute both the notion that awakening is clarity and the notion that it is a lack of clarity.

The Buddha said, "When you refer to 'awakened clarity,' does this clarity of nature refer to what is called 'awakening,' or does it mean that awakening is not clear, and thus it is called 'clear awakening'?

Pūrṇa replied, "If this lack of clarity were called 'awakening,' then there would be nothing to be made clear. The Buddha said, "If there is nothing to be made clear, then there is no 'clarifying through awakening.
To have something before one is not awakening; to have nothing before one is not clarity. Furthermore, this 'lack of clarity' is itself not [the absence of] clarity."

Regarding the phrase "the nature of awakened, profound clarity," this passage consists of three sections: first, from "The Buddha said" downward, he simultaneously interrogates both clarity and non-clarity;
second, from "Pūrṇa" downward, he exclusively accepts the side of clarity while regarding non-clarity as incorrect; third, from "The Buddha said" downward, he refutes both.
Both "clarity" (*prabhāsvara*) and "non-clarity" are incorrect. Previous interpretations have been manifold, yet they damage the text and miss its essential meaning;

I shall not take the time to debate them here, but will simply set forth the explanation so that the meaning may become clear. The initial passage need not be subjected to forced interpretation to make it profound;

rather, let it be understood in its most straightforward sense. The question asks: "Regarding what you call 'awakened clarity' (*bodha-prabhāsvara*), does this refer to the nature having something to clarify such that it is named 'awakening'?"
Is it that what is called "enlightened awareness" (vidyā) is actually non-enlightenment? For this reason, two checkpoints—enlightenment and non-enlightenment—are established to examine the matter.
Pūrṇa then replied: "If this non-enlightenment were called enlightenment, then there would be nothing enlightened.
This implies that there must be something enlightened for it to be termed "enlightened"; thus, he ultimately fell into a logical trap.
This is the section on "The One Who Clarifies. The Buddha then refuted both [positions] together, saying:

"If you claim that if there were nothing to clarify, then there would be no 'clarifying awareness,' you must necessarily assume that there is something to be clarified. To know that there is something [to be clarified] is not the nature of awakening.
Having thus refuted the error of what he had grasped, fearing that he might shift his calculation toward the notion of "non-illumination," the Buddha again restated and refuted it, saying: "Non..."
Furthermore, "not being ignorance" does not mean there is no ignorance; "yet not being the nature of profound clarity" means there is no such thing as a nature of awakened, limpid clarity.

The phrase "not being awakening" reveals that this nature of awakening does not fall into the trap of being "clarity," while the two phrases "not being non-clarity" reveal that this nature of awakening does not fall into the trap of being "non-clarity.
Precisely because it is neither clarity nor non-clarity, it fundamentally does not belong to either.
Delusion and awakening serve as the basis for delusion and awakening. Second, the specific explanation of delusion and awakening has two parts:
first, explaining how sentient beings delude themselves regarding the truth and thus produce the false; second, explaining that the Buddhas awaken to the fact that the false is nothing but the true.

Within the first part, there are three sections: first, explaining the causes from which the false arises; second, explaining the false fruits produced by those causes; third, returning the fruit to its cause. Now...

First: The nature of awareness is inherently luminous, yet through delusion it becomes "luminous awareness. This awareness is not something that can be made luminous; rather, because of this luminosity, an object is established.

Once that object has been falsely established, your false subjectivity arises. Within that which is neither identical nor different, a blazing diversity is formed; based on that diversity of objects, identity is established.

From the manifestation of identity and difference, there further arises the establishment of neither-identity-nor-difference; thus, through such agitation and mutual dependence, weariness is produced.
As this weariness persists for a long time, it raises up dust, causing one's own characteristics to become turbid. From this, the afflictions of worldly toil are incited.
This precisely reveals that within a single moment of the mind of ignorance, there are spontaneously present the three kinds of continuous causes for the world, sentient beings, and karmic fruits.

The phrase "the nature-awareness must be luminous" (性覺必明) carries the same meaning as the previous expressions "the nature-awareness is wondrously luminous" (性覺妙明) and "fundamental awareness is luminously wondrous" (本覺明妙).
It means that the nature-awareness must inherently possess true luminosity; this luminosity is not a delusion that involves directed objects.
This "illumination" (*ming*) is not the same as the darkness of non-awakening that characterizes ignorance (*avidyā*).

Rather, it is the inherent function of *tathatā* (Suchness) manifesting in accordance with conditions. Because this has never been awakened to since beginningless time, an unawakened thought arises and falsely constitutes "illuminating awareness.
Therefore, the nature of awakening is fundamentally not something that can be illuminated; from this false illumination, there subsequently arises the false object of perception.
Having falsely established [distinctions], you immediately give rise to deluded capacities;
