Since the true is fundamentally without delusion, the nature of delusion is inherently empty; how could there be a cause?
Were there a cause, it would not be delusion. Thus, the two lines regarding the "cause of delusion" do not mean that delusion arises from a cause of delusion.
This is because the preceding passage has already refuted both the cause of delusion and the cause of awakening;
now it is said that such a "cause of delusion" is actually the correct cause, for delusion fails to reach the state of causelessness. Thus, while it is not existent, it is eternally self-existent.

If one realizes that delusion fundamentally lacks a cause, then one will know that false conceptualization has no intrinsic nature and nothing further upon which to rely; even at the very beginning, it does not exist.
Once it has arisen and then perished, what can one do? It is exactly like an object in a dream; once awake, how could it be grasped?
Furthermore, since it is without cause and fundamentally non-existent, how could it have any causal conditions—any more than the case of Yan-rda-da-da (Śaṇmukha) in that city?
When one who was running from the fear of losing their head suddenly has the madness cease, the head is not obtained from outside; even if the madness has not ceased, what has been lost?
The false nature of Pūrṇa is just like this: for what reason would it have a location?
Continuing from the preceding text: Objects within a dream cannot be grasped at all upon waking; how much more so this delusion, which is entirely without cause and fundamentally non-existent?
It is just like the case of Śreṇika Bāhula running about in a frenzy;
one can never say that looking into a mirror was the cause of his madness, for many people look into mirrors yet do not run about crazily. Therefore, we know that his sudden frenzy has simply ceased.

The head is not something obtained from without; it may be used as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s wondrous, enlightened, perfect clarity. Even if one has not yet ceased their madness, what has been lost?
This may be used as a metaphor for the fundamental, perfect, and wondrous luminosity of sentient beings. Thus, it can be known that the binding of delusion is without cause.
Second, explaining that even the True [Nature] is without attainment, which has two parts: first, the Dharma; second, the analogy. Now, for the first:

"If you merely do not follow after the three kinds of continuous succession—worldly phenomena, karmic fruits, and sentient beings—the three conditions will be severed, and the three causes will not arise.
Then the madness-nature of your own mind’s *yantradada* (the 'running-about' one) will naturally subside; this subsiding is itself Bodhi."
The supreme, pure, and luminous mind pervades the entire Dharma-realm; it is not obtained from others, so why rely on arduous effort or painstaking cultivation and realization?

Although Pūrṇa and the others have already realized the outflow-free state and severed the three conditions, because they have not yet shattered their attachment to dharmas, they do not realize that the three types of continuity—worldly karma, its fruits, and sentient beings—are entirely devoid of substantial reality; therefore, they follow along with these.
Through false discrimination, one falsely claims there is a triple world from which to escape and a nirvana to be realized;

this is like the case of Pūrṇa, who, terrified of his own head, ran about in a frenzy. Now, one need only not follow this false discrimination, and the three conditions and karma will already be severed first;
the delusive causes for the threefold continuity will likewise not arise, and the nature of madness will naturally subside. When it subsides, [the mind is at peace].
This is precisely Bodhi. "Keng-qi" (the knotty parts) refers to places where tendons and sinews converge; what need is there to rely on toil for the cultivation and realization of these knotty parts?
This means that such words do not require the laboring of sinews or the suffering of bones. This is said in reference to those like Pūrṇa who have already severed their afflictions.
However, if one discusses the essential path of cultivation and realization in general, it is to not follow discursive discrimination, but rather to proceed from principle.

To open the perfect understanding, because the three conditions are severed, one proceeds from the phenomenal to initiate actual practice; only when both principle and phenomenon advance together can one directly realize the ultimate truth.
Although the three conditions may be severed, if one still follows conceptual discrimination, one will produce the false fruits of the human, celestial, or two vehicles.
Conversely, if one does not sever the three conditions yet claims not to follow conceptual discrimination, one falls into the state of mere goodness.

The Bhikṣu Xing [stated that] one must proceed with both principle and phenomena because of the precedent of past errors. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise":
since there is no karma of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, there are no sentient beings; and since there are no sentient beings, there is no world.
This is like one who blocks the source first so that the current dries up, or like one who splits bamboo by first breaking its base.
The second analogy:
Suppose there is a person who has tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within his own garment, yet remains unaware of it;
he wanders abroad in poverty and destitution, begging for food, and though he is truly impoverished, the jewel has never been lost. Suddenly, a wise person points out the jewel to him.
When one’s wishes are fulfilled according to the mind and great wealth is attained, one finally realizes that the divine jewel was not obtained from without.
This differs from the parable of the jewel in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;

in that parable, the sixteen princes establish a connection with the "cause-of-attainment" (了因) jewel, whereas this parable illustrates that each individual inherently possesses the "cause-of-nature" (正因) jewel. The wise person points out the jewel as an analogy, just as follows:
To come and reveal the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Second, the response to Ānanda’s renewed adherence to dependent origination, which has two parts: first, the inquiry;
second, the demonstration and answer. Now, the first:
At that moment, Ānanda, amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, rose, and addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, you have now spoken...”

Because the three conditions for the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are severed, the three causes do not arise; when this is realized within the mind, the nature of madness naturally subsides.
Once it has subsided, Bodhi is attained—not from another person. Thus, the principle of cause and condition is clear and manifest.
Why, then, did the Tathāgata suddenly discard cause and condition? It was precisely through cause and condition that I attained enlightenment. World-Honored One, why is this meaning unique [to you]?
We young śrāvakas in training— such as Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and Subhūti here in this assembly—
having heard the causes and conditions of the Buddha from the aged brahmin, have resolved our minds, attained awakening, and achieved the state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*). Now,
if you say that bodhi does not arise from causes and conditions, then it would be the "spontaneity" (*svayambhū*) taught by Kauśārī and others in Rājagṛha.

The first section refutes doubt, and the second provides admonitions and exhortations. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, the refutation through analogy; second, the application of the analogy to the dharma to conclude the demonstration.
Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, the establishment of the two attachments; second, the refutation of the two attachments. This is the first [of those two].
The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is just as with the case of the mad nature of Rāvaṇa in the city;
if that madness is eliminated, the state of non-madness naturally emerges. Thus, the principle of natural causes and conditions is exhausted herein."
Ānanda originally raised an objection based on the following passage concerning the dharma and its analogy; now [the Buddha] answers and explains it by means of that very dharma and analogy.
When the principle is exhausted at this point, he says: "The principles you maintain regarding causality and spontaneity are fully exhausted here.
What follows is the refutation of their lack of substantial reality. Second, the refutation of the two attachments, which is further divided into two parts. First:
Correctly destroying the two attachments and awakening to the fact that both are fundamentally non-existent. This first section has two parts: first, destroying [the notion of] the head;
second, destroying [the notion of] madness. Now, for the first:
Ānanda, the head of the yakṣa Rāvaṇa was originally natural. It was originally so of itself; there is no "so-ing" apart from its own nature. What cause could there be for it?
If it is because of conditions that the head becomes terrified and runs mad, then why does the natural head not likewise go mad due to those same conditions?

If it is because of conditions that one loses the original head, then why does one not lose it when going mad? Since the head undergoes no change whatsoever, what need is there for conditions? It is merely that deluded fear arises.
This clarifies that the head does not arise from spontaneous causes and conditions, serving as a metaphor for the fact that the true essence does not arise from spontaneous causes and conditions.

First, it clarifies that the head is not spontaneous; thus it says: "Suppose that Daṭṭa’s head were originally spontaneous—then it would be spontaneously so by its very nature, and there would be no 'so-ness' that is not itself.
For what cause and condition, then, would one fear the head and run about in a frenzy? Next...
Since the head at the front is not produced by causes and conditions, it is said:

"If this naturally existing head were truly dependent on causes and conditions, why does it not likewise perish according to those causes and conditions? Now, this original head is neither lost nor destroyed;
yet out of madness and fear, false heads are produced. Since this [original] head has never undergone any change, what need is there for causes and conditions?"
This is the true essence; upon it, there is absolutely no principle of either spontaneity (*svabhāva*) or dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to be found.
Second, refutation by means of madness:

If madness were spontaneous and inherently present, then prior to the onset of madness, where would that madness have been latent? If it were inherently non-mad, how could it become mad spontaneously?
The head is fundamentally without delusion; why then do you run about in madness?

This clarifies that madness is not a natural occurrence through causes and conditions, using this as a metaphor to show that delusion likewise is not a natural occurrence through causes and conditions.
First, to clarify that madness is not natural, it says: "If madness were natural from the beginning, then it would be inherently present even in the absence of fear."
Furthermore, before one has gone mad, where could madness be latent? Next, it clarifies that madness is not due to causes and conditions, stating:
"Even if one were not mad by nature, madness would necessarily rely upon causes and conditions. Now, since the head is fundamentally without delusion, why run about in madness?
How could madness have causes and conditions? Thus, within these illusory phenomena, there is absolutely no such thing as naturalness or causes and conditions."

The principle of this can be understood: if one seeks the principle of spontaneity and conditions within both the realms of the real and the false, and finds them both unattainable, then is that principle not ultimately exhausted? Both awakenments are fundamentally non-existent.
If one awakens to the original head, one realizes that the causes and conditions for running mad are naturally both mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
To awaken to the original head means to know that this head does not change, yet follows conditions; therefore, there are the differences between running mad and the cessation of madness.

Thus, it is not "natural" [in the sense of being unconditioned], for one knows this head follows conditions without changing, and does not depend on the running mad or the cessation of madness [to exist].
Because it exists and because it does not exist, it is neither through causes and conditions nor through consciousness. One knows the madman by knowing that madness has no intrinsic nature;
thus it is not spontaneous. One knows madness has no provenance; thus it is not through causes and conditions. Second, the conjunction of dharmas to manifest the three [points]:
first, the direct conjunction of dharmas; second, the repeated exclusion of what is not; third, the correct indication of what is. Now, the first.
Therefore, I say that because the three conditions are severed, it is itself the bodhicitta.
This statement is an abbreviated expression; in full, it should be said: "Because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise, and the nature of madness naturally subsides;
this subsiding is itself bodhi. Now, when one speaks of the severing of the three conditions and the non-arising of the three causes, there appears to be a resemblance [to the following].
If it arises through causes and conditions, yet you say it is identical to the bodhicitta—this would be like a head that is not obtained from without;
how could it then be due to causes and conditions? Furthermore, if it is identical to the bodhicitta, it would seem to be spontaneous (*svabhāva*);

yet it must be because the three conditions are severed that it is finally "rested," which is the bodhi. This is like one who has ceased their madness and only then realizes his original head; how could this be spontaneous?

When nature is fully perfected through cultivation and cultivation is fully manifested through nature, this is the true Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*). Second, the double negation of what is not [the path]:
when the Bodhicitta arises and the mind of birth-and-death ceases, both arising and ceasing are exhausted; this is the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*).

If there is spontaneity (*svabhāva*) in this way, then it is clear that the spontaneous mind gives rise when the mind of arising-and-ceasing arises and ceases when the mind of arising-and-ceasing ceases; this [arising-and-ceasing] is itself arising-and-ceasing.

That which is without arising or ceasing is called spontaneity. It is like how, in the world, various phenomena that blend together to form a single entity are called the nature of combination (*saṃyoga-svabhāva*), while that which is not so combined is termed the nature of suchness (*tathatā-svabhāva*).

This is because the conceptual calculations of arising and ceasing have not yet been forgotten; thus, one might still give rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding the dharma that is free from proliferation.
Therefore, it is necessary to repeatedly examine and sweep away these notions. The intent is this:

when I say that "because the three conditions are severed, it is the bodhicitta," I do not mean that there are three conditions to be extinguished or that a bodhicitta begins to arise anew. If one follows the words [too literally], one will fall into error.
To resolve that the arising of the bodhicitta of false conceptualization is the cessation of the mind of birth-and-death merely results in the proliferation of the play of birth and death.
Only when both arising and cessation are extinguished is there the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), and only then is there the dharma free from proliferation.
Furthermore, what is called the path of effortlessness is not something natural; if one were to again conceptualize effortlessness as...

If one claims that there is such a thing as spontaneity (*svabhāva*), and further asserts that through this spontaneity the mind of arising is produced and the mind of ceasing is extinguished, this too merely results in the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of arising and ceasing.
However, this dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing is precisely the dharma free from conceptual proliferation, yet it is not "spontaneity" either.
If one were again to designate that which is without arising and ceasing as "spontaneity," it would be just like...

In the world, when various phenomena combine and merge into a single entity, this is termed "the nature of conjunction" (*saṃyoga-svabhāva*); that which is not so combined is called "the original nature" (*prakṛti*).
Both of these are merely false designations established through relative opposition; all such names are but conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). This is what is correctly pointed out here.

"Fundamental suchness is not suchness; harmony is not harmony; being both harmonious and such, one is detached from both; being detached from both harmony and suchness, one is detached from both—this phrase alone is called the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
This follows the preceding text which, having eliminated and brushed away all conceptual proliferation, indicates it by saying: 'How can one know fundamental suchness?'"
Although its nature is unchanging, it follows conditions with its entire substance; therefore, it is not a phenomenon of spontaneous conjunction.
Although it follows conditions, its entire substance remains unchanging; therefore, it is not a conjunction. Thus, both conjunction and spontaneity are equally transcended.
Both transcendence and conjunction are likewise non-existent. Only this phrase is called the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Transcendence.
"Neither conditioned nor spontaneous" is a phrase that doubly negates; "both conditioned and spontaneous" is a phrase that doubly illuminates.
Because both negation and illumination are absent, it is said that "neither union nor separation applies. Second, there are two parts:
first, a warning against mere hearing being fruitless; second, an exhortation that true cultivation is beneficial. Now, the first part:
Bodhi and Nirvana still lie far away; they are not to be realized through your diligent cultivation over kalpas.

Although you may remember and uphold the pure and wondrous principles of the twelve divisions of the Tathāgatas’ scriptures throughout the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—this only increases your frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Though you discourse upon causes and conditions and spontaneity with clarity and certainty, among men you are called the foremost in erudition.
If even those who have accumulated the熏習 (vāsanā) of extensive learning over many kalpas cannot escape the peril of the Mātanga woman, why wait for my Buddha-Usnīṣa Divine Mantra?
The fire of lust in the mind of the Mātanga woman has been instantly extinguished; she has attained the stage of Anāgāmin and become a forest of diligence within my Dharma.
The river of craving has been dried up, and you have been granted liberation.
Second, it encourages that true cultivation is beneficial.
Therefore, Ānanda, though you have for kalpas retained the Tathāgata’s secret and wondrous adornments in memory,

it would not equal a single day of cultivating untainted karma and remaining far removed from the two sufferings of worldly hatred and love, as was the case with Mātanga, who was formerly a courtesan.
By the power of divine mantras, their passions were extinguished within the Dharma; they are now known as the Bhikṣuṇī Śīlā and Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula.
Together they awakened to their past causes, realizing that throughout successive lifetimes, craving and attachment had been the source of suffering.

Because both of these women had cultivated untainted goodness through a single thought-moment, some attained the realization of the third fruit and emerged from the entanglements, while others realized the fourth fruit and received the empowerment of the Supreme Honored One.
The Record asks: "How is it that you deceive yourself by still lingering to observe and listen?
It further asks: "Previously it was said, 'How could one rely on toil and labor for realization?

whereas here it says, 'It is not through your diligent cultivation over kalpas that you have realized this. Why are these statements contradictory? The answer is: "Pūrṇa has already exhausted all outflows; he merely harbors lingering doubts."
Because of remorse, doubt and regret are both removed, and one attains direct realization. Although Ānanda has already attained awakening, his residual habitual outflows have not yet been eliminated;
to realize true wisdom and true severance, he must cultivate the supreme karma of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Yet even this untainted karma is merely the non-following of the threefold continuity of conceptual discrimination—that is, it consists precisely in purifying the true cause through what has been realized.
It is merely the manifestation of karma; there is no separate dharma to be cultivated. Since cultivation is itself non-cultivation, it is said that "resting is itself Bodhi.
Yet, this non-cultivation is not a failure to cultivate; thus it is said that "it is better to cultivate untainted karma for even a single day.
What is called the mutual fulfillment of nature and cultivation, and the non-duality of nature and cultivation, perfectly complement one another—how could they be contrary? Indeed, they are not.
If one cultivates [this practice], even a single thought-moment is superior to a whole day, and how much more so if one practices throughout successive kalpas!

If one does not cultivate it, then even the vast learning accumulated over many kalpas offers no real benefit; how much less so for one who has heard nothing at all. This is a direct exhortation to practice, intended to introduce the following passage:
"Those who still linger in seeing and hearing" is a reproach of those who are unable to turn their vision to see their own nature (*svabhāva*) and turn their hearing to hear their own nature.

Yet one still pursues delusive conditions. From the beginning of the "Section on the Correct Teaching" up to this point, the first major section—revealing the wondrous true suchness-nature of the *Tathāgatagarbha* and the perfect principle of the three truths—is concluded.

Second, demonstrating non-arising and non-extinction as the fundamental cause for cultivation, the wondrous gate of the three contemplations, which has two parts: first, showing the fundamental root of perfect penetration according to the needs of the audience.
The second part demonstrates the methods for the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) for the sake of those in the final age. This section has two parts: first, praising and restating the request;
second, proclaiming the meaning of the Dharma. Now, the first part:
Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instructions, had their doubts eliminated; their minds awakened to the true reality (dharmatā), and their bodies and minds [were transformed].
Attaining a tranquility such as he had never experienced before, he wept again with deep sorrow, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Unsurpassed King of Pure Jewels of Great Compassion, you have skillfully opened my mind;

by means of these various causes, conditions, and expedient means, you have uplifted and guided those submerged in darkness out of the sea of suffering. World-Honored One, although I now receive [your teaching]...”

Upon hearing such a Dharma sound, he realized that the Tathāgata-garbha—the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind—pervades the worlds of the ten directions, encompassing and nourishing the lands of the Tathāgatas throughout the pure, jewel-adorned realms of the Wondrous Enlightened Kings.

The Tathāgata further rebuked him for his fruitless erudition and failure to engage in cultivation, saying: "I am now like a traveler who has suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King."

"Though one may obtain a great mansion, it must be entered through its gates. I only pray that the Tathāgata will not forsake his great compassion, but reveal to those of us in this assembly who are obscured by darkness:
how we may abandon the Lesser Vehicle and fully attain the Tathāgata’s nirvana without remainder; what was the original path of our resolve;
how those with awakening may subdue their past objects of attachment; and how they may obtain *dhāraṇī* and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and waited with single-minded devotion for the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.
This passage consists of three sections: first, the narrator describes the scene; second, from "The Unsurpassed Great Compassion" onwards, the audience addresses the Buddha;
third, from "Having spoken these words" onwards, the great assembly awaits his teaching. In the first section, doubts and delusions are eliminated.
As for "removing," it is because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of names and words have been naturally eliminated and swept away;

as for "the mind awakening to the true reality (*dharmatā*)," it is because the true understanding of the *dharmakāya* increases and becomes doubly clear; as for "body and mind being light and at ease," it is because one is able to subdue the heavy obstacles (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Next, the formal address according to the occasion is divided into two parts: first, from "The unsurpassed great compassion" to "emerges from the sea of suffering."
The passage beginning with "I now [request]" below this is a description of the request for instruction. "Nurturing" (*han-yoku*) is as explained above;

because both the environment and its inhabitants throughout the ten directions are objects within the wondrous mind, they are called "contained" (*gan*); because they all manifest from the wondrous mind itself, they are called "nurtured" (*yoku*).
The metaphor of "traveling and lodging" (*ryuhaku*) represents those who have long turned their backs on true nature, while the "Heavenly King" (*Ten-ō*) serves as the metaphor for the Buddha.
The metaphor of the Dharma King’s Flowered Mansion refers to the secret treasury of the three virtues realized by the Tathāgata.

Although this secret treasury of the three virtues has been my ancestral home for a long time, I was lost and unaware of it; its discovery through the Buddha’s instruction signifies that it is a gift bestowed by the Buddha.

As for the "gate," it refers to conduct as the gate of principle, which is what is called the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*; this is the opening of the perfect and sudden [teachings] mentioned above.
Having understood that the initial expedient means has already been explained, he now directly requests entry through the gateway of the expedient means of the "Flower House.
As for the Tathāgata’s nirvana without remainder, it is the fruit of ultimate perfection, revealed as not being the nirvana without remainder realized by the two vehicles.

Regarding the path of the original aspiration, it is the cause of perfect practice; attaining the *dhāraṇī* and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision— [The above is the translation of the provided Chinese text.]
By means of the Great Dharani Gate of the Threefold Contemplation within a Single Mind, one enters the stage of the Buddha of Sublime Enlightenment through the Threefold Wisdom within a Single Mind.
Part Two: Proclaiming the Meaning of the Dharma, which has two sections: First, the Narrator’s Preface; Second, the Tathāgata’s Formal Exposition. Now, the first section.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those among the assembly— both pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas— who were not yet sovereign in their bodhicitta,
and for the sake of future sentient beings in the age of the Dharma’s decay who shall resolve upon bodhicitta after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
proclaimed the path of the sublime practice of the Unsurpassed Vehicle to Ānanda and the great multitude.
Because the objects of perception (*ālambana*) have not yet been subdued, although one has awakened to Bodhi, one has not yet attained self-mastery;

it is now shown that the correct practice for subduing these objects of perception is essential. This practice applies both to the present and after the passing [of the Buddha], such that there is none who does not rely upon it to realize Bodhi.
Second, the Tathāgata’s correct exposition has two parts: first, a general indication of the causal mind; second, a detailed manifestation.
Cultivation and Realization. Regarding the first two [sections], there are two parts: first, the explicit clarification of the two meanings; second, the resolution of doubts and obstructions.
The first part also has two sections: first, a general inquiry; second, a detailed explanation. Now, the first [section].
"You all must resolutely give rise to the Bodhicitta; regarding the wondrous samādhi of the Buddha-Tathāgata, you should not give way to weariness.
You ought first to clarify the two definitive meanings of the initial mind that awakens. What are these two definitive meanings of the initial mind?"
The "wondrous samādhi" refers to the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama King Samādhi;

because the entirety of the nature gives rise to cultivation, and the entirety of cultivation resides within the nature, it is called "wondrous. Since the qualities of cultivation must have merit for the qualities of the nature to manifest, one must not give rise to weariness.
Because initial awakening is brought forth from fundamental awakening, it is called "arousing the initial mind of awakening. "Decisive" means to resolve.
Regarding "ascertainment" (*niścaya*): one must first ascertain these immutable principles at the very moment of generating the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*).
Otherwise, one will not enter the true assembly of those destined for enlightenment (*samyaktvaniyāma*).

Thus, although this meaning is inherently certain, it is called the "meaning of certainty" because it is only through ascertainment that it becomes known. Second, the detailed explanation has two parts; first, one should examine [the following]:
Regarding the contemplation of the arousal of the mind in the causal stage, one should carefully examine the root of afflictions. This section has two parts:
first, a general exhortation to contemplate with scrutiny; second, the actual demonstration of such scrutiny. Now, the first part.

Ānanda, as for the primary meaning: if you wish to cast aside the vehicle of the śrāvakas and cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully examine whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is identical to or different from the awakening at the stage of the fruition.
Ānanda, if, at the causal ground, you take a mind of arising and ceasing as the fundamental practice while seeking the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, [you will not attain it].
This is impossible.

This correctly demonstrates that because the cause must accord with the resultant awakening, and since the cause is true and the result is correct, one must necessarily take the unborn and unceasing as the fundamental basis for cultivating the cause;
yet the nature of the unborn and unceasing is entirely present within arising.
Within cessation, it is like space being entirely present within the vessel-world, or pure water being entirely present within turbid water;
therefore, one must examine them with scrutiny and make a definitive discernment. Second, the actual demonstration of the examination has two parts: first, establishing the analogy;
second, demonstrating the dharma. Now, the first part:
For this reason, you should illuminate that all conditioned phenomena within the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) are subject to transformation and extinction.
Ānanda, observe the conditioned phenomena of the world: which among them does not decay? Yet, one never hears of empty space decaying or rotting.
Why is this? Because space is not something conditioned; therefore, from beginning to end, it is without destruction or extinction.
This uses the phenomena of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) as a metaphor for the phenomena of the sentient-being-world (*sattva-loka*).

Specifically, all conditioned phenomena of the vessel-world are used to metaphorize the various phenomena of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and sense-objects (*viṣaya*) within the bodies of sentient beings;

and the space of the vessel-world is used to metaphorize the fundamental nature of the sense-faculties, sense-objects, consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth. Second, the demonstration of the Dharma has two parts; first, the exclusion.
The characteristics of false arising and ceasing may be used as an analogy for the two [aspects of] dependence; the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing may be used as an analogy for empty space.

Regarding the first of these two, there are two parts: first, pointing out the falsity to provide a general indication; second, explaining it in detail according to its specific meaning. This is the first part.
Thus, within your body, solidity is earth, moisture is water, warmth is fire, and movement is wind.
Bound by these four elements, they divide your profoundly still, perfect, wondrous, and luminous mind into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing;
from beginning to end, these five layers become turbid.
The four great elements within the body, as well as seeing, hearing, and cognition, are like conditioned phenomena; the profound, perfect, and luminous mind is like empty space.
That these four entanglements are divided into seeing, hearing, and so forth, is precisely what was meant in the preceding text by the statement:
"Once that which is falsely established exists, the principle of clarity does not overstep it. Indeed, it is because these four entanglements partition the wondrous mind.
It is like using the physical world (bhājana-loka) to demarcate empty space;
the four entanglements (catvāraḥ saṃyojanāni) may change and perish, yet the wondrous mind can never be destroyed—just as the physical world may be destroyed while empty space cannot.
However, since the physical world does not exist outside of empty space, one knows that the four entanglements likewise do not exist outside of the wondrous mind.
Beyond this, if you know that emptiness is fundamentally without division and that all divisions are entirely illusory,
then not only can the four entanglements be destroyed, but even seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing can be destroyed.

If you know the meaning of "form-nature being true emptiness" and "emptiness-nature being true form," then not only is the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing itself profoundly still (*zhan*), [but it is also unconditioned].

The perfectly wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind is indestructible; thus, even the nature of the four entanglements within the body is itself that perfectly wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind, which is likewise indestructible.
Therefore, while the characteristics of the eighteen realms may all be subject to transformation and decay, the nature of the eighteen realms is like empty space—indestructible.
Regarding the five turbidities from the beginning to the end: "beginning" is a provisional designation for the phase of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) which has no starting point;
"end" is a provisional designation for the ultimate virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) of wondrous enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*).

Since even a portion of the ignorance of the phase of birth remains undestroyed prior to wondrous enlightenment, a corresponding portion of the subtle characteristics of the five turbidities likewise has not yet been entirely eliminated.

This is because the fundamentally profound, perfect, wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind delusively divides into the two parts of the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*).

The perceived object-part is termed the "dharma of form" (*rūpa-dharma*), and the perceiving subject-part is termed the "dharma of mind" (*citta-dharma*). The dharma of form is precisely the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), yet there is no form apart from the mind;

the dharma of mind is precisely [the aggregates of] sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*), yet there is no mind apart from form. Therefore, as for these two—mind and form...

Since dharmas are fundamentally inseparable, from the beginningless past until the stage prior to wondrous enlightenment, within every moment of thought, the five turbidities have been fully present without exception.
Second, the detailed explanation according to their meanings, which has two parts:
first, a general demonstration of the meaning of "turbidity"; second, a specific explanation of the names of the turbidities. Now, the first part.
"What is meant by turbidity? Ānanda, it is like clear water that is pure and pristine by nature, while the dust, ash, and sand are by their very substance obstructive and solid.
These two entities are such that their natures do not accord with one another.

If there is a person of the world who takes that dust and throws it into the pure water, the earth loses its solidity and the water loses its clarity; their appearance becomes turbid, and this is what is called turbidity."
The turbidity of you sentient beings and the fivefold turbidity are likewise thus.
Previously, in order to demonstrate the nature of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing, the analogy of empty space and various vessels was employed;

now, in order to demonstrate the characteristics of purity and turbidity, the analogy of water and earth is employed. One should know that these are the five [aspects] of the dharma-nature within the Buddha-realm.
The *āyatanas* (spheres) are likened to clear water, while the nine realms of delusion and the five *skandhas* (aggregates) are likened to dust, soil, ash, and sand mixed together.

Nevertheless, within the single wondrous mind, both the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) portions are present; this is likened to the presence of both earth and water within the great void of space.
If one realizes that the nature of water is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true water, then earth and water are truly one.
If emptiness were the true land, it would not need to extinguish earth and water before manifesting; the great void space is like this.

If one realizes that these views and conditions are fundamentally the wondrously pure and luminous essence of Bodhi, then it is unnecessary to extinguish the two divisions of appearance and perception before manifesting the single wondrous mind.
It is simply because one does not realize that appearance and perception are themselves the wondrous mind.

Therefore, by grasping at delusive appearances and casting them into delusive views, one ultimately forms the five turbid aggregates (*pañca-kaṣāya*), which are as murky as failing to realize that earth and water are themselves the nature of emptiness.
Thus, by grasping at delusive earth and casting it into delusive water, one results in this turbid appearance.

Consequently, the subsequent passage speaks of "settling the turbid to reach the clear"; it simply means that if the two divisions of seeing and appearance do not entwine, then seeing and hearing [will be pure].
To awaken to this knowledge is to accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity. It is like removing the mud so that the pure water becomes bright;
its essence is refined and pure, which accords with the meaning of the true emptiness of the nature-water.

One must not cling to the preceding metaphor to challenge the subsequent one by claiming that clear water still belongs to the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and thus must be removed. Furthermore, the following section will demonstrate:

Because Ānanda cultivates the Path based on the nature of hearing, water is used as a metaphor for the natures of seeing, hearing, and so forth, while earth is used as a metaphor for objects and consciousness.
If one were to contemplate the six objective realms (*viṣaya*), water can likewise be used as a metaphor for the nature of the objects and earth as a metaphor for the faculties and consciousness.
Furthermore, if one were to contemplate the six consciousnesses, water can again be used as a metaphor for the nature of consciousness and earth as a metaphor for the faculties and objects.

This must be understood. Second, the detailed explanation of the names of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*): first, the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), up to the fifth, the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*).

Now, for the first: Ānanda, do you see that empty space pervading the worlds of the ten directions? Space and seeing are not distinct; there is emptiness, yet it has no substance, and there is seeing.
The false weaving together of the characteristics of non-cognition constitutes the first layer, which is named the *kalpa-turba* (the turbidity of the eon).
This directly points to the form-aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) of the nine realms as the turbidity of the eon. The character "seeing" (*dṛṣṭi*) subsumes hearing, cognition, and awareness;
it is the seeing-portion of one's own mind, metaphorically like clear water. "Space" (*ākāśa*) subsumes the four great elements and the six sense objects.
This is the manifestation of one’s own mind, which is likened to dust, ash, and sand.
You perceive empty space pervading the ten directions, yet space and seeing cannot be separated at their boundaries; this is likened to water and soil being blended together.
If there were only space and no seeing, then space would have no substance; if there were only seeing and no space, then seeing would likewise [have no substance].

Lacking true awakening, they now perceive through delusive marks, and as these two aspects interweave, they falsely construct the various distinct states of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Consequently, within the true suchness of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there arise the distinctions of the three lands—the Land of Real Reward, the Land of Expedient Means, and the Land of Common Residence—collectively termed the "Dust of the Kalpa" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
As for why this dust of the kalpa is called the first layer, it is because...
Because its characteristics are the coarsest and easiest to perceive, there is second, the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

Your body presently takes the four great elements as its substance; seeing, hearing, smelling, and knowing are congested and obstructed, while water, fire, wind, and earth revolve to produce the perception of characteristics that are falsely interwoven. This second layer is called the turbidity of views.
This directly points to the five aggregates of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) within the nine realms as the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

When it says, "Your body currently takes the four great elements as its substance," this refers specifically to the body of the shared dwelling (*sahā-vāsa*) within the realm of segmented existence (*bhūta-bheda*).

One must understand that although the bodies of the stage of skillful means (*upāya*), true recompense (*dharmatā-svabhāva*), and the Dharma-nature lack the coarse and heavy four great elements, they still possess subtle and wondrous forms (*rūpa-dharma*) and may likewise be called "realms" (*dhātu*).
The four external elements are the natures of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and cognition. Their nature is fundamentally empty and pervasive;
now they are congested and made obstructive, like water losing its clarity. Water, fire, wind, and earth are fundamentally devoid of conscious awareness;
now they revolve and produce cognition, like earth losing its solidity. Because of these false appearances, the two parts interweave, and through this delusion, the six [sense organs] are formed.

The faculty of sensation (*vedanendriya*) experiences the preceding sense objects; thus, regarding that which is neither self nor non-self, one has a conventional view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) while dwelling together with it, and a real view of non-self (*anātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, there is a view that [regards] both self and non-self as real. This is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
This turbidity is designated as the second layer because its characteristics are likewise easy to understand. Third is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
Furthermore, within your mind, the nature of recollection, cognition, chanting, and study gives rise to discernment and vision, which appear as the six sense objects;

yet apart from these objects there is no form, and apart from awareness there is no nature. These characteristics are interwoven through delusion to form this third layer, called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
This directly points out that the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception) within the nine realms constitutes the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). It means:

when you recall past events in your mind, perceive present events, or rehearse various future matters, the nature of your consciousness already gives rise to the cognition and views of the grasper (*grāhaka*), and the appearances of the six sense objects (*viṣaya*) as the grasped (*grāhya*) manifest accordingly.
If separated from these objects, the cognition and views would be without characteristic; if separated from awakening, [the perception] ceases.
Thus, the six sense objects have no inherent nature; the objects are the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect) and awareness is the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect).

Furthermore, because these illusory aspects of seeing and perceived are interwoven, various conceptions and minds arise. Hatred and love arising within the *sahā-lokadhātu* (Shared Residence Land) are called the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
Hatred and love arising within the *upāya-bhūmi* (Land of Expedient Means) are called the afflictions of dust and sand (*rajas-kleśa*).
In the *sambhogakāya* realm (*shibao tu*), hatred and attachment are termed ignorance and afflictions; therefore, they are called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
This constitutes the third layer because, compared to the preceding two aspects, it is more integrated. Fourth is the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

Furthermore, as you arise and perish morning and evening without ceasing, your perceptions and views constantly desire to remain in this world, while the operations of karma perpetually shift the lands;
these interwoven delusions constitute the fourth layer, known as the turbidity of sentient beings.
This directly points to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (行陰) of the nine realms as the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

That which arises and ceases incessantly from morning until evening is the characteristic of the birth-and-death of the shared dwelling (*sahā-vāsa*) and the segmented (*paricchinna*) nature; it is likewise so for the characteristics of the birth-and-death of the provisional means (*upāya*), the true reward (*bhūta-puṇya*), and the transformative (*pariṇāma*) nature.
When knowledge and vision constantly desire to remain in the world, this is the ordinary person’s greedy attachment to the three realms and the two vehicles’ sinking [into quiescence].

The Bodhisattva Who Delights in the Stillness of Space is attached to karmic retribution. As for the constant shifting of lands through the movement of karma: ordinary beings are shifted by good and evil karma;
those of the Two Vehicles are shifted by untainted (anāsrava) karma; and Bodhisattvas are shifted by karma pertaining to the two extremes.
This is understood through the metaphor of water for knowledge and vision, and earth for the movement of karma; their mutual interweaving of delusion forms the nine realms.
The second death is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*); this is designated as the fourth layer because, compared to the preceding ones, it is more obscure and hidden.
Fifth is the turbidity of life (*āyus-kaṣāya*).

You all have seen and heard that originally there is no difference in nature; though separated by the various defilements, you recognize one another within the state of being born differently without cause.

When the characteristics of the middle [state] oppose one another, the standards for identity and difference are lost; they interweave delusively to form this fifth layer, which is called the turbidity of life.
This directly points to the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) of the nine realms as the turbidity of life. You all see and hear that fundamentally there is no difference in nature;
it is like space, which has neither interior nor exterior, and like water, which is originally pure. It is only due to the obstruction of various defilements.

The Transcendent One then gave this command: "Those who are deluded and ordinary are like one who takes a *piṅgala* bird's bottle and blocks both its openings, thereby causing the interior and exterior to be separated from one another;
they are also like throwing dust into water, destroying its purity.
Therefore, within their nature, they still possess mutual cognition—just as the ear-faculty hears the Dharma-body, yet the mouth cannot ask about it—and this cannot be called the six faculties."

These are distinct, yet when functioning within the Middle Way, they are all mutually opposed; for example, the ear does not see forms and the eye does not hear sounds—it cannot be said that the six faculties are identical.
Whether one claims they are the same or different, both lose their standard of measurement.

This is merely because the subjective aspect of seeing and hearing and the objective aspects of the various sensory objects interweave through delusion to form the nine realms; thus, the consciousness-mind subsequently possesses its respective [distinctions].
The grasping of the physical body and life-force differently is called the turbidity of lifespan; this is termed the fifth "heavy" [turbidity] because it is extremely subtle.
Second, regarding the reliance on the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, there is a conjunction with the analogy of space. This has two parts: first, abandoning the turbid for the clear;
second, applying the analogy to the dharma. Now, the first part:

Ānanda, if you now wish to cause seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to reach far back in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity, you should first select the root of birth and death and rely upon the nature that is unborn and undying, the perfect and profound stillness. By means of this stillness, turn back its false delusions so that arising and ceasing are extinguished, thereby restoring the original awakening.
Realizing that this fundamental, luminous awakening possesses a nature free from birth and death, you should take it as the mind for the causal ground; only then—
The cultivation and realization of the fruit-stage of Buddhahood is fully accomplished.

The characteristics of the eighteen realms are none other than turbid water; the nature of the eighteen realms is entirely the Tathāgata-garbha, which is none other than the nature of clear water within turbid water.
Now, because I wish to lead Ānanda to cultivate and realize [the truth] through the gateway of the ear, I specifically point to it.
The nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is like the nature of clear water within turbid water.
You say that if you wish to cause this present-day seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to ultimately accord with the permanence,
bliss, self, and purity of the Tathāgata’s stage of fruition, then while at the stage of names and words, you must first select and eliminate these five layers of interwoven characteristics.
Taking the fundamental nature— which is originally unborn and undying, originally perfect and originally tranquil— as the basis for the root of birth and death,
one accomplishes the merit of contemplative practice; by means of this originally tranquil nature, one reverses its false delusions and extinguishes arising and ceasing,
so that coarse afflictions fall away spontaneously first, and one returns to the original awakening, taking the originally luminous awareness as having a nature free from birth and death.

Having perfected the true causal-ground mind at the initial stage of the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), one subsequently perfects the cultivation and realization of the fruition-ground until reaching the ultimate state of *miao-jue* (wondrous enlightenment).
This is what is meant by the identity of principle between the causal mind and the resultant awakening from beginning to end.

Within this, the nature of seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition—which is unarisen, undying, perfectly still, and profound—is analogous to the preceding metaphor of empty space being indestructible; this constitutes the fifth layer [of analogy].

The mutual entanglement of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) as the root of birth and death is universally pointed out as being illusory; this corresponds to the preceding analogy of the workable substance.
Second, the application of the analogy to the dharma:
it is like settling turbid water by storing it in a still vessel; when it is deep and motionless, the sand and silt naturally sink, and the clear water appears before one.
This is called "first subduing the adventitious afflictions," where the mud is removed and only pure water remains;

it is called "permanently severing fundamental ignorance," where the characteristics of clarity are refined and pure, such that all transformations and manifestations do not become afflictions, but instead accord with the pure and wondrous virtue of Nirvana.

Since previously the act of throwing soil into water was used as a metaphor for the characteristic of turbidity, it is now likewise used—through the clearing of that turbidity to attain clarity—as a metaphor for the characteristics of cultivation and realization.
The "still vessel" is a metaphor for the fundamentally non-arising and non-ceasing, perfectly湛 (zhàn) and profound nature;

just as one must store turbid water in a still vessel to clarify it, so too, to break through the five aggregates (*skandhas*), one must contemplate the fundamental nature of the aggregates (*āyatana*), sense bases (*dhātu*), and elements (*dhātu*).
The Tathāgatagarbha is tranquil, profound, and unmoving, which is analogous to the depth of the power of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).

The sand and soil naturally settling is analogous to the two divisions of appearance and perception no longer interweaving; having perfectly subdued the afflictions of the five abodes, the coarse impurities fall away spontaneously first.
The clear water appearing before one is analogous to the manifestation of the principle of True Truth (*satya*); this is likewise similar to seeing the three truths.

This is the principle: first, one subdues the adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*), which clearly clarifies the subduing of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-vikalpa*) within the realm, while subduing the ignorance (*avidyā*) outside the realm.
The metaphor of removing the mud to reveal pure water illustrates the severance of the distinct delusions outside the realm;

from the initial stage of the Perfect Teaching’s First Abode (*prathamābhūmi*), these are severed partially, until they are ultimately exhausted at the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). Therefore, it is said that the fundamental ignorance is "permanently severed. If...
When the pure radiance of the dawn reaches its peak, one attains the Buddha-realm, the unsurpassed Dharma-nature.

Although the five aggregates (skandhas) flow equally through the nine realms and manifest as all phenomena—whether good, evil, or indeterminate, outflowing or non-outflowing—all such five-aggregate dharmas are merely skillful applications of the dharma-gate of inherent evil.
Because they are not employed by evil dharmas, it is said that they are "not defiled."
The afflictions (*kleśa*) are known to be intrinsically evil, yet this very nature is intrinsically good; when their function is fully realized, it is identical to their essence.

Since the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) are none other than permanence, bliss, self, and purity (*nitya-sukha-ātma-śubha*), it is said that they all accord with the pure, wondrous virtue of *nirvāṇa*. Indeed, the Buddha-dharmadhātu possesses both the provisional and the real aspects of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
As for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the real [aspect], these are the true, good, and wondrous form (*rūpa*) of the Buddha-realm, and so forth.
The provisional five aggregates, such as the *āmalavijñāna*, demonstrate their identity with the form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness of the nine realms.
Whether provisional or real, they are all pure and not turbid. When real, they are called the "pure essence of the mark of clarity";

when provisional, they are called "all-encompassing manifestations. This is analogous to thoroughly understanding that the nature of water is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true water.
Water may cause waves to surge and billows to crash, even manifesting as turbid or clear, or appearing separately as earth, fire, or wind;

yet the essential nature of water is never lost. Therefore, by directly taking its turbid aspect, it can be clarified—corresponding to the aforementioned "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) which are destructible—and by taking its luminous aspect of pure essence, it corresponds to the aforementioned "space" (*ākāśa*), which is indestructible. This is truly due to the third [element].
The middle fascicle has already clarified that both emptiness and water are in their nature and essence the True.

Furthermore, one should know that the entirety of our present seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is entirely illusory, yet it is also entirely true. This is because they arise conditioned by seeing and the cause of light, which constitutes the illusory;
whereas being unmoving, unchanging, non-returning, and not seeing, etc., constitutes the True. It is like clay and water mixed together in one place.
In this regard, one must first recognize that within these turbid waters there exists the nature of pure water;

only then may one employ skillful means to remove the turbidity and attain clarity. One must certainly not abandon the turbid water to seek pure water elsewhere, nor should one mistake the turbid water for pure water.
Second, one should carefully examine the root of afflictions. Part One: General Exhortation.
Regarding the detailed examination of the two correct demonstrations, this is the first.

As for the second point: if you all truly desire to give rise to the bodhicitta and generate great courage and resolve within the Bodhisattva Vehicle, you must thoroughly examine the root of afflictions;
since beginningless time, these have been associated with all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Who initiates karma and moistens rebirth? Who acts and who receives [the results]?
Ānanda, if you cultivate bodhi without carefully examining the root of afflictions, you will not know where the false roots and objects are inverted;
if you do not even know their location, how can you subdue them to attain the rank of Tathāgata?

In the first sense mentioned above, the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya) were discussed; this clarifies that when the false arises from the absolute truth, one must discard the false to return to the true.
Now, in the second sense, the six sense faculties are discussed; this clarifies that since the false completely contains the true, one must awaken to the true to harmonize with the false.
The ignorance that initiates karma (*karmotpādaka-avidyā*) is the cause of karma, while the ignorance that moistens birth (*janmārdrīkaraṇa-avidyā*) is the condition for rebirth.
That is to say, karma and its conditions—these two pervade both within and beyond the realms and are collectively termed "afflictions. As for the questions "Who acts?

and "Who receives?", this is precisely to examine their fundamental basis; the underlying intent is to reveal that the agent consists of the six sense organs and the recipient likewise consists of the six sense organs.
Since there are no afflictions apart from these present six sense organs, one must uproot their adhesive clinging. (2)
The second part, "Correctly Demonstrating Thorough Examination," has two sections: first, establishing the analogy; second, demonstrating the dharma. Now, for the first:
"Ānanda, observe those in the world who untie knots: if they do not see what was knotted, how can they know it has been untied?
You have not heard of empty space being torn asunder by you. Why is this? Because empty space has no form or characteristics, and thus there is neither knotting nor untying."

This uses the metaphor of "knots" to illustrate the false state of clinging between the faculties, objects, and consciousness, while using the metaphor of "empty space" to illustrate the fundamental *tathāgatagarbha* (store-nature) of the faculties, objects, and consciousness.
Part Two: Demonstrating the Dharma, which has two sections: First, a detailed demonstration of the locus of inversion, corresponding to the metaphor of the knots;

Second, a formal exhortation to discern and subdue [the afflictions], corresponding to the metaphor of knowing and understanding. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, a general demonstration.
The characteristics of the fetters are shown in two distinct parts; this is the first.
That which is before you—your eyes, ears, nose, tongue, as well as your body and mind—these six act as the intermediaries for thieves who plunder the family’s treasures.
Because of this, since beginningless time, the world of sentient beings has been bound by entanglements, such that they are unable to transcend the vessel-world (the physical environment).
This means that because your six present sense organs act as intermediaries for the external thieves of the six sense objects, they instead plunder the treasures of your own home;
consequently, since beginningless time, you have been bound by the world of the six classes of ordinary beings,
such that you cannot transcend the shared world, and you have even been bound by the worlds of the two vehicles of practitioners.
Because Bodhisattvas cannot transcend the world of skillful means due to the arising of fetters within the realm of sentient beings, they likewise cannot transcend the world of retribution.
As the subsequent text states: "How much more so regarding the divisions, measures, and enumerations of birth, abiding, change, and extinction within this?
Here, "within this" refers specifically to the birth, abiding, change, and extinction occurring among the six sense faculties.
The "number of portions" refers specifically to the distinct afflictions of ignorance;

thus we know that the fetters of the six sense organs pervade all nine realms, and only upon reaching the stage of Sublime Enlightenment can they be completely untied, becoming like empty space, incapable of being shattered or torn asunder.
Question: Previously, the six consciousnesses were identified as the thieves; why do you now point to the six sense objects? Answer: It is precisely because of those six [consciousnesses]...
Because the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) act as thieves, it is said that "the eye is plundered by forms, the ear is plundered by sounds," and so forth.
Furthermore, these six objects are called the "six decays" (*ṣaḍ-hāni*), signifying their ability to cause decay and harm.

In summary, when one is deluded, the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are internal thieves, the six sensory objects are external thieves, and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are both internal and external thieves, acting as mutual intermediaries.
Therefore, if they did not adhere to one another, each and every one would be a virtuous citizen. Second, specifically showing the characteristics of their entanglement:
first, clarifying the number of delusions by way of the world of sentient beings; second, traversing the six sense faculties by way of the delusive numbers of the world.
Now, the first [part].
Ānanda, what are called the world of sentient beings? "World" (*loka*) refers to the constant flux of time, while "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial orientation.
You should now know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the realms;
the past, future, and present constitute the worlds. There are ten directions and three periods of time. All sentient beings are woven together by delusive falsehood.
Within the body formed by mutual correspondence, worlds trade with one another and interpenetrate;

yet while the nature of these realms may be clearly defined according to the fixed positions of the ten directions, the mundane world is merely designated by east, west, south, north, above, and below. There is no fixed position for the center, and the four numbers must be clearly evident as they interpenetrate with the mundane.
Three times four and four times three revolve into twenty, flowing and transforming through three layers of ten.
One hundred thousand.
What is called the "sentient-being world" refers simply to all that migrates and flows within this present body, which is termed "world" (*loka*);
all its spatial orientations are termed "realm" (*dhātu*). There are ten such orientations, and the number of these flows constitutes the three types of sentient beings.
Since beginningless time, birth and delusive weaving have formed one another within a single body; through their mutual exchange and flux, they cause the worlds to interpenetrate one another.
By taking these fixed directions as a basis, they intersect with those shifting three periods of time.
Each of the three periods possesses its own four directions, totaling twelve directions; likewise, each of the four directions possesses its own three periods, thus forming [the same total].
Because there are twelve, it is called "twelvefold winding. One body becoming twelve is the first layer of transformation;
within each of these twelve, there must be ten, which constitutes the second layer of transformation into one hundred and twenty;
within each of these one hundred and twenty, there are again ten, which constitutes the third layer of transformation.
Regarding the "one thousand two hundred," the current statement of "ten, one hundred, and ten thousand" merely cites a large number for illustrative purposes.

However, concerning the threefold transformation of the *liúbiàn* (flowing changes), there has been no definitive ancient interpretation. The explanation by Youxi seems to accord most closely with reason; I shall now excerpt it. Youxi says:
"The first cycle calculates the three periods for each of the four directions, totaling twelve (three times four). The second cycle..."
Regarding the transformation of one into ten across the three periods of time in the eastern direction, this is spoken in terms of the nine periods within a single *kṣaṇa*.
Just as, in the fundamental [structure], one period of the past has already been transformed into the three periods, each of those further becomes three periods;

thus, there are nine periods—namely, the past-of-the-past, the present-of-the-past, and the future-of-the-past; the past-of-the-present, the present-of-the-present, and the future-of-the-present; and the past-of-the-future, the present-of-the-future, and the future-of-the-future.
The past is equal to the present, the present is equal to the future, the future is equal to the past, and the future is equal to the present;
by adding these future states to the fundamental single period mentioned previously, ten periods are established.

This is what is meant by "the ten periods—past, present, and future, beginning and end—do not depart from a single thought-moment. Furthermore, each of the two periods of the present and the future likewise possesses ten periods.
However, regarding the third cycle of thirty aeons together: in the east, each of the thirty aeons transforms into ten, totaling three hundred;

likewise for the four directions, there are twelve hundred Buddhas in total. This is likely intended to mean that the world of sentient beings necessarily possesses spatial orientation and cyclical flux;
every direction has its aeons, and every aeon has its directions. In a single thought-moment, the ten directions comprise nine *kṣaṇas*.
Life after life, throughout the stages of arising and ceasing, the nature of phenomena is thus; this refers to the number of merits within a single kṣaṇa.
If it were for a single moment or a single day, how could there be any limit? What is called "merit" (guṇa) refers to "power" (bala) as the "function" (guṇa);
that is, each of the six sense faculties possesses a power and function that is vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive. This precisely clarifies the *dhātu*.
Although the world undergoes trade and transformation, and although it flows and migrates, there exists that which is unchanging and non-migratory.

This is verified by the "Flying Light" (Feiguang) for its immobility, and demonstrated by the "Ten Sections" (Shike) for its universal perfection. Furthermore, the striking of the bell below serves as verification of its permanence; all these are matters of this very principle.

This constitutes the most urgent matter regarding the selection of the fundamental root of perfect penetration. Personally, I say there is yet another explanation to offer: [Insert the remainder of the text here]
Regarding the three layers of flowing transformation: the first layer consists of three times four, which makes twelve;
the second layer means that within each of the ten realms—both spatially and temporally—each realm possesses the other nine, so that twelve becomes one hundred and twenty;
the third layer means that within each of these realms, each again mutually possesses the ten realms, so that one hundred and twenty becomes one thousand two hundred. Therefore...

The meaning of the following passage regarding the faculty of mind (*manas*) states that it silently encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

This section has two parts: first, an analysis according to the deluded enumeration of the world to examine the six faculties; second, an initial clarification of the essential nature as fundamentally perfect and interfused, followed by a clarification of the differentiation of their functions into superior and inferior. Now, for the first part:
Summarizing from beginning to end, within the six sense organs, each possesses one thousand two hundred merits.
Multiplying one by twelve marks the start of the numerical sequence; multiplying one hundred and twenty by ten marks the end of the sequence at one thousand two hundred.
Although this is the total number for the entire body, the six organs likewise each obtain their full complement. For example:
Just as six people looking at the same moon each perceive the entirety of the moon, such is the natural law of the nature that is eternally true within the delusory.
Second, clarifying the distinctions of superiority and inferiority in function:

this is merely because the sentient beings of this world are immersed in delusion and inversion, and thus their functions are mutually opposed; therefore, within the fundamental nature which is devoid of superiority or inferiority, they falsely [perceive it].
This establishes the characteristics of superiority and inferiority. The text is divided into two parts: first, a general explanation; second, a specific demonstration. This is the first part:
"Ānanda, you should further determine the relative superiority and inferiority among them."
Second, the specific exposition of the six [sense organs]. First, clarifying the characteristics of the eye organ (up to) sixth, clarifying the characteristics of the mind organ.

Now, for the first: as the eye perceives, what is behind is dark while what is before is bright; the front is entirely bright while the back is entirely dark; looking to the left and right, it covers two-thirds [of the side];
in sum, regarding the functional efficacy produced, it is not complete. One-third is said to be its function, while one-third is said to be without such efficacy.
One should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits:
two hundred each for the four cardinal directions and one hundred each for the four intermediate corners, totaling twelve hundred.

The front half is entirely luminous, which refers to the central square and two corners, totaling four hundred; the rear half is entirely dark, which likewise refers to the central square and two corners.
"Four hundred at each corner" means that when observing from the left and right sides, one sees two hundred in each of the four cardinal directions;
this is also what is meant by "seeing. Regarding the phrase "two-thirds," it is a total calculation showing that eight hundred are seen while four hundred are not.
As for the statement that "three parts represent function," it means that nature is inherently complete; the "one part lacking virtue" refers to the partiality of its application. (2)
This clarifies the characteristics of the ear faculty (*śrotra-indriya*).
Just as the ear listens all around to the ten directions without omission—whether in motion, it reaches both the near and the far;
in stillness, it has no boundaries—one should know that the ear faculty is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits in full perfection.
When sound is heard and movement occurs, it seems as though there is nearness or distance; this is merely the deluded perception arising in accordance with karma.
When the hearing is still, there is fundamentally no boundary; this is the essence of that which is eternally true within the midst of delusion. This is the third:
the characteristics of the nose faculty.
Just as the nose’s act of smelling depends upon the passage of inhalation and exhalation— where there is an out-breath and an in-breath— and lacks the intermediate junction,
one should know that when one of the three parts of the nose faculty is missing, it possesses only eight hundred merits.

When it goes out, it takes up fragrance; when it comes in, it perceives fragrance; at the interval between these two states, there is no functional capacity, and thus it is said that "one-third is missing.
Regarding the characteristics of the tongue faculty (*jihvendriya*):
like the tongue proclaiming all mundane and supramundane wisdom, its verbal expression has spatial divisions while its principle is inexhaustible.
One should know that the faculty of the tongue is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits.
The tongue has two functions: first, the discernment of flavors; second, speech and discourse. If judged by the discernment of flavors, its merit is inferior;
however, if judged by speech and discourse, its merit is superior. Youxi (Yuanxiao) said: "This merely cites the proclamation [of the Dharma] to manifest the excellence of the tongue."
"Being able" does not mean that one lacks virtue when not proclaiming [the Dharma]. Regarding "having spatial divisions," this is because worldly and world-transcending dharmas differ.
Regarding "the principle being inexhaustible," this is because both coarse words and subtle speech are all of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
Fifth, the characteristics of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
Just as the consciousness that perceives touch through the body can discern when there is contact with what is disagreeable or agreeable, yet cannot discern separation when one is apart;

and just as the single and the combined are verified through the three aspects of the body-faculty—if one of these three parts were lacking, it should be known that the body possesses only eight hundred merits.

Because it does not know anything at all when separated from its objects, it is considered "one"; because it simultaneously recognizes both the favorable and the adverse when in conjunction with them, it is considered "double.
Sixth, the characteristics of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*):

Just as the mind silently encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena of the ten directions and the three periods of time—whether pertaining to the sages or the ordinary—[so too does the mental faculty].
There is nothing it does not encompass, exhausting all its boundaries; you should know that the faculty of mind is perfected with one thousand two hundred merits.
All phenomena that arise are manifestations of the mind alone; this present momentary thought, however slight, is by nature vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive.
Even if it is clouded by confusion and delusion, its essence remains unchanged; therefore, it is said to silently contain all things.
Regarding all dharmas: first, the formal exhortation to discern, subdue, and understand through analogies;
second, the detailed demonstration arising from doubt. Now, for the first:

Ānanda, if you now wish to go against the current of the flow of birth and death, and desire to trace it back to its source until you reach that which is neither born nor extinguished, you must verify it.

Among these six faculties of reception, which are conjoined and which are disjoined? Which are deep and which are shallow? Which constitute the faculty of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), and which are not fully perfected?
If one can awaken to this faculty of perfect penetration and turn back the beginningless flow of fabricated karmic delusions, one will follow the path of perfect penetration;

compared to those faculties that are not perfectly complete, the difference between a day and an eon will be multiplied tenfold. I shall now fully reveal the six faculties of profound stillness and perfect luminosity as they originally are.
The measure of these merits is as follows; you should carefully examine and select those that are appropriate for you, and I shall clarify them so that you may progress.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions all attain supreme enlightenment through the complete fulfillment of each and every practice within the eighteen realms;
among these, there is no superiority or inferiority. It is only because you are currently inferior that you have not yet been able to perfect yourself therein.
