Because of wisdom, I proclaim this for you: simply enter deeply through one gate; once you have entered that One without delusion, those six faculties of cognition will simultaneously become pure.
Although the six faculties differ in their relative strength and may be said to be entirely illusory, each nonetheless possesses a vertical depth that reaches to the ultimate.

As for the merit of horizontal pervasiveness, it further involves the entirety of the delusory containing the real; therefore, one must turn back from this to return the delusory to the real, using the real to dissolve the delusory.

Regarding "the flow of birth-and-death and desire," this generally refers to both types of birth-and-death, all of which arise because there is grasping and attachment toward phenomena, and are thus collectively termed the "flow of desire.
"Tracing back to the root of the flow" and so forth means to sever the cycle of arising and ceasing.
The root source lies in acceding to the nature that is without arising or ceasing. One should examine these illusory six sense-faculties:
which accords with this nature and which departs from it; which accords deeply and which departs shallowly;

and which both accords deeply and constitutes perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), while which both departs shallowly and is not complete. If one cultivates contemplation from such a state of meditative concentration, progress will be slow.
Because they differ in terms of speed, permanence, and superiority, one must carefully discern them.
The "beginningless flow of delusory karma" refers to the characteristics of the arising of the six sense organs as explained in the following text;
since each is composed of woven delusions, every single organ possesses five layers of turbidity that must be reversed and clarified—the remainder of the text makes this clear. Second, the cause.
The detailed exposition of the doubt has two parts: first, the inquiry arising from doubt; second, the detailed exposition. Now, for the first:

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, how is it that by flowing against the current and penetrating deeply into a single gate, one can cause all six faculties to become pure simultaneously?"
The intention [of this objection] is as follows: since there are already six sense faculties (*indriya*), why is it necessary to enter through only one gate?

This doubt arises by taking up the preceding text. Second, the extensive demonstration has two parts: first, a general demonstration by means of analytical refutation; second, a specific demonstration by way of the characteristics of practice (*ākāra*).

Within the first part, there are three sections: first, analytical refutation based on the phenomena themselves; second, revealing the principle by means of a metaphor; third, applying the dharma to the analogy.
Metaphor. First:

The Buddha told Ānanda, "You have now attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and have already extinguished the delusions of sentient beings in the triple world that are abandoned through the path of seeing;
yet you still do not know the beginningless, empty habitual tendencies accumulated within the faculties."

If even the attainment [of results] severed by the cultivation of the Path is thus difficult to fathom, how much more so the distinctions and enumerations of arising, abiding, change, and cessation within this [attainment]?
Now, Ānanda, observe these six sense-faculties before you: are they one, or are they six?

Ānanda, if you say they are one, why does the ear not see, why does the eye not hear, why does the head not tread, and why do the feet not speak? If these six faculties were definitively established as one...
"Sixth, as I now proclaim this subtle and wondrous Dharma-door to you in this assembly, which of your six sense organs comes to receive it?
Ānanda replied, "I hear with my ears. The Buddha said, "Your ears hear for themselves; what concern is this for your body or mouth?

It is the mouth that asks about the meaning, and the body that rises to show reverence. Therefore, you should know that [the self] is not one, yet it is never six; nor is it six, yet it is never [not] one."
Ānanda, you should know that these faculties are in truth neither one nor six.
Because of the inverted and deluded transmigration since beginningless time, the conceptual meanings of "one" and "six" have falsely arisen within the perfectly湛 (zhan) and luminous nature.
Although you, as a Srotāpanna, have attained the dissolution of the six [faculties], you have not yet eliminated the notion of "one."

*Srotāpanna* (須陀洹) is translated here as "Entering the Stream," the name for the first fruit. The "accumulated empty habits" from beginningless lifetimes refer to the delusions of thought (*viparyāsa*).
"Among these" refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). "The divisions and counts of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing" refers to the specific delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Attaining the dissolution of the six" means not entering into form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; thus, [the delusions] have not yet been extinguished.
First, because they do not yet know the root-source of the fetters (*bandhana*), and because they have not yet eliminated even one of them,

they continue to form fixed views regarding the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and do not believe in the method whereby one enters deeply through a single gate so that all six faculties are simultaneously purified. Second,
the principle is revealed by means of a metaphor.
Just as the great void of space combines with various vessels, and because the shapes of the vessels differ, one speaks of "different spaces";
yet when the vessels are removed and one contemplates the space, that space is said to be one—how could that great void of space be established for you as either identical or different?
How much less can it be called "one" or "not one"?
The great void is used as a metaphor for true nature (*tathatā*), and the various vessels as a metaphor for the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

Just as the void is designated differently according to the differing shapes of the vessels, so too is the perfectly湛 (profoundly still) nature differentiated by those false six sense objects into the distinct functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing;
this is what was referred to in the preceding passage as "the meaning of 'one' and 'six' arising," and that which will be discussed in the following passage.

The arising of delusion from the Truth results in the six functions being partial and restricted. The statement that "removing the vessel and contemplating emptiness, one speaks of emptiness as one" is a metaphor for the dissolution of the six [senses] while the "one" has not yet been extinguished.
The phrase "that great void space," etc., serves as a metaphor for the preceding passage on being neither one nor six;
it also serves as a metaphor for the subsequent passage on the mutual functioning of the six faculties and the supreme cognitive awareness, which is perfectly enlightened, luminous, and wondrous.
Third, applying the analogy to the Dharma:
your understanding of the six faculties of sensory reception is likewise so.
The four sense-objects and the physical organs are like the vessel, while the nature within the faculties is like the emptiness within the vessel; it is neither six nor one.

Second, the detailed demonstration of the distinctions according to their modes of activity (*ākāra*). This has two parts: first, clarifying how delusion arises from the True [Nature], wherein the six functions are partial and restricted;

second, clarifying the return from delusion to the True [Nature], wherein the six sense organs function interchangeably. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the specific demonstration of the causes for their arising;

second, the summary of the characteristics of their partiality and restriction. Within the first of these, there are six subsections. First, the demonstration of the formation of the eye-organ’s knot. (Up to...)
Sixth, the illustration of the formation of the eye-faculty. First:
Through the two types of appearances—light and darkness—in contrast with the wondrous perfection, the clarity of stillness becomes adhered to, giving rise to vision.
This essence of vision reflects forms, binding with form to form the faculty. The root of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements"; its substance is like a cluster of grapes.
The floating faculties, with their four sensory objects, flow and rush toward forms.
This precisely reveals the characteristics of what has been bound, so that people may know what to understand.

For when one falsely takes delusion as the cause of enlightened awareness, and based on that light establishes the objective realm, there naturally arise the two kinds of phenomena—light and darkness—which define one another. From this, within the wondrous...
Within the nature of roundness, it adheres to that luminous stillness and gives rise to the essence of vision.

This essence of vision reflects upon colors such as light and darkness, and by coagulating with these colors, it forms the ultimate sense organ (*paramārtha-indriya*). This can only be seen by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and cannot be seen by the physical eye;
therefore, it is called the "pure four great elements. The phrase "resembling a cluster of grapes" refers to the ultimate sense organ, which is hollow.
Since delusive appearances exist, there must be the "floating dust" eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), which takes the coarse and turbid four great elements as its substance;

it constantly flows in dissipation and rushes toward forms. This is called "deluding the truth to produce the delusive," and thus the eye-faculty exists. Herein, "brightness and darkness" refer to the *bhāga* (objective portion) of one's own mind;
"tranquility" refers to the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving portion) of one's own mind. The characters "adhere" (*nian*) and "reflect" (*ying*) precisely [indicate this relationship].

This is analogous to the meaning of the character "weave" (*zhi*) in the preceding text; it signifies that when the sense organ (*indriya*) is mentioned, the object (*viṣaya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) must necessarily be present;
when the object is mentioned, the sense organ and consciousness must necessarily be present; and when consciousness is mentioned, the sense organ and object must necessarily be present.
Thus, within each individual phenomenon, there is a fivefold entanglement and turbidity. Second, this demonstrates the manifestation of the knotting of the ear-faculty.

Due to the mutual impact of the two aspects of movement and stillness within the wondrous perfection, the clarity of the profound stillness becomes attached and gives rise to hearing. The essence of hearing reflects sound;
when it withdraws from sound, it forms the sense organ. The root of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements. Its substance is like a freshly curled leaf;
as a floating organ among the four objects, it flows and scatters, rushing toward sound.
To falsely conceive of clarity and awareness is the very mark of the initial movement of ignorance;

continuing thus until the mutual dependence gives rise to agitation, and the establishment of solidity and clarity creates obstruction—this is called the two kinds of marks of "movement" and "stillness" striking one another, which are likewise the objective portions (*nimitta-bhāga*) of one's own mind.
Other instances may be understood by analogy with the preceding explanation. Third, the manifestation of the knot of the nose-faculty is shown.

From the two aspects of penetration and obstruction, within the wondrously perfect state, the clarity becomes adherent, giving rise to the sense of smelling; the essence of smelling reflects the fragrance and receives it, thereby forming the faculty.
The root-source of this faculty is termed the "pure cause of the four great elements," and the substance of the nose is like a pair of hanging claws.
This floating faculty flows and scatters among the four objects, rushing toward fragrances.
Obscurity and darkness constitute emptiness, which possesses the characteristic of penetration; the binding of darkness constitutes form, which possesses the characteristic of obstruction.

Therefore, these are called the two kinds of manifested characteristics, which are also the objective divisions (nimitta-bhāga) of one's own mind. Fourth, the manifestation of the characteristics of the tongue-faculty is shown.
Due to the intermingling of the two aspects of tranquility and change within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes adhered, giving rise to tasting;
the essence of tasting reflects flavor, and the binding of flavor forms the faculty. The source of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements," and its substance is like a crescent moon.
This floating faculty pursues the four sense-objects, rushing toward flavors.

When the blazing [fire] becomes distinct, there is immediately the appearance of change; because of this distinction, identity is established, and there is immediately the appearance of tranquility. "Tranquility" means being bland, not being sweet.
These two kinds of appearances intermingle; they are also the appearance-aspect of one's own mind. Fifth, the manifestation of the body-faculty’s characteristics.

Through the two modes of separation and union, they rub against one another within the wondrous perfection; this adhesion to the stillness gives rise to awareness. The essence of awareness reflects upon contact, and through the grasping of that contact, the sense organ is formed.
The source of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements," which serve as its cause; it is called the body, resembling the head of a waist-drum.
The floating root [the eye] flows out toward the four objects, rushing toward contact.
Once there is subject and object, there is union and separation; the mutual friction of these two is also a manifestation of the self-mind’s *bhāga* (perceptual portion).
Sixth, this illustrates the formation of the characteristics of the sense-faculty of the mind (*manas-indriya*).

Through the two types of continuity—arising and ceasing—within the wondrous perfection, it adheres to the profound stillness to give rise to cognition; this essence of cognition reflects upon phenomena.
Grasping at phenomena forms the faculties; the root of these faculties is designated as "purity. The four great elements are named the cause of mental intention (*manas*).
Like seeing floating objects in a dark room, the four sense-faculties flow outward and rush toward phenomena.
Since the initial movement of ignorance is not the arising of false views, there is no birth of various dharmas; yet, because of the transformation of false views, there is also no cessation.
It is said that the cessation of these two continuities is also the manifestation-part (*nimittabhāga*) of one's own mind, like what is seen in a dark chamber;

it refers to the shadows conditioned by the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) which sentient beings falsely reckon as the manifestations of their own minds. "The four objects of the floating faculties" is spoken with reference to the physical heart-mass (*māṃsapiṇḍa-citta*).
Second, a summary of the characteristics of partiality and limitation.
Ānanda, these six faculties arise from the luminosity of that awakened clarity; yet when this luminous clarity loses its essential discernment and becomes stuck in delusion, light is emitted.

Therefore, at present, if you are removed from darkness and light, the essence of seeing does not exist; if you are removed from movement and stillness, the substance of hearing fundamentally has no reality.
Without penetration or obstruction, the nature of smelling does not arise; it is neither change nor tranquility, and the sense of tasting has no place of emergence—yet it does not depart.
It is not possible for contact to be perceived, for it is fundamentally non-existent; there is neither cessation nor arising, so where could the cognition find its resting place?

To say that the six sense organs are false and form their distinct characteristics without any other cause is merely because the true nature of awakened clarity gave rise to the delusion of "deluded clarity.
Thus, one loses that essence of pure discernment and becomes stuck to those false objects, thereby emitting deluded light.

To provisionally name it as "seeing" is to mean hearing, awakening, and discerning. What was previously called "adhering to the profound stillness" (*zhan-zhan*) referred to that which adheres and that which is adhered to;
what is now called "adhering to delusion" refers to the capacity to adhere and that which is adhered to. Although the subject and object differ, their false nature is one and the same.

Thus, the meaning of the passage beginning with "Therefore, you now... is to reveal that because of delusive confusion, one becomes partial and restricted, just as in the previous text it was said that hearing does not go beyond [the ear].
The view that sound does not transcend form is identical in meaning to [the claim] that it is not the case that the six faculties are collectively devoid of nature.

Second, clarifying the return from delusion to truth through the mutual functioning of the six faculties: first, clarifying the round extraction of returning from delusion; second, clarifying the mutual functioning upon returning to truth.
Returning from delusion is like removing the vessel; mutual functioning is like the great void. Now, the first [part].

If you merely do not follow these twelve characteristics of conditioned existence—movement and stillness, union and separation, tranquility and agitation, penetration and obstruction, birth and death, light and darkness—and instead uproot one of them, you will detach from the stickiness [of sensory clinging] and settle inwardly. As you settle back into the fundamental reality, the original radiance will manifest;
once the nature of this radiance is illuminated, all the remaining five types of stickiness will naturally be uprooted and you will achieve complete liberation.

The two characters "not following" (*bùxún*) constitute the immediate and intimate practice for taking up the work; they are like the two characters "not following" (*bùsuí*) in the previous passage regarding "not following discrimination.

The two characters "distancing oneself from" (*yuǎnlí*) in the second fascicle regarding "distancing oneself from all conditions of conjunction and non-conjunction" are likewise like the character "discarding" (*qì*) in the subsequent passage regarding "discarding arising and ceasing," and the phrase "knowing that seeing is no-seeing."
There is not a single character that is not taken up, yet there are no two characters such as "non-illusion" that are not taken up;
this extends even to the character "whirlpool" in "whirling the flow," which attains the "whirlpool of non-delusion. Once one is liberated, all are liberated.

Since the ear has already ceased to adhere to movement and stillness, yet the other faculties still adhere to union and separation and so forth, it is called "universal liberation. However, at the initial stage of extraction, one must focus on a single faculty.
This is merely the beginning. Second, explaining the mutual application of returning to the True [Nature] has two parts: first, verifying the characteristics of mutual application;
second, clarifying the reason for mutual application. Now, the first:

"Not arising from the objects before one through cognition and vision, then the fundamental clarity does not follow the six faculties, yet it does not fail to rely upon the six faculties to manifest."
From this, the six sense organs are thus able to function for one another. Ānanda, do you not know that within this assembly, Aniruddha sees without eyes;
the Naga Baddhālana hears without ears; the goddess of the Ganges smells fragrances without a nose;
Gavāmpati perceives flavors with a different tongue; and the Śūnyatā-deva experiences touch without a body?
Reflected within the light of the Tathāgata, it appears for a moment; yet being of the nature of wind, its substance is fundamentally non-existent.

While the śrāvakas who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation perceive silence, Mahākāśyapa here in this assembly has long since extinguished his mental faculties, yet he possesses perfect and clear understanding that does not depend on mental ideation.
Bhadanta is here translated as "Virtuous Joy" (Xiánxǐ). The Gaṅgā River is named Gavāmpati, which is translated as "Cow-Chewer";
he possessed an extraordinary tongue that was not like ordinary sense organs.

One whose mental faculty (*manas*) has long been extinguished has severed all innate self-clinging (*ātmagrāha*), such that no further signs can be perceived, like seeing within a dark chamber. Although various proofs have been cited in succession...
Whether it be through the fruition of karma or through the attainment of the Way, its clarity in not following the sense organs is one and the same.

Second, showing the reason for their mutual functioning, which is further divided into three parts: first, showing that the essence of delusion is fundamentally true; second, pointing to direct perception as proof;
third, showing how cultivation reveals the nature. Now, the first part.

Ānanda, if your faculties were now to be completely uprooted and their inner radiance were to shine forth, then these superficial phenomena and the various changing appearances of the vessel-world would,
like ice melting in hot water, transform into supreme awareness at the very thought of it.

The various changing marks of floating dust are fundamentally the unsurpassed enlightened awareness; that is to say, this seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi.
Following the defiled conditions of ignorance is like water forming ice, while employing the pure conditions of wisdom is like ice melting into water.
To speak of "hot water dissolving ice," the hot water and the ice are of one and the same substance.
The nature of water is merely that the fire of wisdom can melt the solid rigidity of ignorance; this is illustrated by the metaphor of hot water.

This refers to the cultivation of virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), wherein one overturns delusion and returns to awakening, and is thus called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). If, however, one refers to the inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), there is neither decrease nor increase, and they are not two separate things;
then it is said that "afflictions are themselves bodhi" and "birth-and-death are themselves nirvāṇa. Second.
He points to direct perception as proof:

"Ānanda, it is like when people of the world gather their vision upon the eyes; if one were to suddenly close them, the appearance of darkness would manifest before them, and the six sense organs would become dark and indistinct, with head and feet appearing alike.
Even though that person cannot see [the specific features], they can still use their hand to trace around the exterior of the body."
First, it is established that perception is identical.

Although the mutual functioning of the six sense organs was previously pointed out and both its phenomenal and principled aspects were clearly elucidated, there remains a fear that those who are stubbornly deluded might claim this is achieved through cultivation and is unrelated to the inherent nature. Therefore, [the text] further cites a worldly example.
Valid cognition serves as the means of proof. All the false views held by worldly people are concentrated solely in the visual faculty;

even if one were to suddenly close one's eyes and darkness appeared before them, although others might stand right in front, their six sense faculties would be obscured and they would appear as mere indistinct shapes of head and feet.

However, if one causes that person with closed eyes to use their hand to trace around the other person’s body once, then [the visual faculty]— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation above reflects the available portion.)
Although one does not see them, the head and feet are clearly distinguished and the perception is identical; is this not a clear proof that consciousness does not follow the sense organs?
An ancient master once identified touching a pillow in the middle of the night as the "thousand hands and eyes" of Great Compassion;
this, too, carries the same meaning. Third, he demonstrates the cultivation of the manifestation of the nature.

Because seeing depends on causes such as light and darkness to constitute "non-seeing," yet when there is no light, seeing itself arises spontaneously; thus, all appearances of darkness can never again obscure it.
Since the sense organs and their objects have already dissolved, how could this enlightened clarity not be perfectly wondrous?
Following the above instruction, the nature of sentient beings' cognitive awareness fundamentally does not depend upon the eye-organ;
however, because that vision which constantly conditions sensory objects relies upon the appearance of light, it becomes non-vision in the presence of darkness.

If one can cultivate in accordance with this nature, giving rise to the original luminous radiance so that the nature of this radiance does not depend on the condition of light but can manifest spontaneously, then—

All dark signs can never again obscure it; since the delusions of the sense organs and their objects have thus been dissolved, how could the nature of enlightened clarity not achieve the perfect and wondrous ultimate fruit?
This concludes the clarification of the two meanings. Second, resolving and removing doubts and obstructions. Part one:
clarifying that both cause and effect are eternal, thereby resolving the first meaning. Part two: clarifying that bondage and liberation are non-dual, thereby resolving the second meaning.
This is the second section on the general meaning. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the posing of the question; second, the presentation of the answer.

This is the first. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, if one seeks the permanently abiding awakened mind at the causal stage, it must correspond in name and designation with the resultant stage.
World-Honored One, if within the resultant stage there are Bodhi, Nirvana, True Suchness, and the Buddha..."
The nature of the *amala-vijñāna*, the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom— though these seven names differ, their essence is pure and perfect,
firm and solid like a diamond king, eternally abiding and indestructible. If one perceives this hearing as being free from light and darkness,
motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction, it ultimately has no substance, just as the mind of recollection is devoid of its preceding objects.
Dust is fundamentally non-existent; how can one take this ultimate annihilation as a causal factor for cultivation in order to obtain the fruit of the Tathāgata’s sevenfold eternal abiding?
World-Honored One, if one is free from light and darkness, seeing ultimate emptiness, then—as there are no external objects—the thoughts of self-nature are extinguished.
Whether advancing or retreating, through repeated and subtle investigation, one finds that originally there is neither a self-mind nor any mental factors associated with a self.

Who could establish a cause for seeking unsurpassed enlightenment? If the Tathāgata’s previous teaching that [the self] is profound, pure, perfect, and eternal contradicts his truthful words, it ultimately becomes mere frivolous discourse.
How can the Tathāgata be said to speak words of truth? I pray only that you will grant us great compassion and dispel our ignorance and hesitation.
The wisdom-virtue that is free from the two obstacles is called *bodhi*; the abandonment of virtue that is free from the two deaths is called *nirvāṇa*.
That which is non-false is called "True" (*satya*); that which is non-different is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*); that which is indestructible and unchanging is called "Buddha-nature.
To discern all things without being defiled by them is called the *amala-vijñāna*; that there is only the single true mind and nothing else is called "Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).
The Tathāgatagarbha illuminates all phenomena while remaining free from discrimination; this is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
If, upon hearing the following explanation of how delusive and biased appearances were previously shown, one were to instead suspect that true nature is annihilated, consider these words:
these six faculties—seeing, hearing, and so forth—are ultimately devoid of inherent substance when separated from the six objects, such as light and darkness.
It is as explained in the first fascicle: when the mind of recollection is examined, it is found to be detached from objective phenomena and fundamentally non-existent.
How can one take this ultimate annihilation as a cause and seek the fruit of non-arising and non-ceasing?
"Deluded attachment" refers to clinging due to ignorance; the rest of the text may be understood accordingly. Second, showing the answer, which has three parts: first, rebuking delusion.
This consists of three parts: the permission to speak, the explanation of the two fingers to dispel doubt, and the comprehensive summary and conclusion. First:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Though you have studied much learning, you have not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).
In your mind, you merely know the cause of inversion, but when inversion manifests before you, you truly cannot recognize it."
One merely knows that the entirety of the six sense faculties is delusion, yet one does not know that within this total delusion, the true nature is never extinguished.
Second, removing doubts by pointing to specific phenomena, which has two parts: first, interrogating the sense organs and their objects to reveal delusive inversion;
second, demonstrating the permanence of the cause through the nature of hearing. Now, the first part.
"Fearing that your cognitive mind has not yet attained faith and submission, I shall now test you with various mundane matters to eliminate your doubts.
Immediately, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula to strike the bell once and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear it now?
Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "We hear it. When the bell had ceased and there was no sound, the Buddha again asked, "Do you hear it now?"
Ānanda and the great assembly both said, "We did not hear it. Then Rāhula struck it once more, and the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear it now?
Ānanda and the great assembly replied once more, "We all hear it. The Buddha asked Ānanda, "In what way do you hear?
Why did you say you did not hear? Ānanda and the great assembly together addressed the Buddha, saying, "If the bell is struck, then we hear it."
When the striking has long ceased, the sound has vanished, and both resonance and echo have utterly perished, this is called the Tathāgata of No-Sound.
Furthermore, the Buddha commanded Rāhula to strike the bell and asked Ānanda, "Do you now hear the sound? Ānanda and the great assembly replied together, "There is a sound.
After a short while, when the sound had vanished, the Buddha asked again, "Do you now hear the sound? Ānanda and the great assembly answered, "There is no sound. A moment later, Rāhula...
When the bell was struck again, the Buddha asked once more, "Do you now hear a sound? Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "There is a sound.

The Buddha asked Ānanda, "In what way is there sound, and in what way is there no sound? Ānanda and the great assembly all addressed the Buddha, saying, "If the bell is struck, it is called 'having sound.
When it has been struck for a long time and the sound has faded until both the resonance and the echo have ceased, it is called 'having no sound.'"
The Buddha said to Ānanda and the great assembly, "How is it that you now speak with such deceptive confusion?
The great assembly and Ānanda simultaneously asked the Buddha, "In what way, O Buddha, is this called deceptive confusion? The Buddha said, "I ask you whether you hear, and you say 'I hear';
I ask you about sound, and you say 'sound. Since your answers regarding hearing and sound are thus inconsistent, this is called confusion."
Why is this not called evasive or confused?
The first answer—that there is no hearing—is incorrect; the second answer—that there is no sound—is correct; the meaning of these texts is clear.
Second, [the text] demonstrates the cause of permanence based on the nature of hearing.

Ānanda, when the sound has vanished and there is no resonance, you then falsely claim that there is no hearing. If, in reality, there were no hearing, then the nature of hearing itself would have ceased, becoming like a withered tree;

even if the bell were struck again, how could you know it? You should understand that knowing "there is" and knowing "there is not" pertains only to the presence or absence of the auditory object (the sound-dust).
How could that nature of hearing be subject to existence or non-existence for you? Even if the hearing were real...
If you say there is no [hearing], who then is it that knows there is no hearing? Therefore, Ānanda, it is the sound-objects within the nature of hearing that possess arising and ceasing;
it is not the case that because this sound arises when you hear it, or because this sound ceases when you hear it, that your own nature of hearing becomes existent or non-existent.
You are already inverted and deluded, mistaking sound for hearing; how much more so, then, that you are confused and take the permanent to be impermanent?
In the final analysis, one should not say that there is a separation from movement and stillness, or that there is hearing through the opening and closing [of the ears].
Since [all things] ultimately lack intrinsic nature, it is like a person in a deep sleep, lying soundly on a bed and pillow; while he sleeps, someone in the house pounds silk or husks rice.
In his dream, he hears the sounds of pounding and husking, yet he perceives them as something else—either as the beating of a drum or the striking of a gong.
While dreaming, the man was startled by the sound of the bell, which he took to be made of wood or stone. Suddenly waking up, he immediately realized it was the sound of the pestle.
He told his family, "While I was dreaming, I was confused by this sound of pounding and mistook it for the sound of a drum.

Ānanda, how could that person in his dream have recalled the stillness of the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*) or the opening, closing, permeability, or obstruction of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*)? It was merely that his physical form was asleep.

The nature of hearing is definitively not subject to obscuration; taking this as proof, you should know that even if your physical form were to dissolve and the radiance of your life-force were to pass away, how could this nature ever be extinguished for you?
This passage precisely identifies the nature of non-arising and non-extinction within the midst of false sense organs and objects as the true cause for cultivation.
It specifically takes the nature that is able to hear the sound of pounding as the object of focus, rather than taking the delusion of the bell and drum;

for to take the delusion as the bell and drum is the inverted mark of the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This concludes the third assembly by synthesizing and demonstrating the point.
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, clarifying that because of delusion, the permanent is itself impermanent; second, clarifying that because of awakening, the impermanent is itself permanent.
Now, for the first:
since beginningless time, all sentient beings have followed after forms and sounds, flowing with every thought without ever attaining awakening.

The nature is pure, wondrous, and constant, yet it does not follow its own constancy as it pursues all that arises and perishes; consequently, birth after birth, it flows through the cycle of defilement.
Second, because of awakening to this, impermanence is itself permanence.
If you abandon arising and ceasing to maintain the true permanence, the eternal light will manifest before you; the faculties, objects, consciousnesses, and mind will dissolve simultaneously.
When both conceptual marks—which act as dust—and the conscious emotions—which act as grime—are removed, your Dharma-eye will become clear and bright at that moment.
How could you then fail to achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?
To abandon arising and ceasing is to discard the deluded perception of arising and ceasing within the state of true permanence.
To maintain true permanence is to maintain the essential nature that is inherently true and permanent even amidst arising and ceasing.

Phenomenal appearances are dust, yet fundamentally there is no real dust; the perceptions of consciousness are defilements, yet fundamentally there is no real defilement. If one can now realize this, then—
At that moment, one becomes detached from them, and the Dharma-eye naturally becomes clear and bright.

Part Two: Resolving that Bondage and Liberation Are Non-dual. Section Two: First, the formal exposition that bondage and liberation are non-dual. Second... [text continues].

This also reveals that the six are resolved and the one is extinguished. Regarding the first of these two sections, there are two parts: first, the request born of doubt; second, the opening instruction.

Now, for the first: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has explained the gateway of the second meaning, when I observe those in the world who attempt to untie a knot, if they do not know the origin from which it was tied, I believe such people will ultimately never be able to untie it."
World-Honored One, it is likewise for the śrāvakas in training within this assembly: from beginningless time, they have arisen and ceased simultaneously with various forms of ignorance.
Although they have attained such roots of goodness through extensive learning and are called "those who have left the home life," they are like those suffering from quotidian malaria.
We pray that the Great Compassionate One will take pity on us who are submerged in suffering; today, what is this bondage of our bodies and minds, and from what does it arise?
He further resolved that all sentient beings suffering in the future might be liberated from saṃsāra and not fall into the three realms of existence.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself before the great assembly with his five limbs touching the ground; shedding tears and raising his heart in sincere devotion, he waited for the unsurpassed instruction of the Buddha, the Tathāgata.
The causes for the arising of the six sense organs shown in the preceding text not only manifest their characteristics clearly, but the very essence of their binding also remains present;
yet, because Ānanda is obscured by innate delusions and fails to realize that the six organs are themselves the source of this binding, he makes this request once more.
This is like one suffering from a quotidian malaria: although the *śrotāpanna* has already severed the delusions of views, [the afflictions remain].

This is because although the afflictions of thought have not yet been eliminated, upon entering the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), one is like a strong person; yet at the time of emerging from that contemplation, the habitual defilements remain.
Second, the opening instruction has two parts: first, the manifestation of auspicious omens; second, the formal exposition. Now, the first part.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who were still in training,

and also to serve as a cause for transcendence and as eyes for the future for all sentient beings, rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head with his hand— shining with the purple-gold light of Jambūnada gold. Immediately,
the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions shook in six ways, and the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust [appeared].
Those dwelling in their respective worlds each had jewel-radiance issue from their crowns;

at that same moment, this radiance came from those worlds to the Jeta Grove and drenched the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, such that this great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.
The touching of Ānanda’s crown is intended to manifest the Unsurpassed Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dharma within Ānanda’s present body.

The fact that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions emit light from their own crowns to consecrate his crown demonstrates that the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dharma possessed by Ānanda is none other than the Uṣṇīṣa Dharma realized by all Buddhas, without any distinction.
Second, the actual exposition, which has two parts: first, the common proclamation by all Buddhas; second, the personal teaching of Śākyamuni. Now, the first part.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly together heard the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, speaking with one voice and in different mouths, saying to Ānanda:
"Excellent, Ānanda! You wish to recognize and know the co-nascent ignorance that causes you to revolve in saṃsāra."
The root of birth and death’s fetters is none other than your six faculties; there is no other thing.
Furthermore, if you wish to know the unsurpassed Bodhi that enables you to swiftly realize peaceful liberation and the wondrous, eternal tranquility—that too is your six faculties and nothing else.
This is because Ānanda specifically sought out the root of the knots; thus, the six sense organs were directly pointed out as the root of the knots of birth and death, and nothing else.
Precisely because they are the very root of the knots of birth and death, they are also the very essence of bodhi, permanence, and bliss.
It is like water entirely becoming ice, such that the entire ice is water; or like a cloth entirely forming a knot.
Therefore, it is simply because this [text] concludes with the "towel" (the ear-fan) that one must further understand:

for those such as Ānanda, who constitute a specific class of recipients, though they have accumulated much learning over many kalpas, they were unable to realize the truth within hearing itself; instead, they blamed their extensive learning for their failure.
Consequently, the faculty of the ear—the perfect penetration of Avalokiteśvara—is selected to serve as an antidote. Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara also proceeds from hearing and reflection.
For one who cultivates entry into samādhi, when has the hearing ever been abandoned? It simply does not follow after sounds to wander.
Since the faculty of hearing is used to manifest perfect penetration, the faculties themselves are taken as the Dharma-realm; thus it is said: "It is only your six faculties, and nothing else.
If, in ordinary discourse, one says that all phenomena are but consciousness, then one might likewise say: "It is only your six consciousnesses."

Furthermore, it is not any other thing; rather, it is simply your eight consciousnesses—not any other thing—meaning that as they follow the flow of the eight consciousnesses and as they are transformed into the four wisdoms, there is ultimately no duality of substance.

Moreover, according to the principle of "only form" and "only fragrance," one may also say that it is simply these six sense objects and nothing else, for it is through craving and attachment that various afflictions arise.
It is because when there is no attachment, one is inherently in a state of Great Peace. Furthermore, it is said that the "root" (organ) subsumes the "dust" (object) and "consciousness";

"consciousness" subsumes the "root" and "dust"; and "dust" subsumes the "root" and "consciousness. This is because these three dharmas arise through mutual conditionality and are not separate from one another;
for all three share a common source and all three lack intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, regarding the ten...
By practicing each of the eight elements one by one, one attains the perfect and unsurpassed Bodhi;

furthermore, there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority among them. Therefore, Tiantai excluded the *dhātus* (elements) and *āyatanas* (bases) from the three categories, further excluded the first four *skandhas* (aggregates) from the five aggregates, and within the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate), he further excluded the other seven, observing only a single moment of the present six consciousnesses.
This is called "cauterizing the ailment to hit the vital point.

Now, among the three categories [of objects], one eliminates the coarse objects (*viṣaya*), and among the six sense bases (*indriya*), one eliminates five of the sense organs, taking only the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) as the object of contemplation.

This may also be described as "cauterizing the ailment to hit the vital point," such that for the six masters beginning with Dignāga, each takes a single atom (*paramāṇu*) as the object of contemplation—atom by atom.
There is nothing that is not a true point; if one applies moxibustion to them, all can be cured instantly. Thus, the eighteen realms (*dhātus*) and the seven elements (*mahābhūtas*) are all points.
If one carefully determines which ailment is present, one should know which point to moxibusture. If one finds the correct point, the disease is healed;
if one does not find the correct point, the disease cannot be healed. One must not say that this is a point while that is not. Therefore, [the twenty-five...]

After each of the Sages had described their own perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), the World-Honored One emitted precious light from his five limbs, which reached far to drench the crowns of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Those Tathāgatas likewise emitted precious light from their five limbs, coming to drench the crowns of the Buddha and the members of the assembly.
Does this not manifest that the entire body is a cavity, and that the entire body is capable of giving rise to illness?
In these twenty-five chapters, there is nothing that is not the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dharma. Second, Śākyamuni’s personal exposition, which has two parts:
first, the inquiry; second, the response. Now, for the first:
although Ānanda had heard such a sound of the Dharma, his mind was still not yet clear, so he prostrated himself and addressed the Buddha, saying: "How may you cause me..."
The cycle of birth and death, saṃsāra, bliss, and wondrous permanence are all these six faculties and nothing else.

This means that the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness constitutes the eighteen realms; when deluded, they are entirely birth and death, but when awakened, they are entirely the Tathāgatagarbha.
For what reason do the Tathāgatas of the ten directions speak only of birth and death and bliss in relation to the six faculties alone?
Second, the response and explanation, which has two parts: first, the long prose, and second, the verses. Now, the first part:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "The sense organs and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual. The nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky.

Ānanda, knowledge arises because of objects, and characteristics appear because of the sense organs. These characteristics and the act of seeing lack inherent nature, being like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another. Therefore..."
If you now establish knowledge within what you perceive and see, this is the very root of ignorance; if you perceive and see that there is no seeing, this is nirvana—taintless, truly pure.
How could any other thing be admitted within this?

Among these, the first four lines demonstrate that the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are fundamentally inseparable; therefore, by mentioning the six faculties alone, the objects and consciousness are already subsumed.

Next, the four lines beginning with "Next, from the objects, cognition arises" provide a further explanation of how the faculties and objects share the same source and how the nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky. The section beginning with "Therefore, you now... is as follows:
Regarding the initial statement that "the faculties and objects share the same source" in the context of the non-duality of bondage and liberation:

it should properly be stated that the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses—these three—share the same source. This is because they are all the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, which remains immutable while responding to conditions (*ananyathābhāva-anuvṛtti-pratyaya*), such that its entire substance manifests as the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses.
Therefore, these three—the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses—are, while responding to conditions, nonetheless immutable; they remain, in their entirety, identical to [the *tathāgatagarbha*].

Regarding the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, where bondage and liberation are non-dual: if one thoroughly realizes that the sense faculties and their objects are themselves the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, and does not erroneously conceive of the faculties as the grasper and the objects as the grasped, this is called "liberation.

Even at the time of liberation, the sense faculties and their objects have never been annihilated. If, however, one does not realize that the faculties and objects are merely one's own mind, one will erroneously conceive of the faculties as...

The capacity to grasp objects as the "grasped," extending even to the sensory faculties and the four types of sense-objects, where the mind flows and rushes toward forms and so forth—this is called "bondage.
Even at the time of bondage, the faculties and objects have never truly existed; therefore, they are non-dual.

Regarding the phrase "the nature of consciousness is illusory," it should fully be stated that the nature of the faculties, objects, and consciousness are all collectively illusory; this is a mutual abbreviation with the preceding text.
The true nature of the ear, its objects, and consciousness is precisely the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
This nature of the Tathāgatagarbha remains unchanging while responding to conditions, manifesting its entire substance as the faculties, objects, and consciousness.

To seek the unconditioned dharma of the Tathāgatagarbha apart from the conditioned dharmas of the faculties, objects, and consciousness is like seeking empty space apart from flowers; therefore it is said: "It is still..."
It is like flowers in the sky. In the subsequent passage, it is said that if cognition arises from objects, then the single sense organ cannot be established;
if characteristics arise because of the sense organ, then the single object cannot be established.

Since both the characteristic and the seeing lack self-nature and are like two reeds leaning against each other, the consciousness produced in the space between them—like the hollow within those leaning reeds—how could it possibly have self-nature? Therefore, you now [should understand] this equality.
The two characters "knowledge" (zhī) and "vision" (jiàn) refer to the true substance.

The establishment of the two characters "knowledge" reveals the root of delusion—namely, that which is called "delusion as luminous awareness," and "because of luminosity, the objective field is established," and so forth. This is precisely the root of ignorance;

it is not actually bondage, yet it is spoken of as bondage. It is that which is bound, the very source of the knots, and the fundamental knot itself. Next, the two characters "knowledge" and "vision" refer to the original [nature].

The two characters "no-seeing" (*amukha*) within the term "nature" (*prakṛti*) reveal the wondrous cultivation, namely: not following after conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) and not pursuing movement or stillness.
This is precisely the Nirvana that is untainted (*anāsrava*), truly pure; it is "non-liberation" yet called "liberation," meaning it liberates that which was bound.
How can other things be further admitted within this? The answer is: how could they?
These are both questions concerning the six sense faculties. The two verses are divided into two parts:
the first praises the dharma-gate of teaching, and the second praises the dharma-gate of extolling. Within the first part, there are two sections:

the first is a reiteration of the preceding text, and the second is an independent verse. Within the first of these, there are again two sections: the first reiterates the proximate text to reveal the nature as the basis for cultivation.
The preceding text of these two verses demonstrated that cultivation is performed in accordance with the wondrous nature. Now begins the first [section].
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The true nature is empty of conditioned phenomena, Because they arise dependently, like illusions. Unconditioned phenomena have no arising or ceasing; They are unreal, like flowers in the sky."
The statement of falsehood reveals the various truths; yet falsehood and truth are equally both false. Since they are neither true nor not true, how can there be a seer and that which is seen?
In the interval between them, there is no substantial nature. Therefore, whether they are intertwined like reeds or disentangled, the cause is the same;

there are no two paths for the holy and the ordinary. You should observe the nature within this interweaving: it is neither empty nor dualistic. Delusion and obscuration constitute ignorance; illumination and clarity result in liberation.
Within this context, the two characters "true nature" (*zhēn xìng*) first indicate the essence that is neither true nor false;

this is what is referred to in the first fascicle as the "ever-abiding true mind, the essence of purity and luminosity," in the second and third fascicles as the "wondrous true thusness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha," in the fourth fascicle as "the wondrous luminosity of the nature-awakening" and "the luminous wonder of original awakening," and in the sixth fascicle... [as previously cited].
This refers to the nature of the ocean of awakening, which is serene and perfect; its serenity and perfection mean that the fundamental awakening is primordially subtle and wondrous.

It continues through the tenth fascicle, referring to what is called "the essential truth, the subtle and luminous, the fundamentally awakened, and the perfectly pure. "Conditioned" refers to the characteristics of the sense organs, objects, and consciousness—the phenomena of conditioned existence.
Their substance is fundamentally empty because they arise dependently; thus, they are likened to illusory things. "Unconditioned" refers to the nature of the sense organs, objects, and consciousness.
The unconditioned dharma is likewise not real, because it fundamentally lacks arising and ceasing; it is likened to flowers in the sky.
Next, he explains further: Why are both the conditioned and the unconditioned empty and unreal?
Because using the false to manifest the true is a dharma of relative opposition; since the false is false, the true is also false, and they are both alike.
Both are false. Since even the wondrous, luminous true nature is neither "true" nor "not true," how could it be the faculty of seeing or the objects seen?
You must know that the internal faculties, the external objects, and the consciousness in between all lack a real nature;
they are merely like bundles of reeds leaning against one another. Because they lack a real nature, [they are empty].
Bondage and liberation share the same cause, for both the holy and the ordinary lack two separate paths. You should examine that central space within the interlaced reeds:
if you call it "empty," the appearance of the reeds remains vivid; if you call it "existent," the center has no substantial reality.
Therefore, both emptiness and existence are non-existent. It is merely through delusion and obscuration regarding this principle of "neither" that one falls into non-existence.
When one clearly illuminates this principle of being neither [ordinary nor holy], liberation is attained. For the true nature is fundamentally neither ordinary nor holy;
when obscured by delusion, it becomes bondage, fetters, and the state of an ordinary person; when illuminated, it becomes liberation, release, and the state of a sage.
Since ordinary sentiments do not arise and sagely understanding is also empty, the preceding verse says: "It is still not 'not-true'..."

Since conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are truly empty, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are likewise not real. These two verses summarize the preceding text to demonstrate that cultivation must accord with the wondrous nature.

Regarding the sequence for untangling the knots: once the sixth knot is untied, even the first knot vanishes; by selecting the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-vyūha*) from among the faculties, one enters the stream and achieves true enlightenment.
This verse from afar summarizes the passage from the second section on the "Definitive Meaning" to demonstrate the skillful means of cultivation.

Building upon the preceding point that although bondage and liberation pertain solely to the six sense faculties, the untying of the knots must necessarily follow a sequential order, one must enter deeply through a single gateway;
once the six are untied, even the "one" vanishes, whereby the various corresponding floating phenomena are transformed through mindfulness.
Unsurpassed enlightenment requires that, at the very outset of practice, one must select from among the six sense faculties that which is most perfectly penetrating (*yuan-tong*).
By entering the stream of the Dharma-nature from this point, one achieves perfect awakening; thus, there is a difference as vast as that between a day and an eon.
Second, the verse of independent origination.
The subtle *ālayavijñāna*, with its habitual tendencies forming a violent torrent—fearing that one might confuse the real with the unreal, I have never openly taught it.

To grasp at one’s own mind is to take what is not illusory and turn it into an illusory dharma; if there is no grasping, there is nothing that is not illusory. Since even the non-illusory does not arise, how could illusory dharmas be established?

In Sanskrit, *ādāna* means "grasping" or "holding. Although the preceding passage clarifies the selection of faculties for entry into the stream [of liberation], these six faculties are actually that which are grasped and held by the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
This subtle *ādāna*-consciousness possesses habit-energies (*vāsanā*) and seeds (*bīja*) capable of forming a violent torrent;
if one calls it "real," it is the very root of birth and death, yet if one calls it "unreal," it is not so.
If one seeks water apart from the waves, that is called "the real" being distinct from "the unreal. I speak thus because I fear people will become deluded and attached;
for this reason, I do not constantly expound it. Indeed, all sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses are manifestations of the Mind alone.
If one relies on the organs to grasp objects, or abandons the objects to grasp the organs, or even abandons both organs and objects to grasp consciousness—[all such approaches are deviations].
To discard the six consciousnesses and grasp only the eighth consciousness and so forth is entirely a case of the self-mind returning to grasp its own mind,

thereby causing the nature— which is fundamentally not illusory and false— to become entirely an illusory and false phenomenon. If one who practices can realize that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind,
quiescent and non-arising, and thus refrain from grasping or attachment, then not only will there be no illusion.
Furthermore, there is nothing that is not illusion; since even non-illusion itself does not arise, how could illusory phenomena be established?
It is like empty space, which does not even give rise to flowers—how could there be any arising at all? Thus, "the self-mind grasping the self-mind" is also a reiterative verse;
"establishing cognition upon cognition" means that what is not illusion becomes illusory phenomena—this too is a reiterative verse, for ignorance is fundamentally non-existent.
The two characters "take" (qu) also constitute a reiterative verse; the thirteen characters "knowing and seeing, no seeing, nothing that is not illusion," etc., also constitute a reiterative verse.
This is precisely the Nirvana that is untainted, true, and pure. "Nothing that is not illusion" means there is no reality and no Nirvana of the Two Vehicles.
"No illusion" means there is no delusion and no birth-and-death of ordinary beings. There is also no Nirvana.
The absence of birth and death is called the Great Nirvana of Non-abiding;
because it arises in isolation yet is combined with verses in praise, the subsequent eulogy describes it as "a refined amalgamation. Second, two verses praise the Dharma-gate.
This is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Vajra King, the Jewel-like Awakening, the Illusion-like Samādhi, which transcends the stage of no-more-learning with a mere snap of the fingers;
it is this Abhidharma, the single path to Nirvāṇa for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.
The first three phrases reveal the name of this samādhi; the next single phrase manifests its preeminent efficacy;
and the final three phrases clarify that it is universally honored by all the sages. The first three phrases must be read in a single breath, stating:
"What is the name of this samādhi? It is the Wondrous Lotus, the Vajra King, the Jewel-like Awakening, which is like an illusion."
As for samādhi: because its true nature and wondrous principle exist within the conditioned yet are not existent, and exist within the unconditioned yet are not non-existent;
because it is pure and unattached in the face of defilement and untainted by it—it is therefore called the "Wondrous Lotus.

Because the wondrous wisdom of prajñā touches existence and finds existence destroyed, touches non-existence and finds non-existence ruined, such that neither extreme can be grasped and one does not abide even in the middle way—it is therefore so named.
The Vajra-King’s Precious Enlightenment, through its wondrous practice of liberation, regards the conditioned as like an illusion and the unconditioned as like an illusion;
it regards both extremes as like an illusion and the Middle Way as like an illusion. Therefore, it is called "Like an Illusion" (*yathā-māyā*).
When these inconceivable three virtues are unified into one right concentration, it is called *samādhi*. This is the Great Buddha-Crown [Dhāraṇī].

The Śūraṅgama King Samādhi is also known by various names and various interpretations—such as the Vajra King, the Illusory, the Inconceivable, and the True Mother of Buddhas—yet it ultimately possesses no dual essence.
Therefore, those who transcend the stage of "no-more-learning" (aśaikṣa) with a mere snap of the fingers certainly transcend it through the partial realization that destroys ignorance;
even those at the stage of "semblance" (sādharmya) transcend it, for they suppress ignorance. Thus one should contemplate.

Because its practice also transcends and can perfectly subdue [the afflictions], and because its names and words also transcend [ordinary discourse] through the knowledge of the Buddha-nature, *Abhidharma* is also called *Abhiddhamma*.
Translated, this means "Incomparable Dharma" (*anupama-dharma*). Generally speaking, the Śrāvaka Piṭaka of the Hīnayāna may also bear this name, for it cannot be compared with worldly dharmas.
Specifically, however, it is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the One Vehicle that truly corresponds to this name.
Because it cannot be compared to the vehicles of the provisional teachings, "Bhagavān" is a sublime title for the Buddha that encompasses six meanings;
thus, the original sound is retained: first, sovereignty; second, brilliance; third, majesty; fourth, renown;
fifth, auspiciousness; and sixth, nobility. The first fascicle states: "One enters through the gate of the wondrously adorned path. First, the gate—

The subsequent path involves first understanding and then proceeding; this so-called "Single Path to the Gate of Nirvana" involves first the path and then the gate, first the journey and then the entry.
The former is the gate for emerging from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); this is the gate for entering nirvana.
Furthermore, in delusion, one's own hometown is entirely a foreign land; in awakening, the entire world is one's native home. In delusion, one departs from nirvana...

Entering birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and awakening to transcend birth-and-death and enter the gate of *nirvāṇa*—in terms of their conventional meaning, these are spoken of as two, yet in essence they are not two. This second section further clarifies that while the six [realms] are resolved, the one is lost. It consists of two parts: first, the request based on doubt; second, the response that provides instruction. The first part also has two sections: first, describing the benefits; second, requesting clarification regarding the doubt. Now, the first [section]: The text states: "Entering birth-and-death and awakening to transcend birth-and-death and enter the gate of *nirvāṇa*—in terms of their conventional meaning, these are spoken of as two, yet in essence they are not two. This means that although the gates of entering *saṃsāra* and entering *nirvāṇa* appear distinct when analyzed according to their conventional designations, in their ultimate nature they are non-dual. Furthermore, by resolving the six [realms], the notion of "one" vanishes. This section comprises two parts: first, the request based on doubt; second, the response that provides instruction. The first part also contains two sub-sections: first, describing the benefits; second, requesting clarification regarding the doubt. Now, the first [sub-section]: [The text continues: "Furthermore, the World-Honored One previously spoke of the 'One Vehicle' (*ekayāna*), which is the true reality of all phenomena. Why then do you now speak of three? If there is truly only one vehicle, why must sentient beings undergo suffering for immeasurable eons? If it is said that there are three vehicles, how can this not contradict the principle of the One Vehicle? Moreover, the Buddha’s past teachings stated that the three realms are like a burning house and that all conditioned things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless. Yet now you say that within the three realms there is a place of peace and bliss, and that within the conditioned there is a state of permanence, joy, purity, and self. If this is so, then the previous teachings were false. If the previous teachings were not false, then the present teaching must be false. If both are true, then the Dharma is contradictory. If both are false, then the Buddha is not omniscient. I am now deeply confused and cannot resolve these doubts. I hope the Tathāgata will compassionately explain them for me. Thus ends the first section. The second section follows. The third section is the response that provides instruction. This also has two parts: first, the praise and encouragement; second, the actual explanation. The first part also has two sections: first, the praise; second, the encouragement. Now, the first [part]: [The text states: "At that time, the Buddha addressed Mahākāśyapa: 'Excellent, excellent! You have raised this question because you wish to benefit and bring peace to many beings, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake of gods and humans. You have asked well. Thus ends the first part. The second part follows. The second part is the actual explanation. This also has two sections: first, the general explanation; second, the specific explanation. Now, the first [part]: [The text states: "The Buddha told Mahākāśyapa: 'The Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle is indeed the true reality of all phenomena. However, because sentient beings have various faculties, dispositions, and inclinations, I provisionally teach three vehicles. The reason I speak of three is to guide those who are attached to the Lesser Vehicle and to cause them to enter the Great Vehicle. If I did not speak of three, those of dull faculties would remain in the Lesser Vehicle and would never attain liberation. Therefore, I speak of three to lead them to the One. Thus, although the gates of entering *saṃsāra* and entering *nirvāṇa* are conventionally described as two, in their ultimate essence they are non-dual. Thus ends the first section. The second section follows. The second section is the specific explanation. This also has two parts: first, the explanation of the One Vehicle; second, the explanation of the three vehicles. Now, the first [part]: [The text states: "What is called the 'One Vehicle' is the true nature of all phenomena, which is neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Because all phenomena are thus, the Buddha’s wisdom is also thus. Because the Buddha’s wisdom is thus, the path is also thus. Because the path is thus, the fruit is also thus. Because the fruit is thus, the liberation is also thus. Because liberation is thus, the knowledge and vision of liberation is also thus. Since all these are thus, they are collectively called the 'One Vehicle. This is the ultimate truth, not a provisional teaching. Thus ends the first part. The second part follows. The second part is the explanation of the three vehicles. This also has two sections: first, the explanation of the three vehicles as a provisional means; second, the explanation of how the three ultimately return to the One. Now, the first [section]: [The text states: "However, because the capacities of sentient beings differ, I provisionally teach three vehicles. For those who delight in small matters, I teach the Śrāvaka vehicle; for those who seek intermediate matters, I teach the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; for those who aspire to the great, I teach the Bodhisattva vehicle. These three are taught as skillful means to lead sentient beings toward the One Vehicle. Thus ends the first section. The second section follows. The second section is the explanation of how the three ultimately return to the One. This also has two parts: first, the analogy; second, the application to the principle. Now, the first [part]: [The text states: "It is like a great physician who, seeing his children have ingested poison, uses various medicines to expel it. Although he prescribes different remedies according to the severity of the illness, once the poison is removed, the children are all restored to health. In the same way, the Buddha, seeing that sentient beings are afflicted by the poison of ignorance and craving, provisionally teaches three vehicles to remove their afflictions. Once the afflictions are removed, they all enter the One Vehicle. Thus ends the first part. The second part follows. The second part is the application to the principle. This also has two sections: first, the application; second, the conclusion. Now, the first [section]: [The text states: "Just as the physician’s intention was always to cure the children, the Buddha’s intention is always to lead all beings to the One Vehicle. There is no other vehicle apart from the One. Therefore, although the gates of entering *saṃsāra* and entering *nirvāṇa* are conventionally described as two, in their ultimate essence they are non-dual. Thus ends the second section. The third section is the conclusion. This also has two parts: first, the summary; second, the exhortation. Now, the first [part]: [The text states: "In summary, the One Vehicle is the true reality of all phenomena. The three vehicles are merely provisional teachings used as skillful means. Those who understand this will not be confused by the words of the Buddha. Thus ends the first part. The second part follows. The second part is the exhortation. This also has two sections: first, the exhortation to practice; second, the exhortation to propagate. Now, the first [section]: [The text states: "You should all diligently cultivate this One Vehicle Dharma-gate. Do not cling to the provisional teachings of the three vehicles. Only by practicing the One Vehicle can you truly transcend birth-and-death and enter *nirvāṇa. Thus ends the first section. The second section follows. The second section is the exhortation to propagate. This also has two parts: first, the exhortation; second, the promise of merit. Now, the first [part]: [The text states: "If you can propagate this sutra, you will benefit immeasurable sentient beings. You will cause them to cast off the bonds of birth-and-death and attain the eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa. Thus ends the first part. The second part follows. The second part is the promise of merit. This also has two sections: first, the promise of worldly merit; second, the promise of supramundane merit. Now, the first [section]: [The text states: "Whoever upholds, reads, recites, or explains even a single verse of this sutra will, in this life, receive protection from all deities and spirits. They will be free from all calamities and obstacles. Thus ends the first section. The second section follows. The second section is the promise of supramundane merit. This also has two parts: first, the attainment of the fruits of the path; second, the realization of Buddhahood. Now, the first [part]: [The text states: "Furthermore, such a person will gradually advance through the stages of the path, from the stage of dry wisdom to the stage of the Arhat, until they finally attain the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction—
composed of *geya* and *gāthā*, refined and pure, exquisite and lucid— felt their minds and eyes opened and enlightened, and they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
*Ge-yeh* (Geya) is translated here as "repeated verse" (*chóng-sòng*). *Gāthā* is sometimes called "isolated verse" (*gū-qǐ*) and is also termed "recited verse" (*fěng-sòng*).

It is said that the *geya-gāthā* which expresses [the meaning] is a refined synthesis of various elements, while the sublime principle it expresses is pure and penetratingly clear. Second is the "requesting of doubts."
Ānanda joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to him: “I have now heard the Buddha’s words on the unobstructed great compassion, the pure, wondrous, and eternal true Dharma;
yet my mind has not yet fully realized them. I do not understand the sequence for loosening the knots and the dissolution of the six into one.
I pray that you will extend your great kindness once more to pity this assembly and those of the future, bestowing upon us the sound of the Dharma to wash away our deep-seated defilements.”

This restates the meaning from the preceding verse regarding the sequence for untying the knots—whereby the six knots are untied one by one until even the "one" is lost—and thereby raises the questions.

There are six points of inquiry: first, the question of the six untyings; second, the question of the disappearance of the one; third, the question of the unfolding; fourth, the question of the knotting;

fifth, the question of how the unfolding and knotting each possess their own categories; and sixth, the question of how the unfolding and knotting each possess their own sequential order. This [is the introduction].

I shall provide this enumeration according to the sequence of the text; however, as for the answers, first the order and categories within the "tying" are answered, followed by the "six unravelings and one disappearance," and finally the order and categories within the "unraveling"—these will be evident from the text itself.
Second, the demonstration of the two [analogies]: first, the analogy of tying the cloth to represent delusion; second, the analogy of unraveling the cloth to represent awakening. Now, the first.
At that moment, the Tathāgata, upon his lion throne, adjusted his inner robe (nirvāṇasaṃghāṭī), gathered his outer robe (saṃghāṭī), and took up a seven-jeweled armrest.
Extending his hand over the armrest, he took the flowered cloth offered by the deva Kāpila and, before the great assembly, tied it into a single knot.
He pointed to it and asked Ānanda, "What is this called? Ānanda and the entire assembly replied together to the Buddha, "This is called..."
Thereupon, the Tathāgata again tied the folded flower-cloth into another knot and asked Ānanda once more, "What is this called?
Ānanda and the great assembly again addressed the Buddha, saying, "This is also called a 'knot'. In this manner, he successively tied the folded flower-cloth until six knots were formed in total;
as each knot was completed, he took the knot formed in his hand and held it up to ask Ānanda.
[The assembly] challenged this, asking: "What is this called, Ānanda? The great assembly likewise responded to the Buddha in succession:
"This is called a 'knot'. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "When I first tied the cloth, you called it a 'knot. This folded flower-cloth was originally a single strip;
as for the second and third [folds], why do you all again call them 'knots'? Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
"This precious silk cloth, woven and stitched into a headcloth, is originally a single entity;
yet as I contemplate it, when the Tathāgata ties it once, it receives the name 'one knot,' and if tied a hundred times, it is ultimately called 'a hundred knots.
How much more so for this cloth, which has only six knots—it never reaches seven, nor does it remain at five. Why then, O Tathāgata, do you allow only the first, second, and third [knots]?"
"It is not called 'knots. The Buddha told Ānanda: 'This precious flowered cloth—do you know that this cloth originally consists of but a single strand?
When I tied it six times, there were six knots. Examine this closely: the substance of the cloth is the same, yet it appears different because of the knots.
What do you think? The first time it was tied, it was called the first knot; and so on, until the sixth knot arose.'"
"I now wish to take the name of the sixth knot and [re]establish it as the first; can this be done? "No, World-Honored One.

If the six knots still exist, this sixth name will ultimately never become the first. Even if I were to exhaust my eloquence throughout successive lifetimes, how could I cause these six knots to change their names?
The Buddha said: "It is so. These six knots are not the same; if one traces them back to their original cause..."
If one attempts to weave a turban from these materials, they will become disordered and can never be completed; so too it is with your six sense organs:
ultimately, within their common origin, they produce ultimate differences.
This first answers the sequence and categorization of the questions you asked. *Nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (涅槃僧) is translated here as [the monastic robe].
