how then can one attain perfect penetration? If, at the initial stage, one contemplates the nature of fire [as being merely] a distaste for existence, this is not the principle that the true nature is fundamentally detached;
since it is not the subtle skillful means of the union of cause and effect at the initial stage, how can one attain perfect penetration? If, at the initial stage...

If one contemplates the nature of wind, there is movement; yet if there is stillness, it is not without its counterpart. Since a counterpart is not the Unsurpassed Enlightenment, how can one attain perfect penetration?

If one with an initial mind contemplates the nature of emptiness, that which is dark and dull was not originally the nature of awakening. Without awakening, one is distinct from Bodhi; how can one attain perfect penetration?
If one with an initial mind contemplates the nature of consciousness, the consciousness being contemplated is subject to arising and ceasing, and is therefore not eternal.

The mind that dwells upon and contemplates objects is itself illusory; how can one thereby attain perfect penetration? All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and the nature of thought is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing;
since cause and effect now manifest as distinct experiences, how can one thereby attain perfect penetration?

In this context, the nature of earth, the nature of water, and so forth, refer for the time being to what is conceived by deluded minds—namely, that hardness is the nature of earth, moisture is the nature of water, and so on up to the conceptualization of discernment as the nature of consciousness; these are not the true nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

The text is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent" and so forth, it means that if a beginner relies upon the sense faculties and the great elements to practice mindfulness of the Buddha...
Since the roots of the fetters have not yet been uprooted, the six sense organs belong only to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), whose nature is impermanent;

thus, the faculty capable of mindfulness is itself fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing. In this case, because that which is characterized by arising and ceasing serves as the cause, it is difficult to evoke a fruit that is non-arising and non-ceasing.
Therefore, how could such a distinct response be identical to the wondrous samādhi of Śrī-Prabhūtaratna? (2) Manifestation.

This [passage] consists of seven parts: first, a general clarification of what is appropriate for entering the Path in this land; second, a clarification of the persons and dharmas for leaving suffering and attaining bliss;
third, a formal clarification of the dharma-gate practiced by Avalokiteśvara; fourth, an exhortation for the audience to listen attentively and practice accordingly;

fifth, a praise of the excellence of the Dharma to encourage cultivation; sixth, a description of the intent for attaining Buddhahood to conclude and indicate the selection; and seventh, [the conclusion].
I prostrate and request that you clarify the reality. First:
I now address the World-Honored One: when a Buddha appears in this Sahā world, the true essence of the teaching in this direction is pure and resides within hearing.
If one wishes to attain *samādhi*, it is truly through entering by means of hearing.
"Saha" is translated here as "Endurance"; it is the general name for the three-thousandfold world system.

In the Buddha-lands of other directions, the faculties of sentient beings vary—some being sharp and others dull—and according to their respective capacities, all six sense objects serve as the substance of the teaching.

In this land, however, three sense objects are predominantly employed; specifically, in the case of yellow scrolls and red tablets, the sense object of form (*rūpa*) serves as the substance of the teaching, through which one attains awakening upon hearing the Dharma.
Thus, while sound is the substance of the teaching when observed through the sequence of dharmas, the dharma-object (*dharmadhātu*) is the substance of the teaching when observed analytically;

however, since in the Buddha’s own time those who attained realization by hearing sounds were numerous, and even in the degenerate age many still attain awakening through the indications of speech, it is said:
"In this land, the true substance of the teaching is pure within the hearing of sound. Second, the clarification of the two [aspects].
The human dharma of leaving suffering and attaining happiness;

the noble Avalokiteśvara who leaves suffering and attains liberation. Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you have entered Buddha-lands as many as motes of dust, attaining the power of great mastery and bestowing fearlessness upon sentient beings.
O Avalokiteśvara of Wondrous Sound, with your Brahma-voice and ocean-tide voice!
The Savior brings all to peace; by transcending the world, one attains eternal abiding.

Those who leave suffering behind depart from the afflictions of the nine realms and the five turbidities; those who attain liberation obtain the true bliss of liberation regarding the five aggregates within the *dharmatā* of the Buddha-realm—this is the accomplishment of self-benefit.
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one vertically exhausts the three [times].
Pervading the lands as numerous as motes of dust horizontally throughout the ten directions, he universally bestows fearlessness through great mastery;
this is the accomplishment of benefiting others. He realizes that all sounds are the Tathāgata-garbha—that which remains unchanging while following conditions is called "wondrous sound.
He realizes that the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha’s sound is true emptiness, and that the sound of true emptiness is pure and fundamental.

Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, manifesting in accordance with the minds of sentient beings and the scope of what they should know, appearing according to their karma, there are thus the ten realms of distinctions between the primary and secondary environments and their sounds.
Specifically, that which is called "Unchanging yet Following Conditions" is named Avalokiteśvara; these two aspects are also spoken of in relation to his own practice.
The wondrous Dharma he expounds accords with principle and is pure, which is termed "Brahma-sound. The wondrous [Dharma] he expounds...
The Dharma skillfully responds to the various capacities of sentient beings without missing its proper time; this is called the "Sound of the Ocean Tide.

These two [aspects] also summarize the merit of benefiting others by establishing all in peace through transformation and worldly salvation. Obtaining eternal abiding in the supramundane summarizes the merit of self-benefit.
Third, the correct elucidation of the dharma-gate practiced by Avalokiteśvara.
I now address the Tathāgata regarding what Avalokiteśvara has said: "Suppose a person is dwelling in stillness when drums are struck simultaneously in all ten directions;
they hear them all at once. This is the true perfection of the ear. The eyes do not see beyond obstructions; the same is true for the mouth and nose.
(This phrase should follow below. The body knows only through contact. (This phrase should follow above. When the mind’s thoughts are in disarray, one can hear sounds across a wall."

The resonance can be heard both far and near, yet the five sense faculties are not uniform in their reception. This is the penetration of the true nature of sound: whether in motion or stillness, it exists within hearing;
yet when there is no sound, one speaks of "no hearing," which is not truly no hearing, for it lacks a fixed nature. Since sound is non-existent, its cessation is also non-existent;
since sound exists, its arising is likewise non-arising. When both arising and ceasing are perfectly transcended, this is the eternal reality—even if one is in a dream.
It is said that this is not a state of non-thought, nor is it free from vitarka and vicāra; it transcends discursive thought such that body and mind cannot reach it.
This statement means that a beginner can awaken to the perfect penetration of the three virtues through the faculty of hearing.
Thus, as explained by Avalokiteśvara, one speaks of the Dharma of the ear-faculty as taught by Avalokiteśvara.
That you possess this perfect, universal, and common reality of the three truths does not necessarily mean it was spoken directly from the mouth of Avalokiteśvara.

The term "for example" (*yathā*) is a word used to cite an instance; it is not a mere metaphorical illustration, but rather a discussion based directly upon direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), rather than inference (*anumāna*).
This is precisely what is meant by being muddled and deluded: the principle exists of itself. As for "perfect," there is no measure that is not [encompassed].
Pervasion is the virtue of prajñā; unimpeded function is the virtue of liberation;
and constancy is the virtue of the dharmakāya, as its essential nature remains unchanging. Furthermore, these three virtues are all perfect, all pervasive, and all constant, as explained previously.
Fourth, the exhortation to listen attentively and practice accordingly, which has three parts: first, showing how it accords with one's capacity;
second, encouraging diligent cultivation; and third, concluding with its true nature. Now, the first part.

Now, in this Sahā world, the science of phonetics (*śabda-vidyā*) has been proclaimed and clarified for sentient beings who are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; because they follow after sounds, they wander through saṃsāra.

Ānanda, despite your powerful memory, you cannot avoid falling into deviant thoughts. Is it not the case that by following what you have sunk into, you must now turn back the flow [of consciousness] to attain freedom from delusion?
To falsely claim that listening to the Dharma with a conditioned mind is itself perverse thinking is because such a conditioned mind is merely a reflection of the sounds of the Dharma being heard;
it is certainly not the true fundamental hearing that is capable of listening to the Dharma. Is this not following along with delusions and thereby sinking into saṃsāra?
If one can turn back the flow and awaken to that fundamental hearing, then one will immediately attain freedom from delusion. (2)
Observe their skillful cultivation.
Ānanda, listen attentively as I, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic authority, proclaim the *Vajrarāja-māyopama-acintya-buddhamātṛ-bhūta-samādhi*.
If you hear the secret gates of all the buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, yet do not first eliminate the outflows (*āsrava*), [you will not attain them].

Accumulating learning leads to error; if you hold onto what you have heard, how can you hear the Buddhas? Why do the Buddhas not hear by themselves? Hearing does not arise spontaneously; it exists because of sound and names.
When hearing turns away from sound, one becomes detached. Once detached, who is there to be named? When one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties attain liberation.
Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the sense-faculties are removed, [all delusions vanish].
When the dust of delusion is cleared away, awareness becomes perfectly pure; when purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere. In silent illumination, it encompasses the void.

Returning then to observe the world, it is like an event in a dream. Mātaṅgī is but a dream—whence could she retain your physical form? It is like a skillful magician who conjures various men and women;
though their faculties appear to move, they are all drawn by a single mechanism. When that mechanism ceases, all returns to stillness.
All illusions are devoid of inherent nature; the six sense faculties are likewise so. Originally, they depend on a single luminous intelligence, which divides to form the six harmonious unities.

When these are brought together in one place, they return to stillness, and the six functions cease to operate. Defilements vanish the moment they are thought upon, becoming perfectly clear, bright, pure, and wondrous.
Once all remaining traces of dust are eliminated, one is a student; when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata.
The *Vajrarāja-māyopama-acintya-buddhamātṛ-samādhi* may also be read as a single phrase:
"Piercing all delusions" is the virtue of the Vajrarāja Prajñā; "establishing all dharmas" is the virtue of the Māyopama Vimukti;
and "the simultaneity of piercing and establishing" is the virtue of the Acintya Dharmakāya. All.
All Buddhas emerge from this samādhi; therefore, it is named the True Samādhi of the Mother of Buddhas.

The six sense organs grasping at the six sense objects are collectively termed "outflows of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*). Now, using the ear to grasp the sound of the Dharma is precisely such an outflow of desire.
Taking this hearing as the subject that grasps (*grāhaka*) and that sound as the object grasped (*grāhya*), the mutual adhesion of subject and object results in error. For this reason:
If you employ this faculty of hearing to uphold the Buddha-dharma spoken by the Buddha, why not turn inward and reflect upon the nature of that hearing itself?
This faculty of hearing does not arise spontaneously; it exists only because of sound and thus receives its name.

If you can reverse the mechanism of hearing so that it becomes detached from the object of sound, and once detached from that sound-object, with whom would you further wish to designate the "faculty of hearing"?
Ah! When this single faculty of hearing returns to its source, all six faculties become liberation.
Consequently, the various faculties of seeing and hearing are all like illusory cataracts, and the dusty phenomena of the three realms are entirely like flowers in the sky.

Once the nature of hearing is restored and the cataracts of the faculties have been removed, the dusty appearances are completely dissolved, and the essence of awakening becomes perfectly pure. The remainder of the text may be understood; it concerns the illusionist.
The metaphor of the power of ignorance’s illusion drawing upon a single stimulus illustrates how a single luminous essence adheres to delusion to emit light.
"Perfectly luminous" refers to *prajñā* (wisdom); "pure" refers to *vimukti* (liberation); and "wondrous" refers to the *dharmakāya*. "Remaining dust" points to subtle ignorance;
"Tathāgata" points to the ultimate fruit of wondrous enlightenment. These three summarize its reality.
The great assembly and Ānanda: turn back that inverted faculty of hearing and listen instead to the nature of hearing itself. When this nature is realized, it constitutes the Unsurpassed Way;
such is the true and perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*).
To speak of "true and real perfect penetration" means there is no other method apart from this: simply reverse your own deluded habit of following sounds and listening outwardly.
When the faculty of hearing is reversed, the self-nature of this hearing is realized; by attaining the nature of seeing, one immediately achieves the Unsurpassed Way.
Fifth, he praises the excellence of the Dharma to encourage its cultivation.
This is the single path to nirvana for countless buddhas;

all Tathāgatas of the past have accomplished this gate, all Bodhisattvas of the present now each enter its perfect clarity, and those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this dharma.
I, too, have realized it through this, not only Avalokiteśvara.

One should know that this contains two meanings: first, regarding those of initial capacity who enter deeply through a single gate, the "Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ" (ear-root perfect penetration) is not limited to Avalokiteśvara alone;
indeed, throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, those who have entered the Way through this ear-gate are truly numerous.
Thus, even when considered solely in terms of this one dharma-gate, it is itself vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive.
Secondly, regarding the ultimate, perfect, and universal nature, the "perfect penetration of the ear-faculty" (*śrotra-indriya*) is itself the twenty-five kinds of perfect penetration;
furthermore, all other perfect penetrations, as well as the various Dharma-gates of the ten directions and the three periods of time, may all be called the "perfect penetration of the ear-faculty.
This is the principle that one gate is all gates, and all gates are one gate.
Therefore, it is said that there is "only one path to the gate of nirvāṇa. Is it appropriate to say that the twenty-four sages have not yet reached this principle and remain outside the gate?

Is it appropriate to say that for these twenty-four sages there are further divergent paths? (6) This concludes the exposition on the intent of attaining Buddhahood, summarizing the selection of those who are qualified.

Truly, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, inquired of me regarding the various skillful means for saving those in the final age who seek to transcend the world and achieve the mind of *nirvāṇa*, I replied that Avalokiteśvara is the foremost;

all other skillful means are the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, which causes beings to abandon their defilements through immediate circumstances. These are not for the long-term cultivation and study of sentient beings in this land, nor are they taught at the same level of depth.
This is the Dharma.
To abandon worldly afflictions through these very phenomena is what is meant by "returning home via the path. Other gates of universal penetration reach this state only at the profound levels;
those at shallow levels do not know it. Furthermore, these methods can only be effective for individuals who have achieved a specific kind of innate spiritual capacity (*gotra*) from past lives.
The capacity to universally benefit the three faculties resides solely in this faculty of hearing; while its marvelous efficacy lies particularly in skillfully benefiting those of inferior faculties.
Seventh, prostrating, he requests the addition of the illumination of reality.
I prostrate to the Tathāgatagarbha, the untainted and inconceivable one;

may you bestow your grace upon those of the future so that they may be free from doubt regarding this gateway, easily achieve its skillful means, and be fit to teach Ānanda and those submerged in the final age.
By cultivating perfect penetration through this faculty alone, it surpasses all others—such is the true mind.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the essence of the principle of intrinsic purity; the "outflow-free and inconceivable" refers to the fruit of wisdom realized through ultimate and perfect enlightenment.
The principle is called the Dharma Jewel, and the wisdom is called the Buddha and the Sangha; this is the meaning of the Three Jewels as a single entity.
When it says "the true mind is thus," it means that the essential core of the true mind does not exceed this.
The assembly gained benefit throughout the three periods of the day.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great multitude attained clear understanding in both body and mind,

receiving a profound revelation that the contemplation of the Buddha’s Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa is like a person who has traveled far away on business and, though not yet returned, clearly knows his home.
The multitude gathered on the road where they were traveling—consisting of devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings; those still in training and those of the two vehicles;
and all the bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds—numbered as many as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers.

They all attained their original mind, became free from dust and defilement, and achieved the purity of the Dharma-eye. Upon hearing these verses, the bhikṣuṇī Śrīprabhā attained arhatship, as did an immeasurable multitude.
All who are born therein give rise to the peerless *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind.
The nature of hearing in this present single thought-moment is fundamentally perfect, fundamentally penetrating, and fundamentally constant. "Perfect" refers to the Bodhi of Real Wisdom;
"penetrating" refers to the Bodhi of Expedient Means; "constant" refers to the Bodhi of True Nature; and "perfect" refers to the Perfectly Pure Nirvana. "Penetrating" refers to...
The expedient means of the purity of nirvāṇa is constant; this is precisely the nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity.

Thus, there is the nirvāṇa of principle, up to the ultimate nirvāṇa of bodhi. Because these six are constantly identical, it is said that although one has not yet attained them, one returns to the six.
Because they are constantly identical, one treads the road back to one’s hometown at every step. One who attains the original mind realizes this.

This is the fundamental essence of the single thought-moment present before us; because it is far removed from the delusive dust of conceptual signs and free from the empty defilements of discriminative consciousness and emotion, it is said that one "attains the purity of the Dharma-eye.
This is the Tathāgata’s treasury of the True Dharma-eye, not the "Dharma-eye" among the five eyes of sequential progression.
Upon hearing this verse, the nun Śīlinī became an Arhat; this is what is meant by "attaining [enlightenment] through the Great Teaching."
Attaining a small benefit therein is precisely for the sake of the Bodhisattvas, while incidentally for the sake of the two vehicles; this is clear from the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) section.
Those who give rise to the "unequaled and equal" mind have no dharma that can be equaled; this mind is able to equalize all dharmas.

This refers to those who, upon first hearing the perfect principle, either give rise to the mind through contemplative practice (*guanxing*) or give rise to the mind at the level of names (*mingzi*). This is the initial stage.
The demonstration of the fundamental root of perfect penetration by the practitioner is concluded. Second, showing the methods for the site of practice (*maṇḍala*) for the sake of future generations.
Part one: The request; part two: The granting of praise; part three: The proclamation. Now, the first.

Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms in reverence before the great assembly, and prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet. His mind and its traces were perfectly clear and bright, and he was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy.
Desiring to benefit all sentient beings of the future, he bowed his head and addressed the Buddha, the World-Honored One of Great Compassion:
“I have now awakened to the Dharma-door of attaining Buddhahood; by practicing within it, I have attained freedom from doubt and confusion. I have often heard the Tathāgata speak in this manner.”

To say that one who has not yet crossed over oneself first crosses others refers to the Bodhisattva’s initial resolve; to awaken oneself fully and then be able to awaken others refers to the Tathāgata appearing in the world.
Although I have not yet crossed over myself, I vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final kalpa.

World-Honored One, these sentient beings are gradually moving further away from the Buddha; false teachers preach the Dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. [I wish] to gather their minds and lead them into...
How does samādhi cause one to be established in the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), remain far from all demonic activities, and attain non-retrogression in the mind of bodhi?
Youxi said: "Mind" refers to the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*; "traces" refers to the path elucidated therein. Wuxing said: "Compassion."
One feels sorrow because of not having heard [the teaching] in the past; one feels joy because of attaining awakening now;

furthermore, one feels sorrow because of considering sentient beings of the future who have not yet awakened, and joy because of observing that the great assembly present before one has gained benefit. Second is praise and approval.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, praised Ānanda, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
As you have asked, regarding the establishment of the site of enlightenment to rescue and deliver sentient beings drowning in the final age—listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly responded, "So be it," and respectfully awaited his instruction.
Because it accords with the capacity of those who practice the Way during the final kalpa and aligns with the Tathāgata’s intent to preach, he again utters "Excellent.
Third, the proclamation of the two parts: first, clarifying the fundamental precepts; second, clarifying the recitation of mantras to treat habitual tendencies.

Regarding the first of the two introductory sections: first, a general exposition of the three trainings with precepts as the foundation; second, a specific demonstration of the four grave prohibitions to reveal the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*). Now, for the first:
The Buddha addressed Ānanda, "You have often heard me, within the *Vinaya*, proclaim the three definitive principles of practice."

What is called "gathering the mind as the precept" (*śīla*), "arising of concentration from the precept" (*samādhi*), and "the emergence of wisdom from concentration" (*prajñā*)—these are named the Threefold Training of the Outflows (*anāsrava-śikṣā*).
The *Vinaya* also states that *vinaya* is the *Vinaya-piṭaka*. Regarding the phrase "gathering the mind as the precept," the character "as" (*wei*) serves as a term of definition (*xùn*).
The statement that one must restrain the mind through the practice of the precepts indicates that the mind must necessarily be governed by the observance of the *śīla*.

If the mind were not restrained by the precepts, by what means could one distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox? Furthermore, it is only when the mind is restrained that one can truly be said to possess the precepts;

this clearly demonstrates that the practice of observing and violating the precepts does not merely consist of binding the body. Thus, through the *pratimokṣa* precepts, one first restrains the mind, and only thereafter...
The arising of concentration and the development of wisdom—this is what is called the three untainted trainings (*trīṇy aśaikṣāṇi*).

If one lacks this precept, even if meditative concentration and much wisdom manifest before one, one will inevitably fall into the realm of demons and heterodoxy, becoming tainted (*sāsrava*). Question:
Does the gathering of the mind as a precept gather the true mind or the deluded mind? If it gathers the deluded mind, since the delusion has no inherent substance, how can it be gathered?

Regarding "inclusion": if it is the true mind that is included, what further need is there for inclusion? Furthermore, although the dharma of precepts is one, there are four distinct differences in the wisdom of contemplation according to the four teachings;
I do not yet understand how the mind must be included for the circular (perfect) precepts to be established.

If you say that the precepts are themselves outflow-free (*anāsrava*), then could the retribution of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who maintains the precepts in the realms of humans and devas also be called outflow-free? If [it were], then...
Question: Can that which is with outflows (sāsrava) still be called pure precepts? Answer: True mind and deluded mind are originally not two distinct entities.

When following conditions of defilement, the entirety of the true becomes deluded, just as water becomes ice; when following conditions of purity, the entirety of the deluded returns to the true, just as ice becomes water.
To speak precisely, the delusion of the true and the arising of delusion occur solely because delusion is taken for luminous awareness—this is what is meant by "knowing."

“Seeing” (jian) establishes the awareness; “knowing” (zhi) identifies the error. The character for “establishing” (li) is precisely the mind’s grasping at its own mind; the character for “grasping” (qu) is the recognition within awakening that is itself delusion;
and the character for “recognizing” (ren) refers to returning from falsehood to truth. In short, it is simply a matter of not following the three types of continuous conceptualization.
Thus, “knowledge and vision are without seeing”—the merit lies in the character for “without” (wu), which means not grasping at anything, yet there is nothing that is not illusion.

The "not taking" (bùqǔ) of the two characters, the "maintaining" (shǒu) of the phrase "maintaining true permanence," and the "subduing" (fú) of the phrase "adhering inwardly and subduing" are all identical to the present term "gathering" (shè).
Thus, one knows that if the mind is not gathered, the true mind becomes a deluded mind;
if it can be gathered, the deluded mind becomes the true mind. As for the wondrous method of gathering the mind, nothing surpasses the precepts.

To be in accord with the sublime precepts in every thought-moment is what is meant by "gathering" (*saṃgraha*); it does not mean that the precepts have spatial dimensions, nor does "gathering" imply bondage. As the subsequent text states:

"One must ensure that the impulse toward lust is severed in both body and mind, and even the nature of this severance is non-existent. Here, the severance of the body refers to the *prātimokṣa-saṃvara* (the discipline of individual liberation);

the severance of the mind refers to the *dhyāna-saṃvara* (the discipline co-arising with meditative concentration); and the non-existence of the very nature of severance refers to the *anāsrava-saṃvara* (the untainted discipline co-arising with the Path).
Furthermore, because both body and mind are severed, one does not abide in saṃsāra; because the nature of severance is also non-existent, one does not abide in nirvāṇa.

Moreover, because the body is severed, this is the precept of the ultimate truth that transcends birth and death; because the mind is severed, this is the precept of the conventional truth that plays with spiritual powers and supernatural faculties.
Because the nature of severance is also non-existent, one realizes that the very nature of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and falsehood is itself the Buddha.
The nature [of reality] is such that there is nothing further to be severed; this is the precept of the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The sutra text further states:

"Sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and fail to attain true purity because they follow along with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. By reversing these three [actions], one gives rise to [the state of] being without killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct.
Those who possess these names belong to the realm of ghosts; those who lack them belong to the celestial realms. Between existence and non-existence..."
When mutual inclinations give rise to the view of saṃsāra, if one attains the wondrous arousal of *samādhi*, then there is wondrous and eternal stillness;

both existence and non-existence are absent, and even non-duality is extinguished. This is identical in meaning to the principle herein that body and mind are simultaneously severed, and the very nature of severance is also absent.
Only this may be called pure precept (*śīla*); only this may be termed the gathering of the mind; only this is the untainted (*anāsrava*).
To learn from those who move humans and devas through the goodness of their precepts is like using a mani jewel to trade for a single garment or a single meal;
there is no inherent superiority or inferiority in the things obtained through what is not the Dharma.

Therefore, if one now wishes to collect the mind, one should first clearly prepare the precepts as the objective field, and subsequently deeply clarify contemplative wisdom to achieve its fruition; in this way, one will perhaps draw near to that goal. (2)
A separate exposition of the fourfold gravity to manifest the state of being free from outflows. Part one: the restatement of the inquiry; part two: the detailed exposition. Now, for the first:
Ānanda, how does one collect the mind? That which I call "precept" (śīla).
The question is: "How is it that by skillfully restraining the mind so that body and speech are simultaneously pure, one may be called 'possessing the precepts'?
This passage generally demonstrates that without the precepts, one can never restrain the mind; and without restraining the mind, one can never be said to possess the precepts.

Second, a detailed exposition of the four [precepts]: first, the precept against sexual misconduct; second, the precept against killing; third, the precept against stealing; fourth, the precept against false speech.
Regarding the precepts of speech, these constitute the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*) of a bhikṣu; they are the very foundation of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
First, the precept against sexual misconduct is presented at the outset because desire, as the root of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), is the foremost [affliction].
If the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor lustful hearts, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death.
You cultivate samādhi precisely to emerge from worldly toil; if you do not eliminate the lustful heart, you cannot escape the dust of the world.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall into the path of demons—becoming a high-ranking māra-king at best, or a demon subject at worst.
These low-grade māras and their various demonic followers each claim for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.

After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such demonic adherents will flourish in the world, widely practicing greed and lust while posing as "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra).
They cause sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and false views, losing the path to Bodhi. You must instruct the people of the world [to beware of them].
To cultivate samādhi while first severing sexual desire in the mind is called the Tathāgata’s foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction from previous Buddhas and World-Honored Ones.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one cultivates dhyāna-concentration without severing sexual desire, it is like steaming sand and gravel in the hope that it will become rice;
even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it would still only be called hot sand. Why is this? Because this is not the fundamental substance of rice; it is sand.

Since stone becomes [jewels], you may seek the Buddha’s wondrous fruit with a lustful body; yet even if you should attain wondrous awakening, it will all have its root in lust. With lust as its fundamental basis, you will revolve through the three miserable realms and certainly be unable to escape. As for the path to cultivating and realizing the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, you must ensure that the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind, such that even the nature of this severance is non-existent. Only then can you hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha. Thus it is said: If you wish to attain the Way, first eliminate lust; If you do not eliminate lust, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate lust and cultivate the Way, You will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate lust and yet cultivate the Way, It is like trying to grow grain from ashes— Even if you labor for a hundred thousand kalpas, You will never attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate anger. If you do not eliminate anger, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate anger and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate anger and yet cultivate the Way, it is like trying to grow grain from frost—laboring for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate ignorance. If you do not eliminate ignorance, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate ignorance and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate ignorance and yet cultivate the Way, it is like trying to grow grain from weeds—laboring for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate greed. If you do not eliminate greed, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate greed and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate greed and yet cultivate the Way, it is like trying to grow grain from salt—laboring for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate arrogance. If you do not eliminate arrogance, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate arrogance and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you eliminate doubt and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate delusion. If you do not eliminate delusion, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate delusion and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate delusion and yet cultivate the Way, it is like trying to grow grain from wind—laboring for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain the Way. If you eliminate pride and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you eliminate envy and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate envy and yet cultivate the Way, it is like trying to grow grain from dust—laboring for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate jealousy. If you do not eliminate jealousy, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate jealousy and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you eliminate stinginess and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate flattery. If you do not eliminate flattery, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate flattery and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate flattery and yet cultivate the Way, it is like trying to grow grain from sand—laboring for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate hypocrisy. If you do not eliminate hypocrisy, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate hypocrisy and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate hypocrisy and yet cultivate the Way, it is like trying to grow grain from ice—laboring for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate conceit. If you do not eliminate conceit, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate conceit and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate conceit and yet cultivate the Way, it is like trying to grow grain from vapor—laboring for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate arrogance. If you do not eliminate arrogance, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate frivolity and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way.
