If you eliminate distraction and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate distraction and yet cultivate the Way, it is like trying to grow grain from shadows—laboring for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate negligence. If you do not eliminate negligence, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate negligence and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate negligence and yet cultivate the Way, it is like trying to grow grain from echoes—laboring for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate indolence. If you do not eliminate indolence, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate indolence and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate indolence and yet cultivate the Way, it is like trying to grow grain from dreams—laboring for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish to attain the Way, you must first eliminate sloth. If you do not eliminate sloth, you will never reach the Way. If you eliminate sloth and cultivate the Way, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not eliminate sloth and yet cultivate the Way, it is like trying to grow grain from illusions—laboring for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain the Way. Furthermore, if you wish
"What I have here taught is called the teaching of the Buddha; to speak otherwise is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
This statement does not merely require that the body refrain from sexual misconduct; it requires that the mind likewise refrain from it.

Even those with great wisdom and meditative concentration would still become companions of Māra [if they fail here], let alone those lacking concentration and wisdom who fall directly into ruin—of this there is no doubt. One must know well what it means to be a companion of Māra."

If consciousness manifests an appearance of compassion yet does not sever the mind of lust, one falls into the pit of craving; if one falsely claims that lust does not obstruct the Path, one falls into the pit of views.
Having fallen into these deep pits, one will forever be estranged from the path to enlightenment.
Indeed, the lustful mind is the root of birth and death and can never correspond with the fruit of Buddhahood; it is just as sand and gravel can never be the basis for cooked rice.
The cultivation through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is illustrated by the metaphor of steaming;

taking non-arising and non-ceasing as the fundamental cause of cultivation, one subsequently achieves the perfect realization of the stage of fruition, which is like steaming rice to produce cooked grain.

To achieve otherwise is to produce the perverse blessings of Māra, which is like steaming sand to produce only heat. "Severing the body" refers to the *vinaya* precepts; "severing the mind" refers to the dhyāna precepts. Severing—

"The nature is also non-existent" refers to untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*); this is the meaning of entering emptiness. "The body is severed" refers to the restraint of discipline (*saṃvara*) and that which is concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja*);
"the mind is severed" refers to that which is concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahaja*). "The nature of severance is also non-existent" means that while engaging with objects, one is not defiled;
this is the meaning of emerging from the stages. "The body is severed" means realizing the untainted; "the mind is severed" means engaging with objects [without attachment].
If even the nature of defilement and severance is non-existent, then both severance and non-severance are quiescent; this is the meaning of the Middle Way.
Regarding the "trigger of lust," as the previous verse says: "Though one sees the movement of the various faculties, they must be drawn out by a single trigger.

If this trigger is not extinguished, then even if one can suppress and sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), the illusory root has never been permanently removed; therefore, one must proceed directly toward it.
If you penetrate the character "ji" (mechanism), then both "killing" and "not killing" are simultaneously extinguished. Second, the precept against killing:
Ānanda, furthermore, if the beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor a mind of killing, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
You cultivate samādhi to fundamentally emerge from worldly toil; if the mind of killing is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust. Even if you possess [other virtues],...
Those with much wisdom whose meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) manifests before them—if they do not cease killing—will surely fall upon the path of the spirits.

Those of the highest grade will become powerful ghosts; those of the middle grade will become flying *yakṣas* and various ghost generals; those of the lowest grade will become earth-walking *rākṣasas*.
These various ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way. When I pass into extinction...
In the degenerate age after my passing, many such ghosts and spirits will flourish in the world, claiming that by eating meat one finds the path to Bodhi.
Ānanda, I have permitted bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat; these meats were all produced through my supernatural power and originally possessed no life-force.
You, O Brahmin, live in a land where the ground is mostly damp and humid, further compounded by sand and stones, so that grasses and vegetables do not grow there.
I empower this with the spiritual power of great compassion; it is through the influence of great kindness and pity that it is provisionally called "meat.

How could you, having tasted its flavor, do so after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa? To eat the flesh of sentient beings while calling oneself a son of the Śākya—know this, you must understand:
even if such meat-eaters achieve mental clarity that resembles *samādhi*, they are all great rākṣasas who, when their retribution ends, will surely sink into the depths.
In this sea of suffering of birth and death, those who are not disciples of the Buddha continue to kill, devour, and consume one another without end;
how could such people ever escape the three realms? You have taught the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, and next to that, to sever the taking of life.
This is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past. Therefore, Ānanda...
If one who does not cease killing practices meditative concentration, it is like a person who blocks their own ears and shouts at the top of their voice, yet seeks for others not to hear them;

such people are said to be "the more they try to hide, the more they reveal. Pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas walk along forked paths without treading upon living grass, let alone plucking it with their hands;
how much less could those of great compassion ever take hold of sentient beings [in such a manner]?

If blood and flesh are their sustenance, then if bhikṣus do not wear the silks, cottons, or floss-silk of the East, nor the boots, leather footwear, furs, woolens, curds, milk, or clarified butter of this land, such bhikṣus are truly liberated from the world and have repaid their karmic debts from past lives;
they shall no longer wander within the three realms. Why is this? To wear the products of their bodies is to become bound by those very conditions, just as if one were eating the earth itself.

One who eats only a moderate amount of grain, whose feet do not leave the ground, and who ensures that for all sentient beings there is no attachment to the body or its parts, and that neither the body nor the mind—these two paths—is served or consumed;
I declare such a person to be one truly liberated. What I have spoken thus is called the word of the Buddha;
what is not spoken thus is the word of Pāpīyān.
This statement means that one must not only refrain from killing with the body, but the mind must likewise refrain from killing. Regarding the five kinds of pure meat:
those not seen to be killed, not heard to be killed, and not suspected to have been killed for oneself; as well as meat from animals that died naturally or was left over by birds.
In the five regions of India, all are called Brahmins because it is a venerable clan. Question: Since the Buddha is fully endowed with supernatural powers...

"Why do you not manifest as grass and vegetables, but instead manifest as the five kinds of pure meat? He replied: "The Buddha accords with the requirements of the time and does not establish what is extraordinary.
Since this land originally did not produce grass and vegetables, if they were to suddenly appear now, people would regard it as a marvel.
Furthermore, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, even if one were to encounter grass and vegetables that do not grow, how could one possibly [rely on them]?"

For this reason, when the Buddha and his bhikṣus encountered a famine in the world, Maudgalyāyana offered to take the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) and the naturally grown non-glutinous rice from Uttarakuru;
the Buddha refused both, saying, "In future ages, when there is no Maudgalyāyana, what will you do?
One should know that the transmission and succession of the Buddha-dharma is such as this. It is a false claim [to think otherwise].
To kill living beings and eat their flesh without reaping the karmic retribution is as impossible as covering one's own ears while shouting loudly and hoping not to be heard;
it cannot be achieved. One who cultivates *dhyāna* seeks to transcend birth and death, and thus is called "desiring concealment.
One who kills living beings yet seeks to accumulate merit through continuous enmity is called "exposed. There are two kinds of clothing: the first is *vastra*.
Regarding the two types of clothing: "wearing" refers to garments made of silk, gauze, cotton, floss silk, leather boots, and fur;
"consuming" refers to dairy products such as milk, curd, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Although these are generally prohibited here, according to various sūtras and vinayas there are distinctions.
For instance, regarding silk, cotton, and gauze, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles strictly forbid their use.

Because these [items] result in the killing of many lives, leather boots, furs, and woolen garments are permitted unconditionally in the Hīnayāna, whereas in the Mahāyāna they are not entirely prohibited;
this is because one does not kill specifically for their sake.

Regarding milk, curd, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*), both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna permit them, even to the point that the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* still allows for their consumption. This sūtra likewise...
It is said that you always carry your alms bowl among the assembly during the two meal times; therein, one may encounter milk, curd, or clarified butter (ghṛta), which are called "superior flavors.
Later, in the ritual protocols of the literary altar (wen-tan-chang), these are still used for offerings to the Triple Gem because they are merely the residual moisture and do not harm life.
To say now that one does not consume them is an expression of carrying a category to its ultimate limit.

It is said that it would be even better not to consume them at all. For example, as for those who "eat the essence of the earth" (*pṛthivīrasa*), the humans at the beginning of the eon were able to fly through the air;
because they consumed the essence of the earth and naturally grown non-glutinous rice, their feet did not leave the ground.

This is used as a metaphor for how consuming the physical constituents of sentient beings prevents one from being able to permanently leave the category of sentient beings. As for the body, it is blood... [text fragment ends]
Regarding parts of the body such as skin and hair, since one does not wear them on the body, one does not eat them;
furthermore, one’s mind never harbors the thought of greedily seeking to consume them. Is this not the mark of a truly liberated person?
Question: The followers of the Hīnayāna seek liberation from birth and death; why, then, do they instead permit the five kinds of pure meat, as well as items such as leather boots and sandals?

Question: Since the primary task of those who ride the Great Vehicle is to deliver sentient beings, why on the contrary do you strictly prohibit [certain actions]? Answer: Those of the Hīnayāna seek only their own deliverance;
it suffices for them merely not to commit acts of killing, as this is sufficient to unimpede their transcendence of the world.

This may be compared to a person who has fled from their entire family: they need not repay small debts. Those of the Mahāyāna must extensively transform sentient beings within the triple world; this may be compared to a person [who remains in their home].
If a person of great lineage or a householder in this land owes even a hair’s breadth to another, they will immediately feel shame and lose their composure;
such people cannot freely perform acts of transformation. Those who practice the bodhisattva path should reflect on this. This is the third precept against stealing.
Ānanda, furthermore, if the minds of sentient beings within the six realms of this world do not harbor theft, they will not follow along with the continuous succession of birth and death.
You practice samādhi in order to fundamentally emerge from worldly toil; if the mind of theft is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust of the world.

Even if you possess great wisdom and dhyāna-samādhi manifests before you, if you do not sever the mind of theft, you will inevitably fall into the paths of the heterodox—becoming either a superior-grade spirit or a middle-grade one.

Those possessed by the various demons of the lower grade of malevolent spirits and wicked people—these various evil ones also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, such demonic and perverse beings will flourish in the world;

they will lurk in secret, practicing deceit while calling themselves "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra), each claiming for themselves that they have attained the dharmas of a superior person (uttarapudgala-dharma), thereby deluding and confusing others.
Those without wisdom fear that their minds will be lost; wherever they pass, their households fall into decay.
My teaching is for bhikṣus to wander in all directions begging for food, so as to cause them to abandon greed and achieve the path to Bodhi.

These bhikṣus do not cook for themselves, but rely on the remnants of life, lodging as travelers within the Three Realms, demonstrating a single coming and going after which there is no returning. How can these thieves falsely claim to be my followers?

Those who trade in clothing and profit from the Tathāgata by committing various kinds of evil deeds, claiming that "the Buddha-dharma ought to be thus," while instead slandering and reviling ordained bhikṣus who possess the precepts,
asserting that they follow the path of the Hīnayāna— by such delusions they mislead immeasurable sentient beings,
causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell. If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be a bhikṣu who resolves his mind to cultivate *samādhi* and is able to...

If, before an image of the Tathāgata, one lights a single lamp, burns a finger joint, or burns a single incense stick upon one’s own body, I say that such a person has at once repaid all karmic debts from beginningless time.
They bid a long farewell to the world and are forever liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*).
Although they have not yet clearly illuminated the path to supreme enlightenment, their mind is already resolved regarding the Dharma. If...

Even if one were to attain the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) through such a minor cause as giving up one's body, one would inevitably be reborn as a human being to repay past debts, just as in my own case with the horse-barley;

it is exactly the same. Your teaching for people of the world to practice *samādhi* and subsequently sever the habit of stealing is called the third definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past. Therefore, Ānanda, if...
One who constantly steals away their practice of meditative concentration is like a person pouring water into a leaking cup, seeking to fill it;
even if they pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be restored.

If a bhikṣu does not store even a fraction of what remains from his robes and alms-bowl, and gives whatever surplus he receives from begging to hungry sentient beings, then at a great assembly, when joining his palms to pay homage to the multitude, even if someone strikes or reviles him, [he remains equanimous].
In praising [this teaching], one must cause both body and mind to renounce themselves; one should share one’s own flesh, bones, and blood with all sentient beings.
One must not take the Tathāgata’s teachings of provisional meaning and turn them into one’s own interpretation to mislead beginners. The Buddhas seal such a person as having attained true samādhi.
What I have spoken is called the Buddha’s teaching; that which is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

This statement means that not only must one refrain from stealing the body, but the mind must also not steal. Regarding "those of heterodox paths," this refers to those who are deceitful and fraudulent.
Regarding "spirits," these are those who steal the vital essence of the sun and moon to become divine spirits.

Regarding "vicious demons," these are those who steal the vital essence of humans to become demonic apparitions. Regarding "ghosts who wander for alms according to their methods," this refers to those who follow established rules and procedures.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, begging for food is termed *piṇḍapāta*. "Piṇḍa" means distributing alms to the community of monks, and "pāta" means protecting the power of the Path.
Master Zhaolun stated that there are briefly four intentions for begging for food: first, to bring benefit and merit to sentient beings; second, to subdue arrogance;
third, to recognize that the body is subject to suffering; and fourth, to eliminate attachment and the pursuit of profit.
The Tathāgata is one who attaches himself to the Buddha-dharma and greedily traffics in gain and offerings. As for "kindling a single lamp upon one's own body" and so forth:
because one gives rise to a thieving mind based on the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), one uses the minor cause of relinquishing the body as an antidote to the karma of theft.

Wēn-líng says: "Of all things difficult to relinquish, none is like one's own body; if one can relinquish that which is difficult to relinquish, then all other attachments and cravings will certainly [be overcome]."
Because one is able to relinquish [them], it is said that this person’s mind regarding the Dharma is already resolved.

If one were merely to sacrifice the body while the mind is not resolved upon relinquishment, it would be of no benefit to the Path; therefore, the following passage states: "One must cause both body and mind to be abandoned together.
As for the phrase "my horse-barley and so forth," in a past life the Buddha once rebuked a bhikṣu, saying he might as well eat horse-feed.
He ate barley for three months within the city of Vairaṇyā to demonstrate that past debts must inevitably be repaid.

His meditative concentration is like water; his thieving mind is like a leaking cup. He does not store even a fraction of what remains from his robes and alms bowl, thereby completely abandoning greed.
He gives away the surplus of his begged food to hungry beings, thereby completely abandoning stinginess. At the Great Assembly...

When one joins their palms and pays homage to the assembly, this is the completion of abandoning the mind of pride; when one encounters someone who strikes or reviles them and treats it as equal to praise, this is the completion of abandoning the mind of anger.

Regarding the phrase "not taking [the Buddha's] teachings of provisional meaning," the preceding passage refers to the permanent severance of the mind of theft regarding the two types of retribution—the environment and its inhabitants;
this, however, refers to the permanent severance of the mind of theft regarding the Buddha-Dharma itself. That is to say:

If one wishes to preach the Dharma to benefit sentient beings and guide beginners, one must thoroughly investigate the various scriptures of the Tathāgata’s Great and Small Vehicles to understand the causes and conditions of the four *siddhārtha* (purposes).
One must not merely cling to a single meaning or interpretation, considering it to be the only truth, thereby misleading beginners as well.
[This concludes] the precept against the four great lies.

Ānanda, although the beings of the six realms in this world may have already perfected their physical and mental conduct by being free from the three actions of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, if they engage in great falsehoods, their *samādhi* will not attain purity. They become demons of craving and views, losing the seed of the Tathāgata.

This refers to those who claim to have attained what they have not attained, or say they have realized what they have not realized, or who seek to be the most honored, supreme, and foremost in the world.
To say to another, "I have now attained the fruit of a *srotāpanna*, a *sakṛdāgāmin*, an *anāgāmin*, the path of an *arhat*,
or the vehicle of a *pratyekabuddha*," or to seek the prostrations and repentance of Bodhisattvas at the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and those prior to the stages for the sake of their offerings—
this is a *icchantika* who destroys the seeds of the Buddha, like a person cutting down a *tāla* tree with a sword.

The Buddha has prophesied that such persons have eternally destroyed their roots of goodness and lack further wisdom or insight; they sink into the ocean of the three sufferings and shall not attain samādhi.

After my parinirvāṇa, I shall command the various bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest bodies within that age of the final dharma, assuming all manner of forms to deliver those wandering in saṃsāra—whether as śramaṇas, laypeople, householders, kings, or officials.
Whether with boys or girls, or even with courtesans, widows, thieves, butchers, or merchants, he associates with them and praises the Buddha Vehicle, causing their bodies and minds to enter samādhi.

Yet he never says of himself, "I am a true Bodhisattva" or "I am a true Arhat," lest he reveal the Buddha’s secret cause before those who have not yet studied. He does so except at the time of death, when his *skandhas* remain.
The entrustment says: "How can such a person delude sentient beings and commit a great falsehood?

You must teach the people of the world to practice *samādhi* and subsequently eliminate all great falsehoods; this is called the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the Buddhas of the past.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever this great falsehood, it is like carving..."
To take human excrement and shape it into sandalwood, hoping to find its fragrance—such a thing is impossible.

I teach my bhikṣus that at the altar of the straightforward mind, even amidst all actions within the four modes of deportment, there must be no pretense whatsoever; how then could one falsely claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior man?
It is like a destitute person who falsely styles himself an emperor, only to bring about his own destruction; how much more so for one who would dare to act thus toward the Dharma King?
If you falsely claim that your ground is not true, the fruit you will reap will be circuitous; seeking the Buddha’s Bodhi is like a man trying to bite his own navel—who can achieve it?
If there are bhikṣus whose minds are as straight as bowstrings, who are entirely truthful and enter samādhi, they will forever be free from demonic affairs.
I certify that such people shall achieve the unsurpassed awakening of a Bodhisattva. What I have spoken is called...
What the Buddha has spoken is not as you have said; that is the speech of Pāpīyān.
Those who possess the demon of craving and views give rise to a slight degree of attainment and thereby develop overweening pride—this is the demon of craving.
To cling to this as being real while regarding all else as false is the demon of views. Furthermore, to use this to greedily seek offerings and honor is the demon of craving.
The Māra clings to inherent nature and abandons cultivation, falsely claiming that he has already attained equality with the various sages; this is to see the Māra.
The stages prior to the [first] ground—namely the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and penetration—as well as the *icchantika*, are all *icchantikas*.
The fruits of the Three Vehicles are like sandalwood, while the evil mind is like filth. As for the "person who bites his own navel," it refers to a person who...
The ability to bite one's own navel is used as a metaphor for remorse that is too late to avail;

some say it refers to a musk deer being pursued by humans who bites its own navel—though it may bite its navel, it ultimately cannot escape its peril. All other points may be understood according to the text.
The Sixth Fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas;
Explanatory Text of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
Fascicle Seven: Words and Phrases.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra during the Tang Dynasty;
the words and phrases [commentary] by the Dharma Master, Bodhisattva-śrāmaṇera Zhixu of Ancient Wu.
Second, explaining the recitation of mantras to cure habitual tendencies. This has two parts: first, summarizing what preceded; second, the actual explanation. Now, for the first:
"Ānanda, regarding your question on concentrating the mind, I shall now first explain the wondrous gate for practicing and learning the entry into *samādhi*.
One who seeks the path of a Bodhisattva must first maintain these four kinds of precepts, as pure as ice and frost, so that [evil] cannot arise within them."
Branches, leaves, mind, and mouth—these four arise without cause.
Ānanda, if these four matters are not lost, the mind will not even take as its object form, sound, smell, taste, or touch; how then could any demonic activities arise?
This is the formal conclusion clarifying that to collect and restrain the mind, one must necessarily uphold the precepts.
"All branches and leaves" refers to all other subtle rules of discipline, such as the four verbal and three mental precepts within the ten wholesome actions,
the latter six articles among the śrāmaṇera precepts, the remaining two hundred and forty-six articles among the bhikṣu precepts, and so forth.
The six grave precepts and forty-eight light precepts that follow the Bodhisattva Precepts are all fully encompassed by these four fundamental mental precepts, leaving nothing out;
therefore, it is said that there is no possibility for the "three of the mind and four of the body" to arise.

Since all demonic activities necessarily manifest by relying upon the six sense objects, if the mind does not take form, sound, smell, taste, or touch as its conditions, [then such activities cannot arise].
The celestial Māras have no means to deploy their arts; therefore, the three trainings in the absence of outflows (trīṇi śikṣāny anāsravāṇi) must necessarily take the precepts as their foundation.

Second, the correct elucidation of the two [aspects]: first, a brief indication of what should be maintained; second, a detailed manifestation of the ritual procedures. Within the first [section], there are two parts:

first, a brief exhortation to recite and maintain [the precepts] to manifest the benefits; second, a brief indication of the methods for the practice site (maṇḍala). Within the first [of these], there are again two parts.
The first part encourages the upholding [of the mantra], and the second reveals its benefits. Now, for the first:

"If there are those with past habitual tendencies whom you cannot eliminate, you should teach such people to single-mindedly recite this unsurpassed divine mantra of mine, the Buddha-Usnīṣa-Vidyotana-Mahā-sāttvata-praṇidhāra; this is the Tathāgata’s Unseeable Summit."
The Unconditioned Mind-Buddha emits radiance from the crown of his head and, seated upon a precious lotus flower, speaks this Heart Mantra.

Now, while the power of the *mokṣa* precepts is certainly capable of warding off external māras, when past habitual tendencies are particularly strong, one must rely on divine mantras for secret purification.
*Mahā-satvata-pratara*, which is translated as "Great White Parasol."
The essence being without counterpart is called "Great"; the appearance being detached from worldly defilement is called "White"; and the function covering all things is called the "Parasol.
Furthermore, because these three are all beyond dependence, their essence, appearance, and function are termed the "Three Greats.

Moreover, as all three are inherently pure and all three cover all things, they are simply alternative names for the secret treasury of the Three Virtues of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. [This concludes] the fifth assembly of the spirit.
Mantras are the secret means for elucidating this wondrous mind; therefore, they are called "mind-mantras" (*cittamantra*) and also "mantras of the mind.
Second, the manifestation of benefits:
Furthermore, your karmic conditions with Mātaṅgī over successive kalpas, as well as the habitual tendencies of affection and love, do not belong to a single lifetime alone.

Furthermore, for one entire kalpa I proclaimed the Dharma, and through my compassionate heart, they were forever liberated [having first realized the stage of Anāgāmin and continuing until now] to become Arhats.
Even she, a courtesan who lacked the intent to practice, was secretly aided by my supernormal powers and quickly realized the state of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
How much more so, then, for you śrāvakas assembled here, who originally sought the Supreme Vehicle and are destined to attain Buddhahood? It is like this: for example, with...
When dust is carried by a favorable wind, what difficulty or peril can there be?
Youyu (幽溪) said: "The practice of Dhanagiri is profound while that of the bhikṣu is shallow; Dhanagiri is lowly and base while the śrāvaka is noble;
Dhanagiri has no mind for cultivation while you all seek the Supreme Vehicle; Dhanagiri belongs to the group of those fixed in error."

That they will certainly attain Buddhahood constitutes the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Wu Xing (Wu-xing) says: "Dust" is a metaphor for past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and "wind" is like a divine incantation (*mantra*).
Second, a brief presentation of the methods for the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*): first, the preliminary means (*upāya*); second, the actual cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Now, the first [section].
If there are those in the final age who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment, they must first uphold the pure prohibitions of a bhikṣu;

they should specifically select a foremost śramaṇa whose precepts are pure to serve as their teacher. If they do not encounter such a truly pure monk, their observance of the precepts will certainly not be perfected.
Once the precepts have been perfected, they should don new, clean robes, burn incense, and dwell in seclusion.
Recite this divine mantra spoken by the Buddha of the Mind one hundred and eight times.

Regarding the śramaṇa—here translated as "one who is diligent and at rest"—he must be a foremost śramaṇa, such as one described in the Vinaya as having completed ten years of ordination and being endowed with the ten virtues.
Not only must the teacher be a foremost śramaṇa, but the monastic community must also [be so].
Because it is truly pure, one knows that the three masters and seven witnesses—or alternatively, the five persons from a border region—must be carefully selected;
they must not be excluded. Youxi said: "The expedient means in this text correspond to the twenty-five kinds of expedient means in the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan), and are likewise largely the same.
First, one maintains the pure prohibitions of a bhikṣu; this is the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
Donning new, clean robes, he was fully provided with food and clothing; dwelling in seclusion, he stayed in quiet places and ceased all worldly affairs.

Taking the foremost śramaṇa as his teacher, he drew near to virtuous friends. In the preceding passage, his mind did not even dwell upon forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tangibles—this is the censure of the five desires.
In the subsequent passage, his mind extinguished greed and lust, remaining awake for twenty-one days—this refers to [the practice of] *śīla*.
Having abandoned the five hindrances, one sits upright in tranquil abiding; one must harmonize the five matters and practice the five methods during the time of seated meditation.
Zhenji said: "Reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times symbolizes the extinction of the one hundred and eight afflictions. Second is right cultivation.
Thereafter, having established the boundary and set up the *maṇḍala*,

one should pray to the Unsurpassed Tathāgatas currently residing in the lands of the ten directions to emit the light of great compassion and descend to anoint their crowns. Ānanda, if bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs,
or lay donors (*dānapati*) in the final age extinguish greed and lust, uphold the pure precepts of the Buddha, and resolve upon Bodhicitta within the *maṇḍala*...
"Śākyamuni, I vow that if you enter and exit for bathing and practice the Way throughout the six periods of the day and night without sleeping for twenty-one days,
I shall manifest my own body before you, stroke your head to comfort you, and cause you to attain awakening."

The "delimitation of the boundary" (sīmābandha) refers to the ritual methods for the altar described below. According to the various Secret Mantra sections, when one intends to practice, one selects a day to establish the altar;
once the practice is completed, one must immediately dissolve the characteristics of the altar and must not allow them to remain until the appearance of the dawn light.

Since the square and round altars measuring sixteen feet are eight-cornered altars, and no specific height for their construction is mentioned, they should be understood as being identical to those in the Secret [Mantra] tradition.
The sections are demarcated on the ground to perform this samādhi, which is accessible to the fourfold assembly; "lay donors" (upāsaka) refers specifically to pure-faith men and women.
However, regarding the method for entering the maṇḍala, it is absolutely necessary that each group remains distinct;
there is no principle whatsoever for monks and laity to intermingle or for men and women to be mixed together. Alternatively, an upāsaka may be permitted to follow along with the assembly of bhikṣus.
It is permissible for a *vayasyā* (female companion) to follow a *bhikṣuṇī*, yet she must remain at the very end of the line;

she is absolutely not permitted to count toward the number of ten monks, as the text below specifies "ten *bhikṣus*. When the Buddha himself manifests his body and places his hand upon one's head, this is precisely what the practitioner seeks and is therefore not an act of Māra.
However, one must simply contemplate that all is mind-only (*cittamātra*) and must not grasp at anything external to the mind.
Section on the Object. Part Two: Extensively Revealing the Ritual Procedures. This has two sub-sections: first, the formal presentation of the rules for the *maṇḍala*;
second, the reiterated proclamation of the Buddha-śikhara mantra. Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the response. Now, the first [the inquiry].

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, having received the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Tathāgata, my mind has already been awakened and I know for myself that by relying on this Ear-Faculty Perfect Penetration (*karṇendriya-pariśuddha-avavāda*), one can achieve the realization of the path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*). However, as for those practicing during the Dharma-ending age (*paścima-dharma*), they must establish a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
I do not yet know how they should perform the ritual boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) in accordance with the pure rules of the Buddha, the World-Honored One."

Second, the demonstration of the answer, which has two parts: first, the specific demonstration; second, the general summary. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the method for establishing the maṇḍala;

second, the method for performing the practice. Within the first of these, there are again two sections: first, the method for setting up the maṇḍala; second, the method for making offerings. This is the first [section].

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people in the final age wish to establish a site for the Way, they must first obtain a powerful white ox from the Snowy Mountains that eats the fatty, fragrant herbs of those mountains.
This ox drinks only the pure water of the Snowy Mountains; its dung is fine and subtle.
One should take this dung and mix it with sandalwood to plaster the ground. If it is not from the Snowy Mountains, the ox will be foul-smelling and filthy."
As the ground was unfit for coating, they separately excavated five feet of earth from a level plain;

taking the yellow soil from below that depth, they mixed it with sandalwood, aloeswood, *suhaka*, frankincense, saffron, resin, *candana*, *jintong*, *linglang*, *gansong*, and clove—these ten kinds being finely ground into powder.
This was blended with the earth to form a mud plaster, which was then used to coat the site.
A square and round altar, sixteen feet in circumference, is made into an eight-cornered altar.
Regarding this method of the altar, there is both the phenomenal aspect (*sō*) and the noumenal principle (*ri*). The phenomenal aspect may be understood from the text;

as for the noumenal principle, the ritual methods serve to symbolize something. If one does not understand that which the ritual methods symbolize, then the phenomenal forms are applied in vain—how could they provide contact [with the truth]?

The objective realm is established through sublime contemplation; however, while various commentaries of the past have each presented their own explanations—each possessing its own insights yet failing to accord closely with the fundamental tenets of the sutra’s preceding and succeeding sections—I shall not take the time to debate them here.

For now, I shall tentatively provide a separate interpretation based on my own private reflections, awaiting the discernment of those of superior intelligence. "Snow Mountain" (*Himavat*) symbolizes the Dharma.
The nature-principle (*dharmatā*) is as follows: the great powerful white ox symbolizes the wisdom of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*).
The lush, fatty fragrant herbs and clear water in the mountains symbolize the various merits of the conditions and causes inherently present within the essence of nature.

The subtle fineness of its dung symbolizes the wondrous cultivation arising from the three causes inherent in nature. The sandalwood symbolizes the wondrous, unconditioned precepts inherent in nature.
"Smearing the ground with clay" represents the true cause of cultivation. If it were not for the snow mountains, the oxen would be foul-smelling and unfit for smearing the ground;
this signifies that if one takes birth and death as the fundamental cause of cultivation, one cannot achieve the perfect realization of the stage of fruition.
"The plain" represents the six ordinary faculties of experience. "Digging five feet into the ground" represents the shattering of the five aggregates (*skandhas*).
The yellow earth represents the Middle Way Buddha-nature at the gateway of the six sense faculties.
"The sandalwood and so forth" of the Upādhyāya represents the complete upholding of the ten kinds of precepts, namely:

the precept of being unimpaired, the precept of being unbroken, the precept of being unpierced, the precept of being unmixed, the precept of following the Path, the precept of non-attachment, the precept praised by the wise, the precept of mastery, and the precept of accordance with... [the Dharma].

The perfection of the precepts of meditative concentration refers to the ten kinds of fine *śīla* ground powder, which symbolizes that the ten types of precepts mutually encompass and interpenetrate one another, without fixed boundaries or sequential order.
Their combination to form mud symbolizes the simultaneous cultivation of both the precepts (*śīla*) and the vehicle (*yāna*).
Their application to the site of the ritual field symbolizes the mind of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi-citta*). The six patterns, such as the square and the circle, symbolize the eight [precepts].

The Eightfold Right Path subsumes the eightfold wrong path; its eight corners are square yet circular, and circular yet square, symbolizing the non-duality of phenomena and principle, and the common convergence of the provisional and the real.
For those of superior capacity, it is simply a matter of not following the three kinds of continuous discrimination;
because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise, and the nature of madness naturally subsides—this subsiding is itself Bodhi.
It is illustrated by the analogy of mixing white ox dung with sandalwood. If you cannot immediately bring this madness to rest, you must understand the two definitive meanings of cultivation:
at the gateway of the six sense faculties, break through the turbidity of the five aggregates to attain the fundamental luminous awareness and the nature free from birth and death;
using this as the mind of the causal ground, and refining it with the mutual strictness of the precepts, one will only then achieve the wondrous cause. This is the illustration.
It is like mixing yellow earth with the ten perfumes. Regarding the two methods of offering, there are again two parts: first, the offerings within the mandala;
second, the adornments outside the mandala. Now, for the first:
place a lotus flower made of gold, silver, copper, or wood at the center of the mandala; upon the flower, set a bowl; and within the bowl, first fill it with...
In the eighth month, take whatever lotus petals are available from the dew in the water; take eight round mirrors and place them in each of the directions surrounding the flower bowl.
Outside the mirrors, establish sixteen lotuses and sixteen incense burners, alternating between flowers and incense burners as a solemn adornment.
Burn only aloeswood incense in the burners so that the flames are not visible. Take white cow’s milk and place it in sixteen vessels.
One should offer milk pancakes, various sugar cakes, oil cakes, milk porridge, storax, honey, ginger, pure ghee, and pure honey, each surrounding the lotus flower sixteen times.
Outside the flowers, these are offered to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
At every mealtime, or during the middle watch of the night, one should take half a *sheng* of honey and three *he* of ghee, and set them apart before the altar.
Using a small brazier, one should prepare scented water by boiling *turuṣka* incense; with this water, one bathes the charcoal and kindles it until it blazes fiercely.
Then, casting ghee and honey into the flaming brazier, one burns them until the smoke has vanished, thereby making offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
As for the materials—gold, silver, copper, or wood—the intention is that one should act according to one's capacity; it is not necessary to be rigidly bound by these requirements.

Nevertheless, they collectively symbolize the principle of ultimate reality (*tathatā*). The lotus flower symbolizes the simultaneity of cause and effect, signifying that that which is produced precisely represents the principle that is neither cause nor effect, yet is capable of accomplishing all causes and effects.
The bowl is called the "appropriate vessel" (*saṃbhoga-pātra*), used to symbolize the mutual correspondence between phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*dharmatā*).
The dew on the lotus leaves in the eighth month symbolizes the wondrous samādhi of the Middle Way; the placement of flowers and leaves accordingly symbolizes the wondrous prajñā of the Middle Way.

Taking eight circular mirrors and placing them in their respective directions symbolizes that sentient beings inherently possess the great light of meditative concentration and wisdom, which abides securely by relying upon the Eightfold Noble Path.
The arrangement of flower bowls surrounding [the central vessel] symbolizes that wondrous wisdom is constant.

This is based on the sublime principle. The establishment of lotus flowers and incense burners outside the mirror signifies that the flowers of wisdom and the fragrance of precepts arising from the nature each require sixteen;
this represents the eightfold noble path for one's own practice and the eightfold noble path for transforming others.
The interspersed arrangement of flowers as adornment signifies that precepts and wisdom mutually serve as adornments for one another. The incense burners are used exclusively for burning [incense].
The fact that the incense sinks and does not allow fire to be seen represents the upholding of the wondrous precepts of signlessness (*animitta*).

The cakes made from white cow’s milk, along with various granulated sugars and the like, represent the flavor of the Dharma arising from meditative joy (*dhyāna-prīti*) in accordance with one's nature;

this is also the flavor of the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), each consisting of sixteen [aspects], which represents that within each individual path, one possesses both self-cultivation and [the cultivation of others].
The two kinds of transformation for others consist of the Eightfold Noble Path.
That which is offered to the Buddhas and Great Bodhisattvas symbolizes the aspiration to accord with the fruit of virtue by means of the flavor of the true path of dhyāna-joy realized within oneself.
The fact that it is consumed at midday and midnight symbolizes reliance upon the Middle Way. Honey is the essence of flowers and ghee is the essence of milk; both are the finest among flavors.
The "superior flavor" symbolizes the wondrous principle of perfect penetration (*yuantong*). The measure of "half a *sheng*" represents the number three;

as the number three is the central number, it signifies that the Middle Way must necessarily possess the three virtues (*triguṇa*). A small brazier is separately placed before the altar to symbolize the mental state associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*);
the twenty-five states of perfect penetration must all individually rely upon this as the subject of contemplation (*ālambaka*).
The *tālīśa* incense—also called white mugwort (*śvetadarbha*)—is used to boil water for bathing and charcoal for burning;

this signifies that both the primary and auxiliary practices are fully perfected. As for the casting of the *ghṛta*, honey, and other substances, it symbolizes the application of wondrous principle into wondrous wisdom, thereby causing one to directly enter the stream, lose all objective referents, and perfectly transcend the five turbidities to ascend and unite with the realm of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is the realization of the essential nature. Second, regarding the external adornments of the two altars:
one should cause banners and flowers to be suspended everywhere on the four outer sides.

Within the altar chamber, images of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all the Bodhisattvas should be arranged; specifically, Vairocana, Śākyamuni, and Maitreya should be displayed facing forward.
The great transformations of Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Avalokiteśvara, as well as Vajragarbha, should be placed at the left and right [of the central image].

Śakra, Brahmā, Ucchuṣma, and Lambodara, along with the Cāmuṇḍīs, Vighnāntaka, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Pināyaka, should be arranged on the left and right sides of the entrance. Furthermore, take eight mirrors.
Hang [the banners] suspended in the void so that they face the mirrors installed within the ritual arena, causing their forms and reflections to interpenetrate one another in layers.

As for hanging the banners, flowers, and so forth throughout, these collectively symbolize the possession of all auxiliary practices: the banners represent the Dharma-gate of the Five Repentances, and the flowers represent...
The [statues of] the Six Pāramitās represent the myriad practices; the Tathāgatas of the ten directions represent the ultimate fruition;

the images of the Bodhisattvas represent the true cause. Vairocana is the wisdom of the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya); Śākyamuni is the compassion of the Response Body (Nirmāṇakāya); Maitreya is the future teacher;
Akṣobhya—translated as "Immovable"—is the name of the Buddha of the East, representing immovability.

Ji Mítuó (智彌陀), here translated as Immeasurable Life (*Amitāyus*) and also as Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*), is the name of the Buddha of the Western Quarter; this name signifies his unconditional compassion (*nirālambana-karuṇā*).

The various great transformations of the forms of Avalokiteśvara—such as those with multiple heads, arms, and eyes—as clarified in the preceding text, represent the true master of universal penetration according to the Exoteric Teachings (*kengyō*).
Vajragarbha (*Vajragarbha*), however, is the true master of universal penetration according to the Esoteric Teachings (*mikkyō*).
The Lord is stationed at their left and right, manifesting the mutual adornment of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings. Śakra is the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
Brahmā is the lord of the First Dhyāna. Ucchuṣma is the Fire-Head Vajra; Kālarātri is the Blue-Faced Vajra;
Cundā is also a name for a Vajra; and Bhṛkuṭī is the present Three-Eyed One who holds her hair in a topknot.

The Four Heavenly Kings—Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the East, Virūḍhaka of the South, Virūpākṣa of the West, and Vaiśravaṇa of the North—as well as Piṇāka, the boar-headed messenger, and Nāga, the elephant-nosed messenger:

these external protectors collectively symbolize the power and function of subduing the heterodox and manifesting the orthodox. The eight mirrors suspended in space symbolize the fruition stage of all Buddhas.

The great samādhi and the light of wisdom are without dependence or abiding; they face the mirrors within the altar from all directions, causing their forms and reflections to interpenetrate one another in layers.
This represents the inconceivable mutual fusion of the living beings and the Buddhas, and the wondrous intersection of resonance and response.
Indeed, when the eight mirrors in space reflect the mirrors on the altar, this signifies that the fruit penetrates to the source of the cause. Within the altar, the eight...

A mirror reflects within emptiness; thus, the mirror as cause encompasses the ocean of fruition. If one fixes one’s gaze upon this point, one will know the wondrous principle that the Buddha, sentient beings, and the mind are non-different in three ways, and will thereby be able to awaken to and enter the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena.

Fundamentally, the sublime purport of this sutra does not go beyond the ten modes of contemplation (*daśa-dhyāna*). The first three and a half fascicles of the sutra explicitly discourse upon the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*);
the divine mantras of the fifth assembly esoterically elucidate the inconceivable realm; and these altar rites symbolize the inconceivable realm.
Because the mirror of emptiness and the mirror of the altar reflect while remaining eternally quiescent, they are termed "sublime" (*miao*).
Because the various adornments are profound and the environment and its inhabitants correspond to one another, it is called the Ground of Total Retention (*dhāraṇī*).

Because its essential nature is the quiescence of empty space, it is called Immovable. Furthermore, because the mirror is wondrously profound, the ground and the empty space of the adornments are both wondrously profound.
Because the adornments constitute total retention, the mirror, the ground, and the empty space are all total retention. Because the ground and the empty space are immovable, so too is the mirror.

Furthermore, both the adornments and [the state of] immovability are such because they are wondrously profound and clear (*miāozàn*). Thus, it is called "white" because of total retention (*zǒngchí*);
it is called a "parasol" (*sàngài*) because of immovability; and it is called "great" (*dà*) because it is also wondrously profound, white, and a total retention.
Since total retention is like a parasol, wondrous profundity and immovability are both like a parasol. Because immovability is great, wondrous profundity and total retention are also [great].

It is "Great" (Mahā); furthermore, because the three meanings of the Great White Parasol (*Mahāsitātapatra*) are one essence, it is "Wondrously Profound" (*Miaozhan*); because this one essence possesses the three meanings, it is "Upholding All" (*Zongchi*);
and because the three, the one, and the one-three are inconceivable, it is "Immovable" (*Budong*).

Therefore, it is said that whether expressed through the Exoteric, explained through the Esoteric, or indicated by symbols, its nature as the inconceivable realm is one and the same. One should single-mindedly cultivate the aspiration.
"Correctly arousing the Bodhicitta, reciting mantras, and practicing seated meditation" refers to calming the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

"Examining the mind and discerning views" refers to the universal penetration of phenomena (*dharmaparyeṣaṇā*). "Not conceiving oneself as a sage" is called a "wholesome state. "Recognizing what is unobstructed and what is obstructed" refers to the three gradual stages (*trīṇi kramāṇi*).
"The harmonization of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and the observance of discipline" and "the holding of mantras" refer to the "aids for remediation" (*pratipakṣa-sahāya*).
The opening of the fifty-five stages and so forth signifies knowing the sequence of positions;

practicing *dhyāna* in its proper place and awakening without delusion signifies being able to abide in patience and flow into the "middle of the middles," until reaching the fulfillment of *bodhi* and returning to non-attainment, which signifies the departure from attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
Furthermore, this very altar-dharma fully represents the ten vehicles, while the substance of the altar can represent the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*).
The lotus can symbolize the true bodhicitta; water placed within the bowl and a flower placed within the water can symbolize the skillful settling of the mind in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Eight mirrors placed at the eight directions of the altar can symbolize the "pervasive penetration of phenomena.

The floral decorations between the incense burners must not allow the fire to be seen, which can symbolize the discernment of the open and the obstructed. There should be sixteen vessels for each of the eight flavors.

The incense burner represents the harmonious practice of the *dharmaparyāya*; the fragrant water bath represents the remedial aids for awakening; the Buddha and Bodhisattva images represent the stages of the path;
the various Dharma-protecting deities on the left and right sides of the gates represent the perfection of patience;

and the eight mirrors in the void represent the detachment from attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). These ten sublime principles of the vehicle, when integrated as a whole, constitute one inconceivable reality.

This is because each vehicle mutually encompasses the others. Second, the explanation of the method of cultivation has three parts: first, the formal presentation of the practice; second, the exclusion of those who cannot achieve it; third, the clarification of the benefits obtained. Within the first part, there are two sections:

first, the seven-day practice of the path and the subsequent repentance; second, the actual cultivation. Now, for the first section: The text states: "Because the vehicles mutually encompass one another. Second, the explanation of the method of cultivation has three parts: first, the formal presentation of the practice; second, the exclusion of those who cannot achieve it; third, the clarification of the benefits obtained. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, the seven-day practice of the path and the subsequent repentance; second, the actual cultivation. Now, for the first section.
During the first seven days, one should with utmost sincerity prostrate to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and those bearing the title of Arhat;

constantly reciting mantras at the six periods of the day and night, one should circumambulate the altar with a sincere heart and practice the Way, performing one hundred and eight recitations at each session.
During the second seven days, one should single-mindedly and exclusively resolve upon the Bodhisattva vow, maintaining it without interruption according to my Vinaya.
Previously, during the third seven-day period of the instructions on making vows, they single-mindedly recited the Buddha’s *Bhadrakarātrī* mantra throughout the twelve periods of the day;

by the seventh day, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions appeared simultaneously at the point where their reflected lights intersected, and they received the Buddhas’ touching of their heads with their hands.
Regarding those who say that performing one hundred and eight circumambulations at all times signifies the accomplishment of the one hundred and eight samādhis:
some claim this refers to reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times, but this is incorrect. If one were to recite the entire mantra, the task would certainly be impossible;
yet if one were to designate only the portion from *tadyathā* onwards as the "mantra-heart," this would likewise be logically untenable upon examination.
The subsequent passage states: "If this person’s mind is dull and unable to recite or memorize [the entire text], they may carry it on their person or write it within their home;
if they were to merely count a few phrases as the *zhoushen* (heart-mantra), how could their mind be so dull as to be unable to recite or memorize them?
Furthermore, even if these few phrases alone constituted the *zhoushen*, why would there not be a single word concerning them in the sutra? Thus, one knows that... [the latter part].

The arbitrary speculations and forced interpretations of people are truly lamentable. Regarding the Vinaya, there was previously a vow-based teaching which should be identified with the ten great vows in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and so forth;

by single-mindedly upholding the Buddha’s *Pañcarakṣā* (Bhadrakarātrī) dhāraṇī, one’s every thought becomes uninterrupted, and through this secret formation of inconceivable perfuming, on the seventh day, one is able to receive [the transmission] at the point where the light of the mirror intersects.

The Buddha’s usnīṣa is the very place where the lights of these mirrors intersect; it is precisely the locus where the cause encompasses the fruit and where the states of birth and Buddhahood are equal.
If one cannot realize the principle through the phenomenon, by what means could one cause the Tathāgatas of the ten directions to appear simultaneously?
May practitioners employ this perfect and sudden sublime understanding throughout all ritual procedures and phenomena.
It would suffice to merely perform useless ascetic practices. Second, regarding the formal cultivation following repentance:
by practicing *samādhi* within the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*), one can cause the body and mind of those training in this degenerate age to become as clear and pure as lapis lazuli.
When the twenty-one days have concluded, the ritual procedures for the altar should be suspended, yet the site itself remains as it was; thus, one cultivates samādhi right here.
As for this samādhi, specifically it refers exclusively to the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, but generally it may also follow the cultivation of any one of the other faculties.
One must know that the two types of auxiliary practices mentioned previously—the precepts and the altar rituals—serve solely to assist this primary practice.
If the intent of practicing or correctly practicing is not clear, then all auxiliary practices will be in vain; one must be cautious indeed.
Second, distinguishing those who do not succeed:
Ānanda, if among this bhikṣu’s original preceptor or the ten bhikṣus in the assembly...
If there is one who is impure, such a place of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) will for the most part not achieve success.
Regarding the "ten bhikṣus," this is stated based on the maximum number, which does not exceed ten;

according to other rules of conduct, even if there are no like-minded companions, it is permissible to practice alone—it is not necessary to insist on completing the number of ten people to the point that purity cannot be attained.

Furthermore, within this context, there are two matters that exclude those who do not share [the same practice]: first, receiving the precepts improperly; second, practicing together improperly. Alas!
In the Dharma-ending age, bhikṣus have the name but lack the substance. If one seeks accomplishment, how could it be possible?
They spend their entire days discussing "perfection" (pūrṇa), yet they do not know what the bhikṣu precepts actually are. This is precisely what was stated in the preceding text.

This refers to those who, though having left home and received the full precepts as bhikṣus, mislead sentient beings by harboring doubts regarding the path of the Lesser Vehicle, thereby causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell—how lamentable!
As for the benefits obtained through the Three Knowledges (traividyā), they are as follows: [text continues].
After the three weeks, they sat in meditative retreat for one hundred days; those of keen faculties attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* without rising from their seats.
Even if the physical and mental bodies had not yet fully realized the holy fruit, they knew with certainty that their attainment of Buddhahood would not fail.

The previous statement that "not sleeping for three weeks" was a regulation requiring constant walking; the present statement that "sitting upright for a hundred days" is a regulation requiring constant sitting.
Regarding the *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer), this is the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which encompasses two meanings:

first, in terms of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it refers to the First Abode of the Initial Resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*), which is the most superior; second, according to the *Āgama* teachings...

Regarding "perfect," this refers to the initial stage of the position of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), such as that of Ānanda, who perfectly realized the *tathāgatagarbha* and suddenly attained the *dharmakāya*;

this may also be called "sharp. As for the phrase "even though his body and mind [are still bound]," it means that he has recently achieved the five grades of understanding with clear and distinct realization;
that is to say, an ordinary person still bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) is able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is certain.
He knew for certain that his attainment of Buddhahood was not in error. Second, the general conclusion:
"As you have asked regarding the establishment of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it is thus.
Second, the repeated proclamation of the Buddha-peak divine mantra (*uṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī*): First, Ānanda’s request; second, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition.
The Vow of Dharmapāla, Part One.

Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to the Buddha: "Since I left the household life, relying on the Buddha’s affectionate love and seeking much learning, I have not yet realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Consequently, I was obstructed by the evil arts of that Brahmā; though my mind was clear, my power was insufficient."
I, Svayambhū, have attained liberation through meeting Mañjuśrī; yet, although I have secretly received the power of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-uṣṇīṣa dhāraṇī-mantra, I have not yet heard it directly.

I pray that, out of great compassion, you will proclaim it once more for the sake of the practitioners in this assembly, as well as those in the future who remain within saṃsāra, so that by receiving the secret sound of the Buddha, their bodies and minds may attain liberation. At that time—
The entire assembly within the gathering all prostrated themselves, awaiting the hearing of the Tathāgata’s secret verses.

Second, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition of the two [sections]: first, the manifestation of transformation Buddhas and their recitation of the mantra; second, the description of its merits and exhortation to uphold it.
The first of the two introductory sections consists of: (1) the manifestation of the transformative display of the Dharma, and (2) the formal recitation of the divine mantra. Now, for the first:
At that time, from within the *uṣṇīṣa* on the Buddha’s crown, there surged forth a hundred jewel-lights;

from within those lights, there emerged thousand-petaled jewel lotuses, upon which transformed Tathāgatas sat amidst the precious flowers. From their crowns, ten streams of hundred-jewel radiance were emitted, and from each individual ray of light...
Throughout all places, ten *gaṅgā*-sands of Vajrapāṇis appeared, holding mountains and vajras, filling the entire realm of empty space;

the great assembly gazed upward, feeling both awe and affection, seeking the Buddha’s compassionate protection as they listened with single-minded devotion to the World-Honored One of the Unseen Crown,
the Tathāgata Emitting Light, as he proclaimed this divine mantra.
The inner topknot is the mark of the invisible crown, known as the Great Buddha-Crown (*Mahā-uṣṇīṣa*). "Hundred-jeweled radiance" symbolizes the wisdom-light of the hundred realms.
The thousand-petaled precious lotus symbolizes the cause and effect of the thousand suchnesses (*sahasra-tathatā*).

The fact that an emanation Tathāgata sits within the precious flower signifies that these causes and effects of the thousand suchnesses are precisely what all Buddhas have realized. Furthermore, the emanation Tathāgata...

This signifies that within the *dharmas* of the "Crown" (*mūrdha*), which represent the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by sentient beings, each of the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) is fully present, and within each realm there are one hundred *dharmas*.
Regarding the phrase "each and every light," this signifies that within each and every *dharma*, there is inherently the light of wisdom;
all are like adamant (*vajra*), indestructible, and capable of shattering the sands-of-the-Ganges of afflictions (*kleśa*) across the ten realms. They are all capable of...
This demonstrates the ocean-like, boundless virtues and functions of the ten realms: because he possesses majestic power that subdues, the great assembly all stands in awe;
