with thought or without thought— in such evil places, if these sons of good family read, recite, copy, transcribe, wear, or preserve [this teaching],
and make various kinds of offerings to it, they shall not be born into poverty, lowliness, or unpleasant states throughout kalpa after kalpa.
The "first kalpa" refers to the initial moment of generating the resolve and maintaining the mantra;
the "final body" refers to the single body that attains Buddhahood at the very end. These four are identical to the merits of a Buddha.
Even if these sentient beings do not personally perform meritorious deeds themselves, all the merits of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions shall be bestowed upon them.
By this means, for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—incalculable, unspeakably unspeakable—they shall always be born in the same place as the Buddhas;
their immeasurable merits will be like clusters of akṣa fruits, perfuming one another in that same location.
By practicing this without ever allowing for distraction, one is able to cause those who have broken the precepts to purify their roots of discipline;
those who have not yet attained the precepts to attain them; those who lack diligence to attain diligence; those who lack wisdom to attain wisdom;
and those who are impure to quickly attain purity. Even those who do not observe the fasts and precepts will spontaneously fulfill them.
The merit cultivated by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions was originally intended to be bestowed universally upon all sentient beings;
however, because sentient beings do not realize that the dharma-nature is of one essence, they are unable to receive it.

Now, by upholding this mantra, one comes to know that the Buddhas are the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings, and that sentient beings are the sentient beings within the minds of the Buddhas; therefore, [the merit] is attained.
Third, there is no distinction [between them], like a cluster of akṣa fruits, as they are cultivated together in the same place. Fifth, it can purify karmic obstacles.

Ānanda, when these good men uphold this dhāraṇī, even if they have violated prohibitive precepts, provided that before they received [the dharma]—that is, after they have begun upholding the dhāraṇī—they vow never to violate them again, then all their accumulated offenses of breaking the precepts, regardless of whether they are light or heavy, will be extinguished at once.

Even if one has in the past indulged in drinking alcohol, eating the five pungent roots, or various kinds of impurities, after holding this mantra, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, celestial immortals, ghosts, and spirits will no longer regard these as transgressions.
Even if one wears impure or tattered clothing, whether walking or staying still, one is entirely pure.
Furthermore, even if one does not construct a ritual altar, enter a *maṇḍala*, or practice [the rites], [one is nonetheless purified].
If one recites and upholds this mantra, it is identical in merit to entering the altar to perform the Way; there is no difference between them.

Even if one has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution or the four parājikas and eight saṃghāvaśeṣas of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, once this mantra has been recited, such heavy karma will be completely eradicated—just as a fierce wind blows apart a heap of sand—leaving not even a hair’s breadth remaining.

Question: A sūtra states that even if one has violated the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them, all transgressions of the precepts—regardless of their gravity—are extinguished at once following the recitation of this mantra.

Now, for practitioners in the末法 (mofa/dharma-ending age) who have committed violations of the precepts, must they first perform ritual repentance before reciting this mantra to be able to extinguish their offenses, or is this not necessary?
If one performs the ritual by simply maintaining single-minded concentration while reciting the mantra, can one thereby extinguish sins and realize non-arising?

Or, if the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*) is not yet clear, can one still extinguish sins by merely reciting the mantra of phenomena (*shi-zhou*)? Or must one advance simultaneously in both understanding and practice before being able to extinguish karmic obstacles and realize non-arising?
The answer is: The Sūtra states that after reciting the mantra, all transgressions are completely extinguished.
This is not merely to manifest the majestic power of the divine mantra; rather, because this mantra is itself the esoteric expression of the nature of mind, it is called the "Mantra of the Mind.
If one conceals one's transgressions and does not perform the ritual, since this is neither a direct mind nor direct speech, how could it possibly accord with the essence of the divine mantra?
It is clear that such a person cannot swiftly eliminate their karmic obstacles. As for sincere heart...

After having confessed one's transgressions, if one refrains from further committing them and single-mindedly upholds this mantra, vowing never to let it lapse or be deficient, there will be great benefit regardless of whether one understands its meaning or not.
If one understands it, one is capable of racing side by side with Ānanda; even if one does not understand it, one is still worthy of being ranked alongside Devadatta.
Furthermore, for those who do not perform the ritual procedures but merely uphold the mantra, one must know that there are three additional cases.
First, because there is fundamentally no pure master or monk toward whom one may perform the ritual of repentance, one instead confesses before an image;
this confession is equal in merit to performing the ritual before a person. Second, although there is a person toward whom one could perform the ritual, one harbors shame and fails to repent;

yet, by being able to permanently sever the continuity of transgression, one gradually diminishes the offense—though one will certainly not realize the non-arising of dharmas. Third, [the third case is omitted in the source].
Even if such a person knows how to maintain the dhāraṇī, if they still commit the aforementioned transgressions, their guilt will not be extinguished; there will merely be distant benefit.
Sixth, it can eliminate past karma:
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who, from immeasurable and incalculable kalpas ago, have committed all manner of light and heavy offenses...
If hindrances have followed one from previous lives and one has not yet had the opportunity to repent them, yet can read, recite, copy, or wear this mantra upon the body,
or place it in one’s dwelling, house, garden, or villa— then such accumulated karma will be dissolved like snow in boiling water, and before long,
one shall all attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Seventh, it can fulfill all wishes.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if there is a woman who has not yet given birth to children and desires to conceive,
if she can recollect this mantra with a sincere heart, or wear this *Sītātapatrā* (White Parasol) [dhāraṇī] upon her body, she will immediately give birth to a child endowed with merit.
Virtuous sons and daughters who seek long life shall immediately obtain long life; those who desire that their karmic rewards be swiftly fulfilled shall have them swiftly fulfilled.
It is the same for their physical life, complexion, and strength. After their lives end, they will be reborn in the lands of the ten directions according to their vows;
they will certainly not be born in border regions, among the lowly, or in inferior forms—how much less so in mixed or hybrid shapes.
Eighth, it can protect the national borders.
Ānanda, if there are lands, prefectures, counties, or villages suffering from famine, pestilence, or the calamities of war, bandits, strife, and all other such misfortunes,
one should transcribe this divine mantra and install it at the four gates of the city as well as in all [other locations].
Whether at a *caitya* or atop a *stūpa*, let all sentient beings within that land welcome this mantra, prostrate to it with reverence, and make offerings with single-minded devotion.
Let every person among the populace wear it upon their bodies or place it in their respective dwellings;
thus, all calamities and misfortunes shall be entirely extinguished. Ānanda, wherever there are sentient beings in any land—
Wherever this mantra exists, devas and nāgas rejoice; wind and rain follow their proper seasons; the five grains flourish in abundance; and the myriad people are peaceful and happy.
Furthermore, it can subdue all malevolent stars and the strange portents that arise in various directions, so that calamities and obstacles do not arise.
People suffer no untimely deaths; they are not bound by shackles, fetters, or stocks. They sleep peacefully day and night, never having evil dreams. Ānanda, this is the [Sā]... [mantra].
In this world-system, there are eighty-four thousand calamitous transformations and malevolent stars, with twenty-eight great malevolent stars as their leaders.

Furthermore, there are eight great malevolent stars that act as their sovereigns; when they manifest in various forms in the world, they can produce all manner of calamities and anomalies for sentient beings.
Wherever this dhāraṇī exists on earth, these shall all be completely extinguished within an area of twelve yojanas.
Within the boundaries of this consecrated site, all evil calamities and portents can never enter.
*Cetiya* is translated here as "a place worthy of offerings"; *dhvaja* is translated as "banner.

The twenty-eight great malevolent stars do not necessarily refer to the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), for the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* explicitly states that there are twenty-eight lunar mansions.
These are all manifestations of Bodhisattvas appearing to protect the world; they should not be called malevolent stars.
Third, the exhortation:
Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims this mantra to protect beginners and all practitioners in future ages.
Entering samādhi, body and mind are serene and you attain great peace and stability;
furthermore, no demons, spirits, ghosts, or deities, nor any karmic debts from beginningless time, calamities, or past offenses shall come to afflict or harm you.
You, along with all those among the assembly who are still in training, and all practitioners of future ages, shall rely upon my maṇḍala and maintain the precepts according to the Dharma.
If the preceptor from whom one received the precepts encounters a pure monk and does not give rise to doubt or regret regarding this mantra-heart,
yet this good son fails to attain mental penetration within this body born of his parents, then the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsely.
To seek a response from the Buddhas, one must possess four dharmas: first, one must rely upon my ritual altar; second, one must maintain the precepts according to the Dharma;
third, one must have pure and virtuous teachers and monks; fourth, one must not give rise to doubt or regret.
If these four dharmas are deficient, yet one claims that the Tathāgata speaks falsely—is this possible? III. The Protector of the Dharma States His Vow (Part Two): First, the Eight Classes of Beings.
Second, the assembly of bodhisattvas. First:

Having spoken these words, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of vajrapāṇis in the assembly simultaneously joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Buddha has taught, we shall protect with sincere heart those who thus cultivate awakening."
At that time, the Brahma King, together with Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Four Great Kings, also simultaneously prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:

"If there are indeed such virtuous persons who practice and study in this way, we shall protect them with all our hearts and utmost sincerity, ensuring that everything they do throughout their lives shall be fulfilled according to their wishes.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable yakṣa generals and rākṣasa kings.

The King of the Pūtanas, the King of the Kumbhāṇḍas, the King of the Piśācas, the Vināyakas, and all the great ghost kings and generals of spirits also joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We also vow to protect and uphold these people, causing their bodhicitta to quickly reach full perfection. Furthermore, there were immeasurable sun and moon deva-kings.

The Masters of Wind, the Masters of Rain, the Masters of Clouds, the Masters of Thunder, along with the Lord of Lightning and other annual circuit officials, as well as the retinues of all the stars, also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet within the assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“We, too, shall protect these practitioners of the path, establishing them in the site of practice so that they may attain fearlessness. Furthermore, there are immeasurable mountain deities, ocean deities, and all earth deities.”
The spirits and deities of the myriad things moving in water, on land, and through the air, together with the Wind Devas and the gods of the Formless Realm,
simultaneously prostrated themselves before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We, too, shall protect these practitioners so that they may attain Bodhi,
forever free from the interference of Māras."

The eight classes of outer protectors do not emerge from the two worlds: the Vajra-holders, Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Kings, the ghost generals, and so forth, are the lords of the *sattva-loka* (sentient world);
the sun and moon deities, up to the wind kings, are the lords of the *bhājana-loka* (receptacle world).
Even the deities of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) belong to the *sattva-loka*, yet they do not even exist within the provisional teachings.

If those who merely listen to the Dharma are thus able to protect it, how much more so those who encounter this most perfect and ultimate Dharma-gate, which enables them to make vows in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Second, the assembly of Bodhisattvas:
At that time, there were eighty-four thousand nayutas of *koṭis* of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were Vajragarbha Kings.
In the midst of the great assembly, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, as for those such as we who have long accomplished our meritorious deeds and attained Bodhi, yet do not enter Nirvana, we shall constantly follow this mantra to protect and deliver those in the final age who cultivate Samādhi and practice correctly.
World-Honored One, for those who thus cultivate the mind and seek right concentration...”
Whether they are in a place of practice (*maṇḍala*), on a walking path, or even wandering with a distracted mind through a village, we and our followers shall always follow and protect such a person;
even if Māra or Maheśvara were to seek an opportunity against them, they would ultimately find none.
As for minor spirits and deities, they shall remain ten *yojanas* away from such a virtuous person, except when they have generated the resolve for enlightenment.
O World-Honored One, for those who delight in practicing dhyāna, if an evil Māra or his retinue should come to harass such virtuous persons,
I shall shatter their heads with my precious vajra-pestle until they are like fine dust, and I shall ensure that these people’s endeavors always succeed according to their wishes.

This constitutes internal protection; he is the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lord of the World. Having long ago attained Bodhi, his three types of awakening are already perfected, and no further delusions remain.
Yet, not entering Nirvana, he remains in harmony with the nine realms of existence, never again subject to extinction.
For all Great Bodhisattvas, the practice of causes following the attainment of the fruit—driven by great compassion and great vows—is of this nature. Thus ends the *Ratnadaṇḍa*.
The "Shattering of Māra’s Head" is so named because it crushes the heterodox and manifests the orthodox Dharma as is its proper function;

whether through compassion or majesty, it is like parents, for both subduing and gathering are means of uprooting suffering; and it employs the skillful application of the dharma-gate of inherent evil.

From the fourth fascicle, "Requesting Entry into the Flowered Hall," up to this point constitutes the second major section, which demonstrates that non-arising and non-extinction are the fundamental basis.

The section on the Threefold Sublime Contemplation as the Cultivation of Causes is concluded. Third, the clarification of the stages of the threefold perfect virtues achieved through the primary and auxiliary practices, which consists of three parts:
first, the formal request; second, the granting of permission; and third, the actual exposition. Now, the first part.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We are dull-witted and fond of mere erudition;

regarding our minds, which are still subject to outflows (*āsrava*), we had not yet sought liberation. Having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, we have attained correct cultivation, and both body and mind feel a sense of joy, gaining great benefit.
World-Honored One, such is the cultivation and realization of the Buddha’s *samādhi*, though we have not yet reached *nirvāṇa*."

"What is meant by the stage of 'Dry Wisdom' (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*)? From what point do the forty-four mental states begin, and through what gradual sequence does one attain the vision of cultivation?
To what destination must one go to be said to have entered the stages (*bhūmi*)? And what is meant by the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*)?

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; the great assembly, with single-minded attention, awaited the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing up at him in rapt wonder.
Those who cultivate and realize the Buddha-samādhi proceed from beginning to end by means of the Buddha’s knowledge and the Buddha’s vision;
this refers to what are called the samādhis of the Buddha in name, up to and including the ultimate samādhi of the Buddha.
Nirvāṇa is the fruit that is ultimate, perfect, and supreme; "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-prajñā) is the cause consisting of the initial stage of contemplative practice. 4.
The "fourteen minds" refer to the stages of faith (*śraddhā*), abiding (*sthiti*), practice (*caryā*), and direction (*pratipatti*), as well as the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*).
To the question of at what gradual sequence one attains the "eye of cultivation," the answer is: it occurs after the fourteen minds and before the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-jñāna-bhūmi*).

This clearly demonstrates that these three gradual sequences are practices capable of being traversed from beginning to end, and are not restricted to the initial mind alone. The rest may be understood accordingly.
2. Praise and Approval.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
You have been able to universally [instruct] the great assembly and all sentient beings of the future age who cultivate *samādhi* and seek the Mahāyāna, from the level of ordinary persons..."
"In the Great Parinirvāṇa, I shall reveal the path of supreme, correct practice; listen attentively now, for I shall speak for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms, hollowed out their hearts, and silently received the instruction.

Third, the correct exposition has two parts: first, a general clarification of the three virtues; second, a specific demonstration of delusion and enlightenment. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, clarifying that principle transcends names and marks; second, clarifying how the true is established based on delusion. This is the first section.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, you should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and characteristics; fundamentally, there have been no worlds or sentient beings.

'Wondrous nature' refers to the essence of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the virtue of the *dharmakāya*. 'Perfectly luminous' means it illuminates and exhaustively penetrates all phenomena."
The characteristic of the realms (*dhātu*) is the virtue of *prajñā*; that which is free from all names and characteristics cannot be designated by any name nor represented by any characteristic.
Its unobstructed and unhindered function is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*).
That which is fundamentally without a world is precisely the ten realms (*daśadhātu*), wherein the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) are the very substance itself.

Fundamentally unobtainable: since the characteristics of the three lands—the land of shared residence, the land of expedient means, and the land of true retribution—are absent, the characteristics of the land of serene light are likewise unobtainable.
That "sentient beings have originally not existed" refers to the provisional names of the ten realms;
their very substance is fundamentally unobtainable. Since the names of the nine dharma-realms do not exist, [the Buddha...]
Even the name "dhātu" (element) is likewise unobtainable. Yet this wondrous nature is precisely the direct pointing to what is present before us;
it is the mind-nature of a single moment of thought that has been thus from the very beginning.
It does not mean that something was originally non-existent in the past and now exists as a delusion; rather, the single moment of thought of the present is itself inherently so.
Because it is inconceivable and its suchness is eternally constant, it is called the wondrous nature.
Because it is fundamentally vertical and horizontal, pervasive and ever-knowing, it is called perfect clarity.

Because the ten realms of existence—both the environment and the beings therein—are inherently complete within it, yet these ten realms of environment and beings cannot be described by names or characteristics, it is called being free from all names and marks.

Originally, there have been neither worlds nor sentient beings; yet, if one cannot directly realize this and return to the state prior to the kalpa of emptiness, then one is like a person who loses their head and recognizes only its reflection—this would be a profound betrayal of the Perfect Sound.

Furthermore, it should be understood that just as the three virtues were pointed out in relation to the dharmas of the mind, they are likewise pointed out in relation to the dharmas of the Buddhas and the dharmas of sentient beings.

The three virtues are all thus; for every single dharma of the Buddhas and every single dharma of sentient beings is none other than the wondrous nature’s perfect luminosity, and all are inherently free from names and marks. Reflect upon this, reflect upon this!
Second, it clarifies how the True is established based on the delusory:
because of the delusory there is birth, and because of birth there is cessation; birth and cessation are termed "delusory," while the cessation of delusion is termed "True.
These are the two designations for the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa, which represent the two transformations of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

Birth arises because of delusion; it does not mean that there is truly something born. This statement reveals that birth exists solely because of confusion and delusion, and is therefore not truly born—it is merely called "birth" due to delusion.
Since this non-birth is mistakenly perceived as birth, it is likewise not extinguished—it is merely perceived as extinction due to delusion.
Therefore, both birth and extinction are termed "delusion"; one should understand that both delusions are ultimately unattainable.

The nature is fundamentally quiescent and extinguished; it is forcibly designated as "True" and is called by the two names of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa, which refer to the two types of *parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis).
It is because sentient beings are deluded regarding this very nature of the present single thought-moment that they cling to appearances and calculate names;
this is what is meant by transforming the basis of Bodhi into afflictions and transforming the basis of Nirvāṇa into birth-and-death.
Just as water forms ice, the Tathāgata has realized that the nature of this present single thought-moment is a wondrous, perfect, and luminous nature, free from all names and marks.
This is called the transformation of the basis of afflictions into Bodhi, and the transformation of the basis of birth-and-death into Nirvana.

Just as ice becomes water, it is merely a transformation of names; fundamentally, there is no real nature [to be transformed]. Therefore, it is said that these two are designated by the name "transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti), yet there is no transformation.

Regarding the progression of the stages (*bhūmi*), there are distinctions ranging from the "transformation of names" up to the "ultimate transformation. First, opening the perfect understanding that all phenomena are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished is the "transformation of names.
The stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna-bhūmi*) is the "transformation of contemplative practice" (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).

The stage of the Ten Faiths is the "transformation of semblance. The four types of preparatory practices (*prayoga*)—the ten abodes, ten conducts, and ten directions—as well as the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth, constitute the subsequent transformations.
Awakening as a partial realization is the transformation toward the supreme fruit of wondrous awakening;

as the ultimate transformation, the nine realms of sentient beings transform their basis from afflictions to bodhi and from birth-and-death to nirvana, resulting in the distinctions of the twelve classes of beings.
When the realm of Buddhas transforms its basis from afflictions to bodhi and from birth-and-death to nirvana, there are fifty [classes].
The seven stages are distinct; Bodhi is the three wisdoms that are the illuminators, and Nirvana is the three virtues that are the illuminated.
Furthermore, Bodhi belongs to wisdom, which is the virtue of Prajñā; Nirvana belongs to cessation, which is the virtue of Vimukti.
Afflictions are themselves Bodhi, and birth-and-death are themselves Nirvana. There is nothing to be transformed; the Dharma-realm as it is in its own essence is itself the Dharma.

The virtues of the body from beginning to end are entirely the secret treasury of the three virtues; because they are neither vertical nor horizontal and are inconceivable, it is said that this "comprehensively clarifies the three virtues.
Second, the specific demonstration of delusion and awakening has two parts:

first, clarifying how delusion regarding the truth gives rise to falsehood, forming the twelve classes of beings and their inverted dharmas; second, clarifying how the extinction of falsehood is named truth, establishing the sixty stages of the sages.

Regarding the title "The Transformation of the Basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): the first part consists of two sections—the initial general exposition of the intent, and the subsequent detailed demonstration according to its characteristics. Now, for the first:
Ānanda, if you now wish to cultivate true *samādhi* and proceed directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you must first...
To recognize these two kinds of inverted causes within the world of sentient beings so that inversion no longer arises—
this is the Tathāgata’s true samādhi.
This true samādhi is precisely the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King Samādhi, wherein cultivation arises from the full nature.

Because the entirety of cultivation resides within the nature, it is called "True. To "directly proceed to the Tathāgata’s Great Nirvāṇa" means that with a direct mind and right mindfulness of True Suchness (*tathatā*), from the initial stage of naming through to the ultimate consummation, one employs the Buddha’s awakening entirely as one's own mind, remaining forever free from all signs of deviousness or circuitousness in the interim.
The two characters for "sentient beings" (*sattva*) refer, in terms of afflictions and karma, to...
Regarding the "ten realms" (*daśadhātu*) as provisional designations in contrast to *bodhi*, the two characters for "world" (*loka-dhātu*) refer to them from the perspective of karmic retribution;
this refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the ten realms as actual phenomena, namely the so-called twelve classes of beings.

When contrasted with *nirvāṇa*, these refer to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) rather than referring solely to the physical world (*bhājana-loka*). This is because mentioning the primary retribution (*pratyaya-phala*) necessarily encompasses the secondary environment (*upādāya-phala*).
Now, apart from sentient beings, there are no twelve categories; apart from the twelve categories, there are no sentient beings—and yet all exist within the state of deluded and inverted emotion.
Apart from the wisdom of Bodhi, there is no principle of Nirvana; apart from the principle of Nirvana, there is no wisdom of Bodhi.
All of this ultimately derives from the essence of the non-arising of wondrous awakening. Indeed, the principle of inversion is itself [the truth].
Sentient beings perceive birth within that which is unborn; by realizing this principle of non-birth, one attains what is called "non-birth as a name.
This non-birth as a name is the true samādhi, and when it reaches ultimate non-birth, it is the ultimate true samādhi.
Second, distinguishing the characteristics to provide an exposition [of the two truths]. First, clarifying sentient beings.
The second part clarifies the perversion of the world; this is the first.

Ānanda, what is meant by the perversion of sentient beings? Ānanda, because the nature of the mind is luminous and the luminous nature of the mind is perfect, one takes that luminosity as a basis to give rise to a "nature.
From this, deluded vision arises. Out of that which is ultimately non-existent, there is established that which is ultimately existent. This existence and its objects [constitute perversion].
That which is not the cause of causes, nor the abode of abodes, is fundamentally without root. Based upon this non-abiding, the worlds and all sentient beings are established.
They are deluded regarding their own original, perfect luminosity, thereby giving rise to what is false. This false nature has no substance and has nothing upon which it relies.

When one seeks to return to the truth, that which is sought as "truth" is already not true; the nature of True Suchness is not something that can be attained by seeking it back, for such a pursuit merely results in the manifestation of a false characteristic.
Neither arising nor abiding, neither mind nor dharmas, they arise from one another; the power of arising brings forth illumination, which perfumes and forms karma.
Through the mutual resonance of shared karma, there is the cause of karmic response, wherein phenomena cease and phenomena arise. It is for this reason that sentient beings exist in delusion.

This fully elucidates the causes of delusion for sentient beings within the nine realms. If one refers to the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is free from names and transcends all marks, then the ten realms are none of them "ten realms.
If one refers to the provisional names and provisional marks that arise according to conditions—whether defiled or pure—then the ten realms are all designated as "sentient beings.
However, it is only the nine realms that, by deviating from the true nature at this moment, are termed "deluded beings."
The text states: "Only those born [in this world] who perfectly accord with the sublime principle of the Buddha may be called non-perverted sentient beings. This passage consists of three sections.

The first, from "By virtue of their nature they clarify the mind" to "and all sentient beings," generally clarifies the causes of perversion within the nine realms, as described in the first fascicle:
"All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have undergone various forms of perversion."

1. "The same as" (Section Two): From "Following delusion regarding the fundamental perfect brightness" to "completely forming non-characteristics," this specifically clarifies the causes of the inversions of the three vehicles, demons, and externalists, which is like what was stated in the first fascicle:
"Various practitioners of cultivation cannot achieve unexcelled Bodhi," and so forth. 2. "From neither arising nor abiding" to "therefore there are sentient beings' inversions" (Section Three).

This section on the fetters clarifies the characteristics of perversion within the nine realms, similar to what was stated in the first fascicle regarding how "all arise from not knowing the two kinds of roots," and so forth.
In the opening lines, the phrase "the nature is inherently luminous" corresponds to what is said in the fourth fascicle, "the nature-awareness is necessarily luminous.
The phrase "due to luminosity, the nature is manifested" corresponds to what is called "delusively taking luminosity as awareness."

"The nature of deluded perception arises" (yè xìng wàng jiàn shēng) refers to what is called "establishing an object based on the cause of illumination; once the object is falsely established, your deluded subjectivity arises.
"From ultimate non-existence" (cóng bìjìng wú) refers to what is called "within the absence of sameness and difference, a blazing diversity is formed.
"Not due to a cause for the cause" (fēi yīn suǒ yīn) refers to what is called "being deluded regarding the original lack of cause. This is what is meant by "only" (zhǐ).

Because the mind of original true luminosity is by nature inherently bright and perfect, it possesses only the virtue of its fundamental nature (*xing-de*) but not yet the virtue of cultivation (*xiu-de*).
Consequently, while this luminosity manifests from within the nature, deluded views suddenly arise within that very nature;
thus, from ultimate non-existence, one falsely constructs the appearance of ultimate existence. However, the substance of this "existence" is itself void.
Delusion is like flowers in the sky or objects in a dream; it is truly not caused by any cause.

Even the present state of that which dwells and the characteristics of that which is dwelt upon are likewise utterly devoid of a fundamental basis. It is merely based on this non-dwelling that worlds and all sentient beings are established.
This explanation of sentient beings' inversions while simultaneously addressing the world precisely reveals the nature of the world.
The realms and sentient beings exist solely because of this single delusion; there is no second dharma.

The meaning of the subsequent passage is that delusion regarding the essence of the fundamentally luminous nature gives rise to the false. Therefore, the nature of falsehood has no inherent substance of its own, nor does it have anything else upon which to rely.
Those Bodhisattvas of the provisional vehicles and those of the two vehicles, wishing to abandon this falsehood, [proceed as follows].

Furthermore, if even those who seek to restore the true by means of the true have already departed from the nature of True Suchness (tathatā), how much more so for Māras and non-Buddhists who seek restoration through that which is not true—does this not result all the more in the formation of non-characteristics?
The third intention reveals that the dharmas of the mind, in their arising and abiding, are fundamentally without self-nature;
thus, for all sentient beings, as well as for those of the three vehicles, Māras, and non-Buddhists, there is herein neither arising nor abiding.
It is neither mind nor dharmas, yet through false vision there arise birth, abiding, mind, and dharmas. From this delusion, they successively give rise to the power of birth;

this power of birth manifests and perfumes [the seeds] to form karma. Through the mutual resonance of shared karma, there is extinction and birth, and thus the sentient beings of the nine realms fall into perversion.
From that which is non-existent, they falsely perceive existence; indeed, it is not birth at all.
To falsely perceive the existence of birth, up to and including the existence of non-dharmas where there are no dharmas—this is precisely delusion (*moha*).

That the power of birth is manifested is due to delusion giving rise to karma (*karma-samutthāna*). That beings with similar karma respond to one another is due to karma summoning its retribution (*vipāka*).
If, within the nature of dharmas—which is without birth, without abiding, without mind, and without phenomena—one falsely perceives similarity, [this is likewise delusion].
Dwelling within the three realms, the mind-states of birth and abiding are the dharmas of delusion;

these are the outflowing karmas of wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable deeds, perfumed by the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), which give rise to the birth and death of the shared realm of segmented existence (*sahā-loka*).

If, within the nature of dharmas—which is unborn, non-abiding, mindless, and devoid of phenomena—one falsely perceives the mind-states of birth and abiding in the provisional three realms, this is perfumed by the afflictions of the dust-like [delusions] (*rajas-kleśa*).
When one accomplishes the karma of the universally true and untainted, it evokes the extinction of birth through the transformation of means (*upāya-nirmāṇa*).

If, within the nature of dharmas—which is non-arising, non-abiding, mindless, and without phenomena—one falsely perceives the existence of real retribution and the mental states of birth and abiding in the triple world, this is the result of being perfumed by ignorance;
it is evoked by karma that is both tainted and untainted, resulting in the extinction of real retribution and transformation.

Furthermore, not knowing that the mind-states of birth, abiding, and dwelling within the three lands—the Land of Common Residence, the Land of Expedient Means, and the Land of Real Reward—are in their very essence empty constitutes the affliction of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);
not knowing that these various provisional names for the mind-states of birth, abiding, and dwelling within the three lands constitute the affliction of dust-like sands (*rajas-kleśa*);

and not knowing that the entire substance of these mind-states of birth, abiding, and dwelling within the three lands is the Middle Way constitutes the affliction of ignorance (*avidyā-kleśa*). Thus it is said.
Finally, because karma arises from afflictions and retribution is summoned by karma, there are the inverted characteristics of sentient beings in the nine realms.
Second, the explanation of the inversion of the world has two parts: first, designating the name based on its cause; second, explaining its characteristics based on its result.
First: Ānanda, what is meant by the inversion of the world? It is that which exists as having something belonging to it, wherein fragmented delusions arise;

because of this realm, there is established that which is not a cause yet is taken as a cause, and that which is not a dwelling yet is taken as a dwelling. Because of this, there is constant flux and instability, and thus the world of the three periods of time is formed.
The four directions harmonize and intermingle through transformations, forming the twelve classes of beings. Thus, the world arises from motion there is sound;
from sound, form; from form, fragrance; from fragrance, touch; from touch, taste; and from taste, one perceives phenomena (*dharma*).
These six types of deluded conceptualizations constitute the nature of karma; therefore, the twelve divisions revolve by means of this cycle. For this reason...
The world of sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles undergoes twelve transformations and returns to a single cycle;
driven by this wheel of inverted appearances, there exist worlds of egg-birth, womb-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth; those with form and those without form;
those with perception and those without perception; those that are neither with nor without form; and those that are neither with nor without perception.
This is precisely a restatement of the aforementioned cause of the delusion of sentient beings as the characteristic of the delusion of the world.
Previously it was said: "That which exists here has no root whatsoever—neither cause nor caused, neither abode nor abiding.
Now, by taking the single phrase "that which exists here" from above, it constitutes the "world" (*loka*); and by taking the three phrases "neither cause nor caused," it constitutes the "delusion."

Thus, worldly discourse arises as false existence; where there is such existence, the forms of segmented divisions falsely come into being, and from this, the boundaries of the four directions are established.
Since this false existence does not arise from a cause, it has no locus;
because it has no locus, it further flows on without abiding, and from this, the characteristics of the three periods of time are formed. Thus it is.
When these three periods of time and those four directions harmonize and interpenetrate one another, through this transformation, sentient beings are formed into twelve categories.
Therefore, in a single thought-moment, due to the non-awakening of ignorance, the mind moves; as it moves, there is sound;
with sound, the six sense objects—form, fragrance, touch, taste, phenomena, and so forth—are suddenly complete, and chaotic thoughts proliferate, leading to delusion.
Karma is the root of action, and retribution is the basis of karma; from retribution, delusions arise again, like the clusters of the akṣa fruit, which are forever inseparable.
To discuss this from a remote perspective, the source of movement lies in the beginningless past; to discuss it from a proximate perspective, it is simply the present thought.

When not a single thought arises, the six delusions naturally cease. Thus, the triad of delusion, karma, and suffering is like flowers vanishing into the void; therefore, they are called "perversions."

That which is non-arising is the Tathāgata’s true samādhi. Form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena arise in mutual dependence, mutually contain one another, and mutually give rise to one another.
Taking sound as the primary example, it necessarily encompasses all six sense objects;

this is likewise true for form and smell. Regarding the sense objects in relation to the sense faculties, they are termed the twelve divisions, which exhaustively encompass the twelve categories of beings.

These transformations constitute one cycle within the nature of karma; therefore, among the twelve classes of beings, each class mutually contains the others and each class mutually gives rise to the others.

Thus, from the stage of Equal Enlightenment downward, as long as even a fraction of subtle ignorance has not been severed, there remains within each of these twelve classes a portion of the cause for rebirth that has not yet been exhausted. Therefore, these twelve...
The inverted characteristics of the world of rebirth are the direct opposite of Great Nirvana. This is precisely what is meant by:

when deluded, one turns toward Nirvana as being dependent upon birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), whereby there exist the segmented birth-and-death of the hells up to the transformational birth-and-death of Bodhisattvas;
when awakened, one turns toward birth-and-death as being dependent upon Nirvana, whereby there exists the Nirvana of names and designations.

This continues up to ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, although the characteristics of the twelve classes of beings described in the subsequent text may at first glance seem to pertain only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
they must nonetheless be explained by referring to both phenomena and principle, as well as to both the internal and external realms, so that—
through the successive layers of the twelvefold single-and-multiple combinations in the later text— the wondrous enlightenment may fully realize the Unsurpassed.
The purport of the Way is unity. Second, the explanation of the characteristics by way of the fruit has two parts: first, the specific clarification; second, the general summary.

First, the specific clarification has twelve sections, beginning with the characteristics of egg-birth and ending with the characteristics of non-ideation. Now, the first [section]: The characteristics of egg-birth. (Up to: The twelfth, the characteristics of non-ideation. Now, the first:

Ānanda, because the world is characterized by the delusory cycle of saṃsāra and the inversion of movement, the combination of vital energies (*vāyu*) gives rise to eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking;
thus there exist egg-born beings, such as *kalala* embryos, who circulate through the lands as fish,
birds, turtles, and snakes, filling every category.
The "world" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as substantial dharmas. "Vanity" refers to delusion (*moha*). "Movement" refers to karma (*karman*).
"Vital energy," along with the retributions of flying and sinking, refers to the fruit of maturation (*vipāka*). Because the egg-born are produced solely through thought, they are called "vain.

Since delusion is the root of karma and its retribution, it is termed "saṃsāra. Because thought is characterized by much agitation, it is called "movement. Since karma must necessarily be induced [by thought], it is described as "toppling."
The inverted egg [conception] occurs through the mingling of vital energies (*vāyu*), such as when the male calls from upwind and the female from downwind; hence it is called "harmonious union.

Energies are formed and each arises from the transformations induced by eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*); thus it is said that there are eighty-four thousand "flying and sinking" disordered thoughts.
*Kalala*—translated here as "coagulated mucus"—is the initial stage of birth for those born from eggs.
Birds are the category of those that fly; fish, turtles, and snakes are all categories of those that sink. "Pervading" means vertically exhaustive and horizontally universal.

To explain this according to its meaning: the delusions of *darśana-heya* (delusions abandoned by insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions abandoned by cultivation), the delusions as numerous as motes of dust, and the delusions of ignorance—these are the very roots of the two cycles of transmigration, *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence) and *pariṇāmi-bhava* (transformative existence).
They are movements of evil, movements of good, movements within the out-flowing (*āsrava*) realm, and movements within the non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*) realm.

Movement toward either of the two extremes is entirely the mark of inverted karma. The energetic constituents of humans and animals; those of male and female; those of the realms of form and formlessness;
those of meditative concentration; those of the skillful means for nirvana; those of the supernormal powers of provisional emergence;

and those of the Buddha-nature of the Middle Way—all these, when scattered and disordered, result in flight; when dull and obscure, they result in sinking. Insight and wisdom lead to flight; stillness and concentration lead to sinking.

The contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is "flying," while true cessation (*bhūtasthiti*) is "sinking. The contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) is "flying," while skillful means that accord with conditions (*upāya-anuvidhāna-sthiti*) is "sinking.
The middle way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) is "flying," while the cessation of dualistic discrimination (*anta-dvaya-vikalpa-sthiti*) is "sinking.

The shell of the egg of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa-aṇḍakośa*), the shell of the egg of *pāramitā*-obstructions (*rajas-aṇḍakośa*), and the shell of the egg of ignorance (*avidyā-aṇḍakośa*): in brief, all nine realms are termed "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*); only the Buddha breaks [this shell].
Within the concentration of the shell of ignorance, wisdom and samādhi are equal; neither flying nor sinking, delusive thoughts are forever extinguished.
The habitual shadows of conditioning are stilled and motionless, free from inversion, truly and eternally abiding. It is not born from an egg.

Furthermore, because the Buddha has forever severed the subtle causes for birth from an egg, he is able to manifest birth from an egg within the nine realms. Moreover, birth from an egg is characterized by inversion.
The inversion is fundamentally non-arising; by penetrating this principle of non-arising, one proceeds from the severance of names to ultimate severance.

Therefore, there are fifty-five stages on the true path of Bodhi. Furthermore, sentient beings of the nine realms do not know that the essence of all phenomena is illusory, mistakenly taking them to be real;
for this reason, they are unable to exercise sovereign power through supernatural transformations.

Because the mind cannot move the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) nor harmonize with it, the ten realms manifested from one's own mind appear as various forms of flight and descent according to their respective elemental constituents.
Only the Buddha thoroughly realizes the illusory nature of these phenomena and skillfully manifests the shifting transformations of the dharma-realm;
he takes the nine realms to be the Buddha-realm and the Buddha-realm to be the nine realms, thereby bringing them into harmony.
Within the nine realms combined, the portion of the Buddha-realm manifests the flying and sinking of the Buddha-realm;
within the Buddha-realm, the portions of the nine realms manifest the flying and sinking of the nine realms. Therefore, only the Tathāgata is called the ultimate;
he is the ultimate egg-born being, the ultimate fish, the ultimate bird, the ultimate tortoise, and the ultimate snake—the one ultimate.
The ultimate consummation of all things reveals the true nature of egg-birth, which is precisely the path to attaining Buddhahood:
delusory saṃsāra is the true nature of prajñā; the movement of inversion is the true nature of liberation; and the rising and falling of the vital breath (prāṇa) is the true nature of the dharmakāya.
Furthermore, because delusion, movement, and the rising and falling of the breath are all themselves the Middle Way, they are so named.

Because the wondrous nature is identical with form, it is called "perfectly luminous" (*yuanming*); because it is identical with the provisional (*jia*), it is free from all names and marks (*nāman-lakṣaṇa*).

When this true nature is thus revealed—whether as a partial revelation, a complete revelation, or even the ultimate revelation that constitutes wondrous enlightenment—the subsequent sections should be understood accordingly;
they will not be explained in full here. Second, the characteristic of birth from a womb.
Due to the causes of the world’s defiled cycle of rebirth and the perversions of desire, eighty-four thousand transverse and vertical disordered thoughts are combined and nourished;
because of this, there exist the stages of the embryo, the *arbuda*, and so forth, as beings transmigrate through various lands—
humans, animals, dragons, and seers— filling all categories.
The cause of the womb is delusion arising from emotional attachment, which is termed "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*). The entanglement of craving and affection, driven by karma, is termed "desire.

The mingling of semen and blood is termed "nourishment and obstruction" (*pu-tan*); this refers to the *arbuda* stage, translated here as "blister," which is the appearance of the gradual differentiation of the embryo and ovum during the second week.

"Human and Immortal" refers to the vertical orientation, while "Beast and Dragon" refers to the horizontal; in terms of their underlying meaning, these represent the defilements of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*).
The dust-like sands of ignorance, the defilements of male and female desire-love, the flavor of dhyāna-desire-love, the love of partial truth, the love of supernatural powers,

the love of the *butzhong* (limited-middle) [truth], the nourishment provided by semen and blood, the nourishment provided by the ten links [of dependent origination], the nourishment provided by the flavor of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas,

the nourishment provided by the flavor of dharmas for emerging into the provisional, the nourishment provided by the flavor of the Middle Way, and the three virtues within the nature— [all these are nourished].

The middle three virtues cultivated horizontally serve as the vertical cause, while the middle three virtues [attained] vertically serve as the vertical fruit; the lower three virtues are horizontal—these are what are to be severed.

Just as there is no wisdom outside of Suchness and no Suchness outside of wisdom, taking the dharmas of affliction as the wife of joy and the flavor of the Dharma of the Three Truths as the nourishment for the six senses, this "constancy" is precisely what is horizontal.
Furthermore, the constant six [elements] form the vertical axis; this is what is revealed here. Third is the characteristic of moisture-born beings.
Due to the world’s attachment to the inverted realms of saṃsāra, the combination of warmth produces eighty-four thousand types of chaotic and inverted thoughts.
Because of this, there exists the moist characteristic of *piśāca* (or *pīśita*), which flows and turns within the lands, containing crawling and wriggling creatures.

Their kind fills [the world]. Moisture causes them to conjoin through mutual attraction; this attraction is called "clinging" (*abhiniveśa*). To attach oneself to power and hasten toward influence is called "karma. To move toward fire and water in mutual formation is called "heat" (*uṣman*).
That which is pursued without fixed direction is called "turning back and forth" (*viparyāsa*). *Bī* (蔽) refers to "flesh"; here it is translated as "soft flesh" (*mṛdu-māṃsa*).

This is the initial characteristic of moisture-born birth (*saṃsvedaja*). To summarize the meaning: the attachments of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); the attachments of the sands of phenomena and ignorance (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*); the realms of existence, emptiness, the extreme, and the middle;
the stage of warmth in the shared realm (*sahabhū-nikāya-sabhāga*), the stage of warmth in the provisional means (*upāya*), and the stage of warmth in the true retribution (*bhūtaphala*).

Wherever there is turning away toward something, there must be something covered and turned away from. The moisture that causes rebirth through view and thought is the moisture of the sands of phenomena and ignorance.

The moisture that arises is called the characteristic of dampness; this is what is to be severed. Only when one has thoroughly exhausted the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena can one then engage in attachment.
Take any single phenomenon—into it all phenomena enter, and they do not transcend this entry. Within all phenomena there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss.
Skillfully observing them is like drilling wood to produce fire: once one intends to ignite the wood, the true [fire] appears.

The characteristics of warmth within the conventional truth and the characteristics of warmth within the ultimate truth: the ten realms are simultaneously present, which constitutes overturning the ten realms rather than covering them.
When the mind flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* and connects with the Dharma-stream of the Buddha-Tathāgata, this is called the characteristic of moisture;
this is what is manifested. Fourth, the characteristic of transformational birth (*upapāduka*).

Due to the causes of the world’s shifting cycles and the provisional nature of inverted perceptions, the conjunction of contact gives rise to eighty-four thousand types of new and old disordered thoughts;
because of this, there exist transformed beings, *kalala* embryos, those that flow through lands, those that undergo metamorphosis,
and those that fly— such species fill the world.

That which was non-existent suddenly comes into being, its appearance altered and its form changed; all such instances are termed "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). Transformation that responds through separation and delusion is termed "change.

That which repeatedly turns back and forth without reality is termed "provisional" (*prajñapti*). That which follows whatever it encounters is termed "contact" (*sparśa*). Because it is what is newly pursued, it is what is shed.
*Kalala*—here translated as "hard flesh"—is the initial phase of transformational birth (*upapāduka*). This is explained in terms of... [text ends].

"Meaning" refers to the transformation of views and thoughts; the transformation of the *rajas* (dust-like) and *avidyā* (ignorance); the formation of provisional continuities; the provisional of mutual dependence; the provisional of cohabitation;
all contacts of the provisional stage; all contacts of the stage of true retribution; and all contacts within and beyond the realms.

These are transmitted and transmitted anew, and transmitted and transmitted as old—whether through karmic transformation, vow-transformation, or mind-transformation. This is that which is to be severed.
The unchanging following conditions is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*); all is provisional, and the three truths are all provisional.
In the Great Parinirvāṇa, one touches the eight masteries; [all] is manifested by the mind alone. Taking the new cause as the mind, it constitutes the substance;
this extends even to the unmanifested transformations—this is what is revealed. Fifth, the characteristics of form and color.

Due to the obstruction of the world’s causes of stagnation and the cycle of rebirth, and because of inverted views, these combine and coalesce to form eighty-four thousand types of turbid and radiant deluded thoughts.
Consequently, there exist material forms—*kalala* in their various stages—that circulate through the lands, manifesting as auspicious or inauspicious spiritual potencies;
such beings fill the world.
The delusion of stubborn attachment to false conceptualization is called "obstruction" (*pratigha*); karmic activity that is stagnant and fails to flow through is called "hindrance" (*āvaraṇa*);

and the brilliance of refined clarity is called "attachment" (*abhiniveśa*). Above, the sun, moon, and stars are termed auspicious or calamitous; below, oyster pearls and fireflies are termed portents or omens—all of these are termed "possessing form.
To explain this according to its meaning: the objects of the views and thoughts that cause obstruction are the *dharmas*.

The sands [of phenomena] are characterized by ignorance, obstruction, the outflows (*āsrava*), the hindrance of partial emptiness, the hindrance of the two extremes, and the manifestation of illusory forms, the manifestation of *nirvāṇa*, and the manifestation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Therein lie tainted form (*sāsrava-rūpa*) and untainted form (*anāsrava-rūpa*), both of which are like illusory forms;

these are what are to be severed. Their nature and characteristics are eternally abiding, yet they are termed "obstructions" because they hinder the evil realms, obstruct the path, and block the outflows.

Obstructing the two extremes is called "obstruction"; the manifestation of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the manifestation of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and the manifestation of the middle truth (madhyama-satya) is called "clinging.
This extends even to true, good, and wondrous forms; these are what is manifested. Sixth are the six formless characteristics (arūpa-lakṣaṇa).
Because the world dissolves due to the delusions and inversions of saṃsāra, the conjunction of darkness forms eighty-four thousand thoughts of obscured and chaotic confusion;
thus there exist the formless *kalala* realms of transmigration, where beings are filled with the nature of empty dispersion and sinking dissolution.
To loathe existence and cling to emptiness, to extinguish the body and return to non-existence, and to harbor delusions—these are called "dissipation.

To be confused by outflows and lack the hearing of the Way, failing to penetrate the principle of emptiness, such karmic activity is called "delusion. Relying on the darkness and obscurity of empty names, it is called "darkness.

Because it cannot be seen or heard, it is called a "skandha" (aggregate). Its characteristics are stubborn and dull, thus it is called *kalala*. It disperses and sinks into emptiness; it does not specifically refer to non-existence.

The deities of space (*ākāśa-devatā*) residing in all places—such as the four heavens of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), great rivers, valleys, remote and perilous regions, and dark places—are all of this same category.
To explain the underlying meaning: they are those who dissipate form and color; who dissipate *nirvāṇa*; who dissipate the two truths;

who are deluded regarding true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*); who are deluded regarding wondrous existence (*miao-you*); who are deluded regarding the Middle Way; and who are mired in stubborn emptiness, obscure and partial emptiness, or mere darkness.

The lack of all dharmas within the middle is what is to be severed; it is the dispersal of the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the dispersal of the *rajas* and *sahasrāra* ignorance (*avidyā*).
It is like a magician who can delude all and entice his children to place them within the secret treasury.
I, too, shall before long enter therein myself. This meaning of the secret treasury is like darkness, and it is also called the "First."
The emptiness of meaning (*artha-śūnyatā*) is that which is revealed. Seventh is the characteristic of having perception (*sa-saṃjñā-nimitta*).
Because the world’s causes consist of the revolving shadows of delusive appearances and inverted views, the combination of memories forms eighty-four thousand latent knots of chaotic thoughts;
thus, there exist those with perception, such as *kalala* (embryonic stages), who transmigrate through lands of spirits, ghosts, and numinous essences.
These types fill the space;
they seem to exist yet are as if non-existent, and their delusive name is "Wangxiang" (the Unseen). Tracing footprints and clinging to shadows, their karmic name is "Youyin" (Shadowy Darkness).
Within the hidden depths, they falsely construct appearances, all of which are formed by the power of commonality (*sabhāgatā*) and false recollections and conceptions; thus they are named "Names."
To recollect that there is no substantial form, but only the appearance of perception (*saṃjñā*):

according to this principle, one sees the phantom-like dust of deluded thoughts, the phantom-like ignorance as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the shadows of tainted karma, the shadows of untainted karma, and the shadows of karma from the two extremes all coexisting within the expedient means of recollective thought.
One recollects the true recompense through this recollective thought; this is what is to be severed. This is the attainment of the principle.
Wisdom is named "the phantom-like" (*wangxiang*); all phenomena within the dharma-realm are like shadows. The ocean of perfect universal knowledge arises from the mind and its perceptions;
this is termed "recollection," and it is that which is manifested here. Eighth is the characteristic of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā-lakṣaṇa*).
Due to the causes of worldly ignorance, dullness, cyclic existence, delusion, and inversion, these combine with stubbornness to form eighty-four thousand parched and disordered thoughts;
thus there exist the realms of the "unconscious kalala," where spirits are transformed into earth,
wood, metal, and stone, such that their kinds fill the world.

The delusion that fails to comprehend the principle of the Truths is called "dullness" (*yùdùn*); the stubborn adherence to obstructive karma is called "delusion" (*chī*). That which is characterized by obstruction and ignorance is called "obstinate" (*wán*).

Although it is said to be withered and parched, it is still a state of distracted conceptualization, because there are no phenomena external to the mind; all phenomena are but the mind itself. In terms of their specific meanings:

the dullness of *duṣṭhula-kleśa* (afflictions) and *darśana-heya-kleśa* (afflictions abandoned through insight) constitutes "dullness," while the dullness of *pāramitā-saṃkhyeya-kleśa* (afflictions of the dust-like sands) and *avidyā* (ignorance) constitutes "obstinate."
There is the delusion of outflows (*sāsrava-moha*), the delusion of partial emptiness (*ekānta-śūnyatā-moha*), and the delusion of the two extremes (*antadvaya-moha*).

Because the three truths (*triratna*) and the flow of the Dharma (*dharmadhātu*) do not moisten these states—which are characterized by the stubbornness of fragmented existence (*paricchinna*) and the stubbornness of transformation (*pariṇāma*)—they are called "withered. These are what are to be abandoned.

Not discriminating among any phenomena is termed "dullness" (*jaḍa*); having nothing to grasp or reject is termed "delusion" (*moha*). The principle of the three truths is eternally quiescent and unchanging.
The names "stubborn delusion," "karma," and "suffering" signify that these three no longer give rise to fear; this is what is meant by "withered.

Ninth, there are no material characteristics, because due to the world's causal interdependence, cyclic existence, falsehood, and inversion, they combine with defilement to form eighty-four thousand [afflictions].
Because of such disordered thoughts, there exist non-material forms that take on material characteristics as *kalala* (embryonic stages), flowing through the lands;
these include various sea-squirts and similar creatures that use shrimp as their eyes, filling the world in great numbers.

Skillful deceit and false pretenses delude by relying on names and appearances; they possess no reality. Activity is called "deceit" (*māyā*), and that which is grasped as foul and impure is called "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*).

These two are of different natures yet serve as mutual causes and conditions for one another. They are like the *siphonophora* (water-mother), which takes sea foam for its body and the shrimp for its eyes;
originally it has no color of its own, but depends on other things to manifest color, being unable to function independently.

Regarding the mutual dependence of things for utility: the *siphonophore* (water-mother) gains the ability to move by means of the shrimp, while the shrimp obtain food by relying on the *siphonophore*.
Thus, it is said that "dependent and causal deluded thoughts" arise. In terms of doctrinal meaning: the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are mutually dependent;

emptiness and existence are mutually dependent; the center and the periphery are mutually dependent. Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are like illusions, they are false; because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not truly real, they are also false. Within the realms, these are defiled.
The defilements and so forth outside the realms are what is to be severed. The "box of principle" and the "lid of wisdom" are called mutually dependent phenomena;
that which lacks a real nature of self or other is called a false dharma-body. The harmony of merit and virtue is like mercury mixed with pure gold;
therefore, it is called "defiled. This is what is revealed. Ten: non-forms do not exist as signs.

Due to the nature of inverted delusion that causes beings in the world to draw one another into the cycle of saṃsāra, mantras combine to form eighty-four thousand types of disordered thoughts of summoning;
because of this, there exist those who are neither of material nor immaterial form, such as *kalala* and *arbuda*, who flow through various lands,
producing curses and spells that fill every realm.
The mutual incitement of delusions is called "mutually inducing habituation" (*xi*). When these form seeds and karma, they are termed "nature" (*xing*).

When names are invoked by means of sounds, they are called "mantras. It is not that they were originally formless; rather, one now curses them to become formless while secretly invoking their function. Regarding the underlying meaning:
the views and thoughts mutually induce one another, as do the *cīra-saṃsāra* (dust-like) afflictions and ignorance; thus, both evil natures and good natures exist.

The nature of outflows (*āsrava*), the nature without outflows (*anāsrava*), worldly spells (*laukika-mantra*), and world-transcending spells (*lokottara-mantra*)—these are that which is to be severed.

The three vehicles, the drawing forth of the Great Vehicle, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the revealing cause (*jñāna-pratyaya*), the unsurpassed spell, and the peerless spell—these are that which is to be revealed.
(11) The characteristic of non-perception (*asaṃjñā-lakṣaṇa*).
Because the world arises from the convergence of causes with delusive saṃsāra and inverted views, various combinations form eighty-four thousand types of reciprocal and chaotic thoughts.
Thus, there exist the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages where non-existent perceptions and existent perceptions combine to form thought; these flow and circulate through the realms of existence.
Among them, creatures such as the *pulu* (maggots) are formed through the transformation of different substances, and their kind fills all places.
The second is the false conjunction that gives rise to what is called the "conjoined false nature. Its essence is empty and false, and its karma is termed "deception" (*wang*).
Because this and that are not the same, it is termed "difference" (*yi*). Because they are fundamentally different yet are made identical through mutual inversion, it is termed "inverted confusion.
The *puluo* is the mulberry worm; various bees with slender waists cannot raise their own offspring, so they take [other insects], incant over them, and before long they become [bees].
Originally there was no perception of a bee, yet now suddenly the perception of a bee has arisen. To explain this according to its meaning:

the delusive objects of views and thoughts, the sands of afflictions, and the delusive conditioned dharmas of ignorance are all non-existent; even the unconditioned dharmas are likewise non-existent. Within the realm, they have a different substance;
outside the realm, they have a different substance—this is that which is to be severed. These views and their conditions are fundamentally Bodhi.
Because the essence of wondrous purity and clarity is conjoined with deluded vision, the conditions of seeing, and the perceived forms—like flowers in the sky—it is called "entrapment" (wang).
Because the natures of the twelve dharma-realms are fused into a single nature, it is called "conjunction" (he).
Because all sentient beings of the nine realms are designated as disciples, it is called "interchangeability" (huihu). These are what is revealed. Twelve. Not.
This is the characteristic of non-perception.

Due to the world’s cycle of enmity and harm, and because of the perversion of killing, these factors combine to produce the strange notion that there are eighty-four thousand who perceive their parents as food;
thus, there exists this characteristic of non-perception, wherein the *kalala* (embryonic stage) of non-perception flows through the lands.
Just as the earth-owl and its kind take clods of earth for their offspring, and the "broken-mirror" bird takes the fruit of poisonous trees to raise its young—
once the offspring are grown, both parents meet their end by being eaten by them— and such creatures abound everywhere.

To harbor resentment and plot harm while being deluded is called "enmity and injury. To take another's life is called the karma of "killing," which is named "cruelty. Constantly harboring poisonous thoughts is named "monstrosity.
Regarding the fruit as a child, it is not that there is no thought of a child; yet for the child to eat its own parents is something beyond the reach of one's imagination.
In terms of their meaning, the enmity and injury of views and afflictions (*kleśa*) are like the dust and sands [of the Ganges], while the enmity and injury of ignorance (*avidyā*) are even more so.
In the realm of the cohabitation of the principle of killing, one partakes of the "strange food" of the Father of Ultimate Truth and the Mother of Emptiness-Wisdom;

in the realm of skillful means, one partakes of the "strange food" of the Father of Conventional Truth and the Mother of Path-Wisdom; and in the realm of the true reward, one partakes of the "strange food" of the Father of the Wisdom of All Seeds and the Mother of Reality.
These are what must be severed. One must kill the father of ignorance and harm the mother of craving; to protect life, one must indeed kill, and only when killing is exhausted does it begin.
The hostility of the *anukampaka* (one who feels compassion) toward harm is the gateway for all phenomena within the *dharmadhātu*;
that there is no gateway beyond this is what is being revealed here. Second, the summary:
these are called the twelve types of sentient beings.
