Although they all equally belong to the stage of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*), there nonetheless remain distinctions of depth and shallowness: "opening" differs from "demonstrating," "demonstrating" differs from "awakening," and "awakening" differs from "entering.
Now, by means of the distinct nature of awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one enters into the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
It is of the same nature; being free from defilement, it is pure, and when purity reaches its ultimate limit, luminosity arises spontaneously—therefore, it is called "Radiant" (*prabhākarī*).

Radiance is itself clarity, and when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, awakening becomes spontaneously fulfilled—therefore, it is called "Blazing Wisdom" (*arciṣmatī*). When awakening is fulfilled, one can illuminate the inconceivable principle;
having illuminated the inconceivable principle, one also illuminates inconceivable phenomena. Thus, one illuminates both the principle and the phenomena.
Because it illuminates both phenomena and principle, it cannot be reached by any mundane wisdom of a different nature;
because it reaches [the ultimate], it cannot be reached by any mundane wisdom of a different nature.

This is because while the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*) can only obliterate identity and difference, this [stage] harmonizes and integrates identity and difference; thus, it transcends both mundane and supramundane wisdoms.

None can surpass it; thus it is named the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*durjayā*). Whether in terms of phenomena or principle, their essential nature is entirely unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) true suchness (*tathatā*), which is fundamentally pure.
Now that this has been illuminated and made manifest, it is named the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī*).
Since all dharmas are thus true suchness, one then reaches the ultimate limit of true suchness, which is named the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā*). This is the limit of true suchness.
Transversely pervasive and vertically exhaustive, it is unified within the single mind; how could there be entering or exiting? Therefore, it is named "Immovable.

Having realized the immovable whole of True Suchness (Tathatā), one must necessarily manifest the great function of True Suchness following conditions; therefore, it is named "Excellent Wisdom" (Sādhumati).
"Excellent Wisdom" means that both the provisional and the ultimate wisdoms are excellent. From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to this point, although all are indeed without [outflows],...
The path of effortful application (*prayoga-mārga*) still refers to the merit of cultivation arising from conformity with the nature (*dharmatā*);

from this point onward, including the cultivation of effortless application (*anābhoga*), the task is completed, and as the merits of great wisdom and great compassion are both fully perfected, these nine stages are likewise designated as the "stage of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-avasthā*). As for the tenth stage, however...

Because there is no longer any self-interest and it consists purely of benefiting others, one uses the wondrous cloud of the *maitrī*-canopy to cover the ocean of the primordially existing *nirvāṇa*-nature of sentient beings, spontaneously uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness; this is called the *Dharmameghā-bhūmi*.
These ten stages may also be described as ranging from the stage of the Buddha in principle (*li-ji fo-di*) to the ultimate stage of the Buddha (*jiong-jing fo-di*); for now, however—
To speak in terms of partial realization, there are further two meanings: the vertical and the horizontal. Vertically, one penetrates deeply stage by stage;

horizontally, within a single stage, all stages are present, and within all stages, a single stage is present. For example, just as the ten great mountain kings all rely upon the same great earth, so too the ten kinds of wisdom-stages of a bodhisattva are but the single Buddha-stage. This is the perfect awakening to the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*).

The Tathāgata flows against the current; likewise, when a Bodhisattva proceeds in accordance with the flow until their realization reaches the boundary where it intersects with that [of the Buddha], they are called an Equal-Enlightened One (*samyaksambuddha*).

It is said that the Tathāgata has already realized the true flow of the Dharma-nature and, emerging from within that Dharma-nature against the current, flows together with the nine realms to deliver sentient beings.
In this way, the Bodhisattva flows against the stream of birth and death while proceeding in accordance with Nirvana.
When it flows back into the source of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), on one hand it returns to the essence from its function, and on the other hand it arises as function from the essence.
It is like two people: one enters through a gate and the other exits through it;

though their going and coming differ, the fact that each has one foot inside and one foot outside is identical. Therefore, this is called "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Indeed, it is thus.
When provisional wisdom descends to respond to the capacity of sentient beings, it is called the Bodhisattva "Quiescent Illumination" (Jizhao);

when true wisdom ascends to accord with the awakened mind, it is called "Illuminating Quiescence" (Zhaoji). The meanings of "illuminating quiescence" and "quiescent illumination" are identical. Thus, viewed from the perspective of a Buddha, one is still termed a bodhisattva;
yet viewed from below, one is already like a Buddha. This concludes the section on the "Partial Realization of the Transformation of the Basis."
The fourth is the name for the ultimate transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

Ānanda, from the stage of the Dry Wisdom Mind (*śuṣka-vijñāna-citta*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), awakening has begun; it is only upon attaining the Vajra Mind that one first reaches the stage of Dry Wisdom.
Thus, through these successive layers—both single and double—the twelve stages are fully exhausted, whereby one perfects Wondrous Enlightenment and achieves the Unsurpassed Way.

This statement proves that even after attaining equal enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), one must still employ that Vajra-contemplation wisdom to once again traverse all the stages previously realized,
so that the views and thoughts, the dust-like and sand-like afflictions, ignorance, and all residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) are swept away without remainder,
thereby achieving wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*). Therefore, from the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*kan-hui*) up to this Equal Enlightenment, this awakening is merely...
Upon attaining the Vajra-mind, one first traverses the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*);

from this Vajra Dry Wisdom, one again passes through the stages of faith, abiding, practice, direction, and application, totaling two sets of twelve stages before finally reaching the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and accomplishing the Unsurpassed Way.
Regarding the phrase "repeatedly traversing the single and double twelve," it means that at the beginning there is first the single stage of Dry Wisdom, followed by the twenty stages of faith.

The thirty abodes, the forty practices, the fifty dedications, the six stages of warmth, the seven stages of summits, the eight stages of patience, the ninth stage of the worldly supreme, the tenth stage of the ten grounds, the eleventh stage of equal enlightenment, and the twelfth stage of the diamond-mind—these constitute the first single set of twelve sequential stages.
Furthermore, within the single diamond-mind: first is the wisdom of dry insight; second is the ten faiths within the diamond-mind.
From the tenth *vajra-citta* through to the twelfth *vajra-citta*,
the final *vajra-citta* constitutes the second cycle of the double twelve; having thus exhausted both the single and double cycles of twelve,
ignorance along with its residual habits is forever exhausted without remainder, there is nothing further to be severed, and one thoroughly realizes the original nature of the mind.
It is called "Sublime Enlightenment" (*samyag-bodhi*) because it constitutes the ultimate transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and the unsurpassed path.

Second, the specific elucidation of the various stages concludes with the designation of that which is transformed. Third, the combined conclusion of the various stages is established through three aspects:

first, a general conclusion by means of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; second, a formal conclusion by means of the three practices; and third, a further conclusion by means of the erroneous and the correct.
First: these various stages are all entered into progressively and deeply through the śamatha of the ten profound metaphors for viewing all things as illusory with a diamond-like discernment,
and through the purification and realization of the vipaśyanā of all Tathāgatas.
The "various stages" refers to the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*) up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi-bhūmi*).
"Vajra" is a metaphor for the wisdom that performs the contemplation; "like an illusion" is a metaphor for the objects contemplated.

All wisdom of contemplation arises in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*); because it can destroy all things yet cannot be destroyed by anything, it is called "vajra. [This applies to] all objects.
All realms are manifestations of mind alone; because they are neither annihilated nor eternal, neither empty nor existent, they are said to be "like an illusion.
As for the ten profound metaphors: first, a magical person; second, a mirage; third, the moon in water;

fourth, flowers in the sky; fifth, an echo; sixth, a city of the *gandharvas*; seventh, a dream; eighth, a reflection; ninth, an image; and tenth, a transformation. Thus, in the various Mahāyāna sūtras...
The items listed differ slightly and need not be harmonized; what is valued is simply grasping the intended meaning. Furthermore, the analogy of the illusory person applies across all four teachings:
if it is called "illusory" because it arises from causes and conditions and lacks self or what belongs to a self, this is the intent of the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao);

if it is called "illusory" because causes and conditions are themselves empty, this is the intent of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao); [and so on for the Distinct and Perfect Teachings regarding] illusory dharmas.
That which is unreal transforms according to the mind; its provisional names are immeasurable—this is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*).
That illusion is itself the dharma-realm, and that all dharmas tend toward illusion is itself the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—inconceivable;

this is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*). Now, we specifically adopt the meaning of the Perfect Teaching, and therefore it is called a "profound metaphor. *Śamatha* is precisely the single mind.
The three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are precisely the single mind and the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).

When it is said that all Tathāgatas employ *vipaśyanā*, this refers exactly to taking the fruition-awakening (*phala-bodhi*) entirely as the causal mind. Because the entirety of nature gives rise to cultivation and the entirety of nature achieves realization, it is called "pure cultivation and realization.

Since the six [perfections] are eternally present within the one, it is called "gradual"; yet since the one is eternally present within the six, it is called "simultaneous. Thus, it is both gradual and simultaneous.

Because it is eternal, it is said that one enters deeply into it; this means penetrating both the fruit and the cause, and contemplating them collectively as the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
To propagate this sutra while simultaneously disparaging *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is like making offerings to Śakra while reviling Kauśika;
such delusion and confusion are truly extreme. Second, the conclusion is made by summarizing the three practices.
Ānanda, it is precisely because of these three progressive advancements that one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi.
These three advancements are none other than the aforementioned three types of progressive cultivation; they consist of the integration of both the primary and auxiliary practices.
Regarding the statement that one can accomplish the true path to Bodhi through the fifty-five stages— namely, the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices,
ten transferences, four preparatory practices, ten grounds, and Equal Enlightenment— it is evident that these three types of practice are not restricted to the initial stage alone,
for it is through the progressive advancement of these three from beginning to end that accomplishment is achieved. Thus, it is clear that "Dry Wisdom" (Gāndhī) constitutes the path.
The True Sublime Enlightenment is not [merely] "true" because it is not a path; therefore, it is not so described.

Furthermore, although Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) is that which is accomplished, its stage lies within the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), and thus it also possesses the function of being that which accomplishes.

Although Sublime Enlightenment is likewise that which is accomplished, its stage lies in the ultimate, and thus it is entirely devoid of the characteristics of being something accomplished. Therefore, the preceding text merely says: "only then is the sublime exhausted."
Awakening by means of wondrous awakening is simply the inherent nature originally possessed by sentient beings; it merely involves bringing this to its ultimate, thorough completion.
Just as with the head of Sudatta or the pearl within one's clothing—since these were never lost in the first place, what could possibly be gained now?
Therefore, the subsequent text further states: "Perfecting Bodhi, one returns to non-attainment. Thirdly, regarding the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox:
[The Buddha] said:
"One who practices this contemplation is said to practice right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to practice wrong contemplation.
This contemplation refers specifically to the Tathāgata’s *vipaśyanā* (insight), which must be distinguished by means of three matters.
Regarding the identity of the heterodox and the orthodox: first, knowing that the nature and practice of the perfect and sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā* are non-dual is called orthodox;

otherwise, it is heterodox. Second, knowing that while the six [realms] are always identical with the unborn, one does not succumb to despondency, and while they are identical, the six are always present, yet one does not give rise to arrogance—is called orthodox;
otherwise, it is heterodox. Third, knowing that progress is advanced by means of the three [practices].
Cultivating both the primary and auxiliary practices while being equally urgent regarding both the precepts and the vehicle is called "correct"; otherwise, it is "erroneous.

The third major section, clarifying the stages of the threefold perfect virtues achieved through the cultivation of the primary and auxiliary practices and the subduing and severing [of delusions], is now complete.

Fourth, the conclusion establishes the title of the sutra to manifest its perfect essence, perfect doctrine, and perfect function. Part one consists of two sections: first, Mañjuśrī’s question; second, the Tathāgata’s answer.
First: At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should this sutra be named? How should I and all sentient beings uphold it?"

Since the nature, cultivation, cause, effect, understanding, practice, wisdom, and abandonment have already been fully revealed, I now wish to subsume the particulars into the general, to lead the particulars by means of the general, and to derive the extensive from the concise;
for it is through the concise that the extensive is attained. Therefore, I inquire after the title of this sutra and the method for its upholding.
However, regarding these three—the perfect and sudden teaching, practice, and principle—it is impossible to realize them without the fundamental, ultimate wisdom.
Because one must thoroughly take responsibility for this, Mañjuśrī first asks about the title of the sutra, desiring that people seek the essence by means of the name;

he next asks about its upholding, desiring that people establish the principle (the *zong*) based on that very essence. Once the principle and the essence are established, there is then power and function;
thus, we know that these questions concern nothing other than these three dharmas. Furthermore, "name" (*ming*) generally designates the three dharmas, while "sutra" (*jing*)...
That is to say, he takes the three dharmas as the essence of the sutra: principle is the core, practice is the function, and teaching is the exposition.
Those who uphold [the sutra] employ these three dharmas for their own cultivation and for the transformation of others. Second, the Tathāgata’s response has two parts:
first, the individual responses to the five names; second, the general response regarding upholding. Now, the first part.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "This sutra is named 'The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Śītata-Pāṭala Unsurpassed Jewel Seal, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions.

It is also named 'The Savior and Protector of Kinsmen and Causes, Delivering Ānanda and the Bhikṣuṇī of this Assembly from their Nature, Causing Them to Attain Bodhicitta and Enter the Ocean of Universal Knowledge. It is also named 'The Tathāgata.'"

The Definitive Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause; also known as the Great Vaipulya Wondrous Lotus King, the Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions;
also known as the Chapter of Consecration, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi that is the Foremost of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
The first three characters, *Dàfódǐng* (Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa), establish the name based on its essence; both the Exoteric and Esoteric traditions take the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa as their essence.

*Siddhārthapāṇḍarā Anuttara-ratnamudrā* (The Unsurpassed Jewel Seal of Siddhārthapāṇḍarā) refers to both the Exoteric and Esoteric traditions taking the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa as the seal, with the term "seal" indicating the esoteric interpretation. *The Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions*—
Both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings are the Great Buddha-Topknot, the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma; "manifest" (*khyen*) here refers specifically to the Exoteric exposition.

Next is the title "Savior of Kinsmen and Causes": "kinsmen and causes" refers to immediate conditions. In this assembly, Ānanda represents the kinsmen and the courtesan Pañcaśikha represents the causes;
all such kinsmen and causes are saved and protected by means of these two expositions, the Exoteric and the Esoteric.

There is none who does not receive deliverance; it shall certainly cause them to attain the Bodhicitta and enter the ocean of universal knowledge before coming to rest—this is the naming based on its function.
The third name, "The Definitive Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata," is a name established according to its essence:
the nature of the Great Buddha-Crown is precisely this unarisen and undying true cause, which encompasses both cause and fruit.
The name "Secret Cause" (*guhyahetu*) also concurrently refers to the meanings of *mudrā* and *pañcara*, yet it emphasizes explicit exposition.

The fourth name, "Great Vaipulya Wondrous Lotus King Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions," establishes its title based on its essence (*tattva*) and school (*śarīra*), referring specifically to the esoteric exposition;
"Vaipulya" is simply another term for the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa.

The name is also an alternative designation for the *Mahāsitātapatra* (Great White Parasol). This refers to the essence (*tattva*), which signifies the principle of the simultaneity of cause and fruit.
The title "Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions" signifies the principle of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) regarding cause and fruit. This refers to the school (*siddhānta*);
although it is explicitly taught therein that it is also called the "Wondrous Lotus," the "Vajra King," the "Jewel Awakening," and the "Illusory Samādhi. Furthermore...
The phrase "Vajrarāja-māyā-acintya-buddhamātṛ-sat-samādhi" emphasizes its esoteric interpretation.
Fifth is the title "Mantra-Phrases for Consecration," which establishes its name based on its function: the *Śūraṅgama* of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas.
The four characters "Mantra-Phrases for Consecration" signify the application of the esoteric interpretation, referring to the upholding of this mantra upon the level of fruition.
The mind can receive the empowerment and prediction of Buddhahood from the Buddhas of the ten directions while still within the causal stage by upholding this mantra-heart;

likewise, one receives the prediction of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions. The single phrase "Śūraṅgama," the foremost of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas, refers to the function of manifesting the ultimate truth:
through awakening that the aggregates, sense-bases, elements, and the seven great elements are all the Tathāgatagarbha, the single mind is thus able [to achieve this].
When the ten thousand practices are complete, every matter can be realized as perfect penetration; the rest is explained as in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
Second, the general response regarding upholding: "You should uphold this."
To uphold [this teaching] there is no other method than to recognize the meaning of these words and bring them back to oneself.

However, since the question asked how "I" and "sentient beings" should uphold it, my answer that "you should uphold it" precisely reveals that the one who transmits the Dharma must provide instruction by example; you must be able to uphold it in accordance with the Dharma.
If one maintains this, all sentient beings will naturally act without being commanded.

To "overcome oneself and return to propriety" in a single day, and for the world to turn toward benevolence—this is what must be deeply contemplated and diligently strived for when propagating the sutras in the final age. The fourth major section, concluding the title of the sutra, is finished.
Fifth, taking the evil dharma of breaking the precepts as the starting point of the inquiry, [the text] extensively demonstrates seven points.

The distinction regarding the realms (gati) is intended to show that if there were no supramundane sublime ethical discipline (*śīla*), there would certainly be no supramundane sublime wisdom (*prajñā*).
In the three evil destinies and among the asuras, there is no *vinaya* (discipline); among humans, rishis, and the desire-realm devas, there is no dhyāna-discipline;

and among the form and formless realm devas, there is a lack of untainted (*anāsrava*) discipline. Because they lack discipline, wisdom does not arise, and they do not transcend birth and death. The text is divided as follows:
Second, the initial request and the subsequent response. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the narration by the sūtra compiler;
second, the formal request of the audience. Now, for the first section.
Having spoken these words, Ānanda and the great assembly immediately received the Tathāgata’s revelation of the secret seal.
The meaning of "Pañcāla" encompasses both hearing this sūtra of definitive meaning and its titles;

it refers to the sudden awakening to dhyāna, the progressive advancement through the stages of sainthood, the superior and wondrous principle of the mind becoming empty and concentrated, and the severing of the six grades of subtle afflictions within the three realms through mental cultivation.

The benefits derived from this are profound and far-reaching: first, one receives the revelation of the meaning of *paṇḍara*, which is the reiteration of the divine mantra from the preceding text, describing its benefits and exhorting its retention;

second, it anticipates the cultivation and advancement through the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*), namely the three types of progressive development and the fifty-seven established stages; third, it concurrently provides a thorough understanding through hearing.
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to a name or designation. *Dhyāna* is translated here as "calm contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), which is another term for correct observation (*vipaśyanā*).
This corresponds to what was mentioned in the preceding text: "within *śamatha*, one employs the various *vipaśyanās* of the Tathāgatas for pure cultivation and realization.
It is "empty and congealed" because observation is free from stagnation; it is "empty and still" because there is no distraction or agitation. This is the power of hearing the Dharma.
This is because he is being provided with the support of concentration and wisdom.

Among the eighty-one grades of afflictions to be severed through the cultivation of the mind within the three realms, Ānanda has now severed six grades of afflictions in the desire realm and realized the second fruit, that of the Sakṛdāgāmin;

this is spoken of in terms of his outward manifestation. Second, the formal request of the one suited to the occasion, which has two parts: first, praise and gratitude; second, the presentation [of the request].
[The second] doubt. Herein is the first [section]:
immediately rising from his seat, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, whose compassionate voice is all-pervading and who skillfully opens the subtle, sunken delusions of sentient beings, you have caused my body and mind today to experience such joy.”
Nevertheless, they obtained great benefit.
Second, the expression of doubts: first, a general doubt that the Truth cannot tolerate falsehood; second, a specific doubt regarding whether the hells are collective or individual;
third, the conclusion requesting a definitive revelation. This was Ānanda’s manifestation of the Great Compassion of the same essence (*sāmānya-kāya-mahākaruṇā*), foreseeing the future末法 (mofa) age.
Among them, there are those who falsely cling to the principle of a perfect permanence, asserting that both heaven and hell are equally one true permanence, and thus feel no dread of the evil realms;
there are those who falsely calculate upon the name of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) while stubbornly acting as a sovereign creator and denying cause and effect;
and there are those who, having a vague notion of the purity of mind and the purity of the land, go so far as to claim that hell has no fixed location.
This refers to those who merely see that the hells and other realms each have fixed locations, and who cling to them as ultimately and truly existent without realizing they are "mind-only";
thus they pose this question so that practitioners may advance both in understanding and practice without falling into the net of delusion.
It is also the ultimate reflection for upholding the Vinaya while discussing the eternal. First, there is a general doubt that the Truth cannot tolerate the false.
World-Honored One, if this wondrously bright, truly pure, and wondrous mind is fundamentally pervasive and perfect,

such that even the great earth, grasses, trees, crawling insects, and all sentient beings are fundamentally True Suchness (Tathatā)— which is the very essence of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood—
and if the Buddha-essence is thus truly real, how can there further be the paths of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas, World-Honored One?
Is this path something that has existed inherently from the beginning, or does it arise from the deluded habitual tendencies of sentient beings?

Although this constitutes a general doubt regarding the fact that the Truth cannot admit of falsehood, its intent differs from the "difficulty concerning phenomena" raised by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra in the fourth fascicle;
for Pūrṇa’s inquiry was based upon the textual passage concerning the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
The intent of this objection is that the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* should not suddenly give rise to various conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) characteristics;

therefore, the Buddha must answer by explaining that while delusion of the truth results in the false, the false is fundamentally non-arising. The present text accepts the principle of the two kinds of *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis) to further clarify the dharma-gate of the inherent nature (*prakṛti-prakṛta*).
If one transformation entails the transformation of all, then the essence of the Buddha would not be accommodated.
Furthermore, regarding the six realms: if the one mind inherently possesses the ten dharma-realms, then the six realms should be able to coexist with the Buddha-realm.
Therefore, the Buddha must explain that these arise from deluded thought and do not exist originally;

even when you create them through your own delusion, it is not the fault of Bodhi. In the response to this, the passage beginning with "if this wondrous clarity" up to "originally pervasive and perfect" [addresses this].
This refers to the preceding statement that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and characteristics;

it refers to the fundamental true suchness (*tathatā*), which is the true body of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood, and to the preceding statement regarding the extinction of delusion called "the True" and the two designations for the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
As for this Way, does it exist inherently from the beginning? This concluding phrase asks: what is the reality of the Buddha-body?
Furthermore, there are the hardships of the six realms of existence. For these sentient beings, deluded habits arise;

the phrasing below implies that they each privately experience their own fixed destinies, leading to two doubts with which they inquire. Second, the specific doubt concerns whether the hells are common or individual.
World-Honored One, it was like the case of the bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā, who upheld the bodhisattva precepts yet secretly engaged in sexual misconduct.
She falsely claimed that "sexual conduct is neither killing nor stealing, and thus carries no karmic retribution.

Having uttered these words, a great, fierce fire first broke out from her female organ, and subsequently, fierce fires blazed up from every joint of her body until she fell into the Avīci Hell—just as it happened to King Vairōcana and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra.
"Kūṭa-vaiḍūrya, because he falsely proclaimed that all phenomena are empty to Śuklodana of the Gautama clan,

his physical body fell into the Avīci Hell. Do these various hells have fixed locations, or do they arise spontaneously so that each person receives their retribution privately according to the karma they have individually generated?"

This specific citation of a current event as a question regarding physical appearance is intended to demonstrate that karma and its fruits are solely of the mind, thereby awakening those who are mired in delusion within the three realms.
As for Bao-lianxiang, his private indulgence in lust constitutes a violation of the precepts; his false claim that there is no retribution for such acts constitutes a violation of right view.
Since both his conduct and his views were destroyed, he fell directly [into hell]—of this there is no doubt. This is just like Virūḍhaka, who usurped the throne by killing his own father.
To execute those of the Gautama clan in order to avenge the insult of a single word is neither a case of violating the precepts nor a denial of cause and effect;
it is simply because their hatred has intensified that they invite rebirth in hell.

Although Sunakṣatra falsely taught the emptiness of dharmas—which constitutes a violation of view—and thus had not yet broken the precepts, he likewise fell into these various hells. This is clearly known.
All these arise from the production of delusive habits; it is simply that one does not yet know whether they have fixed locations or whether each receives their own private portion.

To receive one's own private portion is precisely to have no fixed location. Although this question specifically asks whether the hells have fixed locations, its intent actually encompasses all six realms of existence.
The answer below states that while beings indeed invite their own retribution, there are also original lands.
Although there are fixed locations, they belong only to the floating and empty congealing of deluded thoughts;
thus, the principle that "the three realms are but the mind" becomes even more clearly manifest. Third, I request you to provide a definitive teaching.

I pray that you will bestow great compassion to enlighten this ignorant youth, so that all sentient beings who uphold the precepts may hear this definitive meaning, receive it with joy and reverence, and remain pure and unoffending.
By examining this concluding inquiry, one knows that its intent lies in supporting the Vinaya. Part Two: The Response, which has two sections; first, the praise and approval.
Second, the formal exposition. Now, for the first part:
The Buddha addressed Ānanda, "Excellent indeed is this question, which prevents all sentient beings from entering into false views. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you."
To falsely claim that the six realms of existence have existed from the beginning and cannot be extinguished is a false view;
to falsely claim that the six realms are themselves the true nature and need not be extinguished is also a false view;

to falsely claim that the six realms exist solely within the mind and have no fixed location is a false view; and to falsely claim that the six realms have a fixed location and do not exist solely within the mind is likewise a false view.
This too is a false view, falsely claiming that the nature of karma is emptiness and thus does not entail retribution; this is a false view.
To falsely claim that karmic obstacles have substantial reality and cannot be transformed is likewise a false view.

Now, through this inquiry, I shall once again provide an exposition so that you may know that the six realms of existence are all the congealing of delusive thoughts and do not exist from the beginning; thus one will understand that...
That the nature is empty constitutes the nature's inherent presence; that the nature's inherent presence is itself the nature's emptiness.

Not falling into the first two false views, one comes to know that what is summoned is one's own delusion; furthermore, by possessing the primordial ground, one knows that the triple world is mind-only.
Not falling into the next two false views, one comes to know that the wondrously manifested samādhi forever eliminates the three delusions, and only then can one realize the wondrous.

If one knows that in quiescence and permanence there is no self, no agent, and no experiencer, yet the karma of good and evil does not perish—if one can thus exhaust the old without creating the new and extinguish hindrances as if overturning the great earth—then because one does not enter the latter two types of false views, this question may be called "excellent. This section demonstrates the seven destinies and the three fetters to encourage cultivation. Regarding the first of these three parts: first, there is the dual presentation based on delusion regarding the Truth;
second, the specific demonstration based on emotional thoughts; and third, the clarification of the pure and mixed states and their respective ascent or descent. Now, the first part.

Ānanda, all sentient beings are in truth fundamentally true and pure; it is because of that deluded vision that deluded habits arise, and because of this, they distinguish between the internal and external divisions.
These two divisions—internal and external—are merely distinguished based on the currently deluded body and mind of sentient beings; in reality, they do not exist.

Although one transcends both good and evil karma, taking evil as one's internal portion is like what is meant in the Vinaya when it says that for a layperson to commit a transgression is their "internal portion.
Now, internal and external portions arise solely from delusive habituation; delusive habituation arises solely from delusive views;
and delusive views have no further cause. If they had a cause, how could they be called "delusive"? Therefore, we know this.
Mad flowers dance in confusion, yet the substance of space remains as it was; though deluded habits are chaotic, the reality is fundamentally pure and true.
Second, a specific demonstration based on feelings and perceptions:
Ānanda, the internal division is precisely the division within sentient beings; due to various defilements of craving, deluded feelings are initiated, and these feelings accumulate.
The water of craving can arise incessantly; therefore, when sentient beings recall delicacies in their minds, saliva flows from their mouths.

When they remember people of the past, whether with pity or resentment, tears fill their eyes. When greedily seeking wealth and treasures, the mind produces amorous saliva, making the entire body glisten and moist.

When the mind is attached to sexual intercourse, the two organs of male and female naturally flow with fluids. Ānanda, although these various forms of craving differ, [they all arise from the same source].
The flowing fetters are identical in their moistening nature; they do not ascend but naturally fall downward—this is called the internal portion, Ānanda.

The external portion refers to the external factors of sentient beings: through various forms of longing and aspiration, they give rise to empty conceptions which accumulate without ceasing, thereby producing a superior vital energy.

For this reason, when sentient beings maintain prohibitive precepts in their minds, their entire bodies become light and pure; when they maintain mantras and mudrās in their minds, their glances [are transformed].
When a courageous mind desires to be born in heaven, dreams of flying upward; when the mind dwells upon the Buddha-land, sacred realms manifest in the darkness;
and when one serves spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) while disregarding one’s own body and life—Ānanda, although these various thoughts differ, their lightness and elevation are the same.
This soaring and movement, which is naturally transcendent and does not sink, is called the "external division" (bāhyabhāga).
Because sentient beings are entirely immersed in delusion, they take defiled and evil emotions as their internal domain and aspire to wholesome thoughts as their external domain;
this can be understood from the text. Third, the clarification of the pure and the mixed, and of ascent and descent. Part one: the formal explanation of ascent and descent. Part two:
the conclusion answering the question regarding identity and difference. Now, the first part.
Ānanda, in all worlds, the cycle of birth and death continues: birth proceeds from habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and death proceeds from transformation and flow.

At the moment of the end of life, before body heat and sensation have departed, the good and evil of one’s entire lifetime manifest simultaneously and instantaneously. Death is contrary to the flow while birth is with the flow; these two tendencies intersect.
If one consists purely of thought, they immediately ascend and will certainly be born in the heavens. If within that ascending mind there is a combination of merit and wisdom, as well as...
With pure vows, their minds naturally open and they behold the Buddhas of the ten directions and all their pure lands; according to their wishes, they are reborn therein.

With few worldly emotions and abundant contemplation, they attain lightness of body and are not far from becoming flying immortals, powerful ghost-kings, flying yakṣas, or earth-walking rākṣasas who roam through the four heavens, moving everywhere without obstruction.
Among them, if there are those with virtuous vows and virtuous hearts, they shall be protected and sustained.

In my Dharma, some protect the prohibitions and precepts according to those who uphold the precepts; some protect divine mantras according to those who uphold mantras; and some protect meditative concentration to preserve and sustain the patience of the Dharma.
These individuals dwell intimately beneath the seat of the Tathāgata, their mental conceptions being equalized: when thoughts are not flighty, they do not fall; they are born among humans.

When their thoughts are clear, they are sharp-witted; when their thoughts are obscure, they are dull-witted; and when their thoughts are many, they are few in substance, flowing into [the cycle of existence].

Those with seven emotions and three thoughts are born horizontally as the heavy-furred beasts or the light-feathered fowl. Those with nine emotions and one thought sink below the water-wheel and are born at the boundary of fire;
they receive their breath from fierce flames and become hungry ghosts, constantly scorched by fire.

Water can only harm them, and lacking both food and drink, they pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas. Those with nine emotions and one thought descend through the fire-wheel; their bodies enter the intersection of wind and fire.

Those who pass through the various hells and are reborn in the Intermittent Hells (*sāntara-niraya*) or the Uninterrupted Hells (*avīci-niraya*)— the latter being exclusively for sentient beings whose consciousness sinks directly into the Avīci Hell—
will, if they harbor slander toward the Mahāyāna, violate the Buddha’s prohibitions, preach deceptive and false doctrines, greedily covet offerings of faith, or unworthily receive respect,
further give rise to the five heinous crimes and the ten grave offenses, and will subsequently be reborn in the Avīci Hells throughout the ten directions.
Birth proceeds from habitual tendencies means that karma arises from afflictions, each following its own respective habit-energy.
Death proceeds from shifting flux means that one receives retribution according to karma, having no autonomy whatsoever.
When death’s shifting flux and birth’s habitual tendencies intersect—meaning when a person is approaching the end of life—the state of death’s shifting flux and birth’s habitual tendencies meet.

Matters such as these manifest simultaneously through the two types of habitual tendencies; according to the power of one's wholesome or unwholesome karma, rebirth is drawn forth without the slightest deviation.
Pure thought refers exclusively to the superior grade of the ten wholesome deeds: merit leads to supramundane precepts; concentration and wisdom lead to supramundane insight;
and pure vows lead to the four supramundane great vows, various vows for rebirth, and so forth. Therefore—
Riding upon the power of these pure thoughts and wholesome roots, one attains the opening of the mind, beholds the Buddha, and is reborn according to one's vows.
With nine thoughts and one emotion, one becomes a flying immortal; with eight thoughts and two emotions, a powerful ghost-king;
with seven thoughts and three emotions, a flying yakṣa; and with six thoughts and four emotions, a land-walking rākṣasa—all of whom belong to the lineages of benevolent deities.
If those who are the counterparts of the various devas further cultivate virtuous vows and a virtuous mind, they become the eight classes of Dharma-protecting beings.

When emotional desire (*kleśa*) and conceptual thought (*saṃjñā*) are equal, this constitutes the collective retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*) of the human realm. Within this state of equality, if conceptual thought predominates, one is clear and intelligent;
if emotional desire predominates, one is obscure and dull-witted—these constitute the individual retributions (*viśeṣa-vipāka*) of the human realm.

This is the karma [of such beings]. When "feeling" (qing) is predominant and "thought" (xiang) is scarce, it refers to the six feelings and four thoughts; within these six feelings, they are further divided into heavy and light.
The heavy are the "furry herds" whose feet do not leave the ground; the light are the "winged tribes" who are still able to fly.
As for water being able to harm oneself, even when one obtains water, it transforms into molten copper, boiling excrement, and so forth. There is also the light birth... [text truncated]

The phrase "uninterrupted" (ānantarya) refers generally to those with eight afflictions and two thoughts who are reborn in the uninterrupted realms; it specifically refers to those with nine afflictions and one thought whose pure emotions sink into Avīci.
This corresponds exactly to those with pure thought who are certain to be born in the heavens.

Therefore, the lifespan in the Avīci hell is equal to that of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven. If the sinking mind is further accompanied by the slandering of the sutras, [the retribution is even more severe].
The various evils of violating the precepts are directly opposed to merit, wisdom, and pure vows;

therefore, they result in rebirth in the Avīci hell throughout the ten directions, which stands in contrast to those who attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Thus we know that the power of good and evil karma is equally inconceivable;
it is like casting images or weapons from the same metal, by the same craftsman, using the same tools.
If one can turn this single pivotal point, then the ten directions of Avīci will become the pure lands of the ten directions;
the proofs provided by Aṅgulimāla and Pūraṇa are clearly present—how can one fail to reflect upon this? Second, the conclusion summarizes the identity and difference.
Regarding the phrase "following the commission of evil karma," although one invites [retribution] for oneself, within the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) there are also the original lands.

By saying "inviting it for oneself according to karma," it is evident that this is not something originally possessed; by saying "possessing it within the *sabhāga*," it is evident that there is no lack of a fixed location.

This follows the convenience of the text in concluding the discussion of evil karma. If, however, it concerns the celestial realms (*deva-gati*) and so forth, one should instead say "following... [the commission of good karma].
Although the performance of wholesome karma brings about one’s own rebirth within a particular *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class of beings), it also includes the primary realms therein.
Second, the seven destinies (*gati*) are specifically shown, which constitute seven sections: first, the hell realm; [and so on] up to seventh, the asura realm.
Regarding the first of these, there are three parts: first, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation; and third, a summary. This is the first part.
Ānanda, all these are what is induced by the karma of those sentient beings themselves; they have created the ten habitual causes and received the sixfold intersecting retributions.
These two characters, "these" (cǐ děng), refer back to the aforementioned hells. What is meant by "induced by their own karma"? It refers to that which is not... [the text here is incomplete].
It descends from heaven, it is not born from the earth, nor is it bestowed by humans, nor is it a fruit falsely summoned without cause.
Second, the detailed explanation has two parts: first, clarifying the ten causes; second, clarifying the six retributions. This is the first part.
What are the ten causes? Ānanda, first is the habit of sexual desire. Through the act of union, it is triggered by mutual friction;
as this grinding continues without ceasing, a great and fierce fire is ignited within. It is like two people rubbing their hands together, where the sensation of warmth appears before them.
Because these two habits ignite one another, there arise such things as iron beds and copper pillars. Therefore, throughout the ten directions...
All Tathāgatas characterize sexual misconduct with the same name: the fire of desire. When a Bodhisattva perceives desire, he avoids it as if avoiding a pit of fire.
Second, the habit of greed involves mutual plotting that gives rise to mutual attraction; this attraction and grasping do not cease.

Because of this, there is accumulated cold and solid ice, freezing and chilling within. It is like a person drawing in wind through the mouth, whereby a sensation of cold arises. These are the two habits.
Because they insult one another, there arise the states of *ṭha-ṭha*, *pa-pa*, *ra-ra*, as well as the blue, red, and white lotuses, and the cold hells;
therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate excessive seeking with the same name: the "Water of Greed. Bodhisattvas view greed as they would avoid a sea of miasma.
Third, the habit of pride involves mutual insults arising from mutual arrogance, flowing on incessantly; because of this, there arise—
Surging and rushing, accumulated waves become water; just as the mouth and tongue of a person create a continuous flavor, water is thereby produced.
Because these two habits strike against one another, there arise such phenomena as rivers of blood, rivers of ash, hot sands, poisonous seas, and the swallowing of molten copper poured upon one.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize this arrogance as "drinking the water of delusion," and Bodhisattvas perceive it as pride.

Fourth, like avoiding a great drowning, the habit-energy of anger clashes and collides, manifesting as mutual antagonism. When this antagonism knots together without ceasing, the heat of the mind ignites fire, forging the vital breath into metal.
Thus, there arise mountains of knives, iron stakes, sword-trees, sword-wheels, axes, halberds, spears, and saws.

Just as when a person bites out an enemy, their murderous breath flies forth and moves; because these two habits strike one another, there exist punishments of imprisonment, dismemberment, beheading, and hacking.
Because of various acts such as hacking, stabbing, and beating with clubs, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate hatred as the "Sharp Sword.
When Bodhisattvas see hatred, they avoid it as they would an execution. Fifth, through the habitual practice of deceitful enticement, mutual flirtation arises, leading to instability;
thus there are bonds, wooden stocks, and strangulation, like water soaking a field where weeds and grass grow.
Because these two habits extend into one another, there arise shackles, fetters, stocks, manacles, whips, staves, clubs, and cudgels;

for this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions identify such craftiness and falsehood by the same name: "the slanderous thief. When a Bodhisattva sees such deception, he fears it as he would a jackal or a wolf.
Sixth, the habit of delusion involves mutual cheating that arises from mutual entrapment; when deceptive speech does not cease, the mind flies about to create villainy in this manner.
Therefore, there are impurities such as dust, excrement, urine, filth, and uncleanness, like dust driven by the wind where nothing can be seen;

because these two habits combine, there arise various occurrences such as drowning, tossing about, flying, falling, drifting, and sinking. For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize deception with the same name:
"Robbery and Murder. When a Bodhisattva encounters deception, it is as if they were treading upon a venomous snake. This is the seventh.

When the habit-energy of resentment and mutual hatred arise from harbored enmity, there result such things as flying stones, thrown rocks, being confined in boxes or carriage-cages, or being stored in jars and bags;
like a person of hidden malice who harbors and nurtures evil, these two habits devour one another, resulting in acts of throwing, seizing, striking, shooting, tossing, and snatching.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate the enemy as their "target."

The eighth is the mutual illumination of the two habits, which is like the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and various karmas arising from false awakening that provoke resistance and give rise to opposition.
Thus, there are kings, messengers, officials, and clerks who hold legal documents and records, just as travelers on the road come and go and see one another; this is the second habit.
Because they intersect, there is the authority to interrogate, to employ stratagems, to examine and cross-examine, to investigate and search out, to scrutinize and illuminate good and evil.
A youth holds a register in his hand and adjudicates all matters; therefore, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate this evil view with the same name:
"The Pit of Views. When Bodhisattvas see all such falsehoods and pervasive attachments, it is as if they were facing a precipice of poison. This is the ninth.

When the habits of perversion and entanglement combine to give rise to false slanders, there consequently arise mountains and stones that crush, grind, plow, and rub, just as slanderous thieves oppress and wrong the virtuous.
Because these two habits clash with one another, there occur various matters such as being pressed down, crushed, squeezed, strained, and measured.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions identify the act of malicious slandering by the common name "the Slanderous Tiger."
The Bodhisattva views injustice as if encountering a thunderbolt. Tenth, the habit of litigation and mutual clamor arises from concealment;
thus, there is the faculty of discerning vision that illuminates like the midday sun, unable to hide one's shadow.

Because these two habits present themselves together, there are evil companions, the karma-mirror, and the fire-pearl, which reveal past karmas and verify all matters. Therefore, throughout the ten directions, all...

The Tathāgata designates concealment (*mrakṣa*) by the same name as "hidden thieves" (*chāyā-caura*). A Bodhisattva views concealment as if wearing a high mountain upon one's head while treading upon a vast ocean.
Since it is said that the ten causes must necessarily yield their fruits, the three phases of delusion (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*) are here fully set forth.
Sexual desire is the most grievous among delusions of greed and is the very root of birth and death; therefore, it is clarified first.

The joining of the two organs is its characteristic of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*); the friction that ignites fire, resulting in such things as the iron bed and the copper pillar, is its characteristic of suffering (*duḥkhalakṣaṇa*).
As for the "two habits," they refer to the two habits of death being contrary [to the Way] and birth being compliant with it. Their mutual kindling results in birth.
Previously, the fire of desire from individual karma arose; subsequently, the fire of suffering from the common lot (sabhāgatā) appears simultaneously, and they ignite together.

Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have perfected awakening and profoundly understand all causes and effects of karma, regarding the single act of sexual intercourse, they have definitively designated its name and form, calling it the "fire of desire," so that all sentient beings may know to be wary and fearful.
Because all Bodhisattvas have attained awakening from delusion, they view desire as one would avoid a pit of fire, vowing never to tread upon it;
the following cases should be understood accordingly. Greed (*lobha*) is a root affliction; its nature is to be stained by and attached to existence and the requisites of existence.
Its characteristic activity is conceptual calculation (*parikalpa*), which draws things together and generates freezing cold, resulting in the suffering of ice.
*Chata-chata*, *papa-rala*—these are all the sounds of those in hell enduring the cold.
The red, white, and blue lotuses are all the colors of the freezing chill in hell. Pride (*māna*) is also a root affliction;

its nature is to be haughty toward others by relying on oneself, and its function is to cause mutual disparagement. It causes one to rush and flow like waves, leading to being drenched and swallowed [by suffering].
Regarding all matters as having the characteristic of suffering, anger (*krodha*) is also a root affliction;
its nature is one of hatred and resentment toward suffering and the instruments of suffering, and its functional characteristic is to cause conflict and obstruction.
Deceit (*māyā*) is also called guile (*śāṭhya*); it is a minor derivative affliction whose nature is to falsely contrive differences for the purpose of deluding others.

Guile (*māyā*) has deceitful crookedness as its intrinsic nature; its functional characteristic consists in enticement through social interaction, extending even to such matters as the use of shackles and fetters, which constitute its aspect of suffering.
Deception (*śāṭhya*), also a minor secondary affliction, has the feigning of possessing virtues for the sake of gain and reputation as its intrinsic nature;
its functional characteristic consists in the practice of mutual deception, whereby one brings about ruin through the commission of fraud and treachery.
To harbor resentment toward various matters as a mark of suffering is *upanāha* (enmity); it is also a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*).

Because it takes *krodha* (anger) as its precursor and has the nature of harboring malice without relinquishing it—thereby binding one in enmity—it functions with the characteristic of mutual dislike as its karmic activity.

By harboring enmity and accumulating evil, it leads to the casting of insults and other such matters as marks of suffering. Seeing this as a fundamental affliction (*mūlakleśa*) regarding the [Four Noble] Truths...
Because its nature is defiled wisdom that investigates in a distorted manner regarding principles, it takes mutual illumination as its functional characteristic (*karmalakṣaṇa*).

There are five distinct varieties of this view-characteristic (*dṛṣṭicaritalakṣaṇa*): first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which consists of grasping at the five aggregates of clinging as "self" or "mine," ranging from twenty to sixty-five permutations;
second, the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which refers to [the grasping] toward various views...

The attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) refers to regarding the precepts and observances that accord with various views, as well as their underlying aggregates (*skandha*), as supreme and capable of bringing about purification.
The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) refers to adhering to either annihilationism or eternalism with respect to the five aggregates.
The five types of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) refer to those that deny cause and effect and engage in such actions.
Based on actual facts, all other false attachments apart from the four views are termed "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
What is now called "false awakening" encompasses the two views of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
When these arise from rejection and produce opposition, the moment one view is raised, it immediately contradicts all other views; each claims, "This alone is the truth, and all others are false."
It is false and deceptive. To interrogate others regarding their words and various affairs constitutes its characteristic of suffering.
To wrongfully impose what is not rational—taking the straight for the crooked—is subsumed under harm; it is also a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*).

Because its nature consists of lacking compassion toward sentient beings and causing them injury and distress, its functional characteristic (*karmalakṣaṇa*) is that of making false accusations. It extends even to [the act of] weighing and measuring.
To litigate over the characteristics of suffering is an evil karma resulting from concealment;
this concealment is a minor secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) whose nature is to hide one's own committed offenses out of fear of losing profit or reputation.

Because I conceal my offenses, others will eventually expose them, thereby forming the karma of litigation that leads to the karmic mirror of various bitter retributions and the company of evil friends. As the Preface to the Precepts states: "Repent."

Thus, one may find peace and happiness; yet if one does not repent, their transgressions will deepen further. One should reflect deeply upon the metaphors of "bearing a mountain" and "treading the sea" regarding those who uphold the precepts.
Question: There are twenty-six afflictions, including the root and secondary afflictions; why is it that these ten alone are designated as the causes for habitual practice (*abhyāsa-hetu*)? Answer:

The Buddha, possessing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), profoundly understands the causes of the delusions and karmic actions of sentient beings. Therefore, he has specifically identified these ten as the primary causes for the persistence of afflictions.
Regarding the differentiation of the results, these ten causes are able to encompass all afflictions (*kleśa*).

Among the root afflictions, the two types—delusion (*moha*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—as well as the two medium-level secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and the eight major secondary afflictions, all arise in association with these ten causes.

Among the minor secondary afflictions, the two—anger (*krodha*) and resentment (*upanāha*), as well as envy (*īrṣyā*)—are subsumed under hatred (*dveṣa*); while arrogance (*mada*) is subsumed under pride (*māna*).

Since the inclusion of stinginess is subsumed under greed, citing these ten causes fully encompasses the twenty-six types of afflictions, as well as all afflictions, karmas, and sufferings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Second, the six retributions are explained.
What are the six retributions? Ānanda, for all sentient beings, the evil retributions summoned by the karma created through the six consciousnesses emerge from the six sense organs.
How do these evil retributions emerge from the six organs? First, regarding the retribution of the eye faculty that draws forth evil fruits:

when this visual karma intersects with other conditions, at the moment of death, one first sees fierce fires filling the ten directions, and the deceased’s spirit-consciousness flies downward into them.
Riding on smoke, they enter the Avīci Hell, wherein two manifestations arise: first, seeing clearly, they see all manner of evil things and give rise to immeasurable fear;
second, seeing in darkness, they perceive only silence and nothingness, giving rise to immeasurable dread.

Thus, when they see fire, it burns their hearing and becomes boiling cauldrons and molten copper; when it burns their breath, it becomes black smoke and purple flames; and it burns their sense of taste.
It can burn the body like glowing pellets, molten iron, or scorching contact; it can scorch the heart like hot ashes, furnaces, or charcoal;
and it can produce sparks that scatter and fan through the void. Second, hearing the retribution invites the drawing forth of evil fruits.

When this hearing and karma intersect, at the moment of death one first sees waves and tides, drowning in heaven and earth; the deceased’s consciousness descends and flows along with the current into non-existence.
The intermediate hells manifest two aspects: first, when the doors are open, one hears various clamors that cause the spirit to become bewildered and disordered;

second, when the doors are closed, one hears nothing in the silence, and the dark soul sinks into despair. Thus, the waves of hearing pour forth: when hearing pours forth, it can become reprimands and interrogations;
when seeing pours forth, it can become thunder and roars, as well as noxious poisonous vapors; when breathing pours forth, it can become rain.
Mist is sprayed upon various venomous insects that completely cover the body; when their flavors are infused, they become pus and blood, as well as various kinds of filth.
When their touch is infused, they become animals, ghosts, excrement, and urine.

When their thoughts are infused, they become lightning and hail that shatter the heart and soul. These three—smell, retribution, and the summoning of evil fruits—converge when the karma of smelling is activated.

At the time of death, one first perceives poisonous vapors filling the near and far surroundings; the deceased’s consciousness then surges from the earth and enters the Avīci Hell, manifesting two signs:
first, "penetrating hearing," where one is overwhelmed by various foul vapors that intensely disturb the mind;

second, "obstructed hearing," where the vapors block the senses so completely that one faints upon the ground. Thus, as these vapors strike the breath, they become the substantial basis for perception.
When encountered by sight, it can become fire or a torch; when encountered by hearing, it can become drowning, submersion, boiling, or seething;
when encountered by taste, it can become hunger or a bitter distaste;

when encountered by touch, it can become tearing, rotting, or a great mountain of flesh with hundreds of thousands of eyes that incessantly devour; and when encountered by thought, it can become ash, pestilence, or flight.
Fourth, the retribution of taste attracts evil fruits;
when this karmic action of taste intersects with others, at the time of death, one first sees an iron net of fierce, blazing flames covering the entire world.

The deceased’s consciousness passes through the iron net and hangs upside down with its head downward, entering the Avīci Hell. Two manifestations appear: first, the inhaled breath solidifies into form.
The cold ice freezes both body and flesh; the exhaled breath flies forth as a fierce fire that sears the marrow and bones.

Thus, when tasting flavors, through repeated tasting one can become a vessel of endurance; when seeing sights, through repeated seeing one can become like burning gold and stone; when hearing sounds, through repeated hearing one can become like sharp weapons;
when breathing, through repeated inhalation and exhalation one can become like a great iron cage covering the entire land; and when touching, through repeated contact...
Then one can become a bow, an arrow, a crossbow, or an archer; through repeated contemplation, one can become a flying red-hot iron ball falling from the sky.

These five are the retributions of contact that summon evil fruits. When these karmic contacts intersect, at the moment of death, one first sees a great mountain approaching from all four sides with no way out.
The deceased’s consciousness then sees a great iron city filled with fire-snakes.
Fire-dogs, tigers, wolves, lions, ox-headed hell-wardens, and horse-headed rākṣasas, holding spears and halberds in their hands, drive them through the city gate toward the Avīci Hell.
This gives rise to two types of manifest contact: first, *saṃsparśa* (contact by collision), where mountains press against the body, crushing the flesh and bones until the blood flows;
second, *viṣparśa* (contact by separation), where blades and swords strike the body and mind, carving and tearing open the liver and heart. Thus they undergo both *saṃsparśa* and *viṣparśa*.

When it encounters the Way, it becomes a path; when it encounters contemplation, it becomes a hall; when it encounters a table, it becomes a desk. When it encounters what is seen, it becomes burning and incineration;
when it encounters what is heard, it becomes clashing, striking, stabbing, and shooting. When it encounters what is breathed, it becomes a casket, a bag, an examination, and a binding.
When it encounters what is tasted, it becomes plowing, tongs, hacking, and cutting. When it encounters what is thought, it becomes a fall.
Whether it be flying, boiling, or roasting—these six ways of thinking about retribution attract and draw forth evil fruits.

When such thoughts of karma intersect, at the moment of death, one first sees an evil wind blowing away and destroying the land. The deceased’s spirit-consciousness is blown upward into the void, only to swirl down and fall, carried by the wind, into the Avīci Hell.
This manifests two signs: the first is that, failing to awaken, delusion reaches its extreme, and one runs about in wild panic.
If one does not cease these two, one will not be deluded regarding awakening and cognition; yet suffering is immeasurable, a scorching heat so deep it is difficult to endure.
Thus, when perverse thoughts form knots, they can become a square for binding and a mirror for testimony;
when they knot the hearing, they can become a great confluence of stones, ice, frost, earth, and mist; when they knot the breath, they can become a great [obstruction].
When bound by the touch of fire-chariots, fire-ships, and fire-cages, one may experience great wailing, remorse, and weeping;
when bound by the touch of [other] fetters, one may become large or small, undergo ten thousand births and ten thousand deaths within a single day, and be cast face-down or face-up.

The triad of faculty (*indriya*), object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is like a cluster of *akṣa* fruits. If there were no faculty and object, by what means would consciousness create karma?

If there were no object and consciousness, by what means would the faculty receive retribution? Therefore, Wu Xing said: "In creating karma and attracting retribution, the faculty and consciousness must coexist.
That one now takes consciousness as the karma while retribution emerges from the faculty is because karma proceeds contrarily from the mind, whereas retribution follows the faculty.

This is primarily because it concerns the physical form (*rūpa*). "The intersection of seeing and karma" refers to the moment when the evil karma created by the faculty of sight is about to undergo death—the time when the two tendencies of the "inverse at death" and the "concordant at birth" intersect.

This clarifies that those with extremely heavy evil karma enter directly into the Avīci Hell without passing through an intermediate state (*antarābhava*); this is what is meant in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* when it states that "extreme goodness and extreme evil [both bypass the intermediate state]."

There is no intermediate state (antarābhava). To clarify the two aspects [of perception], it is said that in ordinary times, when the sense organs produce offenses, there are originally two kinds of differences:
first, those arising from seeing in light; second, those arising from seeing in darkness.

Therefore, the retribution received now also differs according to the delusions and karma, manifesting through either light or darkness. First, the evil retribution summoned by one organ causes the remaining five [organs] to...

That the sense organs also experience [retribution] for one another is truly because, at the time of committing an offense, although one consciousness may serve as the primary agent, it must have once stirred up and harmonized with the other consciousnesses; thus, one now experiences this retribution.

Had there been even a single consciousness absent or inactive at the time of committing the offense, then at the time of receiving retribution, one would likewise be spared from that particular suffering. This applies to the ear-consciousness as well.
The fundamental nature of transgression inherently possesses two aspects: opening and closing; likewise, the consciousness that creates transgression inherently possesses two aspects:
delusion and awakening. The meaning of the evil retributions summoned by these states can all be understood. As for the "mind-only hells" and "hells that are mind-only":

when one is deluded regarding *prajñā*, confusion arises; when one is deluded regarding liberation, karma arises; and when one is deluded regarding the *dharmakāya*, suffering arises. When reading the sutras and reaching this point—
One who does not feel a sense of urgency to sever the three conditions of birth and death, nor one who does not experience a sudden awakening to the three causes of intrinsic virtue, is no true man.
This concludes the third section.
Ānanda, these ten causes and six effects of the hells are all created by the deluded ignorance of sentient beings. If...

If sentient beings collectively commit evil karma and enter the Avīci Hell to undergo immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas, it is because their six sense organs each committed offenses, as well as the actions performed through those organs and their respective objects.
Such persons enter the Eight Uninterrupted Hells (*aṣṭāv-avīcika-naraka*).

If one commits the three acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, one enters the eighteen hells. If the three karmas are not combined, one falls into the intermediate hells.
If one commits a single act of killing or a single act of stealing, that person enters thirty-six hells;
if they commit a single offense with a single faculty, they enter one hundred and eight hells. Thus, sentient beings act and create individually, entering the common ground within the world;
these are produced by delusive thoughts and do not exist from the beginning.
"Creating evil karma together" refers to the ten causes being created simultaneously by all six sense-faculties at all times.
"Each of the six sense-faculties creates [karma]" means that although each of the six faculties has its own offenses, they do not create them at one time;

or it refers to the inclusion of only several of the ten causal objects, or the inclusion of only several of the six sense-faculties. Regarding the three actions of body, speech, and mind, these refer to killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

To "diminish three of the six faculties" means to lack seven of the ten causes. To say that "the three karmas are not simultaneous" means that among body, speech, and mind, any one of them may be missing.
Alternatively, it refers to performing only one act of killing or one act of stealing, meaning that any one of the three unwholesome karmas may be absent.
"Seeing with only one faculty" means that among the six faculties, only a single faculty is used to create karma.
Citing "seeing seeing" serves as an analogy for "hearing hearing" and so forth. "Committing a single karma alone" refers to creating only one of the ten causes.
"Separately acting and separately creating" clarifies that evil karma invites its own retribution.

"Entering the stage of the same category" clarifies that this is accompanied by the delusive thoughts of the original ground, which arise and do not exist from the beginning. "The reality is fundamentally true and pure" clarifies that it is inherently authentic and stainless.
That which exists is precisely non-existent, for like a flower in the sky it lacks substantiality; thus it is said to be "non-existent.
This does not mean that what was originally non-existent later becomes existent—reflect on this, reflect on this. Second, showing the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati).
Part one: general indication; part two: specific manifestation; part three: concluding demonstration. Now, the first [general indication].

Furthermore, Ānanda, these sentient beings—having violated the codes of discipline, transgressed the bodhisattva precepts, and defiled and cast aside nirvāṇa, as well as having performed various other miscellaneous karmas—are burned for kalpas;
only when their retribution is exhausted do they receive the forms of various hungry ghosts.

The *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhikāra* states that there are four distinctions regarding the realm of ghosts (*preta-gati*): first, those who directly incur retribution due to the cause of minor ten non-virtuous actions;
second, those whose retribution is suddenly drawn forth by the power of past ripening karma (*vipāka-karma*);

third, those who first experience the "flower-retribution" (*pūrvanimitta*) prior to entering hell; and fourth, those who receive this residual retribution after emerging from hell. To state it briefly, these are the seven [categories].
Those who proceed toward future existence can all proceed to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*);

within this single destination, there are further distinctions of three categories—those with wealth, those with little wealth, and those without wealth—and nine grades. What has been stated here is merely a general and brief explanation regarding the remaining retribution for those in the hells.
Second, a detailed exposition.
If one commits the offense of greed for material objects, when that person's retribution is exhausted, they encounter matter and take form; such a being is called a "monster ghost" (*guāiguǐ*).
If one commits the offense of greed for sensual beauty, when that person's retribution is exhausted, they encounter wind and take form; such a being is called a "drought demon ghost" (*bóguǐ*).

If one commits the offense of greed for delusion, when that person's retribution is exhausted, they encounter an animal and take form; such a being is called a "seductive ghost" (*mèiguǐ*). If one commits the offense of greed for resentment, when that person's retribution is exhausted...

When they encounter insects and take form, they are called *gudu* (poisonous) ghosts; their sin was greed for memory. When these people have finished their retribution and encounter decay, they take form as *li* ghosts;
their sin was greed for arrogance. When they have finished their retribution and encounter vapors, they take form as hungry ghosts;
their sin was greed for deception. When they have finished their retribution and encounter the obscure, they take form as *yan* ghosts; their sin was greed for light.
When this person’s retribution for their sins has ended, they encounter refined essence and take on form, named a *wangliang* ghost; their sin was greed for success.

When this person’s retribution for their sins has ended, they encounter brightness and take on form, named a *yishi* ghost; their sin was greed for factions. When this person’s retribution for their sins has ended, they encounter human beings and take on form, named a *chuanzong* ghost.
Coveting objects is the habit of greed; because one is attached to various things, one now encounters objects and becomes a *guài* (a monster).
Coveting beauty is the habit of lust; because one is fanned by the winds of lust, one now encounters wind and becomes a *pó* (a drought-demon) who creates the calamity of drought.
Coveting delusion is the habit of deceit; because one has made flattery one's nature, one now encounters livestock [and takes possession of them].
Becoming a *mei* (possessing spirit) is like the class of *yaohu* (fox-spirits), which still seeks to seduce and delude people;
