greed and resentment are the habitual tendencies of *dveṣa* (hatred), for because the mind harbors poisonous malice, one now encounters insects that form *gu* (poisonous spirits) to inflict harm upon people.

Greed and recollection are the habitual tendencies of *vaira* (enmity), for because one clutches at resentment without forgetting it, one now manifests as a pestilence in response to misfortune, bringing early death.
Enmity and greediness constitute the habit of arrogance;

because one prizes their own spirit and relies on themselves, they now encounter this spirit and become a hungry ghost (*preta*), which is the severe retribution for being "empty-stomached and high-minded. Greed and deception constitute the habit of litigation;
because one obscured others and committed villainy, they now encounter the darkness and become a nightmare-ghost (*yamaloka-peta*), continuing as before to ride upon others.
To be startled by a nightmare while lying down is the habit-energy of greed for light;

because of such perverse awakening and perverse attachment, one now encounters a *piśāca* ghost formed from this refinement—appearing lofty and brilliant when viewed from afar, yet lacking any true majesty or virtue upon closer approach.
To be greedy for success is the habit-energy of perversion; because of leading others into transgression by pointing to darkness as light, one now encounters...
The Ming spirits serve as messengers for ghosts to assist humans in accomplishing their affairs. Those who are greedy and factional are those habituated to litigation;
because they expose the private secrets of others, they must necessarily involve bystanders as witnesses.
Thus, when they encounter humans, the ghosts employ them to transmit all manner of secret matters. These ten classes of beings each have their own distinct experiences of suffering and joy.
That the retributions differ is also omitted from the explanation and can be inferred through reasoning. Third, the summary indication:

Ānanda, these people all fall due to their pure delusion; scorched by the fires of karma, they emerge above as ghosts. All such beings are summoned and led forth by the karma of their own false imaginings.
If one awakens to Bodhi, then the wondrous, perfect, and luminous nature is fundamentally non-existent [of such states].
Regarding all such beings:
those referred to as "humans" originally descended from the human realm due to having created the ten habitual causes;
although they have been scorched dry by the fires of karma and emerged above as ghosts, their former habits remain, and thus one must be cautious regarding past conditioning.
It is likewise so; since it is said that awakening to bodhi is fundamentally non-existent, how could it truly exist now while one is precisely in a state of delusion?
It is simply that a film obscures the eye, causing illusory flowers to fall in confusion. How lamentable! Third, the demonstration of the animal realm has three parts:
first, a general heading; second, a detailed exposition; third, a concluding indication. This is the first.
Furthermore, Ānanda, once the karmic retribution of the ghost is exhausted, both emotion and thought become empty;
only then, when encountering the person to whom one originally owed a debt in the world, does one take the body of an animal to repay that past debt.

Regarding the explanation of the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*), there are also four distinctions: first, those who directly incur retribution due to the cause of the ten non-virtuous actions of middling degree;
second, those whose retribution is suddenly drawn by the power of past ripening karma (*vipāka-karma*); third, those who immediately repay their debt upon emerging from hell;
and fourth, those who repay their debt after coming from the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). To state it briefly, these are the seven [categories].

All those who proceed toward future existence may likewise proceed into the realm of animals; yet within this single destination, there are further distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior grades, each consisting of three different types.
What has been said here regarding the exhaustion of karmic retribution for hungry ghosts is merely a general statement.
As for the claim that both feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are entirely empty, it refers to those who previously fell into hell, or—
This refers to those who are purely insentient and without thought, or those with nine feelings and one thought,
eight feelings and two thoughts, and so forth, even within the realm of hungry ghosts, or those with seven feelings and three thoughts— these directly invite [rebirth]. Now, however,

because the power of the accumulated evil feelings and virtuous thoughts has been exhausted and no longer invites the retribution of suffering in those two realms, it is said that they "become empty."
This does not mean that one simultaneously empties past karmic debts, nor does it mean that one can empty the very substance of delusion. Second, the specific manifestations:
ghostly creatures of strange objects are dissolved when their retribution is exhausted; those born in the world are mostly of the *xiāo* (owls) class. Ghosts of wind and drought...
When the retribution for their wind-nature is exhausted, they are born into the world mostly as omens of calamity;

the ghosts of beasts and enchantments, when their retribution for being animals is exhausted, are mostly born into the world as foxes; the ghosts of insect-pestilence, when their retribution for being vermin is exhausted, are mostly born into the world as poisonous species;
and the ghosts of decay and exhaustion, when their retribution for decay is exhausted, are born into the world.
For the most part, those who were of the *huí* class become ghosts that receive vital breath;

when their retribution for this is exhausted, they are reborn into the world, mostly as the *shí* class of ghosts dwelling in deep obscurity. When their retribution for this is exhausted, they are reborn into the world, mostly as the *fú* class of ghosts of harmonized essence.

When their retribution for this is exhausted, they are reborn into the world, mostly as the *yìng* class of ghosts of luminous spirits. When their luminosity fades and their retribution is exhausted...
Those born into the world as omens of good fortune for the most part belong to the category of ghosts that depend on humans;
when their retribution is exhausted and they are reborn into the world, they mostly follow their previous species.

As for those of the *xiāo* (owls) class, due to the habitual tendencies of thievery and greed, they form offspring from clods of earth. Furthermore, among those with the gravest habits of thievery and greed, none surpasses this.
Just as eating meat leads one to harbor resentment and seek revenge, resulting in the perception of one's parents as food, so too do all signs of anomaly portend impending calamity.
Through the habit of lust, one becomes a demon or a malevolent spirit; through the habit of deceit, one becomes a fox; through the habit of malice, one becomes a venomous creature;
and through the habit of resentment, one becomes a parasitic worm that preys upon human vulnerabilities—all of these are likewise [the results of past karma].

It should be understood that because of arrogance, one falsely claims that Heaven created all things fundamentally to nourish humanity, taking the flesh and blood of sentient beings to satisfy their own hunger;

thus, as retribution, they now become food for others. Furthermore, because the habit of arrogance led them to insult others, they now receive this ultimate insult by having their own flesh served as food.
As for those belonging to the category of clothing, such as silkworms and various furs and hides—
To provide clothing, oxen, horses, and mounts for riding because of past deceits, and to repay debts with these now—
such things as the "sociable swallows" (*sèyàn*) and the "cold-swans" (*hán hóng*) that arrive according to the seasons— are remnants of various wrong views concerning time and direction.
As for "auspicious omens" (*xiūzhēng*), these range from the magnificent phoenix and the auspicious qilin down to the chirping of magpies.
Those such as the "retribution for joy" (happiness) result from having wronged others in the past and committed offenses; therefore, they now recompense people with good fortune to repay them.

Those that "follow their kind," such as cats and dogs, result from having greedily sided with factions and brought lawsuits against others in the past; thus, they now remain submissive and compliant toward people.
Regarding the statement that these occur "mostly," this is said by way of general outline to demonstrate that it is not necessarily the case in every instance.
Ānanda, these three cases illustrate that all such beings have their karmic debts exhausted by the fire of their own karma, yet they remain as animals as collateral for those debts.
These states, too, are all summoned and drawn forth by one's own deluded karma; if one awakens to Bodhi, then these deluded conditions are fundamentally non-existent.
All such evil karmas as those of Ratnapadmagandha and others you mentioned, as well as that of King Vaidūrya and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, originally arose from their own minds;
they did not descend from heaven, nor emerge from the earth, nor were bestowed by humans. They were summoned by one's own delusions and must be experienced by oneself.
Within the mind of Bodhi, they are all merely solidified accumulations of floating and empty false thoughts.
Due to the fire of afflictions (*kleśa*), the fire of karma (*karman*) is produced; due to the fire of karma, the fire of retribution (*vipāka*) is experienced.

What is now called the "drying up of the fire of karma" means that evil karma is like fuel: as long as the fuel is not exhausted, the fire will not cease. This is explained in terms of the effect following from its cause.

If one awakens to Bodhi and first transforms the fire of afflictions into the fire of wisdom (*jñāna*), then all the fuel of karma— *Note: The sentence appears to be incomplete, but the translation reflects the provided text.*
If it is burned away in the present moment, what need is there to wait for the fires of hell to burn one? It is simply because one is deluded regarding Bodhi that it becomes affliction;
because one is deluded regarding liberation that it becomes evil karma; and because one is deluded regarding the Dharma-body that it becomes the retribution of suffering.

Nevertheless, the nature of affliction is not separate from Bodhi; how could the nature of evil karma differ from liberation? And how could the nature of the retribution of suffering differ [from the Dharma-body]?
Is it not because the external dharmas are the body [of reality] that they are called Bodhi? Within the mind, all things are merely the congealing of floating, empty, and false imaginings;
it is like mistaking space for flowers or freezing water into ice. How could there be flowers outside of space, or ice outside of water?
IV. Showing the Human Realm (in three parts): 1. General Statement; 2. Specific Explanation; 3. Concluding Indication.
Now, first:
Furthermore, Ānanda, when these beings from the animal realm repay their former debts, if the debtor pays more than what is required to settle the debt,
these beings shall again become human and must repay the excess, provided that the creditor possesses the power to enforce it.
If one possesses both merit and virtue, one will not lose the human body among humans, but will repay that person’s labor.

If one lacks merit, one will instead be reborn as an animal to repay the remaining balance. Ānanda, you should know that if one uses money or goods, or employs their labor, the debt is settled and the cycle ceases;
however, if in the interim one kills their life or eats their flesh—and so forth—[the consequences follow].
For as many eons as there are atoms, they devour and slaughter one another like a turning wheel, rising and falling in alternation without rest;
this cannot cease except through *śamatha* or the appearance of a Buddha in the world.

This clarifies the signs of returning to the human realm from within the three evil destinies, and provides a detailed demonstration that the karma of killing is difficult to cease, in order to warn those who are deluded.
To speak specifically of the human realm, there are also three distinctions:

first, those who take the five precepts and the medium grade of the ten wholesome actions as their cause, directly attaining their fruit; second, those who come from superior classes, such as celestial beings and immortals.
Third, those who come from the evil realms are further divided into four categories: namely, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras.

Here, we speak only in terms of those who were animals and have now resumed human form; this is merely a general and brief explanation. Within the process of mutual retribution, there are two distinctions:
first, the power of retribution; second, the retribution for killing. Regarding the power of retribution, there are again two [aspects]. First...
Those with the power of merit repay their debts within human form, while those without such power are reborn as animals to repay them.
There are two ways in which they repay the debt of killing: first, by being eaten by one another as animals; second, by slaughtering one another among humans.
Since humans kill animals, animals likewise harm humans; through this karma of mutual devouring and mutual slaughter, enmities are bound together and grudges continue until the end.

There is no day on which one may rest, except when one practices the single mind of the three types of cessation (*samatha*) and forever transcends birth and death, at which point one may finally cease;

or when the Buddhas appear in the world and, through the power of inconceivable great compassion and great supernormal powers, resolve enmities and untie knots for one, at which time one may also cease. Apart from these two paths, even if one passes through...
Though kalpas as numerous as motes of dust have constantly passed like the turning of a wheel, the path of śamatha is exceptionally difficult to reach;
that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is so remote and hard to encounter—how lamentable this is! How terrifying! This is the second part: the specific explanation.
You should now know that those of the owl class, having fully expiated their retribution, will take rebirth in the human realm among the dull-witted;
those of the omen-sign class, having fully expiated their retribution, will take rebirth in the human realm among the eccentric;

those of the fox class, having fully expiated their retribution, will take rebirth in the human realm among the mediocre; and those of the venomous class, having fully expiated their retribution, will likewise take rebirth.
Those who, having been born among humans, were combined with the category of the stubborn—those of the class of worms—once their retribution is fulfilled, they take form again among humans;
those who were combined with the category of the subtle—those of the class of food—once their retribution is fulfilled, they take form again among humans;

those who were combined with the category of the supple—those of the class of clothing—once their retribution is fulfilled, they take form again among humans; and those who were combined with the category of the laborious—those of the class of service.
Having fulfilled their retribution and returned to life within the human realm, they join the class of the refined, like those who possess auspicious omens;

having fulfilled their retribution and returned to life within the human realm, they join the class of the enlightened, like those who follow the social order; having fulfilled their retribution and returned to life within the human realm, they join the class of the accomplished.

The human realm inherently possesses the true causes, namely the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions. Now, because these have been fully requited and one has returned to a physical form, they are all said to be "intermingled.
Because of eating, one becomes ignorant and stubborn—this is what is meant by "profit dulls the intellect.

Because of lust, one becomes strange and perverse—this is what is meant by "disrupting kinship and destroying principle. Because of much deceit, one becomes vulgar and contemptible. Because of harboring anger, one becomes cruel and poisonous.

Because one harbors resentment despite benevolence, one is base and insignificant, unworthy of being ranked among men; because of arrogance, one loses one's own power and majesty; because of being weak and yielding, one allows oneself to be deceived by others;
because of the burden of repaying debts, one exhausts the body; because of false views, one skillfully adorns one's speech with rhetoric;

because of the habit of litigation, one possesses a small measure of wisdom and keen discernment; and because of the habit of worldly affairs, one is adept at practical matters—none of these are the ways to span the heavens and weave the earth.
These texts represent the clarity of observing what is above and examining what is below, and the penetration of brilliant intelligence and sagely wisdom. [The Buddha] showed this three times.

Ānanda, all these beings have fully repaid their past debts and returned to human form; yet, from time immemorial, their karmic calculations have been inverted, leading to mutual birth and mutual killing.
Had they not encountered the Tathāgata and heard the True Dharma, they would have remained as they naturally were amidst the dust and toil of worldly afflictions.
These types of people who revolve in this cycle are called the pitiable.
Although they have resumed human form, they give rise to delusions and create karma within the human realm; before long, they fall again into the wheel of suffering.
Because of lustful desire, they give birth to one another; because of killing and stealing, they kill one another. It is like pressing upon the eyes, causing flowers to appear in a blur.
That such things occur is truly pitiable; should not those who cultivate their minds regard the severing of karma as an urgent task?
Part Five: Showing the Realm of Immortals (3): First, a general indication; second, a detailed exposition; third, a concluding demonstration. Now, the first [the general indication]:

Ānanda, furthermore, there are followers who do not rely on perfect enlightenment to cultivate *samādhi*, but instead cultivate deluded thoughts to preserve their forms through visualization, roaming in mountain forests and remote places inaccessible to ordinary people; these are the ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*).
The phrase "furthermore, there are those who follow others" intends to clarify that for advancing toward Bodhi, only the human path is easy;

now that one has fortunately obtained a human body and furthermore possesses some knowledge of cultivation and progress, it would be most regrettable not to rely on the Perfect Enlightenment to cultivate *samādhi*, but instead to cultivate deluded thoughts.
"Not relying on Perfect Enlightenment" means not employing the correct [method].

Taking awakening as the fundamental cause for cultivation yet failing to practice samādhi means not employing the Śūraṅgama Samādhi to advance toward the ultimate fruit, but instead separately cultivating deluded thoughts;
this clearly demonstrates that apart from the Buddha-dharma, there is absolutely no true cultivation.

To maintain the body by fixing the mind on mental images clearly shows that although the ten types of immortals differ in their methods, their ultimate aim is the same: none transcend the solidification of their deluded forms.
There are two kinds of forms: first, the ephemeral sense organs (*rajas-mūla-indriya*), and second, the ultimate sense organs (*paramārtha-indriya*).

If one desires that [the self] remain eternally together with the physical body, then one is clinging to the ephemeral form. If one desires to cast off the ordinary carcass and undergo transformation, then one is clinging to the ultimate form.
One calculates these ultimate sense organs to be the original life-spirit (*prāṇa-ātman*) and does not realize their [true nature].
"Just as the *kinnara* jar is merely a color-form produced by the illusory delusions of birth and death, and is not the true self; secondly, to distinguish and reveal:
Ānanda, those sentient beings who take solid food and drink without ceasing, and whose path of eating is perfected, are named the Stage of Earth (*bhūmi*)."
The Immortal of Firmness of Wood and Grass attains the Way of Medicinal Efficacy and is named the Flying Immortal; he remains firm without ceasing.
The Immortal of Firmness of Metal and Stone attains the Way of Transformation and is named the Wandering Immortal; he remains firm without ceasing.

The Immortal of Firmness of Movement and Stillness attains the Perfection of Vital Energy and Essence and is named the Space-Walking Immortal; he remains firm without ceasing. The Immortal of Firmness of Saliva and Fluids attains the Virtue of Moistening and remains firm without ceasing.
The perfection of the name "Heavenly Practice Immortal" consists in the firmness of vital essence and color without ceasing;

the perfection of the name "Pervasive Practice Immortal" consists in the firmness of incantations and prohibitions without ceasing; the perfection of the name "Path Practice Immortal" consists in the firmness of contemplation without ceasing;

the perfection of the name "Illuminating Practice Immortal" consists in the firmness of recollection without ceasing; the perfection of the name "Mutual Union Practice Immortal" consists in the firmness of sexual union without ceasing.
Those who attain perfection through the response of resting are called *jingxing-xian* (Perfected Beings of Refinement); they possess firm transformations yet do not cease their practice.
Those who attain perfection through awakening are called *juexing-xian* (Perfected Beings of Transcendence).
As for those who firmly apply medicinal elixirs, because they consume substances that prolong life and do not avoid fire or smoke, they merely attain longevity and are thus so named.
The earth-walking immortals (*bhūcaras*) who fortify themselves with plants and trees do not employ fire or smoke, but instead consume pine, cypress, yellow essence (*huangjing*), and the like;

thus their bodies can ascend lightly, and they are called flying immortals (*khecaras*). Those who fortify themselves with metals and minerals use the five metals and five stones to refine external elixirs (*bāidāna*);
therefore, they can transform their forms, change their bones, and by taking up earth and dotting stones, they sport among humanity.

Those known as Wandering Immortals (*cāraṇa-ṛṣi*) who are firm in their movements and stillness regulate their breath and consolidate their essence, casting off their physical forms to traverse the void;

thus, because their vital energy and essence are perfected, they are called Void-Walking Immortals (*ākāśa-cārin*). Those who are firm in their fluids strike the "Heavenly Pond" and swallow their saliva, remaining untainted by worldly desires;
consequently, their skin becomes like ice and snow, and their graceful elegance is like that of a maiden, making them no different from the heavens.

Those called *devacara* (Heavenly-Walking) Immortals possess firm and pure vital essence; because they inhale wind and drink dew, and gather the refined quintessence of the sun and moon, they are able to penetrate the processes of transformation (*zaohua*).
Those called *vidyacara* (Wisdom-Walking) Immortals possess firm mastery of incantations and prohibitions;

because they specialize in esoteric arts and methods, they are able to command ghosts and spirits to manifest their spiritual power. Those called *margacara* (Path-Walking) Immortals are those who, in this manner, propagate the Way.
Furthermore, among the followers of [Zhang] Ling, there are those who rely on the Esoteric (Mijiao) division of the Inner Teachings; some have even erroneously produced this [practice].

Those who maintain firm contemplation may visualize the spirit emerging from the crown of the head, or fix the mind on the *dantian* to refine the vital breath (*qi*), or send their thoughts to Mount Penglai to cast off their mortal shells.
Because they can achieve clear illumination and responsive resonance through long-term, concentrated, and refined reflection, it is called "Illuminating Practice" (*zhàoxíng*).

Regarding the "Immortal’s Firm Union": taking the heart as the Li-fire and the kidneys as the Kan-water, one causes the fire to descend and the water to ascend so that they may unite and form the Immortal Embryo;
thus, through the perfection of resonance, it is called the "Essential Practice for the Firm Transformation of the Immortal. Regarding the "Firm Transformation of the Immortal":
this refers to the principle of maintaining mental visualization for transformation; because the mind follows false awakenings, one is able to give rise to great transformations.
Their transformative practices are transcendent, and they are known as the "Transcendent Immortals of Extraordinary Conduct.
Although these ten types of immortals differ in their levels of attainment, each maintains that one must be firm and unceasing to achieve perfect realization;
thus, the labor of their refinement is by no means easy. Even the delusive fruits they achieve do not exceed a lifespan of ten million years. If...
If one applies this entire spirit toward cultivating samādhi based on right awakening, how could one not suddenly ascend to the state of eternal abiding?

It is like the medicine that prevents hands from cracking, which can be used to spin fine silk; or like the luminous pearl, which may even be used to shoot at yellow sparrows—how lamentable such a waste would be!
This concludes the third section of the exposition.
Ānanda, these individuals all refine their minds among human beings, yet they do not cultivate true awakening;

instead, they separately attain a mode of existence, living for ten million years in deep mountains or on remote ocean islands far from the realm of men. This, too, is the circulation of deluded thoughts within saṃsāra;
failing to cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more to be scattered and enter the various realms of existence.
Although they refine their minds, they do not cultivate correct awakening; therefore, they remain deluded regarding the non-arising [of phenomena] and instead grasp at a principle of arising.
Once their celestial retribution is exhausted, they revert to flowing according to karma and disperse into the various other six realms of existence.
How can this be considered noble? Section Six: Showing the Celestial Realm, Part Two: First, a specific showing of the various heavens; second, a summary of their falsity.

The first of the three sections [of the initial part] consists of: first, the cause of the desire heavens; second, the specific characteristics of the six heavens; and third, the conclusion establishing the name "desire realm. The first of these [three] also has three parts:

first, a general indication of the causes for the desire heavens; second, a detailed presentation of the characteristics of the six heavens; and third, the conclusion that establishes the designation of the desire realm.
First: Ānanda, people in the world do not seek the eternally abiding; they are unable to relinquish the affectionate attachments to their wives and concubines.
Those who do not seek the eternally abiding lack the wisdom for transcending the world; this is a universal delusion within these three realms.
Those who are able to renounce their affection for wives and concubines yet do not cultivate supramundane precepts and meditative concentration possess these specific afflictions of the desire realm;
because of these two types of affliction, they are thus constantly bound by the desire realm. Second, to specifically indicate the characteristics of the six heavens, they are as follows:
first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, up to sixth, the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations.

First: those who, regarding sexual misconduct, have minds that do not wander or dissipate, but are clarified and polished so that luminosity arises; after their lives end, they dwell in proximity to the sun and moon—this class of beings is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

While the various heavens of the desire realm all share the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions as their cause, the reason this specific instance of sexual misconduct is singled out is that such lust is precisely the root of birth and death;
thus, it is discussed alone to illustrate the principles of ascent and descent, while the others may be understood by analogy.
According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, the merit of abstaining from killing is so preeminent that it can [lead one to]... [the heavens].
Having been born in this heaven, if one’s mind does not now flow toward or stray into sexual misconduct, then it goes without saying that one will not commit killing.
Regarding the Four Heavenly Kings: Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east is the king of the gandharvas; Virūḍhaka in the south is the king of the kumbhāṇḍas;
Virūpākṣa in the west is the king of the nāgas; and Vaiśravaṇa in the north is the king of the yakṣas.
O King, this deity dwells forty-two thousand yojanas above the human realm;
his body is one-quarter of a krośa in height—equivalent to seventy-five zhang by the local *zhou* measure—and his lifespan is five hundred years, with one day and night equaling fifty human years.
Calculated by human reckoning, this amounts to nine million years. It is likewise so.
Among those who meet with premature death, at the time of passing away, the five signs of decline appear, causing them extreme suffering and distress.

Second, as for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, their sensual desire for their own wives is slight; however, when they dwell in the Pure Abodes, they cannot fully savor that bliss, and thus, after their lives end, [they fall].
Surpassing the brilliance of the sun and moon and dwelling at the summit of the human realm—this class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Because their sexual desire is also diminished, they surpass the preceding heavens.

According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, through the superior merit of abstaining from killing and stealing, one can be born in this heaven and dwell at the summit of the human realm; this refers specifically to the peak of Mount Sumeru. Now, looking toward it...
That which appears as a vast blue expanse is this very realm. Situated eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above the earth, it comprises the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*).
This consists of eight celestial palaces located in each of the four directions, together with the palace of Śakra, the King of Devas, at its center;
because these are arranged side by side, it is called the Heaven of the Thirty-three. The bodies of the deities therein are all half a *krośa* in height.
When measured by the Zhou *chi*, one hundred and fifty *zhang* equals the height of Śakra, which is one *krośa*;

this is equal to the height of the gods of Tuṣita Heaven. Because he extensively cultivated the karma of reverence in the past, his lifespan is one thousand years, with one human century constituting a single day and night;
calculated by human reckoning, this amounts to thirty-six million years.
There are also those who die prematurely in their youth, as well as the suffering of the manifestation of the five signs of decay; these [sufferings] are the same for all four lower heavens.
Third is the Yama Heaven (Suyāma).
When encountering desire, they engage briefly and then depart without lingering thoughts; in the human world, they are active for little and tranquil for much. After the end of their lives...
Abiding serenely in the midst of empty space, the radiance of the sun and moon cannot reach them from above;
these beings possess their own natural light, and such a class is named the Suyāma Heaven.

Having little movement and much stillness means that by practicing both seated meditation and [walking meditation], one is able to transcend the earth-dwelling realms and achieve residence in the sky-dwelling realms.
According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, through the superior merit of abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, one can be reborn in this heaven.
It is situated sixteen thousand *yojanas* above this earthly realm; there is a ground like clouds, radiant and clear.
The Abhāsvara Heaven (Suyāma) is so named because its day and night are distinguished solely by the opening and closing of lotus flowers;
it is also translated as "Time-Portion" (Śubhakṛtsna) or "Exquisite Goodness.

Its inhabitants are two hundred twenty-five *zhang* in height (measured by the human *chi*), and they have a lifespan of two thousand years, with one human year of two hundred years constituting a single day and night for them. Fourth is Tuṣita.
The Deva of the Station of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). At all times tranquil, even when contacted by sensory objects, they are unable to be disturbed;

after death, they ascend to the subtle and refined realms, not descending to the levels of humans or devas of the lower realms, nor being affected by the three calamities when the kalpa is destroyed. Such is this class of beings.
It is named Tuṣita Heaven.

Because it is always tranquil and has already attained meditative concentration within the Desire Realm, it is able to remain detached from the sensory realms of the various humans and devas of the lower levels;
this refers generally to the outer precincts. Furthermore, even when the kalpa is destroyed by the three calamities, this place remains beyond their reach.
Referring to the inner court, Tuṣita is also called Dṛṣṭā; this translates as "Contentment" (Zizu) and also as "Wondrous Contentment" (Miaozu).
According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, through the superior merit of the threefold physical and fourfold verbal virtuous precepts, one can be reborn in this heaven.
It is located thirty-two hundred thousand yojanas away from this world; there is a ground like clouds above it.
The gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati) have bodies that are three hundred *zhang* in circumference;
they take four hundred human years as one day and night, and their lifespan is four thousand years.
I am free from desire and merely comply with your actions; when we lie together, the experience is like chewing wax.
After death, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati). This class of beings is called the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations.

Chewing wax is used as a metaphor for being without flavor; this refers to the state of one who has already attained concentration within the desire realm and is further cultivating the *anāgamya* (unattained) stage.

As for those who transcend transformation, they are called the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati*) because they can surpass the lower realms and exercise the power of transformation.
They are also called *Suyāma* in Sanskrit. They depart from this world-system.
Sixty-four thousand yojanas above, there is a ground like clouds upon which they dwell;
their bodies are three hundred and seventy-five zhang tall, one day and night is equivalent to eight hundred years of the human world, and their lifespan is eight thousand years.
This is the sixth [heaven], the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Without a worldly mind, they perform worldly deeds; yet while engaging in such activities, they clearly transcend them.

After the end of life, they are able to universally transcend and transform both realms of transformation and non-transformation. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).

To be clearly transcendent amidst the activities of worldly interaction is to have already accomplished the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the concentration of the stage not yet reached), wherein even the taste of chewing wax is absent.
To transcend the realm of transformation (*nirmāṇa-rati*) means to transcend the fifth heaven, the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations;

to transcend the realm of non-transformation (*para-nirmita-vaśavartin*) means to transcend the four heavens preceding it. In the Sanskrit language this is called *paranirmita-vaśavartin*, which in Chinese is translated as "Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations."
One million two hundred and eighty thousand yojanas away from this world, there is a ground like clouds upon which beings dwell;
they are four hundred and fifty *zhang* in height, and their one day and night is equivalent to one thousand six hundred years of human reckoning, with a lifespan of sixteen thousand years.
Furthermore, the palace of Māra is also located in this heaven.
It is said that between the two realms of desire and form, there exists a separate palace of Māra. The three fetters (saṃyojana) constitute the name "Desire Realm.
Ānanda, although the forms of these six heavens transcend [the lower states], the traces of their mental activity still intermingle; from this point downward, they are named [the Desire Realm].
Regarding the Desire Realm:
although their forms have emerged from movement, it is said they emerge from the human realm, which is a sphere of distraction;

their mental traces still intersect with the physical, meaning that in the four lower heavens, both mind and traces intersect. In the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations and the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations, although the mind does not intersect, the traces still intersect.

This is stated in terms of the causal stage; if stated in terms of the resultant stage, the Four Heavenly Kings and humans are alike in that their two organs touch one another, yet they emit only wind and have no impurity. In the Yāma Heaven, embracing constitutes desire;

in Tuṣita, grasping hands constitutes desire, which is the intersection of both mind and physical trace; in Nirmāṇarati, laughing together constitutes desire; and in Paranirmita-vaśavartin, [mere gazing] constitutes desire.
If mutual gazing constitutes desire, then while the minds may be joined, the physical traces are not;

nevertheless, because from the causal stage to the resultant stage the degrees of gravity differ, yet in all cases one has not yet escaped the sensual craving for male and female, it is collectively termed the "Desire Realm" (kāmadhātu).
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,

Scroll Eight: Explanatory Text of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
Fascicle Nine: Words and Phrases.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra during the Tang Dynasty;
Words and Phrases composed by the Dharma Master, Bodhisattva-Śrāmaṇera Zhixu of Ancient Wu.

Second, regarding the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are three parts: first, a general presentation of its causes; second, a detailed explanation of its characteristics; and third, a summary of its names. Now, for the first:
Ānanda, among all those in the world who cultivate the mind, if they do not rely on *dhyāna* (meditative absorption), they will lack wisdom; yet they are nonetheless able to...
Holding the body and refraining from sexual desire, whether walking or sitting, one is free from all such thoughts.
This generally clarifies the cause for the fourth dhyāna. Because it can subdue the afflictions of the lower stages, it is also called "cultivating the mind";
because it does not cultivate supramundane wondrous samādhi, it is said that "it does not rely on dhyāna. Because it does not cultivate... [text truncated]
Because he lacks supramundane sublime wisdom, it is said that he possesses no wisdom;

because he does not cultivate supramundane sublime precepts but only cultivates mundane precepts of conduct and mundane dhyāna, it is said that he can only restrain his body and refrain from sexual desire, such that whether walking or sitting, all conceptual thoughts are absent.
Now, if one refrains from sexual desire, the body is constantly pure, which constitutes the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala*).
When one achieves the precepts of action and is free from both conceptualization and mental attachment, the mind is likewise purified;
the tenfold virtues then arise, yet these are not called the "transcendent sublime precepts" or "sublime concentrations.
This is because such is the method of the old physicians, established by ordinary people and non-Buddhists, and is not the *prātimokṣa* ordained by the Tathāgata. Thus it is said.
The Tiantai school has analyzed the guest-natures of morality, concentration, and wisdom in considerable detail; it is truly lamentable that people generally overlook and fail to examine this.
Second, to specifically clarify their characteristics, there are four sections: first, clarifying the first dhyāna (up to) fourth, clarifying the fourth dhyāna.
Now, the first.

When attachment does not arise and there is no lingering desire for the realm of desire, such a person should regard their own body as a companion of Brahmā; this class of beings is called the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārṣadya).
Once the habituation to desire has been eliminated and the mind of detachment manifests, they take pleasure in and accord with all forms of discipline;

such a person is able at that time to practice the virtues of Brahmā; this class of beings is called the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita), whose body and mind are wondrously perfected.
With their dignified deportment unimpaired and their pure precepts reinforced by clear awakening, such persons are able to lead the Brahma hosts as Great Brahma Kings at the appropriate time.
This class of beings is called the Mahābrahmā Heaven. Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction;
although they have not yet attained the true Samādhi of the Correct Cultivation, within their pure minds all outflows [āsravas] are exhausted.
Immovability (*aniñjya*) is called the first dhyāna.
Because it is pure and free from desire, it is called "Brahma"; the Brahma-realm assembly (*brahmakāyika*) refers to the Brahma-ministers (*brahmapurohita*).
The term "discipline" (*vinaya*) also refers to subtle worldly prohibitions and need not necessarily be the Buddha's precepts. The Brahma-ministers are the ministers of Brahmā; since the mind...
Because the body of one free from desire accords with the moral discipline (*saṃvara*), it is said that "body and mind are wondrously perfect.

These characters "wondrous" (*miao*) and "perfect" (*yuan*) are specifically used in reference to that heaven; being far removed from all the coarse and turbid [states] of the desire realm is called "wondrous," while having the merits of the two preceding heavens fully satisfied is called "perfect.
Furthermore, "enlightened understanding" refers precisely to the cultivation of the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).

Because he has accomplished the mind of measure (*pramāṇa-citta*), he attains the status of a Brahmā King. As for the term "superior stream" (*viśeṣa-srotas*), it refers to being progressively superior to the lower stages;
all subsequent instances should be understood accordingly. "All suffering and affliction" specifically refers to the eight sufferings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The two characters for "outflows" (*āsrava*) likewise refer to the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) within the desire realm. "Dhyāna" is a Sanskrit term, fully called *dhyāna*, which is translated here as "calm contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).

Because in stillness it differs from the distracted movement of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and in reflection it differs from the obscurity of the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), it is also called *samādhi* (equipoise).
Within the nine stages, the first dhyāna is termed the "stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion" (*vivekaja-prītisukha-bhūmi*);

this means that by being secluded from the mixed evils of birth in the desire realm, one attains pure bliss. In the Vinaya, this is metaphorically compared to the thorough soaking and moistening of a bath.

Wuxing said: "In the first dhyāna, one cultivates five factors (*dharma*), abandons five hindrances (*ānuśaya*), accomplishes five branches (*aṅga*), possesses eight tactile sensations (*spraṣṭavya*), and manifests ten meritorious qualities.

The five factors are desire (*chanda*), thought (*vitarka*), diligence (*vīrya*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*). The five hindrances are sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), sloth and torpor (*styānamiddha*), restlessness and remorse (*auddhatyakaukṛtya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

The five branches are initial application (*vitarka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind. The eight tactile sensations are movement (*iñjita*) and itching (*kaṇḍūya*)."
Coolness, warmth, lightness, heaviness, roughness, smoothness, and furthermore, there are eight tactile sensations: agitation, tranquility, cold, heat, buoyancy, sinking, hardness, and softness.

Although these eight are largely identical to the aforementioned tactile sensations, when analyzed in detail, they are not without slight differences. Taken together, they are called the sixteen tactile sensations.
As for the ten merits: first, concentration; second, emptiness; third, clarity and purity; fourth, joy and rapture; fifth...

1. Joy; 2. the six wholesome minds; 3. clear and lucid knowledge and vision; 4. liberation from entanglements; 5. the manifestation of the objective realm—these ten mental states are harmonious and supple.
The lifespan of the Brahmakāyika devas is twenty minor kalpas, and their bodies are half a yojana in height.
The lifespan of the Brahmapurohita devas is forty minor kalpas, and their bodies are one yojana in height. The lifespan of the Mahābrahmā devas is sixty minor kalpas, and their bodies...
They are one and a half *yojanas* in height, with bodies resembling those of youths; they wear garments of white silver and gold, and take the joy of meditation as their food.
Furthermore, the *Qishi yinben jing* (Sutra on the Causes and Origins of the World) states: "The gods of the Form Realm do not wear clothes, yet it is no different than if they were wearing them.
Although they have no topknots, it is as if they were wearing celestial crowns. They lack male or female characteristics, and their forms are of a single kind. (*Fayuan zhulin*).

The Forest [of Saṃjīva] said: "The Great Brahmā Heaven has no separate dwelling place; it is situated upon a high, prominent, and magnificent tiered terrace within the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers (Brahmapurohita).
The Great Brahmā King alone dwells atop this to distinguish himself from the multitudes below.

Among these three heavens, the Brahma-pārṣadyas are the common people, the Brahmapurohitas are the ministers, and the Mahābrahmās are the sovereigns. Only in this First Dhyāna does such a distinction exist."
From this point upward, the distinctions between ruler, minister, and commoner are entirely absent.

Now, examining the subsequent text regarding the four heavens of the four dhyānas, as well as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* which mentions the heavenly kings of the second and third dhyānas, we know that this statement is likewise not exhaustive.
As for the fact that the fire at the end of a kalpa can reach up to this heaven, it is due to its internal [nature].
Because there is the fire of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), [the second dhyāna] is clarified.

Ānanda, next is the Brahmā Heaven, where the Brahmās preside over the Brahma-folk and fulfill the Brahma-conduct; their minds are serene and unmoving, and from this profound stillness, light is produced.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*); light upon light shines forth, its radiance inexhaustible, reflecting throughout ten [directions].
The surrounding realms are entirely composed of lapis lazuli; such a class is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābha*).

They absorb and sustain circular radiance to perfect the essence of the teaching, manifesting pure applications of transformation that are inexhaustible; such a class is called the Heaven of Light-Sound (*Ābhāsvara*).
Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be assailed by any anxieties or regrets; yet, although they are not the true cultivation of *samādhi*, they are nonetheless free from all afflictions.
When the coarse outflows within the mind have been suppressed through the purity of the stage, it is called the Second Dhyāna.
"The perfection of the Brahma-conduct" refers back to the previous mention of the Brahma King.

"The tranquil mind is unmoving" means that one is simultaneously free from the two factors of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), thereby accomplishing the four factors of internal clarity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind. This is the reflection.
Regarding the "ten directions," for the time being, the medium chiliocosm is indicated as these ten directions. Light constitutes the essence of the teaching;
it is metaphorically called "Light-Sound" (Ābhāsvara) because, in the human world, sound serves as the vehicle of instruction. This does not mean that light actually possesses sound.

Since the first dhyāna involves vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), there is still anxiety and unrest, which are also termed "coarse outflows" (audārika-āsrava). Now, when both vitarka and vicāra are abandoned, anxiety...
Because the coarse outflows (*āsrava*) have been subdued without being forcibly suppressed, it is called the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration (*samādhi-jā-prīti-sukha-bhūmi*).

This means that the water of concentration moistens the mind, which is likened to a spring on a mountain peak. The eight contacts (*spraṣṭavya*) and ten qualities (*guṇa*) are the same as in the first dhyāna;
however, they differ in that they arise together with internal purity (*adhyātma-saṃprasāda*), and the lifespan is two great kalpas, while the body is two yojanas.

The lifespan of those with immeasurable light is ten great kalpas, and their bodies are forty yojanas in height; they possess light forty yojanas in extent. The lifespan of those in the Ābhāsvara Heaven is twenty great kalpas, and their bodies are eighty yojanas in height.
The calamity of fire does not reach them, but the calamity of water can reach them, because within their own minds there is the water of joy.
The three knowledges and the three dhyānas:

Ānanda, when these devas and humans have already perfected their radiant halos and attained the power of speech, they now further shed that radiance and speech (to reveal the traces of the teaching), manifesting the wondrous concentration and giving rise to pure practice that penetrates the bliss of cessation.
This class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven (the Heaven of Universal Purity).
When emptiness manifests before one, it expands and extends limitlessly, bringing about physical and mental pliancy and accomplishing the bliss of cessation.

In this same manner, for a certain class [of beings], the world of the *Śubhakṛtsna* (Utterly Pure) gods—wherein body and mind are entirely pure and perfected with pure virtues—is manifested as the supreme object of reliance;
they take refuge in the bliss of cessation. This class is called the *Śubhakṛtsna*.
"Ānanda, these three superior streams possess great conformity; body and mind are at peace, and they attain immeasurable bliss.
Although they have not yet truly attained the samādhi of reality, because they are fully endowed with joy within a peaceful mind, this is called the third dhyāna."
This third dhyāna possesses five factors of merit: first, equanimity; second, mindfulness; third, wisdom; fourth, bliss; and fifth, one-pointedness of mind.
Having departed from the agitation of the preceding joy, it gives rise to pure bliss. This bliss, together with its object, emerges from the nature of purity, which is serene and tranquil;
therefore, it is called the "bliss of cessation. However, it is not the untainted (anāsrava) bliss of cessation.

Emerging from this state, one is eternally free from the agitation of joy; this is called "serenity" (*praśrabdhi*). Within this serenity, one attains immeasurable bliss, which is still termed "joy" (*prāmodya*).
When this stage of sublime bliss, free from joy, is fully perfected, no worldly pleasure can surpass it.
In the Vinaya, this is likened to a lotus that has emerged from the earth but has not yet risen above the water: its roots, stems, flowers, and leaves are all thoroughly moistened.
The Parīttābha (Limited Light) devas have a lifespan of sixteen great kalpas and a body height of sixteen yojanas;

the Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light) devas have a lifespan of thirty-two great kalpas and a body height of thirty-two yojanas; the Ābhāsvara (Radiant) devas have a lifespan of sixty-four great kalpas and a body height of sixty-four yojanas.
The calamities of water and fire do not reach them, but the calamity of wind does reach them. By virtue of this...
Because they have not yet departed from inhalation and exhalation. Fourth, the four dhyānas are further explained in two parts: first, the four heavens of ordinary beings;
second, the five heavens of non-returners (*anāgāmin*). This is the first part.

Ānanda, furthermore, gods and humans are no longer oppressed by body or mind, for the causes of suffering have been exhausted. [They] realize that pleasure is not permanent and does not endure for long.

Because they must destroy birth, they simultaneously and instantaneously abandon both the mind of suffering and the mind of pleasure; the coarse and heavy characteristics are extinguished, and a pure nature of merit arises.

This class of beings is called the Heaven of Merit-Birth (*Puṇyaprasava*). Their minds of equanimity are perfectly integrated, their resolute conviction is pure, and within unobstructed merit, they attain wondrous conformity that extends to the end of the future.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasādā*). Ānanda, from this...

Within the Heaven of Meritorious Love (*Puṇyaprasava*), there are two divergent paths. If, within the previously cultivated immeasurable pure radiance, one dwells having perfected and realized merit and wisdom, such a class is called the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*).

If, within the previous state of mind, one simultaneously detests both suffering and pleasure, diligently cultivating a continuous and uninterrupted state of equanimity (*upekṣā*) until the path of equanimity is fully perfected, and both body and mind are extinguished while the mental faculties become ashen and stilled—[this is the other path].

After five hundred kalpas, because these beings have taken the cessation of the arising and ceasing of suffering and pleasure as their cause, they are definitively unable to manifest the nature that is fundamentally non-arising and non-ceasing.
Thus, when they are born in heaven, their conceptual mind first ceases during the first half-kalpa, and only in the second half-kalpa does the conceptual mind arise again.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva). Ānanda, these four superior streams are among all the worlds.

Though unmoved by any objects of suffering or pleasure, although it is not the truly unconditioned Immovable Ground (*aniñjya-bhūmi*), the state in which the mind of attainment and all effort have reached full maturity is called the Fourth Dhyāna.

Since the causes of suffering are exhausted, the virtues of the preceding three dhyānas—though long maintained—are shown to be subject to decay and rebirth; this reveals the limitations of those three dhyānas.
By transcending the two states of mind—suffering and pleasure—one below manifests the true practice of the fourth dhyāna. This dhyāna possesses four factors of merit:
first, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure; second, equanimity; third, purity; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind.

Regarding the phrase "extending to the limits of the future," this refers to the nature of its merit increasing such that its lifespan is doubled compared to the first dhyāna heaven; it does not mean that it truly exhausts the limits of the future.

Those who dwell in the cultivation and realization of perfect and luminous merit and virtue do so by perfuming their meditative merit with the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), thereby becoming free from the defilements of the lower stages. The "Vast Fruit" (*Bṛhatphala*) refers to the fruit brought about by vast merit and virtue.

As for the Heaven of Non-conception (*Asaṃjñisattva-deva*), within the span of four hundred and ninety-nine kalpas, the six types of perception (*ṣaḍ-saṃjñā*) do not function, like water held between the fingers.
The fish is like grass pressed down by a stone; this is called the Stage of Purity of Equanimity and Mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*).

In the Vinaya, it is compared to bathing and putting on a new, clean robe, or like a lamp inside a sealed house. In another sutra, it is called the "Arising of Merit" or "Cloudless" (*anabhraka*). Regarding the term "Cloudless":

although they dwell below in the empty space, they still rely upon the clouds to stay. The retribution of this heaven is so ethereal and subtle that it is indistinguishable from the clouds themselves.
The Śubhakṛtsna [deities] likewise do not exist; their merit results in a lifespan of one hundred and twenty-five great kalpas and a body one hundred and twenty-five yojanas in height.
The Puṇyaprasava [deities] have a lifespan of two hundred and fifty great kalpas and a body two hundred and fifty yojanas in height.
The Bṛhatphala and the Asaṃjñisattva all have a lifespan of five hundred great kalpas and a body five hundred yojanas in height. [They are destroyed by] fire, water, and wind.
No calamities can reach this place. The *Fayuan zhulin* states that the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*) has no separate location;
it shares the same site as the Heaven of Vast Results (*bṛhatphala*). Because it is inhabited by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), it is distinguished by a separate name.
Second, the explanation of the five non-returner heavens (*anāgāmin*).

Ānanda, herein there are further five non-returner heavens where the nine grades of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) within the lower realms are extinguished simultaneously, and both suffering and pleasure have perished.
Because there is no longer a dwelling place below, they are established within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*).
Dwelling there, Ānanda, both suffering and pleasure are extinguished, and the contentious mind no longer engages; such a class of beings is called the Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha).
Their mental mechanisms function in solitude, with no ground for the friction of contact; such a class of beings is called the Heaven of No Heat (Atapa).

Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, their wondrous vision is perfectly clear and serene, with no further appearance of dust or phenomena, and all heavy impurities are gone; such a class of beings is called the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa).
With refined vision manifest before them, they mold and transform without obstruction; such a class is named the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
Having reached the ultimate limit of all multitudes and exhausted the nature of form, they enter the boundless; such a class is named the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Ānanda, as for these Anāgāmin heavens, the various kings of the four stages of the fourth dhyāna can only hear of them with admiration, yet they are unable to know or see them.
Because the wildernesses, deep mountains, and sites of the sacred path in this world are all sustained by Arhats, they cannot be seen by coarse worldly people.
In the Sanskrit language, *Anāgāmin* means "Non-returner"; these [beings] in the Five Regions of India are all saints of the third fruit who dwell there temporarily.
Regarding "dwelling place": the lower realm refers to the desire realm; "habitual tendencies" refers to the habitual tendencies of the nine grades of afflictions of thought.
When these habitual tendencies are all extinguished, one cannot choose to dwell in the desire realm, as there is no karma for rebirth there.

When both suffering and pleasure have vanished, one cannot choose to dwell in the first, second, or third dhyānas, as there is no karma for rebirth there. This refers to the *sattvasabhāgatā* (commonality of sentient beings) of the mind of equanimity.
This refers to the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven, which is collectively named the "Stage of Purity of Equanimity and Mindfulness" (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*).

Because the afflictions of volition (*saṃskāra-kleśa*) have not yet been exhausted in the higher realms, it is necessary to establish a dwelling place within this stage. "Striving mind" (*yudha-citta*) refers to the mind that has simultaneously abandoned both suffering and pleasure;
"mechanism" (*yantra*) refers to the state where both suffering and pleasure are forgotten; "intense heat" is called "affliction" (*kleśa*), and subtle affliction is called "defilement" (*mala*).
"Heating the worlds of the ten directions" refers collectively to the lands of the great trichiliocosm.

"Dust-like appearances and deep-seated defilements" refer to the obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) within the four *dhyānas*. "Smelting and casting without hindrance" describes how his concentration and wisdom are refined to brilliance and fused into a state of sovereign mastery.

"Ultimate" (*jìngjiù*) carries the sense of exhaustive investigation; "incipient" (*jǐ*) refers to the subtle movement [of thought]. Through the exhaustive investigation of many moments of thought, one reaches...
Because it occurs in a single thought-moment, it is called "ultimate. To "exhaust the nature of form" means that even this exhaustion is itself ultimate.
Since the mind has already perfumed [the seeds] from many to few, form is also exhausted from coarse to subtle. This exhaustion of the very nature of form borders upon emptiness and is without limit;
because this is the highest point of the realm of form, it is named the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha). It is profound.
The Master Xi said: "In the beginning, there is no need for complexity; one simply practices the lower grade of mixed cultivation (*vyavakiraṇa*).

This means that after the practitioner has first entered the fourth dhyāna, within this concentration they first give rise to a continuous succession of many moments of untainted (*anāsrava*) mind, followed by a continuous succession of many moments of tainted (*sāsrava*) mind, and then again a continuous succession of many moments of untainted mind."
In this manner, it gradually diminishes until there are two moments of untainted (anāsrava), two moments of tainted (sāsrava), and two moments of untainted.
At this point, the preliminary practice (prayoga) of mixed cultivation is said to be perfected. Next, one moment of untainted, one moment of tainted, and one moment of untainted arise;
reaching this stage is called the perfection of the fundamental [practice]. By means of this, the tainted and untainted are cultivated in alternation.
Therefore, it is called "mixed cultivation" (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) and also "intermingled perfuming meditation" (*vyavakīrṇa-vāsanā-dhyāna*).

Because the use of the untainted (*anāsrava*) intermingles with and perfumes the tainted (*sāsrava*) form-concentration, making it increasingly luminous and its karmic fruition increasingly superior, one passes away from the Bṛhatphala Heaven due to this support and this karma, and is reborn in the Avṛha Heaven.
Being slightly free from the hindrances of concentration, it is called "without affliction" (*avṛha*); "affliction" (*vṛha*) refers to the hindrances, and the hindrances are suffering.
Delighting in dual combat, one next reaches the Heaven Free from Heat (*Atapa*). Within the intermediate mixed cultivation (*miśrabhāvanā*), there are six moments of mind;
taking the three moments of the preceding inferior grade as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), one further induces three moments.

A single moment of untainted (*anāsrava*) and tainted (*sāsrava*) [mind] serves as the fundamental [attainment], utilizing its former karma to pass away from the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*) and be reborn in the Heaven Free from Heat by transcending the Heaven Without Affliction (*Abṛha*).
In the preceding stage of the "striving mind" (*prāyogika-citta*), although it does not intersect with suffering or pleasure, there is still that which does not intersect;

in the present stage, however, the mechanism operates alone, and since there is no ground for refining the intersection, its intensity likewise lacks the three wholesome [aspects]. When one observes the superior grade of mixed cultivation, nine mental states are employed:
the first six mental states serve as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), and three further mental states are generated as the fundamental [stage] (*maula*).
Relying on their former karma, they pass away from the Bṛhatphala Heaven and are born in the Sudarśana Heaven.

Because their untainted merit is manifest, and because the obstacles to concentration and wisdom have perished, they possess a wondrous vision that is perfectly clear throughout the worlds of the ten directions; thus they are named the Sudarśana Heaven.

Although the previous heaven was free from heat, it still possessed the mechanism of the trigger [of rebirth], and those who dwelt there alone could not be called "Sudarśana" (Good Vision); now, however, they are solitary.

The mechanism of practice is likewise such that the ten directions of the world are but a single wondrous vision. The fourth, "Manifestation" (Sudṛśa), consists of the superior grade of mixed cultivation;
it employs twelve moments of mind, using the first nine as preparatory application (*prayoga*) and further inducing three moments as the fundamental (*maula*).
By relying on past karma, it transcends three births. Although the preceding stage was "Good Vision" (Sudarśana), it was not yet able to effect this transformation.

Transformation occurs spontaneously in the present; since there are currently no external objects, the latent defilements are like a potter who, having applied a small amount of clay to a wheel, gives it a single turn so that vessels of various sizes follow his movements and are produced—there is nothing he cannot accomplish.

Because he transcends the fourteen types of transformation and possesses mastery, he is named "Well-Appeared" (Subhūti). The five colors reach their ultimate perfection, which is the culmination of the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas.

This chapter contains fifteen states of mind. The first twelve states of mind serve as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), while three further states of mind are induced as the fundamental [attainments].

By relying on these, one is able to transcend the four heavens of the form realm. In the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the lifespan is one great eon (*mahākalpa*) and the body is one thousand *yojanas* in height.
In the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the lifespan is two thousand great eons and the body is two thousand *yojanas* in height. These are the wholesome [states].

In the Heaven of Seeing (*Darśana*), the lifespan is four thousand great kalpas and the body is four thousand yojanas; in the Heaven of Good Appearance (*Sudṛśa*), the lifespan is eight thousand great kalpas and the body is eight thousand yojanas;
in the Heaven of Ultimate Purity (*Akaniṣṭha*), the lifespan is sixteen thousand great kalpas and the body is sixteen thousand yojanas.

Regarding the statement in the section on fetters (*saṃyojana*) that the Four Heavenly Kings cannot perceive them, it is because they [the Kings] are ordinary beings while these [heavens] are realms of the noble ones (*ārya*).

This is because they follow different paths. However, according to such sutras as the *Lokotpatti-sūtra*, the five heavens of the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are situated one above the other in double increments.
According to the intent of this present sutra, it appears that [the Non-returners] occupy the same location as the fourth dhyāna, with ordinary beings and sages merely following distinct paths.

One should fear that this is also like the relationship between the *Upāya* (Convenient) and *Sahabhu* (Co-resident) heavens, which possesses both horizontal and vertical theories and cannot be restricted to either alone.
This is a biased adherence to a single path. To explain in detail, a question is asked:

"If that Heavenly King is already a Bodhisattva, why is he unable to know and see the realms of the three fruits [of the non-returner]? The answer is: "Precisely because he manifests as a Bodhisattva, his traces are identical to those of the various devas;
thus they together respectfully hear of the five types of Non-Returners (Anāgāmin) born there, who have produced the roots of goodness for transcending the world."
Third, a summary of their names:
Ānanda, these eighteen heavens are solitary and without companions; as long as the burden of form is not yet exhausted, from this point downward they are called the Realm of Form (rūpadhātu).
"Walking alone without companions" indicates that they lack emotional desires (*kāma*), distinguishing them from the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

"Not yet exhausted the burden of form" indicates that they still possess physical substance (*rūpa*), distinguishing them from the four Formless Heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*). Therefore, they are collectively termed the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the three Formless Realms:

first, those who have turned their minds [toward liberation] but do not enter are excluded; second, the characteristics of the four Formless Heavens are specifically elucidated; third, they are further categorized.

First, a general distinction between the two classes—ordinary beings and sages—is made regarding the differences between kings and subjects; fifth, the conclusion establishes the name "Formless" (*ārūpya*) for itself.
Now, for the first [section]:
Furthermore, Ānanda, from within this limit of form at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are again two divergent paths therein.

If, through the mind of equanimity, one illuminates wisdom such that the light of insight becomes perfectly penetrating, one then transcends the realm of dust to become an Arhat and enters the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas;
such a class of individuals is called a "Great Arhat who has turned the mind."
This first clarifies that among those in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, one class of individuals with sharp faculties whose nature of wisdom is predominant does not enter the four spheres of emptiness;
together with another class of individuals with dull faculties who do enter the four spheres of emptiness, these are collectively termed the two types of divergent paths.
Second, it specifically clarifies the characteristics of the heavens of the four spheres of emptiness.

If, within a mind of equanimity, one achieves the relinquishing of aversion and perceives the body as an obstruction, such that obstructions dissolve and one enters emptiness—this class of beings is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Once all obstructions have dissolved, even the non-obstruction itself ceases;

therein remains only the *ālayavijñāna* in its entirety, along with a portion of the *manas* and the subtle *manovijñāna*. This class of beings is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
When both emptiness and form have vanished and the conscious mind is entirely extinguished, the ten directions are silent and utterly devoid of any destination.

This class of beings is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Their consciousness-nature is unmoving; through the exhaustive investigation of extinction, they manifest the nature of exhaustion within the inexhaustible.
It is as if it exists yet does not exist, as if it is exhausted yet not exhausted. This class of beings is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Regarding the "state":
if one refers generally to the category of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta-pada*)— namely, the stage of pure mindfulness and equanimity within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*)—

it appears as if it speaks solely of the dull-facultied *anāgāmin*, yet in fact it also encompasses the Bṛhatphala gods, the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), and ordinary worldlings who are non-Buddhists.

Changshui said: "There are two ways of relinquishing the mind: first, if one uses the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) to sever afflictions and enter emptiness, this is the 'joyful concentration' (*sukha-samādhi*) of relinquishment;
second, if one uses the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*) at the Fruit of Vastness (*bṛhatphala*) to suppress afflictions and enter emptiness, this refers to ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists.
These words correctly describe the *ālayavijñāna*, which is translated here as..."
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is named *ālaya* because it possesses the meanings of being that which stores, that which is stored within, and that which is clung to as a self.
This refers to the eighth consciousness. *Manas* is translated here as "defiled"; this refers to the seventh consciousness.

Since beginningless time, this seventh consciousness has falsely grasped the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as an internal self; what is now stated applies entirely to this *manas*.
This reveals that innate self-clinging remains entirely intact, without having been suppressed or severed even in the slightest degree.
"Half a minute portion" refers to the sixth consciousness, which no longer has external objects as its cognitive domain and possesses only an internal object;

this "half-portion" still remains, yet its characteristic is subtle—not only is it not form (*rūpa*), but it is also not space (*ākāśa*). For this reason, it constitutes the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
When the conscious mind is entirely extinguished, even that which internally conditions the sixth consciousness is suppressed; therefore, it is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The nature of the eighth consciousness has been fundamentally unmoving and cannot be severed or extinguished.
Now, by using this mind of delusive extinction to forcibly apply exhaustive investigation to this inexhaustible nature, one falsely proclaims that the nature is exhausted.
It is caused by the eighth consciousness, whose nature exists yet does not exist because it is invisible;

and by the seventh consciousness, whose sense of self is both exhausted and yet not exhausted because it clings to these delusions of birth and death as being real, and has not yet severed its craving for the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
Therefore, this state is merely called "separation" because one is free from the coarse perceptions of the lower stages.

Because it is not non-perception, yet does not reach the state where false imaginings lack intrinsic nature; because it does not enter *nirvāṇa*, yet is the true path of non-perception, it is therefore called the "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The lifespan in the Sphere of Infinite Space is twenty thousand great eons; the lifespan in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness is forty thousand great eons;

the lifespan in the Sphere of Nothingness is sixty thousand great eons; and the lifespan in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is eighty thousand great eons. This concludes the third [section].
Distinguishing between the two classes of ordinary beings and sages:

those who exhaustively investigate emptiness yet do not fully realize the characteristic of emptiness— such as this one class who reach the end of the noble path from the Heaven of Non-returners and are called "dull-witted Arhats who do not turn their minds"—
and those who exhaustively investigate emptiness from among the various non-Buddhist heavens of the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva).
Returning to delusion and leaking through the lack of hearing, they immediately enter the cycle of saṃsāra.
These [practitioners] exhaustively pursue emptiness: having already used emptiness to extinguish form, they further use consciousness to extinguish emptiness;
they further use non-existence to extinguish consciousness, and they further use the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to extinguish non-existence. Thus—
One may indeed be said to have exhausted all one's mental and physical strength regarding the realm of emptiness; however, the principle of emptiness does not abide outside of form.

Since one now seeks emptiness apart from form, how could this exhaust the principle of emptiness? This is why those *anāgāmins* of dull faculties share in the same state of confusion as ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists.
Yet, if within this state one follows the noble path from the heaven of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) to its ultimate conclusion, then directly—

Those who wait until the eighty thousand great kalpas of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are exhausted before emerging from the triple world to be born in the impure land of Skillful Means—
known as those of dull faculties whose minds do not turn back— are called "Arhats with non-turning minds.

If they come from among the non-Buddhist heavens of the Unconscious or from ordinary beings of the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*), they seek only the single flavor of emptiness and do not know how to turn their heads to observe the Reality.

The principle of emptiness is called "ultimate emptiness" (kūṅ-k'ung), yet they do not return to it; this is because they are deluded regarding the heavens of outflows (sāsrava) and conceive of them as Nirvana.

Since they have not heard the true Dharma-gate that transcends the world, when their retribution is exhausted, they fall back down and continue to revolve through the seven destinies according to their former karma.
Fourth, a general comparison of the differences between kings and subjects.
Ānanda, those various beings among the devas who are still ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) are subject to the retribution of their karmic fruits;
