once that retribution is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra). Those celestial kings, however, are bodhisattvas who, while traversing samādhi, gradually advance along the path of practice dedicated toward the assembly of the noble ones (ārya-gaṇa).
This passage ought to follow after the subsequent section, as it is a general conclusion concerning the three realms; since it is now misplaced here as a separate section, I shall explain it:

"These various heavens" refers collectively to the six heavens of the desire realm, the thirteen of the form realm, and the four of the formless realm—excluding only the five heavens of the non-returners (anāgāmin), which are not indicated here.
Because it is not a place where ordinary beings repay their karma, it is called "the path practiced by Bodhisattvas.
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the third stage (*bhūmi*), one mostly becomes Śakra, King of Devas; in the fourth stage, one mostly becomes Suyāma, King of Devas;

and so on, up to the eighth stage, where one mostly becomes a Brahmā of a small thousand-world system (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*); and in the ninth stage, one mostly becomes a Brahmā of a medium thousand-world system (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*).
The King of the Ten Stages is generally one such as the Great Brahmā Heaven King of a trichiliocosm, and so forth. Gushan says:
"Wandering in samādhi" refers to the Bodhisattva’s skillful entry into, emergence from, and abiding in hundreds of thousands of samādhis;
thus, while dwelling in this concentration, he acts as a heavenly king. The nine successive concentrations (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) are called "skillful."
Entering the Lion’s Boundless Prowess is called the Samādhi of Skillful Emergence and Transcendence;
it is called the Skillful Abiding because each [state] can profoundly penetrate the true mark (dharmatā). It is named the Śūraṅgama because it binds the five fetters into the formless realm.
Ānanda, in these four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the body and mind are extinguished, and the state of fixed nature (*niyāma*) manifests;
from this point until the end, it is called the formless realm.

The dissolution of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is termed the "extinction of the body," while the subtle refinement of the other four aggregates is termed the "extinction of the mind. The manifestation of the state of fixed nature...
The former [the form realm] still possesses matter that is the result of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), yet lacks matter that is the result of karma (*karma-phala-rūpa*).

Because it cannot be seen by the two types of eyes—the physical eye of ordinary beings and non-Buddhists (*bāhya*) and the fleshly eye of devas—it is called the "Formless Realm" (*ārūpya-dhātu*). Regarding the phrase "from this until the end":

this means that beyond this there are no other separate heavens; one should know that the illusory characteristics of the three realms (*tri-dhātu*) culminate here. This concludes the first section on distinctions.
Having finished showing [the states of] the devas, the second part is a summary of their falsity:
"All these arise from failing to understand the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind; through the accumulation of delusions, the three realms of falsity are produced.
Within them, beings falsely follow the seven destinies, sinking and drowning, with each *pudgala* following its own kind."
*Pudgala* is translated here as "sentient being" (*sattva*) and also as "one who repeatedly takes up existence" (*pudgala*).

This refers to sentient beings who, giving rise to afflictions and performing karma, take birth according to their respective realms; thus, within the three realms, they repeatedly grasp at and become attached to [existence].
Seventh, the demonstration of the *asura* realm.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms there are four classes of asuras.

Those who belong to the realm of hungry ghosts, who by the power of protecting the Dharma ride upon spiritual penetrations to enter the void—these asuras are born from eggs and are categorized among the hungry ghosts.
Those who, having descended from the heavens due to a loss of merit, dwell in proximity to the sun and moon—these asuras...
Born from a womb and categorized among the human realm, there is an Asura King who upholds the world;

his power is profound and fearless, and he can vie for authority with Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings. This Asura, due to his transformations, is also categorized among the celestial realms.
Ānanda, there is also a separate class of inferior Asuras who are born within the great ocean and sink into its depths.
At dawn they roam the void, and at dusk they return to dwell in the waters; these asuras, due to their moisture-nature, are categorized within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
As for the asuras who possess the power to protect through the Dharma, this is their prior cause, as explained previously in the section on the ghost realm (*preta*).
Those who ascend by the power of goodness descend from the heavens with virtue; likewise, those who fall due to the power of karma are also preceded by this cause.

Those who sustain the world can also command spirits and deities to bring fortune or calamity to humanity, yet their authority does not reach that of the heavens; therefore, they frequently become enraged and contend with it.

Originally, they contended for power with Śakra, and thus... [the four]... (Note: The final fragment "而四" appears to be an incomplete phrase, likely referring to the four kings or the four guardians of the quarters.)
The King constantly serves as the vanguard for Śakra; at times, when Śakra is not victorious, he also seeks the assistance of Brahmā and others.
This is the king among the asuras, whose dwellings are all within the great ocean beneath Mount Sumeru;
those inferior asuras are merely the subjects under his rule. Gu Shan says: "If one relies on..."
Regarding the relative superiority and inferiority of the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*), the asuras are ranked below the human destiny;
they are placed at the end here because their classification is not fixed. Youxi said: "The inclusion of the six destinies each has its own definite place;

however, the fact that the asuras are included within four destinies not only reveals that there are four kinds of karmic retribution, but also indicates that within each of those types, there is further mixture."

Although four causes are present, one must consider which cause is predominant to determine into which realm one falls. For instance, the medium grade of the ten unwholesome actions serves as the cause for the realm of hungry ghosts;
the lower grade serves as the cause for the animal realm; and the medium grade serves as the cause for the human realm.

Furthermore, the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions serves as the cause for the heavenly realm. If wholesome or unwholesome karma is dull, one will accordingly experience rebirth as a hungry ghost, an animal, or a human.
Heaven’s retribution may be sudden: one moment performing good, the next committing evil; one moment descending, the next ascending.
Sometimes good and evil contend throughout a lifetime; sometimes the higher and lower realms clash within a single thought.
Furthermore, when the mind harbors suspicion and seeks to surpass others, it causes one to receive retribution at the very end, with the stronger force drawing one forward first.
Some are born from eggs as beings of the realm of ghosts, and others are born from moisture as beings of the animal realm;

yet, though they belong to the realm of ghosts, they can still ride upon spiritual powers to enter the void, and though they belong to the animal realm, they can still roam through the empty sky at dawn—is this not the enjoyment of both human and celestial merit?
As for those included within the two destinies of humans and devas, although they dwell in proximity to the sun and moon, their power is [limited].
In the Avīci Hell, there are still instruments of suffering that operate day and night during the three periods; is this not a punishment shared with ghosts and animals?
Thus, when the devas and asuras wage war, they always prognosticate victory or defeat based on the relative amount of good and evil in the human realm:
if goodness prevails, the devas win; if unwholesomeness prevails, the asuras win. One day, while they were engaged in battle, the Heavenly Emperor—
The alternating victories and defeats are due to the fact that in this world there is a person who, wishing to do good, is suddenly interrupted by an evil thought;
or wishing to do evil, is again interrupted by a good thought. Because they harbor such indecision, it causes the Lord of Heaven to act in this manner.
I observe that those who practice the Way today are muddled by a mixture of right and wrong, beauty and ugliness.
Even for those of divine disposition, if thoughts of suspicion and jealousy remain, and a mind that prizes victory persists, one must likewise take this as a warning.

This concludes the second section, which separately demonstrates the seven realms of existence. Third, the conclusion and demonstration of the exhortation to practice, which has two parts: first, the conclusion and demonstration of delusive error;
second, citing awakening to exhort practice. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, concluding that the fruits of delusion are fundamentally empty; second, [the subsequent section].
A further demonstration of the delusive causes of perversion. Herein is the first:

Ānanda, thus the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, seers and immortals, devas, and asuras—having scrutinized these seven realms, they are all states of昏沉 (dullness and stupor), characterized by the conditioned existence of *saṃskāra*.
They undergo birth through false conceptualization and follow their karma through false conceptualization, within the Wondrous [Nature].
The perfectly luminous, unconditioned original mind is like flowers in the sky, fundamentally without anything to which it clings; it is merely a single delusion, devoid of any root or continuity.
"Thoroughly investigating" means subtle and minute analysis. Torpor is affliction (*kleśa*); conditioned existence is karma; and taking birth follows from these.
Karma is its retribution; what are called delusion, karma, and suffering are like the clusters of akṣa fruits. Suffering is the *dharmakāya*, and is therefore termed "wondrous";
delusion is *prajñā*, and is thus called "perfectly luminous"; karma is *vimukti*, and is named "unconditioned.
Know that this wondrous, perfect, luminous, and unconditioned original mind is like the great void, wherein delusion, karma, and suffering—these three—are [non-existent].
Since all are but manifestations of the Flower, it is said that there is "only one delusion (vithapana) with no further root or source.

Since it is stated that from the beginning there is nothing to which one clings, we know that the seven realms of existence (sapta-gati), being delusions, fundamentally do not obstruct the true body of the Buddha.

Since it is stated that there is no further root or source, we know that this path does not exist from the very beginning. [This concludes] the second section, showing the cause of delusion and its inversion.
[The Buddha said:

"Inverted! Ānanda, these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and undergo this cycle of birth and death for immeasurable kalpas, failing to attain true purity because they follow along with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
If they turn away from these three, they will instead give rise to non-killing."

Theft, sexual misconduct, and [false speech] have names; the realm of ghosts has no name; and the celestial realms exist. As existence and non-existence incline toward one another, the nature of saṃsāra arises.

This "birth" refers to the absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, specifically pointing to the ten wholesome precepts of the former physicians, as well as the practices of aspiration and revulsion and the dhyāna of affairs.
Regarding those with names in the realm of ghosts: they are currently the causes for the three evil destinies, and in the future...

It is certain that one will incur the fruits of the three evil realms. As for those who lack the name of "heavenly realm," they possess the causes for the three good realms in the present and will certainly incur the fruits of the three good realms in the future.

Regarding those who assert existence while denying non-existence, or those who deny existence while asserting non-existence—failing to realize the sublime morality, sublime concentration, and sublime wisdom that transcend the world—they will ultimately remain within saṃsāra alone. This is what is meant by "one."
Is this not like someone with cataracts whose eyes see empty flowers falling in confusion? Thus we know that emptiness originally has no flowers;
though there is no need to sweep them away, one must still rely on the golden probe for the cataracts within the eye. Second, citing awakening to exhort practice, which has two parts:
first, directly citing the realm of awakening; second, concluding with an exhortation to true cultivation. Now, the first part.
If one attains the sublime arising of samādhi, then there is sublime and eternal stillness; both existence and non-existence are absent, and even non-duality is extinguished.
Since there is not even the notion of "not killing," "not stealing," or "not committing sexual misconduct," how could one further follow after the acts of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct?
The phrase "wondrously giving rise to samādhi" means that the wondrous supramundane precepts are developed based upon the Śūraṅgama King Samādhi.
If these wondrous precepts are given rise to, then the *prātimokṣa* precepts are themselves untainted (*anāsrava*) precepts;
thus, "permanence" refers to the dhyāna-precepts, and "quiescence" is as previously stated: the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind, and even the nature of this severance is [severed].
Furthermore, there is neither equality nor difference; because both existence and non-existence are absent, one does not fall into the stage of ordinary beings.

Because even non-duality is extinguished, one does not fall into the stages of the Two Vehicles. Thus, since even the characteristics of non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexual misconduct cannot be apprehended, how could there still be such matters as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct?
Only upon attaining this single phrase does one come to know the signless (*animitta*).
Sublime precepts do not consist in breaking the precepts; if there are instances of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, one remains merely within the realm of ghosts and spirits.
How can such shameless individuals use these as excuses? Second, the exhortation to cultivate true practice.

Ānanda, you have not yet severed the three karmas; each has its own private causes, and because these private causes are shared among many, they constitute a commonality of destiny (*sabhāgatā*) that is not without a fixed location.

These arise from your own delusions; their arising is illusory and without cause, such that they cannot be traced back to an origin. You must exert yourself in practice. If you wish to attain Bodhi, you must eliminate the three delusions.
If you do not exhaust these three delusions, even if you should obtain supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), they will all be mundane and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If the habit-energies of effortful practice are not extinguished, one falls into the path of Māra; though wishing to eliminate delusion, one instead redoubles one's hypocrisy.
The Tathāgata says such a person is to be pitied. This delusion is self-created; it is not the fault of Bodhi.
To speak thus is called the correct teaching; for anyone else to say otherwise is the speech of Māra.
Each individual’s private karma is their distinct karma (*bipākakarma*).

The commonality of these private karmas is the realm of dependence (*āśraya-dhātu*) collectively induced by those similar distinct karmas. From this, there arise the fixed locations of the seven destinies (*gati*).
These various distinct karmas and fixed locations are all produced from one's own delusion; they arise from delusion and have no other cause. Therefore, they do not exist [independently].
One may investigate this by simply eliminating the three delusions within the mind; thus, the causes will be exhausted and karma will be ended.
It is like when cataracts are removed, the floating flowers vanish of their own accord, and when the flowers vanish, the empty space naturally manifests.

These three delusions are precisely the mind of lust, the mind of killing, and the mind of theft. Since karma arises from delusion, one must sever the delusions to eliminate the root of falsehood. This concludes the Great Chapter.
The fifth section, which extensively demonstrates the seven destinies, is concluded.
The sixth section takes the unlearned bhikṣu as its introductory pretext to fully clarify the demonic realms of the five aggregates;

its underlying intent is to reveal that if one lacks the wondrous wisdom of the Middle Way, one simultaneously loses the wondrous precepts of the Middle Way. This is because of possessing only a semblance of Middle Way wisdom.
Therefore, some fall into the realm of Māra and break their precepts, while others fall into external paths and destroy their views;
breaking precepts and destroying views are both violations of the *prātimokṣa* because one lacks the wisdom that partially realizes the Middle Way.
Consequently, some become *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*, thereby destroying the bodhicitta precepts. Thus it is said: "Lacking wisdom... and so forth.

The section on the absence of precepts is divided into two parts: first, the formal elucidation of the meditative realm; second, the further severing of remaining doubts. Within the first part, there are three sections:
first, concluding the previous topic and introducing the subsequent one; second, the assembly awaiting instruction; third, the general and specific explanations. This is the first.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata, having concluded his discourse from the Dharma-seat upon the lion throne, took up a seven-jeweled armrest and, turning toward the Purple Gold Mountain, leaned against it once more.
He addressed the great assembly and Ānanda, saying:

"You who are still in training—whether pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas—who today turn your minds toward the Great Bodhi and the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment: I have now expounded for you the method of true cultivation."
You have not yet recognized the subtle demonic activities that arise during the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Fearing that such demonic realms may manifest before you and that you will fail to recognize them, your mind will be unsettled and fall into false views;

or you will encounter the *skandha-māra*, or the celestial *māra*, or become possessed by spirits, or be beset by malevolent demons. With your mind thus clouded, you will mistake a thief for your own son. Furthermore, regarding...

To attain a small measure [of realization] and consider it sufficient—like a bhikṣu who lacks learning in the fourth dhyāna (whose initial cause was failure to penetrate the characteristics of dharmas)—falsely claims to have realized the state of an arhat.
(And so on, until: when the retribution of the heavens has ended and the signs of decline appear before him, he does not realize that he has not yet attained the fruit;

instead, he gives rise to slanderous thoughts, thinking, "I am now an arhat. Consequently, his body still encounters future existence. Because of this false speech and this mind of slander, he falls into the Avīci Hell. You should listen attentively as I shall now explain for you.
"You must discern this with meticulous care;
for among the demonic realms manifested within this *dhyāna*, none but one of omniscience can identify them.
Therefore, now turning his body of purple-gold, he speaks without being questioned—this is his final profound compassion. 'Washing the mind' is not the primary meaning."
"One cannot cleanse the mind with the True Dharma. Youxi said, "There are two meanings to 'cleansing the mind.

First, when practicing meditation, one must first wash away the prior mind; all former erroneous views and attachments must be repented and severed, just as one must remove poisonous honey and wash with incense ash before storing ambrosia. If even a trace remains, it will immediately become..."

Regarding the two points that give rise to Māra: the cultivation of the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) is the water of wisdom that washes away afflictions and delusions.
If this does not correspond with the three types of *śamatha* and the three types of *vipaśyanā*, it is not the correct path and one will fall into the way of Māra.

As for "your various *skandha*-māras" and so forth: generally speaking, all fifty levels of the objective realms are called *skandha*-māras, as they all depend upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Because they arise separately, the ten objects of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) are merely the "demon of the aggregates" (*skandhamāra*) manifesting within the aggregates themselves.

The ten objects of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) involve external demons entering the mind and encountering malevolent spirits (*chimei*). The ten objects of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) additionally involve the demon of heaven (*devamāra*) and attachment to ghosts and spirits.
The twenty layers of objects of the aggregates of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) and consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) all pertain to those who take little as sufficient.
This refers to their general categories. Furthermore, the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) explains the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*) in detail:

first, the aggregates, realms, and bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*); second, afflictions; third, illness; fourth, karmic signs; fifth, demonic activities; sixth, meditative concentrations; seventh, various views; eighth, arrogance; ninth, the two vehicles; and tenth, bodhisattvas.
Among these, only the aggregates, realms, and bases are the objects constantly contemplated by those at the initial stage of the path; the remaining nine are not.
Objects are observed only when they arise; if they do not arise, they are not observed.

Now, taking these twenty-five objects as the gateways to perfect penetration is precisely for the beginner to constantly observe the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

These five aggregate-objects encompass the characteristics of afflictions, karma, demonic activities, meditative concentrations, various views, and the arrogance of the two vehicles, yet they alone lack the object of illness.
And as for the Bodhisattvas' ears, although the teaching is directed specifically toward the Bodhisattvas, it may also be applied to the realms of the Two Vehicles; thus it is shown in general:
"If you awaken to dhyāna in its own place without delusion, then those demonic affairs will be powerless against you.
This is precisely what is meant by "observing only when [the affliction] arises, and not observing when it does not arise. At that time, the assembly waited expectantly for his instruction.
Ānanda rose together with the other practitioners in the assembly; filled with joy, they prostrated and waited in reverence to hear his compassionate instructions.
This section has three parts: first, a general clarification of the causes of demonic activity; second, a specific revelation of the signs of the arousal of the objective realm;

and third, a concluding exhortation to respectfully receive the teachings and practice accordingly. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the actual explanation of the causes for the movement of demons.
Second, the exhortation regarding the loss and gain of delusion and awakening. First:

The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly, saying, "You should all know that within this world of outflows, the twelve classes of beings—right now before you—possess a fundamentally enlightened and wondrous clarity;
the essence of their awakened, perfect mind is from the beginning no different from that of the Buddhas of the ten directions."

Your deluded conceptualization and failure to realize the principle are the fault; from ignorance and craving, birth arises, and as birth and arising cause universal delusion, the nature of space appears.
As this delusion transforms without ceasing, the world-systems arise. Thus, these lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are not free from outflows;
they are all established through stubborn, deluded, and false conceptualization. You should know that space arises within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing in the sky.

If all the worlds within the Great Qing are situated within empty space, then when even one of you develops true realization and returns to the source, this empty space of the ten directions (as perceived through emotional views) will entirely dissolve and vanish. How could the lands existing within that space not tremble and shatter?
You who cultivate dhyāna and adorn yourselves with samādhi [should know that you are] equal to the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the various ones free from outflows.
The mind of the Arhat is thoroughly proficient and profoundly serene in its own place.
To all the Māras, yakṣas, and ordinary devas, their respective palaces appear to collapse without cause, the great earth quakes and splits apart, and the waters and lands surge and fly upward;
thus there is none who is not struck with terror. Because ordinary worldlings are shrouded in darkness, they do not perceive this transformation.
They all attained the five supernormal powers, with the sole exception of the exhaustion of outflows; yet they were attached to this worldly toil.
How could you cause them to shatter that place? For this reason, when you were in samādhi, ghosts, spirits, celestial māras, and all manner of goblins and demons came together to harass you.
Adorn and embellish with merit and wisdom; when the Dharma-body is adorned with merit and wisdom, cultivated virtue becomes efficacious and the innate nature (xingde) is then manifested.

Thus, the minds of Bodhisattvas and Arhats are pure, lucid, and profoundly still. As for ordinary people who are obscured and ignorant, failing to perceive their own shifting delusions—it is like a person inside a large boat:
even as the boat moves along, the person does not even realize it, let alone [perceive its speed].
The world shook; how could ordinary beings know this? The rest is as stated in the text. Second, the exhortation regarding the gain and loss of delusion and awakening, which has two parts:
first, the exhortation to awaken, which constitutes gain; second, the warning against delusion, which constitutes loss. This is the first part.
However, although those various Māras may be filled with great rage within their realm of defilement, they are like wind blowing against light or a sword cutting through water;
they cannot touch you at all. You are like boiling water, while they are like solid ice; as the warmth gradually approaches, the ice will melt away in no time.
They merely rely on their supernatural powers, acting only as guests who bring about disruption and chaos, all because of what arises from within your own mind.
The five aggregates are like a host, and the host is like a master. If the master is deluded, the guests take advantage of the situation.

But if you attain awakening through *dhyāna* and are free from confusion, those demonic affairs will be powerless against you. When the aggregates dissolve and you enter into clarity, all those various evils will receive their dark breath;
now that clarity can destroy darkness, they will perish on their own. How could they dare remain to disturb your meditative concentration?
In this context, four metaphors are generally cited: first, wind blowing upon light; second, a sword cutting through water;
third, hot water dissolving ice; and fourth, light dispelling darkness. These illustrate that there is no harm because they are neither moved nor injured;
furthermore, they show that one can not only avoid harm but even transform the realm of Māra into the realm of the Buddha. For those who cultivate the mind, this is...
Should you not exert yourself? Second, if one is deluded, one will surely fall into error.

If you do not attain clear awakening and break through that which you are deluded by regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), then you, Ānanda, will inevitably become a child of Māra and achieve the state of a Māra-man, just like the Mātangī;
you would be utterly inferior. He [the Māra] would merely use his spells against you to destroy the Buddha’s code of discipline (*vinaya*) among its eighty thousand practices.
If one destroys but a single precept, yet the mind remains pure, one has not yet sunk into ruin; nevertheless, this [violation] destroys your entire body of precious enlightenment.
It is like a high minister’s family suddenly encountering a confiscation of their property: they will fall into utter decay, beyond all hope of rescue.

Since all objective realms arise based upon the aggregates (*skandha*), it is said only that one is "deluded by the aggregates"; for apart from the five aggregates, no devas, ghosts, or spirits can be found.
Regarding "confiscation" (*jimen*), it means to eliminate their registration in the official records.

Second, a detailed explanation of the characteristics of how the objective realms arise, in five parts: first, explaining the objective realm of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)... [up to] fifth, explaining the objective realm of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

The first of the three sections at the beginning consists of: (1) a general indication of the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*); (2) a detailed explanation of the manifestation of their characteristics; and (3) a conclusion that points out the faults and offers exhortation.
The first of these [three] further has four parts: (1) citing and indicating the perfect, penetrating correct practice; (2) directly indicating the domain of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*);
(3) provisionally indicating the state when the aggregate of form is exhausted; and (4) concluding by indicating that it is fundamentally nothing but deluded thought. This is the first part.
Ānanda, you should know that when you sit at the site of enlightenment, all thoughts must be dissolved and eliminated.

When these thoughts are exhausted, then all states of clarity and brilliance that are free from thought will remain unmoved by motion or stillness, and recollection and forgetfulness will become one as a single unity. You should abide in this state and enter samādhi.

A "site of practice" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is the field for cultivating the Way. If one relies on the Buddha’s era or the final age (*paścimaka-kāla*), those of sharp faculties need only take a place where they can dwell in peace as their site of practice.

However, if one wishes to cultivate both phenomena and principle (*dharma* and *tattva*) and attain realization within a fixed period, then following the ritual procedures of the three-week altar, one should immediately cultivate *samādhi* at this very location, continuing until one sits upright and at ease.
Dwelling for a period of one hundred days is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). To cause all thoughts to dissolve and fall away is to enter the flow and lose the object;

this is the true practice of cultivation, wherein one employs the single-minded, perfect, and sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā* to observe each object so that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the emotional calculations of birth and death are dissolved.
It is like a great furnace smelting gold; therefore, it is called "dissolving," which causes those defilements to be removed.
Therefore, it is called "the falling away of thought. As for "exhaustion" (*jìn*), if taken generally, it refers to the progression from contemplative practice (*guānxíng*) to ultimate exhaustion;

if distinguished specifically, it refers to what is termed "exhaustion" within the context of contemplative practice—that is, the initial ascent to the five grades where one perfectly subdues the afflictions of the five abodes.
As for "separation from thought," all such clarity and precision also proceeds from separation through contemplative practice to ultimate separation. Thus, there is [this distinction].
From the clarity and vigor of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) up to its ultimate perfection, we shall for now discuss it in terms of contemplative practice itself.
Once one has ascended to this stage of contemplative practice, one is able to remain unmoved by either motion or stillness, and recollection and forgetfulness become one.
This is what Avalokiteśvara meant by "that which is entered is already tranquil. To abide in this state and enter *samādhi* constitutes the initial application of the practice.
The power of cultivation (*kungfu*) should indeed be like this. However, there are two meanings here: first, concerning contemplation (*guan*); second, concerning the objects (*jing*).

Regarding contemplation, it refers to the state of brilliant clarity where thought has been eliminated. Regarding the objects, they consist of the two realms of phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*), each having both general and specific aspects.
As for the general aspect, the twenty-five gates constitute the realm of phenomena; within each gate, there are those things possessed [by it], such as...

The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) as the nature of the coming-and-going is merely the realm of principle (*li-jing*), whereas the faculty of hearing is the realm of phenomena (*shi-jing*).
The nature of hearing is fundamentally perfect, fundamentally penetrating, and fundamentally constant; this is the realm of principle. Now, we shall clarify this precisely:
by abiding in the faculty of the ear through this observation of brilliant clarity free from thought, one may enter *samādhi*. This is for those of sharp faculties.

Then, from this point, one transcends directly and enters [the state beyond]. If the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) are strong, then a realm of profound darkness manifests before one.
Second, the correct demonstration of the realm of the aggregate of form.
It is like a person with clear vision situated in great, profound darkness; though the essence of the mind is wondrously pure, its light has not yet emerged.
This is what is called the domain of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
This clarifies the manifestation of the aggregate of form within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*); because the perfect understanding has already opened, it is as described.
Because those with clear vision have not yet broken through the obstructions of the person, they are as if situated in great, profound darkness.

Since they understand that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, it is said that its essential nature is wondrously pure; yet because the principle and the object have not yet appeared, it is said that the mind has not yet emitted light.
Being covered and obstructed by this illusory material substance, the true nature is concealed; therefore, it is called the "domain of the aggregate of form. *Qu* (區) means a partition or enclosure.
The "bureau" refers to the dwelling place. The three suspended [mirrors] demonstrate the signs of the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
If one's vision becomes clear and bright, such that the ten directions open up like a cavern and there is no longer any darkness, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of form.
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
That the ten directions open up completely with no further darkness or obscurity refers precisely to what is called "the two aspects of movement and stillness clearly not arising," and so forth—
because all various dualistic phenomena, such as light and dark, penetration and obstruction, tranquility and change, union and separation, and birth and death, have all clearly ceased to arise,

it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the transcending of the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Thus, one dwells together with the ten directions opening up completely.

When [the gates] open, the color-aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) of the six classes of ordinary beings is exhausted; when the ten directions are opened through skillful means (*upāya*), the color-aggregate of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) is exhausted;

when the ten directions are opened through true retribution (*samyak-vipāka*), the color-aggregate of the Bodhisattvas is exhausted. Thus, one successively transcends the three lands and the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

Furthermore, there is the opening of the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*); when the practice is exhausted, one transcends it through contemplative practice, continuing up to the ultimate opening of the ultimate stage.

To fully and ultimately transcend these differences, one must cross-reference this with the commentary on the five aggregates in the second fascicle and the commentary on the "Perfect Penetration" (yuan-tong) in the sixth fascicle;
only then will the structural connections and underlying purport of this text become clear.
Fourth, the summary: these are fundamentally nothing but false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
When one examines their origin, one finds that solidified conceptualization (*dṛḍha-vikalpa*) constitutes their root.
Now, among the sentient beings of the nine realms, who would not regard these outflowing and non-outflowing forms as definitely possessing real dharmas?

This is truly because one has never carefully observed its origins. Now, when the Buddha-eye illuminates the source of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it is found to be nothing more than the delusion of solidity.
That is to say, it manifests according to the minds of sentient beings, in accordance with the scope of what they know, and in conformity with their karma;
how could there truly be any solid, substantial form? It is merely a delusive thought.
This means that if one takes the solid ear and solid deluded thoughts as the foundation, then there is no foundation at all;

thus, when the sudden and perfect *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) arises once, those [delusions] are exhausted accordingly. Suppose there were real dharmas—how could they ever be exhausted?

Suppose one does not realize their source and they are not real dharmas, but merely belong to deluded thoughts—how then could the sudden and perfect *śamatha-vipaśyanā* be established? Reflect upon this.
All subsequent sections following this reflection shall be understood according to this principle. Second, the specific clarification of the manifestations of arousal, in ten parts:

first, the essence becoming clear and overflowing externally so that the body can be obstructed... [up to] tenth, the perverse mind harboring demonic influences, leading to false visions and false speech.
These ten objects may occur earlier or later, they may arise or not arise, they may arise simultaneously, or they may arise repeatedly; their occurrences are not uniform. Now...
I shall merely list them in sequence in detail so that the practitioner may know these as the objects of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). First:

Ānanda, if within this state you investigate the subtle luminosity until the four great elements no longer interweave, and in a brief moment your body can pass through obstructions—this is called the overflowing of pure essence (*vimala-prabhāsvara*) into the external field;
it is merely a temporary attainment through spiritual effort and is not [the ultimate state].

To realize the state of sagehood without giving rise to the thought of being a sage is called a "wholesome realm"; if one instead forms the conception of being a sage, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.
Herein, "this place" refers to the principle-realm within the immediate phenomena, as mentioned in the preceding text. "Thoroughly investigating" refers to the efficacy of contemplative practice;
"subtle and luminous" refers to the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature. These apply generally to all twenty-five realms, yet they are distinguished here.
At the gateway of the ear, by means of his refined study of the wondrous luminosity, he was able to cause the four great elements to cease their interweaving;

therefore, in a brief moment, his body was able to pass through obstructions. As for "the body being able to pass through obstructions," this refers to the names of the objects manifested within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) where the essence and brilliance overflowed.
The phrase "this is merely the efficacy [of the practice]" clarifies that it is simply the function [of cultivation].
The reason for the arising of this objective realm stems from mental effort (*prayoga*); when effort reaches this point, it is indeed "well-manifested" (*suvyakta*).

However, since this is not yet a realization of the Noble Ones (*ārya*), one must by no means conceive of it as a state of sainthood. Now, Māra, when he takes possession of a person, invariably watches for moments of fear or joy;
by stating that this is not a realization of the Noble Ones, he cuts off such false joy, and by stating that it is called "well-manifested," he [affirms its status].

The reason for severing their deluded fears is that those who cultivate the mind understand this. Second, when the vital essence overflows internally and picks out the *rāhu* (threadworms) and *krimi* (parasites),

Ānanda, if one again uses this mind to investigate the wondrous clarity until it penetrates the interior of the body, this person will suddenly— within that [body]— [...at which point the sentence is left incomplete in the source text.]

If one picks out worms or roundworms from within the body and their physical forms remain perfectly intact without any injury or destruction, this is called the overflowing of refined essence throughout the physical form.
This is merely a temporary attainment resulting from refined practice; it is not a realization of the Sage. If one does not conceive the thought of being a sage, it is called a "wholesome state";
if one interprets it as a realization of the Sage, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.
This "mind" also refers to the mind of contemplative practice; "refined conduct" (*jingxing*) likewise refers to spiritual effort (*yònggōng*). The rest may be understood accordingly.
Third, regarding the union and separation of the refined essence and the soul, one hears the Dharma within space.

Furthermore, by using this mind to investigate both internally and externally, at that time the refined essence, the soul, the will, and the spirit—excluding the body which is subject to grasping—[are liberated].

The rest all involve mutual interpenetration, acting as host and guest to one another; suddenly, one may hear the sound of preaching the Dharma in the air, or hear the secret meanings being expounded simultaneously throughout the ten directions.
This is called the alternating separation and union of the vital essence and the soul, whereby the seeds of goodness are perfected and one temporarily attains such experiences.

These are not holy realizations; if one does not regard them as such, they are called "auspicious states. If one interprets them as holy realizations, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.

In the first passage, although it speaks of "thoroughly investigating the wondrous clarity," this is primarily an external investigation; therefore, the vital essence and clarity overflow into the external objects before one.

In the second passage, although it likewise speaks of "thoroughly investigating the wondrous clarity," this is primarily an internal investigation; therefore, the vital essence and clarity overflow into the physical form.
Now, however, as both the internal and external are investigated simultaneously, the *po*, *hun*, will, and consciousness, as well as the vital essence, [are affected].

The spirit merely removes the body that is grasped as a collective retribution; all else then interpenetrates one another, each acting as both guest and host, whereby the principles of the Dharma are heard throughout the ten directions from within space. A medical treatise states:

"The liver stores the *hun*, the lungs store the *po*, the spleen stores the *yi*, the gallbladder stores the *zhi*, the kidneys store the *jing*, and the heart stores the *shen*. One should know that these are subject to mutual separation and union.
That they act as guest and host to one another is precisely due to this: all things are mind-only, and all phenomena manifested by the mind alone are inconceivable.
Fourth, when the soul is defiled or awakened, one sees the Buddha seated upon the platform.
Furthermore, when this mind becomes clear, luminous, and transparently penetrating, its internal radiance shines forth, causing the ten directions to appear everywhere as the color of Jambūnada gold;

all kinds of things are transformed into Tathāgatas. At that moment, one suddenly beholds Vairocana seated upon a terrace of celestial light, surrounded by a thousand Buddhas, with ten billion lands and lotus flowers appearing simultaneously. This is called the "soul of the mind."
When the mind is permeated by spiritual awakening, its luminosity becomes refined and clear, illuminating all worlds; such a state may be attained for a time, yet it is not a holy realization.
If one does not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome state"; if one interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.
"Transparency" (*ting*) is the function of wondrous stillness (*miāozhǐ*); "manifestation" (*lù*) is the method of wondrous observation (*miàoguān*).
Through transparency via wondrous stillness and manifestation via wondrous observation, this mind becomes bright, pure, and translucent;

thus, inner radiance is revealed, and the *bào-tǔ* (retribution land) momentarily appears as Vairocana—here translated as "Universal Radiance"—who is the unified body of the *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*. This occurs within the sphere of contemplative practice (*guānxíng*).
The form-aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) that is observed is fundamentally not restricted to the realm of cohabitation (*sahabhāva*).

Now that the light of the mind has been refined and clarified, further enhanced by spiritual awakening (*prajñā*), how could that which is permeated lack the power of momentary illumination? It is simply that one must not mistake this for a sign of saintly realization (*ārya-pramāṇa*).
Regarding what is called "permeation through spiritual awakening," it refers to the seeds formed by the habitual hearing of the teachings and the prior knowledge of the *Avataṃsaka* realms.
This refers to the heart-mind and the spirit. When the five refined essences press upon the void and manifest as jewel-like colors,
and one further uses this mental essence to investigate the wondrous luminosity with uninterrupted observation— suppressing, subduing, restraining, and transcending— at that moment,
the void of the ten directions suddenly becomes the color of the seven treasures or a hundred treasures, simultaneously filling all space.
When forms such as blue, yellow, red, and white appear purely and distinctly without mutual obstruction, this is called a temporary attainment resulting from excessive forceful suppression;

it is not a realization of sainthood. If one does not regard it as a state of sainthood, it is known as a "wholesome realm"; if one interprets it as a realization of sainthood, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.

"Suppression, subjugation, and restraint are all the merit of the 'perfect subduing' of the five stages of dwelling; the two characters 'transcending' (chao-yue) indicate that one's application of effort is excessive.
This is a temporary, horizontal vision of the realm of *sambhogakāya* light (*jiguang*) within the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), arising from the power of perfect understanding;
it does not involve the severance of delusions, and therefore one must not mistake it for the realization of a sage. (6)
When the mind’s vision is subtle and clear, one perceives objects within a dark room.
Furthermore, by using this mind to investigate until it is transparent and penetrating, its refined radiance remains undisturbed;
suddenly, at midnight in a dark room, one sees various objects no different from those seen in broad daylight, yet the objects in the dark room do not vanish. This is called the subtlety of the mind.
If you can clarify your vision so that what you behold penetrates the profound depths, and for a time attain such a state, do not regard it as a holy realization;
if you do not conceive of it as a holy mind, it is called a "wholesome realm. If you instead interpret it as a holy attainment, you will immediately fall prey to various delusions.

That which is transparent and penetrating is the essence of tranquil illumination; because it has been refined through investigation so that its radiance is not disturbed, one is able to see strange objects even in a dark room.
Indeed, spirits, ghosts, and those in the various realms of existence constantly dwell intermingled with humans, yet they do not obstruct one another nor see one another.
Now, because the mind is subtle, what it perceives penetrates the profound darkness, and only then can one distinguish the various anomalies.
When encountering objects, even in a dark room, the objects do not cease to exist, and thus they still do not obstruct one another.
The seven types of sensory particles enter together into a state of pure burning and cutting without obstruction.
Furthermore, when this mind enters perfectly into emptiness and fusion, the four limbs suddenly become like grass and wood, such that they may be burned by fire or cut by a blade.
One has no sensation whatsoever; furthermore, the firelight cannot burn or scorch, so that even if one’s flesh were cut, it would be like shaving wood.

This is called the "simultaneous exclusion of sensory objects" (chen bing pai), wherein the nature of the four great elements enters exclusively into purity for a time. Although such a state may be attained, it is not a realization of the Sage.

If one does not conceive of it as a realization of the Sage, it is called a "wholesome state" (shanjian jingjie); if one interprets it as a realization of the Sage, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.
The essence of the mind is fundamentally empty and harmonious; it is only through solidified false conceptualization that obstruction arises within emptiness.

Now, by means of the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one enters perfectly into this nature of empty harmony. One deeply contemplates that the nature of the four great elements internally and the four great elements externally are both manifestations of the mind alone, devoid of self and what belongs to a self.
Therefore, one eliminates the nature of the four great elements and causes the marks of sensory objects to vanish.
The same applies to simultaneous dissolution; however, since this is merely the temporary accomplishment of contemplative practice, how could it be permitted to equate this with the state of a sage?
Eighth, through the transformation manifested by concentrated visualization, one perceives all realms everywhere.
Furthermore, when this mind achieves purity and the power of the pure mind reaches its peak, one suddenly sees the great earth and the mountains and rivers of the ten directions.
One sees all [lands] becoming Buddha-fields, complete with the seven treasures and filled with radiant light;

one further sees Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges filling the void of space, their multi-storied palaces magnificent and resplendent. Looking down, one perceives the hells; looking up, one beholds the celestial palaces, attaining unimpeded vision.

This is called the deepening of focused contemplation through the alternation of joy and revulsion. Through long-term cultivation, these visions transform into the non-conceptual state. One must not regard this as a sign of saintly realization, nor harbor thoughts of being a sage.
What is called a "wholesome realm," if interpreted as a realization of the holy, leads one to accept various forms of heterodoxy.

"Delight and aversion" refers to the mind that rejoices in purity and loathes impurity. Although purity and impurity coexist, they are merely manifestations of the mind; this does not prevent the intense arising of delight and aversion.
If delight and aversion reach their extreme, even the absence of such delight and aversion is not on a different track from them. Therefore, this is the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching].
Practitioners should simply seek birth in the Pure Land; however, although the sacred realms may manifest, one must not give rise to the conceit of being a sage.

The ocean of the Buddhas' perfect and universal knowledge arises from the mind’s conceptions; this mind is the support, this mind is the reality, this mind is the support, and this mind is the reality.
One should understand that these are merely mental constructions; through long-term transformation, they cease to be grasped as "sacred" experiences, just as in the case of Master Huiyuan.
Third, as for seeing sacred images, what compulsion could there be? If one takes this to be a realization of the sacred, it becomes a delusion.
Ninth, the mind flies out and sees the distant regions at night;
furthermore, by investigating with this mind into the profound and far-reaching, suddenly in the middle of the night one sees from afar the markets, streets, and alleys of distant lands.

If one's kinsmen or relatives hear these words, they will feel their hearts oppressed and constrained to the point of flight; thus, many will see them as separated from the truth, yet this is not a sign of saintly realization.

If one does not regard them as signs of sainthood, they are called auspicious states; if one takes them to be signs of sainthood, one will immediately fall under the influence of various heterodoxies.
Those who investigate the profound observe the essential nature of phenomena and principles as vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive;
even that which is forced out in flight is but a temporary state. As long as the shadows of conditions have not been shattered, how can this be the realization of a sage?
These ten types of deviant minds harbor demonic influences, resulting in deluded visions and false teachings.
Furthermore, when you investigate with this mind to the point of extreme refinement, you may see the physical form of the spiritual teacher (kalyāṇamitra) undergo transformations;

in a brief moment, it shifts and changes in various ways without apparent cause. This is called a deluded mind harboring demons, or being possessed by a celestial Māra entering one’s heart and belly, who speaks of the Dharma and masters subtle meanings without basis.
Do not mistake this for a holy realization, nor harbor thoughts of holiness; then the demonic activities will subside.
If one forms a holy understanding of this, one will immediately succumb to various heterodoxies.

Those who have reached the ultimate refinement of their practice say that when the power of their research reaches such a depth, the mind-essence of the Bodhisattvas and Arhats is about to merge with the color-aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*), which is on the verge of breaking down and the void is about to collapse; thus, demonic activities arise from this point. Or...

Within meditative concentration, one may falsely perceive the forms of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) undergoing sudden and inexplicable transformations, appearing as Buddhas or manifesting supernatural powers;
know that this is called a false vision caused by a perverse mind that has harbored demons (chimei), and it is not a true vision of the signs of the sages.
Furthermore, one may occasionally encounter a celestial Māra who enters one’s heart and belly, causing this practitioner to, without cause, [experience such delusions].
If one preaches the Dharma with a thorough understanding of its subtle meanings, know that this is brought about by the power of Māra and is not the genuine opening of the mind.
Although this [practice] guards the mind, it is not sufficiently secret, which allows demonic influences to enter.

If one does not give rise to the notion of being a sage, then the activities of Māra will ultimately dissolve and cease; it is only because of falsely claiming to have attained the realization of a sage that these are the schemes of the celestial Māras.
The third section: Admonition regarding the faults [of these states].
Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifest states during *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a conflicted manner within the *rūpa-skandha*; thus these phenomena appear.
When sentient beings are stubbornly deluded and fail to reflect upon themselves, they encounter these conditions and, being confused, do not recognize them for what they are, saying:
To claim to have attained sainthood through great falsehood is to fall into the Avīci Hell.

You all should, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, proclaim and reveal this meaning so that no celestial Māras may find an opportunity; protect and sustain it so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

To say that these ten kinds of objects manifest from within *dhyāna* is because the beginningless, false aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the present mind of wondrous *śamatha-vipaśyanā* interact as subject and object; thus these phenomena appear.
Indeed, the observing mind is like the drill, the observed aggregates are like the wood, and the inherent nature (*prakṛti*) hidden within the aggregates is like the fire.

Various manifested objects are like smoke produced by drilling wood for fire; when one perceives smoke, one knows that the fire is not far away. Therefore, each [of these] is called a "wholesome object.
If one sees the smoke and stops [the drilling], then the fire cannot be obtained. This is like damaging the wood or failing in the craftsmanship;

it is as if one were to become confused midway and instead fall under the influence of various evils. The following cases should be understood accordingly. Second, the explanation of the objects of the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate).

Third, there are three parts: first, a general indication of the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*); second, a detailed explanation of the manifestation of their characteristics; third, a conclusion on the faults and an exhortation to insight. Within the first part, there are four sections:

first, concluding the previous section on the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); second, correctly indicating the domain of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); third, providing a forward indication of the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation;
fourth, concluding by showing that it is fundamentally nothing but deluded thought. Now, the first section.
Ānanda, when those good men, while practicing samādhi and śamatha, have exhausted the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha),
they see the minds of all Buddhas appearing like reflections manifested in a clear mirror.

In the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the King of Great Buddha-Ushnīṣas, both beginning and end take *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) as their essence and function; what is now stated regarding *śamatha* cites *śamatha* to encompass *vipaśyanā*.
Within the shared realm (*sahā-loka*), when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, one sees the Buddha’s mind of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-citta*);

within the realm of skillful means (*upāya-rūpa-skandha*), when the aggregate of form is exhausted, one sees the Buddha’s mind of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā-citta*); and within the realm of true recompense (*vipāka-rūpa-skandha*).

To fully perceive the Buddha’s mind of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) and further realize that the form-aggregate (*rūpaskandha*) of the three lands is emptiness is called "fully perceiving the Buddha’s mind of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
To realize that the form-aggregate of the three lands is provisional is called "fully perceiving the Buddha’s mind of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).
To realize that the form-aggregate of the three lands is the Middle Way is called "fully perceiving the Buddha’s mind of all-encompassing wisdom. Thus it is.

There are differences between those who possess contemplative practice—ranging from partial insight to ultimate insight—and those of sharp faculties, for whom all is exhausted in one exhaustion and all is seen in one seeing.

However, if the habitual tendencies of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) are strong, then within the stage of contemplative practice, the realms of adventitious heterodoxy will again manifest.
Second, this correctly demonstrates the realm of the aggregate of sensation.
If one has attained something but is unable to employ it— like a person who loathes their own hands and feet, whose sight and hearing are unimpaired and undeluded,
yet whose mind is struck by an external evil spirit such that they cannot move— this is called the domain of the skandha of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Because one perceives the Buddha-mind through contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), if there is still something attained, it has not yet interfused with the flow of the Dharma;

therefore, it cannot yet be put into use. "Reception" (*vedanā*) takes the meaning of receiving and assimilating external objects. Now, although the six sense-faculties do not currently engage with their respective objects, the habit of receiving them remains;
this is why it is said that one understands the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*) to be fundamentally suchness, like a person who has awakened from a nightmare.
Because the ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness) is present, it is compared to hands and feet; seeing and hearing are complete and unconfused.

The three lands (*tri-bhūmi*) and their false *vedanā-skandha* (aggregate of sensation) are compared to an external guest or demon who cannot go or stay as it pleases, and thus cannot move [the host].
Although these external demons are not truly existent, this very domain of the *vedanā-skandha* is precisely the guest-demon that contacts the mind. Part Three: The Suspended.
This demonstrates the signs of the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

If the affliction of nightmares ceases, and the mind detaches from the body to look back at one's own face, such that going and staying are free and there is no further obstruction, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation.
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
When that which is heard is exhausted, it is like the cessation of the affliction of a nightmare; because there is nothing further to grasp or receive, the mind attains liberation.

Being free from the body of segmented existence (*vipāka-kāya*), one gains freedom of movement and abiding within the realm of common residence (*sahā-loka*). Being free from the body of transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), one gains freedom of movement and abiding within the realms of skillful means (*upāya*) and true reward (*dharma-niṣyanda*).
The remainder is as explained in the section on the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing. Fourth, the conclusion and indication of the fundamental source.
Delusive conceptualization.
Observe its origin: empty clarity and delusive conceptualization constitute its root.

Because of adverse or favorable delusive objects, various gains and losses arise; one delusively experiences them as having real existence. This clarity that is perceived is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Examine this empty clarity: it is merely a delusive thought and not a truly existent empty clarity. Once you recognize its root, you will no longer be deceived by it.

Second, the detailed explanation of the manifestation of signs has ten parts: first, the suppression of faults gives rise to compassion (up to) tenth, the culmination of attachment becomes greed. Now, the first part.

Ānanda, that good man, while within this state, shall attain great radiance; his mind becomes luminous, yet because he suppresses it excessively within, a boundless compassion suddenly arises within him.
Thus, even when looking upon mosquitoes or gadflies, he regards them as his own infants, giving rise to a heart of pity and involuntarily shedding tears.
This is called the "excessive suppression and crushing" of the practice; if he awakens to this, [he will transcend it].
"Absence of fault" does not constitute proof of saintliness; it is merely the realization of non-delusion, which will naturally dissipate over time.

If you take this to be the mark of a sage, then the demon of pity will enter your heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, you will weep and wail boundlessly, losing your correct meditative absorption and inevitably falling into ruin.
"Among these" refers to the midst of the samādhis of contemplative practice regarding the two objects of fact and principle.
Because the objective realm of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is shattered by the power of contemplative practice, one is able to attain great radiance;

however, because the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) has not yet been shattered, various realms of sensation arise. There are five kinds of sensation: first, suffering; second, pleasure; third, grief; fourth, joy; and fifth, equanimity.

The compassionate heart of today arises from being conditioned by the suffering sensations (*duḥkhavedanā*) of sentient beings; though it resembles great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), it actually relies upon the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
It arises solely because of excessive internal suppression; how could it enter the stages of the sages?
What is valued is awakening and clarity without delusion, so as not to invite demons or incur failure. Second, being moved to gratitude gives rise to valor.

Ānanda, furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons who perceive the dissolution of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the clarity of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), with superior signs appearing before them, may suddenly experience an excess of agitation.

Within this state, they give rise to limitless courage; their minds become fierce and sharp, and their resolve becomes equal to that of all Buddhas, claiming that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment.
This is called "the transgression of overreaching through the exertion of effort"; if one awakens to it, [it is not an obstacle].
Being free from fault does not constitute proof of saintliness; rather, it is the realization of awakening without delusion, which naturally dissipates over time.
If you take this state to be the mark of a sage, then a mad demon will enter your heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, you will boast with an arrogance beyond compare;
your mind will reach such a point that you see neither Buddha above nor people below. Having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), you shall surely fall into ruin.

Within the meditative concentration of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-samādhi*), one strips away a layer of the objective realm of form-obstruction (*rūpāvaraṇa*) to reveal a state of empty luminosity (*śūnyaprakāśa*).
Consequently, because this [revelation] is so intensely stimulating, courage arises; this is triggered by the pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) within one's own mind.
The meaning of these passages is all readily understandable. Third, when wisdom declines, mindfulness (*smṛti*) is formed.
Furthermore, within that state of concentration, those good sons may see the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) become clear;
yet, having nothing new to realize before them and having lost their former dwelling, their power of wisdom declines and they fall into a state of desolation.

Seeing nothing at all, a great parching thirst suddenly arises in their hearts, and at all times they remain submerged in this unceasing recollection, taking this very state to be the mark of diligent vigor.
This is called cultivating the mind without wisdom; one loses the realization for oneself, yet there is no fault in that. It is not a sign of saintly attainment.

If one mistakes this for such an attainment, the demon of recollection will enter one's heart and viscera. Morning and evening, it will seize the mind and suspend it in a single place, causing one to lose right concentration and inevitably fall into ruin.

Because the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has not yet been destroyed, there is no new realization; because the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has already dissolved, one loses the former dwelling place.

Due to these conditions, based on one's own mind, one abandons equanimity and gives rise to parched thirst. The illness lies in an excess of concentration (samādhi) over wisdom (prajñā), which causes the memory to sink and the mind to hang suspended.
Thus, the four types of wisdom are superior, while this state is inferior.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons may perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright.

If their power of wisdom exceeds the limits of concentration and they lose its sharp intensity, they may harbor various superior natures within their minds; their own minds then become suspicious, thinking, "I am Vairocana," and they settle for a small attainment as sufficient.
This is called losing constant examination through the application of the mind, resulting in being submerged in cognitive views; yet, if they awaken to this, there is no fault.
This is not a sign of saintly realization; if you mistake it for such realization, the demon of inferiority and complacency will enter your heart and mind.
Seeing others, you will claim, "I have attained the supreme, ultimate truth," thereby losing your correct meditative absorption and falling into ruin.

This is the superior state arising from the condition of joyful sensation (*saumanasya*). The ailment lies in wisdom (*prajñā*) exceeding concentration (*samādhi*), whereby constant discernment is lost.
This constitutes the fifth loss, which gives rise to sorrow.

Furthermore, within that concentration, those sons of good family perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear; yet they have not yet attained a new realization.
Therefore, when the mind has already perished and one surveys the two temporal limits, difficulties arise spontaneously within the mind;

suddenly, inexhaustible sorrow arises, as if sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a poisonous drug. The heart no longer desires to live and constantly seeks someone to end its life so that it may quickly attain liberation.
This is called "cultivating the mind while losing the skillful means"; if one awakens to this, there is no fault, yet it does not constitute a realization of the holy.
If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, then a portion of the demons of constant sorrow will enter their heart and viscera;

grasping swords and blades, they will cut their own flesh, rejoicing in the relinquishing of life, or being constantly sorrowful, they will flee into mountains and forests, unable to bear the sight of people,
and having lost right concentration, they shall fall into ruin.
"New realization not yet attained" refers to the fact that the *vedanā-skandha* has not yet been destroyed; "the mind already lost" refers to the prior dissolution of the *rūpa-skandha*.

Because one seeks self-harm due to these conditions of sorrowful sensation, both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are deficient. Sixth, when wisdom is deficient, it results in joy (*prīti*).

Furthermore, when those good sons within that samādhi see the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) become clear and pure, their minds become peaceful and secure.
Thereafter, suddenly and spontaneously, an infinite joy arises within their hearts, such that they cannot restrain their own exultation.

This is called "light ease" (*praśrabdhi*). If one lacks wisdom and restrains oneself [from further progress], there is no fault; however, it is not a holy realization (*ārya-siddhi*). If one takes this to be a holy realization, [it is a delusion].
Then there is a class of demons who delight in pleasure and joy who enter their hearts and bellies;

seeing people, they laugh by the side of the road, singing and dancing to themselves, claiming to have attained unimpeded liberation, yet they have lost right concentration and are destined for downfall.
This arising of the sensation of joy based on pliancy is likewise a case where meditative concentration surpasses wisdom.

Furthermore, within that state of concentration, those sons of good family perceive the dissolution of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) and the clarity of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha), whereby they become conceited, thinking they have already attained sufficiency.

Suddenly, groundless and great pride arises; thus, from pride (*māna*) through excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), or overweening pride (*abhimāna*), or even the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*), they all erupt simultaneously.
Within their minds, they hold even the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in contempt, let alone those of lower rank such as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This is called "seeing oneself as superior. If one lacks wisdom, there is no way to save oneself; yet if one awakens to this, there is no fault.
This is not a sign of saintly realization; if one mistakes it for such realization, then a portion of the Great Māra of Arrogance will enter their heart and viscera.
They will fail to pay homage to stupas and temples and will destroy scriptures and images. They will say to donors, "These [images] are merely gold and copper, or perhaps clay and wood;
these scriptures are but tree leaves or woven silk. Thus, while their own physical bodies—which are truly eternal—are not respected by them, they instead venerate clay and wood.

This is indeed a perversion; those who hold such deep faith will, because of this destruction, bury it in the earth, leading deluded sentient beings into the Avīci Hell and causing them to lose right concentration, thereby falling into ruin.

To consider oneself already sufficient is also to give rise to various forms of conceit (*māna*) based on joy and pleasure. To rely on oneself and look down upon others is called "great conceit" (*adhimāna*).

To be arrogant toward those of equal virtue is simply called "conceit" (*māna*). To compete for superiority with equals is called "excessive conceit" (*atimāna*). To compete for superiority with those who are superior is called "conceit exceeding conceit" (*mānātimāna*).
To claim to have attained what one has not attained is called "puffed-up conceit" (*abhimāna*). To take pride in one's own inferiority is [called] "self-conceit" (*ūnamāna*).
The pride of considering oneself inferior, such as failing to pay homage to stupas and shrines, is itself a form of perverse pride;

since these seven types of pride are seen only within the superior states of meditative concentration, it is said that they lack wisdom and cannot save themselves. Eighth is the pride of being self-sufficient through light ease (*praśrabdhi*).
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons see the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) become clear.

Within their brilliant clarity, they perfectly realize the principle of essence and attain great compliance. Suddenly, their minds give rise to immeasurable lightness and ease, whereupon they claim to have attained sainthood and achieved great self-mastery.
This is called "attaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom. If this realization is [properly] understood, there is no fault; it is not yet a true realization of sainthood.
If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, then a portion of the "light-and-pure" demon will enter their heart and viscera;

they will consider themselves satisfied and no longer seek progress. Such individuals mostly become unlearned bhikṣus who mislead sentient beings, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell and lose right concentration, thereby falling into ruin.
Among those who are clever and discerning, the realm in which form is dissolved is fully realized as the subtle principle;

one who awakens to this realizes that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. Attaining great conformity is also the cause for the two sensations of joy and pleasure.

Having obtained various forms of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) through wisdom, one then considers oneself sufficient; yet because this remains a state where concentration (*samādhi*) exceeds wisdom (*prajñā*), it results in being "without hearing" (*aśruta*).
Monks, this is precisely because they have not attained mastery over the characteristics of dharmas. Their realization of the nine emptinesses leads to annihilationism.
Furthermore, while in that state of concentration, those sons of good family see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear;
within this clarity of awakening, they attain a nature of empty luminosity. Suddenly, they turn toward eternal extinction, repudiating cause and effect, and enter exclusively into emptiness.

When the realization of the empty mind manifests before one, and even when the mind gives rise to the understanding that growth, cessation, and severance are all resolved, there is no fault; yet this is not yet a holy realization.
If one mistakes this for a holy realization, the "empty demon" will enter one's heart and viscera, leading one to slander those who uphold the precepts as being merely followers of the Small Vehicle.

Such a person, claiming to have realized emptiness, asks what "observing" or "violating" precepts could possibly mean; they will constantly drink wine and eat meat while receiving offerings from faithful donors.
