Widely practicing lewd and impure acts due to the power of demonic influence, they entice those before them so that no suspicion or slander arises; once the ghost-mind has long entered them,
they may consume excrement, urine, wine, meat, and the like— all of which are equally empty— thereby violating the Buddha’s disciplinary code,
leading others into transgression, losing right concentration, and inevitably falling into ruin.

The clarity and awakening within this state is precisely the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*) by which the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has been dissolved; the empty and luminous nature therein is the very nature of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*).

This, too, arises from being conditioned by neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*) and results in an understanding of emptiness; it is the fault of having an excess of wisdom and a deficiency of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
I frequently observe that those who claim to be "men of knowledge" nowadays, though they may not dare to eat meat or engage in sexual misconduct, [yet fail in] the monastic precepts (*bhikṣu-śīla*).
Rarely is there anyone who does not judge this to be the Lesser Vehicle; such a view borders on demonic teaching—is it not perilous?
The ten kinds of craving constitute extreme greed.

Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those sons of good family perceive the aggregate of form dissolving and the aggregate of sensation becoming clear and bright, savoring its empty luminosity.
When this penetrates deeply into the marrow of one's heart, a boundless love suddenly arises within the mind; when this love reaches its peak, it gives rise to madness, which is then called greed.

This is known as the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) entering the mind with ease and compliance, yet lacking the self-sustaining power of wisdom. One mistakenly enters into various desires, though there is no fault if one subsequently awakens to them.

It is not a true realization of the holy (*ārya*). If one takes this to be a holy realization, then the demon of desire (*kāma-māra*) will enter one’s heart and viscera, leading one to speak exclusively of desire.
To transform laypeople for the sake of the path to Bodhi, he causes them to practice desire with equanimity; those who thus practice desire are called "sons of the Dharma.

By the power of spirits and ghosts, during the final age, they gather the common and ignorant, numbering up to a hundred, or even one hundred, two hundred, five, six, or seven hundred, or as many as ten million.
Thereupon, the demons develop a mind of weary detachment, and their bodies [perish].
Lacking majestic virtue, they fall into royal calamities; misleading sentient beings, they cause them to enter the Avīci Hell and lose right concentration, inevitably descending into ruin.

By savoring the empty clarity of the aggregate of feeling, they give rise to craving and become crazed; this also arises from the presence of pleasant feelings, whether in meditative absorption or otherwise.

This is an error of wisdom. To admonish against the errors of the three fetters, Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states that appear during dhyāna are all manifestations resulting from the interaction between the mind and the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation); therefore, these matters appear.
When sentient beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to exercise self-reflection, they encounter such conditions and, being confused and unaware of themselves, claim:

To claim to have attained sainthood through a great falsehood is to fall into the Avīci Hell. You all should likewise take these words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them during the Final Dharma;
cause all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning, and do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity.
Protect and preserve them so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

The third section concerns the perception-aggregate (*saṃjñā-skandha*). It has three parts: first, a general demonstration of the characteristics of the aggregates; second, a specific clarification of the manifestation of its characteristics;

and third, a conclusion on the faults and an exhortation to insight. Within the first part, there are four sections: first, concluding the preceding description of the exhaustion of the sensation-aggregate;

second, formally demonstrating the domain of the perception-aggregate; third, pre-emptively demonstrating the exhaustion of the perception-aggregate; and fourth, concluding by showing that it is fundamentally nothing but deluded thought. Now, the first [of these four].
Ānanda, when that good man cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, although his outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet extinguished,
his mind has already separated from its physical form like a bird escaping from a cage. He is then able to achieve the body of intent-birth (*manomaya-kāya*),
ascending from this ordinary body through the sixty sagely stages of a bodhisattva, proceeding everywhere without obstruction.
Regarding the characteristics of the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), one must refer to the three lands and the six stages of realization (*ṣat-samyaktva*).

What is now said—“although the outflows are not yet exhausted”—is for the time being stated from the perspective of the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching; it is precisely the realm where the faculties first attain liberation.

Because the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) still remains, the outflows are not yet exhausted; however, because the discriminative grasping at a self (*vikalpita-ātma-grāha*) has already been severed, the mind is detached from it.
Its form is like a bird emerging from its cage, as previously described in the text regarding "freedom in going and staying.
As for the "sixty stages of the sages," the three gradual sequences constitute the means of advancement (*abhyudaya*), while the fifty-seven stages constitute that which is advanced.

When the means and the object are combined, they collectively form sixty. Within these sixty, the three methods of advancement apply universally to both ordinary beings and sages; it is that which is advanced [which constitutes the stages].

The stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) constitutes the outer ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), while the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) constitute the inner ordinary beings; the remaining forty-six stages are designated as "sages" (*ārya*).
Here, however, they are collectively termed "sages" because the principle of cause and effect is the same for those entering from the state of an ordinary being into the state of a sage.

Having ascended to the first stage of faith (*prathama-śraddhā*), one first severs the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); the momentum is then like splitting bamboo—there is only progress and no retreat—due to the subsequent stages of the sages.
This ensures that the meritorious practices of the preceding stage of ordinary beings are not in vain; thus, they are designated as the "sixty stages of the sages.
Regarding the "body born of mind" (*manomaya-kāya*): because it reaches wherever the mind intends, it is said to proceed without obstruction. There are three types:
first, the body born of mind through entry into the bliss of *samādhi*, which can be attained at the initial stage of faith; second, the body born of mind through awakening...
The *dharmatā-svabhāva-manomaya-kāya* (body of mind-made of the self-nature of phenomena) can be attained through the eight stages of faith;
the three kinds of *anābhoga-manomaya-kāya* (spontaneously produced bodies of mind-made) can be attained through the ten stages of faith.

Upon reaching the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), one partially realizes the Tathāgata’s single body that is yet infinite bodies—namely, the Middle Way *Dharmakāya*, the source of the *Sambhogakāya* and *Nirmāṇakāya*. It is like the moon in the heavens universally reflected in a thousand rivers.
It is also called the "mind-born body. Second, the actual demonstration of the domain of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*):
For example, suppose there is a person who sleeps soundly and speaks in his sleep;

although this person has no distinct awareness, the words he utters possess rhythmic cadence and sequential order, causing those who are not asleep to fully understand his speech. This is what is called the domain of the aggregate of perception.
When those of sharp faculties exhaust the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), all is exhausted at once, and they are able to attain a vast and clear great awakening.

For those whose habitual tendencies regarding the aggregate of sensation are strong, although the aggregate of sensation appears empty and wondrous during their contemplative practice, it further manifests as a state of dreaming and somnambulism within the realm of experience.
The unbroken aggregate of sensation is likened to deep sleep, while the emptiness and wondrous nature of the aggregate of sensation are likened to dreaming.

The phrase "there is no separate object of knowledge" is used as a metaphor for the fact that when afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) have not yet been severed, one does not reach the true realm.

The phrase "forming a rhythmic sequence" is used as a metaphor for the fact that when the merit of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) is profound, the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are forever suppressed, and one is able to border upon the stage of the Sages.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likened to those who do not sleep, for they fully know and fully see this good man and his [attainments].
In the practice of contemplation, the mind attains mastery, as illustrated by the analogy of one who understands another's words;

yet, because they are separated by the aggregate of false conceptualization (*parikalpita-saṃjñā-skandha*), it is like a person who is awake being able to understand the talk of one who is asleep, while the sleeper does not know of the waking person’s understanding.
Third, this is the provisional indication of the signs of the exhaustion of the aggregate of conceptualization.

If all stirring thoughts are exhausted and floating perceptions are eliminated within the awakened, luminous mind—like removing dust and grime—one will perfectly illuminate the beginning and end of a single cycle of birth and death;
this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (kleśa-kaṣāya).
When the luminous mind of awakening is cleansed of its dust and defilements, this is what is meant by "the emptiness of that which perceives and that which is perceived.

Regarding the two categories of birth and death: "category" (*lun*) here carries the sense of "kind. Birth and death through segmented portions (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*) constitute one category, while birth and death through transformation (*pariṇāmi-saṃsāra*) constitutes another.
"Beginning" refers to exhausting their origin; "end" refers to investigating their ultimate conclusion. Thus one comes to full knowledge.
The two kinds of birth and death come from nowhere and go nowhere; this is called "perfectly illuminating the beginning and the end.

When all stirring thoughts in the Stage of Co-residence (Sahā-bhūmi) are exhausted, one removes the defilements of *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *kleśa-āsrava*, and perfectly illuminates the beginning and end of *paricchinna-janma-maraṇa*.

When all stirring thoughts in the Stages of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*) and True Reward (*samyak-vipāka-bhūmi*) are exhausted, one removes the defilements of *paryavasthāna-āsrava* and *avidyā-āsrava*, and perfectly illuminates the beginning and end of *pariṇāmi-janma-maraṇa*.

From the beginning to the end of birth and death, there is the practice of contemplation; exhausting the practice of contemplation, one proceeds through contemplation to perfect illumination, and even to the ultimate limit;
exhausting the ultimate limit, one proceeds to the ultimate intent and achieves perfect illumination. The rest is as explained in the section on Perfect Penetration.
Fourth, the conclusion shows that [birth and death] are fundamentally nothing but deluded thoughts.
Manifesting its origins, it takes pervasive delusion as its basis.
Only this aggregate of perception can effect such fusion and transformation, causing the mind to follow objects and objects to follow the mind;
yet this very fusion is in truth nothing but delusion—there is no other nature of fusion to be found apart from it. To know this perception...
If the aggregates (*skandhas*) are empty, false, and without foundation, one will not be deluded by them. Second, a detailed explanation of the manifestations [of afflictions], in ten parts:
first, the thought of craving for skillful means (up to) tenth, the thought of craving for long life. Although afflictions are many, craving is the foremost;
once there is something craved, one falls into the net of Māra—how can one not be cautious? Now, the first.

Ānanda, when that son of good family’s aggregate of perception (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes luminous.
At this time, his mind comes to cherish this perfect luminosity; he sharpens his refined contemplation and greedily seeks out skillful means.

Then, a celestial Māra, watching for such an opportunity, dispatches a refined spirit to possess a person, who speaks of sutras and dharmas. The person is unaware they are possessed by a māra and says of themselves:
That is to say, having attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, he goes to the place where that seeker of skillful means—a son of good family—is, spreads out a seat, and preaches the Dharma.
For a brief moment, his form may appear as a bhikṣu so that the person may see him;
or he may become Śakra, or a woman, or a bhikṣuṇī, or lie in a dark room while his body emits radiance. This person, deluded by folly, mistakes him for a bodhisattva and places their faith in him.

They convert others by agitating their minds and violating the Buddha’s discipline, secretly practicing greed and desire. They are fond of speaking of calamities, auspicious signs, and strange transformations;
they may claim that the Tathāgata has appeared in a certain place, or speak of the kalpa-ending fires, or describe the terrors of war, causing people's wealth and property to dissipate without cause.
These are called "strange ghosts" who, having grown old, become demons to harass and disturb others.
If this person becomes weary and satisfied, giving rise to thoughts of departure from the other's body, both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal peril;
you must be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth, for through delusion and ignorance, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Regarding the "emptiness and subtlety of the aggregate of sensation": this means that during the stage of contemplative practice, one realizes that the aggregate of sensation is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha;
thus, the ten kinds of demonic activities do not arise, or if they do arise, one awakens to them and is not deluded.

Therefore, it is said that one does not encounter perverse anxieties. Since one originally cultivates perfect concentration based on perfect understanding, one now does not encounter the perversities within the aggregate of sensation.

If one contemplates, the tainted (*sāsrava*) meditative absorption will transform into the untainted (*anāsrava*) right absorption; therefore, it is said that "perfect concentration brings forth illumination.

Once perfect concentration has brought forth illumination, one need only apply oneself with skillful diligence according to the Dharma, progressing from the samādhi of contemplative practice (*darśana-mārga*) into the semblance, the partially true, and the ultimate samādhis.
Thus, what skillful means could there be that is not attained?
What realm of phenomena is not traversed? What principle of capacity is not in accord? What fundamental root is not severed?
What response to resonance is not accomplished? What state of tranquility is not entered? What past lives are not known?
What supernormal powers are not possessed? What profound emptiness is not realized? What...?
Failing to abide permanently in the eternal while suddenly giving rise to a mind of attachment and greed for acquisition is like this:

it is as if one whose scales and horns are not yet formed should immediately think of leaping into flight, or whose feathers and down are not yet complete should already intend to soar through the air;

or as if one should seek office before their learning is refined, or consume elixirs before the alchemical refinement is complete—is this not possible? Therefore, know that all such acts invite demonic interference and lead to downfall.
The fault lies solely in the delusive imaginings of one’s own mind. Each paragraph contains three sections:
first, from "That good son" to "greedily seeking skillful means," which clarifies the delusive imaginings arising within meditative concentration;
second, from "At that time, the heavenly Māra" to "both fall into royal calamity," which clarifies the demonic affairs summoned by those delusive imaginings; third, from "You should... [to the end].
The section on "The Foremost Awakened One Falling into the Avīci Hell" explains the gains and losses resulting from the awakening of the deluded through exhortation.
The first part is self-evident. The second part has four sections: first, from "At that time" to "his body was radiant," which clarifies the characteristics of the demonic activities;

second, from "This person, being foolish and deluded" to "secretly practicing lust," which clarifies how he is enticed and confused by demons; third, [the section on] his mouth... Good words lead to nothingness and thus dissipate; this further clarifies the deeds performed by Māra.
Fourth, these are called "strange ghosts" down to "all falling into royal calamity," which concludes the matters accomplished by Māra.
The initial phrase "waiting for an opportunity" means that one finds an opening in the practitioner’s greedy thoughts to exploit them. "A flying essence attaching itself to a person" refers to this.
Because the practitioner’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, demons cannot attach themselves to them; therefore, they instead attach themselves to others.
Such a person is one to whom a demon has attached itself. Though possessed by the demon, the person is unaware of it.
Riding upon the power of the demon, [the demon] comes before this practitioner and manifests various skillful means to pander to what the practitioner craves. Next is this person...

1. This refers to practitioners who cultivate meditative concentration; because they are deluded by those possessed by demons, they mistake them for Bodhisattvas, thus believing their teachings and secretly engaging in lustful desires.
2. Those who speak pleasant words with their mouths are likewise people possessed by demons;
not only do they delude and disturb this particular group of individuals, but they also universally delude everyone else. 3. This... [fourth point]... here.
Regarding the name "Guaiguī" (Strange Ghost), this refers to the names of malevolent spirits; its intent is to cause the practitioner to perceive them first and then to denounce and shatter them.
"Disciple" refers to one who practices meditative concentration, while "Master" refers to a person possessed by a demon.
Because demonic karma is so rampant, the demon departs only after the person has first encountered royal calamity and subsequently falls into the Avīci Hell. You must perceive this beforehand.
The first two lines exhort one to awaken; if one fails to do so, they result in delusion and ignorance. The latter two lines warn against being lost in confusion;

if one heeds them, one achieves what is called "prior awakening. This may involve restraining and examining the mind to prevent greed from arising, or being able to immediately perceive and shatter greed as soon as it first arises, or remaining unmoved by the clever deceptions manifested by demonic beings. Through these means, one can avoid the cycle of rebirth.
If, however, one were to believe their teachings and violate the Buddha’s Vinaya, even if one were to realize it was the work of Māra from that point on, it would already be too late for repentance.
The subsequent passages are identical and need not be explained further; they may be understood by analogy.
Second is the craving for experiences.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when a son of good family’s aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within the samādhi.
At that time, his mind loves to wander, and he flies with his refined reflections, greedily seeking out various experiences. Then, the celestial Māra watches for this opportunity.

He then sends forth his refined essence to attach itself to a person’s mouth, causing them to preach the Dharma; yet that person remains unaware, being possessed by a māra, and claims for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
He comes to the dwelling of the son of good family who seeks to travel [the path], spreads out a seat, and preaches the Dharma;
his own form undergoes no change, but those listening to the Dharma suddenly see themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers, their entire bodies transformed into purple-gold.
Within this assembly of the Radiant Multitude, each listener has thus attained what was never before experienced. These people are deluded by folly, taking themselves to be bodhisattvas;
their minds are licentious and they violate the Buddha’s Vinaya, secretly practicing greed and desire. They are fond of saying with their own mouths: "A certain Buddha has appeared in the world;
such-and-such a person in such-and-such a place must be the emanation-body of that Buddha come here; such-and-such a person is precisely that bodhisattva."
When these beings come to transform the human realm, people who see them will develop a heart of longing and thirst;

thus, false views will secretly arise, and the wisdom of the All-Knowing One will extinguish them—these are called *pūtana* ghosts who have become demons in their old age. They afflict and disturb these people until they become weary and satisfied, at which point they leave the person's body.

Exposition by the Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera Zhixu of Ancient Wu. Section Four: The Sphere of the *Saṃskāra-skandha*. Part One:

A General Demonstration of the Characteristics of the *Skandhas*. Part Two: A Specific Explanation of the Manifesting Characteristics. Part Three: A Conclusion on the Faults and an Exhortation. Within the first part, there are four sections:
First, a conclusion regarding the characteristics of the exhaustion of the *saṃjñā-skandha*; Second, the formal demonstration of the boundaries of the *saṃskāra-skandha*.

Section Three: Displaying the Signs of the Exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the Aggregate of Mental Formations). Section Four: Concluding that it is Originally Only Delusive Thought. Now, for the first part:
Ānanda, when those good sons who practice *samādhi* have exhausted the *vijñāna-skandha* (the Aggregate of Consciousness), their ordinary dreams and fantasies are extinguished;
whether awake or asleep, they remain constantly one. Their awakened clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky, no longer burdened by the heavy, coarse objects of the external world.
Contemplating the phenomena of shadows, one observes that the great earth, mountains, and rivers of all worlds are like a bright mirror: they come without attachment and pass away without trace;
they receive reflections in emptiness, yet leave no habitual residue, being solely the single, pure, and true reality.
The five aggregates of false delusion all take conceptualization as their root; therefore, when the aggregate of perception is exhausted, ordinary dreams and fantasies are extinguished.

Since the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* clarifies that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages all have dream omens, we know that it is only upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood that one is called "ultimately awakened. However, even these dreams and fantasies—
There are six distinct levels of difference: the views and thoughts of the six classes of ordinary beings can be extinguished by the Two Vehicles;
the dust-like delusions and dreams of the Two Vehicles can be extinguished by Bodhisattvas; the ignorance and dreams of Bodhisattvas can only be extinguished by the Buddha.
Furthermore, there are differences ranging from extinction through contemplation and analysis to ultimate extinction.
If one possesses sharp faculties, then all is dissolved in a single moment;

even if the faculties are unequal, it may still occur without following a sequential order—this is merely spoken of as a sequence for the sake of instruction. The luminous awareness, empty and still, is like a cloudless sky;

this corresponds to the preceding passage which describes the state where "within the mind of luminous awareness, one removes the dust and grime," such that both the subject that perceives and the object perceived are found to be empty. It is empty.
That which receives and responds is empty yet capable of receiving, like a valley responding to an echo; it illuminates and responds, like a mirror reflecting an image.
"Completely devoid of habitual traces" means there are no such traces. These habitual traces are shadows of past sensory objects that have fallen away.

To be completely devoid of these shadows of dust is precisely like the sound of an echo or the reflection in a mirror: when they come, there is nothing to which they adhere; when they pass, they leave no trace. This is what is meant by "seeing."
When the thought-veil (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, one contemplates the world of co-residence (*sahā-loka*); having exhausted all lingering habits, there is only the single true emptiness.

When the thought-veil of dust-like delusions is exhausted, one contemplates the world of skillful means (*upāya-loka*); having exhausted all lingering habits, there is only the single wondrous existence.

When the thought-veil of ignorance (*avidyā*) is exhausted, one contemplates the world of true recompense (*samyak-vipāka-loka*); having exhausted all lingering habits, there is only the single Middle Way, the principle of ultimate truth. (2)
This correctly reveals the domain of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
From this, the root-source of arising and ceasing is disclosed; one sees all twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, each fully categorized by its kind.

Although the specific origins of their respective lives have not yet been fully understood, they are seen to share a common basis of birth, shimmering and turbulently agitated like a mirage in the wild.
To reach the ultimate pivot and aperture of the floating sense-faculties and their objects is what is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha*.
The shifting, flowing, and active creation is termed *saṃskāra*, which is the very root-source of the two kinds of birth-and-death: the segmented (*paricchinna*) and the transformative (*pariṇāma*).
Now, within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*), as the mind of conceptualization has already been subdued, the objective sphere of the *saṃskāra-skandha* [emerges].

Although this has been revealed, the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate) has not yet been discerned; thus, the individual origins of their respective destinies have not been fully understood.

It is precisely this *saṃskāra-skandha* (formative aggregate), however, that serves as the fundamental basis for the rebirth of the twelve classes of beings and the pivotal gateway to the floating sense organs and objects.
Were it not for this shimmering false nature, how could the twelve classes of beings undergo rebirth? As for these floating sense organs...
By what cause do the dust motes open and close? It is by means of their exhaustion and their continuous succession.

"Wild horses" refers to the floating vapors reflected in the sun upon the water, also known as a mirage (*marīci*); when viewed from afar they appear like water, yet when approached they lack substance.
The shadow of the moon is likewise without substantial nature. A "pivot" (*shu*) is the door-axle; a "socket" (*xue*) is the place where the axle rests. By [these means, movement occurs].
Because the pivot-holes are thus, the gates can open and close; because of the activity-aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the sense-faculties and their objects falsely undergo arising and ceasing.
Third, a preliminary indication of the signs of the exhaustion of the activity-aggregate:

If this turbid agitation subsides and the fundamental nature flashes forth, such that the nature enters the fundamental clarity, and with a single clarification the fundamental habits vanish like the extinguishing of waves and ripples.
It transforms into clear water, which is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings.
It is said that if this fundamental nature—which is clear yet agitated, shimmering and never still—is dissolved, its nature enters the essence of clear water;
there is only the single, profoundly tranquil fundamental habit of clarity. It is like when waves and ripples have ceased, they transform into clear water.
This is the emptiness wherein that which is emptied is extinguished; as arising and ceasing are both extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests before one.

Therefore, it is said that the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is exhausted and one transcends the turbidity of sentient beings. The nine realms and the six stages of realization are fully explained as in the section on Perfect Penetration.

Regarding "the primordial clarity of fundamental habit," this refers to the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha). It is called "primordial clarity" because it is originally pure, yet it is also termed "fundamental habit" because it contains...
The storage of all seeds of habitual tendencies still belongs to the continuous flow of the true and permanent;

this is what the subsequent text refers to when it says, "This stillness is not the True Suchness (tathatā), like a rapid stream appearing tranquil. Fourth, the conclusion shows that [the mind] is fundamentally nothing but deluded thought.
Observe its origin: obscure and hidden delusive thoughts constitute its root.

The characteristics of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) are exceedingly obscure and hidden; yet this obscurity is merely produced by delusive thoughts—how could there be any other root?
Second, specifically clarifying the manifestation of these signs, in ten parts: first, calculating two types of non-causality.
(Up to) the tenth calculation, five [types] manifest *nirvāṇa*. These correspond in number to the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭigata*) elucidated in the Āgamas;
however, their doctrinal characteristics differ: those are originally non-Buddhist paths, whereas these arise from errors committed during mental cultivation.
Now, for the first [point].

Ānanda, you should know that when these good men who have attained right awareness within *śamatha*—possessing a concentrated, luminous, and upright mind—the ten classes of celestial Māras find no opportunity to interfere.
Only then are they able to investigate with refinement to exhaust the root of all living beings.

When the generative source of beings is revealed within its fundamental nature, and they observe that profound, pure, and perfectly agitated source of movement, those who give rise to conceptual calculations within that perfect source [fall into error].
Such a person falls into two kinds of causeless theories. First, this person perceives that there is no fundamental cause.

Why? Because this person, having fully broken through the vital mechanism of birth and relying on the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty, sees all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas as their karmic streams meander and wind, dying here and being born there; they see only the cycle of rebirth of these beings within those places.
Beyond ten thousand kalpas, there is a profound darkness where nothing can be observed; one then forms this interpretation:

"These sentient beings of the ten directions in this world have existed spontaneously without cause for eighty thousand kalpas. By such conceptualization, they lose right and universal knowledge and fall into the ranks of external paths, deluding their own nature of Bodhi.
Second, these people see that the end has no cause. Why? Because these people, when observing birth, already see...
Their roots know that humans are born as humans and birds are awakened as birds; crows have always been black and cranes have always been white.

Human beings are originally upright, while animals are originally horizontal. White is not made by washing, nor is black created by dyeing. From eighty thousand kalpas ago, there has been no further change or shifting;
even now, at the end of this physical form, it is likewise so. Since I have never seen Bodhi from the very beginning, how could it exist?
Furthermore, regarding the matter of attaining Bodhi, you should know that all phenomena today are fundamentally without cause.
From such deliberations, one loses right and universal knowledge and falls into the ranks of externalists, deluding oneself regarding the nature of Bodhi;
this is called the first type of externalist who establishes the doctrine of causelessness.

The text consists of three sections. From the beginning up to the second section, the "Theory of No Cause" (ahetuvāda) provides a general explanation of how conceptualizations arise based on the aggregates (*skandha*).
From the third section, "This person... up to "the nature of awakening is deluded," there is a specific explanation of the characteristics of erroneous conceptualizations.

From "Thus it is called... onwards, the text concludes by clarifying that these constitute the treatises of external paths (*tīrthika*); all subsequent passages follow this pattern and will not be further elaborated upon here. The initial term "coagulated" (*niṣyanda*)...
To clarify the right mind means that through the power of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), one does not give rise to the ten kinds of deluded thoughts and greedy seeking;

thus, the ten demons cannot find an opportunity to exploit them. From this point, by refining and investigating the root of the twelve classes of beings, the fundamental source of birth and death is revealed.
Consequently, one is able to contemplate the profound purity and the perfect movement within the turbid world.

Originally, one simply should not give rise to arbitrary conceptualizations regarding this sphere of the perfect and original realm. The "root of movement" refers precisely to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) as the source of all movement.
Because the objective sphere of this *saṃskāra-skandha* is difficult to comprehend, it is called "profound" (*yōu*).

Because it is not a coarse or heavy external object, it is called "clear" (*qīng*). It serves as the foundational basis for the arising of homogeneous categories, wherein they mutually contain and mutually encompass one another.
Because it is complete, it is called "perfect" (*yuan*); because within true permanence there is the false flow of continuity, it is called "agitated" (*rao*).
Among the eighteen views of the externalists' fundamental kalpas and fundamental perspectives, there are two views that arise without cause:
one is that from the realm of non-thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), they claim that what was originally non-existent now exists; the other is that through rapid observation, they falsely claim—
Without cause, there exists the present practitioner whose original purpose was to cultivate correct universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha-jñāna*) in order to attain the fruit of Bodhi;

yet, due to the arising of deluded conceptualization, they have mistakenly fallen into this state. Therefore, it is said that they have lost correct universal knowledge and fail to realize the nature of Bodhi.

"The capacity for birth is completely destroyed" refers to the destruction of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). By means of the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), one is able to see.

"Eighty thousand kalpas" refers to the strength of the power of perfect contemplation (*parivarta*). "Fundamentally without cause" refers to karma as the "root" (*mūla*) and to the place of origin as the "root.
"Ultimately without cause" refers to the phenomenal form (*nimitta*) as the "branch" (*anta*) and to the resulting fruit as the "branch.

Since all are fundamentally without cause, one should say they are ultimately without cause; it is likely that the character "root" (*ben*) is an error for "branch" (*mo*). This pertains to the ten objects of meditation (*daśa-viṣaya*) within *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Belonging to the realm of perceived objects, the perceived realm depends upon the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations);

since the *saṃskāra-skandha* is fundamentally rooted in subtle and hidden delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*), I now investigate and reveal its source, fully clarifying the characteristics of delusion so that those who practice authentically do not fall into it.

Although this is said to arise within the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), there is also the sense of its arising at the stage of profound realization; however, for those at the stage of profound realization, their merit...
It is only because their power is not yet sufficient that they do not fall into the paths of externalists; as the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"If a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage lacks wholesome mindfulness and right meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he falls into the deviant paths of externalists.

That a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage is intoxicated by the "intoxication of the bliss of cessation" and conceives a false notion of *nirvāṇa* is precisely what this means. Now, it is said that the seventh stage in the *Laṅkāvatāra* appears similar [to this].

If one speaks in reference to the ten stages common to the three vehicles, this corresponds to the stage within the vertical discourse on the five aggregates where the characteristics of the aggregates have been exhausted, but thought has not yet been exhausted;
this position lies within the seventh stage of faith. If one refers to the distinct stages, however, one must discuss the five aggregates outside the realms (*dhātu*).
Second, they calculate four types of pervasive permanence.

Ānanda, when these good sons within *samādhi* have concentrated their luminous and upright minds such that Māra finds no opportunity, yet they fail to exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and instead contemplate that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source—those who give rise to speculative calculations within this perfect and eternal state fall into the four theories of universal permanence.
The first is when a person investigates the nature of the mind and its objects and finds that both are without cause; having cultivated this [view], they fall into the theory of universal permanence.

First, they are able to know all births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions within twenty thousand kalpas; these cycles revolve without ever being lost, and they reckon them to be permanent.
Second, these people exhaustively investigate the source of the four great elements and the permanence of their four natures;

through cultivation, they are able to know all births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions within forty thousand kalpas, all of which are fundamentally constant and never... [lost].

Third, those who reckon that which is lost as being permanent are people who have exhausted the six faculties (which should be called the six consciousnesses), the manas, and the eighth [consciousness].

Because they grasp at the fundamental source and abiding nature within mind, thought, and consciousness as being eternally constant, through their cultivation they are able to know that, throughout eighty thousand kalpas, the circulation of all sentient beings does not lose its original state;
it is fundamentally and eternally abiding, and even in exhaustion it does not lose its nature. They thus reckon it to be permanent.
Regarding these four as permanent: once this person has exhausted the source of ideation (*saṃjñā-mūla*), their fundamental nature no longer undergoes flowing, ceasing, moving, or revolving;

the ideating mind of birth and death has now been eternally extinguished. Within this principle, there naturally arises that which is neither born nor extinguished. Because of the mind’s calculations, they take this to be permanent.
Due to this calculation of permanence, they lose correct and universal knowledge and fall into the ways of external paths, deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the second heterodox school that establishes the doctrine of the perfect and eternal.
Because this *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) has continued to evolve without beginning and appears as if it were eternally abiding, it is named "perfect and eternal.
Among the eighteen views of the heterodox schools, there are four views concerning a self and the eternity of the world; the first three of these correspond [to this].
These are all identical to the fourth [type], which is named the Wisdom of Swift Characteristics. Three [of these] reckon one portion as permanent.

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, if a demon finds no opening and they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, observing that profound, pure, and constant source of agitation within themselves and others, and then give rise to conceptual calculations, such people fall into [the error of permanence].
Regarding the first type of the partial view of permanence within the four inverted views—the doctrine that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent:
this person contemplates the wondrous, luminous mind as pervading the worlds of the ten directions, regarding its profound stillness as the ultimate *ātman*.

From this, they calculate that their self pervades the ten directions, remaining concentrated, luminous, and unmoving; thus, they hold that all sentient beings are born and die within their own mind, and that their own mind-nature is [eternal].

To call that which arises and perishes "permanent" is truly the nature of impermanence; these two views arise because this person does not contemplate their own mind, but instead contemplates the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Seeing places where kalpas are destroyed, they call them the ultimate nature of impermanence;
seeing places where kalpas are not destroyed, they call them the ultimate permanence. Thirdly, this person separately contemplates their own mind as being subtle, refined, and profound.

It is like fine dust circulating through the ten directions, its nature remaining unchanging; it can cause this body to arise and perish in an instant, yet its indestructible nature is called the "eternal nature of the self.
All death and birth flow forth from this self, which is called the "nature of impermanence.

Fourth, when this person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted and sees the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) flowing on, they calculate this constant flow of the *saṃskāra-skandha* to be the "constant nature."
The cessation of form, sensation, perception, and so forth is called impermanence;

because one calculates based on this that one part is impermanent while another part is permanent, one falls into the path of externalists and becomes confused about the nature of Bodhi. This is called the third type of externalist doctrine:
the theory of partial permanence.
First, one calculates that oneself is permanent while others are impermanent; second, one calculates solely that others are permanent or impermanent;
third, one calculates solely that oneself is permanent or impermanent; fourth, one calculates that both oneself and others are both permanent and impermanent.
Among the eighteen views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), there are these four types of theories asserting that the self and the world are half-permanent and half-impermanent.

However, their characteristics differ from those [other views]: first, they claim that one Brahmā is eternal while the self is impermanent; second, they claim it is impermanent because of playful laughter;
third, they claim it is impermanent because of mutual gazing; and fourth, they claim it is both eternal and impermanent through rapid observation.
Fourth, the four calculations regarding the finitude of existence.
Furthermore, among those sons of good family within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, the māras find no opportunity.

As they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, those who engage in conceptual calculations regarding its various states fall into error.
Regarding the four theories on finitude: first, there are those whose minds reckon that the source of birth flows and functions without ceasing;
they reckon that the past and future are finite, while the continuity of the mind is infinite.

Second, there are those who observe eighty thousand kalpas and perceive that before those eighty thousand kalpas, sentient beings were silent, with nothing heard or seen; this state of no hearing and no seeing is reckoned as infinite.

There are sentient beings whose state is called "having limits" (antavān). Third, these people conceive of themselves as possessing universal knowledge, thinking they alone have attained the nature of the infinite (ananta);

yet all those people appear within the scope of their own knowledge, while they themselves do not know the nature of those others' knowledge (which is likewise each individually and universally knowing)—thus they consider those others to lack the infinite mind and instead possess only a limited nature. Fourth is...
When people are in a state of spiritual poverty, their mental faculty (*manas*) becomes empty;

they use the path of their own perceptions to speculate about all sentient beings within a single body, calculating that each consists of half-birth and half-extinction. They clarify that within this world, all things are half-finite and half-infinite.
From such calculations regarding the finite and the infinite, they fall into the ways of external paths (*tīrthika*), becoming deluded regarding Bodhi.
This nature is called the fourth heterodox school’s doctrine of establishing the existence of limits (*antavāda*).
Within the true permanence of this nature, how could there be sequential stages? Based upon the stages of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, deluded notions of these stages arise;
the first two [schools] both calculate the stages of the three periods of time. The first regards the past and future as having limits, while the present—a single moment of continuity—is...
1. Regarding the mind as infinite: one considers that which is within eighty thousand kalpas to be finite and that which is beyond eighty thousand kalpas to be infinite.
2. Regarding the distinction between subject and object: because one takes the self to be the knower, it is infinite;

because those objects are what is known, they are finite. 3. Regarding the distinction between arising and ceasing: the nature of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) consists solely of arising and ceasing. Arising is...

There is the view that what has a limit is extinguished into the limitless; this is also found among the eighteen views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika), specifically within the four theories concerning the finite and the infinite.
However, their doctrinal characteristics differ: first, the perception of finitude; second, the perception of infinitude;
third, finitude above but infinitude in the four directions; fourth, neither finite nor infinite; fifth, the doctrine of equivocation (amarāvikkhepa).
Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi* who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, the Māras find no opportunity.

As they exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, those who engage in conceptual calculations regarding their perceptions and views fall into four kinds of perverse, indecisive, and chaotic "immortal" sophistry—universal speculations on emptiness. The first is when such a person contemplates the source of transformation.
Seeing the place of transition is called "change"; seeing the place of continuity is called "permanence"; seeing the place of what is seen is called "arising";

not seeing the place of seeing (which is to say, the place where seeing does not see) is called "cessation"; the place where the nature of the cause of continuity is uninterrupted is called "increase";
and within the midst of correct continuity, the place where one is detached from the center is called "decrease. [Each]...
The arising of each respective place is called "existence," and their mutual absence is called "non-existence.

When observing this through principle as a whole, yet perceiving it with a biased mind, there are those who seek the Dharma and come to inquire about its meaning. To them, he replies: "I am now both arising and ceasing;
both existent and non-existent; both increasing and decreasing. At all times, he confuses his speech in such a way that the person before him is left bewildered.
Second, those who have lost the verses and phrases carefully observe that their minds have no mutual locus; because there is nothing to grasp, they attain realization.
When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying merely "non-existence," and beyond this non-existence, they have nothing further to say.
Third, those who carefully observe that their minds each have their own distinct locus attain realization because of this existence. When someone comes to question them, they...
Answer: A single word merely indicates that it is "is" or "is not"; beyond this, there is nothing further to be said.
Fourth, as for the person who holds the view that both existence and non-existence apply to their object, their mind is likewise distracted.

When someone comes to question them, they answer, "It is both existent and non-existent," or "Within being non-existent, it is not the case that it is also existent. This is entirely evasive and confused; there is no way to exhaustively interrogate such a person.
This speculative, evasive, and nihilistic falling away into the ways of external paths that delude the nature of Bodhi is called the fifth type of external path:
the fourfold nature of perversion, the evasive discourse on immortality, and the pervasive false theorizing.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Arising from arising cannot be spoken of, and even non-arising from non-arising cannot be spoken of;

yet because there are causes and conditions, it can also be spoken of. Thus we know that the distinction between the false and the correct within the four phrases and four gates is exceedingly subtle.

If one has not yet attained the wondrous principle of the Tathāgatagarbha—wherein phenomena follow conditions without changing, and which remains unchanging while following conditions—it will be difficult to realize this in practice.
From within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), cognition and views arise; following these cognitions and views, one gives rise to conceptual constructions.

There is nothing among them that does not constitute perversion, confusion, or sophistry. Because they are of the nature of false discrimination, they are called "pervasive construction" (*parikalpita*); because they ultimately possess no real meaning, they are called "vain discourse.

The fundamental source of these transformations refers precisely to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Within this mutual interplay of non-existence, there is no arising amidst extinction, nor extinction amidst arising.

Because they are non-arising and so forth, all phenomena are equally devoid of individuality; for it is said that at the time of arising there is arising, and at the time of ceasing there is ceasing, and so on.

Thus, regarding arising and ceasing as being both existent and non-existent, one perceives that at the time of arising there is arising but no ceasing, while at the time of ceasing there is ceasing but no arising.
Furthermore, at the time of arising, there is the arising of arising and the ceasing of ceasing.
At that time, because arising and ceasing, as well as ceasing and arising, are equal, existence is itself non-existence and non-existence is itself existence.
It is entirely because they do not realize that arising, ceasing, going, and coming are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha that they conceive these illusory dharmas to be truly real;
being unable to reach a definitive conclusion for themselves, they fall into sophistry and empty discourse. These are the eighteen views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
Within this, there are also different questions and different answers regarding the four views; however, they differ only in their doctrinal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
It says: "First, is there retribution for good and evil, or is there no retribution? Second, is there a future world, or is there no future world? Third, what is wholesome and what is unwholesome?
Fourth, being ignorant, deluded, dull, and obtuse, one follows the words of others in providing answers. Zizhong said: "According to the *Abhidharma*..."
The *Śāṃkhyakārikā-bhāṣya* explains that non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) reckon the eternal nature of the heavens as "immortality" and reckon freedom from confusion as "rebirth in those heavens.
If one were to answer abruptly when not truly knowing the answer, there is a fear of falling into equivocation (*vibhrama*).
Therefore, when questioned, one says, "This is secret terminology; it should not be spoken," or provides an indefinite answer. The Buddha’s Dharma rebukes this, saying: "This is truly [equivocal]."
Because it is evasive, it is called "the evasive discourse on immortality" and "vain speculation. It consists of the six views and the sixteen modes of existence.

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi* who have stabilized their upright minds so that Māra finds no opportunity, they investigate the origin of all living beings and observe that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.

Those who harbor speculative calculations regarding this inexhaustible flow fall into [the following error]: [The text continues with the description of the first of the four types of "Evasive Discourse on Immortality."]

Regarding the notion that there is a sign after death, one may give rise to a perverted resolve by either clinging to the body and saying "form is the self," or seeing the self as encompassing and pervading the lands and saying "the self possesses form," or observing that external objects revolve according to the self and saying "form belongs to the self," or again,
observing the continuity within the activities of the self and saying "the self is in form. All such conceptualizations are termed the view that there is a sign after death.
Thus, in this cycle, there are sixteen aspects. From these, some may calculate that ultimate affliction and ultimate bodhi—these two natures—proceed side by side without ever touching one another;
because they calculate that there is existence after death, they fall into the ranks of the externalists and delude themselves regarding the nature of bodhi.
This is called the sixth externalist school’s establishment of the aspect of "existence after death" within the five aggregates.
The Treatise on the Perversions of Mind.
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is called the "inexhaustible flow" because it has been continuously evolving since beginningless time. [The perversions are as follows:
"Form is the self," which means "form is the self"; "I possess form," "the self is large while form is small," or "form is within the self."
Form belongs to me; there is a self apart from form; form is merely mine; the self is within form—wherein the self is large and form is small, or the self is equal to form.
These four propositions applied to each of the three aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations constitute sixteen aspects.
From this, one may further develop a deeper layer of conceptualization, meaning that [the self] arises through volitional construction (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, because afflictions exist through conditioning, awakening exists through conditioning; this conditioning is precisely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Since the aggregate of formations can never be exhausted, neither afflictions nor awakening can ever be exhausted.

Thus, both natures are driven into the exhaustion of the future limit, yet they do not mutually disparage one another. This, however, is a mistaken understanding of the Perfect Teaching of the inherent nature (*xingju yuanzong*).
To err by even a hair’s breadth from the sublime purport is to fall into a mistake as vast as the distance between heaven and earth. How perilous! How perilous!
Among the forty-four views of external paths and the views of the final age, there are sixteen views concerning the existence of perception in the world;
yet their characteristics differ. They are: first, the view that there is form; second, the view that there is no form; third, the view that there is both form and no form... [and so forth].
1. The view of form; 2. the view of the non-material; 3. the view of the immaterial; 4. the view of neither material nor immaterial;
5. the view of finitude; 6. the view of infinity; 7. the view of both finite and infinite; 8. the view of neither finite nor infinite;
9. the view of happiness; 10. the view of suffering; 11. the view of both happiness and suffering; 12. the view of neither suffering nor happiness; 13. the view of unity.

The fourteen perceptions (saṃjñā), the fifteen various perceptions, the sixteen limited perceptions, and the seventeen immeasurable perceptions: it is said that the first four views rely on the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha);

next, the four views such as "having limits" rely on the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha); next, the four views such as "possessing pleasure" rely on the aggregate of feeling (vedanāskandha);
next, the four views such as "one perception" rely on the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha). The seventh is the calculation [of existence], and the eighth is signlessness (animitta).
Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi* who have stabilized their minds with right concentration, the Māras find no opportunity.

As they exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings and observe that profound, pure essence which is the source of constant agitation, there may be those who first eliminate form, sensation, and perception, yet still give rise to conceptual calculations.
Such persons fall into the delusion of "formlessness after death," developing an inverted view that perceives the extinction of form as being without any underlying cause for the physical shape.
Observe that as perception ceases, the mind has nothing to which it is bound; know that as sensation ceases, there is no further connection, and the nature of the aggregates dissolves.
Even if the physical processes of life persist, being devoid of sensation and perception, one is the same as grass and trees;

such a substance cannot be found even while manifest before one’s eyes—how much less could any signs exist after death? By examining this through such cycles, one finds that the signs of death are likewise non-existent. Thus the cycle continues.
There are eight signless states from which some reckon that the causes and effects of nirvana are entirely empty, existing merely as names, and ultimately subject to total annihilation.
Because they speculate that there is nothing after death, they fall into the path of externalists and delude themselves regarding the nature of bodhi.
This is called the seventh externalist school, which establishes the theory of the "signless state after death" within the five aggregates, resulting in a perverted mind.

The "physiological" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Since the other four aggregates cannot be found either while manifesting in life or after death, both cause and effect would be non-existent;

this is called the "eightfold signlessness. Furthermore, calculating that since the causes and effects of the four aggregates in the mundane world do not exist, how could there be causes and effects for supramundane *nirvāṇa*?
Thus, they establish the inverted doctrine of annihilationism. These constitute the forty-four views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Within this [category], there are also eight views concerning the worldly doctrine of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), which differ in their characteristics from those [previously mentioned].
They are: (1) having form; (2) being formless; (3) having form; (4) neither having form nor being formless;
(5) being finite; (6) being infinite; (7) being both finite and infinite; (8) being neither finite nor infinite. These eight reckonings all share the same [status of] "neither."
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, the māras find no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, and eternal source of agitation within the movement of consciousness. While abiding in the state of mental activity (*saṃskāra*), they simultaneously suppress feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*). By dualistically calculating existence and non-existence, their own essential natures cancel each other out.

These individuals fall into the nihilistic view that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence, giving rise to inverted theories regarding form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*).

Seeing existence as non-existence, observing the flux of conditioned formations, and internally contemplating neither existence nor non-existence—thus cycling through these states until the aggregates (*skandhas*) and elements (*dhātus*) are exhausted—one encounters the eightfold "neither-nor" characteristics.
Whichever single condition one grasps, one claims that after death there are both characteristics and no characteristics.

Furthermore, calculating that the nature of all formations (*saṃskāras*) is subject to change and distortion, the mind gives rise to a penetrating realization that both existence and non-existence are neither true nor false; from this, such speculative reckonings arise.

Because after death there is neither [existence nor non-existence], and because the subsequent limit is dark and obscure such that nothing can be said, they fall into the path of externalists and delude themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the eighth externalist doctrine of the inverted mind within the five aggregates, which asserts that after death there is neither [existence nor non-existence].
Because existence is negated by non-existence and non-existence is negated by existence, it is said that their essential natures mutually negate one another.

First, taking the formations (*saṃskāra*) as an example for the aggregates (*skandha*), one sees that existence is non-existence; taking the flux of formations as an example for form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations themselves, one contemplates that non-existence is not non-existence.
Therefore, each of the four aggregates has two aspects of "neither," which are called the eightfold "neither. Next, again considering them solely from the perspective of formations:

The aggregates (*skandhas*) undergo gradual transformation and deceptive arising; if they were existent, they would not be subject to momentary change and extinction, and if they were non-existent, they would not be subject to momentary birth.
Furthermore, because they do not abide, they are not existent; because they form a continuous succession, they are not non-existent, nor are they empty.

Among the forty-four views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), there are eight views concerning the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); their names and characteristics are as follows: [list of views].
The preceding [section on] the theory of non-perception is the same. Ninth, there are those who calculate seven types of annihilation.

Furthermore, among these sons of good family within samādhi, having stabilized their minds in right concentration so that Māra finds no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that which is profound, pure, and yet the source of constant agitation.
Those who subsequently engage in speculative calculations regarding the absence of future births fall into this state.

The seven theories of annihilationism—whether one calculates the extinction of the body, the extinction of desire, the extinction of suffering, the extinction of extreme bliss, or the extinction of extreme equanimity—and so on, cycling through these until the seven limits are exhausted;

to claim that what is presently extinguished will, once extinguished, never again undergo such calculation regarding annihilation after death—to fall into such views is to be a follower of external paths who deludes the nature of Bodhi. This is what is called...
The ninth heterodox school establishes the inverted view that the mind is annihilated after death within the context of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Regarding the "seven theories of annihilation" (*sapta-vināśavāda*), they calculate that for humans and devas, death results in immediate annihilation across seven locations:
first, upon the death of the human body, there is immediate annihilation; second... [text continues].

First, when the lifespan of the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is exhausted, they immediately perish; second and third, those in the first and second dhyānas whose suffering has ended all return to death and extinction;
fourth, those in the third dhyāna, despite their ultimate bliss, likewise return to death and extinction;

fifth and sixth, those in the fourth dhyāna who have abandoned both suffering and pleasure, as well as those in the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) who have abandoned the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), also return to death and extinction. Therefore, it is said that they exhaustively reach the seven limits.
All are extinguished. Among the forty-four views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), there are also seven views of annihilationism:

first, extinction upon the destruction of the body; second, extinction in the desire heavens; third, extinction in the form heavens; fourth, extinction in the sphere of infinite space; fifth, extinction in the sphere of infinite consciousness; sixth, extinction in the sphere of nothingness;

This opens up the four dhyānas and merges them with the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

Among those who count ten stages and manifest five types of nirvāṇa, there are also sons of good family within samādhi who stabilize their minds in right concentration so that Māras cannot find an opening.

Yet, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, and eternally quiescent source as being subject to agitation. Those who subsequently harbor conceptual calculations regarding rebirth fall into this [error].

Regarding the five theories on *nirvāṇa*, some take the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as the true basis of transformation (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), because one perceives the brilliant and perfect objects of the six heavens of the desire realm and gives rise to longing for them;

or they take the first dhyāna as such because its nature is free from sorrow (having transcended the faculty of sorrow); or they take the second dhyāna because the mind is free from suffering (having transcended the faculty of suffering);
or they take the third dhyāna because of the presence of extreme bliss; or they take the fourth dhyāna because both suffering and pleasure have ceased.
Because they experience the nature of arising and ceasing within saṃsāra, they are deluded regarding the tainted heavens (*sāsrava-dhātu*) and conceive them as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

They calculate these five abodes to be temporarily secure and take them to be the supreme purity and the ultimate refuge. Thus they revolve through these five abodes, ultimately calculating them to be the five forms of manifest nirvāṇa.
Falling into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they confuse the nature of bodhi; this is called the tenth type of externalist.
Established within the five aggregates, they hold the inverted view that the five present states constitute *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding "subsequent existence," they claim it refers to the moment-to-moment arising of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Previously, they calculated that *nirvāṇa* occurs only after extinction at seven locations;

now, they maintain that peace and security at five locations constitute the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). Among the forty-four views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), this is one such position.
There is also the present existence of the five views of *nirvāṇa*: first, it is said that indulgence in the five desires of the present life is itself *nirvāṇa*;
the remaining four [views] are all the same as those in this sutra. This concludes the section on the faults of the three fetters and the exhortation to instruction.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded understandings resulting from *dhyāna* are all manifestations of the interaction between the mind and the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Because sentient beings are stubborn and deluded, they fail to reflect upon themselves; when these states appear before them, they mistake their confusion for realization and claim to have attained the ranks of the sages.
Having committed such great falsehoods, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You must take the words of the Tathāgata as you hear them from me.
After my parinirvāṇa, transmit and reveal this to the age of the final dharma (*mappō*), causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand this meaning.

Do not allow mental demons to give rise to deep calamities within themselves; maintain and protect them so that false views are extinguished. Teach their bodies and minds to awaken to the true meaning, so that they do not encounter byways on the unsurpassed path.
Do not let their hearts pray for little and consider it sufficient; become great awakened kings of purity.
The pointing finger.
Those with deluded understandings rely on the views and afflictions arising from the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Because these arise from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are also called "awakening," yet because they turn their backs on perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), they remain delusions of the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness). Since the celestial Māras have already been subdued, they can no longer find an opportunity.
The sixty-two views of today are all merely demonic growths arising from one’s own mind. Alas!
The stream of those in the degenerate age who possess dark realization and false enlightenment is even more shallow and vulgar than these non-Buddhists;
yet they hold their own gateways high and arrogantly claim to be patriarchal masters throughout the realm—this too is truly lamentable. "Biao" (標) means to set up a banner or to designate.

This refers to the guiding finger; furthermore, the words of the Buddha, King of Awakening, are like that finger. Regarding the five vidyās and the objective realm of the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha), there are three parts:

first, a general indication of the characteristics of the aggregates; second, a detailed explanation of the manifestation of their characteristics; and third, the refutation of errors and the establishment of the correct. Within the first part, there are four sections:
