The characteristics of exhaustion reveal that the four knots are fundamentally nothing but deluded thoughts. Herein begins the first:

Ānanda, when that virtuous man practices *samādhi* and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the subtle, clear, and agitated commonality of all worldly natures—the vital impulses of living beings—suddenly shatter;
the fine meshes of the net and the *pudgala* who recompense their karma [are likewise dissolved].
The profound resonance of the pulse is suspended and severed;
"all worldly gates" refers universally to the three lands of the Shared, Expedient, and Real-Response.

All classes of beings within the nine realms are likened to the meshes of a net, while the submerged and subtle *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) is likened to the main cord of the net—namely, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Because the karmic retributive channels of the six classes of ordinary beings are exhausted, their resonance with the profound pulse is suspended;
because the conditioned practices of the two vehicles based on partial truth are exhausted, the karmic retributive channels of those sentient beings are suspended;
and because the practices of the two extremes are exhausted, the karmic retributive channels of Bodhisattva beings are suspended. Thus, the sentient beings of the nine realms each, by virtue of...
The delusions and karma manifested by one’s own mind serve as the "inducers," while the retributions manifested by one’s own mind serve as the "respondents.

Now that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted, both inducement and response are severed; this is precisely the realm where what is to be emptied by emptiness has been extinguished, and where birth and death have ceased.
For those of sharp faculties, with the extinction of this [aggregate], all are extinguished, and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) likewise ceases.
This is not merely a matter of emotional sentiment. Second, this clearly elucidates the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha*.
When one is about to attain great awakening within the sky of *nirvāṇa*, it is like the crowing of a cock; looking toward the east with courage, one perceives that there is already a refined luster.

The six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are empty and still, no longer wandering or escaping; internally and externally, they are profoundly clear and luminous, entering a state where there is nowhere to enter, deeply penetrating the ten directions.
Observing the twelve kinds of origins of receiving life and the various categories of grasping, which do not summon one from the ten directions,
and having attained their commonality, when the subtle essence does not sink but reveals what is hidden and secret— this is called the domain of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).

This refers to those for whom the habit-energy of the *vijñāna-skandha* is strong; although they have realized the emptiness of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*) during their contemplative practice, the realm of profound stillness and clarity manifests once again.
Both forms of birth-and-death are like a long night: if one realizes the emptiness of conditioned formations, then the Great Light of Perfectly Pure Nirvana (*pariśuddha-nirvāṇa*) will soon dawn;
if one awakens to the emptiness of formations through the realization of partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*), then the [realm of] Expedient Purity (*upāya-śuddha*) will appear.

The "Heaven of Nirvana" refers to the imminent dawn of great awakening; to practice the emptiness of the two extremes is the imminent dawn of great awakening within the Heaven of Innate Purity and Nirvana.

Regarding the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*), they are that which the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) clings to and receives, and that which the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) opens and closes.

Within the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), the aggregate of formations has already been shattered; thus, there is stillness and tranquility, and no further wandering or dissipation. Yet, the aggregate of consciousness remains.
Because it exists, there is no actual entry, yet one still speaks of "inside" and "outside. This is because the nature of consciousness is itself the *tathāgatagarbha*;

however, being shrouded by ignorance, it is like the space inside a *piṅgala* (kalavinka) jar, which falsely creates the distinction of interior and exterior. Therefore, it is called an "aggregate" (*skandha*).

Since the aggregate must be shattered, it appears as if there is something entered; yet the nature of consciousness and the nature of the treasury are fundamentally not two natures, just as the interior [of the jar] is not separate from the space.
Beyond emptiness, emptiness is fundamentally not dual; because it is empty, there is originally nowhere to enter.

Since the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been shattered and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) manifests before one, one deeply penetrates the source from which the twelve classes of beings receive their life-force.
This is precisely why this aggregate of consciousness is called "the master who departs later and arrives first. Because it lacks a pivot-hole, its origin can be understood.
Because one contemplates that there is no flux, the source can be grasped; because there is no mechanism for birth, the various classes of beings do not summon one another;
because one thoroughly understands that all phenomena are consciousness-only, one has already attained identity with the ten directions and the world;

because one’s contemplative practice is profound and one is able to see the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, the subtle color of the refined essence is no longer submerged, and the hidden rational nature emerges from its obscurity.
This realization is the manifestation of the state of true quiescence, yet it has not yet been suddenly transcended; the rest is as explained in the section on Perfect Penetration.
Third, a preliminary indication of the signs of the exhaustion of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).
If, having already attained the unification within the collective, one has worn away the six gates so that they are harmoniously opened and closed,

achieving the accomplishment of mutual interchangeability in seeing and hearing such that the worlds of the ten directions, as well as body and mind, are as pure as Vaiḍūrya crystal, transparent both inside and out—
this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).

The "summoning of the multitude" refers to the aforementioned various classes that were not summoned; "attaining the same" refers to the aforementioned attainment of sameness throughout the ten directions.
Using the six sense-faculties as a single faculty is called "accomplishment through integration"; using a single faculty as the six faculties is called "accomplishment through differentiation.
The world and the body-mind are like *vaiḍūrya* crystal; this is precisely what is meant by "suddenly."
However, the manner of transcending both the mundane and supramundane realms is as explained in the section on "Perfect Penetration.
Fourth, the conclusion indicates that the root is solely deluded thought: when one examines its origin, it is found to be based upon a phantom-like voidness and inverted, deluded thoughts.
Illusory and false, it appears to have a name called "the formless" (*wangxiang*); its nature and substance are empty and still, thus it is named "emptiness" (*xuwu*).
To be deluded and turn one's back on the true nature is called "inversion. There is no real dharma whatsoever; only this deluded thought serves as its root.

If one thoroughly understands that deluded thought has no inherent nature, then since even its root does not exist, how could the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) exist? Therefore, it is said that the aggregate of consciousness is illusory and false.

This is the Tathāgatagarbha. Second, the specific explanation of the manifestation [of the stages], in ten parts: first, attachment to causes and their causes, up to tenth, the nature-determined pratyekabuddhas. Now, the first:

Ānanda, you should know that these good sons have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), returned to the source within consciousness, and have already extinguished arising and ceasing.

Yet, while their subtle and wondrous state of quiescence is not yet perfected, they are able to cause the sense organs of their own bodies to either merge or separate, and they can also communicate with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions through a pervasive awareness. They are able to enter the perfect source;

if, regarding that to which they have returned, they establish it as the cause of true permanence and develop a superior conviction therein, such a person falls into the attachment to a "cause of the cause," which is the *tattva* (Principle) of the *Sāṃkhyas* to which they have returned.

Forming such a partnership, they become deluded regarding the Bodhi of the Buddha and lose their true knowledge and vision; this is called the first [type of practitioner] who establishes a mind based on what has been attained and achieves a fruit based on what is sought as a refuge.
Thus, they remain far removed from perfect penetration, turn their backs on the city of Nirvana, and give rise to the seeds of external paths.

It is said that within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), one has already been able to exhaustively investigate how the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is empty. One is about to subdue the nature of consciousness and restore original enlightenment (*pūrvabodhi*).

Although birth and death have ceased and quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) has manifested before one, because there is still the state of quiescent extinction lingering within the mind, it is said that "the subtle and wondrous is not yet perfected.
At this time, the six sense faculties gradually attain purity; therefore, it is said that "one can cause oneself... [to be so].

Because the body-faculty (kāyendriya) can discern that there is no difference between the three—sentient beings, Buddhas, and the mind—whether in states of union or separation, it is said that "it also universally awakens all categories throughout the ten directions.
Although this perfect primordial object is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, it is entirely comprised of inverted deluded thoughts;
for apart from those [aggregates of] form, sensation, perception, and formations, there is no separate "perfect primordial" entity. It is not something distinct.
Since all dharmas are fundamentally perfect and complete, this [entity] is not truly eternal; one should not falsely give rise to a resolute conviction regarding it.
If one erroneously establishes this as the refuge and claims, "This is the cause from which the myriad dharmas arise;

this cause is eternal while the myriad dharmas are impermanent," then one is taking what is not a cause to be a cause, thereby falling into the attachment to causes and their underlying causes. This is indeed the *sāṃkhya*.
Vikara likewise, within his meditative contemplation, used the sixth consciousness to differentiate the substance of the eighth consciousness;
not knowing it was merely the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha appearing according to karma, he falsely gave rise to attachment to dharmas.

This is what was referred to in the preceding text as Kauśika and others mistaking it for the "Dark Principle" (Tattva). Now, because of these errors, he established the term and its superior designation.

To know and see [these] is called the second establishment of capacity as mind; it accomplishes the fruit of functional efficacy, yet it is remote from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of the Great Brahma Heaven’s universal and pervasive "I."

Previously, one reckoned the eight consciousnesses as "other," thereby forming attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*); now, one reckons the eight consciousnesses as "self," thereby forming attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*).
Because one falsely conceives that which is not the agent to be the agent, it is called the "attachment to the agent and the non-agent.
Maheśvara—here translated as "Great Sovereign"—has three eyes and eight arms. This is the third: the attachment to the permanent and the impermanent.

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished birth and death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*) is not yet perfected, may have a sense of a place of refuge and rely upon such a refuge.
He then suspects that his own body and mind flow forth from that [refuge], and that the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it.
Consequently, regarding that ground from which everything flows forth, he conceives the understanding that it is a true, eternal body, free from birth and death.
Within the midst of arising and ceasing, they prematurely reckon it to be eternally abiding; thus they are deluded regarding non-arising and confused about arising and ceasing.
Those who dwell in this deep-seated confusion yet form a superior resolve toward it will fall into the attachment to permanence and impermanence, taking the *Īśvara* as their companion.
They lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit true knowledge and vision; this is called the third [delusion]: establishing causes based on the mind to produce false conceptualizations of results.
To deviate from and distance oneself from perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), turning one’s back on the city of Nirvāṇa, is to give rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.
This differs from the *tattva* (ultimate principle) of the *Mīmāṃsaka* in that while the latter calculates other dharmas, this calculates other heavens;

because it falsely calculates what is impermanent as permanent, it is said to be "permanence. This attachment to permanence is fundamentally born of the mind, yet people conversely claim it is produced by Heaven.
Heaven and earth give birth to humans, hence they are named "inverted and round. This is the fourth stage: the attachment to the knowledge of non-knowledge.

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished arising and ceasing, yet the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction has not yet become perfect:

if, regarding that which is known, one’s knowledge is universally pervasive, and because of this knowledge one establishes a view such that all grasses and trees in the ten directions are called sentient beings; this is the fourth stage.
He is no different from others; he regards grasses and trees as human beings, and when humans die, they become the grasses and trees of the ten directions without distinction.

One who develops such a superior understanding falls into the view that "knowledge is non-knowledge. He becomes an associate of the Pāṣaṇḍas and the Sāṃkhyas, who cling to the notion of a universal consciousness (*sarvajña*).
He is deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and loses his true knowledge and vision. This is called the fourth type: calculating the all-encompassing mind.
This produces false and erroneous results, which are far removed from perfect penetration and turn one’s back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of inverted cognition.
To be ignorant yet delusively cling to it as knowledge is called "knowing while being ignorant"; this refers to the two non-Buddhist teachers, Pāṭa and Śreṇika.
As for what is said regarding the presence of nature within insentient things, it means that all phenomena are the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Because these objective aspects are all in resonance with the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, it is said:

The Buddha-nature is also so called because the Dharma-Buddha possesses no dual nature. Furthermore, O son of good family,

If one seeks the light of fire within the universal transformation that gives rise to all things, or delights in the purity of water, or craves the circulation of wind,

or contemplates the sensory objects (rajas), thereby accomplishing various esteemed practices and establishing the view of permanence based on these manifold objects as the fundamental causes of arising and creation—
O Kāśyapas, such a person falls into the attachment to birth within non-birth.
Furthermore, there are Brahmins who diligently employ their minds and bodies to serve fire and revere water, seeking to transcend birth and death and making these their companions;
they are deluded regarding the Bodhi of the Buddha and have lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the fifth attachment:

being deluded in mind by the pursuit of external objects, establishing false causes through seeking and hoping for false fruits; thus they stray far from perfect penetration, turn their backs on the city of Nirvana, and give rise to the seeds of perverted transformations.
The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are unborn, yet they are falsely reckoned as the fundamental source of birth; therefore, this is called the "attachment to the unborn within the born.
This is because one does not know that within the *tathāgatagarbha*, the four great elements are inherently complete, fundamentally pure, and all-pervasive throughout the *dharmadhātu*.

Consequently, they manifest according to the minds of sentient beings, in accordance with the capacity of their cognition, and in conformity with their karma. Yet, [the ignorant] directly reckon these four great elements [to be the source of birth].
To claim that this is the "perfectly interfused wondrous nature" is a mistaken interpretation; it is to erroneously equate the Dharma-gates of earth, water, fire, and wind with heaven and earth.
This is the sixth: the attachment to non-attainment as attainment.

Furthermore, if a good man has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished birth and death, yet his subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected;

and if, within this perfect luminosity, he reckons that this very light is inherently empty and still, and thus seeks to transcend the manifold transformations of existence by taking eternal extinction as his refuge and generating a resolute conviction therein—
such a person falls into the attachment of "seeking a refuge where there is no refuge" and is reborn among the gods of the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).
(And those of the four formless realms,) the various Śūnyatās become their companions; they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision.

This is called the sixth fruit: the "perfectly void and mindless attainment of the state of emptiness. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of nihilism.
Because one falsely calculates that which is not a refuge to be a refuge, it is said that one takes refuge in non-refuge.
By clinging to the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), one causes the non-constant mental states and mental factors to cease;

by causing the *śūnyatā* (space) beings to extinguish their obstructive material forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*), one calculates all things as void and thereby achieves annihilationism. Seventh is the clinging to greed as non-greed.

Furthermore, if a good son, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished birth-and-death, has not yet perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*),
and if he seeks within that perfect permanence to solidify his body so that it remains eternally, becoming identical with the subtle and perfect essence and never again decaying or passing away—
should he give rise to such a superior resolve, this person falls into the attachment of craving for what is not to be craved. He becomes one of those Āsuras who seek long life.
Their companions have lost their way regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have forfeited their true knowledge and vision; this is called the seventh [delusion]:

clinging to the source of life, establishing a solid cause of delusion that leads to the fruit of long-lasting toil, straying far from perfect penetration, turning one's back on the city of Nirvana, and giving rise to the seeds of protracted falsehood.
Because one greedily craves what is not to be craved, it is called "craving for what is not craving.

Asita—translated here as "Incomparable"—is the name of a long-lived immortal (ṛṣi). His illusory physical body belongs entirely to the realm of worldly toil; if one now seeks to solidify it, one will only prolong that toil.
Eighth is the attachment to the non-true as true.

Furthermore, there are good sons who, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), have extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*śānti*), they have not yet perfected it.

(If) they contemplate this source of life as mutually interpenetrating, they may consequently retain their worldly defilements (*kleśa*) for fear that [the roots of goodness] will be entirely consumed.

Thus, at this juncture, they sit within a Lotus Palace, extensively manifesting the seven treasures and increasing the number of precious women, indulging their own minds. Those who develop such superior resolve—
Such a person falls into the attachment to "the real" within what is not real, becoming a companion to the Tārkikas; they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision.
This is called the eighth: giving rise to the cause of perverse thinking and establishing the fruit of blazing dust;
it is to be far removed from perfect penetration, to turn one's back on the city of Nirvana, and to give birth to the race of celestial Māras.
Because that which is not real is falsely grasped as real, it is said that "reality is devoid of reality. *Vāmā* refers to a beautiful woman;
*Cakrīkara* is also the name of a māra king. The nine classes of śrāvakas with fixed natures.

Furthermore, there is a good man who, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), has extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, he has not yet perfected it.

Within the clarity of his life-force (*jīva*), he discriminates between the refined and the coarse, and distinguishes the true from the false. He views cause and effect as reciprocating, seeking only to provoke a response, thereby turning his back on the path of purity.
This is what is called "seeing suffering and abandoning accumulation, realizing cessation and cultivating the path," where one rests content once cessation is attained and no longer proceeds further.

If one who advances by means of superior understanding falls into the category of those of fixed nature as Śrāvakas, they will become companions to the assembly of unlearned monks who harbor overweening pride;
they will be deluded regarding the Bodhi of the Buddha and lose their knowledge and vision. This is called the ninth:

when the perfect essence corresponds to the mind, it results in the attainment of the fruit of quiescence; it is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvāṇa, giving rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.

The "Essential Brightness of the Consciousness-essence" (*vijñāna-dhātu-sāra-prakāśa*) is the fundamental source of the life-span for the nine realms; it is the basis of existence. To falsely claim that the subtle marks of transformation and change (*pariṇāma*) are permanent is "subtle";
to regard the physical form of birth-and-death through segmented divisions (*bheda-jāti-maraṇa*) as coarse; to consider untainted superior karma (*anāsrava-viśiṣṭa-karma*) as true;

and to consider tainted mixed karma (*sāsrava-miśra-karma*) as false. The fruit of transformation and change is the retribution for untainted causes, while the fruit of segmented birth-and-death is the retribution for tainted causes.

For this reason, one relies solely on the supramundane path to induce supramundane cessation; turning one's back upon the fundamental [world], this is the pure path that transcends both the mundane and the supramundane.

That is to say: seeing the three realms as actual suffering, severing the actual accumulation of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and realizing the quiescent extinction of partial truth (*pradeśa-satya-nirodha*), one then cultivates the untainted true path. Once one has attained entry into cessation, one then claims—

They have realized that there is nothing to be known other than the Single True Truth, yet this has not yet been fully manifested; how could they ever perceive the conventional truth or the middle truth?
Merely responding to the causal mind with perfect purity, they achieve the minor fruit of quiescence, becoming entangled in emptiness and unable to turn their minds toward the provisional.
These people of true overweening pride arise because they lack the power of hearing and cultivation.
Furthermore, there are those of the tenth stage, the Determined Nature Pratyekabuddhas.

Again, O Good Man, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), they have extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, they have not yet perfected it.
If, within this perfectly integrated, pure, awakened clarity, they investigate and cultivate its profound subtlety, they will establish themselves in *nirvāṇa* and not advance further.

Those who give rise to such superior resolve fall into the category of those fixed in the nature of the Pratyekabuddhas—those solitary practitioners who do not turn their minds back [toward the Mahayana].
They become companions to that class, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the tenth:

the fruit of the "surging mind" (*yongxin*) becoming a profound clarity (*zhanming*), which is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the City of Nirvana; it gives birth to the "untransformed" (*buhua*) seed of circular enlightenment and clarity.

The perfectly interfused, pure, awakened clarity pervades all phenomena; even when one single atom is raised, there is nothing that is not the entire body of the perfectly luminous nature of awakening.
Now, you have isolated this profound and wondrous state as "Nirvana," not realizing that every dharma is both profound and wondrous.
Therefore, although you call it "awakening," you have not yet reached the perfection of transformation. To be so named while existing in the world of Buddhas is called... [the name of the stage].
Pratyekabuddhas who appear in an era without a Buddha are called "Solitary Realizers" (pratyekabuddha); they are nonetheless those of fixed nature whose realization is merely partial truth.

Third, the refutation of the heterodox and the establishment of the orthodox. This section has two parts: first, the refutation of the heterodox; second, the establishment of the orthodox. Now, the first part.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* may lead to madness midway through their practice due to confusion;
by mistaking what is incomplete for a realization of fulfillment, they fall into this state because the mind of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) functions in mutual conflict.
Beings who are stubbornly deluded do not reflect upon themselves; when these states manifest before them, each seeks rest according to their own cherished former habits and deluded minds.
Claiming that you have attained the ultimate state of refuge and that you have fulfilled unsurpassed Bodhi is a great falsehood;

such will cause you to be influenced by external paths and demonic spirits, and when your karma is exhausted, you will fall into the Avīci Hell. You who are Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas will not achieve further progress.
Therefore, maintain your resolve and uphold the Way of the Tathāgata, and after my parinirvāṇa, transmit this Dharma-gate to the final age.
May all sentient beings universally awaken to and understand this meaning, so that they do not allow Māra to cause them to create their own calamities;

may they be protected, comforted, and rescued, having the false conditions extinguished, so that their bodies and minds enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, achieving it from the very beginning without encountering divergent paths.
In the first fascicle, the text explicitly states that "practitioners who cannot achieve supreme Bodhi,
but instead become Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or followers of external paths, devas, māras,
and the retinues of māras," which refers precisely to these various realms of the *skandha-māra*. These are the manifestations produced by externalists and malevolent spirits.
Those who produce false fruits—namely, the various celestial and demonic retinues and the ten kinds of immortals—will, upon the exhaustion of their karma, inevitably fall into the Avīci Hell.
Thereafter, they must again pass through the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, and then take human form; eventually, some may even become asuras.
Thus, practitioners of cultivation are merely equal to these various deluded sentient beings; only śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are exempt from this.
The wheel of suffering of the fragmented stages likewise does not cease; rather, it transforms into the birth and death of the shifting state (*pariṇāma-vaiparītya*).
This is entirely because one does not know the two kinds of fundamental roots and is deluded regarding the eternally abiding true mind, thereby employing various false thoughts.
If one were to know that each of the twenty-five gates possesses the five aggregates as illusory realms, then these very illusory five aggregates—[would be seen for what they are].
Originally, all are the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; there is not a single thing to be grasped and not a single thing to be abandoned.
To be deluded by it is the root of the two kinds of birth-and-death; to awaken to it is the fundamentally pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvāṇa.
How could one go so far as to follow the deluded mind of one's own particular attachments and prior habits, thereby becoming insane midway? Even seeing demons is likewise [an expression of this].
The "demon of the mind" refers to the arising of dualistic attachments to self and phenomena based on the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); therefore, it is called the "demon of views.
It should be understood that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are likewise subsumed under these dualistic attachments to phenomena. Second, the formal conclusion.
In this way, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in past ages, Tathāgatas as many as motes of dust have relied upon this mind to open up and attain the Unsurpassed Way.
When the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is exhausted, your present sense faculties will function interchangeably;

from within this mutual functioning, you can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*). Your perfectly clear and refined essence of mind will manifest transformations therein, like pure lapis lazuli.
Internally containing the Jewel Moon, one thus transcends the ten faiths, ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, and the four preparatory minds;
through the conduct of the Bodhisattvas of the ten vajra stages and equal enlightenment, one attains perfect clarity and enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment,
fulfilling bodhi and returning to non-attainment.
The mutual functioning of the sense organs is precisely what is called the state of "sudden transcendence.

When the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) is exhausted, one enters the stage of semblance (*xiangsi*), thereby attaining the purity of the six sense organs. When the stage of semblance is exhausted, one enters the stage of partial realization (*fenzheng*), thereby attaining the mutual functioning of the six sense organs.
When the stage of partial realization is exhausted, one reaches the ultimate stage and is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s diamond-like *samādhi*.

When wisdom reaches ultimate exhaustion, the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), and the first five consciousnesses are transformed into the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
Thus, from within this perfectly luminous and refined mind, three classes of transformation bodies are manifested to universally quench the wheel of suffering.
Therein, the principle of suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*) are transparently clear both internally and externally, like lapis lazuli.
Containing the Jewel Moon, one suddenly transcends the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and penetration to achieve the wondrous enlightenment of the Unsurpassed Way.

To say "thus transcending" precisely clarifies that the practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden path enters directly in a single leap, without relying on the laborious cultivation and realization of gradual effort.
Furthermore, within the mutual application [of the stages], one is immediately able to transcend into the Vajra Dry Wisdom.
The Vajra-dry-wisdom (Vajra-śuṣka-prajñā) further transcends and enters the ocean of wondrous adornment; thus, the principle of the twelve stages—repeatedly single and paired—is also fulfilled.
It is like a sharp blade that cuts through a thousand sheets of paper at once, or the Great Garuda’s single leap of ninety thousand *yojanas*—truly swift indeed.
Yet, this does not mean that the various stages are entirely discarded. Furthermore, the word "transcend" (*chao*) has two meanings: first, [transcendence in] a single *kṣaṇa*.

Regarding "sudden realization as transcending the two": although one passes through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, because one does not encounter divergent branches along the way, there are forever no signs of detours;
this is also called "transcendence. The "Ocean of Wondrous Adornments" is the ultimate perfection of the myriad practices;
"Bodhi" is the ultimate perfection of the merit of wisdom; and "returning to non-attainment" is the ultimate perfection of the essence of reality (*dharmatā*). Furthermore—
Because it is adorned by merit, adorned by wisdom, and adorned by the purity of self-nature;

because it is an adornment that is neither vertical nor horizontal and is non-dual, it is called the "Ocean of Wondrous Adornments. Because it is the perfection of ultimate wisdom-bodhi, the perfection of expedient means-bodhi, and the perfection of true nature-bodhi;
because it is a perfection that is neither vertical nor horizontal and is non-dual, it is called "Perfect" (Yuan).
The wondrous principle of the three truths of perfect enlightenment is like the head that never loses its divine pearl, which remains within one’s clothing;

thus, there is nothing to be attained regarding principle, for it is the nature-inherent in all practices. These practices are like the tracks of birds in the sky or the multitude of images in a mirror; thus, there is nothing to be attained regarding practice.

The cessation-and-contemplation (śamatha-vipaśyanā) that accords with this nature is like the sun and moon that are inherently luminous, or like a mirror and water that are inherently reflective; thus, there is nothing to be attained regarding wisdom.
Neither vertical nor horizontal, with no dual destination, it is therefore called "taking refuge in non-attainment.

As for those Māras, externalists, and followers of the Two Vehicles, because they all possess attainment, none of them are ultimate. This concludes the second section, which specifically clarifies the characteristics of the arousal [of the mind] regarding the object.
Third, the conclusion, exhortation, and instruction on reverent cultivation.
This is the subtle demonic activity and demonic realm that appears before you during the *vipaśyanā* (insight) within the *śamatha* (calm abiding) of the past Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones; by being able to recognize it, you wash away the defilements of the mind, do not fall into false views,
extinguish the *skandha-māra*, shatter the *deva-māra*, and cause powerful spirits and ghosts to lose heart and flee, while *chi-mei* and *wang-liang* demons vanish.
They shall no longer be subject to rebirth until they reach Bodhi; free from all lack and inferiority, they will advance toward Great Nirvana with minds neither deluded nor distressed.

If there are foolish and dull-witted beings in the final age who do not yet recognize *dhyāna* and do not know how to preach the Dharma, yet delight in practicing *samādhi*, you should fear that they might fall into heterodoxy;
therefore, with a single mind, urge them to uphold this *dhāraṇī-mantra* from the crown of my Buddha-head.
If you are unable to recite or transcribe this, whether in the meditation hall or carried upon your person, no demons whatsoever shall be able to disturb you;
you should then reverently honor these final instructions for ultimate cultivation and progress left by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.

The text consists of two sections. From the beginning up to "the mind is not deluded or distressed," the section concludes with an exhortation to follow and practice the teachings of the Exoteric Vehicle (*khyāna-dharma*).
From "If, in the final age... onwards, the text concludes with an exhortation to follow and practice the esoteric expressions (*guhya-vyākhyāna*). The first section is easily understood.

As for the second section, the phrase "foolish and dull sentient beings" merely refers to those lacking the nature of extensive learning; it does not mean those who are as utterly ignorant as white sheep.
Because they lack wisdom, they have not yet recognized the subtle principle of the Middle Way dhyāna; because they lack eloquence, they do not know how to explain the essential methods of practice.
Nevertheless, having already resolved to transcend birth and death and realize perfect penetration by giving rise to the true and correct bodhicitta, they delight in cultivating samādhi.
This requires that they personally approach an enlightened teacher and receive his transmission.
These twenty-five gates of instruction are taught according to what is appropriate; one should practice by relying on whichever one suits them, for it is not the case that all are identical.
Although there is a lineage of masters, one must still verify through the efficacy of mantra-protection.
In this degenerate age, since teachers are neither conversant with this sutra nor do their mantra-recitation conform to the proper ritual, how many of those who differ from the heterodox are there?
How rare! This concludes the first section, which clearly elucidates the realm of dhyāna. Second, further severing remaining doubts, which has two parts:

first, the inquiry; second, the explanation and resolution. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, receiving the preceding teaching; second, raising three questions; third, requesting a general response. Now, the first [section].
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat; having heard the Buddha’s instruction and admonition, he prostrated himself in reverent acceptance, memorizing it without loss.
In the midst of the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha once more.

He posed two questions and asked three times, which constitute the first three parts: the first question concerns the root of the aggregates as false imagination; the second question concerns the simultaneous and sequential methods for their elimination.
The third question concerns what constitutes the boundary [of the mind]. This is the first part:

as the Buddha has stated that within the characteristics of the five aggregates there are five kinds of false imaginings which serve as the fundamental source-mind, we have hitherto not received the Tathāgata’s subtle and detailed exposition thereof.
This first question asks why the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) have only these five kinds of false conceptualization as their basis and no other basis.
The second question concerns the sequence for eliminating them together:
do these five aggregates need to be eliminated simultaneously, or are they exhausted through a gradual process?
The third question asks what constitutes the boundary for approaching [the preceptor].
Likewise, there are five such layers asking what constitutes the boundary for approaching.
The third [section] provides the general response to these inquiries.
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will manifest great compassion to clarify the minds and eyes of this great assembly, thereby serving as a guiding eye for all sentient beings of the future age.

Part Two: The Response, which has two sections: first, the direct answer to the question; second, the concluding exhortation to transmit and demonstrate. Within the first section, there are three parts. First:

This consists of a broad response regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and fundamental delusion (*parikalpita-vikalpa*), a direct response concerning what constitutes a realm (*dhātu*), and a follow-up response that simultaneously dissolves the sequence.
The first [section] further has three parts: first, a general clarification; second, a specific demonstration; and third, a concluding summary. This is the first [of those three].
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The essential, true, wondrously luminous, fundamental enlightenment is perfectly pure;
it does not harbor birth and death, nor any defilements, even unto empty space—all of these arise because of deluded thoughts.

This is fundamentally the wondrously luminous, true essence of original enlightenment, yet through delusion it gives rise to the various vessel-worlds, just as when Śaṇḍa mistook his own head for a reflection. This delusion has no root cause."
Within the realm of deluded conceptualization, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions; those who are confused about causes and conditions call them "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*).
That nature of space is like a real illusion arising from causes and conditions; both the spontaneous and the causal are all the conceptual reckonings of the deluded minds of sentient beings.

Ānanda, you know that these arise from delusion and speak of the causes and conditions of delusion; yet if delusion were fundamentally non-existent, then speaking of the causes and conditions of delusion would be fundamentally non-existent—how much more so [the objects they produce]?
Because you do not know how to trace back to what is natural, the Tathāgata has revealed to you that the fundamental cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but deluded thought.
That which is essential, true, wondrously luminous, and fundamentally awakened, perfectly pure, also refers to the true nature of the very thought-moment before you.
To speak of it without confusion is called "refined"; to be without falsehood is called "true. "Wondrously bright" means that while quiescent, there is constant illumination;
because from the beginning there has never been non-awakening, it is called "original awakening. "Perfectly pure" means that while illuminating, there is constant quiescence.

"Birth and death" refers universally to both the *paricchinna* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) types; "dust and grime" refers universally to the afflictions and karma of the nine realms. One should know that these arise from delusion.
This means that although one knows there is no arising, because there is delusive dependent origination, one must forcefully explain false causes and conditions;

this is like using medicine to treat an illness. If one fully realizes that the essence of the delusion has never arisen and is not a real arising, yet must still speak of delusive causes and conditions, these too are fundamentally non-existent;
this is like the illness being cured and the medicine discarded. Thus, one understands...
That which arises from delusion is simply the unchanging following conditions; that one realizes the delusion is fundamentally non-existent is simply the following conditions being unchanging.
These two terms, "cause" and "condition," already belong to the realm of forced designations; how much more so, then, to further speculate that they are "spontaneous"?
Therefore, it is revealed that the fundamental cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but delusive thought. Since they are called delusive thoughts, [how could they have any other origin?]
It may be said that the fundamental refers to the false causes and conditions; yet since it is solely deluded thought that constitutes the foundation, how could there be a "foundation" for the false?
It may be said that the source is originally non-existent. Second, the specific demonstration is divided into five parts:

first, clarifying that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is merely solidified deluded thought; [this continues] up to fifth, clarifying that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is merely inverted deluded thought. Now...
First: Your body was originally caused by the parents' thoughts to come into being; had it not been for thought, you could not have come.
As I previously stated, when one thinks of the taste of vinegar, saliva arises in the mouth; when one thinks of climbing a high place, a tingling sensation arises in the soles of the feet.
Since there is no sour substance on the precipice and none has yet arrived, if your physical body were not inherently false and deceptive,
how could this saliva in your mouth be produced merely by speaking of vinegar? Therefore, you should know that this present physical form of yours is called the first false conception of solidity.
People say that form possesses real dharmas, yet they do not realize it is merely solidified deluded thought.
To call deluded thought "solid" implies there is truly something solid; try observing saliva in the mouth—it is formed only by thought.
All dharmas of form are likewise so. Second, it clarifies that the aggregate of sensation is merely empty and luminous deluded thought.

This very state you have described— wherein the mind’s contemplation of heights causes your physical form to truly experience a sensation of astringency, such that through the arising of this sensation the material body is moved—
is known as your current, manifest "empty clarity," the second delusive thought, which is driven by the present alternation between what is favorable and beneficial and what is adverse and harmful.

To follow it brings benefit, while to oppose it causes loss; people say there truly exist these two objective realms of compliance and opposition that are experienced, yet they do not know that these are nothing more than empty, luminous, and deluded thoughts.
To say that deluded thoughts have something clearly perceived—how could there truly be anything clearly perceived?
The numbness and tingling in your feet are formed solely by thought; all sensations are likewise thus.
Thus it is. The third clarity is that the aggregate of perception is merely a pervasive false imagination.

It is due to your thoughts and deliberations that you cause your physical body to exist; yet the body is not of the same category as thought. For what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought?
Various images are grasped as they arise in the mind, taking form in correspondence with thought; when awake, this is the mind of perception, and when asleep, it becomes various dreams.
Thus, the movement of your conceptual thoughts and deluded feelings is called the third false imagination, "interfusion.
Since it has already been stated that the preceding four aggregates are fundamentally nothing but false imagination, how could this aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) have any other basis?
It is simply that the objects manifested by false imagination serve as the very support for that same false imagination. Therefore...

Regarding the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*), one must clarify that outside of perception (*saṃjñā*) there is no external object; now, regarding the aggregate of perception, one must clarify that outside of the external object there is no perception.
This very object that is perceived is merely formed in accordance with perception. If one removes this pervasive deluded thought (*yǒngxiǎng*), how could there be any further fundamental reality?
For people assume that the two dharmas of matter and mind, and the two states of waking and sleeping, are fixed and determinate.
They are not mutually integrated; let us now examine this: it is by virtue of your thoughts that you are able to direct your physical body.
Even if the body were not of the same category as thought, for what reason would your body follow the dictates of thought?

Furthermore, regarding the various images grasped within the mind, once the mind has given rise to a perception, the form follows the object grasped; the object thus grasped must necessarily correspond to what was being thought of.
Furthermore, when one is awake, this constitutes the mind of conceptualization, and when one is asleep, it constitutes various dreams.
Thus, whether it be form or mind, waking or sleeping, how could they ever fail to be mutually integrated and interpenetrating?

One should know that these present perceptions, thoughts, and flickering delusions are not at all real external objects that cause one to waver; rather, they are nothing other than the integration of deluded conceptualizations.
That is all. In the fourth stage, the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), there is only this obscure and hidden false imagination.

The principle of transformation does not abide, but shifts and moves in secret; as nails grow and hair sprouts, the vital breath wanes and the face wrinkles, day and night replacing one another without ever being perceived.
Ānanda, if this were not you, how could it be that the body undergoes change? If it must be truly you, why do you [not perceive it]?
The lack of awareness such that your various formations (*saṃskāra*) do not cease for even a single moment is called the fourth subtle and hidden delusion.
Because it can cause the essence [of the body] to undergo transition, and because it is never awakened to as being inseparable from your own thoughts, it is purely a false fabrication.
Once this subtle and hidden delusion is removed, how could there still be further formations? Fifth, the consciousness aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*) is revealed to be merely...
These are inverted delusions.

Furthermore, as for that which you call "vital clarity," "tranquil stillness," and "unwavering"—if you were to name it "eternal"—it would not, within the body, depend upon seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
If it were truly vital and authentic, it would certainly not admit the cultivation of delusions; for what reason, then, have you all in years past...

Suppose one beholds a marvelous object; though years pass, there is neither memory nor forgetting. Later, suddenly beholding that same former marvel again, the memory is as vivid as ever, without the slightest loss.
Thus, within this state of refined clarity and profound stillness, how could it not be subject to the constant perfuming of momentary thoughts?
Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not true suchness; it is like a swift-flowing stream that appears tranquil from a distance.

The current flows so swiftly that it cannot be seen; this is not because there is no flow. If it were not the fundamental source of the root of false perception, how could it receive the熏習 (xūn xí, perfuming/habituation) of such delusion?

It is because your six faculties do not function interchangeably—opening and closing [in isolation]—that those deluded habituations have nowhere to lodge. Thus, these false perceptions can never be extinguished.

Therefore, within your present seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, you are habituated to a certain degree of turbidity and lack of clarity; internally, you are like a phantom, empty and non-existent.
This is called the fifth inverted, subtle, and refined perception.

Although the *vijñāna-skandha* is said to refer generally to all eight consciousnesses, it must be understood that the eighth consciousness serves as the sovereign of the collective retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*).

This is because the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of this eighth consciousness constantly relies upon the gates of the six sense organs to spontaneously perceive the objects of direct cognition (*pratyakṣa*) and their intrinsic natures; therefore, it is so described.
Within the body, there is nothing that escapes seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. "Shuàn" (串) is the same as "guàn" (慣), meaning constant; "jǐ" (幾) means subtle.
Apart from inverted views and subtle, refined conceptions, how could there further be any illusory, non-existent habitual tendencies?
Thus, the three fetters are formed.
Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) are formed by five kinds of false conceptualization.
They are called the "five aggregates of clinging" because they are that which sentient beings grasp and cling to.

Therefore, the five aggregates are collectively termed "clinging," collectively termed "perception," and it should be known that they are also collectively termed "consciousness," because of [the presence of] feeling and perception.

The three aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) do not exceed the mind-objects (*caitta*) of consciousness, and the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) does not exceed the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of consciousness;

this is why they are so designated. Furthermore, they are collectively termed "formations" because form, sensation, perception, and consciousness are all phenomena characterized by flux and volitional construction (*abhisamskāra*).

Moreover, they are collectively termed "form" because the first [aggregate] consists of resistant and manifest form (*sapratigha-savijñapti-rūpa*), while the latter... [the subsequent aggregates follow].
This is because all four are non-obstructive and non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*). Second, answering by transcending [the question]: What constitutes the realms?
If you now wish to know the depth of the causal realms: only form and space are the limits of form; only contact and its cessation are the limits of feeling;
only recollection and forgetfulness are the limits of perception; and only cessation and arising are the limits of mental formations.
The profound entry into the merging with the profound returns to the limit of consciousness.
Both form and emptiness constitute the limits of the aggregate of form; thus, the form-dharmas of the ten realms are all vertically exhausted and horizontally pervasive.
Both contact and detachment constitute the limits of the aggregate of sensation; thus, the sensations of the ten realms are likewise all vertically exhausted and horizontally pervasive.
Memory and forgetfulness are both the limits of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); cessation and arising are both the limits of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);

Based on this, the moving aspect of this consciousness constitutes the basis of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); its movement necessarily involves grasping objects, which constitutes the basis of perception (*saṃjñā*);

its capacity to grasp the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) constitutes the basis of sensation (*vedanā*); and the objective aspect it grasps (*nimitta-bhāga*) constitutes the basis of form (*rūpa*).

Thus, within a single thought-moment, these five layers are simultaneously present; though turbid, they remain the cause of birth. To seek their ultimate origin, one must look to movement and stillness.

Because the two aspects [of subject and object] are clearly seen as not arising, the nature of form (*rūpa*) is naturally extinguished; because hearing and that which is heard are both exhausted, the nature of sensation (*vedanā*) is naturally extinguished;

because the perceiver and the perceived are empty, the nature of perception (*saṃjñā*) is naturally extinguished; because arising and ceasing have already ceased, the nature of mental formations (*saṃskāra*) is naturally extinguished;
and because one suddenly transcends them, the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is naturally extinguished. This is the fivefold perfect transcendence in a single thought-moment.

Deluded thoughts are still extinguished by removing them from form; because awakening to arising as non-arising, the principle is suddenly realized, and through this realization, all is simultaneously eliminated.

Now, without avoiding prolixity, I shall again provide a clarification: first, I will establish four propositions based on their meanings; next, I will integrate them into a single path.

First, regarding the establishment of the four propositions: (1) sudden enlightenment with sudden elimination; (2) sudden enlightenment with gradual elimination; (3) gradual enlightenment with sudden elimination;

and (4) gradual enlightenment with gradual elimination. As for "sudden enlightenment with sudden elimination," this refers to those of the sharpest faculties whose two obstacles—of phenomena (*dharma*) and of persons (*pudgala*)—are both thin.
From the outset, within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), they ride upon the opening of this mind and directly transcend into the *vajra* [samādhi].

Second, regarding the sudden enlightenment followed by gradual elimination: within the stage of adamantine *śuklavidarśanā* (dry wisdom), one perfects and clarifies the refined mind, suddenly transcending the stages of faith, abiding, practice, orientation, and the [ten] grounds to enter the ocean of wondrous enlightenment.

This is as with Ānanda and others, who first awakened to the *tathāgatagarbha* nature and suddenly attained the *dharmakāya*, and subsequently, through the meditative state of fixed concentration and the cultivation of contemplation, cleansed away the accumulated defilements within the sense faculties.

The third type, "sudden removal through gradual awakening," refers to those such as Pūrṇa-maitrāyaṇīputra; because their cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are heavy, awakening is difficult to achieve.
Since the three conditions have been severed beforehand, it suffices that the three causes do not arise, whereby the deluded mind is suddenly stilled—this stilling is itself *bodhi*.
The fourth type, "gradual removal through gradual awakening," refers to those for whom both obstructions are equally heavy.

This refers to one who must gradually open up perfect understanding through the permeation of hearing, subsequently give rise to true cultivation based on that perfect understanding, and finally undergo diligent practice and realization over successive kalpas.

These four phrases are established solely from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjia) and do not concern the Treasury (Zang), the Shared (Tong), or the Distinct (Bie) teachings; however, it is also possible to establish these four phrases for each of the first three vehicles.
Since this is not what is urgent here, it is not discussed. Next, regarding the single path that encompasses all: as for the principle of phenomena, there is nothing gradual that is not sudden.

That which is called the "sudden" is the complete realization of principle; there is nothing that is sudden which is not gradual.
Even if the five aggregates were to perish simultaneously in a single kṣaṇa, their sequential exhaustion would still remain clearly manifest.

Therefore, the metaphor of the *kalpa* cloth, when applied to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), is horizontal while simultaneously being vertical, because each sense organ contains the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) layered within it;

when applied to the five aggregates, it is vertical while again being horizontal, because within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) one exhausts the five aggregates, and even in the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*) one likewise exhausts the five aggregates. Thus, the dharma and the metaphor are skillfully interwoven.
You should reflect deeply on the initial correct answer that concludes the inquiry. Second, as a summary and exhortation for transmission:
